# Sein und Zeit — Commentary

Niemeyer pagination (SZ 1–437) is cited throughout. A few interpretive guards hold across the whole run, derived from the text and its reception: Dasein is not a synonym for "human consciousness" or "the subject" but names a way of being; being (Sein) is never a being (Seiendes), so no unit may be read as if Heidegger were describing a supreme entity or a property; existenzial (ontological structure) must not collapse into existenziell (ontic self-understanding); Verfallen and Uneigentlichkeit are structural, not moral, determinations; "world" is not the sum of things but a structure of Dasein; Angst is not a psychological state among others; and fundamental ontology is not philosophical anthropology, however much Division One reads like one. Terms retained in German: Dasein, and, once introduced, coinages whose analysis is the text's own business (In-der-Welt-sein, das Man, Sorge — each glossed at first use). Everything else is rendered in consistent English with the German in parentheses where the term is technical.

## Preliminary Remark (1953)

Heidegger records that the treatise first appeared in spring 1927 in volume VIII of Husserl's Jahrbuch für Philosophie und phänomenologische Forschung and simultaneously as a separate printing. The bibliographical fact carries weight: the book was published inside the institutional organ of Husserlian phenomenology, dedicated to Husserl "in admiration and friendship," while its whole Introduction quietly converts phenomenology from a science of consciousness into an ontology of Dasein. The tension between the venue and the content is the first datum of the book's reception history.

The second paragraph certifies the reprint: the text of this ninth edition is unchanged, citations and punctuation have been reviewed, and the pagination agrees with earlier editions apart from slight deviations. The practical consequence is that the Niemeyer pagination functions as the stable scholarly citation system for the work — the convention this commentary follows.

The third paragraph makes the famous admission: the designation "First Half," carried by all previous editions, is struck. After a quarter-century the second half can no longer be joined on unless the first were presented anew. Heidegger thus concedes that Sein und Zeit is and will remain a fragment — the projected third division of Part One ("Time and Being") and the whole destructive Part Two never appeared in this form. But he does not retract: the path of the first half "remains even today a necessary one, if the question of being is to move our Dasein." He reaffirms the way while withholding the destination, which matches his later self-interpretation: the Kehre does not repudiate Sein und Zeit but re-situates it. The conditional is also telling — the question's necessity is indexed to whether it moves our Dasein, an existentiell condition, not a systematic one. The question of being was never meant as an academic exercise.

Finally he refers the reader to the Einführung in die Metaphysik, the 1935 lecture course published by the same house, "for the elucidation of this question." The pointer is doubly significant: it treats the later work as continuous elucidation of the same question, and it directs the reader to the text in which the question of being is renewed by way of the history of metaphysics rather than the analytic of Dasein — a discreet signal of where the unwritten continuation actually went.

## Opening Page (SZ 1)

The book opens, before any heading, with Sophist 244a in Greek and Heidegger's own translation: you have long been familiar with what you really mean when you use the expression "seiend" (being), whereas we, who once thought we understood it, have now come into perplexity (Verlegenheit). The choice of motto sets the entire work under the sign of retrieval: the fundamental question is not new but ancient, and what is to be repeated is not Plato's answer but Plato's perplexity. Heidegger's translation already interprets: by rendering the issue as what one means (meint) by "seiend," he casts the gigantomachia over ousia as a question about meaning and understanding — precisely the register ("the meaning of being," "understanding of being") in which the treatise will pose it. The aporia belongs to the Eleatic Stranger's examination of both materialists and friends of the forms: even the classical positions that pronounce most confidently on beings cannot say what they mean by "is."

Heidegger then asks whether we today have an answer to what we really mean by "seiend" — not at all; so the question of the meaning of being must be raised anew. But are we even in perplexity at not understanding "being"? Again not at all; so first of all an understanding for the sense of this question must be reawakened. The double negative measures a double deficit: the present lacks not only the answer but the very perplexity that made the question live, and the second lack is the deeper one — forgetting a question is worse than failing to answer it. The paragraph then states the whole program in two sentences: the concrete working-out of the question of the meaning of being is the intent (Absicht) of the treatise; the interpretation of time as the possible horizon of any understanding of being whatsoever is its provisional goal (vorläufiges Ziel). Every word is calibrated. The task is to work out the question, not to deliver the answer; time is a horizon of the understanding of being, which binds being from the outset to Dasein's understanding — the transcendental frame of the whole; and "provisional" concedes in advance that even the time-interpretation is preparatory, pointing toward the never-published turn from "Dasein and temporality" to "time and being."

The short closing paragraph notes that this goal, the investigations it demands, and the way (Weg) to it require an introductory elucidation — the warrant for the two-chapter Einleitung that follows. The path-vocabulary is not ornamental: the book presents itself as a way rather than a doctrinal edifice, an emphasis Heidegger retained to the end ("ways, not works").

## Introduction: The Exposition of the Question of the Meaning of Being

### Chapter One: The Necessity, Structure, and Priority of the Question of Being

#### § 1. The Necessity of an Explicit Retrieval of the Question of Being

Heidegger opens with the diagnosis: the question named on the title page has today fallen into forgottenness (Vergessenheit), even though our age credits itself with progress for affirming "metaphysics" again. The barb targets the 1920s metaphysics revival — the post-neo-Kantian turn toward ontology and metaphysics — and makes a sharp point: affirming metaphysics is compatible with, indeed a mode of, forgetting the question of being, since one can traffic in doctrines about beings while sparing oneself the exertion of a rekindled "battle of giants over being" (Plato's gigantomachia peri tēs ousias, again from the Sophist). A three-stage decline follows: the question held the research of Plato and Aristotle in suspense; it then fell silent as a thematic question of actual investigation; what the two won survived only in manifold displacements and "overpaintings" down to Hegel's Logic. The restoration metaphor is exact — an original canvas concealed under layers of retouching — and it prefigures what the destruction of the history of ontology (§ 6) must do: strip the overpainting to recover what was "wrested from the phenomena" in the highest exertion of thought. That phrase already reads the Greeks phenomenologically: their basic concepts were originally answerable to phenomena, and their trivialization is the loss of that answerability. The forgottenness of the question, not merely the lack of an answer, is the target — the seed of what Heidegger will later call Seinsvergessenheit.

Worse than neglect, a dogma has formed on the soil of the Greek beginnings that declares the question superfluous and sanctions the omission: "being" is the most universal and emptiest concept, resists every definition, and needs none, since everyone constantly uses it and already understands what he means. Heidegger's structural point is that this dogma is not an external corruption but grows out of the Greek results themselves once severed from the question that motivated them. What once, as something hidden, drove ancient philosophizing into unrest and kept it there has become sun-clear self-evidence — so much so that whoever still asks is accused of methodological error. This is the book's first model of how disclosure ossifies: an original achievement, transmitted as obvious, becomes the very mechanism that blocks re-asking. § 6 will generalize the model into the concept of tradition as concealing transmission.

The prejudices cannot be treated exhaustively at the outset, Heidegger says, because they are rooted in ancient ontology itself, and ancient ontology can be adequately interpreted — as to the soil from which its basic concepts grew and the adequacy and completeness of its categories — only along the guiding thread of the previously clarified and answered question of being. The circle is stated openly: the critique of the prejudices presupposes the answer they obstruct. So the full reckoning is deferred to the destruction planned as Part Two, and the discussion here is carried only far enough to make the necessity of a retrieval (Wiederholung) evident. "Retrieval" is already a technical term in the making (§ 74 will formalize it): not the reinstatement of an old answer but the re-enactment of a question. Three prejudices are announced.

The first prejudice: being is the "most universal" concept. Heidegger concedes the datum with Aristotle and Aquinas — an understanding of being is always already included in whatever anyone apprehends of beings — and then turns the prejudice against itself. This universality is not generic: being does not demarcate the highest region of beings articulated by genus and species, for "being is not a genus" (Aristotle). Its universality "transcends" all generic universality; medieval ontology called it a transcendens; and Aristotle grasped the unity of this transcendental universal over against the multiplicity of the highest material genera as the unity of analogy — thereby setting the problem of being on a fundamentally new basis, without lighting up the darkness of these categorial connections. The Thomist and Scotist schools discussed the problem endlessly without fundamental clarity, and Hegel, defining being as the "indeterminate immediate," stays within the ancient line of sight while letting Aristotle's problem — the unity of being against the manifold of material categories — slip from his hands. Conclusion: most universal means darkest, not clearest. Two things deserve flagging. The Aquinas citation makes the tradition itself testify to a pre-ontological understanding of being included in all apprehension — the very phenomenon § 2 will make the point of departure. And the analogy problem is autobiographically the origin of the whole enterprise: Brentano's dissertation on the manifold senses of being in Aristotle, which Heidegger names as his first path into philosophy, poses exactly the question of the unity of being's senses that the tradition, on this account, raised and abandoned.

The second prejudice: being is indefinable — correctly inferred from its highest universality, if definition proceeds by proximate genus and specific difference. Being cannot be conceived as a being; "no nature can be added to a being" (enti non additur aliqua natura); it can neither be derived from higher concepts nor exhibited through lower ones. But from this it follows only that being is not something like a being (Seiendes) — the first explicit statement in the book of what Heidegger elsewhere names the ontological difference, here still unnamed. The traditional "definition," legitimate within limits for determining beings and itself rooted in ancient ontology, simply does not apply to being. The prejudice smuggles in a norm: that intelligibility equals definability by genus and species — a rule of logic derived from the ontology of beings and then illegitimately applied to what is not a being. Hence the reversal that closes the paragraph: the indefinability of being does not dispense us from the question of its meaning; it demands the question, since being will require a mode of conceptual determination of its own.

The third prejudice: being is the self-evident concept. In all knowing and asserting, in every comportment toward beings and every comportment toward oneself, use is made of "being," and the expression is understood "without further ado": everyone understands "the sky is blue," "I am glad." Heidegger's counter is the pivot of the section: this average intelligibility demonstrates only unintelligibility — it makes manifest that an enigma lies a priori in every comportment and being toward beings as beings. That we always already live in an understanding of being while the meaning of being is simultaneously shrouded in darkness proves the fundamental necessity of retrieving the question. The very fact invoked to dissolve the question is converted into the phenomenon that motivates it, and this fact — average, vague Seinsverständnis — will become the phenomenal basis of the whole analytic: fundamental ontology is nothing but the interrogation of this everyday understanding.

A short paragraph enlists Kant: appealing to self-evidence in the sphere of basic philosophical concepts, and of all things with regard to "being," is a dubious procedure if the "self-evident" — Kant's "covert judgments of common reason" — is to be and remain the explicit theme of analytics, "the business of philosophers." Self-evidence is philosophy's object, never its warrant. The remark quietly fixes the method to come: phenomenology in § 7 will be defined precisely by its concern with what proximally and for the most part does not show itself, with what lies hidden in what is most familiar.

The closing paragraph draws the section's yield: the consideration of the prejudices has made clear not only that the answer to the question of being is lacking, but that the question itself is obscure and directionless. To retrieve the question therefore means: first of all to work out an adequate way of posing it (Fragestellung). The deficit is displaced from answer to question, and this displacement licenses the entire architecture of the Introduction — beginning with § 2's analysis of what a question as such is, since the question of being must first be constructed before it can be asked.

#### § 2. The Formal Structure of the Question of Being

The question of the meaning of being is to be posed; and if it is a fundamental question, or even the fundamental question, then such questioning needs appropriate transparency (Durchsichtigkeit). Hence Heidegger will briefly discuss what belongs to any question whatever, in order to make the question of being visible as an exceptional one. The move is methodologically deliberate: rather than presume that "ask about being" is an intelligible imperative, he derives its determinate content from the formal structure of questioning as such. Transparency is more than a stylistic ideal here — it names the demand that the questioning comportment become clear to itself in its own constitution, a demand that will shortly pull the questioner into the question.

The formal analysis follows. Every questioning is a seeking, and every seeking is guided beforehand by what is sought. Questioning is a knowing search for beings in their that-being and so-being; it can sharpen into "investigating," which lays free and determines that after which the question asks. Every question has das Gefragte, that which is asked about; asking about is always also inquiring of something, das Befragte, that which is interrogated; and in what is asked about lies das Erfragte, that which is to be found out, the properly intended element in which the questioning reaches its goal. Finally, questioning itself, as the comportment of a being — the questioner — has its own character of being, and it can be enacted casually or as an explicit Fragestellung, whose distinction is that the questioning first becomes transparent to itself in all these constitutive characters. Two features of this apparently dry taxonomy carry the section. First, the triad Gefragtes–Befragtes–Erfragtes provides the grid onto which the question of being will be mapped: being as what is asked about, the meaning of being as what is to be found out, beings — and finally one exemplary being — as what is interrogated. Second, the observation that all seeking takes its direction in advance from what is sought plants the fore-structure of understanding (§ 32) at the root of inquiry: there is no presuppositionless questioning, only questioning that owns or disowns its guidance.

A one-sentence unit turns the analysis to its application: the question of the meaning of being must now be discussed with regard to these structural moments. The brevity is itself the point — the formal inventory was not free-floating logic but scaffolding erected for exactly this employment.

As seeking, the questioning of being needs prior guidance from what it seeks; the meaning of being must therefore already be available to us in some way. This is the Faktum on which everything rests: we move always already within an understanding of being, out of which grow the explicit question and the tendency toward its concept. We do not know what "being" means — but already when we ask "what is 'being'?" we hold ourselves in an understanding of the "is," without being able to fix conceptually what "is" means, and without even knowing the horizon from which its meaning is to be grasped and fixed. This average and vague understanding of being is a fact. The unit dissolves the Meno-style paradox the Sophist motto raised: the search for being is possible because what is sought is pre-possessed non-conceptually. The self-exemplifying character of the question — the "is" operative inside "what is being?" — is the neatest available proof of the Faktum. And the remark about the missing horizon silently defines the book's goal: time will be proposed as exactly the horizon here found lacking.

This understanding of being may fluctuate and blur to the verge of mere acquaintance with the word, yet this very indeterminateness of the understanding of being that is always already available is itself a positive phenomenon needing clarification. An investigation into the meaning of being, however, will not give that clarification at the outset: the interpretation of the average understanding gains its necessary guiding thread only with the developed concept of being, from whose clarity one can first make out what the obscured understanding means and which kinds of obscuring or hindrance of an explicit illumination are possible and necessary. Two commitments surface. Vagueness is dignified as a describable structure rather than a defect to be legislated away — a genuinely phenomenological attitude toward the indeterminate. And the circle announced in § 1 reappears as positive method: the point of departure (vague understanding) receives its definitive interpretation only from the result (the concept of being), so the analysis is essentially provisional and must be repeated at a higher level — the book's spiral architecture, in which Division Two retrieves Division One, is here justified in advance.

A short unit adds that the average understanding may moreover be shot through with traditional theories and opinions about being in such a way that these theories remain concealed as sources of the dominant understanding — and concludes that what is sought in the question of being is not something wholly unknown, though at first something entirely ungraspable. The first half motivates the destruction from an unexpected side: not only academic ontology but everyday self-evidence carries sedimented theory, so even the "natural" understanding is historically contaminated and needs critical sifting. The second half restates the Sophist aporia as a positive epistemic situation: pre-possession without grasp.

Now the grid is applied. The Gefragte of the question to be worked out is being: that which determines beings as beings, that in terms of which (woraufhin) beings, however they may be discussed, are always already understood. The being of beings "is" not itself a being — and the first philosophical step in understanding the problem consists in "not telling a story" (mē mython tina diēgeisthai, Sophist 242c): not determining beings as beings by tracing them back in their origin to another being, as if being had the character of a possible being. Hence being as what is asked about demands its own way of being exhibited, essentially different from the discovery of beings; and the Erfragte, the meaning of being, demands its own conceptuality, essentially set off against the concepts in which beings attain determinateness. This is the densest unit of the section, and three moves must be held apart. First, the formal definition of being as the woraufhin of antecedent understanding: being is that from out of which beings are already intelligible — a horizon-determination, not a property. Second, the Platonic prohibition generalizes the ontological difference into a critique of every explanation of beings by a highest being: the "story" — deriving beings from some arch-being — is precisely the onto-theological pattern the later Heidegger will diagnose in all metaphysics; its rejection is already the founding rule here. Third, the demand for a distinct mode of exhibition and a distinct conceptuality is the systematic reason why the method must be phenomenology (§ 7) and why the book must mint its own terms — the existentials — instead of borrowing categories fitted to beings. The scare-quotes around "is" in "the being of beings 'is' not itself a being" register a difficulty language never stops making: grammar forces the "is" of beings onto what is not a being, a strain on expression Heidegger flags again at the end of the Introduction (SZ 38–39).

Insofar as being means the being of beings, the Befragte of the question is beings themselves: they are interrogated, as it were, with regard to their being. But if they are to yield the characters of their being unfalsified, they must for their part first have become accessible as they are in themselves — so the question demands, with respect to what it interrogates, the winning and prior securing of the right mode of access (Zugangsart) to beings. Yet we call many things "seiend," and in different senses: everything we talk about and mean and comport ourselves toward; what and how we ourselves are; being lies in that-being and so-being, in reality, presence-at-hand (Vorhandenheit), subsistence, validity (Geltung), existence (Dasein), in the "there is" (es gibt). From which being is the meaning of being to be read off? From which should the disclosure of being take its start — is the starting point arbitrary, or does a definite being have priority? Two threads matter. The access-requirement fuses Husserl's maxim of the things themselves with a hermeneutic suspicion the maxim lacks: beings can present themselves falsified, so access is an achievement to be secured, not a given (§ 7's analysis of semblance builds on this). And the catalogue of being's senses is a compressed map of the contemporary scene — Realität from the epistemological debates, Bestand recalling subsistence in the Bolzano–Meinong line, Geltung the Lotzean validity of the neo-Kantians, Dasein still in its traditional sense of existentia (used here innocently one page before its terminological seizure), and es gibt, which the late Heidegger will make the very theme of "Time and Being." The manifold repeats Aristotle's pollachōs legetai in modern dress and re-poses § 1's unity problem as the question of the exemplary being.

The answer is derived, not stipulated. If the question of being is to be posed explicitly and carried through in full transparency, its working-out requires the explication of the way of looking at being, of understanding and conceptually grasping meaning, the preparation of the possibility of the right choice of the exemplary being, and the working-out of the genuine mode of access to it. But looking-at, understanding and grasping, choosing, access-to are constitutive comportments of questioning and thus themselves modes of being of a definite being — of the being that we, the questioners, in each case ourselves are. To work out the question of being therefore means: to make a being — the questioner — transparent in its being. The questioning of this question is, as a mode of being of a being, itself essentially determined by what is asked about in it — by being. This being which we ourselves in each case are and which has, among other possibilities, the possibility-of-being of questioning, we grasp terminologically as Dasein. The derivation is the section's payoff: Dasein's involvement is not anthropocentric preference but structural necessity — since the comportments that constitute the question are ways of being of the questioner, the question cannot become transparent unless the questioner does. The baptism of the term is equally careful: Dasein is introduced as a pure title for the being that questions, defined by a possibility of being rather than a what — and the "in each case ourselves" (je selbst) already carries the mineness (Jemeinigkeit) that § 9 will make explicit.

The objection arrives on cue: does this not fall into an obvious circle — first having to determine a being in its being, and on that basis then posing the question of being? Is not what only the answer should provide already "presupposed" for working out the question? Heidegger's first response is bluntly deflationary: formal objections such as the "circle in proof" argument, always cheaply available in the field of research into principles, are sterile when concrete ways of investigation are being weighed; they contribute nothing to understanding the matter and obstruct entry into the field of investigation. The dismissal is not yet the doctrine — the positive theory of the circle comes with the fore-structure of understanding (§ 32) and the methodological reflection of § 63 — but it fixes the stance: formal-logical proof-theory does not legislate for material inquiry.

The second response is substantive: factually there is no circle in the question as posed. A being can be determined in its being without an explicit concept of the meaning of being already being available — otherwise there could never have been ontological knowledge, whose factual existence no one will deny. Being is indeed "presupposed" in all previous ontology, but not as an available concept, not as that as which it is sought: the "presupposing" of being has the character of an antecedent looking-upon being (Hinblicknahme auf Sein), from out of which the pregiven being is provisionally articulated in its being. This guiding sight grows out of the average understanding of being in which we always already move and which, in the end, belongs to the essential constitution of Dasein itself. Such presupposing has nothing in common with positing a first principle from which a chain of propositions is deduced; a "circle in proof" cannot occur in the question of the meaning of being at all, because answering it is not a matter of derivational grounding but of exhibiting and laying free the ground (aufweisende Grund-Freilegung). The distinction does all the work: presupposition-as-premise versus presupposition-as-prior-sight. The understanding of being functions as the horizon within which beings get articulated, not as an axiom from which theses are derived — and since phenomenology exhibits grounds rather than deducing from them, the deductive circle has no purchase. The argument from the factum of ontological knowledge is a quiet transcendental move: ontology exists, therefore pre-conceptual understanding of being must be operative.

The closing unit converts the alleged defect into the question's distinctive structure: not a circle in proof, but a remarkable back- or fore-relatedness (Rück- oder Vorbezogenheit) of what is asked about — being — to questioning itself as a mode of being of a being. That the questioning is essentially affected by what it asks about belongs to the ownmost meaning of the question of being. This says only: the being with the character of Dasein has a relation, perhaps even a distinctive one, to the question of being itself. But Heidegger immediately audits the books: with this, neither Dasein's priority has been demonstrated nor its possible or even necessary function as the primary being-to-be-interrogated decided; rather, something like a priority of Dasein has announced itself (hat sich gemeldet). The scrupulous bookkeeping is itself methodical — "announced itself" belongs to the phenomenological register of pre-demonstrative givenness, and the actual demonstration is assigned to §§ 3–4. The transparency demanded of the question at the section's start is being practiced on the question itself.

#### § 3. The Ontological Priority of the Question of Being

The opening unit takes stock and reorients: the characterization of the question of being along the guiding thread of the formal structure of questioning has clarified it as a peculiar question, whose working-out — let alone solution — demands a series of fundamental considerations. But its distinction comes fully to light only when the question is adequately delimited with regard to its function, its intent, and its motives. The shift is from the question's internal structure to its justification: what does asking it accomplish? The two priorities that name the chapter's title — ontological here, ontic in § 4 — are the answer.

So far, Heidegger notes, the necessity of retrieval was motivated by the venerability of the question's provenance and above all by the lack of a determinate answer, indeed of an adequate way of posing it. But one may demand to know what the question is for: does it remain — is it perhaps nothing but — the business of a free-floating speculation about the most general generalities, or is it the most fundamental and the most concrete question at once? The suspicion is voiced in order to be reversed, and the reversal's form should be noted: the defense of the question of being will run through the concrete working sciences, so that the accusation of abstraction is answered on the accuser's own terrain.

Being is in each case the being of a being. The totality of beings can, according to its various domains, become the field for the laying-free and delimitation of definite subject areas (Sachgebiete) — history, nature, space, life, Dasein, language — which can then be thematized as objects of scientific investigations. Science performs this lifting-out and first fixing of its areas naively and roughly; the working-out of an area in its basic structures is in a certain way already accomplished by the prescientific experience and interpretation of the region of being in which the subject area is itself delimited. The "basic concepts" that thus arise remain the guiding threads for the first concrete disclosure of the area — and however much the weight of research lies in this positivity, its authentic progress occurs not so much in the collection of results and their storage in "handbooks" as in the questioning after the basic constitutions of the respective area, mostly driven forth reactively out of the growing acquaintance with the things. The unit contains a complete philosophy of science in miniature: every science lives off a pre-scientific interpretation of its region's being, which its basic concepts codify without ever grounding. The Husserlian doctrine of regional ontologies stands in the background, but with a hermeneutic torsion — the region is delimited by prescientific experience and interpretation, not by eidetic intuition — and with the anti-cumulative thesis: progress happens where the foundations, not the results, are in question.

Hence the criterion that made this section famous: the authentic "movement" of the sciences takes place in the more or less radical, more or less self-transparent revision of their basic concepts; the level of a science is determined by how far it is capable of a crisis of its basic concepts. In such immanent crises, the relation of positive investigative questioning to the things interrogated themselves begins to totter — and everywhere today, in the most diverse disciplines, tendencies have awakened to place research on new foundations. The criterion inverts the positivist ideal: security of foundations is not the mark of a science's maturity; capacity for foundational crisis is, because crisis is where a science's relation to its matters is renegotiated. The often-cited anticipation of later crisis-theories of science is real enough, but the point is ontological rather than sociological — a crisis of basic concepts is a reopening of the question what the entities of the domain are.

The panorama that follows names five contemporary crises, each read as a crisis of access to the domain's being. Mathematics, seemingly the strictest and most firmly joined science, has fallen into a "crisis of foundations": the fight between formalism and intuitionism — Hilbert against Brouwer — concerns the winning and securing of the primary mode of access to what is to be the object of this science. Relativity theory grows from the tendency to exhibit nature's own coherence as it is "in itself"; as a theory of the conditions of access to nature itself, it seeks through the determination of all relativities to preserve the invariance of the laws of motion, and thereby runs up against the question of the structure of its pregiven subject area, the problem of matter — Einstein read not as epistemology but as implicit ontology of nature, invariance being the form the "in itself" takes. In biology the tendency awakens to question back behind the determinations of organism and life given by mechanism and vitalism and to determine anew the mode of being of the living as such — the Driesch-era debate dismissed as a false alternative resting on an unclarified ontology of life. In the historical humanities the drive toward historical actuality itself, through transmission and its presentation, has strengthened: literary history is to become the history of problems — Dilthey's program, whose deep appropriation surfaces in §§ 72–77. And theology seeks a more original interpretation of man's being toward God, prescribed by the meaning of faith itself and remaining within it; it slowly begins to understand again Luther's insight that its dogmatic systematics rests on a "foundation" that did not grow out of a primarily believing questioning and whose conceptuality not only fails to suffice for the theological problematic but conceals and distorts it. The theological entry is the most personal: it condenses Heidegger's Marburg proximity to Bultmann and his Luther studies, and it is a template of destruction in one sentence — an inherited (Greek-scholastic) conceptuality distorting the very matter it transmits. The 1927 lecture "Phenomenology and Theology" unfolds exactly this program.

Heidegger then generalizes. Basic concepts are the determinations in which the subject area underlying all thematic objects of a science comes to an antecedent understanding that guides all positive investigation; they receive their genuine demonstration and "grounding" only in a correspondingly antecedent research into the subject area itself. Since each such area is won from the region of beings themselves, this antecedent, basic-concept-creating research means nothing other than the interpretation of these beings with regard to the basic constitution of their being. Such research must precede the positive sciences, and it can: the work of Plato and Aristotle is the proof. This grounding of the sciences differs in principle from a "logic" that limps along behind, investigating the contingent state of a science for its "method"; it is productive logic, in the sense that it leaps ahead, as it were, into a definite region of being, discloses it for the first time in the constitution of its being, and makes the structures thus won available to the positive sciences as transparent directives for their questioning. Thus what is philosophically primary is not a theory of concept-formation in historiography, nor a theory of historical knowledge, nor a theory of history as the object of historiography, but the interpretation of authentically historical beings with regard to their historicity; and the positive yield of Kant's Critique of Pure Reason lies in its beginning to work out what belongs to a nature as such, not in a "theory" of knowledge — its transcendental logic is an a priori logic of the subject matter of the region of being called nature. The polemic runs on two fronts at once: against the neo-Kantian philosophy of science ("limping logic" is aimed at the Rickert school in which Heidegger was trained), and for an ontological reading of Kant that converts the first Critique from epistemology into material ontology of nature — the thesis Heidegger was elaborating in the same Marburg years and would publish as the Kant book. "Productive logic" names ontology's relation to science: pre-cursive disclosure, not retrospective methodology.

But such questioning — ontology taken in the widest sense, without attachment to ontological directions and tendencies — itself needs a guiding thread. Ontological questioning is indeed more original than the ontic questioning of the positive sciences; yet it remains itself naive and opaque if its inquiries into the being of beings leave the meaning of being in general undiscussed. And precisely the ontological task of a genealogy — not deductively constructive — of the different possible ways of being requires a prior agreement about "what we then really mean by this expression 'being.'" This is the decisive escalation of the section: the regional ontologies just vindicated against the sciences are themselves demoted to naivety so long as the meaning of being überhaupt goes unasked. The projected "genealogy of the possible ways of being" — presence-at-hand, readiness-to-hand, existence, reality, and the rest, derived non-deductively from a unified sense — is § 1's analogy problem come back as a task, and the Sophist question returns verbatim as the standard none of them meets.

The priority can now be stated. The question of being aims at an a priori condition of the possibility not only of the sciences, which investigate beings as beings of such and such a kind and thereby always already move within an understanding of being, but of the ontologies themselves that precede the ontic sciences and found them. All ontology, however rich and firmly clamped the system of categories at its disposal, remains at bottom blind and a perversion of its ownmost intent if it has not first adequately clarified the meaning of being and grasped this clarification as its fundamental task. The two-tiered transcendental structure is explicit — sciences rest on regional ontologies, regional ontologies on the clarification of the meaning of being — and the vocabulary of conditions of possibility shows how firmly Sein und Zeit still operates within a transcendental frame (the title of Part One promises time as the "transcendental horizon" of the question). The Kantian echo in "blind" is barbed: a categorial system without the being-question is like intuitions without concepts, and the barb reaches every contemporary ontology, Husserl's regional ontologies and Hartmann's and Scheler's new metaphysics alike.

The closing unit is transitional but does its own work: rightly understood, ontological research itself gives the question of being its ontological priority, beyond the mere resumption of a venerable tradition and the advancement of a hitherto opaque problem. But this objective-scientific priority is not the only one. The demonstrated priority remains sachlich-wissenschaftlich — internal to the enterprise of grounding knowledge — and the pointed last sentence announces that the deeper root lies elsewhere: in the being of the questioner. Whoever reads fundamental ontology as merely a foundations-of-science program has stopped at precisely the point this sentence steps past.

#### § 4. The Ontic Priority of the Question of Being

Science in general, Heidegger begins, can be defined as the whole of a grounding-connection of true propositions — a definition that is neither complete nor reaches science in its meaning. Sciences, as comportments of man, have the mode of being of this being (man), which we grasp terminologically as Dasein; and scientific research is neither the only nor the nearest possible mode of being of this being. Dasein itself, moreover, is distinguished before other beings, and this distinction must be made provisionally visible, the discussion here anticipating analyses that only later become properly demonstrative. Three moves in five sentences: a propositional-logical definition of science is set aside because it misses science's mode of being — science is something Dasein does, an existing comportment, a thesis § 69(b) will unfold as the existential genesis of the theoretical attitude; the term Dasein receives its second, now official introduction, this time via "man" but immediately de-psychologized; and the anticipatory character of the whole Introduction is again flagged — the priority about to be sketched will be earned only by the analytic itself.

Then comes the canonical determination. Dasein is a being that does not merely occur among other beings; it is rather ontically distinguished by this: that in its being, this being is concerned about this being itself (es geht ihm in seinem Sein um dieses Sein selbst). To this constitution belongs that Dasein, in its being, has a relation of being to this being; and this again means: Dasein understands itself in some way and with some explicitness in its being. It is proper to this being that with and through its being, this being is disclosed to it. Understanding of being is itself a determination of being of Dasein — and Dasein's ontic distinction lies in this, that it is ontological. Every clause of the chain matters. The "es geht um" formula is care (Sorge) in embryo — § 41 will define Dasein's being as care, and the "for-the-sake-of" (Worumwillen) of the world-structure descends from this "um." The relation-of-being to one's own being makes self-understanding a way of being rather than an accompanying act of reflection. "Disclosed" (erschlossen) drops, almost casually, the term for the book's master phenomenon, Erschlossenheit. And the closing epigram — the ontic distinction is to be ontological — compresses the whole strategy: Dasein is the being whose way of being includes an understanding of being, which is why interrogating it can answer a question about being.

A terminological unit refines the epigram. Being-ontological here does not yet mean developing an ontology; if "ontology" is reserved for the explicit theoretical questioning after the meaning of beings, then Dasein's being-ontological is to be designated pre-ontological (vorontologisch) — which does not mean simply being ontically, but being in the way of an understanding of being. The triplet ontic / pre-ontological / ontological now structures the whole enterprise: the pre-ontological is the hinge, an understanding that is neither theory nor mere occurrence but a mode of being. It gives fundamental ontology its phenomenal base — the analytic will interpret what Dasein pre-ontologically already "has" — and its criterion: § 42 will invoke a pre-ontological document (the Cura fable) as attestation for the care-interpretation. One textual curiosity deserves note: the text reserves ontology for the theoretical question after the meaning of beings (Sinn des Seienden), where one expects "of being" — the sense being that explicit ontology thematizes beings with regard to their being.

The next unit fixes the second key term. The being itself toward which Dasein can comport in this or that way, and always somehow does comport, we call existence (Existenz). And because the essential determination of this being cannot be accomplished by specifying a material what — its essence lying rather in that it has, in each case, its being to be as its own — the title "Dasein" has been chosen, as a pure expression of being, to designate this being. Existenz is thereby wrenched from its traditional sense: it no longer translates existentia, the mere being-present of something (§ 9 will make the contrast explicit), but names the mode of being proper to Dasein alone. The essence-formula anticipates § 9's "the 'essence' of Dasein lies in its existence": what Dasein is cannot be inventoried as a quiddity because Dasein's what is a to-be, delivered over to it as its own (als seiniges — mineness again). And the naming is justified precisely by this: "Dasein" says no what; it is a title of pure being — the there-being that § 28 will finally read out of the word.

Existence is then given its enactment-character. Dasein always understands itself from its existence, from a possibility of itself: to be itself or not to be itself. These possibilities Dasein has either chosen itself, or stumbled into, or in each case already grown up in; existence is decided — by way of seizing or neglecting — only by the respective Dasein itself. The question of existence can only ever be settled through existing itself; the self-understanding that leads in such existing we call existentiell. The question of existence is an ontic "affair" of Dasein and requires no theoretical transparency about the ontological structure of existence; the question after that structure, by contrast, aims at laying apart what constitutes existence, and the connection of these structures we call existentiality (Existenzialität), whose analytic has the character not of an existentiell but of an existential (existenzial) understanding. Nearly every major doctrine of the book is seeded here in a subordinate clause: to-be-itself-or-not names authenticity and inauthenticity before the terms exist; "stumbled into, grown up in" is thrownness before Geworfenheit is coined; and the existentiell/existenzial distinction becomes the book's methodological firewall — the analytic articulates structures and prescribes no way of life, however hard the later chapters press on that line. The remark that existing needs no ontological theory cuts both ways: it protects everyday existence from intellectualist condescension, and it denies that fundamental ontology could ever substitute for an existentiell decision.

The circle then bites in the reverse direction: insofar as existence determines Dasein, the ontological analytic of this being always already requires a prior sight of existentiality; but existentiality is the constitution of being of the being that exists, and in the idea of such a constitution of being already lies the idea of being in general — so the possibility of carrying out the analytic of Dasein depends in turn on the prior working-out of the question of the meaning of being. Where § 2 argued that the question of being requires the analytic, this unit concedes that the analytic presupposes the idea of being. The mutual presupposition is not embarrassment but architecture: it dictates the spiral of the published book (a preparatory analytic, then its repetition out of temporality) and the projected reversal into "Time and Being" that was to redeem the presupposed idea. It also marks the exact spot the later Heidegger will identify as the limit of the fundamental-ontological approach — the clarification of being was to be reached through a being, however distinctive.

The scope of Dasein's understanding is then widened. Sciences are ways of being of Dasein in which it comports itself also toward beings that it need not itself be; but to Dasein belongs essentially: being in a world. Hence the understanding of being that belongs to Dasein concerns equiprimordially (gleichursprünglich) the understanding of something like "world" and the understanding of the being of the beings accessible within the world. The ontologies whose theme is beings of non-Dasein-like character are therefore founded and motivated in Dasein's own ontic structure, which comprises within itself the determinateness of a pre-ontological understanding of being. In-der-Welt-sein makes its first, still unhyphenated appearance ("Sein in einer Welt"), and with it the operator gleichursprünglich, Heidegger's standing weapon against foundationalist orderings: world-understanding is not derived from self-understanding nor the reverse; both are equally original in the one understanding of being. The founding claim completes § 3's hierarchy from the other end — the regional ontologies are grounded not in a general category-doctrine but in the structure of the being whose understanding of being embraces world.

Hence the one-sentence thesis that names the program: fundamental ontology, from which alone all other ontologies can first arise, must be sought in the existential analytic of Dasein. The sentence deserves its isolation as a paragraph, and its precision deserves notice: fundamental ontology is to be sought in the analytic — the analytic is the way to it, not its completed content. On this hangs Heidegger's later defense against the anthropological reading: the analytic of Dasein is fundamental ontology only as the working-out of the ground on which the question of being can be answered, not as a doctrine of man promoted to first philosophy.

The results are formalized as a triple priority. Dasein has a multiple priority before all other beings: the first is ontic — this being is determined in its being by existence; the second is ontological — on the ground of its determinateness by existence, Dasein is in itself "ontological"; and to Dasein belongs, equiprimordially with these and as a constituent of its understanding of existence, an understanding of the being of all non-Dasein-like beings — hence the third priority, as the ontic-ontological condition of the possibility of all ontologies. Dasein has thus shown itself as that which, before all other beings, is ontologically the primary being to be interrogated. The third priority answers § 2's open question exactly: the Befragte of the question of being is Dasein. Its derivation should be seen: because existence is being-in-the-world, Dasein's self-understanding constitutively includes an understanding of the being of what it is not — which is why interrogating this one being can open the meaning of being in general rather than merely regional self-knowledge.

The counter-rooting follows at once: the existential analytic, for its part, is ultimately existentielly — that is, ontically — rooted. Only when philosophical-investigative questioning is itself seized existentielly, as a possibility of being of the existing Dasein in each case, does there exist the possibility of a disclosure of the existentiality of existence, and therewith the possibility of taking up an adequately founded ontological problematic at all. With this, the ontic priority of the question of being has also become clear. The unit states the hermeneutic honesty that § 63 will elaborate: ontology is an existentiell enterprise, an enactment of a possibility of existence, not a view from nowhere — its "presupposition" of a factical self-understanding is not a defect to be purged but the condition of its disclosive power. The phrase "ontic priority of the question" resolves the section title: the question of being is distinguished ontically because it is rooted in, and radicalizes, the being of the being that asks it.

A historical attestation closes the argument. The ontic-ontological priority of Dasein was seen early, without Dasein itself being grasped in its genuine ontological structure or even becoming a problem so directed. Aristotle: the soul is, in a certain way, beings (hē psychē ta onta pōs estin); the soul that constitutes man's being discovers, in its ways to be — perception (aisthēsis) and thought (noēsis) — all beings with respect to their that-being and so-being, and thus always also in their being. This proposition, which points back to Parmenides' ontological thesis, Aquinas took up in a characteristic discussion: within the task of deriving the transcendentia — those characters of being that lie beyond every possible generic-material determination of a being, every modus specialis entis, and belong necessarily to anything whatever — the verum too is to be demonstrated as such a transcendens, and this happens by appeal to a being that, according to its own mode of being, is apt to "come together" with beings of any kind whatever: this distinguished being, the ens quod natum est convenire cum omni ente, is the soul (anima). The priority of "Dasein" emerging here, though ontologically unclarified, obviously has nothing in common with a bad subjectivization of the totality of beings. The genealogy Aristotle–Parmenides–Aquinas certifies that the tradition itself testified to what § 4 argues: a being whose way of being is openness to all beings grounds even the transcendental determination of truth. That verum is derived through anima is, in Heidegger's optic, the medieval anticipation of § 44's thesis that truth has its primary locus in Dasein's disclosedness. And the last sentence erects a guard the book needs repeatedly (§ 43 will fight on this front): the priority of Dasein is not idealism — beings are not resolved into a subject; rather, one being is distinguished by being the site where beings can show themselves in their being.

The penultimate unit knots the two argument-lines together. The demonstration of the ontic-ontological distinction of the question of being rests on the provisional indication of Dasein's ontic-ontological priority; but the analysis of the structure of the question as such (§ 2) had already run up against a distinctive function of this being within the very posing of the question — there Dasein revealed itself as the being that must first be worked out ontologically if the questioning is to become transparent. Now it has emerged that the ontological analytic of Dasein as such constitutes fundamental ontology, so that Dasein functions as the being that is, in principle and in advance, to be interrogated as to its being. Two independent routes — the formal-structural (transparency of the questioner) and the material (the triple priority) — converge on the same being, and the convergence is the real proof: the analytic of Dasein is demanded both by the method of the question and by its matter.

The chapter closes with a formula that answers § 3's opening suspicion once and for all: if the interpretation of the meaning of being becomes the task, Dasein is not only the being to be primarily interrogated; it is, beyond that, the being that in its being always already comports itself toward what is asked about in this question. The question of being is then nothing other than the radicalization of an essential tendency-of-being that belongs to Dasein itself — of the pre-ontological understanding of being. Philosophy, so understood, does not approach Dasein from outside with an alien question; it makes explicit, and drives to its root, a questioning that Dasein as such already is. The charge of free-floating speculation is thereby not merely rebutted but inverted: nothing could be less free-floating than a question rooted in the very being of the questioner — and nothing more concrete than the radicalization of what each of us, in understanding "is," already does.

### Chapter Two: The Double Task in Working Out the Question of Being. The Method of the Investigation and Its Outline

#### § 5. The Ontological Analytic of Dasein as the Laying-Free of the Horizon for an Interpretation of the Meaning of Being in General

The opening unit recapitulates in order to isolate the unfinished business: in characterizing the tasks lying in the "posing" of the question of being, it was shown that not only must the being that is to function as the primary interrogated be fixed, but the right mode of access to it must be expressly appropriated and secured. Which being takes over the distinguished role has been settled; but how is this being, Dasein, to become accessible and, as it were, sighted in understanding interpretation? Chapter One answered the what of the interrogated; Chapter Two owes the how — and the shift from Befragtes to Zugangsart is what makes the chapter methodological.

The second unit dismantles a natural inference. Dasein's demonstrated ontic-ontological priority could seduce one into thinking this being must also be what is primarily given ontically-ontologically — immediately graspable in itself, its mode of being just as "immediately" pregiven. Dasein is indeed ontically not merely near, or even the nearest: we are it, in each case, ourselves. Nevertheless, or precisely for this reason, it is ontologically the farthest. It belongs to its ownmost being to have an understanding of that being and to hold itself always already in a certain interpretedness (Ausgelegtheit) of it — but nothing says this nearest, pre-ontological self-interpretation can be adopted as an adequate guiding thread, as though it sprang from a thematic ontological reflection on its ownmost constitution. Dasein rather has, according to a mode of being belonging to it, the tendency to understand its own being from the being toward which it essentially, constantly, and proximally comports itself — from the "world." In Dasein itself, and so in its own understanding of being, lies what will be exhibited as the ontological back-reflection (Rückstrahlung) of the understanding of the world onto the interpretation of Dasein. The near/far paradox is not a rhetorical flourish but the methodological crux of the book: the obstacle to the analytic is a structure of the analysandum itself. Because Dasein is being-in-the-world, it reads itself in worldly terms — as a thing, a substance, an occurrence — and this self-misreading by way of the world is what the tradition then codifies (§ 6 will say Greek ontology understands being "from the 'world'"). The concealment the method must overcome is the object's own doing.

Hence the third unit's compressed reversal: Dasein's ontic-ontological priority is itself the ground for the fact that its specific constitution of being — understood in the sense of the "categorial" structure belonging to it — remains covered up from it. Dasein is ontically "nearest" to itself, ontologically farthest, but pre-ontologically not foreign. The triadic formula is exact bookkeeping: the pre-ontological familiarity is what makes the analytic possible at all; the ontological farness is what makes it necessary; and the same priority produces both. The scare-quotes around "categorial" flag terminology under correction — § 9 will reserve categories for non-Dasein-like beings and coin "existentials" for Dasein.

The fourth unit locates the difficulty: an interpretation of this being faces peculiar difficulties grounded in the mode of being of the thematic object and of the thematizing comportment itself — not in some deficient endowment of our cognitive faculty or in a lack of adequate concepts that could seemingly be remedied with ease. The difficulty is ontological, not technical: no improvement of apparatus and no new vocabulary by itself dissolves it, because both the theme (a being that flees itself into the world) and the act of thematizing (itself a mode of that being's being) generate the distortion. The remark is also a quiet self-caution for a book about to mint a formidable terminology: the coinages are answerable to the difficulty; they do not remove it.

The fifth unit situates the analytic against the existing sciences of man. Because understanding of being not only belongs to Dasein but develops or decays with Dasein's respective mode of being, Dasein disposes over a rich interpretedness: philosophical psychology, anthropology, ethics, "politics," poetry, biography, and historiography have pursued, on different paths and to varying extents, Dasein's comportments, faculties, powers, possibilities, and destinies. But the question remains whether these interpretations were carried out existentially as originally as they were perhaps existentielly original. The two need not go together, nor do they exclude each other: existentiell interpretation can demand existential analytic, if philosophical knowledge is grasped in its possibility and necessity. Only when the basic structures of Dasein are adequately worked out in explicit orientation to the problem of being itself will the previous gains of Dasein-interpretation receive their existential justification. The § 4 distinction here becomes a criterion for the human sciences: a work can be existentielly profound — the unstated exemplar is Kierkegaard, whom a note in § 45 will assess in exactly these terms — while remaining ontologically naive, borrowed in its concepts. The analytic does not compete with poetry, biography, or psychology; it grounds their right.

The sixth unit issues the methodological charter. An analytic of Dasein must remain the first concern in the question of being — which makes the problem of winning and securing the guiding mode of access to Dasein all the more burning. Negatively: no arbitrary idea of being and actuality, however "self-evident," may be brought to bear on this being in a constructive-dogmatic way; no "categories" predelineated by such an idea may be forced upon Dasein ontologically unexamined. The mode of access and interpretation must instead be chosen so that this being can show itself in itself from itself (an ihm selbst von ihm selbst her) — and show itself, moreover, in how it is proximally and for the most part (zunächst und zumeist), in its average everydayness (durchschnittliche Alltäglichkeit). In everydayness not arbitrary and accidental but essential structures are to be exhibited, structures that maintain themselves as determinative of being in every mode of being of factical Dasein; with regard to the basic constitution of everydayness the preparatory lifting-out of this being's being then grows. Two decisions of rank are taken here. The self-showing formula anticipates verbatim the definition of phenomenon in § 7 — the method is being derived from the access-problem before it is named phenomenology. And the election of everydayness is the positive counter-move to the tradition's habit of reading man off his exceptional modes (pure thinking, theoretical cognition, the moral act): the average, precisely because it is where Dasein first and mostly is, is where the essential structures must be caught — everydayness is a phenomenal field, not a degraded preliminary, and § 11 will further guard it against confusion with "primitiveness."

The seventh unit draws the analytic's limits. So conceived, it remains wholly oriented to the guiding task of working out the question of being, and thereby its boundaries are determined: it cannot aspire to a complete ontology of Dasein — which would indeed have to be built if anything like a "philosophical" anthropology is to stand on a philosophically adequate basis; with a view to a possible anthropology and its ontological foundation, the following interpretation supplies only some "pieces," though not unessential ones. But the analysis of Dasein is not only incomplete; it is at first also provisional: it initially only lifts out the being of this being, without interpreting the meaning of that being. Rather, it is to prepare the laying-free of the horizon for the most original interpretation of being; once that horizon is won, the preparatory analytic demands its repetition (Wiederholung) on the higher and authentic ontological basis. The double disclaimer — incomplete and provisional — fixes the book's architecture and its self-understanding. Incompleteness wards off the anthropological reading in advance (a defense Heidegger had to repeat for decades, not least against Husserl's charge of anthropologism); provisionality announces the spiral: Division Two is the promised repetition of Division One out of temporality, and a further repetition out of the meaning of being in general was reserved for the division never published.

The eighth unit names the result in advance: temporality (Zeitlichkeit) will be exhibited as the meaning of the being of the being we call Dasein. This demonstration must prove itself through the repeated interpretation of the provisionally exhibited structures of Dasein as modes of temporality. But with this interpretation of Dasein as temporality, the answer to the guiding question — the meaning of being in general — is not yet given; only the soil for winning it is prepared. The unit is a masterclass in scope-discipline: Zeitlichkeit answers the question of Dasein's being, not the question of being. The verification procedure is also stated: the proof that temporality is the meaning of care is nothing other than the success of the repetition — that every structure of Division One lets itself be rewritten as a mode of temporalizing (§§ 67–71 execute this). "Meaning" (Sinn) here carries its technical sense, defined at § 32 and applied at § 65: that from out of which something becomes understandable — the whence of the project.

The ninth unit extends the claim from Dasein to being. Dasein is in the manner of, being, understanding something like being; holding fast to this connection, it is to be shown that that from which Dasein tacitly understands and interprets anything like being at all is time. Time must be brought to light and genuinely conceived as the horizon of all understanding of being and every interpretation of being — which requires an original explication of time as horizon of the understanding of being, out of temporality as the being of the Dasein that understands being. The task includes delimiting this original concept of time against the vulgar understanding of time, which became explicit in the traditional time-concept persisting from Aristotle to beyond Bergson; and it must be made clear that and how this time-concept and the vulgar understanding of time in general spring from temporality — whereby the vulgar concept receives back its own right, against Bergson's thesis that the time meant in it is really space. The order of derivation is the crucial commitment: ordinary clock-time is not to be refuted but derived — shown to be a leveled-off descendant of temporality (§ 81 pays this debt). Hence the double-edged verdict on Bergson: he rightly saw that the traditional concept misses original time, but wrongly diagnosed the miss as spatialization — the vulgar concept is genuine time, only derivative, and calling it space forfeits both its right and its provenance.

The tenth unit assembles the evidence that time already functions ontologically. "Time" has long served as an ontological — or rather ontic — criterion for naively distinguishing regions of beings: one marks off "temporal" beings (the processes of nature, the events of history) against "non-temporal" beings (spatial and numerical relations); one contrasts the "timeless" sense of propositions with the "temporal" course of assertings; one finds a "gulf" between temporal beings and the "supratemporal" eternal and attempts to bridge it. "Temporal" in each case means "being in time" — a determination obscure enough itself. The fact stands: time functions as a criterion for separating regions of being. But how time comes to this distinguished ontological function, with what right precisely time so functions, and whether in this naive employment its authentic possible ontological relevance finds expression — this has been neither asked nor investigated. Time, within the horizon of the vulgar understanding, has drifted "of itself" into this "self-evident" ontological function and held itself there. The inventory is pointed at contemporaries as much as ancients: the "timeless validity" of propositions is Lotze's Geltung, backbone of the neo-Kantian value-philosophy in which Heidegger was schooled; the gulf-and-bridge is the theology of eternity. The argument-form repeats § 1: an unexamined self-evidence — here time's regional-criterial role — is converted from an answer into a question.

The eleventh unit states the counter-thesis in one sentence: on the ground of the worked-out question of the meaning of being, it is to be shown that and how the central problematic of all ontology is rooted in the phenomenon of time rightly seen and rightly explicated. The proviso carries the weight — rightly seen: not time as one region-marking being among beings, but time as the horizon the tradition was unknowingly using.

The twelfth unit draws the terminological consequence. If being is to be conceived from time, and the various modes and derivatives of being do become intelligible in their modifications and derivations from the view toward time, then being itself — not merely beings as beings "in time" — is thereby made visible in its "temporal" character. But then "temporal" can no longer mean merely "being in time": even the "non-temporal" and the "supratemporal" is "temporal" with respect to its being, and this not only privatively, but in a positive sense still to be clarified. Because the expression "temporal" is already claimed by pre-philosophical and philosophical usage, and because it will be claimed in what follows for yet another meaning, the original determinateness of the meaning of being and of its characters and modes out of time is named its Temporal determinateness (temporale Bestimmtheit); the fundamental-ontological task of interpreting being as such therefore includes working out the Temporality of being (Temporalität des Seins), and in the exposition of this problematic the concrete answer to the question of the meaning of being is first given. The three-way split must be kept rigid across the whole book: innerzeitig (in time), zeitlich (Dasein's temporality), temporal (being's time-determinateness). The startling middle claim — that even the timeless is positively temporal — says that mathematical objects, valid propositions, and the eternal are all understood in modes of presence, hence from time. And the last sentence quietly relocates the book's payoff: the concrete answer belongs to the Temporalität-problematic, that is, to the third division that never appeared — the lecture course of summer 1927 (GA 24), with its doctrine of praesens as horizonal schema, is the surviving attempt.

The thirteenth unit forestalls a misreading of what an "answer" would even be. Because being becomes graspable only in the view toward time, the answer cannot lie in an isolated and blind proposition; it is not grasped by repeating what it propositionally asserts, least of all when passed along as a free-floating result, mere notice of a "standpoint" that perhaps deviates from previous treatments. Whether the answer is "new" is of no consequence and remains an externality; what is positive about it must lie in its being old enough to learn to grasp the possibilities readied by the "ancients." According to its ownmost sense, the answer gives a directive (Anweisung) for concrete ontological research to begin its investigative questioning within the laid-free horizon — and it gives only that. Philosophy's results, on this conception, are horizons, not theses: a proposition detached from the path that opened it is "blind" in the Kantian sense the Introduction has already exploited. The polemic against novelty inverts the avant-garde self-presentation one might expect of 1927's most radical book — its ambition is to be old enough for the Greeks.

The closing unit pivots to § 6: if the answer thus becomes a guiding directive for research, it is adequately given only when from it the specific mode of being of previous ontology — the fates of its questioning, finding, and failing — comes into view as something necessary in the manner of Dasein (daseinsmäßig notwendig). The demand is severe: the answer must explain the history of ontology, including its failure, as grounded in Dasein's own way of being — not as a run of avoidable errors. Traditional ontology's oblivion of being must itself be deduced from falling, everyday, world-absorbed understanding. History of philosophy thereby becomes an ontological discipline, and the bridge to the destruction is built.

#### § 6. The Task of a Destruction of the History of Ontology

The section opens with its longest and densest unit, deriving historicity from temporality. All research — not least that moving in the orbit of the central question of being — is an ontic possibility of Dasein, whose being finds its meaning in temporality. But temporality is at the same time the condition of the possibility of historicity (Geschichtlichkeit) as a temporal mode of being of Dasein itself, regardless of whether and how Dasein is a being "in time"; and historicity lies before what one calls history in the sense of world-historical happening. Historicity means the constitution of being of the "happening" (Geschehen) of Dasein as such, on whose ground alone something like "world-history" — and historical belonging to world-history — first becomes possible. Dasein is, in its factical being, in each case how and "what" it already was: whether explicitly or not, it is its past. And not in the manner of a property shoved along "behind" it, a possession of bygones still present-at-hand and occasionally working after-effects in it: Dasein "is" its past in the manner of its being, which — roughly put — in each case "happens" out of its future. In its respective way of being, and so too with the understanding of being that belongs to it, Dasein has grown into and grown up within a transmitted interpretation of Dasein; from this it understands itself proximally and, within a certain range, constantly. This understanding discloses the possibilities of its being and regulates them. Its own past — and that always means the past of its "generation" — does not follow after Dasein but in each case already goes ahead of it. Nearly the whole doctrine of §§ 72–77 is compacted here. Being-one's-past against having-a-past: the present-at-hand model of the past as trailing property is replaced by having-been as a way of being enacted now. The aside that Dasein happens "out of its future" states, two hundred and fifty pages early, the primacy of the future in the structure of temporality (§ 65). "Generation" is Dilthey's concept, silently appropriated: the past that pre-forms me is communal, not private. And the closing inversion — the past goes ahead of Dasein — is the historical deepening of the hermeneutic situation: transmitted interpretedness predelineates the possibilities from which Dasein understands itself, including its possibilities of doing ontology.

The second unit distinguishes historicity from historiography. This elementary historicity can remain concealed from Dasein; it can also be discovered in a certain way and receive its own cultivation. Dasein can discover tradition, preserve it, expressly pursue it; the discovery of tradition, and the disclosure of what it "hands over" and how, can be seized as an independent task. Dasein thereby brings itself into the mode of being of historiographical questioning and research. But historiography (Historie) — more precisely, historicality (Historizität) — is possible as the mode of being of the questioning Dasein only because Dasein is, in the ground of its being, determined by historicity. Where historicity remains hidden, and so long as it does, the possibility of historiographical questioning and of discovering history is denied to Dasein; the absence of historiography is no proof against Dasein's historicity but rather, as a deficient mode of this constitution of being, proof for it — an age can be unhistoriographical only because it is "historical." The argument-form deserves isolation, since the book will reuse it constantly: an apparent absence of a structure is reinterpreted as a deficient mode of that structure, hence as evidence of it (being-alone will be a deficient mode of being-with, mere staring a deficient mode of concernful dealing). The grounding claim — the science of history is founded in Dasein's historicity — is redeemed at § 76.

The third unit turns historicity back onto the being-question itself. If Dasein has seized the possibility lying in it not only of making its existence transparent but of questioning after the meaning of existentiality itself — that is, in advance, after the meaning of being in general — and if in such questioning the view has opened for Dasein's essential historicity, then the insight is inescapable: the questioning after being, already exhibited in its ontic-ontological necessity, is itself characterized by historicity. The working-out of the question of being must therefore hear, from the ownmost being-sense of the questioning itself as a historical questioning, the directive to inquire after its own history — to become historiographical — in order to bring itself, through positive appropriation of the past, into full possession of its ownmost possibilities of questioning. The question of the meaning of being, according to the mode of enactment proper to it as the prior explication of Dasein in its temporality and historicity, is brought by itself to understand itself as historiographical. The destruction is thereby derived, not appended: because questioning is a mode of being of a historical being, the being-question owes itself an inquiry into its own history. The point of the history is expressly positive — appropriation of possibilities, self-possession of the question — which is why the destruction belongs to the working-out of the question and not to a survey of opinions.

The fourth unit introduces the counter-force. The preparatory interpretation of Dasein's fundamental structures in its nearest and average mode of being — in which it is also proximally historical — will make the following manifest: Dasein has not only the inclination to fall onto its world (an seine Welt zu verfallen), in which it is, and to interpret itself out of that world by reflected light (reluzent); in one with this, Dasein falls prey to its tradition, seized more or less expressly. Tradition takes from Dasein its own leading, its questioning and choosing — and this holds not least for that understanding, rooted in Dasein's ownmost being, which is ontological. Verfallen enters the book here, with its structure already double: falling onto the world (self-interpretation by the world's reflected light — "reluzent" preserves a term of art from the early Freiburg lectures) and falling onto tradition. The second is the historical form of the first, and its yield is precise: tradition relieves (nimmt ab) Dasein of questioning and choosing — relief, disburdening, will remain the signature operation of fallenness (das Man, § 27). With this, the concealment § 1 could only report is given its existential ground.

The fifth unit describes the mechanism.
