The tradition that thereby comes to dominance makes what it "hands over" proximally and for the most part so little accessible that it rather covers it up: it consigns the transmitted to self-evidence and blocks access to the original "sources" from which the traditional categories and concepts were, in part, genuinely drawn. Tradition even makes such provenance be forgotten altogether, and it cultivates the felt needlessness of so much as understanding the necessity of such a return. It uproots Dasein's historicity so far that Dasein moves about only in an interest in the multiplicity of possible types, directions, and standpoints of philosophizing in the most remote and alien cultures, seeking with this interest to veil its own groundlessness (Bodenlosigkeit). The consequence: with all historiographical interest and all zeal for philologically "objective" interpretation, Dasein no longer understands the most elementary conditions that alone make possible a positive return to the past in the sense of its productive appropriation. Note the concessive precision: the traditional concepts were in part genuinely drawn from original sources — the destruction presupposes genuine origins to recover, or it would have nothing to do. The polemical target is the historicist culture of the day: typologies of worldviews, comparative panoramas, doxographic connoisseurship — erudition as the mask of rootlessness. The paradox is Nietzschean (the second Untimely Meditation stands behind it, and § 76 will cite it): maximal historical learning coinciding with minimal capacity to appropriate history.

The sixth unit runs the thesis through the actual history. At the outset (§ 1) it was shown that the question of the meaning of being is not only unsettled and not only inadequately posed but, with all the interest in "metaphysics," forgotten. Greek ontology and its history — which through manifold filiations and distortions still determines the conceptuality of philosophy today — is the proof that Dasein understands itself and being in general from the "world," and that the ontology thus arisen falls prey to the tradition, which lets it sink to self-evidence and to mere material for reworking (as for Hegel). This uprooted Greek ontology becomes in the Middle Ages a fixed doctrinal corpus — whose systematics, Heidegger immediately adds, is anything but a mere assembling of transmitted pieces: within the limits of a dogmatic reception of the Greek basic conceptions of being, much unmined, forward-pointing work lies in it. In its scholastic coinage, Greek ontology passes over — essentially by way of Suárez's Disputationes metaphysicae — into the "metaphysics" and transcendental philosophy of modernity, and it still determines the foundations and goals of Hegel's Logic. And insofar as in the course of this history certain distinctive domains of being come into view and thenceforth primarily guide the problematic — Descartes' ego cogito, subject, I, reason, spirit, person — these remain, in keeping with the thoroughgoing omission of the question of being, uninterrogated as to their being and its structure; instead, the categorial stock of traditional ontology is transferred to this being with corresponding formalizations and merely negative restrictions, or else dialectic is called in to help with an ontological interpretation of the substantiality of the subject. This single paragraph is Heidegger's history of Western ontology in miniature, and each joint matters. That Greek ontology arises from the "world" confirms § 5's Rückstrahlung at the level of world-history: the self-misreading from the world is the origin of the tradition, which is why the tradition's failure is daseinsmäßig necessary, as § 5's close demanded. The Suárez claim — that modernity received Aristotle through the Disputationes rather than directly — has become standard scholarship; in 1927 it was a working discovery of Heidegger's lecture courses. And the indictment of modern philosophy is exact in form: the revolution of subjectivity changed the privileged domain of beings while leaving the inherited sense of being untouched — the subject is a res, thought with the categories of the present-at-hand, whether formalized (Kant's "I think" as logical form), negatively restricted (the soul as non-extended thing), or dialectically mediated (Hegel). The critique of the "subject" that runs through the whole book (§§ 10, 13, 25, 43, 64) is grounded here.

The seventh unit gives the task its name. If the question of being itself is to win the transparency of its own history, then the hardened tradition must be loosened up and the concealments it has produced dissolved. This task is understood as the destruction (Destruktion), carried out along the guiding thread of the question of being, of the transmitted stock of ancient ontology — down to the original experiences in which the first and thenceforth leading determinations of being were won. Every element of the definition is load-bearing: destruction operates on the transmitted stock (not on the past itself); its direction is regressive, toward the ursprüngliche Erfahrungen from which the basic concepts were drawn — a phenomenological genealogy that asks of every category what experience originally cashed it; and its guiding thread is the question of being, not historiographical interest, so its selections and verdicts are systematically, not philologically, motivated. The word itself has a prehistory in Luther's destructio of scholastic theology, which Heidegger knew intimately — the § 3 remark on Luther marked the same gesture — and a famous posterity in Derrida's déconstruction.

The eighth unit protects the concept from its obvious misreadings. This demonstration of the provenance of the ontological basic concepts — the investigative issuing of their "birth certificate" — has nothing to do with a bad relativizing of ontological standpoints; and destruction has just as little the negative sense of shaking off the ontological tradition. On the contrary, it is to stake out the tradition in its positive possibilities, and that always means: in its limits, which are factically given with the respective way the question was posed and with the delimitation of the possible field of investigation thence predelineated. Destruction does not comport itself negatively toward the past; its critique strikes the "today" and the dominant manner of treating the history of ontology, be it doxographic, intellectual-historical, or problem-historical. Destruction does not want to bury the past in nullity; it has a positive intent; its negative function remains inexplicit and indirect. Two precisions repay attention. Possibilities and limits are made convertible: to exhibit what an ontology positively achieved is eo ipso to exhibit the boundary drawn by its Fragestellung — genealogy neither debunks (relativism) nor demolishes. And the critique's true target is the present's relation to the tradition: even Problemgeschichte — commended at § 3 as an advance for literary history — is listed among the criticized treatments when it comes to ontology, for a history of "problems" still presupposes that the problems themselves, and the being-question behind them, are already understood.

The ninth unit limits the execution: within the present treatise, whose goal is the fundamental working-out of the question of being, the destruction — which belongs essentially to the posing of the question and is possible only within it — can be carried out only at fundamentally decisive stations of that history. The clause "possible only within it" bears repeating against any reading of Part Two as detachable erudition: without the worked-out question there is no criterion for what counts as decisive, nor any light in which the tradition's concealments could show as concealments.

The tenth unit names the first station. In keeping with the destruction's positive tendency, the first question is whether and how far in the history of ontology the interpretation of being was ever thematically brought together with the phenomenon of time, and whether the problematic of Temporality necessary for this was, or could be, fundamentally worked out. The first and only one who moved a stretch of the investigative way in the direction of the dimension of Temporality — or rather, let himself be driven there by the compulsion of the phenomena themselves — is Kant. Only when the problematic of Temporality is fixed can light be brought into the darkness of the doctrine of the schematism; and on this path it can also be shown why this region had to remain closed to Kant in its authentic dimensions and central ontological function. Kant himself knew he was venturing into a dark region — the schematism, he wrote, is "a hidden art in the depths of the human soul" whose true operations nature will hardly ever let us unveil. What Kant here as it were recoils from must be brought thematically and fundamentally to light, if the expression "being" is to have a demonstrable meaning; in the end, precisely the phenomena to be exhibited under the title "Temporality" are the most secret judgments of "common reason," whose analytic Kant calls the "business of philosophers." Kant is elected precursor on the strongest ground Heidegger's economy knows — compulsion of the phenomena, not doctrinal choice: the schematism chapter is where being (the categories) and time (the schemata as transcendental time-determinations) actually meet in the tradition. The image of Kant's recoil before his own discovery becomes the organizing thesis of the 1929 Kant book (Kant's shrinking back from the abyss of the transcendental imagination). And § 1's Kant citation returns with its cash value: the covert judgments of common reason are now identified — they are the temporal operations of the pre-ontological understanding of being.

The eleventh unit states the Kant-interpretation's program and diagnosis. In pursuing the destruction along the guiding thread of the Temporality-problematic, the treatise will attempt to interpret the schematism chapter and, from there, the Kantian doctrine of time; and it will be shown why Kant had to be denied insight into the problematic of Temporality. Two things prevented it: first, the omission of the question of being in general and, connected with it, the lack of a thematic ontology of Dasein — in Kantian terms, of a prior ontological analytic of the subjectivity of the subject; instead, for all his essential advances, Kant dogmatically takes over Descartes' position. Second, despite drawing the phenomenon of time back into the subject, his analysis of time remains oriented to the transmitted vulgar understanding of time, which in the end prevents him from working out the phenomenon of a "transcendental time-determination" in its own structure and function. Owing to this double after-effect of the tradition, the decisive connection between time and the "I think" remains wrapped in complete darkness — it does not even become a problem. The diagnosis is architecturally elegant: Kant fails at exactly the two joints the destruction's next stations name — the subject's being (Descartes) and the concept of time (Aristotle) — so the regress Kant→Descartes→ancient ontology is not a list but a single genealogy traversed backwards. The missed connection between time and the "I think" is the positive residue: establishing it (temporality as the meaning of the being of the self) is precisely what §§ 64 ff. and the Kant book undertake.

The twelfth unit opens the second station. By taking over Descartes' ontological position, Kant shares in an essential omission: that of an ontology of Dasein — an omission decisive in the sense of Descartes' ownmost tendency, for with the cogito sum Descartes claims to provide philosophy a new and secure ground. But what he leaves undetermined in this "radical" beginning is the mode of being of the res cogitans — more precisely, the being-sense of the sum. Working out the inexplicit ontological foundations of the cogito sum constitutes the stay at the second station of the destructive regress; the interpretation proves not only that Descartes had to omit the question of being but also why he came to the opinion that the absolute "being-certain" of the cogito exempted him from the question of the being-sense of this being. The formula — the sum forgotten in favor of the cogito — is Heidegger's constant shorthand for modernity's founding omission (it recurs at §§ 10 and 43): certainty is put in the place of being, epistemic security substituting for ontological determination, so that the more "radical" the beginning claims to be, the more totally it inherits.

The thirteenth unit shows that the omission was filled — by the tradition. For Descartes does not leave the res cogitans sive mens sive animus in sheer ontological indeterminacy: he carries through the fundamental reflections of his Meditationes by transferring medieval ontology onto this being posited as fundamentum inconcussum. The res cogitans is ontologically determined as ens, and for medieval ontology the being-sense of ens is fixed in the understanding of ens as ens creatum — God, as ens infinitum, being the ens increatum. Createdness (Geschaffenheit), in the widest sense of the producedness (Hergestelltheit) of something, is an essential structural moment of the ancient concept of being. The apparent new beginning of philosophizing unveils itself as the planting of a fateful prejudice, on whose ground the following age neglected a thematic ontological analytic of "mind" (Gemüt) guided by the question of being and, in one with it, a critical confrontation with the transmitted ancient ontology. The deep move is the equation buried in the aside: creation-ontology is production-ontology — ens creatum thinks being as being-produced, and producedness is a Greek structural moment (the artisan model of form and matter), so that medieval theology transmits, and Descartes replants, the ancient horizon. The 1927 lecture course (GA 24, § 11) unfolds this in detail: essentia and existentia both drawn from the comportment of producing. Thus the vacancy at the sum was never neutral — it was immediately occupied by the oldest tenant.

The fourteenth unit converts source-criticism into ontology. That Descartes is "dependent" on medieval scholasticism and uses its terminology — every connoisseur of the Middle Ages sees that. But with this "discovery" nothing is philosophically gained so long as it remains obscure what fundamental import this in-working of medieval ontology has, for the sequel, on the ontological determination — or non-determination — of the res cogitans. That import can be estimated only once the sense and limits of ancient ontology have been exhibited from an orientation to the question of being: in other words, the destruction faces the task of interpreting the soil of ancient ontology in the light of the Temporality-problematic. And here it becomes manifest that the ancient interpretation of the being of beings is oriented to the "world," or "nature" in the widest sense, and that it in fact wins its understanding of being from "time." The external document of this — but only that — is the determination of the meaning of being as parousia or ousia, which means, ontologically and Temporally, "presence" (Anwesenheit): beings are grasped in their being as "presence," that is, understood with regard to a definite mode of time, the "present" (Gegenwart). Here the book's title becomes a historical thesis: being and time were always already conjoined — the tradition understood being from time, namely as presence, without ever knowing it. The philological anchor (ousia as Anwesen, estate, presence) is expressly demoted to a document; the proof lies in the analysis of the comportments from which the Greeks read off being. The concept of being as constant presence, minted here, becomes the master key of Heidegger's entire subsequent history of being — and the standing standard against which Dasein, the being that is its past and happens from its future, cannot be thought.

The fifteenth unit supplies that analysis of comportment. The problematic of Greek ontology, like that of any ontology, must take its guiding thread from Dasein itself: Dasein — the being of man — is delimited, in the vulgar as in the philosophical "definition," as zōon logon echon, the living being whose being is essentially determined by the ability to talk. Legein (cf. § 7 B) is the guiding thread for winning the structures of being of those beings encountered in addressing and discussing something; hence the ancient ontology that takes shape with Plato becomes "dialectic." With the progressive working-out of the ontological guiding thread itself — that is, of the "hermeneutic" of the logos — grows the possibility of a more radical grasp of the problem of being: dialectic, which was a genuine philosophical embarrassment, becomes superfluous, and Aristotle "no longer had any understanding" for it because he set it on a more radical footing and sublated it. Legein itself — or noein, the plain perceiving of something present-at-hand in its pure presence-at-hand, which Parmenides had already taken as the guide for interpreting being — has the Temporal structure of the pure "making-present" (Gegenwärtigen) of something: the being that shows itself in and for this perceiving, and is understood as the authentic being, accordingly receives its interpretation with regard to the pres-ent — it is conceived as presence (ousia). The argument closes a circle opened at § 4: every ontology takes its clue from Dasein, and the Greeks took theirs from one privileged comportment — pure assertion and perception. Since making-present is a mode of temporality (§ 68 will place it within the structure of the present), the temporal analysis of this comportment explains why Greek being means presence: what shows itself to a pure making-present can only show itself as the presently-abiding. Two asides carry polemical charge: the definition of man is rendered "able to talk," deflating animal rationale in advance of § 10's critique; and Aristotle's dismissal of dialectic is ranked as progress — a pointed inversion of Hegel's scale.

The sixteenth unit states the Greeks' double blindness: this Greek interpretation of being is accomplished without any explicit knowledge of the guiding thread functioning in it, without acquaintance with — let alone understanding of — the fundamental ontological function of time, and without insight into the ground of the possibility of this function. On the contrary: time itself is taken as one being among other beings, and the attempt is made to grasp it in its being-structure from the horizon of an understanding of being that is itself tacitly and naively oriented to time. The circle is exquisite and damning: the Greeks interrogate time using categories (presence, the now as vorhanden) that feed on time as their concealed horizon — the horizon is treated as an item within the field it opens. This is why a Greek treatise on time is the perfect diagnostic site for the whole ancient ontology.

The seventeenth unit selects the specimen: within the present fundamental working-out of the question of being, the detailed Temporal interpretation of the foundations of ancient ontology — above all of its scientifically highest and purest stage in Aristotle — cannot be communicated; in its place stands an interpretation of Aristotle's treatise on time (Physics IV 10–14), which may be chosen as the discrimen of the basis and the limits of the ancient science of being. Discrimen: the test that separates — the treatise where the tacit horizon becomes explicit theme, so that both the power and the boundary of the Greek understanding of being must show themselves at once. This is the third station of the projected Part Two.

The eighteenth unit justifies the choice by influence: the Aristotelian treatise on time is the first detailed interpretation of this phenomenon that has come down to us, and it has essentially determined all subsequent conceptions of time — Bergson's included. From the analysis of the Aristotelian time-concept it becomes retrospectively clear that the Kantian conception of time moves within the structures Aristotle set out — which means: Kant's basic ontological orientation, for all the differences of a new questioning, remains Greek. The arc announced at § 5 (the vulgar concept "from Aristotle to beyond Bergson") is now grounded, and the stations interlock into a single proof: if Kant's time is Aristotle's, then the sole modern advance toward Temporality was made with ancient instruments — which is exactly why it had to stall.

The nineteenth unit states what the destruction yields for the question itself: only in carrying out the destruction of the ontological tradition does the question of being win its true concretion; in the destruction the question procures for itself the full proof of the inescapability of asking after the meaning of being, and so demonstrates the sense of talk of a "retrieval" of this question. The claim completes § 1's deferral: the necessity of the question, there only motivated, is fully proven only historically — by showing that the tradition lived off an answer (presence) it never grounded. Retrieval now has its exact sense: asking again, as a question, what the tradition transmitted as self-evidence.

The final unit ends the section on a note of severe modesty. Every investigation in this field, where "the matter itself is deeply veiled" (Kant), will keep itself free of overestimating its results; for such questioning constantly forces itself before the possibility of disclosing a still more original and more universal horizon, from which the answer to the question "what does 'being' mean?" could be drawn. Such possibilities can be seriously and productively negotiated only when the question of being has first been awakened again at all and a field of controllable disputes has been won. The concession is remarkable and easily missed: even time is not guaranteed to be the ultimate horizon — the book expressly holds open a horizon more original than its own answer. Read forward, the sentence is quietly prophetic of the later self-displacement, when the transcendental-horizonal approach of fundamental ontology is itself set aside. Read in 1927, it defines the work's scientific ethos: not a worldview to be believed, but the reopening of a question and the winning of a field in which disagreement can be controlled — argued, checked, decided.

#### § 7. The Phenomenological Method of the Investigation

The opening unit refuses the obvious route to a method. With the provisional characterization of the investigation's thematic object — the being of beings, or the meaning of being in general — its method seems already predelineated: setting being off against beings and explicating being itself is the task of ontology. But the method of ontology remains questionable in the highest degree so long as one would seek counsel from historically transmitted ontologies or similar attempts; and since "ontology" is here used in a formally broad sense, the path of clarifying the method by pursuing ontology's history forbids itself of its own accord. The refusal is principled, not merely prudent: § 6 has just shown that the transmitted ontologies embody the very concealments at issue, so their procedures cannot be normative — the discipline's past supplies material for destruction, not methodological authority.

The second unit widens the refusal to the concept of a discipline as such. Using the term "ontology" is not to speak for some definite philosophical discipline standing in connection with the others; the aim is not to satisfy the task of a pregiven discipline, but the reverse — from the substantive necessities of definite questions, and from the manner of treatment demanded by the "things themselves," a discipline may at best take shape. Questions precede disciplines; disciplines are precipitates of questioning, never its warrant. The remark generalizes § 3's picture of science (basic concepts answerable to the subject area, not to the guild) to philosophy itself, and it quietly reserves the right to a hermeneutics of Dasein that fits no existing departmental map.

The third unit names the method and immediately guards the name. With the guiding question of the meaning of being, the investigation stands at the fundamental question of philosophy in general, and the manner of treating this question is the phenomenological. But the treatise thereby subscribes neither to a "standpoint" nor to a "direction," because phenomenology is neither and can never become either, so long as it understands itself. "Phenomenology" primarily signifies a concept of method: it characterizes not the substantive what of the objects of philosophical research but the how of that research. And the more genuinely a concept of method works itself out, the more comprehensively it determines the fundamental conduct of a science, the more originally it is rooted in the confrontation with the things themselves, and the farther it stands from what we call a technical device, of which the theoretical disciplines also have many. The unit performs a delicate double gesture toward Husserl: it adopts the phenomenological banner while detaching it from any doctrinal content — including, tacitly, Husserl's own (transcendental idealism, the reduction, the primacy of consciousness are all "standpoint" on this accounting). Method rooted in the matters versus technical device also sets the standard by which Heidegger will justify departing from Husserlian procedure: fidelity to phenomenology may require abandoning its school-form.

The fourth unit gives the maxim and meets the shrug it invites. The title "phenomenology" expresses a maxim that can be formulated: "to the things themselves!" — against all free-floating constructions and accidental findings, against the adoption of concepts only seemingly demonstrated, against the pseudo-questions that often spread themselves for generations as "problems." One might reply that the maxim is abundantly self-evident, an expression of the principle of any scientific knowledge whatever, and hardly worth putting in a research program's title. Heidegger accepts the challenge on § 1's terms: it is indeed a "self-evidence," and precisely such self-evidences are what philosophy must bring closer — as far as matters for illuminating the procedure of this treatise. We are expounding, he says, only the preliminary concept (Vorbegriff) of phenomenology. The word "Vorbegriff" carries the section's whole modesty and its promise: the full concept of the method can be won only from the investigation itself (§ 83 ends the book on this note), so what follows is a formal anticipation, not a methodology delivered in advance.

The fifth unit sets the etymological program: the expression has two components, phenomenon and logos, both going back to Greek terms — phainomenon and logos. Taken externally, "phenomenology" is formed like theology, biology, sociology — science of God, of life, of community — and would accordingly be the science of phenomena. The preliminary concept is to be exhibited by characterizing what each component means and by fixing the sense of the name composed of them; the history of the word itself, which presumably arose in the school of Wolff, is of no significance here. The dismissal of the word's actual history is itself a methodological act: what legitimates the title is not Lambert's or Kant's or Hegel's usage but the Greek phenomena the components name — the procedure of § 6 (back to the sources beneath the transmitted term) applied to the method's own name.

##### A. The Concept of Phenomenon

The first unit derives the term and its shadow. The Greek phainomenon derives from the verb phainesthai, to show itself; phainomenon therefore means: that which shows itself, the self-showing, the manifest. Phainesthai is a middle-voice formation of phainō, to bring to the day, to set in brightness; and phainō belongs to the stem pha-, like phōs, the light, the brightness — that in which something can become manifest, visible in itself. So the meaning of "phenomenon" to be held fast is: the self-showing-in-itself (das Sich-an-ihm-selbst-zeigende), the manifest; the phainomena are the totality of what lies in the day or can be brought to the light — what the Greeks sometimes simply identified with ta onta, beings. Now beings can show themselves from themselves in various ways, according to the mode of access to them; the possibility even exists that a being shows itself as what it in itself is not — in such self-showing it "looks like..." This self-showing we call seeming (Scheinen), and so in Greek phainomenon also means: what looks like, the "seeming," semblance (Schein) — phainomenon agathon is a good that looks like, but "in actuality" is not, what it gives itself out to be. Everything depends on seeing how the two meanings hang together structurally: only insofar as something at all pretends, by its very sense, to show itself — to be a phenomenon — can it show itself as what it is not, can it "merely look like..." The meaning of semblance thus already includes the original meaning, phenomenon as the manifest, as founding it. The title "phenomenon" is assigned terminologically to the positive, original meaning, and phenomenon distinguished from semblance as its privative modification. But what both terms express has at first nothing whatever to do with what is called "appearance" (Erscheinung), let alone "mere appearance." The founding argument is the unit's philosophical core: semblance is not the opposite of self-showing but its parasite — deception is only possible for what by its sense claims to show itself. This founding of the privative on the positive will recur as a schema (falsehood founded on uncovering in B; covering-up as counter-concept in C), and it silently rebukes any epistemology that starts from illusion: semblance presupposes manifestation.

The second unit introduces appearance by its natural home, the symptom. One speaks of "appearances (symptoms) of illness": occurrences in the body that show themselves and, in showing themselves, "indicate" something that does not show itself. The emergence of such occurrences, their self-showing, goes together with the presence-at-hand of disturbances that do not show themselves. Appearance, as appearance "of something," accordingly means precisely not: showing itself, but the announcing-itself (Sichmelden) of something that does not show itself, through something that does show itself. Appearing is a not-showing-itself — but this "not" must never be thrown together with the privative not that determines the structure of semblance: what does not show itself in the manner of the appearing thing can never seem either. All indications, presentations, symptoms, and symbols have this formal basic structure of appearing, however they may differ among themselves. The taxonomy is doing surgical work: appearance is a referential relation (something present announces something absent), categorially distinct both from the phenomenon's self-showing and from semblance's distorted self-showing. The medical example is well chosen because there the indicated (the disturbance) is a being that happens not to show itself — keeping the analysis at first ontic and neutral.

The third unit fixes the dependence. Although appearing is never a self-showing in the sense of phenomenon, appearing is possible only on the ground of a self-showing of something; but this self-showing that co-enables appearing is not the appearing itself. Appearing is announcing-itself through something that shows itself. If one then says that with the word "appearance" we point to something wherein something appears without itself being appearance, the concept of phenomenon is not thereby delimited but presupposed — and the presupposition stays covered up, because in this determination of "appearance" the expression "appear" is used ambiguously: that wherein something "appears" means that wherein something announces itself, i.e., does not show itself; while "without itself being 'appearance'" means the self-showing, which belongs essentially to the "wherein." Phenomena are therefore never appearances, but every appearance is dependent on phenomena. If one defines phenomenon with the help of an — additionally unclear — concept of "appearance," everything is stood on its head, and a "critique" of phenomenology on this basis is a peculiar undertaking. The polemical coda has contemporary addressees (critics who took "phenomenon" to mean the merely subjective show of a hidden reality), but the argument is general: appearance-talk borrows its intelligibility from self-showing at every joint, so the phenomenon cannot be a species of appearance — the order of definition runs the other way.

The fourth unit inventories the ambiguity: "appearance" can itself mean two things — the appearing in the sense of announcing-itself as not-showing-itself, and the announcer itself, that which in its self-showing indicates something that does not show itself; and finally one can use "appearing" as a title for the genuine sense of phenomenon, the self-showing. If one designates these three different states of affairs indiscriminately as "appearance," confusion is unavoidable. The unit is pure disambiguation, but its yield is a lexicon the whole book relies on: the relation (announcing), the relatum that shows (the announcer), and the self-showing as such must be separable on demand wherever "appearance" occurs in the tradition.

The fifth unit adds the fourth and philosophically heaviest sense. The confusion is essentially heightened in that "appearance" can take on yet another meaning: if the announcer — what in its self-showing indicates the non-manifest — is grasped as what emerges on the non-manifest itself, radiating out from it, such that the non-manifest is thought as what is essentially never manifest, then appearance means as much as bringing-forth or the brought-forth, which however does not constitute the authentic being of what brings it forth: appearance in the sense of "mere appearance." The brought-forth announcer does show itself — but in such a way that, as emanation of what it announces, it constantly veils that very thing in itself. Yet this veiling not-showing is, again, not semblance. Kant uses the term "appearance" in this coupling: appearances are for him, first, the "objects of empirical intuition," what shows itself in it — the self-showing, phenomenon in the genuine original sense — and at the same time "appearance" as the announcing emanation of something that conceals itself in the appearance. The analysis quietly performs a diagnosis of the thing-in-itself doctrine: Kant's "Erscheinung" fuses the phenomenon (what empirical intuition gives) with a production-and-emanation relation to an essentially unshowable X — and the fusion of categorially distinct structures under one word is what generates the classical antinomies of the doctrine's reception. Note also the guard within the guard: even "mere appearance" is not semblance — the veil is not a lie.

The sixth unit stacks the structures to show their founding order. Insofar as a phenomenon is constitutive for "appearance" in the sense of announcing-itself through a self-showing thing, and this phenomenon can privatively modify itself into semblance, appearance too can become mere semblance: in a certain lighting someone can look as if he had reddened cheeks, and this showing redness can be taken as an announcement of the presence-at-hand of fever, which in its turn indicates a disturbance in the organism. The little chain — semblance feeding a symptom feeding an inference — is not an ornament: it demonstrates that the categorial distinctions just drawn compose, and that the analysis can track an everyday case through all its layers without confusion. That is the pragmatic test of a formal taxonomy.

The seventh unit summarizes the order of foundation. Phenomenon — the self-showing-in-itself — means a distinctive way something can be encountered (Begegnisart); appearance, by contrast, means a referential relation that is itself a being within beings, such that the referrer (announcer) can satisfy its possible function only if it shows itself in itself — only if it is a phenomenon. Appearance and semblance are themselves, in different ways, founded in the phenomenon. The confusing multiplicity of "phenomena" named by the titles phenomenon, semblance, appearance, mere appearance can be disentangled only if the concept of phenomenon is understood from the start: the self-showing-in-itself. The unit's terminological precision — phenomenon names a Begegnisart, a how of encounter, not a class of entities — is what allows the concept to be formalized in the next step and then filled ontologically in section C.

The eighth unit distinguishes formal from vulgar phenomenon. If in this version of the concept it remains undetermined which being is addressed as phenomenon, and open whether the self-showing is a being at all or rather a character of the being of beings, then only the formal concept of phenomenon has been won. If what shows itself is understood as a being accessible, say, in Kant's sense through empirical intuition, the formal concept finds a legitimate application: phenomenon in this use is the vulgar concept of phenomenon — which is not the phenomenological one. Within the horizon of the Kantian problematic, what phenomenology understands by phenomenon can be illustrated (other differences aside) thus: what in the appearances, the vulgarly understood phenomenon, in each case already shows itself in advance and alongside, though unthematically, can be brought thematically to show itself, and this self-showing-in-itself-as-such ("the forms of intuition") are the phenomena of phenomenology. For space and time must evidently be able to show themselves so — must be able to become phenomena — if Kant claims a transcendentally grounded assertion when he says that space is the a priori "wherein" of an order. The Kantian illustration is exquisitely chosen: it locates the phenomenological phenomenon as the unthematic accompaniment of ordinary givenness (that which co-shows in whatever shows), and it enlists Kant's own practice as witness — a transcendental claim about space is empty unless space itself is somehow given, i.e., unless the a priori can be phenomenon. The vulgar concept is thereby honored (a legitimate application) and demoted in one stroke.

The ninth unit closes the section with the dependency of concepts: if the phenomenological concept of phenomenon is to be understood at all — however the self-showing may be more closely determined — insight into the sense of the formal concept and its legitimate application in a vulgar meaning is an indispensable presupposition. And before fixing the preliminary concept of phenomenology, the meaning of logos must be delimited, so that it becomes clear in what sense phenomenology can be a "science of" phenomena at all. The transitional sentence carries a real question, not politeness: given that phenomena in the emphatic sense are precisely what does not show itself proximally, the "-logy" cannot mean neutral registration — what logos must be, for a science of the hidden-yet-showable to make sense, is the burden of section B.

##### B. The Concept of Logos

The first unit clears the ground of translations. In Plato and Aristotle the concept of logos is ambiguous, and in a manner in which the meanings drift apart without being positively guided by a basic meaning — but this is in fact only a semblance, which maintains itself so long as interpretation fails to grasp the basic meaning adequately in its primary content. If we say the basic meaning of logos is discourse (Rede), this literal translation becomes fully valid only from a determination of what discourse itself means. The later history of the word's meanings, and above all the manifold and arbitrary interpretations of subsequent philosophy, constantly cover up the authentic meaning of discourse, which lies open enough to view: logos gets "translated" — that is, always interpreted — as reason, judgment, concept, definition, ground, relation. How is "discourse" supposed to be able to modify itself so that logos can mean all of these, and within scientific usage at that? Even if logos is understood as assertion, and assertion as "judgment," this seemingly legitimate rendering can still miss the fundamental meaning — especially if judgment is conceived in the sense of some contemporary "theory of judgment": logos does not mean, and in any case not primarily, judgment, if by that one understands a "combining" or a "taking of a stand" (acknowledging — rejecting). The unit's strategy replicates section A's: beneath a drifted multiplicity of senses, find the one founding sense from which the drift can be derived. The named targets are the neo-Kantian and Brentanian judgment-theories of the day (judgment as synthesis of representations; judgment as acknowledgment or rejection) — precisely the frameworks in which the young Heidegger was trained and from which the promise "discourse" now breaks.

The second unit gives the positive determination. Logos as discourse means rather the same as dēloun: to make manifest what one is "talking about" in the discourse. Aristotle explicated this function of discourse more sharply as apophainesthai: the logos lets something be seen (phainesthai) — namely, what the discourse is about — and lets it be seen for the speaker (the middle voice) or for those speaking with one another. Discourse "lets something be seen" apo...: from that very thing which the discourse is about. In discourse (apophansis), so far as it is genuine, what is said should be drawn from what is talked about, so that discursive communication makes manifest, in what it says, what it is talking about, and thus makes it accessible to the other. That is the structure of the logos as apophansis. Not every "discourse" possesses this mode of making-manifest in the sense of exhibiting letting-be-seen: requesting (euchē), for example, also makes manifest, but in a different way. Everything in the book's later theory of assertion (§ 33) and discourse (§ 34) is seeded here. Letting-be-seen-from: the apo- prescribes that genuine speech draws its said from the matter itself — an ethics of speech built into its structure, whose violation (talk that circulates without the matter) will define idle talk (§ 35). The middle voice matters: showing is for the involved speakers, not the production of representations. And the closing concession — prayer also discloses, otherwise — leaves room for the non-apophantic modes of discourse the tradition flattened.

The third unit adds the medium: in its concrete enactment, discoursing (letting-be-seen) has the character of speaking, vocal utterance in words. Logos is phōnē, and indeed phōnē meta phantasias — vocal utterance in which, in each case, something is sighted. The gloss inverts the traditional order of definition: voice is not sound plus attached meaning; it is utterance in which something is already seen — sighting is internal to speaking. § 34 will draw the consequence: language (Sprache) is the worldly being of discourse (Rede), not its foundation.

The fourth unit reinterprets synthesis. Only because the function of the logos as apophansis lies in the exhibiting letting-be-seen of something can the logos have the structural form of synthesis — where synthesis does not mean combining and connecting representations, a manipulating of psychic occurrences regarding whose combinations the "problem" is then supposed to arise how they, as inner, agree with the physical outside. The syn has a purely apophantic meaning: to let something be seen in its togetherness with something — to let something be seen as something. The as-structure makes its first appearance in the book, and with it the dissolution of a pseudo-problem: once synthesis is read apophantically (showing a thing as thus-and-so) rather than psychologically (gluing ideas), the correspondence-problem of inner and outer never gets started. § 33 will distinguish this apophantic "as" from the deeper hermeneutic "as" of circumspect interpretation — the founding relation runs from the latter to the former.

The fifth unit derives truth and falsity. Again: because the logos is a letting-be-seen, therefore it can be true or false — and everything depends on keeping free of a constructed concept of truth as "agreement" (Übereinstimmung), an idea by no means primary in the concept of alētheia. The being-true of the logos as alētheuein means: to take the beings that are being talked about, in legein as apophainesthai, out of their concealment — to let them be seen as unconcealed (alēthes), to uncover (entdecken). Likewise being-false, pseudesthai, amounts to deceiving in the sense of covering-up: putting something in front of something (in the manner of letting-be-seen) and thereby passing it off as something it is not. This is the germ of § 44 and of everything Heidegger will ever say about truth: alētheia read privatively as un-concealment; truth as an achievement of uncovering rather than a property of propositional agreement; falsity as a mode of covering that exploits the same letting-be-seen. The structure mirrors section A exactly — as semblance was the privative modification of the phenomenon, falsity is the privative exploitation of uncovering — one schema now legible across both components of the method's name.

The sixth unit dethrones the proposition. Because "truth" has this sense and the logos is one definite mode of letting-be-seen, the logos precisely may not be addressed as the primary "place" of truth. If one determines truth, as has today become thoroughly customary, as what "properly" pertains to judgment, and appeals moreover to Aristotle for the thesis, the appeal is without right and, above all, the Greek concept of truth is misunderstood. In the Greek sense, what is "true" — and more originally than the logos just discussed — is aisthēsis, the plain sensuous perceiving of something: insofar as an aisthēsis aims at its idia, the beings genuinely accessible only through and for it (seeing at colors), perceiving is always true — seeing always uncovers colors, hearing always uncovers tones. And "true" in the purest and most original sense — only uncovering, never able to cover up — is pure noein, the plainly regarding perceiving of the simplest determinations of being of beings as such: noein can never cover up, never be false; at most it can remain a non-perceiving, agnoein, insufficient for plain, adequate access. The Aristotelian doctrine (from De anima and Metaphysics IX 10) is deployed against its supposed heirs: where the exhibiting is simple — without the as-structure — error is impossible and only missing remains; error requires synthesis. The hierarchy (noein above logos as locus of truth) explains retroactively why Greek ontology took pure perceiving as its guide (§ 6) and prepares § 44's thesis that assertion-truth is founded, not primary.

The seventh unit states the founding relation from the side of falsity: whatever no longer has the form of enactment of pure letting-be-seen, but in exhibiting recurs in each case to something else and so lets something be seen as something, takes over, with this synthesis-structure, the possibility of covering-up. "Judgment-truth" is only the counter-case to this covering-up — a phenomenon of truth founded in multiple ways. Realism and idealism, Heidegger adds, miss the sense of the Greek concept of truth with equal thoroughness — the concept from which alone one can understand the very possibility of something like a "doctrine of ideas" as philosophical knowledge. The aside is a program in one sentence: Plato's forms become intelligible as an answer to the question of uncoveredness (what must already be sighted for beings to show as what they are), not as an inflationary ontology — and both realism and idealism, quarreling over judgment's agreement with the real, share the derivative concept of truth and so miss the ground of the doctrine they fight about.

The eighth unit derives the drifted meanings, redeeming the promise of the first. Because the function of the logos lies in the plain letting-be-seen of something, in letting beings be perceived, logos can mean reason (Vernunft). Because logos is used not only in the sense of legein but also of legomenon — the exhibited as such — and because this is nothing other than the hypokeimenon, what already lies present at the ground for every approaching address and discussion, logos qua legomenon means ground, ratio. And because, finally, logos qua legomenon can also mean what is addressed as something, what has become visible in its relation to something, in its relatedness, logos receives the meaning of relation and proportion (Beziehung und Verhältnis). The derivation is the proof that "discourse" was the right basic meaning: each traditional rendering — reason, ground, relation — is generated by a determinate slippage (act to content, content to substrate, addressed-as to relatedness), so the drift is now guided, and the semblance of guideless ambiguity from the first unit dissolves exactly as promised.

The ninth unit closes: this interpretation of "apophantic discourse" may suffice to clarify the primary function of the logos. The modesty is scoped precisely — apophantic discourse only; the fuller existential analysis of Rede, and of its non-apophantic and fallen modes, is business for §§ 34–38.

##### C. The Preliminary Concept of Phenomenology

The first unit composes the two results. Bringing concretely to mind what was set out in the interpretation of "phenomenon" and "logos," an inner relation between the two leaps to the eye. Phenomenology can be formulated in Greek: legein ta phainomena; but legein means apophainesthai; so phenomenology says: apophainesthai ta phainomena — to let what shows itself be seen from itself, just as it shows itself from itself. That is the formal sense of the research that gives itself the name phenomenology. And so nothing else comes to expression than the maxim formulated above: "to the things themselves!" The definition earns what the maxim merely asserted: the two Greek components, each independently analyzed, compose into precisely the maxim — self-showing (from A) entrusted to a letting-be-seen that draws only on the matter (from B). Method and matter are welded: the how (exhibiting) is defined entirely by the what (self-showing), which is why phenomenology can be a "standpoint" only by self-betrayal.

The second unit contrasts the title's logic with its lookalikes. "Phenomenology" differs in sense from designations like "theology": those name the objects of the science in their respective material content, whereas "phenomenology" names neither the object of its researches nor characterizes their material content — the word gives information only about the how of the exhibition and manner of treatment of what is to be treated. Science "of" phenomena means: such a grasping of its objects that everything up for discussion about them must be treated in direct exhibition (Aufweisung) and direct demonstration (Ausweisung). The fundamentally tautological expression "descriptive phenomenology" has the same sense: description here does not mean a procedure on the model of, say, botanical morphology — the title again has a prohibitive sense, the keeping-away of all non-demonstrating determination. The character of description itself, the specific sense of the logos, can be fixed only from the "thinghood" of what is to be "described," brought to scientific determinateness in the encounter-mode of phenomena. Formally, the meaning of the formal and vulgar concepts of phenomenon entitles one to call any exhibition of beings, as they show themselves in themselves, phenomenology. Two consequential claims hide in the density. Description is defined prohibitively (no smuggled constructions) rather than positively (no inventory-taking) — so what description concretely is depends on the described, leaving room for the coming identification of description with interpretation. And the closing sentence concedes that the formal concept licenses a merely vulgar phenomenology (any honest exhibition of beings) — flagging that the phenomenological concept proper still awaits its deformalization.

The third unit poses the deformalizing question. With respect to what must the formal concept of phenomenon be deformalized into the phenomenological one, and how does the latter differ from the vulgar? What is it that phenomenology is to "let be seen"? What must, in a distinctive sense, be called "phenomenon"? What is, by its essence, necessarily the theme of an explicit exhibition? Manifestly such a thing as proximally and for the most part does precisely not show itself — something that, over against what proximally and for the most part does show itself, is concealed, but which at the same time belongs essentially to what proximally and for the most part shows itself, and indeed so as to constitute its meaning and ground. The answer's paradoxical form is the section's hinge: the theme of the science of the self-showing is the proximally hidden — not another realm behind the shown, but the unthematic dimension of the shown itself (its meaning and ground), exactly as the Kant illustration in A prefigured with the forms of intuition.

The fourth unit names it. What remains concealed in an exceptional sense, or falls back into covered-up-ness, or shows itself only "in distorted form," is not this or that being, but — as the preceding considerations have shown — the being of beings. It can be covered up so extensively that it is forgotten, and the question of it and its meaning stays away. What therefore, in a distinguished sense and from its ownmost material content, demands to become phenomenon, phenomenology has taken thematically into its "grip" as its object. The three modes of hiddenness named in passing (never yet discovered; buried again; disguised) will be systematized two units below; here the identification does the work: phenomenon in the phenomenological sense = the being of beings. The whole Introduction converges in the equation — the forgotten question of § 1, the concealment-analysis of §§ 5–6, and the formal apparatus of § 7 A meet in a single determination of the method's theme.

The fifth unit draws the identity of disciplines. Phenomenology is the mode of access to, and the demonstrative manner of determination of, what is to become the theme of ontology: ontology is possible only as phenomenology. The phenomenological concept of phenomenon means, as the self-showing, the being of beings — its meaning, its modifications and derivatives. And this self-showing is nothing arbitrary, nor anything like appearing: the being of beings can least of all ever be something "behind which" something else stands, "which does not appear." The thesis "ontology only as phenomenology" cuts both ways at once: against constructive ontology (category-systems without exhibition — § 3's "blind" ontologies), and, in the last sentence, against any two-worlds reading of being — being is not a hidden entity announced by beings; the appearance-model, so carefully quarantined in A, is expressly barred from ontology. Concealment, yes; back-world, no.

The sixth unit fixes the counter-concept: "behind" the phenomena of phenomenology stands essentially nothing else — but what is to become phenomenon can be concealed. And precisely because the phenomena are proximally and for the most part not given, phenomenology is needed: covered-up-ness (Verdecktheit) is the counter-concept to "phenomenon." The little unit contains the method's whole raison d'être in two sentences: if being showed itself of itself, no phenomenology would be needed — the discipline exists because and only because its theme is proximally hidden; its work is not registration but wresting from concealment (§ 44 will make truth itself a Raub, a robbery).

The seventh unit classifies the modes of covered-up-ness. A phenomenon can be covered up in the sense that it is still altogether undiscovered — neither knowledge nor ignorance of it exists. It can be buried over (verschüttet): once discovered, it has fallen back into coveredness — which can become total, or, as is the rule, what was discovered remains visible, though only as semblance; yet as much semblance, so much "being." This covering-up as disguise (Verstellung) is the most frequent and most dangerous, for here the possibilities of deception and misdirection are especially stubborn: structures of being, available but veiled in their native ground, may claim their right within a "system," presenting themselves — on the strength of their constructive interlocking in a system — as needing no further justification, as "clear," and hence as fit to serve as the point of departure for progressive deduction. The typology maps directly onto the destruction: the buried and the disguised are the tradition's forms of transmission (§§ 1, 6 said as much historically; here it is said structurally). The proverb-like "wieviel Schein, soviel 'Sein'" repeats A's founding thesis in the register of danger — precisely because semblance feeds on genuine showing, disguised truths are the hardest to correct; and the sting of the last sentence lands on systems: systematic coherence can function as a machine for laundering ungrounded concepts into "clarity."

The eighth unit distinguishes accidental from necessary covering and turns the danger inward. Covering-up itself — whether as concealment, burying-over, or disguise — has in turn a twofold possibility: there are accidental coverings and necessary ones, the latter grounded in the way the discovered endures (in der Bestandart des Entdeckten). Every phenomenological concept and proposition, drawn originally, stands — as a communicated assertion — in the possibility of degeneration: passed along in an empty understanding, it loses its native ground and becomes a free-floating thesis. The possibility of the hardening and ungraspability of what was originally "in grip" lies in the concrete work of phenomenology itself, and the difficulty of this research consists precisely in making it critical against itself in a positive sense. This is among the most consequential paragraphs of the Introduction: concealment is not only the method's enemy but its own product — genuine discoveries necessarily degenerate in transmission, because communicated assertions can be repeated without the uncovering that grounded them (§ 35's idle talk gives the existential mechanism; § 44 the truth-theoretic one). Phenomenology therefore has no safe results, only enactments to be renewed; the destruction of § 6 turns out to be phenomenology's permanent self-relation, not a one-time clearing of the past.

The ninth unit draws the methodic consequence: the way being and its structures are encountered in the mode of phenomenon must first be wrested from the objects of phenomenology. Hence the point of departure of the analysis, the access to the phenomenon, and the passage through the dominant coverings demand their own methodical securing. In the idea of the "originary" and "intuitive" grasping and explication of phenomena lies the very opposite of the naivety of an accidental, "immediate," and unreflective "beholding." The last sentence adjusts an account with the school: Husserlian watchwords (originary givenness, intuition) are retained but re-glossed as achievements of a secured passage through concealment — against the popular picture, and perhaps the temptation within phenomenology itself, of intuition as effortless inner looking. Seeing, here, is the hard-won end of a way, not its beginning.

The tenth unit fixes two adjectives: on the basis of the delimited preliminary concept, "phenomenal" names what is given and explicable in the encounter-mode of the phenomenon — hence talk of phenomenal structures; "phenomenological" names everything belonging to the manner of exhibition and explication, and what constitutes the conceptuality demanded in this research. Housekeeping, but load-bearing: the book will constantly distinguish the phenomenal findings (what shows) from the phenomenological apparatus (how it is brought to show), and the distinction disciplines the reader against mistaking terminology for the matters.

The eleventh unit restores the vulgar concept to service. Because phenomenon in the phenomenological understanding is always only what constitutes being, while being is in each case the being of beings, the aim of laying being free requires first that the beings themselves be brought forward rightly — they too must show themselves in the mode of access genuinely belonging to them. Thus the vulgar concept of phenomenon becomes phenomenologically relevant: the prior task of a "phenomenological" securing of the exemplary being, as point of departure for the analytic proper, is always already predelineated from that analytic's goal. The unit welds § 7 back to § 5: the demand there — that Dasein show itself from itself, in its average everydayness — now stands revealed as the vulgar-phenomenal pre-task assigned by the phenomenological goal; the ontological difference governs the method's two tiers (get the being to show, in order to let its being show).

The twelfth unit names the method's concretion: hermeneutics. Taken in its material content, phenomenology is the science of the being of beings — ontology; and the elucidation of ontology's tasks gave rise to the necessity of a fundamental ontology, whose theme is the ontically-ontologically distinctive being, Dasein, such that it brings itself before the cardinal problem, the question of the meaning of being in general. From the investigation itself it will emerge: the methodical sense of phenomenological description is interpretation (Auslegung). The logos of the phenomenology of Dasein has the character of hermēneuein, through which the authentic meaning of being, and the basic structures of Dasein's own being, are made known (kundgegeben) to the understanding of being that belongs to Dasein itself. Phenomenology of Dasein is hermeneutics in the original signification of the word, according to which it designates the business of interpretation. And insofar as, through the uncovering of the meaning of being and the basic structures of Dasein in general, the horizon is exhibited for every further ontological investigation of non-Dasein-like beings, this hermeneutics becomes at the same time "hermeneutics" in the sense of the working-out of the conditions of the possibility of every ontological investigation. And insofar, finally, as Dasein has the ontological priority before all beings — as the being in the possibility of existence — hermeneutics, as interpretation of Dasein's being, receives a specific third sense, the philosophically primary one: an analytic of the existentiality of existence. In this hermeneutics, insofar as it works out Dasein's historicity ontologically as the ontic condition of the possibility of historiography, is rooted what can only derivatively be called "hermeneutics": the methodology of the historical humanities. The paragraph performs the decisive transformation of phenomenology, and its logic should be laid bare. Description of Dasein must be interpretation because its theme is an understanding: what shows itself is always already self-interpreting, so the exhibiting logos addresses an understanding of being and can only proceed as its explication — announcement (kundgeben) to Dasein of what Dasein already understands. The three (plus one) senses are ordered by descent: existential analytic (primary), transcendental hermeneutics (conditions of all ontology), interpretation of Dasein as such — and only at the derivative end Dilthey's and Schleiermacher's discipline, the methodology of the humanities, now re-rooted in an ontology of the interpreting being. Phenomenology, entrusted to Heidegger's hands, has become hermeneutic through and through — the quiet revolution of the whole section.

The thirteenth unit re-grounds the old transcendens. Being, as the basic theme of philosophy, is no genus of a being, and yet it concerns every being; its "universality" is to be sought higher: being and the structure of being lie beyond every being and every possible determination of a being that itself is. Being is the transcendens pure and simple. And the transcendence of Dasein's being is a distinctive one, since in it lies the possibility and necessity of the most radical individuation. Every disclosure of being as the transcendens is transcendental knowledge; phenomenological truth (disclosedness of being) is veritas transcendentalis. The unit retrieves § 1's medieval material and re-mints it: being's trans-generic "universality," there a scholastic doctrine, is now grounded in the ontological difference — being transcends beings, not as a higher being, but as what is never a being. The startling middle sentence couples this transcendence to individuation: because Dasein's being is delivered to it as in each case its own (§ 4), disclosure of being singularizes — the thread that runs to anxiety, death, and conscience, where being-disclosure and individuation coincide. And the closing equation re-appropriates Kant and the scholastics at a stroke: transcendental truth is not the truth of a subject's conditions but disclosedness of being.

The fourteenth unit gives the discipline its final formula: ontology and phenomenology are not two different disciplines belonging, alongside others, to philosophy — the two titles characterize philosophy itself according to object and manner of treatment. Philosophy is universal phenomenological ontology, taking its departure from the hermeneutics of Dasein, which, as analytic of existence, has fastened the end of the guiding thread of all philosophical questioning at the point from which it arises and to which it strikes back (zurückschlägt). The definition compresses the whole Introduction into one sentence, and its final image is exact: the guideline of philosophy is tied at Dasein twice — questioning springs from Dasein's pre-ontological understanding (§ 4's radicalization-thesis) and recoils upon it (the answer transforms the being that asks; ontology is an existentiell possibility, § 4 again). Philosophy is that rare inquiry whose results strike back at its own origin.

The fifteenth unit pays the debt and declares independence in a single gesture. The following investigations, Heidegger writes, became possible only on the ground that E. Husserl laid, with whose Logical Investigations phenomenology achieved its breakthrough; and the elucidations of the preliminary concept show that what is essential to phenomenology does not lie in being actual as a philosophical "direction." Higher than actuality stands possibility: the understanding of phenomenology lies solely in seizing it as possibility. The attached note — folded in here because it settles the sense of the tribute — thanks Husserl personally: whatever steps forward the investigation takes in disclosing the "things themselves," the author owes above all to Husserl, who during the author's Freiburg apprenticeship acquainted him with the most diverse areas of phenomenological research through incisive personal guidance and the freest access to unpublished investigations. Every clause is calibrated. The Logical Investigations — not the Ideas — are named as the breakthrough: Heidegger's phenomenology descends from the categorial intuition and truth-analysis of the sixth Investigation, not from transcendental idealism. The possibility/actuality maxim (itself an application of the book's coming thesis that possibility stands higher than actuality, § 7 here anticipating § 31) converts homage into license: fidelity to phenomenology as possibility can demand infidelity to phenomenology as actual school — the sentence is the charter of the whole hermeneutic transformation just performed, and Husserl read it, in due course, exactly so.

The sixteenth unit begs indulgence for the prose to come — and grounds the plea ontologically. With regard to the awkwardness and "inelegance" of expression in the following analyses: it is one thing to report narratively about beings, another to grasp beings in their being. For the latter task not only are the words mostly lacking, but above all the "grammar." If a reference to earlier, incomparably higher researches in the analysis of being is permitted, compare the ontological sections of Plato's Parmenides, or the fourth chapter of Book VII of Aristotle's Metaphysics, with a narrative section from Thucydides, and one will see the unheard-of character of the formulations Greek philosophers demanded of their language. And where the powers are essentially lesser, and the region of being to be disclosed ontologically far more difficult than that pregiven to the Greeks, the circumstantiality of concept-formation and the harshness of expression will increase. The apology is an argument: grammar itself is fitted to beings — to narrative about the present-at-hand — so an ontology of Dasein must do violence to it (the scare-quoted "is" of § 2 already showed the strain). The comparison with Thucydides measures philosophical language by its distance from narration; and the closing sentence, with its blunt self-assessment ("powers essentially lesser") and its claim that Dasein is ontologically harder terrain than the Greeks' nature, is both modesty and warning — the book's notorious idiom is presented as the price of the matter, not a mannerism.

#### § 8. The Outline of the Treatise

The opening unit binds universality to individuation and system to history. The question of the meaning of being is the most universal and emptiest of questions; but in it lies at the same time the possibility of its own sharpest individualization upon the respective Dasein. Winning the basic concept "being," and predelineating the ontological conceptuality it demands together with that conceptuality's necessary variations, requires a concrete guiding thread. The universality of the concept of being is not contradicted by the "speciality" of the investigation — advancing to being by way of a special interpretation of a definite being, Dasein, in which the horizon for the understanding and possible interpretation of being is to be won. But this being is in itself "historical," so that its ownmost ontological illumination necessarily becomes a "historical" interpretation. The paragraph is the Introduction's own summary, executed as a chain of entailments: the emptiest question individuates most sharply (the § 7 C thesis on transcendence and individuation, applied); universality demands a concrete guide (§§ 2–4); the guide is historical (§ 6) — hence, in three steps, the two-Part plan that follows.

The second unit states the fork: the working-out of the question of being bifurcates into two tasks, to which corresponds the division of the treatise into two Parts. Part One: the interpretation of Dasein with respect to temporality, and the explication of time as the transcendental horizon of the question of being. Part Two: basic features of a phenomenological destruction of the history of ontology, following the guiding thread of the problematic of Temporality. The two Parts codify the "double task" of the chapter's title — the analytic (§ 5) and the destruction (§ 6) — and the wording preserves the strict terminological regime of § 5: Part One runs from Zeitlichkeit to time as transcendental horizon; Part Two is guided by Temporalität. The word "transcendental" in the title of Part One fixes how the book understands itself in 1927: the question of being is pursued as a question about the horizon of understanding — the self-conception the later work will shed.

The third unit gives Part One's divisions: the preparatory fundamental analysis of Dasein; Dasein and temporality; time and being. The three titles map the spiral announced at § 5: the preparatory analytic (published as Division One), its repetition from temporality (Division Two), and the reversal — "Time and Being" — in which the analysis was to turn from Dasein's temporality to the Temporality of being itself and thus to the answer. That third division is the book's famous absence: withheld in 1927 (the accompanying lecture course, GA 24, attempts its content), it was never published in this form, and the Preliminary Remark of 1953 struck the "First Half" that promised it. The reader of the extant book is thereby holding two-thirds of half of the announced work.

The fourth unit gives Part Two's divisions, in the announced reverse chronology: Kant's doctrine of the schematism and of time, as preliminary stage of a problematic of Temporality; the ontological foundation of Descartes' cogito sum and the taking-over of medieval ontology into the problematic of the res cogitans; Aristotle's treatise on time as the discrimen of the phenomenal basis and the limits of ancient ontology. These are the three "stations" of § 6, now in tabular form, and none appeared as such: the Kant division became the 1929 Kant book, the Descartes confrontation was partially absorbed into §§ 19–21 and the lecture courses, and the Aristotle interpretation survives in GA 24 § 19. With this table the Introduction closes: question constructed (Chapter One), method and plan secured (Chapter Two) — the analytic itself can begin.

## Part One: The Interpretation of Dasein with Respect to Temporality and the Explication of Time as the Transcendental Horizon of the Question of Being

### Division One: The Preparatory Fundamental Analysis of Dasein

The division opens with a single orienting paragraph. What is primarily interrogated in the question of the meaning of being is the being with the character of Dasein; and the preparatory existential analytic, in keeping with its peculiar nature, itself needs a predelineating exposition and a demarcation against investigations that seem to run parallel to it (Chapter One). Holding fast to the fixed approach, a fundamental structure is to be laid free in Dasein: In-der-Welt-sein, being-in-the-world (Chapter Two). This "a priori" of the interpretation of Dasein is no pieced-together determinateness but an originally and constantly whole structure, which nonetheless grants different perspectives on its constitutive moments; with the antecedent whole constantly kept in view, these moments are to be set off phenomenally — and so the objects of analysis become: the world in its worldhood (Chapter Three), being-in-the-world as being-with and being-a-self (Chapter Four), being-in as such (Chapter Five). On the basis of the analysis of this fundamental structure, a provisional indication of the being of Dasein becomes possible: its existential meaning is care, Sorge (Chapter Six). The paragraph is a map, but one methodological commitment in it outranks the itinerary: the whole precedes the moments. Being-in-the-world is announced as originally and constantly whole, so the coming chapters do not assemble Dasein from parts (world + who + in-being) but articulate perspectives on one unbroken structure — the anti-Cartesian architecture is fixed before a single analysis has run, and the hyphenated coinage itself, introduced here without ceremony, enacts it.

#### Chapter One: The Exposition of the Task of a Preparatory Analysis of Dasein

##### § 9. The Theme of the Analytic of Dasein

The opening unit gathers the Introduction's determinations into a working characterization. The being whose analysis is the task is in each case we ourselves; the being of this being is in each case mine (je meines). In its being, this being comports itself toward its being; as a being of this being, it is delivered over (überantwortet) to its own being. Being is that which, for this being, is in each case itself at stake. From this characterization a twofold follows — announced here and unfolded in the next units. The new word is überantwortet: delivered over, consigned — mineness is not proud self-possession but a being handed over to the being it has to be, a note of weight and burden that thrownness (§ 29) and facticity will make explicit. Everything in the section derives from this compressed formula of care-before-care.

The first consequence: the "essence" of this being lies in its to-be (Zu-sein). Its what-being (essentia), so far as one can speak of it at all, must be conceived from its being (existentia). And precisely this is the ontological task: to show that when we choose the designation Existenz for the being of this being, the title does not and cannot have the ontological signification of the traditional term existentia — for existentia says, ontologically, as much as being-present-at-hand (Vorhandensein), a mode of being that essentially does not pertain to the being with the character of Dasein. Confusion is avoided by always rendering existentia with the interpretive expression Vorhandenheit, presence-at-hand, and assigning Existenz as a determination of being solely to Dasein. The terminological legislation seals what § 4 began: the scholastic pair essentia/existentia is not applied to Dasein but suspended for it — Dasein's "what" is a "to-be," and the tradition's word for existence names precisely the wrong mode of being (the occurring of things). Vorhandenheit here receives its official coinage as the interpretive translation of existentia — the whole destruction of § 6 (being as producedness, presence) stands compressed inside this rendering.

The third unit states the formula and its corollary. The "essence" of Dasein lies in its existence. The characters exhibitable in this being are therefore not present-at-hand "properties" of a present-at-hand being that "looks" thus and so, but in each case possible ways for it to be, and only that: all so-being of this being is primarily being. Hence the title "Dasein," with which we designate this being, expresses not its what — as table, house, tree do — but being. The quotation marks around "essence" do the philosophical work: the sentence is not an essentialist thesis with existence as the essence (the misreading Sartre would canonize) but the suspension of the essence-question in favor of the to-be. The corollary is methodologically decisive for every page that follows: no analysis of Dasein may take the form "it has the property F" — every existential to come (understanding, disposedness, falling) names a way to be, not an attribute; and the book's title-word for the entity is defended as a pure being-expression.

The fourth unit gives the second consequence: the being at stake for this being in its being is in each case mine. Dasein is therefore never to be grasped ontologically as a case and exemplar of a genus of beings, as of something present-at-hand. To such present-at-hand beings their being is "a matter of indifference" — more precisely, they "are" in such a way that their being can be neither indifferent nor non-indifferent to them. In accordance with the character of Jemeinigkeit, mineness, the addressing of Dasein must always say the personal pronoun with it: "I am," "you are."
