Mineness blocks the logic of instantiation: Dasein is not a token of a type, because the being of each is at issue for that one — a first-person structure that grammar registers in the obligatory pronoun. The precision about stones and tables is characteristic: indifference to being is not their attitude but their lack of the dimension in which indifference or concern could occur; whereas Dasein's seeming indifference to its being (everydayness, fleeing) is a mode of the at-stake-ness, never its absence.

The fifth unit derives the possibility of authenticity. And Dasein is mine, in turn, in each case in this or that way to be: it has always somehow already decided in what way Dasein is in each case mine. The being for which, in its being, that being itself is at stake comports itself toward its being as toward its ownmost possibility. Dasein is in each case its possibility, and does not merely "have" it, as a property, the way something present-at-hand does. And because Dasein is essentially in each case its possibility, this being can, in its being, "choose" itself, win itself; it can lose itself, or never and only "seemingly" win itself. It can have lost itself, and can have not yet won itself, only insofar as it is, according to its essence, possible authentic — that is, its own (sich zueigen). The two modes of being, Eigentlichkeit and Uneigentlichkeit — authenticity and inauthenticity, expressions chosen terminologically in the strict sense of the word — are grounded in the fact that Dasein as such is determined by mineness. But inauthenticity does not signify a "lesser" being or a "lower" degree of being: it can rather determine Dasein in its fullest concretion, in its busyness, its excitement, its interestedness, its capacity for enjoyment. The derivation is strict and worth reconstructing: because the being at issue is mine, it can be enacted as mine or disowned — authenticity and inauthenticity are possibilities opened by mineness, not values imported into it. The etymological ground is flagged by Heidegger himself: eigentlich from eigen, own — being one's own versus being disowned. And the last two sentences erect the guard the reception has most needed: inauthenticity is not deficiency, diminution, or moral failing — it is a full, rich, busy way to be; the pair is ontological-structural, and the analyses of das Man and falling must be read under this protection.

The sixth unit converts the two characters into a methodological problem. The two sketched characters — the priority of "existentia" over essentia, and mineness — already indicate that an analytic of this being faces a phenomenal region of its own kind (eigenartig). This being never has the mode of being of what is merely present-at-hand within the world; hence it is also not to be given as theme in the manner of coming-upon something present-at-hand. Its right pre-givenness (Vorgabe) is so far from self-evident that determining it constitutes an essential part of the ontological analytic of this being: on the secure enactment of the right pre-givenness stands and falls the possibility of bringing the being of this being to understanding at all. However provisional the analysis, it always already demands the securing of the right approach. The unit re-issues § 5's access-problem now armed with § 9's results: because Dasein is possibility and mineness, any procedure that begins by "finding" it as an occurrent object has already substituted another kind of being for it — method is not preliminary to the analytic but part of its subject matter.

The seventh unit fixes the point of departure. Dasein determines itself as a being in each case from a possibility that it is and somehow understands in its being — that is the formal sense of Dasein's existence-constitution. For the ontological interpretation this contains the directive to develop the problematic of its being out of the existentiality of its existence. But this cannot mean constructing Dasein from a concrete possible idea of existence: at the outset of the analysis Dasein is precisely not to be interpreted in the differentiatedness of some determinate existing, but uncovered in its undifferentiated proximally-and-mostly. This indifference of Dasein's everydayness is not nothing, but a positive phenomenal character of this being: out of this mode of being and back into it is all existing as it is. We call this everyday indifference of Dasein averageness (Durchschnittlichkeit). The unit performs a double refusal that defines the book's stance. No existentiell ideal may be smuggled in as the analytic's guide (not the sage, not the saint, not the hero — the analytic starts below the authentic/inauthentic differential, in the modally indifferent everyday); and this indifference is itself dignified as a positive phenomenon, the medium out of which and back into which all existing moves. Methodological honesty about a limit is quietly included: § 63 will concede that even this beginning harbors an existentiell presupposition.

The eighth unit explains why the obvious was never seen, and lets Augustine say it. Because average everydayness constitutes the ontic proximally of this being, it was and is passed over again and again in the explication of Dasein: the ontically nearest and most familiar is the ontologically farthest, unrecognized, and in its ontological significance constantly overlooked. When Augustine asks — what is nearer to me than myself? — and must answer: assuredly I labor here and labor within myself; I have become to myself a land of trouble and inordinate sweat, this holds not only of the ontic and pre-ontological opacity of Dasein but in a heightened measure of the ontological task: not only not to miss this being in its phenomenally nearest mode of being, but to make it accessible in positive characterization. The Confessions citation (X, 16) is more than ornament: it certifies from within the tradition that self-nearness and self-opacity coincide — § 5's paradox given its classic voice — and it aligns the analytic of everydayness with the confessional tradition's discovery that the self is terra difficultatis, a discovery Heidegger had worked through in his 1921 Augustine lectures.

The ninth unit protects everydayness from a first misreading: average everydayness may not be taken as a mere "aspect." In it too, and even in the mode of inauthenticity, lies a priori the structure of existentiality; in it too Dasein's being is at stake for Dasein in a definite way — a way toward which it comports itself in the mode of average everydayness, be it only in the mode of fleeing before it and forgetting of it. The unit's closing clause opens a motif of vast consequence: flight and forgetting are modes of comportment toward one's being — everydayness relates to what it evades, so evasion itself is testimony. Anxiety (§ 40) will be read through exactly this structure: what everydayness flees discloses what everydayness is.

The tenth unit protects everydayness from a second misreading: the explication of Dasein in its average everydayness does not yield merely average structures in the sense of a blurred indeterminacy. What ontically is in the manner of averageness can ontologically very well be grasped in pregnant structures which are not structurally distinct from the ontological determinations of, say, an authentic being of Dasein. The distinction is between the mode analyzed and the precision of the analysis — average being does not entail approximate ontology. And the last clause quietly states the deep formal thesis of the book's two-division architecture: authentic and inauthentic existence are modifications of the same structures (§ 45 will say authenticity is an existentiell modification of das Man, not another set of faculties), which is why structures won from everydayness remain valid when the analysis turns to authenticity.

The eleventh unit coins the book's grammatical regime. All explicata arising from the analytic of Dasein are won with a view to its existence-structure; because they determine themselves from existentiality, we call the being-characters of Dasein existentials (Existenzialien), sharply to be separated from the determinations of being of non-Dasein-like beings, which we call categories — the expression taken up and held fast in its primary ontological signification. Ancient ontology took as the exemplary soil of its interpretation of being the beings encountered within the world; noein, or logos, counted as the mode of access; therein beings are encountered — but the being of these beings must become graspable in a distinctive legein (letting-be-seen), so that this being becomes understandable in advance as what it is and already is in every being. This always antecedent addressing of being in the discussing (logos) of beings is katēgoreisthai — which means at first: to accuse publicly, to say something to someone's face before all; used ontologically the term says: to tell beings to their face, as it were, what they already are as beings — to let them be seen in their being for everyone. What is sighted and visible in such seeing are the katēgoriai: they comprise the a priori determinations of the beings addressable and discussable in the logos in various ways. Existentials and categories are the two basic possibilities of characters of being; the beings corresponding to them demand in each case a different manner of primary interrogation: a being is a who (existence) or a what (presence-at-hand in the widest sense). About the connection of the two modes of characters of being one can treat only from the clarified horizon of the question of being. The unit does three things at once. It legislates the vocabulary that disciplines the whole book (every structure to come is an existential, never a category misapplied). It grounds the legislation in a destructive etymology: "category" carries its origin — the forensic accusing of beings in the logos — so the tradition's table of categories is regionally fitted to what shows itself to assertion, i.e., to the present-at-hand, and its transfer to Dasein (the omission indicted at § 6) is exposed as a category mistake in the strictest possible sense. And it closes with the who/what disjunction as the operational test — with the unity of the two kinds of being-character deferred, once more, to the unwritten answer.

The closing unit widens the stakes: as the Introduction already intimated, the existential analytic co-advances a task whose urgency is hardly less than that of the question of being itself — laying free the a priori that must be visible if the question "what man is" is to be philosophically discussable at all. The existential analytic lies before every psychology, anthropology, and a fortiori biology; in demarcation against these possible investigations of Dasein the theme of the analytic can receive a still sharper delimitation, and its necessity a still more penetrating proof. The unit is the hinge to § 10, and its ordering word is "before" (vor): the priority claimed is not of rank but of foundation — the positive sciences of man presuppose the a priori the analytic uncovers. That the question "what is man?" is here expressly subordinated to the question of being also marks the exact distance from philosophical anthropology, soon to be measured discipline by discipline.

##### § 10. The Demarcation of the Analytic of Dasein against Anthropology, Psychology, and Biology

The opening unit justifies a prohibitive interlude. After a first positive predelineation of a theme, its prohibitive characterization remains of consequence, although discussions of what is not to happen easily become unfruitful. What is to be shown is that the previous questionings and investigations aimed at Dasein — their material fruitfulness unimpaired — miss the authentic, philosophical problem, and hence, so long as they persist in this missing, may not claim to be able to accomplish what they at bottom strive for. The demarcations relate solely to the fundamentally ontological question; "science-theoretically" they are necessarily insufficient, if only because the science-structure of the named disciplines — not the "scientificity" of those working at their advancement — is today thoroughly questionable and needs new impulses that must spring from the ontological problematic. The courtesies are precise, not decorative: the disciplines' material yield and their practitioners' rigor are exempted; what is indicted is a foundation — and the indictment claims to serve the disciplines' own deepest striving, in line with § 3's crisis-doctrine (their basic concepts need what only ontology gives).

The second unit gives the historical shorthand. The intent of the existential analytic can be clarified by Descartes, to whom one ascribes the discovery of the cogito sum as the point of departure of modern philosophical questioning: he investigated the cogitare of the ego — within certain limits — while leaving the sum wholly undiscussed, although it is posited just as originally as the cogito. The analytic poses the ontological question of the being of the sum; only when this is determined does the mode of being of the cogitationes become graspable. § 6's formula returns as a program: the analytic of Dasein is, in one sentence, the making-good of Descartes' omission — determine the "am," and only then can acts of consciousness be ontologically placed. The order of determination is the polemical point: modern philosophy built a doctrine of the cogitare on an unexamined sum.

The third unit immediately retracts the shorthand's convenience. This historical exemplification is at the same time misleading: one of the analytic's first tasks will be to demonstrate that positing a proximally given I and subject misses the phenomenal content of Dasein from the ground up. Every idea of "subject" — unless purified by a prior ontological basic determination — still ontologically posits the subiectum (hypokeimenon) along with it, however vigorously one may protest ontically against the "soul-substance" or the "reification of consciousness." Thinghood itself first needs a demonstration of its ontological provenance, so that one could even ask what is positively to be understood by the non-reified being of the subject, the soul, consciousness, spirit, the person. All these titles name determinate, workable phenomenal domains, but their use always goes together with a remarkable needlessness of asking after the being of the beings so designated — hence it is no willfulness of terminology that we avoid these titles, as also the expressions "life" and "man," to designate the being that we ourselves are. The argument is subtler than its slogan-reception: ontic protest against reification (Heidegger's contemporaries loudly refused soul-substances) is unavailing so long as the ontological schema of the hypokeimenon — an underlying persisting bearer — silently structures every "subject"-concept; one cannot even say what non-reified being would be until thinghood itself has been genealogically accounted for (§§ 19–21 on Descartes' res, § 43 on reality, redeem this). The terminological asceticism of the whole book — never "man," "consciousness," "subject," "life" for the entity that we are — is here grounded once and for all: the avoided words carry the omitted question.

The fourth unit turns to Lebensphilosophie with a barbed compliment: in the rightly understood tendency of every serious scientific "philosophy of life" — the word says about as much as "the botany of plants" — there lies, unexpressed, the tendency toward an understanding of the being of Dasein. What remains striking, and is its fundamental lack, is that "life" itself as a mode of being does not become an ontological problem. The mocking gloss (a philosophy "of life" is as pleonastic as a botany "of plants") carries the diagnosis: the movement's very name betrays that it circles the right phenomenon without ever posing the question of what mode of being "living" names — vitality is presupposed as self-evident precisely where it should be the problem.

The fifth unit pays and measures the great debts. Dilthey's researches are kept in suspense by the constant question after "life"; the "experiences" (Erlebnisse) of this life he seeks to understand in their structural and developmental connection out of the whole of this life itself. What is philosophically relevant in his "human-scientific psychology" is not that it no longer orients itself to psychic elements and atoms and no longer pieces the soul's life together, aiming instead at the "whole of life" and its "shapes" — but that in all this he was above all on the way toward the question of "life." Here too, though, the limits of his problematic show most strongly, and of the conceptuality in which it had to find words; and these limits are shared, with Dilthey and Bergson, by all the directions of "personalism" they determined and all tendencies toward a philosophical anthropology. Even the fundamentally more radical and more transparent phenomenological interpretation of personhood does not reach the dimension of the question of the being of Dasein: for all the differences of questioning, execution, and worldview-orientation, Husserl's and Scheler's interpretations of personhood agree in the negative — they no longer pose the question of "person-being" itself. Scheler's is chosen as the example, not only because it is accessible in print, but because Scheler expressly emphasizes person-being as such and seeks to determine it by demarcating the specific being of acts against everything "psychic": the person, for Scheler, must never be thought as a thing or substance — the person "is rather the immediately co-experienced unity of living-through, not a thing merely thought behind and outside what is immediately experienced"; the person is no thingly substantial being, and its being cannot consist in being a subject of rational acts of a certain lawfulness. The long footnote on Husserl, folded in because it settles what the text's discretion conceals: Husserl's investigations of personhood, Heidegger reports, are as yet unpublished; the basic orientation shows already in "Philosophy as Rigorous Science" (1910), and the investigation is far advanced in the second part of the Ideas — whose first part presents pure consciousness as the soil for the constitution of any reality, while the second brings the executed constitution-analyses of material nature, animal nature, and the spiritual world (the personalistic versus the naturalistic attitude); Husserl there begins by saying that Dilthey grasped the goal-setting problems but did not press through to decisive formulations and methodically correct solutions; and since that first elaboration Husserl has pursued the problems more penetratingly and communicated essential pieces in his Freiburg lectures. The note is a small historical bombshell: Heidegger, who knew the Ideen II manuscripts intimately, certifies that the master's most advanced work — precisely the personalistic constitution-analyses closest to the analytic of Dasein — remained unpublished, and encloses Husserl's own verdict on Dilthey as if to mark the relay of a single question. The paragraph's architecture is the same generous demotion three times over: Dilthey honored for the question, limited by the concepts; Bergson and personalism inheriting the limit; Husserl and Scheler, the most radical, agreeing "in the negative" — the being of the person is what none of them any longer asks.

The sixth unit presses Scheler to the point and widens the deficit to the whole man. The person is no thing, no substance, no object — therewith the same is emphasized that Husserl intimates when he demands for the unity of the person an essentially different constitution than for natural things. What Scheler says of the person he formulates also for acts: an act is never also an object, for it belongs to the essence of the being of acts to be experienced only in their very enactment and given in reflection; acts are something non-psychic, and to the essence of the person belongs that it exists only in the enactment of intentional acts — every psychic objectification, every grasping of acts as something psychic, is identical with depersonalization. The person is in any case given as the enactor of intentional acts bound by the unity of a meaning; psychic being has nothing to do with person-being. Acts are enacted; the person is act-enactor. But — and here the analytic's question lands — what is the ontological sense of "enacting"? How is the mode of being of the person to be determined positively and ontologically? And the critical question cannot stop there: at issue is the being of the whole man, whom one is accustomed to grasp as a bodily-psychic-spiritual unity. Body, soul, spirit may in turn name phenomenal domains thematically detachable for determinate investigations, and within certain limits their ontological indeterminacy may not weigh heavily; but in the question of the being of man, this being cannot be summatively computed from the modes of being — themselves still awaiting determination — of body, soul, and spirit; and even such a procedure would have to presuppose an idea of the being of the whole. What obstructs or misleads the fundamental question is the pervasive orientation to ancient-Christian anthropology, whose insufficient ontological foundations personalism and philosophy of life alike overlook. The traditional anthropology carries in itself two elements — announced here, itemized in the next two units. The critique of Scheler is surgical: everything Scheler says is negative (not thing, not substance, not object, not psychic) plus one positive word — Vollzug, enactment — which is left ontologically blank; the analytic's whole claim is compressed in the question "what is the being-sense of enacting?", to which existence, care, and temporality are the staged answers. And the summation-argument against the body-soul-spirit composite is transcendental in form: any adding of strata presupposes the unity it purports to build — being-in-the-world will be offered as that presupposed whole.

The seventh unit itemizes the first inherited element: the definition of man as zōon logon echon, in the interpretation animal rationale, rational living being. The mode of being of the zōon is here understood in the sense of being-present-at-hand and occurring; the logos is a higher endowment, whose mode of being remains as dark as that of the being thus composed. In two sentences the classical definition is convicted on the § 9 criterion: it is category-work applied to a who — an occurrent animal plus an occurrent faculty, with the being of the composite (and of the "plus") never asked. § 6's rendering ("the living being that can talk") had already loosened the definition philologically; here its ontological cost is booked.

The eighth unit itemizes the second: the other guiding thread is theological — "and God said: let us make man in our image and likeness" (Genesis 1:26). From here, taking up the ancient definition as well, Christian-theological anthropology wins an interpretation of the being we call man; but just as the being of God is interpreted ontologically with the means of ancient ontology, so — all the more — is the being of the ens finitum. In the course of modernity the Christian definition was de-theologized; but the idea of "transcendence" — that man is something that reaches out beyond itself — has its roots in Christian dogmatics, of which one will hardly want to say that it ever made the being of man an ontological problem. This transcendence-idea, according to which man is more than a creature of understanding, has worked itself out in various modifications — its provenance illustrated by Calvin (man's first estate excelled in gifts by which he might transcend even unto God and eternal felicity) and Zwingli (that man looks up to God and his word shows clearly that in his very nature he is born somewhat closer to God, somewhat more after his likeness, has somewhat of an approach to him — all of which flows from his being created in God's image). The analysis is genealogical, not anti-theological: the imago Dei anthropology is faulted not for its faith but for interpreting both God and creature with the borrowed means of ancient ontology (creation as production, § 6). The pointed claim is about secularization: modern doctrines of man's self-transcendence — reaching beyond himself toward the ideal, the infinite, value — are de-theologized dogmatics, inheriting from the imago-tradition both the exalting gesture and the never-asked question of the being of the one who so reaches.

The ninth unit draws the two threads together. The origins relevant for traditional anthropology — the Greek definition and the theological guiding thread — indicate that over the essence-determination of the being "man," the question of its being remains forgotten; this being is rather conceived as "self-evident" in the sense of the being-present-at-hand of the other created things. In modern anthropology the two threads intertwine with the methodical point of departure from the res cogitans, consciousness, the nexus of lived experience; but insofar as the cogitationes too remain ontologically undetermined — or are again taken, unexpressedly and "self-evidently," as something "given" whose "being" is subject to no question — the anthropological problematic remains undetermined in its decisive ontological foundations. The verdict has the Introduction's exact form: essence-determination flourishing over a forgotten being-question (§ 1's oblivion, regionalized to man). And the extension to modernity closes the circle of § 10's opening: even where the given is no longer the created thing but the datum of consciousness, "givenness" functions as the new self-evidence — the Cartesian turn changed the inventory, not the omission.

The tenth unit extends the diagnosis to psychology and biology and fixes the order of founding. The same holds no less of "psychology," whose anthropological tendencies are today unmistakable; nor can the missing ontological foundation be replaced by building anthropology and psychology into a general biology. In the order of possible grasping and interpretation, biology as "science of life" is founded in the ontology of Dasein — though not exclusively in it. Life is a mode of being of its own, but essentially accessible only in Dasein: the ontology of life is accomplished on the path of a privative interpretation — it determines what must be, in order that there can be such a thing as mere-living (Nur-noch-leben). Life is neither pure presence-at-hand nor, again, Dasein; and Dasein, for its part, is never to be ontologically determined by positing it as life — (ontologically undetermined) — and then as something more besides. Two theses of great reach are stated with deceptive brevity. Against the biologism of the day, the order of founding is inverted: biology does not ground anthropology; the ontology of Dasein grounds the science of life. And the method for an ontology of life is fixed as privative: "mere life" is reached by subtraction from being-in-the-world, not Dasein by addition to life — a rejection, in one stroke, of every stratified anthropology (life plus reason, life plus spirit; Scheler's late scheme is the unnamed target) and the program Heidegger executes in the 1929/30 course on the animal's world-poverty.

The closing unit sets the epistemological seal. Pointing out that anthropology, psychology, and biology lack an unambiguous, ontologically sufficiently grounded answer to the question of the mode of being of this being that we ourselves are passes no judgment on the positive work of these disciplines. But it must be brought to awareness again and again that these ontological foundations can never be disclosed hypothetically, after the fact, from empirical material; rather they are always already "there" even when empirical material is merely being collected. That positive research does not see these foundations and holds them self-evident is no proof that they do not lie at the ground — and are problematic in a more radical sense than any thesis of positive science can ever be. The folded-in footnote guards the method's name: disclosure of the a priori is not "aprioristic" construction; through Husserl we have learned again to understand the sense of all genuine philosophical "empiricism" and to handle the tools it requires; apriorism is the method of every scientific philosophy that understands itself, and precisely because it has nothing to do with construction, a priori research demands the right preparation of the phenomenal soil — the nearest horizon to be prepared for the analytic of Dasein lying in its average everydayness. Text and note together fix the two-front position: against empiricism, the a priori cannot be induced from data it always already structures; against rationalism, the a priori is not constructed but seen — on a soil that must be phenomenally prepared. That the paradigmatic "empiricism" of philosophy should be Husserl's a priori intuition is the deliberate paradox on which the whole methodology stands.

##### § 11. The Existential Analytic and the Interpretation of Primitive Dasein. The Difficulties of Securing a "Natural Concept of the World"

The first unit dissolves an equation the title of the section invites. The interpretation of Dasein in its everydayness is not identical with the description of a primitive stage of Dasein, knowledge of which anthropology can supply empirically: everydayness does not coincide with primitiveness. Everydayness is rather a mode of being of Dasein even and precisely when Dasein moves in a highly developed and differentiated culture; and conversely, primitive Dasein too has its possibilities of non-everyday being — it has its specific everydayness. Orienting the analysis of Dasein toward the "life of primitive peoples" can nonetheless have positive methodological significance, insofar as "primitive phenomena" are often less covered over and complicated by an already far-reaching self-interpretation of the Dasein concerned: primitive Dasein often speaks more directly out of an original absorption in the "phenomena" (taken in the pre-phenomenological sense), and its conceptuality, perhaps clumsy and crude seen from our side, can be positively conducive to a genuine lifting-out of the ontological structures of phenomena. The categorial point is decisive against a whole reading of Division One: everydayness is an existential mode, indifferent to cultural altitude — the analytic of the everyday is not evolutionary anthropology in disguise, and modernity has its everydayness as surely as any "primitive" world. The methodological concession is equally calibrated: ethnological material may help not because origins are truer but because thinner layers of sedimented self-interpretation (§ 6's tradition, individualized) leave the structures less disguised.

The second unit withdraws the concession's innocence. So far, our knowledge of primitives is supplied by ethnology; and ethnology already moves, in the very first "taking up" of its material, its sifting and working-over, within determinate preliminary concepts and interpretations of human Dasein in general. Whether the everyday psychology, or indeed the scientific psychology and sociology, that the ethnologist brings along offers scientific warrant for an adequate possibility of access, interpretation, and transmission of the phenomena to be explored is not settled: here the same situation shows itself as with the previously named disciplines — ethnology itself already presupposes a sufficient analytic of Dasein as guiding thread. But since the positive sciences neither "can" nor should wait for the ontological work of philosophy, the ongoing course of research will not take the form of "progress" but of retrieval and the ontologically more transparent purification of the ontically discovered. The folded-in note gives the claim its contemporary address: Cassirer, Heidegger records, has lately made mythical Dasein the theme of a philosophical interpretation in the second volume of the Philosophy of Symbolic Forms (1925), thereby supplying ethnological research with more comprehensive guiding threads; but seen from the philosophical problematic the question remains whether the foundations of that interpretation are sufficiently transparent — whether, in particular, the architectonic of Kant's first Critique and its systematic content can offer the possible outline for such a task at all, or whether a new and more original approach is not needed here; Cassirer himself, the note adds, sees the possibility of such a task, pointing to the phenomenological horizons opened by Husserl, and in a conversation following a December 1923 Hamburg lecture of the author's on the tasks and ways of phenomenological research, an agreement already showed itself in the demand for an existential analytic. Text and note together enact the section's logic: the empirical science of the primitive presupposes an a priori of Dasein it cannot itself supply; even the era's most powerful philosophical framework for myth (Cassirer's neo-Kantian symbolic forms) is queried at exactly this joint — can Kant's architectonic carry an interpretation of Dasein? — with the 1929 Davos disputation between the two men already legible in embryo. And the closing maxim generalizes § 5's Wiederholung into a philosophy of research: since science rightly does not wait for ontology, its history advances by retrieving and purifying its own discoveries, not by linear accumulation.

The third unit names the desideratum behind the whole discussion. However easy the formal demarcation of the ontological problematic from ontic research may be, the carrying-out — and above all the approach — of an existential analytic is not without difficulties. In its task lies enclosed a desideratum that has long disquieted philosophy but at whose fulfillment philosophy fails again and again: the working-out of the idea of a "natural concept of the world." The wealth of knowledge now available of the most manifold and remote cultures and forms of Dasein seems favorable to a fruitful attack on this task — but that is only semblance: at bottom such overabundant knowledge is the seduction to misrecognizing the authentic problem. Syncretistic comparing-of-everything and typologizing does not of itself yield genuine knowledge of essence; the masterability of the manifold in a table does not guarantee actual understanding of what lies there ordered. The genuine principle of order has its own material content, never found through the ordering but already presupposed in it — so the ordering of world-pictures requires the explicit idea of world in general; and if "world" is itself a constitutive of Dasein, the conceptual working-out of the world-phenomenon demands insight into the basic structures of Dasein. The desideratum has a name and address Heidegger's first readers knew: the natürlicher Weltbegriff is Avenarius's phrase and Husserl's problem (the natural attitude, later the Lebenswelt) — announced here as the task philosophy keeps failing, and claimed for the analytic. The argument against comparative typology repeats § 6's verdict on historicist erudition, now with a transcendental edge: classification presupposes the concept it pretends to induce, so a hundred world-pictures cannot yield the idea of world. The final conditional — if world is a constitutive of Dasein — is the exact program of Chapter Three, and its fulfillment (worldhood as an existential) is what turns the old desideratum into a solvable problem.

The closing unit states the chapter's yield and philosophy's self-understanding in two sentences. The positive characterizations and negative considerations of this chapter had the purpose of steering into the right course the understanding of the tendency and question-posture of the following interpretation. Ontology can contribute only indirectly to the advancement of the existing positive disciplines; it has an independent aim of its own — if indeed, beyond any taking-notice of beings, the question of being is the goad (Stachel) of all scientific seeking. The demarcations, that is, were never the point: the analytic is not a better anthropology but something with an eigenständige Abzweckung. The last image deserves its place at a chapter's end — being as the Stachel, the spur or sting of all inquiry: § 4's thesis that the question of being radicalizes a tendency of Dasein itself returns as a claim about science as such, whose restlessness (§ 3's crises) is finally the being-question working in it unasked.

#### Chapter Two: Being-in-the-World in General as the Basic Constitution of Dasein

##### § 12. The Predelineation of Being-in-the-World from the Orientation toward Being-in as Such

The opening unit collects the acquisitions of § 9 in strict order. The preparatory discussions already set off characters of being that are to give the further investigation a secure light, while themselves receiving their structural concretion in that investigation. Dasein is the being that, in its being, comports itself understandingly toward this being — therewith the formal concept of existence is indicated: Dasein exists. Dasein is further the being that in each case I myself am; to existing Dasein belongs mineness as the condition of the possibility of authenticity and inauthenticity, and Dasein exists in each case in one of these modes, or in their modal indifference. The recapitulation is not padding but calibration: existence and mineness are expressly ranked as formal indications awaiting concretion — the analytic will fill them, not deduce from them — and the third possibility, modal indifference, is reaffirmed as the actual starting level of the analysis (§ 9's averageness), so that neither authenticity nor inauthenticity is presupposed in what follows.

The second unit subordinates both characters to the structure that names the chapter: these determinations of Dasein's being must be seen and understood a priori on the ground of that constitution of being which we call being-in-the-world (In-der-Welt-sein) — and the right approach of the analytic consists in the interpretation of this constitution. The subordination is architectural: existence and mineness, the § 9 headline results, are not free-standing; they are ways of being-in-the-world, and any interpretation that detaches them (an existentialism of the self without world) has already lost the phenomenon.

The third unit reads the coinage itself. The composite expression "In-der-Welt-sein" indicates in its very minting that a unitary phenomenon is meant: this primary finding must be seen as a whole. But irresolvability into pieces that could be stuck together does not exclude a multiplicity of constitutive structural moments — the phenomenal finding indeed grants a threefold direction of regard, and if we pursue it while holding the whole phenomenon fast in advance, three moments can be lifted out. The hyphens are the argument: the expression is built to make the unity typographically prior to the moments, and the methodological rule — every analysis of a moment is a seeing of the whole — is issued before any moment is named. This is the standing answer to the Cartesian starting point: there is no worldless subject plus world to be bridged, because the bridge-problem presupposes fragments the phenomenon never yields.

The fourth unit names the first moment: the "in-the-world" — with respect to which arises the task of asking after the ontological structure of "world" and determining the idea of worldhood (Weltlichkeit) as such (Chapter Three). The compressed announcement contains a decision of rank: what Chapter Three seeks is not an inventory of the world's contents but worldhood, the being-structure of world — the shift from world as sum of entities to world as constitutive of Dasein that § 11's "natural concept of the world" demanded.

The fifth unit names the second: the being that in each case is in the way of being-in-the-world — sought with the question "who?"; phenomenological exhibition is to determine who is in the mode of Dasein's average everydayness (Chapter Four). The interrogative discipline of § 9 (a who, never a what) is here scheduled: and the phrasing quietly warns that the answer will not be "I" — who is in everydayness is exactly what must be shown, not assumed (das Man will be the answer).

The sixth unit names the third and sets the order of treatment: being-in (In-Sein) as such — the ontological constitution of "in-ness" (Inheit) itself is to be exhibited (Chapter Five). Every lifting-out of one of these moments means lifting the others with it: in each case a seeing of the whole phenomenon. Being-in-the-world is an a priori necessary constitution of Dasein, but far from sufficient to determine its being fully. Before the thematic individual analyses, an orienting characterization of the last-named moment is attempted. Two governing caveats are lodged here. The co-lifting rule repeats the whole-first methodology as a running obligation, not a preface. And the insufficiency clause keeps the architecture honest: being-in-the-world is the basic constitution, not the full determination — care (Chapter Six) and temporality (Division Two) stand behind it.

The seventh unit begins the orientation by exhibiting the misunderstanding. What does being-in mean? One completes the expression to being-in "in the world" and inclines to understand it as "being in..." — the term for the mode of being of a being that is "in" another as water is "in" the glass, the garment "in" the closet: the "in" then means the relation of being of two beings extended "in" space with respect to their place in that space. Water and glass, garment and closet are both, in the same way, "in" space "at" a place; and the relation can be extended — the bench in the lecture hall, the hall in the university, the university in the city, up to: the bench "in world-space." All beings whose "in"-one-another can be so determined have the same mode of being — presence-at-hand — as things occurring "within" the world; presence-at-hand "in" something present-at-hand, and co-presence-at-hand with something of the same mode of being in the sense of a determinate place-relation, are ontological characters of the categorial kind, belonging to beings not of Dasein's way of being. The analysis of containment is deliberately patient: the nesting series (bench to world-space) shows the categorial "in" iterating indifferently at every scale — which is precisely why it can never reach the existential "in": no widening of the container yields inhabitation.

The eighth unit gives the positive sense through the language's own memory. Being-in, by contrast, means a constitution of being of Dasein and is an existential; it cannot mean the presence-at-hand of a corporeal thing (the human body) "in" a present-at-hand being. Nor does "in" originally mean a spatial relation of the kind described — Grimm's philology, cited in the note, supplies the pedigree: "in" stems from innan-, to dwell, habitare, to sojourn; "an" means: I am accustomed to, familiar with, I tend something — it has the signification of colo in the sense of habito and diligo. The being to which being-in in this signification belongs is the one we characterized as the being that I in each case am; and the expression "bin" (am) is connected with "bei" (at, alongside) — "ich bin" says in turn: I dwell, I sojourn alongside... the world as what is thus and so familiar. Being, as the infinitive of "I am" — understood, that is, as an existential — means: to dwell alongside..., to be familiar with...; being-in is accordingly the formal existential expression of the being of Dasein, which has the essential constitution of being-in-the-world. The etymology is not decoration but destruction in miniature: beneath the sedimented spatial "in" (the container-schema the tradition reads everywhere) the language preserves an older stratum — dwelling, tending, familiarity — and the very copula of the first person ("bin" from "bei") testifies that to be, said of Dasein, means to inhabit. Being-in is intimacy with a world before it is position in space; the late Heidegger's meditations on dwelling (Bauen Wohnen Denken) unfold what is compacted here.

The ninth unit introduces a founded existential and defends the pedantry to come. "Being-alongside" the world (Sein bei), in the sense — still to be interpreted more closely — of absorption in the world (Aufgehen in der Welt), is an existential founded in being-in. Because these analyses aim at seeing an original structure of Dasein's being, in accordance with whose phenomenal content the concepts of being must be articulated, and because this structure is fundamentally not graspable by the transmitted ontological categories, this "being-alongside" too is to be brought closer — again by the route of contrast against an ontologically essentially different, categorial relation of being that language expresses with the same means. Such phenomenal re-presentations of easily blurred fundamental ontological differences must be explicitly carried out, even at the risk of discussing the "self-evident"; for the state of the ontological analytic shows that we have long had these self-evidences far from adequately "in grip," still more rarely interpreted in their being-sense, and even less do we possess the appropriate structural concepts in secure coinage. Two things are fixed: Sein bei — absorbed dwelling-alongside — enters the book's inventory (it will be one of care's three structural moments, § 41); and the method's apparent laboriousness is justified by § 1's own principle — self-evidence is the philosophical theme, and language's use of one preposition for two ontologies is exactly how the fundamental difference gets blurred.

The tenth unit executes the contrast at its sharpest point: touching. "Being-alongside" the world as an existential never means anything like the being-present-at-hand-together of occurring things; there is no such thing as the "side-by-side" of a being called "Dasein" with another called "world." True, we sometimes express the togetherness of two present-at-hand things by saying "the table stands 'by' the door," "the chair 'touches' the wall" — but strictly there can never be talk of "touching," not because exact examination would always find a gap between chair and wall, but because the chair, even were the gap zero, fundamentally cannot touch the wall. The presupposition would be that the wall could be encountered "for" the chair. A being can touch a present-at-hand being within the world only if it has by nature the mode of being of being-in — only if, with its Da-sein, something like world is already discovered to it, from out of which a being can become manifest in touch and so accessible in its presence-at-hand. Two beings that are present-at-hand within the world and moreover in themselves worldless can never "touch" one another; neither can "be" "alongside" the other. And the qualification "moreover worldless" must not be dropped, since even a being that is not worldless — Dasein itself — is "in" the world present-at-hand, or more precisely: can with a certain right, within certain limits, be apprehended as merely present-at-hand, which requires a complete looking-away from, or not-seeing of, the existential constitution of being-in. But this possible apprehension of "Dasein" as something present-at-hand must not be conflated with a way of "presence-at-hand" proper to Dasein: that presence-at-hand becomes accessible not by disregarding the specific structures of Dasein but only in a prior understanding of them — Dasein understands its ownmost being in the sense of a certain "factual being-present-at-hand," and yet the "factuality" of the fact of one's own Dasein is ontologically fundamentally different from the factual occurrence of a kind of stone. The factuality of the fact Dasein, as which every Dasein in each case is, we call its facticity (Faktizität); the involuted structure of this determination becomes graspable as a problem only in the light of the existential constitutions already worked out; and the concept encloses in itself: the being-in-the-world of an "innerworldly" being, such that this being can understand itself as bound up, in its "destiny," with the being of the beings it encounters within its own world. The chair-and-wall argument is among the book's most famous and most misread: it is not panpsychist fastidiousness but a strict point of ontological grammar — touching presupposes encounter, encounter presupposes a disclosed world, and worldless things have none; contact between things is only ever registered within someone's world. The second half then performs a rescue with far-reaching consequences: there is a legitimate, limited apprehension of Dasein as occurrent (I am in the room, I weigh so much), but Dasein's own "that it is" — its facticity — is categorially unlike a mineral's occurrence: it is a that-it-is delivered over to being-in-the-world, entangled with the destiny of what it encounters. Facticity, the early Freiburg lectures' master word, here receives its official definition, and thrownness (§ 29, to which the note points) will be its existential elaboration.

The eleventh unit banks the distinction and reserves space for spatiality. For the present it suffices to see the ontological difference between being-in as an existential and the "insideness" (Inwendigkeit) of present-at-hand things among one another as a category. Demarcating being-in this way does not deny Dasein every kind of "spatiality": on the contrary, Dasein itself has its own "being-in-space" — which, however, is possible only on the ground of being-in-the-world in general. Hence being-in cannot be clarified ontologically by an ontic characterization of the sort: being-in in a world is a spiritual property, and man's "spatiality" a quality of his corporeality always "founded" in bodiliness — for with that one stands again before a being-present-at-hand-together of a spirit-thing so constituted with a corporeal thing, and the being of the composite as such remains darker than ever. Only the understanding of being-in-the-world as an essential structure of Dasein makes possible insight into Dasein's existential spatiality, and it guards against not seeing this structure or striking it out in advance — a striking-out motivated not ontologically but "metaphysically," in the naive opinion that man is first a spiritual thing which is then subsequently transposed "into" a space. The unit sets the program of §§ 22–24 (existential spatiality) and forecloses its standard evasion: the spirit/body division does not solve the problem of Dasein's space but doubles it — the § 10 summation-argument against composites, applied. The closing barb identifies the real motive of the traditional picture as metaphysical (the immaterial soul lodged in extension), not phenomenal.

The twelfth unit descends into the plural everyday and coins the term for its being. With Dasein's facticity, its being-in-the-world has in each case already dispersed or even splintered itself into determinate ways of being-in — an exemplary enumeration: having to do with something, producing something, ordering and tending something, using something, giving something up and letting it get lost, undertaking, carrying through, finding out, asking about, considering, discussing, determining... These ways of being-in have the mode of being — to be characterized in detail — of concern (Besorgen). Ways of concern are also the deficient modes of omitting, neglecting, renouncing, resting — all modes of "merely still" with respect to possibilities of concern. Pre-scientifically the word means carrying something out, settling it, "getting it straight"; also procuring something for oneself; and further, in the idiom "I am concerned lest the undertaking fail," something like fearing. Against these ontic significations, "Besorgen" is used in this investigation as an ontological term (an existential) for the being of a possible being-in-the-world — chosen not because Dasein is proximally and largely economic and "practical," but because the being of Dasein itself is to be made visible as care (Sorge), an expression likewise to be grasped as an ontological structural concept (Chapter Six), having nothing to do with "toil," "melancholy," and the "cares of life," which are ontically findable in every Dasein and are ontically possible, like their opposites carefreeness and gaiety, only because Dasein, ontologically understood, is care. Because being-in-the-world belongs essentially to Dasein, its being toward the world is essentially concern. The enumeration is the analytic's first concrete phenomenology, and its lesson lies in its breadth: from producing to renouncing, from using to merely-resting, everyday being-in is uniformly a matter of attending-to — even omission is a mode of concern (the deficient-mode argument of § 6 again: neglect is concern in privation, not its absence). The terminological note is a preemptive strike against two misreadings at once: pragmatist (Dasein defined by practice — expressly denied as the ground of the word-choice) and pessimist (care as gloom — expressly ruled ontic); Sorge names the structure that makes both busyness and gaiety possible.

The thirteenth unit states the anti-additive thesis in its own right. Being-in, by all that has been said, is no "property" that Dasein sometimes has and sometimes not, with or without which it could equally be. Man does not "be" and then, in addition, have a relation of being to the "world" which he occasionally takes on: Dasein is never "first" a being free of being-in, as it were, that sometimes has the whim of taking up a "relation" to the world. Taking up relations to the world is possible only because Dasein, as being-in-the-world, is as it is. This constitution does not first arise because, besides the being with Dasein's character, other beings are present-at-hand and meet up with it: the other beings can "meet up with" Dasein only insofar as they are able to show themselves from themselves at all within a world. Two directions of derivation are barred in one paragraph: outward (a subject that subsequently adds a world-relation) and inward (a world-relation generated by things impinging on the subject). Encounter itself — the elementary "meeting" of anything with Dasein — presupposes the disclosed world; being-in is thus the condition of every relation, not one relation among others.

The fourteenth unit tests the thesis on a fashionable phrase. The saying, much used today, that "man has his environment (Umwelt)" says nothing ontologically so long as this "having" remains undetermined: in its possibility, the having is founded in the existential constitution of being-in. Because Dasein essentially is in this way, it can expressly discover the beings encountered environmentally, know about them, dispose over them, "have" world. The ontically trivial talk of "having an environment" is ontologically a problem, and solving it requires nothing less than first determining the being of Dasein in an ontologically adequate way. And if biology — above all since K. E. von Baer — makes use of this constitution, one may not infer "biologism" from its philosophical use: for biology, as a positive science, can never find and determine this structure — it must presuppose it and constantly make use of it; the structure can be philosophically explicated as the a priori of biology's thematic object only if it is first grasped as a structure of Dasein, and only from the ontological structure so grasped can the constitution of being of "life" be delimited a priori, by way of privation. Ontically as well as ontologically, being-in-the-world as concern has the priority; in the analytic of Dasein this structure receives its foundational interpretation. The passage takes up the Umwelt-biology of the day (von Baer's line, contemporaneously Uexküll's) with the same double gesture as § 10: the science is right to use the structure and constitutionally unable to ground it; and the direction of founding is reaffirmed — the animal's environment is thinkable only privatively from being-in-the-world, never the reverse.

The fifteenth unit answers the objection its own procedure invites. Has the determination of this constitution so far moved exclusively in negative assertions — do we not hear only what this supposedly fundamental being-in is not? Indeed. But the predominance of negative characterization is no accident: it itself announces the peculiarity of the phenomenon and is thereby positive in a genuine sense, appropriate to the phenomenon itself. The phenomenological exhibition of being-in-the-world has the character of a rejection of distortions and coverings-over, because this phenomenon is always already "seen" in a certain way in every Dasein — it belongs to Dasein's basic constitution and is, with Dasein's being, always already disclosed for its understanding of being — and yet is mostly just as thoroughly misinterpreted or ontologically insufficiently laid out. And this "seeing in a certain way and yet mostly misinterpreting" is itself grounded in nothing other than this very constitution of Dasein, according to which Dasein understands itself — and that means also its being-in-the-world — ontologically at first from those beings and their being which it is not, but which it encounters "within" its world. The unit is the method reflecting on itself with § 7's concepts: the phenomenon's mode of concealment is disguise (Verstellung), and against disguise the appropriate positivity is via negativa — clearing away the misreading is exhibiting the phenomenon. The closing derivation is the deeper point: even the misinterpretation is not bad luck but the § 5 Rückstrahlung operating — Dasein reads its being-in off the innerworldly, and so converts dwelling into containment; the error has an existential etiology.

The sixteenth unit traces the genealogy of epistemology. Within Dasein and for it, this constitution is always already somehow familiar; but if it is now to be known, the knowing that becomes explicit in such a task takes precisely itself — knowing the world — as the exemplary relation of "soul" to world. Knowing the world (noein), or addressing and discussing "world" (logos), therefore functions as the primary mode of being-in-the-world, without being-in-the-world as such being conceived. Because this structure remains ontologically inaccessible while being ontically experienced as a "relation" between beings (world and soul), and because being is at first understood by ontological leaning on beings as innerworldly beings, the relation between those beings is attempted to be conceived on the basis of these beings and in the sense of their being — as presence-at-hand. Being-in-the-world, though pre-phenomenologically experienced and familiar, becomes invisible on the path of an ontologically inappropriate interpretation; one now knows the constitution only — and as something self-evident — in the coinage the inappropriate interpretation gave it; and in this shape it becomes the "evident" point of departure for the problems of epistemology or the "metaphysics of knowledge." For what is more self-evident than that a "subject" relates to an "object" and vice versa? The "subject-object relation" must be presupposed — but it remains a presupposition which, though untouchable in its facticity, is for that very reason fatal (verhängnisvoll) if its ontological necessity and above all its ontological sense are left in the dark. The paragraph is a compressed history of philosophy as pathology: (a) being-in seeks to know itself; (b) the knowing that undertakes this takes itself as the paradigm case; (c) the relation is then ontologized from innerworldly being (presence-at-hand); (d) the product — subject over against object — hardens into the self-evident premise of epistemology. Every step instantiates a structure already exhibited (Greek noein-guidance from § 6, understanding-from-the-world from § 5, tradition's self-evidence from § 1). The verdict is finely balanced: the subject-object relation is factually untouchable — there is such a comportment — and fatal as an unexamined foundation; its facticity is exactly what makes it so durable a disguise.

The closing unit announces § 13's task and names the stakes: because knowing the world mostly and exclusively represents the phenomenon of being-in exemplarily — and not only for epistemology, since practical comportment is understood as the "non-" and "a-theoretical" comportment — and because this priority of knowing misleads the understanding of its own mode of being, being-in-the-world is to be set out still more sharply with regard to knowing the world, and knowing itself made visible as an existential "modality" of being-in. The parenthesis carries the sharpest edge: the tradition's very concept of practice is privative — the not-theoretical — so that even the champions of the practical accept theory as the measure; § 13 will invert the founding, and Chapter Three will then begin from concernful dealings as the positive primary phenomenon.

##### § 13. The Exemplification of Being-in in a Founded Mode. Knowing the World

The opening unit fixes the dialectical situation. If being-in-the-world is a basic constitution of Dasein, in which it moves not only in general but preeminently in the mode of everydayness, then it must also always already be experienced ontically — a total remaining-veiled would be unintelligible, especially since Dasein disposes over an understanding of being of itself, however indeterminately it may function. But as soon as the "phenomenon of knowing the world" was itself grasped, it fell forthwith into an "external," formal interpretation, whose index is the positing — still customary today — of knowing as a "relation between subject and object," which harbors as much "truth" as emptiness. And subject and object do not coincide with Dasein and world. The last sentence is the section's thesis in six words, and it forestalls the assimilation that has dogged the book's reception: being-in-the-world is not the subject-object relation renamed — the pair is a late, leveled interpretation of the phenomenon, true enough to be empty. That the phenomenon cannot be wholly hidden (Dasein always somehow experiences its being-in) repeats § 12's diagnosis: the tradition's error is a misreading of something seen, not sheer blindness.

The second unit lets the traditional approach generate its own riddle. Even if it were feasible to determine being-in ontologically primarily from knowing being-in-the-world, the first required task would still be the phenomenal characterization of knowing as a being in and toward the world. When one reflects on this relation of being, what is at first given is a being called nature, as what is known; knowing itself is not to be met with in this being — and if it "is" at all, it belongs solely to the being that knows. But even in this being, the man-thing, knowing is not present-at-hand — at any rate not externally ascertainable like bodily properties. So, since knowing belongs to this being but is no external quality, it must be "inside." And the more unambiguously one holds fast that knowing is proximally and properly "inside," indeed has nothing of the mode of being of a physical or psychic being, the more presuppositionless one believes one's procedure in the question of the essence of knowledge and the clarification of the relation between subject and object. For only now can a problem arise — namely: how does this knowing subject come out of its inner "sphere" into one "other and external"? how can knowing have an object at all? how must the object itself be thought so that in the end the subject knows it without needing to risk the leap into another sphere? But in this approach, however variously executed, the question of the mode of being of this knowing subject is everywhere omitted — though its way of being is constantly, tacitly, already in the theme whenever its knowing is treated. One hears, to be sure, the assurance that the inside, the "inner sphere" of the subject, is certainly not thought as a "box" or "cabinet"; but what the "inside" of immanence positively means, in which knowing is at first enclosed, and how the being-character of this "being-inside" of knowing is grounded in the subject's mode of being — on this, silence reigns. However the inner sphere is interpreted: as soon as one so much as asks how knowing gets "out" of it and gains a "transcendence," it comes to light that one finds knowing problematic without having first clarified how and what this knowing itself is that poses such riddles. The reconstruction is a masterpiece of diagnostic patience: each step of the epistemological genesis is granted (knowing not in nature; not an outer property; hence "inside"), so that the transcendence-problem is shown to be manufactured by an unexamined ontology of the knower — an occurrent thing with an interior. The exposure of the "not a box, of course" disclaimer is the sharpest cut: the tradition disavows the crude picture verbally while retaining its ontological schema, precisely the ontic-protest-with-ontological-complicity pattern § 10 diagnosed in theories of the subject.

The third unit turns the tables on the anticipated protest. In this approach one remains blind to what is already tacitly co-said with the most provisional thematizing of the knowledge-phenomenon: knowing is a mode of being of Dasein as being-in-the-world; it has its ontic foundation in this constitution of being. To this indication — knowing is a mode of being of being-in-the-world — one will want to object: but such an interpretation annihilates the problem of knowledge; what remains to be asked, if one presupposes that knowing is already alongside its world, which it was supposed first to reach in the subject's transcending? Apart from the fact that this last question again betrays the phenomenally unattested, constructive "standpoint": what instance decides whether and in what sense there is to be a problem of knowledge, other than the phenomenon of knowing itself and the mode of being of the knower? The reply is methodologically pure § 7: problems have no rights of their own; whether "the problem of knowledge" exists is itself to be decided by the phenomena — and a problem generated by a disguise dissolves with the disguise. The charge of annihilating the problem is thus accepted and re-described: what is annihilated is a pseudo-problem (§ 7's Scheinprobleme that "spread themselves for generations").

The fourth unit gives the positive genealogy of knowing. Asking what shows itself in the phenomenal finding of knowing itself, one must hold fast: knowing is antecedently grounded in an already-being-alongside-the-world (Schon-sein-bei-der-Welt), which essentially constitutes Dasein's being. This already-being-alongside is proximally not a rigid gaping at something purely present-at-hand; being-in-the-world, as concern, is taken in (benommen) by the world of its concern. If knowing as contemplative determining of the present-at-hand is to be possible, there is need beforehand of a deficiency of concernful having-to-do with the world: in refraining from all producing, handling, and the like, concern places itself in the sole remaining mode of being-in — the merely-tarrying-alongside... On the ground of this mode of being toward the world, which lets innerworldly beings be encountered only in their pure look (eidos), and as a mode of it, an explicit looking-at what is so encountered becomes possible. Such looking-at is in each case a determinate taking-of-direction toward..., an aiming at the present-at-hand; it takes from the encountered being, in advance, a "viewpoint." Such looking becomes itself a mode of independent sojourning alongside innerworldly beings; in this "sojourn" — as the refraining from every manipulation and use — the perceiving (Vernehmen) of the present-at-hand accomplishes itself, in the manner of enactment of addressing and discussing something as something. On the basis of this interpreting in the widest sense, perceiving becomes determining; and what is perceived and determined can be expressed in propositions, and as so asserted be retained and preserved. But this perceiving retention of an assertion about... is itself a way of being-in-the-world, and may not be interpreted as a "process" by which a subject procures itself representations of something, which remain stored "inside" as thus appropriated — with respect to which the question can then occasionally arise how they "agree" with actuality. This is the celebrated genetic account of theory out of praxis, and its steps deserve enumeration because Division Two (§ 69b) will temporalize exactly them: concernful absorption; its deficiency (refraining, not adding); tarrying-alongside; the pure look (eidos — the Platonic term pointedly re-derived from a modification of concern); directed looking with an antecedent viewpoint; perceiving as addressing-something-as-something; determining; assertion; retention. Theory is thus a founded accomplishment of being-in — born of a stilling of dealings, not of a native spectator-stance — and the representationalist picture (inner copies awaiting comparison with the outer) is unmasked at the exact point where it seemed strongest: even retained knowledge is a way of being-in-the-world, not inner inventory.

The fifth unit states the anti-immanentist result with full rhetorical force. In directing itself toward... and grasping, Dasein does not first go outside of an inner sphere in which it is at first encapsulated; rather, by its primary mode of being, it is always already "outside," alongside beings encountered in the world already discovered. And the determining sojourn alongside the being to be known is no abandoning of the inner sphere: even in this "being-outside" alongside the object, Dasein is "inside" in the rightly understood sense — namely, it itself, as the being-in-the-world that knows, is the inside. And again: perceiving the known is not a returning of the grasping excursion, with its won booty, into the "cabinet" of consciousness; even in perceiving, preserving, and retaining, the knowing Dasein remains, as Dasein, outside. In "merely" knowing about a context of the being of beings, in "only" representing it, in "just" thinking of it, I am no less alongside beings outside in the world than in an originary grasping; even forgetting something, in which every relation of being to what was formerly known seems extinguished, must be conceived as a modification of original being-in — likewise all deception and every error. The paragraph systematically inverts the container-vocabulary it quotes: outside/inside survive only in scare-quotes, redefined (the true "inside" is being-in-the-world itself, which is essentially "outside"). The escalation at the end is the strongest claim: not only perception but memory, mere thought, forgetting, and error are modes of being-alongside — negative and absent relations to beings are modifications of being-in, never lapses into a worldless interior. Intentionality, one may say, is here out-radicalized: where Husserl taught that consciousness is of its object, Heidegger replies that the "of" was never a bridge from an inside, because there never was an inside to leave.

The closing unit banks the section's yield. The exhibited founding-connection of the modes of being-in-the-world constitutive for knowing the world makes clear: in knowing, Dasein wins a new stance of being (Seinsstand) toward the world already discovered in Dasein in each case. This new possibility of being can develop independently, become a task, and as science take over leadership for being-in-the-world. But knowing neither first creates a "commercium" of the subject with a world, nor does this arise from an action of the world upon a subject: knowing is a mode of Dasein founded in being-in-the-world. And therefore being-in-the-world, as basic constitution, demands a prior interpretation. The balance of the verdict should be felt: knowing is genuinely new — a transformed stance that can institutionalize itself as science and even lead existence (§ 3's picture of research as a possibility of Dasein returns, now grounded) — and radically non-original, creating no commerce between subject and world because that commerce, being-in, precedes it. Both classical options for the origin of the knowledge-relation (constituted by the subject's act; caused by the world's impact) are dismissed in one sentence. With that, the exemplification has done its work backwards: precisely the mode the tradition took as primary shows itself founded, and the chapter closes by handing the analysis over to what founds it — the world itself, whose worldhood Chapter Three must now interrogate.

#### Chapter Three: The Worldhood of the World

##### § 14. The Idea of the Worldhood of the World in General

The opening unit lets the naive procedure convict itself. Being-in-the-world is to be made visible first with regard to the structural moment "world" — a task that seems so easy and trivial that one still believes oneself entitled to skip it. What can it mean to describe "the world" as a phenomenon? To let be seen what shows itself in the way of "beings" within the world: the first step is an enumeration of what there is "in" the world — houses, trees, men, mountains, stars; one can depict the "look" of these beings and narrate the occurrences on and with them. But this remains a pre-phenomenological "business" that cannot be phenomenologically relevant at all: the description sticks to beings, it is ontic — while what is sought is being. "Phenomenon" in the phenomenological sense was formally determined as what shows itself as being and structure of being. The unit applies § 7 with textbook precision: inventory is not description of the world, because the world is not the inventoried; and the § 7 C reminder in the last sentence fixes the criterion by which every candidate in this section will be tested.

The second unit tries the obvious ontological upgrade. Describing the "world" phenomenologically would then mean: exhibiting and fixing conceptually-categorially the being of the beings present-at-hand within the world. These are things — natural things and "value-laden" things; their thinghood becomes the problem, and since the thinghood of the latter builds on natural thinghood, the being of natural things, nature as such, is the primary theme; the all-founding character of natural things, of substances, is substantiality — what constitutes its ontological sense? Therewith the investigation has been given an unambiguous direction of questioning. The reconstruction is a portrait of the reigning program — Husserl's stratified constitution (nature founding value-predicates founding the cultural object) is recognizably the model — and its very cogency is the trap: the direction is unambiguous and, the next unit will say, unambiguously wrong.

The third unit springs the trap. Are we, in this, asking ontologically about the "world"? The problematic is without doubt ontological — but even if it achieves the purest explication of the being of nature, measured by the basic assertions of mathematical natural science about this being, this ontology never touches the phenomenon "world": nature is itself a being that is encountered within the world and is discoverable on various paths and at various levels. The argument is short and total: however refined, an ontology of nature is an ontology of an innerworldly being — it presupposes the within-which it was supposed to explain. Regional ontology at its best (§ 3's own program) is here shown to be constitutionally unable to reach worldhood.

The fourth unit tries the other candidate: should we then hold to the beings alongside which Dasein proximally and mostly dwells — the "value-laden" things? Do not they "properly" show the world in which we live? Perhaps they do show something like "world" more penetratingly — but these things too are beings "within" the world. The concession and the rebuttal are both instructive: the cultural object is closer to the phenomenon (its value-character gestures at significance, which worldhood will turn out to involve), yet the same one-line argument fells it — whatever is within the world cannot be the world.

The fifth unit generalizes the result: neither the ontic depiction of innerworldly beings nor the ontological interpretation of their being touches, as such, the phenomenon "world" — in both modes of access to "objective being," "world" is already "presupposed," and in each a different way. The diagnosis has the Introduction's structure: the world is the concealed presupposition of exactly those procedures that claim to capture it — a transcendental invisibility, hidden by functioning.

The sixth unit lets the perplexity pose the real question. Can "world" in the end not be addressed as a determination of those beings at all? Yet we call them innerworldly. Is "world" then a character of being of Dasein? And does then "proximally" every Dasein have its world? Does "world" not thereby become something "subjective"? How is a "common" world still to be possible, "in" which we after all are? And if the question of the "world" is posed — which world is meant? Neither this one nor that one, but the worldhood of world in general. On what path do we encounter this phenomenon? The rapid-fire questions rehearse, in advance, every objection the coming analysis will face — above all the subjectivism worry, which §§ 26–27 (the common world of das Man) and the whole doctrine of transcendence must answer. The resolving move is the formalization: not a world but worldhood — the structure that makes any world (mine, ours, the mathematician's) a world.

The seventh unit fixes the answer's ontological place. "Worldhood" is an ontological concept and means the structure of a constitutive moment of being-in-the-world; but being-in-the-world we know as an existential determination of Dasein — worldhood is accordingly itself an existential. In asking ontologically about the "world" we do not at all leave the thematic field of the analytic of Dasein: "world" is ontologically no determination of the beings Dasein essentially is not, but a character of Dasein itself. This does not exclude that the path of investigating the phenomenon "world" must pass through innerworldly beings and their being; and the task of a phenomenological "description" of the world lies so little open to view that even its adequate determination demands essential ontological clarifications. This is the chapter's thesis-paragraph and the hinge of the whole book's concept of world: world is an existential — which sounds like the subjectivism just worried over, and is its opposite, since Dasein is not a subject but being-in-the-world. The methodological concession matters equally: though world is Dasein's, the way to it runs through the innerworldly — § 15's tool-analysis is thereby licensed as a detour, not a change of theme.
