If the mode of being of being-in-the-world essentially belongs to Dasein, then to the essential stock of its understanding of being belongs the understanding of being-in-the-world. The antecedent disclosing of that toward which the freeing of the innerworldly encountered proceeds is nothing other than the understanding of world, toward which Dasein as a being always already comports itself. The chain from § 4 is closed at world: Seinsverständnis, hitherto the abstract Faktum of the Introduction, receives its first concrete content — it is, at least, world-understanding; the pre-disclosure that § 16 found operative and § 18 found presupposed turns out to be an accomplishment of the understanding that Dasein is.

The eighth unit executes the section's central derivation and defines the phenomenon. The antecedent letting-be-involved at... with... is grounded in an understanding of something like letting-be-involved, of the at-which and the with-which of involvement; such things, and what further underlies them — the for-this as the at-which of involvement, the for-the-sake-of-which to which every what-for ultimately goes back — all this must be antecedently disclosed in a certain intelligibility. And what is that wherein Dasein as being-in-the-world pre-ontologically understands itself? In understanding the named relational context, Dasein has referred itself (sich verwiesen), from a potentiality-of-being for the sake of which it itself is — grasped expressly or not, authentic or inauthentic — to an in-order-to; the in-order-to predelineates a for-this as the possible at-which of a letting-be-involved, which structurally lets something be involved with something. Dasein always already refers itself from a for-the-sake-of-which to the with-which of an involvement — that is, it always already, insofar as it is, lets beings be encountered as ready-to-hand. That wherein (Worin) Dasein antecedently understands itself in the mode of self-referral is that toward-which (Woraufhin) of the antecedent letting-be-encountered of beings. The wherein of self-referring understanding, as the toward-which of letting beings be encountered in the mode of being of involvement, is the phenomenon of world; and the structure of that toward which Dasein refers itself is what constitutes the worldhood of the world. The definition earns every one of its clauses, and the direction of self-referral is its whole content: Dasein does not stand among things and then relate them — it throws itself, from a possibility of its being (the for-the-sake-of), along the in-order-to lines, and the web thus lit up in advance is that within which things can then rest at their involvements. World is the wherein of this self-referral, identified with the toward-which of the freeing; worldhood is the structure of that web. Nothing subjective is asserted — the wherein is no interior — and nothing thing-like: world is the understood relational whole in which any encounter is always already emplaced. The parenthetical modal indifference ("authentic or inauthentic") keeps § 9's discipline: the derivation holds below the existentiell differential.

The ninth unit names the relation and grounds the possibility of this very analysis. That wherein Dasein always already understands itself in this way, with it Dasein is originally familiar. This familiarity with world does not necessarily require theoretical transparency of the relations constituting world as world; but the possibility of an explicit ontological-existential interpretation of these relations is grounded in this world-familiarity constitutive for Dasein, which for its part co-constitutes Dasein's understanding of being. The possibility can be expressly seized insofar as Dasein has set itself the task of an original interpretation of its being and its possibilities, or indeed of the meaning of being in general. § 16's closing question ("familiar with what?") is answered — with the significance-web itself, not with things — and the paragraph performs the book's signature reflexive loop: the analysis of world-familiarity is itself possible only on the ground of world-familiarity; fundamental ontology is the express seizure of a possibility deposited in what it analyzes (§ 4's radicalization-thesis, verified at world).

The tenth unit is transitional but exact about the state of play: with the analyses so far, only the horizon has been laid free within which such a thing as world and worldhood is to be sought; for the further consideration it must first be made clearer as what the context of Dasein's self-referring is to be ontologically grasped. The modesty is § 2's bookkeeping again — the phenomenon is located, not yet conceptually articulated; the articulation follows immediately.

The eleventh unit performs it, minting the chapter's final term. Understanding — to be analyzed more penetratingly later (§ 31) — holds the indicated relations in an antecedent disclosedness: in its familiar holding-itself-within-them, it holds them before itself as that in which its referring moves. Understanding lets itself be referred in and by these relations themselves; the relational character of these relations of referring we grasp as signifying (be-deuten). In familiarity with these relations Dasein "signifies" to itself: it gives itself, originally, its being and potentiality-of-being to understand with respect to its being-in-the-world. The for-the-sake-of-which signifies an in-order-to; this, a for-this; this, an at-which of letting-be-involved; this, a with-which of involvement. These relations are clasped together among themselves as an original totality; they are what they are as this signifying in which Dasein antecedently gives itself its being-in-the-world to understand. The relational whole of this signifying we call significance (Bedeutsamkeit); it is what constitutes the structure of world — of that wherein Dasein as such in each case already is. Dasein, in its familiarity with significance, is the ontic condition of the possibility of the discoverability of beings encountered in a world in the mode of being of involvement (readiness-to-hand), beings that can thus make themselves known in their in-itself. Dasein as such is in each case this: with its being, a context of the ready-to-hand is essentially already discovered — Dasein has, insofar as it is, in each case already referred itself to an encountering "world"; to its being belongs essentially this being-referred-upon (Angewiesenheit). The paragraph completes the chapter's conceptual ladder — reference, involvement, involvement-totality, significance — and its two closing theses balance each other with precision. Dasein is the ontic condition of discoverability: the strongest "idealist"-sounding claim in Division One, immediately counterweighted by Angewiesenheit — Dasein is dependent, referred upon a world it does not posit; conditioning and thrown dependence in one structure. The verb be-deuten, hyphenated, has been carefully de-linguistified: signifying here is the relational movement of the significance-web itself, not yet anything verbal — which sets up the next unit's founding claim.

The twelfth unit issues that claim in one sentence: significance itself, with which Dasein is always already familiar, harbors in itself the ontological condition of the possibility that understanding Dasein, as interpreting, can disclose such things as "significations" (Bedeutungen), which in their turn found the possible being of word and language. The founding order is a quiet revolution stated in passing: world-significance grounds significations, significations ground language — meaning is not deposited in words and projected onto things; words accrue to a significance already articulated in being-in-the-world (§ 34 will say it exactly so: to significations, words accrue). Every semantics that starts from the sign has the order inverted — § 17's subordination of sign to reference, now extended to language as such.

The thirteenth unit is a single-sentence theorem, banked for later use: disclosed significance, as an existential constitution of Dasein — of its being-in-the-world — is the ontic condition of the possibility of the discoverability of an involvement-totality. The compression is deliberate architecture: disclosure (of significance) conditions discovery (of involvements) — the § 16 terminology now runs as a load-bearing formula, and § 44's ordering of truth (disclosedness founding discoveredness) is pre-cast here.

The fourteenth unit voices the objection the whole analysis invites. If we thus determine the being of the ready-to-hand (involvement), and even worldhood itself, as a reference-context — is not the "substantial being" of innerworldly beings volatilized into a relation-system? And since relations are always "something thought," is not the being of the innerworldly dissolved into "pure thinking"? The objection is the era's idealism-charge in its exact contemporary form (world as a system of relations = world as posited by thought — the neo-Kantian construction of the object stands recognizably behind it), and Heidegger lets it speak at full strength before answering.

The fifteenth unit answers with the section's whole apparatus. Within the present field of investigation, the repeatedly marked differences of structure and dimension must be held apart in principle: first, the being of the innerworldly beings first encountered (readiness-to-hand); second, the being of beings (presence-at-hand) that become findable and determinable in an independent discovering passage through what is first encountered; third, the being of the ontic condition of the possibility of the discoverability of innerworldly beings in general — the worldhood of world. This last is an existential determination of being-in-the-world, of Dasein; the two former concepts of being are categories, concerning beings of non-Dasein-like being. The reference-context that constitutes worldhood as significance can be formally grasped as a relation-system — only, such formalizations level the phenomena so far that the authentic phenomenal content is lost, above all with such "simple" relations as significance harbors. These "relations" and "relata" — the in-order-to, the for-the-sake-of, the with-which of involvement — resist, by their phenomenal content, every mathematical functionalization; nor are they anything thought, first posited in a "thinking," but relations wherein concernful circumspection as such already dwells. This "relation-system," as constitutive of worldhood, so little volatilizes the being of the innerworldly ready-to-hand that on the ground of worldhood these beings are first discoverable in their "substantial" "in-itself"; and only when innerworldly beings can be encountered at all does the possibility exist of making the merely present-at-hand accessible in their field. On the ground of its mere-presence-at-hand these beings can be determined mathematically, with respect to their "properties," in "function-concepts" — which are ontologically possible at all only with regard to beings whose being has the character of pure substantiality: function-concepts are always possible only as formalized substance-concepts. The reply operates on three fronts. The three-level table (readiness-to-hand, presence-at-hand, worldhood — two categories and one existential) dissolves the objection's premise: worldhood is not a relation-system among things but the existential condition of there being things to relate. The anti-formalization argument redeems § 17's warning at the decisive spot: the significance-relations are lived-in, not thought — dwelt in by circumspection before any positing — and formalizing them levels precisely what they are. And the closing thrust turns the mathematical ideal against its own champions: Cassirer's celebrated progress from substance-concept to function-concept is reversed in one line — function-concepts are formalized substance-concepts, feeding on the very ontology of the present-at-hand they claim to supersede, and standing at two removes from world.

The closing unit announces the detour: so that the specifically ontological problematic of worldhood may stand out still more sharply, the interpretation of worldhood is to be clarified, before continuing the analysis, against an extreme counter-case. Section B — Descartes' ontology of the world as res extensa, the tradition's most rigorous execution of exactly the error just diagnosed — is thereby motivated from within: the positive analysis pauses to measure itself against its strongest historical opposite, the promised partial payment (§ 14) on Part Two's unwritten Descartes-division.

##### B. The Contrast between Our Analysis of Worldhood and Descartes' Interpretation of the World

The section opens by justifying the detour. The investigation can assure itself of the concept of worldhood, and of the structures enclosed in this phenomenon, only step by step; and because the interpretation of the world at first sets in with an innerworldly being, thereafter never bringing the phenomenon of world into view at all, this approach is to be clarified ontologically in what is perhaps its most extreme execution. Not only a short presentation of the basic features of Descartes' ontology of the "world" is given: its presuppositions are interrogated and characterized in the light of what has been won so far. The discussion is to make recognizable on what fundamentally undiscussed ontological "foundations" the interpretations of the world after Descartes — and those preceding him all the more — move. The rationale is exact: Descartes is not one erroneous world-theory among others but the extreme execution of the standard approach (world read off an innerworldly being), so his ontology serves as the concentrated specimen of what §§ 14–18 argued against diffusely. The closing sentence widens the indictment in both temporal directions — post-Cartesian and pre-Cartesian world-interpretations share his undiscussed foundations — which is why refuting him is not antiquarianism.

The second preamble unit fixes the connection to what follows and the itinerary. Descartes sees the ontological basic determination of the world in extensio; and since extension co-constitutes spatiality — for Descartes is even identical with it — while spatiality remains in some sense constitutive for the world, the discussion of the Cartesian ontology of the "world" offers at the same time a negative foothold for the positive explication of the spatiality of the environing world and of Dasein itself (section C). Three things are treated: the determination of the "world" as res extensa (§ 19); the foundations of this ontological determination (§ 20); the hermeneutical discussion of the Cartesian ontology of the "world" (§ 21) — the consideration receiving its detailed grounding only through the phenomenological destruction of the cogito sum (Part Two, Division Two). The architecture is candid: exposition, genealogy of foundations, critical discussion — a destruction in miniature — with the IOU to the unwritten Part Two explicitly signed; and the bridge to section C explains the placement: because Descartes identifies world with extension, refuting him clears the ground for the positive theory of space.

###### § 19. The Determination of the "World" as res extensa

The opening unit locates the distinction and its unclarified being. Descartes distinguishes the ego cogito from the res corporea; this distinction henceforth determines ontologically the distinction of "nature and spirit." However many ontic variations of content this opposition may receive, the unclarity of its ontological foundations, and of the opposed members themselves, has its proximate root in the distinction Descartes carried out. Within what understanding of being did he determine the being of these beings? The title for the being of something that is in itself is substantia — an expression meaning now the being of a being that is as substance, substantiality, now the being itself, a substance; and this double meaning of substantia, already carried by the ancient concept of ousia, is not accidental. Three theses in five sentences: the modern nature/spirit dualism, in all its later ontic costumes (the Naturwissenschaften/Geisteswissenschaften divide of Heidegger's own day included), is genealogically Cartesian; the distinction was drawn within an unexamined understanding of being; and the systematic ambiguity of "substance" — being of a being versus the being itself — is no lexical slip but a structural symptom, whose diagnosis § 20 will deliver (ontic answers standing in for an ontological question). The alignment with ousia quietly attaches the analysis to § 6's genealogy.

The second unit extracts the definition from the Principia. The ontological determination of the res corporea demands the explication of substance — of the substantiality of this being as a substance. What constitutes the authentic being-in-itself of the res corporea? Substances are accessible in their "attributes," and each substance has a distinguished property from which the essence of the substantiality of that determinate substance can be read off. Which is the property of the res corporea? Extension in length, breadth, and depth constitutes the authentic being of the corporeal substance we call "world." And what gives extensio this distinction? "Everything else attributable to body presupposes extension": extension is the constitution of being of the being in question, which must already "be" before all other determinations of being so that they can "be" what they are; extension must be "assigned" to the corporeal thing primarily. Accordingly the proof for the extension and the extension-characterized substantiality of the "world" proceeds by showing that all other determinacies of this substance — above all divisio, figura, motus — are conceivable only as modes of extensio, while conversely extensio remains intelligible sine figura vel motu. The reconstruction is scrupulously fair — Descartes' criterion (the asymmetry of presupposition: shape and motion presuppose extension, never conversely) is a genuine ontological argument, an a priori of the corporeal — and the fairness is strategic: § 21's "rescue" will credit exactly this as proto-Kantian apriorism, while the critique will strike not the argument but the unasked question beneath its terms (what "being" means in "must already be").

The third unit gives Descartes' own illustration: a corporeal thing can, while retaining its total extension, yet vary the distribution of that extension along the different dimensions in manifold ways, and present itself in manifold shapes as one and the same thing — the Principia passage on one body extended now more in length and less in breadth, soon after the reverse. The wax of the Meditations stands recognizably behind the citation: identity through qualitative variation is anchored in quantity conserved — the same thing is the same because its extension persists — so that permanence is already functioning as the criterion of authentic being, one paragraph before Heidegger names it.

The fourth unit completes the reduction and names the result. Shape is a mode of extensio, and no less motion, for motus is grasped only "if we think of nothing but locomotion and do not inquire into the force by which it is aroused": if motion is a property that is of the res corporea, it must, to be experienceable in its being, be conceived from the being of this being — from extensio, hence as pure change of place; anything like "force" contributes nothing to the determination of this being's being. Determinations like durities (hardness), pondus (weight), color can be taken away from matter, and it remains what it is; they do not constitute its authentic being, and insofar as they are, they prove to be modes of extensio. Descartes shows this in detail for hardness: touch tells us only that the parts of hard bodies resist the motion of our hands; but if, whenever our hands moved toward a place, all bodies there retreated with the same speed as the hands approach, we would never feel hardness — and yet it is in no way intelligible that bodies retreating in this fashion would thereby lose anything of their corporeal nature; hence body's nature does not consist in hardness. In the same manner weight, color, and all other such qualities sensed in corporeal matter can be removed from it while it itself remains intact: its (extension's) nature depends on none of them. What constitutes the being of the res corporea is accordingly the extensio — the omnimodo divisibile, figurabile et mobile, what can change in every manner of divisibility, shaping, and motion, the capax mutationum, that which sustains itself through all these changes, remanet; what in the corporeal thing suffices for such constant remaining is the authentically being element in it, so much so that by it the substantiality of this substance is characterized. The unit is exposition, but the last sentences are already the verdict's premise laid bare: Descartes' operational test for authentic being is survival of variation — what remains is what is. The thought-experiment on hardness, here merely reported, is banked for § 21, where it becomes the star exhibit; and the exclusion of force is worth marking (Leibniz's later counter-attack on precisely this point hovers unnamed): a world of pure extension has room for change of place but none for power, tendency, or the resistant — the ontological poverty the hardness-analysis will expose from the side of experience.

###### § 20. The Foundations of the Ontological Determination of the "World"

The opening unit digs to the first foundation: substantiality as independence, and its theological scale. The idea of being to which the ontological characterization of the res extensa goes back is substantiality: "by substance we can understand nothing other than a thing that exists in such a way that it needs no other thing in order to exist." The being of a "substance" is characterized by a needlessness (Unbedürftigkeit); what in its being is simply in need of no other being satisfies the idea of substance in the authentic sense — this being is the ens perfectissimum. "A substance needing no other thing whatever can be understood as one only, namely God." "God" is here a purely ontological title, understood as ens perfectissimum; at the same time, what is "self-evidently" co-meant with the concept of God makes possible an ontological interpretation of the constitutive moment of substantiality, needlessness: everything that is not God needs production in the widest sense, and conservation. Production toward presence-at-hand, or needlessness-of-production, constitute the horizon within which "being" is understood; every being that is not God is ens creatum. Between the two an "infinite" difference of being obtains — and yet we address the created just as much as the creator as beings: we use "being" in a breadth whose sense embraces an "infinite" difference. So created beings too can with a certain right be called substances: relative to God they need production and conservation, but within the region of the created — the "world" as ens creatum — there are beings that, relative to creaturely production and conservation (man's, for instance), "need no other being." Such substances are two: the res cogitans and the res extensa. The paragraph executes § 6's promissory note in full view: substantiality is cashed as independence, independence is measured on the creator/created axis, and creation means production — so the horizon of Descartes' concept of being is Herstellung, the ancient production-ontology in theological dress. The three-substance architecture (one infinite, two relatively independent finite substances) is thereby shown to be a system of graded needlessness — and the phrase "production toward presence-at-hand" welds § 6's two theses (being as producedness, being as constant presence) into a single horizon.

The second unit finds the buried problem: analogy. The being of the substance whose distinguishing proprietas is extensio would be ontologically determinable in principle only if the sense of being "common" to the three substances — one infinite, two finite — were clarified. But "the name substance does not apply univocally to God and to them, as they say in the Schools": Descartes here touches a problem that much occupied medieval ontology — in what way the signification of being signifies the being addressed in each case. In "God is" and "the world is" we assert being, but the "is" cannot mean each being in the same sense (univoce), given the infinite difference of being between them; were the signifying univocal, the created would be meant as uncreated or the uncreated dragged down to a creature. Nor does "being" function as a mere identical name: in both cases "being" is understood. The Schools grasped the positive sense of the signifying of "being" as "analogous" signification, in distinction from the univocal and the merely homonymous, and — following Aristotle, in whom, as in the approach of Greek ontology generally, the problem is prefigured — fixed various modes of analogy, by which the "schools" also differ in conceiving the signifying function of being. In the ontological working-through of the problem Descartes falls far behind scholasticism (the note pointing to Cajetan's De nominum analogia as the standard of comparison); indeed he evades the question: "no signification of this name that would be common to God and creatures can be distinctly understood." This evasion means: Descartes leaves undiscussed the sense of being enclosed in the idea of substantiality, and the character of the "universality" of this signification. Medieval ontology, to be sure, asked after what being itself means as little as the ancient — so it is no surprise that a question like that of the mode of signifying of being makes no headway so long as it is to be discussed on the ground of an unclarified sense of being, which the signification "expresses"; the sense remained unclarified because it was held "self-evident." The unit is § 1's first prejudice returned with names attached: the analogy problem — Aristotle's unity-of-being question, Brentano's and the young Heidegger's own starting point — is the exact place where Descartes' system needed an ontology and posted instead a declaration of unintelligibility. The judgment is finely graded: scholasticism at least worked the problem (Cajetan's treatise as its high-water mark); Descartes regresses from the tradition he inherits — modernity's "new beginning" as a loss of a question, § 6's pattern confirmed at the letter.

The third unit exposes the second foundation: the inaccessibility of being and the detour through attributes. Descartes not only evades the ontological question of substantiality; he expressly stresses that substance as such — its substantiality — is antecedently inaccessible in and for itself: "substance cannot first be noticed merely from its being existent, because this alone does not affect us." "Being" itself does not "affect" us, therefore it cannot be perceived — "being is no real predicate," in Kant's dictum, which merely renders Descartes' proposition. Therewith the possibility of a pure problematic of being is renounced in principle, and a way out is sought by which the determinations of substances are then won: because "being" is in fact not accessible as a being, it is expressed through ontic determinacies of the respective being — attributes; not arbitrary ones, but those that most purely satisfy the tacitly presupposed sense of being and substantiality. In the finite substance as res corporea the primarily necessary "assignment" is extensio: "indeed we understand extended substance, or thinking substance, more easily than substance alone, omitting that it thinks or is extended" — for substantiality is detachable only ratione tantum, not realiter, not findable like the substantial being itself. The paragraph is a small masterpiece of destruction: the famous Kantian thesis is genealogically returned to Descartes and re-read — not as a critical insight but as a renunciation: from "being does not affect us" the tradition concluded not that being demands a non-ontic mode of access (§ 2's own inference: being requires its own way of being shown) but that ontology must deal in beings' determinacies. The detour through the privileged attribute is thus the structural consequence of an evaded question — being expressed by proxy, the proxy selected by a sense of being nobody examined.

The closing unit draws the balance and vindicates the method of "word-quibbling." Thus the ontological foundations of the determination of the "world" as res extensa have become clear: the idea of substantiality — not only unclarified in its sense of being but declared unclarifiable — presented by the detour through the preeminent substantial property of the respective substance. In the determination of the substance through a substantial being lies also the ground of the term's double meaning: substantiality is intended, and it is understood from an ontic constitution of the substance; because something ontic is made to underlie the ontological, the expression substantia functions now in ontological, now in ontic, mostly in a blurred ontic-ontological signification. But behind this slight difference of signification hides the failure to master the fundamental problem of being; working it through requires "tracking the equivocations in the right way" — whoever attempts this is not "occupied" with "mere word-meanings" but must venture into the most original problematic of the "things themselves" to bring such "nuances" into the clear. The diagnosis announced at § 19 is delivered: the ambiguity of "substance" is the linguistic fossil of a category-substitution — the ontic underlaid beneath the ontological — and thus of the ontological difference suppressed. The closing apologia generalizes the procedure: semantic archaeology of this kind is Sachforschung, not philology; equivocation is where buried ontology surfaces, so the "nuance" is the phenomenon (§ 7 B's method — one word's drifted senses tracked to their ground — justified as first philosophy).

###### § 21. The Hermeneutical Discussion of the Cartesian Ontology of the "World"

The opening unit poses the critical question and answers it without ceremony. Does this ontology of the "world" seek the phenomenon of world at all — and if not, does it at least determine an innerworldly being far enough that its worldly character can be made visible in it? Both questions are to be answered in the negative. The being that Descartes tries to grasp ontologically and in principle with the extensio is rather such as becomes discoverable only in passing through what is first ready-to-hand innerworldly. But granting that, and granting even that the ontological characterization of this determinate innerworldly being (nature) — both the idea of substantiality and the sense of the existit and ad existendum taken up into its definition — leads into darkness, there remains the possibility that an ontology grounded on the radical separation of God, I, and "world" poses and furthers the ontological problem of the world in some sense. If, however, even this possibility does not obtain, then the express demonstration must be produced that Descartes gives not merely a mistaken ontological determination of the world, but that his interpretation and its foundations led to skipping over the phenomenon of world as well as the being of the innerworldly beings first ready-to-hand. The verdict-structure is worth pausing on: "hermeneutical discussion" names the genre — not refutation of theses but exhibition of what a problematic could and could not see from its ground (§ 6's destruction-concept: positive possibilities as limits). And the charge is calibrated as double skipping: world missed, and the ready-to-hand missed — Descartes' extensio-being is the § 13/§ 15 product (reached only through the ready-to-hand and its de-worlding) mistaken for the primary stratum.

The second unit identifies the access-decision that predetermines everything. In the exposition of the worldhood-problem (§ 14) the importance of winning an adequate access to the phenomenon was noted; so the critical question runs: which mode of being of Dasein is fixed as the appropriate mode of access to the beings whose being, as extensio, Descartes equates with the being of the "world"? The sole and genuine access to these beings is knowing, intellectio, in the sense of mathematical-physical knowledge. Mathematical knowledge counts as that manner of grasping beings which can at all times be certain of the secure possession of the being of the beings grasped in it; whatever, in its mode of being, is such as to satisfy the being made accessible in mathematical knowledge, is in the authentic sense. Such beings are what always is what it is; hence, in the experienced beings of the world, their authentic being is constituted by what can be shown to have the character of constant remaining, as remanens capax mutationum. Authentically is what everlastingly remains; such is what mathematics knows; what is accessible through it in beings constitutes their being. So, from a determinate idea of being enveloped in the concept of substantiality, and from the idea of a knowledge that knows beings in this way, the "world" has its being dictated to it, as it were. Descartes does not let the mode of being of innerworldly beings be pregiven by them; rather, on the ground of an idea of being unrevealed in its origin and unattested in its right — being = constant presence-at-hand — he prescribes to the world its "authentic" being. Thus it is not primarily reliance on a science he happened to esteem, mathematics, that determines the ontology of the world, but the fundamental ontological orientation toward being as constant presence-at-hand, whose grasping mathematical knowledge satisfies in an exceptional way. Descartes thereby carries out, philosophically and expressly, the switching-over of the effect of the traditional ontology onto modern mathematical physics and its transcendental foundations. This is the section's — arguably Division One's — central historical thesis, and its causal order is the whole point: not "Descartes mathematized being because he loved mathematics" but the reverse — the inherited equation of being with constant presence selected mathematics as its adequate organ, since mathematics is the knowledge of the invariant. The phrase "being = ständige Vorhandenheit" here gets its canonical formulation, fusing § 6's ousia-as-Anwesenheit with § 19's remanet-criterion; and the closing sentence assigns Descartes his exact world-historical role: the relay-switch through which Greek ontology energizes modern physics.

The third unit notes that the access-problem could not even arise. Descartes has no need to pose the problem of adequate access to innerworldly beings: under the unbroken predominance of the traditional ontology, the genuine manner of grasping authentic beings has been decided in advance — it lies in noein, "intuition" in the widest sense, of which dianoein, "thinking," is only a founded form of enactment; and from this fundamental ontological orientation Descartes delivers his "critique" of the still possible intuitively perceiving mode of access, sensatio (aisthēsis) as against intellectio. The genealogy is compressed but complete: Parmenides' noein (§ 6), ranked above discursive thought since Greek ontology's founding, silently supplies Descartes both his ideal of access and the terms of his sense-critique — the "new" method never chose its court of appeal.

The fourth unit reports that critique in Descartes' own words. Descartes knows very well that beings do not proximally show themselves in their authentic being: "proximally" given is this determinately colored, tasting, hard, cold, sounding wax-thing — but this, and whatever the senses give, remains ontologically without weight: "it suffices to note that the perceptions of the senses relate only to that union of the human body with the mind, and ordinarily exhibit to us what external bodies can profit or harm it." The senses do not let beings be known in their being at all; they merely report the usefulness and harmfulness of "external" innerworldly things for the body-burdened human essence; "they do not teach us what (bodies) are in themselves": through the senses we get no disclosure at all about beings in their being — "the nature of matter consists not in hardness or weight or color or any other mode of affecting the senses, but solely in its being a thing extended in length, breadth, and depth." Heidegger's citation-strategy is a trap lovingly set: Descartes himself testifies that the senses deliver the beneficial and the harmful — that is, in § 18's vocabulary, involvement, the um-zu structure of the environing world — and then discards precisely this as ontologically void. The tradition's text preserves the phenomenon its ontology annuls: prime material for a destruction.

The fifth unit announces the counter-analysis: how little Descartes can let what shows itself in sensibility give itself its own mode of being, let alone determine it, becomes clear from a critical analysis of his interpretation of the experience of hardness and resistance (cf. § 19). A hinge-unit, but its formula is the whole method of the book in one line: the standard is sich vorgeben lassen — letting the phenomenon dictate its own categorial treatment — and the hardness-analysis is the controlled experiment.

The sixth unit performs it. Hardness is grasped as resistance; but resistance, as little as hardness, is understood in a phenomenal sense — as something experienced in itself and determinable in such experience. For Descartes resistance means: not yielding from the spot, that is, undergoing no change of place; a thing's resisting then means remaining at a determinate place relative to another thing changing its place, or changing place with such speed that the other can "catch up" with it. By this interpretation of the experience of hardness, the mode of being of sensuous perceiving is extinguished — and with it the possibility of grasping in its being the beings encountered in such perceiving. Descartes translates the mode of being of a perceiving of something into the only one he knows: perceiving something becomes a determinate side-by-side presence-at-hand of two present-at-hand res extensae; the motion-relation of the two is itself in the mode of extensio, which primarily characterizes the presence-at-hand of the corporeal thing. True, the possible "fulfillment" of a touching comportment requires a distinguished "nearness" of the touchable; but this does not mean that contact, and the hardness announcing itself in it, consist, ontologically taken, in the different speeds of two corporeal things. Hardness and resistance do not show themselves at all unless there is a being with the mode of being of Dasein — or at least of something living. The analysis is § 12's chair-and-wall argument armed and fired at its proper target: Descartes' kinematic reduction of hardness deletes the perceiver — two bodies with matched velocities never touch, but neither do two bodies of any velocities "resist" one another except for a being to whose concern something can be resistant. Resistance is an encounter-phenomenon, indexed to being-in-the-world (or at least to life — the § 10 privative reservation carefully repeated); the reduction does not explain the phenomenon but re-describes a world from which it has been erased. Behind the passage stands a whole contemporary debate — resistance-experience as the proof of the external world (Dilthey; later § 43 confronts Scheler's version) — whose premise Heidegger here undercuts: resistance presupposes disclosed world and so can prove nothing about it.

The seventh unit names the circle: thus, for Descartes, the discussion of possible accesses to innerworldly beings comes under the dominance of an idea of being that is itself read off a determinate region of those very beings. The one-sentence unit is the diagnosis in its tightest form — the epistemology is downstream of a regional ontology (extension), which was itself never interrogated: § 13's order (access-theory presupposing ontology of the knower and the known) confirmed on the corpus.

The eighth unit totals the cost. The idea of being as constant presence-at-hand not only motivates an extreme determination of the being of innerworldly beings and its identification with the world in general; it at once prevents bringing Dasein's comportments ontologically into view in an adequate way — and thereby the way is completely blocked toward seeing the founded character of all sensuous and intellectual perceiving and understanding these as a possibility of being-in-the-world. The being of "Dasein," to whose basic constitution being-in-the-world belongs, Descartes grasps in the same way as the being of the res extensa — as substance. The escalation matters: the casualty-list runs from world through perception to Dasein itself — the res cogitans is the present-at-hand ontology applied to the being it fits least (§ 10's diagnosis of the cogito's undetermined sum, now shown to be not indeterminacy but a positive misdetermination: substance).

The ninth unit voices the fairness-objection: but is not a task being foisted on Descartes with these critical discussions, and then "demonstrated" as unsolved by him, which lay wholly outside his horizon — how should Descartes identify a determinate innerworldly being and its being with the world, if he does not know the phenomenon of world, and hence anything like innerworldliness, at all? The objection is genuinely strong — anachronism is the standing risk of every destruction — and Heidegger states it at full force before answering.

The tenth unit answers with a principle of interpretation. In the field of fundamental confrontation, one may not hold merely to doxographically graspable theses; orientation must be taken from the substantive tendency of the problematic, even if it does not get beyond a vulgar formulation. That Descartes, with res cogitans and res extensa, not only wished to pose the problem of "I and world" but claimed a radical solution for it, is clear from the Meditations (especially I and VI); that his fundamental ontological orientation to the tradition, devoid of all positive critique, made it impossible for him to lay free an original ontological problematic of Dasein, had to obstruct his view of the phenomenon of world, and could force the ontology of the "world" into the ontology of a determinate innerworldly being — this the foregoing discussions were to prove. The hermeneutical principle here formulated — interpret the sachliche Tendenz, what a thinking was reaching for, not only what it managed to say — is the charter of all Heidegger's violent readings (the Kant book will invoke it expressly). It converts the anachronism-charge: measuring Descartes by the world-problem is legitimate exactly because "I and world" is his problem, in vulgar form; the destruction judges a philosophy by its own deepest tendency and shows the tradition blocking that tendency's fulfillment.

The eleventh unit lets the strongest defense speak: the layer-ontology. But — one will counter — granted the problem of world and the being of the environmentally nearest beings remain covered: Descartes has still laid the ground for the ontological characterization of the innerworldly being that founds every other being in its being — material nature. On this fundamental stratum the remaining strata of innerworldly actuality are built up: in the extended thing as such are grounded, first, determinacies that show themselves as qualities but are "at bottom" quantitative modifications of the modes of extensio; on these still reducible qualities rest the specific qualities — beautiful, ugly, fitting, unfitting, usable, unusable — which, in primary orientation to thinghood, must be grasped as non-quantifiable value-predicates by which the merely material thing is stamped a good. With this layering, the consideration does after all arrive at the beings we characterized ontologically as ready-to-hand equipment; the Cartesian analysis of the "world" thus first makes possible the secure construction of the structure of the proximally ready-to-hand — it needs only the easily accomplished supplementation of the natural thing into the full use-thing. The reconstructed position is no straw man: it is, recognizably, the reigning program — the stratified constitution of the cultural object on the founding stratum of nature, the "value-laden thing" of § 15 — here presented at its most plausible, as the friendly completion of Descartes rather than his refutation.

The twelfth unit demolishes it. Setting the specific world-problem aside: is the being of what is innerworldly first encountered ontologically reachable on this path at all? Is not, with material thinghood, a being tacitly posited — constant thing-presence-at-hand — which is so little ontologically supplemented by the subsequent outfitting of beings with value-predicates that these value-characters themselves remain merely ontic determinacies of a being with the thing's mode of being? The addition of value-predicates cannot give the least new disclosure about the being of goods; it merely presupposes again, for them, the mode of being of pure presence-at-hand: values are present-at-hand determinacies of a thing, having their ontological origin solely in the antecedent positing of thing-actuality as the fundamental stratum. But already pre-phenomenological experience shows, in the beings meant as things, something that thinghood does not make fully intelligible — so thingly being needs a supplement. What, though, does the being of values or their "validity" (which Lotze grasped as a mode of "affirmation") mean ontologically? What does this "adhering" of values to things signify ontologically? So long as these determinations remain in the dark, the reconstruction of the use-thing out of the natural thing is an ontologically questionable enterprise — quite apart from the fundamental perversion of the problematic. And does not this reconstruction of the first "skinned" use-thing always already need the antecedent positive view of the phenomenon whose wholeness the reconstruction is to restore? If its ownmost constitution of being is not adequately explicated beforehand, does the reconstruction not build without a blueprint? Insofar as this reconstruction and "supplementation" of the traditional ontology of the "world" arrives, in its result, at the same beings from which the analysis of equipmental readiness-to-hand and involvement-totality set out, it awakens the semblance that the being of these beings has indeed been clarified or even become a problem — but as little as Descartes hits the being of substance with extensio as proprietas, so little can refuge in "value" constitutions bring being as readiness-to-hand even into view, let alone make it an ontological theme. The argument has three blades. Regress: value-predicates inherit the substrate's ontology — decorating the present-at-hand yields decorated present-at-hand, never the ready-to-hand (§ 15's south-wind argument generalized). Vicious presupposition: the reconstruction is guided throughout by an unthematized prior view of the very use-thing it claims to build — assembly without a blueprint, or rather with a blueprint it refuses to acknowledge; the "skinning" metaphor gives the true order of operations away (the natural thing is what remains after de-worlding, not what was there first). Semblance of success: because the layering terminates at the same entities the tool-analysis began from, it looks equivalent — the deep methodological warning, since ontologies are distinguished not by their inventories but by the being they let be seen.

The thirteenth unit fixes Descartes' precise contribution to the error: he sharpened the narrowing of the question of the world to the question of natural thinghood, as the innerworldly being proximally accessible, and consolidated the opinion that the supposedly strictest ontic knowledge of a being is also the possible access to the primary being of the beings discovered in such knowledge. But at the same time one must see that even the "supplementations" of the thing-ontology move fundamentally on the same dogmatic basis as Descartes. The verdict distributes responsibility historically: the narrowing is ancient (§ 6), Descartes radicalized and armed it; and the contemporary value-philosophies, self-styled correctors of naturalism, are convicted of Cartesianism at the foundation — the § 10 pattern (ontic protest, ontological complicity) at the scale of a whole century's philosophy.

The fourteenth unit re-grounds the failure in Dasein and names the condition of legitimate critique. We already indicated (§ 14) that skipping over the world and the beings first encountered is not accidental, not an oversight simply to be made up, but grounds in an essential mode of being of Dasein itself. Only when the analytic of Dasein has made transparent the most important main structures of Dasein within the frame of this problematic, when the concept of being in general has been assigned the horizon of its possible intelligibility — so that readiness-to-hand and presence-at-hand too first become originally intelligible ontologically — only then can the critique of the Cartesian world-ontology, still fundamentally usual today, be set into its philosophical right. The unit is a candid audit of the section's own epistemic status: the critique so far is provisional, its full right pending the horizon of being (temporality) — the destruction, once more, is possible only within the worked-out question (§ 6), and § 21 confesses itself an installment.

The fifteenth unit posts the questions that would complete it, referring to the never-written Division Three: it must be shown why, at the beginning of the ontological tradition decisive for us — with Parmenides explicitly — the phenomenon of world was skipped over, and whence the constant recurrence of this skipping; why innerworldly beings leap in as the ontological theme in place of the skipped phenomenon; why these beings are found first in "nature"; and why the supplementation of such a world-ontology, experienced as necessary, is carried out with the help of the value-phenomenon. The four questions are the section's findings converted into a research program — occlusion of world, substitution of the innerworldly, privilege of nature, value as prosthesis — each demanding a temporal explanation (why presence dominates) that only "Time and Being" could give; the reference "Part One, Division 3" is among the book's explicit pointers into its own missing third.

The sixteenth unit states what hangs on the answers: only in them is the positive understanding of the world-problematic reached, the origin of its being-missed exhibited, and the legal ground of a rejection of the traditional world-ontology demonstrated. The juridical vocabulary (Rechtsgrund) keeps the destruction honest: until the genealogy is complete, the rejection is motivated but not yet adjudicated.

The seventeenth unit sums the lesson for method: the considerations on Descartes were to bring the insight that the seemingly self-evident point of departure from the things of the world, as little as the orientation to the supposedly strictest knowledge of beings, guarantees winning the soil on which the nearest ontological constitutions of world, Dasein, and innerworldly beings are phenomenally to be met. The two false securities — the obvious (things) and the exact (mathematics) — are precisely the two authorities § 1 diagnosed as the question's suppressors: self-evidence and methodological rigor, both now shown capable of organizing a total miss.

The closing unit performs the promised rescue. If we recall that spatiality manifestly co-constitutes innerworldly beings, a "rescue" of the Cartesian analysis of the "world" becomes possible after all: with the radical exhibition of extensio as the praesuppositum for every determinacy of the res corporea, Descartes prepared the understanding of an a priori whose content Kant then fixed more penetratingly. The analysis of extensio remains, within certain limits, independent of the omission of an express interpretation of the being of extended beings; the positing of extensio as basic determinacy of the "world" has its phenomenal right — even though in going back to it neither the spatiality of the world, nor the spatiality first discovered of the beings encountered in the environing world, nor indeed the spatiality of Dasein itself can be ontologically conceived. The destruction ends, as § 6 promised it always must, positively: Descartes' insight (extension as presupposed by every corporeal determination — an a priori discovery, the ancestor of Kant's) is staked out precisely in its limits — three spatialities lie beyond its reach, and these three (of the ready-to-hand, of being-in-the-world, of Dasein and space) are exactly the three stations of section C, to which the analysis now turns with its counter-case fully measured.

##### C. The Aroundness of the Environing World and the Spatiality of Dasein

The section opens by recalling the negative result that now demands its positive complement. In the first predelineation of being-in (§ 12), Dasein had to be demarcated against a mode of being in space called insideness — an extended being enclosed by the extended boundaries of something extended, both present-at-hand in space. But the rejection of such an insideness of Dasein in a spatial container was not meant to exclude in principle every spatiality of Dasein; it was to keep the way clear for seeing the spatiality constitutive for Dasein — which must now be set forth. And since innerworldly beings are likewise in space, their spatiality will stand in an ontological connection with the world: it must be determined in what sense space is a constituent of the world, which was itself characterized as a structural moment of being-in-the-world. In particular it must be shown how the aroundness of the environing world — the specific spatiality of the beings encountered in it — is founded through the worldhood of the world, and not conversely the world present-at-hand in space. The investigation starts from an analysis of the innerworldly ready-to-hand in space and runs through three stages: the spatiality of the innerworldly ready-to-hand (§ 22), the spatiality of being-in-the-world (§ 23), the spatiality of Dasein and space (§ 24). The preamble's single sentence of doctrine is the founding-thesis in its sharpest form: world is not in space; space is world-founded — the exact inversion of Descartes just measured in section B, now to be earned positively. The three-stage order repeats the book's constant procedure: from the beings encountered, through the encountering being-in, to the phenomenon itself (space) — never the reverse.

###### § 22. The Spatiality of the Innerworldly Ready-to-Hand

The opening unit states the task's continuity: if space in some still-to-be-determined sense constitutes the world, it cannot surprise that the foregoing ontological characterization of the being of the innerworldly had to keep it in view also as inner-spatial; but this spatiality of the ready-to-hand has not yet been expressly grasped phenomenally, nor exhibited in its interlocking with the being-structure of the ready-to-hand — that is now the task. The word Verklammerung (interlocking) announces the method: spatiality will not be added to readiness-to-hand but read out of it.

The second unit finds space already inside the section's basic term. How have we already struck the spatiality of the ready-to-hand? There was talk of the proximally ready-to-hand — which means not only what is encountered first, before other beings, but at once what is "nearby" (in der Nähe): the ready-to-hand of everyday dealings has the character of nearness. Looked at closely, this nearness of equipment is already intimated in the very term for its being, Zu-handenheit — to-handedness. But what is "to hand" has in each case a different nearness, not fixed by measuring distances: this nearness regulates itself out of circumspectively "calculating" handling and use; and circumspection fixes what is near in this way also with regard to the direction in which the equipment is at all times accessible. The directed nearness of equipment means that it does not merely have its position in space, present-at-hand somewhere; as equipment it is essentially installed and accommodated, set up, laid out. Equipment has its place (Platz) — or else it "lies around," which differs in principle from pure occurrence at an arbitrary spatial position. The respective place determines itself, as the place of this equipment for..., out of a whole of places directed toward one another belonging to the environmentally ready-to-hand equipment-context; place and the place-manifold must not be interpreted as the where of some arbitrary presence-at-hand of things. The place is in each case the determinate "there" and "yonder" of an equipment's belonging-there (Hingehören); and the respective belonging corresponds to the equipment-character of the ready-to-hand — its involvement-belonging to an equipmental whole. But at the ground of the placeable belonging of an equipmental whole, as the condition of its possibility, lies the whither in general (das Wohin überhaupt), into which the place-totality is assigned to an equipment-context: this whither of possible equipmental belonging, held circumspectively in advance in view in concernful dealings, we call the region (die Gegend). The paragraph is a phenomenology of everyday space at full density: nearness as a practical magnitude (regulated by use, not metric); place as belonging (the hammer's place on its hook versus a position in a coordinate manifold — even disorder, "lying around," is a mode of place, not its absence); and the transcendental step at the close — places presuppose a prior whither, the region, exactly as § 18's involvements presupposed the totality: the argument-form of the whole chapter, run once more on space.

The third unit unfolds the region and buries three-dimensionality. "In the region of" means not only "in the direction toward" but at once in the circuit of something lying in that direction. The place constituted by direction and de-severedness — nearness is only a mode of this — is already oriented toward and within a region: something like a region must previously be discovered if the assigning and finding of places for a circumspectively available equipmental whole is to become possible. This regional orientation of the place-manifold constitutes the aroundness (das Umhafte), the around-us of the beings encountered environmentally nearest. Never is a three-dimensional manifold of possible positions first given, to be filled up with present-at-hand things: this dimensionality of space is still veiled in the spatiality of the ready-to-hand. The "above" is the "at the ceiling," the "below" the "on the floor," the "behind" the "at the door"; all wheres are discovered through the paths and ways of everyday dealings and circumspectively interpreted — not ascertained and catalogued by an observational measuring of space. Two claims of rank: the "um" of Umwelt receives its promised non-spatial (or pre-metric) reading — aroundness is the regional articulation of belonging, not geometrical surroundment; and everyday spatial deixis is enlisted as evidence — up, down, behind are use-determinations ("at the ceiling," "by the door"), place-names of dwelling, discovered by walking the ways, so that lived space is anisotropic and significant where geometric space is homogeneous and indifferent.

The fourth unit shows regions preceding things — and gives the day and the dead as proofs. Regions are not first formed by things present-at-hand together; they are in each case already ready-to-hand in the individual places. Places themselves are assigned to the ready-to-hand in the circumspection of concern, or are come upon; hence what is constantly ready-to-hand, with which circumspective being-in-the-world reckons in advance, has its place. The where of its readiness-to-hand is put into the reckoning of concern and oriented toward the rest of the ready-to-hand: thus the sun, whose light and warmth stand in everyday use, has — from the changing usability of what it bestows — its circumspectively discovered, distinguished places: sunrise, midday, sunset, midnight. The places of this changingly yet uniformly-constantly ready-to-hand become emphatic "indicators" of the regions lying in them; these celestial regions, which need have no geographical sense at all, pregive the antecedent whither for every particular shaping of regions occupiable by places. The house has its sunny side and its weather side; the distribution of the "rooms" is oriented by them, and within the rooms the "arrangement," each according to its equipment-character. Churches and graves, for instance, are laid out toward the rising and setting of the sun — the regions of life and death, from which Dasein itself is determined with regard to its ownmost possibilities of being in the world. The concern of Dasein, for which in its being this being itself is at stake, antecedently discovers the regions with which, in each case, it has a decisive involvement; the antecedent discovery of regions is co-determined by the involvement-totality toward which the ready-to-hand is freed as encounterable. The examples ascend deliberately: the sun as the primal constant equipment (its "places" — sunrise, noon — the first indicators of regions, and, marked for § 80, of time); the house articulated by sun-side and weather-side; and then, startlingly, the oriented church and grave — East and West as the regions of life and death. The last example carries the section's deepest point: regions are constituted by what Dasein's being is about — even mortality spatializes itself — so that the significance-structure (§ 18) reaches all the way into the layout of the earth; existential space is stretched between birth-directions and death-directions before it is ever measured.

The closing unit gathers the section and hands the ball to § 23. The antecedent readiness-to-hand of the respective region has, in a sense still more original than the being of the ready-to-hand, the character of inconspicuous familiarity: it becomes visible itself only in the manner of conspicuousness, in a circumspective discovering of the ready-to-hand, and specifically in the deficient modes of concern — in not finding something at its place, the region of that place often becomes expressly accessible as such for the first time. The space discovered in circumspective being-in-the-world as the spatiality of the equipmental whole belongs, as its place, in each case to the beings themselves; bare space is still veiled: space is splintered into places. But this spatiality has, through the worldly involvement-totality of the spatially ready-to-hand, its own unity: the "environing world" does not arrange itself in a pregiven space; rather its specific worldhood articulates, in its significance, the involvement-context of a respective totality of circumspectively assigned places. The respective world discovers in each case the spatiality of the space belonging to it. And letting the ready-to-hand be encountered in its environmental space remains ontically possible only because Dasein itself is "spatial" with regard to its being-in-the-world. Every prior structure re-runs at the region: inconspicuous familiarity (§ 16's positive privative — more original here than at the tool), visibility through breakdown (the missing item lights up its region), and the anti-container conclusion: no pregiven space furnished by a world, but a significance-articulated place-whole from which "bare space" must first be extracted. "Space splintered into places" is the formula to retain — unity belongs to the involvement-whole, not to a homogeneous medium — and the final sentence pivots the whole analysis onto its ground: things have environmental space only because the encountering being is spatial; § 23 must say how.

###### § 23. The Spatiality of Being-in-the-World

The opening unit sets the categorial frame and names the two structures. If we ascribe spatiality to Dasein, this "being in space" must manifestly be conceived from the mode of being of this being: the spatiality of Dasein — which is essentially no presence-at-hand — can mean neither occurrence at a position in "world-space" nor readiness-to-hand at a place, both being modes of being of innerworldly beings. Dasein is "in" the world in the sense of concernful-familiar dealings with the beings encountered innerworldly; if spatiality belongs to it in any way, that is possible only on the ground of this being-in — and its spatiality shows the characters of de-severance (Ent-fernung) and directionality (Ausrichtung). The exclusions are § 9's discipline applied to space: Dasein occupies neither position nor place, since both are categories; its spatiality must be an existential pair — and the hyphenated coinage Ent-fernung announces the analysis to come by breaking the ordinary word for distance/removal into its literal opposite: de-distancing.

The second unit defines de-severance. By Ent-fernung as a mode of Dasein's being with regard to its being-in-the-world we understand nothing like remoteness (nearness) or even distance (Abstand): the expression is used in an active and transitive signification. It means a constitution of Dasein's being, with regard to which removing something — putting it away — is only a determinate factical mode. De-severing means making the farness — the remoteness — of something vanish: bringing near. Dasein is essentially de-severant: as the being it is, it lets beings in each case be encountered into nearness. De-severance discovers remoteness; remoteness, like distance, is a categorial determination of non-Dasein-like beings, whereas de-severance must be held fast as an existential. Only insofar as beings in their remoteness are discovered for Dasein at all do "removals" and distances among innerworldly beings, with respect to one another, become accessible: two points are as little de-severed from one another as two things in general, because neither of these beings can, by its mode of being, de-sever — they merely have a distance, findable and measurable in de-severing. The definition inverts the everyday word with philological wit: Ent-fernung, ordinarily "distance," is read privatively (ent- as removal) — the abolition of farness. The grammar carries the ontology: de-severing is transitive, an accomplishment of Dasein, whereas distance is a relation obtaining between things — and the two-points argument re-runs § 12's touching-argument in metric dress: geometry's distances are parasitic on an encountering nearness-bringing that no point can perform.

The third unit gives the tendency and its most modern witness. De-severing is proximally and mostly circumspective bringing-near: procuring, making ready, having to hand — but determinate kinds of purely cognitive discovery of beings also have the character of bringing-near. In Dasein lies an essential tendency toward nearness. All the kinds of increase of speed that we today go along with, more or less compelled, press toward the overcoming of remoteness: with the "radio," for example, Dasein today accomplishes a de-severing of the "world" — by way of an expansion of the everyday environing world — whose sense for Dasein cannot yet be surveyed. The radio-sentence became famous for good reason: written in 1926, it identifies the technological compression of the world as an enactment of an existential structure (the essential tendency toward nearness), refuses to celebrate or lament it, and marks its meaning as still unsurveyable — the seed of the later meditations on technology and of the postwar question (in the Bremen lectures) whether the abolition of all distances yields any nearness at all.

The fourth unit describes everyday estimation and defends its rigor. In de-severing there need be no express assessment of the farness of a ready-to-hand thing relative to Dasein; above all, remoteness is never grasped as distance. If farness is to be estimated, this happens relative to de-severances in which everyday Dasein maintains itself: computationally these estimates may be inexact and fluctuating, but in Dasein's everydayness they have their own, thoroughly intelligible determinateness. We say: it is a walk over there, a stone's throw, "a pipe long." These measures express not only that they do not want to "measure," but that the assessed remoteness belongs to a being to which one goes concernfully and circumspectively. Even when we use fixed measures and say "it is half an hour to the house," the measure must be taken as estimated: "half an hour" is not thirty minutes but a duration that has no "length" at all in the sense of quantitative stretch — a duration interpreted, in each case, out of accustomed everyday "attendings-to." Remotenesses are proximally, and even where "officially" computed measures are known, circumspectively estimated; and because the de-severed is ready-to-hand in such estimates, it retains its specifically innerworldly character. To this belongs even that the accustomed ways to remote beings are of different lengths every day. The ready-to-hand of the environing world is not present-at-hand for an eternal observer exempted from Dasein, but is encountered into Dasein's circumspectively concernful everydayness: on its ways, Dasein does not traverse, like a present-at-hand corporeal thing, a stretch of space — it does not "devour kilometers"; bringing-near and de-severing are in each case concernful being toward what is brought near and de-severed. An "objectively" long way can be shorter than an "objectively" very short one that is perhaps a "hard going" and strikes one as infinitely long — but in such "striking" the respective world is first authentically ready-to-hand. Objective distances of present-at-hand things do not coincide with the remoteness and nearness of the innerworldly ready-to-hand: those may be exactly known, yet this knowledge remains blind — it lacks the function of circumspectively discovering bringing-near of the environing world; one uses such knowledge only in and for a concernful being — one that does not measure stretches — toward a world that "concerns" one. The pipe-length and the half-hour are among the book's finest micro-analyses: the measures of everydayness measure by enactments (a smoke, a walk), not by units, and their apparent vagueness is their own kind of exactness (§ 7 C's warning about mathematical leveling, redeemed) — the "half hour" that is not thirty minutes quietly prefigures Division Two's whole theory of reckoned time. The eternal-observer sentence names the false subject of the objectivist picture; the "hard going" that makes a short way long is not error about distance but the truth of the way as encountered; and the closing verdict — exact knowledge, functionally blind — reprises § 3's Kantian barb at the exact point where geometry meets life.

The fifth unit turns the subjectivism-charge around: one is inclined, from an antecedent orientation to "nature" and the "objectively" measured distances of things, to pass off such interpretation and estimation of remoteness as "subjective." Yet this is a "subjectivity" that perhaps discovers what is most real about the "reality" of the world — a subjectivity that has nothing to do with "subjective" arbitrariness or subjectivistic "apprehensions" of beings that "in themselves" are otherwise: the circumspective de-severing of Dasein's everydayness discovers the being-in-itself of the "true world," of the beings alongside which Dasein, as existing, in each case already is. The unit re-applies § 16's resolution of the in-itself to space: the workday nearnesses are not colorations of a metric substrate but the primary discoveredness of the world — "true world" in scare-quotes turning Nietzsche's phrase to phenomenological use.

The sixth unit demolishes the metric concept of the near with three tools worn on the body. Primary — let alone exclusive — orientation to remotenesses as measured distances covers up the original spatiality of being-in: the supposedly "nearest" is by no means what has the smallest distance "from us"; the nearest lies in what is de-severed within an average reach, grasp, and glance. Because Dasein is essentially spatial in the manner of de-severance, its dealings always maintain themselves in an "environing world" de-severed from it within a certain leeway (Spielraum); hence we proximally always hear and see past what is, by distance, "nearest." Seeing and hearing are distance-senses not on account of their range, but because Dasein, as de-severant, predominantly dwells in them. For someone who wears spectacles — by distance so near that they "sit on his nose" — this used equipment is environmentally more remote than the picture on the wall opposite: this equipment has so little nearness that it is often not even findable at first. Equipment for seeing, likewise for hearing — the telephone receiver — has the marked inconspicuousness of the proximally ready-to-hand. So too, for instance, the street, the equipment for walking: in walking it is touched at every step and is seemingly the nearest and most real of all the ready-to-hand, sliding along, as it were, certain parts of the body, the soles of the feet — and yet it is more remote than the acquaintance one meets "on the street," in such walking, at a "remove" of twenty paces. Circumspective concern decides about the nearness and farness of the environmentally proximally ready-to-hand: that alongside which concern dwells in advance is the nearest and regulates the de-severances. The spectacles, the receiver, and the street form the book's most quoted trio after the hammer, and their lesson is exact: existential nearness is inverse to absorption — what is used most transparently (§ 15's withdrawal) is environmentally farthest, while the friend twenty paces off is nearest because concern dwells with him. The re-derivation of the "distance-senses" is a small gem: sight and hearing carry the far not by physiology but because de-severant dwelling lives in them — a thesis on the existential meaning of the senses the tradition's optics never asked for.

The seventh unit relocates the "here." When Dasein in concern brings something into its nearness, this does not mean fixing something at a spatial position with the smallest distance from some point of the body: "in the nearness" means in the circuit of what is circumspectively proximally ready-to-hand. Bringing-near is not oriented toward the body-encumbered I-thing but toward concernful being-in-the-world — toward what is in each case proximally encountered in it. Hence Dasein's spatiality is not determined by citing the position at which a corporeal thing is present-at-hand. We do say of Dasein that it in each case occupies a place — but this "occupying" must be distinguished in principle from being ready-to-hand at a place out of a region: occupying a place must be conceived as de-severing of the environmentally ready-to-hand into a circumspectively pre-discovered region. Dasein understands its here from the environmental yonder (Dort): the here does not mean the where of something present-at-hand, but the wherein-alongside (Wobei) of a de-severant being-alongside... in one with this de-severance. Dasein, in accordance with its spatiality, is proximally never here but yonder — out of which yonder it comes back to its here, and this again only in such a way that it interprets its concernful being-toward... from what is ready-to-hand yonder. This is the section's most radical stroke: the zero-point of lived space is not the body. Dasein is "proximally never here but yonder" — with the work, at the friend, in the region of its concern — and the here is derivative, understood backward from the there. The de-centering will be confirmed twice over: existentially at § 26 (Dasein is with others out there) and structurally at § 69 (Dasein's being as ahead-of-itself); the body, expressly bracketed in the next unit, waits for a problematic Heidegger admits he does not treat.

The eighth unit adds the strange corollary: Dasein can never cross its own de-severance. Dasein maintains itself essentially in a de-severing; this de-severance — the farness of the ready-to-hand from Dasein itself — Dasein can never cross over. The remoteness of a ready-to-hand thing from Dasein can indeed be come upon by Dasein as distance, when determined in relation to a thing thought as present-at-hand at the place Dasein previously occupied; this between of distance Dasein can subsequently traverse — but only in such a way that the distance itself becomes de-severed. Dasein has so little crossed its de-severance that it has rather taken it along, and constantly takes it along, because it is essentially de-severance — spatial. Dasein cannot wander around within the current circuit of its de-severances; it can only ever change them. Dasein is spatial in the manner of circumspective space-discovery, comporting itself constantly de-severantly toward beings thus spatially encountered. The paradox is precise, not mystical: since de-severance is the structure by which anything far or near is given at all, approaching a thing does not diminish Dasein's de-severance but re-enacts it at the new station — one carries one's horizon of nearness as one carries one's shadow. Distances are crossed; the crossing itself is de-severant.

The ninth unit introduces the second structure. As de-severant being-in, Dasein has at once the character of directionality: every bringing-near has already taken up in advance a direction into a region out of which the de-severed approaches, so as to become findable with regard to its place. Circumspective concern is directional de-severing. In this concern — in Dasein's being-in-the-world itself — the need for "signs" is pregiven: this equipment takes over the express and easily manageable indication of directions, holding the circumspectively used regions expressly open — the respective whither of belonging, going, bringing, fetching. If Dasein is, it has, as directing-de-severing, in each case already its discovered region; directionality, like de-severance, is guided in advance, as a mode of being-in-the-world, by the circumspection of concern. Two threads knot here: the sign-analysis of § 17 receives its existential ground (signs exist because directional de-severing needs its regions held open — the turn-signal retroactively explained), and direction is fixed as equiprimordial with de-severance: nothing is brought near except from somewhere.

The tenth unit derives right and left. From this directionality spring the fixed directions of right and left; like its de-severances, Dasein constantly takes these directions along.
