Dasein's spatialization in its "bodiliness" — which harbors a problematic of its own, not to be treated here — is also marked out along these directions: hence what is ready-to-hand and used for the body, gloves for instance, which must go along with the hands' movements, must be directed to right and left; a craftsman's tool, by contrast, held in the hand and moved with it, does not share the hand's specifically "handy" movement — hence there are, though hammers are handled with the hand, no right and left hammers. The glove/hammer contrast is exact phenomenological jurisprudence: chirality attaches to equipment exactly insofar as it must accompany the lived body's own movement — and the parenthesis on bodiliness is the book's famous confession: the Leib is acknowledged as a problematic of its own and deferred (a deferral Heidegger maintained for decades, and for which the French reception, Merleau-Ponty above all, took up the mortgage).

The eleventh unit grounds even right-left in world — against Kant. It remains to note that directionality, belonging to de-severance, is founded through being-in-the-world: left and right are not something "subjective" for which the subject has a feeling, but directions of directedness into a world in each case already ready-to-hand. "Through the mere feeling of a difference of my two sides" I could never find my way in a world. The subject with the "mere feeling" of this difference is a constructive point of departure that disregards the true constitution of the subject: that Dasein, with this "mere feeling," in each case already is in a world and must be, in order to be able to orient itself at all — as becomes plain from the very example by which Kant tries to clarify orientation. The citation (from Kant's 1786 essay on orienting oneself in thinking, the note supplies) sets up the twelfth unit's demonstration; the diagnostic term is "constructive" — the worldless subject equipped with a feeling is an artifact of theory, § 10's hypokeimenon in sensationist costume.

The twelfth unit works the dark-room example and settles accounts with Kant. Suppose I enter a familiar but dark room which in my absence has been rearranged so that everything that stood on the right now stands on the left: if I am to orient myself, the "mere feeling of the difference" of my two sides helps not at all so long as no determinate object is grasped, of which Kant says in passing, "whose place I have in memory." But what does that mean other than: I orient myself necessarily in and from an already-being-alongside a "familiar" world; the equipment-context of a world must already be pregiven to Dasein. That I am in each case already in a world is no less constitutive for the possibility of orientation than the feeling for right and left; and that this constitution of Dasein's being is self-evident does not entitle one to suppress it in its ontologically constitutive role. Kant does not suppress it either — no interpretation of Dasein does; but constant use of this constitution does not absolve from an adequate ontological explication: it demands one. The psychological interpretation — that the I has something "in memory" — means at bottom the existential constitution of being-in-the-world; and because Kant does not see this structure, he also misses the full context of the constitution of possible orientation. Directedness toward right and left is grounded in the essential directionality of Dasein in general, which is in its turn essentially co-determined by being-in-the-world. Kant, to be sure, is not concerned with a thematic interpretation of orientation: he wants only to show that every orientation needs a "subjective principle" — but "subjective" here will want to mean: a priori. Yet the a priori of directedness toward right and left is grounded in the "subjective" a priori of being-in-the-world, which has nothing to do with a determinateness restricted in advance to a worldless subject. The analysis is a destruction in miniature with the § 21 principle applied generously: Kant's aside ("whose place I have in memory") testifies to what his framework cannot state — the pregiven familiar world — so his example refutes his principle and confirms Dasein's. The closing transvaluation is the section's theoretical yield: "subjective" a priori, rightly understood, means the a priori of being-in-the-world — apriority relocated from the worldless subject into the structure of dwelling, the correction § 24 will repeat for space itself.

The closing unit sums and hands over: de-severance and directionality, as constitutive characters of being-in, determine Dasein's spatiality — its being, concernfully and circumspectively, in discovered, innerworldly space. The explication so far of the spatiality of the innerworldly ready-to-hand and the spatiality of being-in-the-world first gives the presuppositions for working out the phenomenon of the world's spatiality and posing the ontological problem of space. The bookkeeping is exact: two spatialities are in hand (of the ready-to-hand: place and region; of being-in: de-severance and direction); the third — space itself and its being — is § 24's business.

###### § 24. The Spatiality of Dasein and Space

The opening unit welds the spatiality-analysis into the worldhood-analysis. As being-in-the-world, Dasein has in each case already discovered a "world." This discovering, founded in the worldhood of the world, was characterized as the freeing of beings toward an involvement-totality; the freeing letting-be-involved is accomplished in the manner of circumspective self-referral, grounded in an antecedent understanding of significance. Now it has been shown: circumspective being-in-the-world is spatial. And only because Dasein is spatial in the manner of de-severance and directionality can the environmentally ready-to-hand be encountered in its spatiality. The freeing of an involvement-totality is equiprimordially a de-severing-directing letting-be-involved at a region — a freeing of the spatial belonging of the ready-to-hand. In the significance with which Dasein, as concernful being-in, is familiar, lies the essential co-disclosedness of space. The paragraph accomplishes the section's whole systematic labor in advance: § 18's apparatus and § 23's apparatus are shown to be one apparatus — freeing-toward-involvement is eo ipso freeing-into-region — and the conclusion is given its lapidary form: space is co-disclosed in significance. Space is neither a container for world nor a product of it, but a moment of world's own disclosedness.

The second unit locates the region within significance and keeps pure space veiled. The space thus disclosed with the worldhood of the world has as yet nothing of the pure manifold of the three dimensions: in this nearest disclosedness, space remains hidden as the pure wherein of a metric ordering of positions and determining of locations. That toward which space is antecedently discovered in Dasein has already been indicated with the phenomenon of the region: the whither of the possible belonging of the ready-to-hand equipment-context, which is to be encounterable as directionally de-severed — placed. The belonging determines itself from the significance constitutive for the world and articulates, within the possible whither, the hither and thither; the whither in general is predelineated by the reference-whole fastened in a for-the-sake-of-which of concern, within which the freeing letting-be-involved refers itself. With what is encountered as ready-to-hand there is in each case an involvement at a region: to the involvement-totality that constitutes the being of the environmentally ready-to-hand belongs regional spatial involvement (Raumbewandtnis). On its ground the ready-to-hand becomes findable and determinable according to form and direction; with the factical being of Dasein, the innerworldly ready-to-hand is de-severed and directed according to the possible transparency of concernful circumspection. The technical yield is the term Raumbewandtnis: space enters the ontology as a kind of involvement — the region is an at-which within significance, anchored, like everything in § 18, in the Worumwillen — so that the whole spatial order of a world hangs, ultimately, from what Dasein's being is about.

The third unit names Dasein's space-constituting accomplishment. The letting-be-encountered of innerworldly beings, constitutive for being-in-the-world, is a "giving of space" (Raum-geben); this giving of space, which we also call making room (Einräumen), is the freeing of the ready-to-hand toward its spatiality. As discovering pre-giving of a possible involvement-determined place-totality, it makes possible the respective factical orientation. Dasein can, as circumspective concern with the world, rearrange, remove, and "make room" only because making-room — understood as an existential — belongs to its being-in-the-world. But neither the region antecedently discovered nor the respective spatiality is expressly in view: it is present in itself, for circumspection, in the inconspicuousness of the ready-to-hand in whose concern circumspection is absorbed. With being-in-the-world, space is proximally discovered in this spatiality; on the soil of spatiality so discovered, space itself becomes accessible for cognition. Einräumen doubles, in German, as furnishing/arranging and as conceding — Heidegger exploits the ordinary sense (one can tidy a room only because one's being makes room) to name the existential: room-making as the pre-giving of a place-whole. And § 16's law holds for it too: the accomplishment works inconspicuously; its product (space in the spatiality of places) is the soil from which cognition can then extract space itself.

The fourth unit states the section's title-thesis. Space is neither in the subject, nor is the world in space; space is rather "in" the world, insofar as being-in-the-world, constitutive for Dasein, has disclosed space. Space is not to be found in the subject, nor does the subject observe the world "as if" it were in a space; rather the ontologically well-understood "subject" — Dasein — is spatial. And because Dasein is spatial in the manner described, space shows itself as a priori. This title does not mean anything like antecedent belonging to a proximally still worldless subject that casts a space out of itself: apriority means here the antecedence of the encountering of space (as region) in the respective environmental encountering of the ready-to-hand. The double negation dispatches, in one sentence, the two classical positions — realism's container (world in space) and idealism's form (space in the subject) — and the positive formula, space "in" the world, must be read with § 12's care: "in" as belonging to disclosedness, not containment. The re-definition of the a priori completes § 23's transvaluation: apriority de-subjectivized — not prior possession by a mind but prior encounteredness in every encounter; Kant's discovery kept, Kant's proprietor dismissed (the settling of the account § 21's "rescue" opened).

The fifth unit traces the ladder from workshop to geometry. The spatiality of what circumspection proximally encounters can itself become thematic for circumspection, a task of calculation and measurement — in house-building, for instance, and land-surveying. With this still predominantly circumspective thematization of environmental spatiality, space in itself already comes into view in a certain way. The space thus showing itself can be pursued by pure looking, with surrender of the formerly sole possibility of access, circumspective calculation: the "formal intuition" of space discovers the pure possibilities of spatial relations — and here there is a graded sequence in laying free pure, homogeneous space, from the pure morphology of spatial shapes through analysis situs to the purely metric science of space. The consideration of these connections does not belong to this investigation (the note referring to Oskar Becker's phenomenological grounding of geometry, in the same Jahrbuch); within the present problematic only the phenomenal soil was to be fixed ontologically, on which the thematic discovery and elaboration of pure space sets in. The ladder is § 13's genesis of theory rebuilt for space — concern, semi-circumspective measurement (the surveyor), pure beholding, formal intuition — with each rung a further surrender of circumspection; the ordered disciplines (morphology, topology, metric geometry) show that even pure space has its levels of formalization, and the Becker-note quietly marks where phenomenology's own school had carried the problem.

The sixth unit names the price of the ascent. The circumspection-free, merely looking discovery of space neutralizes the environmental regions into the pure dimensions; the places, and the circumspectively oriented place-totality of ready-to-hand equipment, collapse into a manifold of positions for arbitrary things. The spatiality of the innerworldly ready-to-hand loses therewith its involvement-character; the world loses the specifically around-ish, the environing world becomes the world of nature. The "world" as ready-to-hand equipment-whole is spatialized into a context of extended things merely still present-at-hand: homogeneous natural space shows itself only on the way of a mode of discovery of encountered beings that has the character of a specific de-worlding of the worldly character of the ready-to-hand. This is § 14's Entweltlichung executed step by step on space — region to dimension, place to position, belonging to arbitrariness — and it delivers, retroactively, the full verdict on Descartes: the res extensa is real, but it is a product; homogeneous space is what remains of a world when the involvement-character has been methodically stripped, so an ontology that begins there has mistaken the residue for the origin.

The seventh unit refuses to decide space's being by its site. To Dasein, in accordance with its being-in-the-world, discovered space is in each case already pregiven, though unthematically; space in itself, by contrast, remains proximally still covered with regard to the pure possibilities of the sheer spatiality of something enclosed in it. That space shows itself essentially in a world does not yet decide about its mode of being: space need not have the mode of being of something itself spatially ready-to-hand or present-at-hand — nor does the being of space have the mode of being of Dasein. From the fact that the being of space cannot be conceived in the mode of being of res extensa it follows neither that it must be ontologically determined as a "phenomenon" of this res — in being it would then not be distinguished from it — nor that the being of space could be equated with that of the res cogitans and conceived as merely "subjective," quite apart from the questionableness of the being of this subject. The paragraph is a display of ontological restraint rare in any tradition: having grounded space in world, Heidegger declines to classify its being — space is neither thing, nor appearance-of-thing (the Leibnizian option), nor subject-dependent (the idealist option), nor Dasein; the exhaustive-seeming alternatives are all rejected, and the question is left standing.

The eighth unit diagnoses why it must be left standing. The perplexity persisting to this day regarding the interpretation of the being of space is grounded not so much in insufficient knowledge of the material content of space itself as in the lack of a fundamental transparency of the possibilities of being in general and of their ontologically conceptual interpretation. What is decisive for understanding the ontological problem of space lies in freeing the question of the being of space from the narrowness of the accidentally available and, moreover, mostly crude concepts of being, and in bringing the problematic of the being of space — with regard to the phenomenon itself and the various phenomenal spatialities — into the direction of clarifying the possibilities of being in general. The diagnosis universalizes § 3's crisis-doctrine onto philosophy's oldest embarrassment: the antinomies of space-theory (substantivalism, relationism, subjectivism) are symptoms of a poverty of being-concepts — the disputants share three or four crude categories and force space into them; the cure is the book's own question, the genealogy of the possible ways of being that only the meaning of being in general could ground.

The closing unit fixes space's rank and closes the chapter. In the phenomenon of space neither the sole nor even a primary-among-others ontological determinateness of the being of innerworldly beings can be found; still less does space constitute the phenomenon of world. Space can be conceived only by going back to the world: it is not that space becomes accessible only through the de-worlding of the environing world — spatiality is discoverable at all only on the ground of world; and yet space co-constitutes the world, in accordance with the essential spatiality of Dasein itself with regard to its basic constitution of being-in-the-world. The final balance is struck with both hands: against Descartes, space is neither the being of the innerworldly nor the constituent of world; against any spiritualist over-correction, space genuinely co-constitutes world, because the being whose structure world is, is itself essentially spatial. Chapter Three thus ends where it began, with the priority reversed and earned: not world in space, but space from world — and the analysis, its first structural moment secured, can turn from the wherein of being-in-the-world to its who.

#### Chapter Four: Being-in-the-World as Being-With and Being-a-Self. Das "Man"

The chapter opens by justifying its place and mapping its course. The analysis of the worldhood of the world constantly kept the whole phenomenon of being-in-the-world in view, without all its constitutive moments standing out with the same phenomenal distinctness as the phenomenon of world itself. The ontological interpretation of the world, by way of the innerworldly ready-to-hand, was put first because Dasein in its everydayness — the standing theme — is not only in a world at all, but comports itself to the world in a predominant mode of being: Dasein is proximally and mostly taken in (benommen) by its world. This mode of being — absorption in the world — and therewith the underlying being-in in general essentially determine the phenomenon now to be pursued with the question: who is it that Dasein, in everydayness, is? All structures of Dasein's being, hence also the phenomenon answering the who-question, are ways of its being; their ontological characterization is existential — so the question must be rightly posed, and the way sketched by which a further phenomenal district of everydayness is to come into view. Inquiry toward the phenomenon that answers the who leads to structures of Dasein equiprimordial with being-in-the-world: being-with (Mitsein) and co-Dasein (Mitdasein). In this mode of being grounds the mode of everyday being-a-self, whose explication makes visible what we may call the "subject" of everydayness — das Man. The chapter divides accordingly: the approach to the existential who-question (§ 25); the co-Dasein of others and everyday being-with (§ 26); everyday being-a-self and das Man (§ 27). Two decisions are already made in the map. Being-with is announced as equiprimordial with being-in-the-world — not derived from encounters, not added to a prior solus ipse — and the "subject" of everydayness is flagged, in advance and in scare-quotes, as no subject at all: das Man, the "one," whose grammatical impersonality (man sagt, one says) will be promoted to an existential title.

##### § 25. The Approach to the Existential Question of the Who of Dasein

The opening unit convicts the obvious answer of a borrowed ontology. The answer to the question who this being (Dasein) in each case is seems to have been given already with the formal indication of Dasein's basic determinateness (§ 9): Dasein is the being that I in each case am; its being is in each case mine. This indicates an ontological constitution — but only that; it contains at the same time the ontic, though rough, information that in each case an I is this being and not others. The who is answered from the I itself, the "subject," the "self": the who is what maintains itself as identical through the change of comportments and lived experiences and relates itself, in so doing, to this manifold. Ontologically we understand it as what is, in a closed region and for it, always already and constantly present-at-hand — what lies at the ground in a preeminent sense, the subjectum; which, as the selfsame in manifold otherness, has the character of the self. One may reject soul-substance, the thinghood of consciousness, the objectivity of the person: ontologically it remains a positing of something whose being, expressly or not, retains the sense of presence-at-hand. Substantiality is the ontological guiding thread for determining the being from which the who-question gets answered; Dasein is tacitly conceived in advance as present-at-hand — in every case the indeterminacy of its being always implies this sense of being. Yet presence-at-hand is the mode of being of non-Dasein-like beings. The analysis retraces § 10's argument at the exact point of the who: the classical self — identical pole persisting through the flux of experiences — is the hypokeimenon in first-person dress, and the disclaimers of the moderns (no soul-substance, no reified consciousness) change the furniture, not the ontology. The last two sentences spring the § 9 trap: the traditional who-answer applies a category to what demands an existential.

The second unit raises the stakes from ontology to fact. The ontic self-evidence of the assertion that it is I who in each case am Dasein must not mislead one into supposing that the way of an ontological interpretation of what is thus "given" is thereby unmistakably marked out. It remains questionable even whether the ontic content of the assertion adequately renders the phenomenal stock of everyday Dasein: it could be that the who of everyday Dasein is precisely not in each case I myself. This is the section's thunderclap, delivered in the subjunctive: not only is the I ontologically misconstrued — perhaps it is not even, ontically, the everyday answer. The sentence pre-announces § 27's result (the who of everydayness is das Man) and converts the who-question from a formality into a genuine discovery-problem.

The third unit states the methodological stake in one sentence: if phenomenal exhibition from the mode of being of the being itself is to keep priority — even over the most self-evident and time-honored answers and the problem-formulations drawn from them — then the phenomenological interpretation of Dasein must, with respect to the question now to be posed, be guarded against a perversion of the problematic. § 7's maxim, re-armed for the hardest case: nowhere is the "self-evident" more entrenched than at the I, so nowhere is the maxim under more strain.

The fourth unit lets the strongest objection speak — with Husserl's voice. Does it not offend the rules of all sound method if the approach to a problematic does not hold to the evident givennesses of the thematic field? And what is more indubitable than the givenness of the I? Does this givenness not carry the directive to abstract, for the purpose of its original elaboration, from everything else "given" — not only from an existing "world" but even from the being of other "I"s? Perhaps what this manner of giving — the plain, formal, reflective perceiving-of-the-I — gives is indeed evident; this insight even opens access to an independent phenomenological problematic, which has its fundamental, frame-giving significance as a "formal phenomenology of consciousness." The objection is stated with full Cartesian-Husserlian force (the reduction to the sphere of ownness is recognizably sketched), and the concession is carefully measured: the reflective I-givenness is evident, and grounds a legitimate discipline — the question is only whether that discipline reaches Dasein.

The fifth unit turns the evidence into a possible trap set by Dasein itself. In the present context of an existential analytic of factical Dasein the question arises whether the named manner of the I's givenness discloses Dasein in its everydayness — if it discloses it at all. Is it then a priori self-evident that access to Dasein must be a plainly perceiving reflection on the I of acts? What if this kind of "self-givenness" were, for the existential analytic, a seduction — and one grounded in the being of Dasein itself? Perhaps Dasein, in proximally addressing itself, always says: it is I — and in the end says it loudest precisely when it is "not" this being. What if the constitution of Dasein, that it is in each case mine, were the very ground of the fact that Dasein proximally and mostly is not itself? What if the existential analytic, with the approach from the givenness of the I, walked into a trap set, as it were, by Dasein itself and by an obvious self-interpretation of it? What if the ontological horizon for determining what is accessible in plain giving remained fundamentally undetermined? One may always, with ontic legitimacy, say of this being that "I" am it; but the ontological analytic that makes use of such assertions must place them under fundamental reservations: the "I" may be understood only in the sense of a noncommittal formal indication of something that, in the respective phenomenal context of being, perhaps unveils itself as its "opposite" — where "not-I" by no means signifies a being that essentially lacks "I-hood," but a determinate mode of being of the "I" itself, for instance self-lostness (Selbstverlorenheit). The paragraph is among the book's most consequential methodological texts. The loudest-when-least argument gives the reflective evidence an existential etiology: the everyday "I am I" can be flight's own testimony — self-assertion as symptom of self-lostness — so that Descartes' indubitable datum is re-read as the voice of falling. The doctrine of formal indication, elsewhere presupposed, is here stated: the analytic's terms (the "I" above all) are noncommittal pointers whose content the phenomena must fill, possibly with their opposite — the early-Freiburg methodology surfacing by name in all but name. And the closing precision protects against over-correction: the not-I is not an entity without mineness but a mode of mineness — self-lostness presupposes a self to lose (§ 9's derivation of inauthenticity from Jemeinigkeit, applied).

The sixth unit adds the positive bar to the I-start and posts the section's forward reference. Even the positive interpretation of Dasein given so far already forbids the departure from the formal givenness of the I for a phenomenally adequate answer to the who-question: the clarification of being-in-the-world showed that a bare subject without world never "is" proximally, and is never given; and so, in the end, an isolated I without the others is just as little given — the note crediting Scheler's phenomenological exhibitions in the Sympathy book (both editions cited) for this point. But if "the others" are in each case already there-with in being-in-the-world, this phenomenal finding too must not seduce one into holding the ontological structure of what is thus "given" to be self-evident and in no need of investigation: the task is to make the kind of this co-Dasein phenomenally visible in nearest everydayness and to interpret it in an ontologically adequate way. The symmetry is exact and double-edged: as no worldless subject, so no otherless I — but the correction must not itself become a new dogma; that others are given is a phenomenal fact whose ontology (Mitsein) still has to be worked out, against both the Cartesian denial and an uncritical appeal to sociality (Scheler honored and put on notice in one gesture).

The seventh unit generalizes the seduction-pattern: as the ontic self-evidence of the in-itself-being of innerworldly beings misleads one into the conviction of the ontological self-evidence of the meaning of this being, and lets the phenomenon of world be overlooked, so the ontic self-evidence that Dasein is in each case mine harbors a possible seduction of the corresponding ontological problematic — proximally, the who of Dasein is not only ontologically a problem; it remains ontically covered up as well. The parallel welds Chapters Three and Four into one method: the I is to the who-question what the "in itself" was to the world-question (§ 16) — a phenomenal right concealing an ontological task — and the last clause repeats the § 25 thunderclap as settled: even ontically, who one everyday is, is hidden.

The eighth unit finds the true guiding thread. Is the existential-analytic answering of the who-question then without any guide? By no means — but of the formal indications of Dasein's constitution given above (§§ 9 and 12), the one that functions here is not so much mineness as the other: that the "essence" of Dasein grounds in its existence. If the "I" is an essential determinateness of Dasein, it must be interpreted existentially: the who can be answered only by phenomenal exhibition of a determinate mode of being of Dasein. If Dasein is its self in each case only in existing, then the constancy of the self, quite as much as its possible "non-self-constancy" (Unselbständigkeit), demands an existential-ontological way of questioning as the sole adequate access. The substitution of guiding threads is the section's positive yield: from mineness (which tempts toward the given I) to existence (which forbids any given who) — selfhood becomes a way of being, to be won or forfeited, and the pregnant pun Ständigkeit/Unselbständigkeit (constancy/dependence, self-standing/unself-standing) is planted for Division Two, where the constancy of the self will be re-derived from resoluteness and temporality (§ 64).

The closing unit meets the fear of evaporation with the book's most quotable inversion. If the self is to be conceived "only" as a way of being of this being, that seems tantamount to volatilizing the authentic "core" of Dasein — but such fears feed on the perverse preconception that this being at bottom has, after all, the mode of being of something present-at-hand, even if one keeps at bay the massiveness of an occurring corporeal thing. Yet the "substance" of man is not spirit, as the synthesis of soul and body: it is existence. The objection answered is the perennial one (a self that is only a how seems to lose its what), and the answer is § 9 verbatim, now applied: only a substance-ontology could experience the existential self as a loss. The closing sentence — deliberately echoing and correcting the tradition's formula — compresses the section: not even the refined substance (spirit as body-soul synthesis) will do; the "substance" of the who is the to-be.

##### § 26. The Co-Dasein of Others and Everyday Being-With

The opening unit fixes procedure: the answer to the who of everyday Dasein is to be won in the analysis of the mode of being in which Dasein proximally and mostly maintains itself; the investigation orients itself by being-in-the-world, the basic constitution co-determining every mode of Dasein's being. If it was rightly said that with the foregoing explication of world the remaining structural moments of being-in-the-world had also come into view, then the answering of the who-question must in a certain way be prepared by it too. The remark redeems the division-preamble's whole-first rule: the who will not be fetched from elsewhere but read out of the already-analyzed world — the next unit does exactly that.

The second unit finds the others already in the workshop. The "description" of the nearest environing world — the craftsman's work-world — yielded that with the equipment in work the others, for whom the "work" is destined, are "co-encountered": in the mode of being of this ready-to-hand thing, in its involvement, lies an essential reference to possible wearers, to whose "body it is to be cut." Likewise, in the material used, the producer or "supplier" is encountered as the one who "serves" well or badly; the field along which we walk "outside" shows itself as belonging to so-and-so and kept in good order by him; the book we use was bought at..., given by...; the boat anchored at the shore refers, in its being-in-itself, to an acquaintance who undertakes his voyages with it — and even as a "boat strange to us" it shows others. The others thus "encountered" in the ready-to-hand environmental equipment-context are not somehow added in thought to a thing proximally merely present-at-hand: these "things" are encountered from out of the world in which they are ready-to-hand for the others — a world that is, in advance, always already mine as well. The previous analysis restricted the circuit of the innerworldly encountered to equipment and nature — to non-Dasein-like beings — not only to simplify the exposition, but above all because the mode of being of the Dasein of others, encountered innerworldly, differs from readiness-to-hand and presence-at-hand: Dasein's world frees beings that are not only distinct from equipment and things but, in accordance with their mode of being as Dasein, are themselves "in" the world — in the manner of being-in-the-world — in which they are at the same time innerworldly encountered. These beings are neither present-at-hand nor ready-to-hand but are as the freeing Dasein itself is: they are there too, and there with (auch und mit da). Should one insist on identifying world with the innerworldly, one would have to say: "world" is also Dasein. The paragraph is § 15's twelfth unit promoted to a principle: others were in the tool-analysis from the start (wearer, supplier, owner, the stranger of the strange boat), encountered from the world, never inferred to; and the categorial triple is completed — a third mode of innerworldly encounterability, neither zuhanden nor vorhanden but daseinsmäßig: co-there. The closing paradox ("world" is also Dasein) marks how far the finding strains the innerworldly/worldly grid: others are met within my world as beings who each have world.

The third unit forestalls the residual egology and mints the chapter's terms. Yet does not this characterization of encountering others orient itself, once again, by one's own Dasein — starting from a distinguishing and isolating of the "I," so that a passage from this isolated subject to the others must then be sought? To avoid the misunderstanding, note in what sense "the others" is here spoken: "the others" does not mean the whole remainder of the rest besides me, out of which the I lifts itself — the others are rather those from whom one mostly does not distinguish oneself, among whom one also is. This being-there-too with them has not the ontological character of a being-present-at-hand-"with" within a world: the "with" is Dasein-like, the "too" means the sameness of being as circumspectively concernful being-in-the-world. "With" and "too" are to be understood existentially, not categorially. On the ground of this with-like being-in-the-world, the world is in each case already the one I share with the others: the world of Dasein is with-world (Mitwelt); being-in is being-with others (Mitsein mit Anderen); the innerworldly being-in-themselves of the others is co-Dasein (Mitdasein). The redefinition of "the others" is the decisive anti-Cartesian stroke: not the non-I (a contrastive class presupposing the isolated I) but those from whom one mostly does not distinguish oneself — a formula whose second life comes at § 27, where the same indistinction feeds das Man. The three coinages then fall in order: Mitwelt (the shared world), Mitsein (my being's with-structure), Mitdasein (the others' mode of innerworldly encounterability) — and the categorial discipline of § 12 (the existential "with" against the categorial "beside") holds the set together.

The fourth unit secures the direction of encounter and de-centers self-finding. The others are not encountered by way of an antecedent distinguishing grasp of one's own proximally present-at-hand subject from other occurring subjects — not in a primary looking-at-oneself in which the counter-term of a distinction is first fixed. They are encountered from out of the world in which concernful-circumspective Dasein essentially dwells; against the theoretically concocted "explanations" of the presence-at-hand of others, which easily press themselves forward, the exhibited phenomenal state of their environmental encountering must be held fast. Indeed, this nearest and elementary worldly mode of encounter of Dasein goes so far that one's own Dasein too becomes proximally "findable" for itself by looking away from — or not yet at all "seeing" — "lived experiences" and any "center of acts": Dasein finds "itself" proximally in what it pursues, needs, expects, wards off — in the environmentally ready-to-hand with which it is proximally concerned. The symmetry is the argument's elegance: as others are met at their work, so am I — I find myself in my projects and provisions, not in an inner theater; the primacy of reflection falls on both sides of the supposed bridge at once, and the "problem of other minds" loses both its banks.

The fifth unit reads even "I-here" spatially: when Dasein expressly addresses itself as I-here, the locative personal determination must be understood from Dasein's existential spatiality — as already indicated (§ 23), the I-here means not a distinguished point of the I-thing but understands itself as being-in, from the yonder of the ready-to-hand world alongside which Dasein as concern dwells. § 23's de-centered here is now put to work in grammar: the first person locates itself from its world.

The sixth unit calls linguistics to witness. Wilhelm von Humboldt — the note cites the 1829 academy treatise — pointed to languages that express the "I" by "here," the "thou" by "there," the "he" by "yonder": languages that render the personal pronouns by locative adverbs. It is controversial which signification of these locative expressions is original, the adverbial or the pronominal; the dispute loses its footing once one notes that the locative adverbs have their relation to the I qua Dasein. "Here," "there," and "yonder" are primarily not pure determinations of place of innerworldly beings present-at-hand at spatial positions, but characters of Dasein's original spatiality: the supposed locative adverbs are Dasein-determinations, primarily existential and not categorial in signification. Nor are they pronouns: their signification lies before the very difference of locative adverbs and personal pronouns; and the authentically spatial Dasein-signification of these expressions documents that an interpretation of Dasein undistorted by theory sees Dasein immediately in its spatial — de-severing-directing — "being alongside" the world of concern. In the "here," Dasein absorbed in its world does not speak toward itself but away from itself, toward the "there" of something circumspectively ready-to-hand — and yet means itself, in its existential spatiality. The Humboldt excursus is a model of how the analytic uses empirical science: the linguists' either/or (adverb first or pronoun first) is dissolved by exhibiting the common root beneath the distinction — deixis as Dasein's self-articulation in its dwelling — and the closing sentence gives the phenomenon its finest formulation: saying "here," I point away from myself and thereby say myself; the grammar of person is the grammar of being-alongside.

The seventh unit adds the everyday confirmation: Dasein understands itself proximally and mostly from its world, and the co-Dasein of others is encountered in manifold ways from the innerworldly ready-to-hand. But even when the others become, as it were, thematic in their Dasein, they are not encountered as present-at-hand person-things: we meet them "at work" — primarily in their being-in-the-world. Even when we see the other "just standing around," he is never grasped as a present-at-hand human-thing; the "standing around" is an existential mode of being — the unconcerned, uncircumspective tarrying alongside everything and nothing. The other is encountered in his co-Dasein in the world. The standing-around example does for persons what "lying around" (§ 22) did for tools: even apparent idleness is a positive existential mode, not a lapse into thinghood — the perceptual default for others is co-Dasein, never body-plus-inference.

The eighth unit meets the objection from the word "Dasein" and issues the section's central theses. But does not the expression "Dasein" plainly show that this being "proximally" is in unrelatedness to others, subsequently able to be "with" others as well? It must not be overlooked, however, that the term Mitdasein designates that being toward which (daraufhin) the existing others are freed innerworldly; this co-Dasein of others is disclosed innerworldly for a Dasein — and so too for the co-existing ones — only because Dasein is essentially in itself being-with. The phenomenological assertion "Dasein is essentially being-with" has an existential-ontological sense: it does not intend to ascertain ontically that I am factually not present-at-hand alone, that others of my kind also occur. Were that the meaning, being-with would not be an existential determinateness accruing to Dasein from itself, out of its mode of being, but a quality that turns up on the basis of the occurrence of others. Being-with determines Dasein existentially even when an other is factically neither present-at-hand nor perceived: Dasein's being-alone, too, is being-with in the world; the other can be missing only in and for a being-with — being-alone is a deficient mode of being-with; its possibility is the proof of the latter. Conversely, factical being-alone is not removed by a second exemplar of man occurring "beside" me, or ten of them: even with these and more present-at-hand, Dasein can be alone. Being-with, and the facticity of being-with-one-another, therefore does not ground in a co-occurrence of several "subjects." Yet being-alone "among" many does not mean, with respect to the being of the many, that they are then merely present-at-hand: even in being "among them," they are there-with; their co-Dasein is encountered in the mode of indifference and alienness. Missing and "being away" are modes of co-Dasein, possible only because Dasein as being-with lets the Dasein of others be encountered in its world. Being-with is a determinateness of one's own Dasein in each case; co-Dasein characterizes the Dasein of others insofar as it is freed, for a being-with, through that being-with's world. One's own Dasein is co-Dasein — encounterable for others — only insofar as it has the essential structure of being-with. This is the section's doctrinal core, and every joint bears weight. Being-with is a priori: not the registration of company but the structure that makes both company and solitude possible. The deficient-mode argument reaches its most famous instance — loneliness proves Mitsein (only a with-being can miss anyone) — and its converse is equally sharp: crowds do not cure solitude, since being-with was never numerical. The terminological division of labor closes the account: Mitsein on the side of the one who is (mine, always), Mitdasein on the side of the encountered (the others as freed into my world) — and, reflexively, my own encounterability for them.

The ninth unit assigns the new structure its own mode of concern. If co-Dasein remains existentially constitutive for being-in-the-world, then it must be interpreted — like circumspective dealings with the ready-to-hand, anticipatorily termed concern — from the phenomenon of care, as which the being of Dasein in general will be determined (Chapter Six). The being-character of concern cannot pertain to being-with, although this mode of being is a being toward beings encountered innerworldly, as concern is; the being toward which Dasein comports itself as being-with does not have the mode of being of ready-to-hand equipment — it is itself Dasein. These beings are not attended-to as objects of concern (besorgt): they stand in solicitude (Fürsorge). The categorial hygiene is strict: one more mode of being demands one more mode of comportment — persons are not managed as tools are handled — and the forward-reference quietly re-architects the book: Besorgen and Fürsorge will be the two arms of the one care (§ 41).

The tenth unit protects the new term and dignifies the deficient. Even the "procuring" of food and clothing, the nursing of the sick body, is solicitude — but the expression is understood, corresponding to the use of concern, as the term for an existential; "welfare work" (Fürsorge) as a factical social institution, for instance, grounds in Dasein's constitution of being as being-with, and its factical urgency is motivated by the fact that Dasein proximally and mostly maintains itself in the deficient modes of solicitude. Being for, against, and without one another, passing one another by, mattering nothing to one another — these are possible ways of solicitude, and precisely the last-named modes of deficiency and indifference characterize everyday and average being-with-one-another. These modes of being show once more the character of inconspicuousness and self-evidence that belongs to the everyday innerworldly co-Dasein of others just as much as to the readiness-to-hand of daily equipment; and these indifferent modes easily mislead the ontological interpretation into construing this being, at first, as pure presence-at-hand of several subjects. Only slight varieties of the same mode of being seem to be present — and yet ontologically there is an essential difference between the "indifferent" occurring-together of arbitrary things and the mattering-nothing-to-one-another of beings who are with one another. The etymological aside on the German welfare-state term (Fürsorge as an institution grounded in Fürsorge as an existential — urgent because everyday solicitude is deficient) is more than wordplay: it derives a social fact from an ontological structure. And the closing distinction is among the book's finest: mutual indifference between persons is a mode of being-with — a relation of non-mattering — categorially unlike the sheer juxtaposition of stones; coldness is a way of being together, which is exactly why it can wound.

The eleventh unit gives the first extreme of positive solicitude. With regard to its positive modes, solicitude has two extreme possibilities. It can, as it were, take "care" away from the other and, in the attending-to, put itself in his place — leap in (einspringen) for him: this solicitude takes over, for the other, what is to be attended to. The other is thereby thrown out of his place; he steps back, in order afterward to take over the attended-to as something finished and available, or to disburden himself of it entirely. In such solicitude the other can become dependent and dominated — even if this domination is tacit and remains hidden from the dominated. This leaping-in solicitude, which takes "care" away, determines being-with-one-another to a wide extent, and it concerns mostly the attending to the ready-to-hand. The analysis is a phenomenology of domination through helpfulness: leaping-in operates at the level of the other's concerns (doing his tasks) and, precisely by relieving him, displaces him — benevolence's own structure of mastery, the more effective for being invisible to both parties. The vocabulary of disburdening (entlasten) is planted here for § 27, where das Man will be the great disburdener.

The twelfth unit gives the counter-extreme. Over against it stands the possibility of a solicitude that does not so much leap in for the other as leap ahead (vorausspringen) of him in his existentiell potentiality-of-being — not to take "care" away from him but first to give it back authentically as such. This solicitude, which essentially concerns authentic care — the existence of the other — and not a what that he attends to, helps the other to become transparent to himself in his care and free for it. The contrast is drawn along the § 12 line: leaping-in addresses the other's Besorgen (his tasks), leaping-ahead his existence (his having-to-be); the one substitutes, the other liberates — helping the other into his own care rather than out of it. The formula quietly defines everything the book will mean by authentic community (§ 60's resoluteness that first lets others "be" in their ownmost potentiality; § 122's authentic alliance) and supplies, in two sentences, an entire ethics of education, therapy, and friendship the text declines to elaborate.

The thirteenth unit ties solicitude into shared work — and states the paradox of solidarity. Solicitude proves to be a constitution of Dasein's being which, according to its different possibilities, is interlocked with Dasein's being toward the world of its concern as with its authentic being toward itself. Being-with-one-another grounds proximally, and often exclusively, in what is jointly attended to in such being: a being-with-one-another that springs from one's doing the same thing as another mostly keeps not only within outer limits but enters the mode of distance and reserve — the being-with-one-another of those employed at the same affair often feeds only on mistrust. Conversely, common commitment to the same cause (Sache) is determined from the Dasein expressly seized in each case: this authentic alliance first makes possible the right objectivity (Sachlichkeit), which frees the other in his freedom for himself. The sociological aperçu is razor-sharp: mere co-employment breeds rivalry and reserve (sameness of task without ownness of existence), while genuine solidarity presupposes that each has seized his own existence — commonality is grounded in authenticity, not in likeness; and the closing clause fuses the section's two ideals: right objectivity about the cause and the freeing of the other are one accomplishment.

The fourteenth unit places the everyday between the extremes: between the two extremes of positive solicitude — the leaping-in-dominating and the leaping-ahead-liberating — everyday being-with-one-another maintains itself and shows manifold mixed forms, whose description and classification lie outside the limits of this investigation. The disclaimer is the § 5 discipline: the analytic supplies the structural axes; the empirical typology of social forms belongs to the sciences the analytic grounds.

The fifteenth unit gives solicitude its sight: as circumspection belongs to concern as its way of discovering the ready-to-hand, so solicitude is guided by considerateness (Rücksicht) and forbearance (Nachsicht); and both can run through the corresponding deficient and indifferent modes, down to inconsiderateness and the indulgent overlooking that indifference guides. The parallel completes the architecture — every comportment has its sight (§ 15's law) — and the German plays on Sicht (Um-, Rück-, Nach-sicht) bind the three sights into one family of circumspective seeing, each with its privatives.

The sixteenth unit re-founds the whole in worldhood. The world frees not only the ready-to-hand as innerworldly encountered beings, but also Dasein — the others in their co-Dasein. But this environmentally freed being is, according to its ownmost sense of being, being-in in the same world in which, encounterable for others, it is there-with. Worldhood was interpreted (§ 18) as the reference-whole of significance, fastened in Dasein's being toward its ownmost being, with which there can essentially be no involvement — which is rather the being for-the-sake-of-which Dasein itself is as it is. The recapitulation prepares the decisive extension in the next unit: the anchor of significance (the Worumwillen) is about to be shown as plural.

The seventeenth unit performs it. According to the analysis now carried through, being-with others belongs to the being of Dasein, about which, in its being, that being itself is at issue: as being-with, Dasein "is" essentially for the sake of others (umwillen Anderer). This must be understood as an existential statement of essence: even when the respective factical Dasein does not turn to others, believes it has no need of them, or does without them, it is in the mode of being-with. In being-with as the existential for-the-sake-of others, the others are already disclosed in their Dasein; this disclosedness of the others, constituted beforehand with being-with, accordingly co-constitutes significance — worldhood — as which it is fastened in the existential for-the-sake-of-which. Hence the worldhood of the world, thus constituted, lets the environmentally ready-to-hand be encountered in such a way that, in one with it as circumspectively attended, the co-Dasein of others is encountered: it lies in the structure of the world's worldhood that the others are not proximally present-at-hand as free-floating subjects beside other things, but show themselves, in their environmental particular being in the world, from what is ready-to-hand in it. The theorem is the chapter's deepest: § 18's world-structure is revised at its anchor — the for-the-sake-of includes the others (Dasein is umwillen Anderer as essentially as it is umwillen seiner) — so that sociality is built into significance itself, and the workshop-findings of the second unit (others met in the wares) fall out as consequences: the world lets others be encountered because their disclosedness co-constitutes its very worldhood.

The eighteenth unit converts knowing-others into a founded mode. The disclosedness of the co-Dasein of others belonging to being-with means: because Dasein's being is being-with, in its understanding of being there already lies the understanding of others. This understanding, like understanding in general, is not an acquaintance grown from cognition but an originally existential mode of being that first makes cognition and acquaintance possible: knowing-one-another (Sichkennen) grounds in the originally understanding being-with. It moves proximally, in accordance with the nearest mode of being of with-like being-in-the-world, in the understanding acquaintance with what Dasein circumspectively finds and attends to with the others in the environing world; from out of what is attended to, and with the understanding of it, solicitous concern is understood — the other is proximally disclosed in concernful solicitude. The order of § 13 is repeated for persons: understanding-of-others is an existential (given with Mitsein), and mutual acquaintance is its everyday enactment through shared work — one knows the other from what one does with him, and explicit knowledge of persons is downstream of that.

The nineteenth unit explains why acquaintance is work: because solicitude proximally and mostly dwells in the deficient or at least indifferent modes — in the indifference of passing one another by — the nearest and essential knowing-one-another needs a getting-to-know-one-another; and when knowing-one-another loses itself into reserve, hiding, and dissembling, being-with-one-another needs special ways to come near the others or get "behind" them. The unit dignifies the everyday difficulty of intimacy ontologically: the opacity of others is not the metaphysical closure of foreign minds but the practical sediment of deficient solicitude — hiddenness as an achievement of comportment, not a property of consciousness.

The twentieth unit locates the empathy-theory's error of order. But just as self-revealing and self-closing ground in the respective mode of being of being-with-one-another — indeed are nothing other than it — so too the explicit solicitous disclosing of the other grows only out of the primary being-with him. Such disclosing of the other, thematic but not theoretical-psychological, easily becomes, for the theoretical problematic of understanding "foreign psychic life," the phenomenon that first comes into view; and what is thus phenomenally "proximally" a way of understanding being-with-one-another gets taken at the same time as what "initially" and originally makes possible and constitutes being toward others at all. This phenomenon, not exactly happily termed "empathy" (Einfühlung), is then supposed, ontologically as it were, first to build the bridge from one's own subject, given at first alone, to the other subject, at first altogether closed off. The diagnosis is a § 13 replay in the social register: a founded, remedial accomplishment (the special effort of getting behind reserve) is promoted by theory into the constituting origin — Lipps's Einfühlung, and the entire problematic Husserl's Fifth Cartesian Meditation would soon canonize, are caught at the moment of the inversion.

The twenty-first unit reconstructs the projection-theory. Being toward others is indeed ontologically different from being toward present-at-hand things; the "other" being has itself Dasein's mode of being; hence in being with and toward others lies a relation of being of Dasein to Dasein. But this relation, one would like to say, is surely already constitutive for one's own Dasein, which has an understanding of its own being and thus comports itself to Dasein: the relation of being to others then becomes the projection of one's own being-toward-oneself "into an other" — the other is a double (Dublette) of the self. The reconstruction is scrupulous: the projection-theory (analogical apperception, the alter ego as mirrored ego) is granted its premises before the single false one is isolated.

The twenty-second unit isolates it: it is easy to see that this seemingly self-evident reflection rests on weak ground — its presupposition, that Dasein's being toward itself is a being toward an other, does not hold; and so long as this presupposition has not evidently demonstrated its legitimacy, it remains a riddle how it should disclose the relation of Dasein to itself to the other as other. The refutation is two-pronged and exact: the premise is false (self-relation is not other-relation writ small — my being-toward-myself has mineness's structure, not encounter's), and even granted, it proves too little — a projected double is precisely not the other as other; the alterity the theory was to explain is what it structurally cannot reach.

The twenty-third unit re-orders the phenomena. Being toward others is not only an autonomous, irreducible relation of being: as being-with, it already is with Dasein's being. It cannot be denied that the lively mutual acquaintance grounded on being-with often depends on how far one's own Dasein has in each case understood itself — but that means only: how far it has made the essential being-with with others transparent to itself and not dissembled it, which is possible only if Dasein, as being-in-the-world, in each case already is with others. "Empathy" does not first constitute being-with; it is possible only on its ground, and is motivated in its unavoidability by the predominant deficient modes of being-with. The re-ordering is the section's verdict in three clauses: being-with is a priori; self-understanding aids other-understanding only as transparency about the with-structure (not as data for projection); and empathy is real, founded, and necessary — necessary because everydayness is deficient: the bridge-building exists because the with-being mostly passes itself by.

The twenty-fourth unit assigns the residual problem and totals the section. That "empathy" is no original existential phenomenon — as little as cognition in general — does not mean there is no problem regarding it: its special hermeneutic will have to show how the various possibilities of being of Dasein itself mislead and obstruct being-with-one-another and its knowing-one-another, so that a genuine "understanding" is suppressed and Dasein takes refuge in surrogates; and which positive existential condition right understanding of the foreign presupposes for its possibility. The analysis has shown: being-with is an existential constituent of being-in-the-world; co-Dasein proves an ownmost mode of being of innerworldly encountered beings; insofar as Dasein is at all, it has the mode of being of being-with-one-another — which cannot be conceived as the summative result of the occurrence of several "subjects." Coming upon a number of "subjects" itself becomes possible only when the others, encountered at first in their co-Dasein, are treated merely as "numbers": such a number is discovered only through a determinate being with and toward one another — this "inconsiderate" being-with "reckons" with the others without seriously "counting on them" or even wanting "to have anything to do with them." The promised hermeneutic of misunderstanding (surrogates for genuine understanding, the positive condition of Fremdverstehen) is one more of the book's fertile unwritten chapters — the program Gadamer's hermeneutics and a whole literature on intersubjectivity would inherit. And the closing analysis of counting is a small marvel: even the sociologist's aggregate of n subjects presupposes Mitsein — enumeration of persons is itself a mode of being-with, the inconsiderate one that reckons with those it will not count on; the reduction of others to numbers is a social relation, not the absence of one.

The closing unit poses the question that names the next section: one's own Dasein, like the co-Dasein of others, is encountered proximally and mostly from the environmentally attended-to with-world; in its absorption in the world of concern — that is, at once, in its being-with toward others — Dasein is not itself. Who is it, then, who has taken over being as everyday being-with-one-another? The two chapters' results (self found from world, § 26; others constitutive, § 25–26) converge into the question § 25 planted: if everyday Dasein is not itself, someone else answers the who — § 27's das Man stands in the doorway.

##### § 27. Everyday Being-a-Self and das Man

The opening unit banks § 26's yield in a formula: the ontologically relevant result of the analysis of being-with lies in the insight that the "subject-character" of one's own Dasein and of the others determines itself existentially — from certain ways to be. In what is environmentally attended to, the others are encountered as what they are: they are what they pursue. The last sentence is the everyday who-answer in six words — one is one's occupation, the baker at his oven, the colleague at her desk — and it is offered without irony: existential determination of the who means precisely that everyday identity is a way of being (pursuing), not a substrate behind it. On this basis the section can now ask what way of being everyday pursuing itself has.

The second unit uncovers the restlessness inside the everyday. In attending to what one has undertaken with, for, and against the others, there rests constantly the care about a difference from the others — be it only to even out the difference; be it that one's own Dasein, lagging behind the others, wants to catch up in relation to them; be it that Dasein, in priority over them, is out to keep them down. Being-with-one-another is — hidden from itself — disquieted by the care about this distance: expressed existentially, it has the character of distantiality (Abständigkeit). And the more inconspicuous this mode of being is to everyday Dasein itself, the more stubbornly and originally it works itself out. The three cases are exhaustive and deliberately leveling: conformism, ambition, and domination are one structure — comparative care, the constant secret measurement against the others — and the paradox of the diagnosis is its concealment-clause: distantiality rules most where it is noticed least; social existence is disquieted precisely in its calm.

The third unit draws the consequence and names the who. In this distantiality belonging to being-with lies: Dasein, as everyday being-with-one-another, stands in subservience (Botmäßigkeit) to the others. Not it itself is; the others have taken its being away from it (abgenommen). The others' discretion disposes over the everyday possibilities of Dasein's being. These others are, in this, not determinate others: on the contrary, every other can represent them; decisive is only the inconspicuous domination by the others, taken over unawares by Dasein as being-with. One belongs to the others oneself and consolidates their power. "The others" — so called to cover over one's own essential belonging to them — are those who, in everyday being-with-one-another, proximally and mostly "are there." The who is not this one, not that one, not oneself, not some, and not the sum of all: the "who" is the neuter, das Man — the "one," the "they." The paragraph performs the answer § 25 forecast. The expropriation-formula (the others have taken its being away) turns § 26's disburdening into dispossession; the anonymity-clauses do the philosophical work — the dominating others are nobody in particular, infinitely substitutable, and include me (my very phrase "the others" is an alibi concealing that I am of them); and the grammar delivers the ontology: the everyday who is a neuter, the impersonal pronoun of "one says," "one does" — a who that is structurally no one.

The fourth unit shows the dictatorship at work in public life. It was shown earlier how, in the nearest environing world, the public "environing world" is already ready-to-hand and attended to along with it: in using public transport, in employing the news-service (the newspaper), every other is like the other. This being-with-one-another dissolves one's own Dasein completely into the mode of being of "the others" — such that the others, in their distinguishability and explicitness, vanish still further. In this inconspicuousness and unascertainability das Man unfolds its authentic dictatorship: we enjoy ourselves and amuse ourselves as one enjoys; we read, see, and judge literature and art as one sees and judges; we withdraw from the "great mass" as one withdraws; we find "revolting" what one finds revolting. Das Man, which is nothing determinate and which all are — though not as a sum — prescribes the mode of being of everydayness. The tram and the newspaper (the era's mass media, § 23's radio close behind) supply the phenomenal base: publicness as the sphere where each is like the next and the "others" as such disappear into pure substitutability. The famous catalogue is built to close every exit — even withdrawal from the crowd is executed as one withdraws; even indignation is prescribed — nonconformity itself has its conventions, so the dictatorship needs no dictator. And the final clause fixes the strange logic: everyone is das Man, yet no summation yields it — it is a way of being, not a set.

The fifth unit gives das Man its second and third structures. Das Man has its own ways to be. The tendency of being-with called distantiality grounds in the fact that being-with-one-another as such attends to averageness (Durchschnittlichkeit): averageness is an existential character of das Man; in its being, das Man is essentially concerned with it. Hence it maintains itself factically in the averageness of what is proper, what one lets count and what not, what one grants success and what one denies it. This averageness, in predelineating what can and may be ventured, watches over every exception that presses forward: every priority is noiselessly suppressed; everything original is overnight smoothed down as long familiar; everything hard-won becomes handy; every mystery loses its power. The care of averageness reveals once more an essential tendency of Dasein, which we call the leveling (Einebnung) of all possibilities of being. The paragraph is the book's social criticism at its most quotable, and its precision should not be lost in the eloquence: averageness is not a statistical fact but something das Man cares about and enforces — a normativity (what one lets count) whose sanctions are noiseless; and the four aorists of leveling (smoothed, handy, powerless, familiar) describe a temporal mechanism — "overnight" — by which the exceptional is not refuted but assimilated: § 1's trivialization of the Greek beginnings and § 6's tradition now receive their existential motor.

The sixth unit composes the structures into publicness. Distantiality, averageness, leveling constitute, as ways of being of das Man, what we know as "publicness" (die Öffentlichkeit). It proximally regulates all interpretation of world and Dasein and retains the right in everything — and this not on the ground of a distinguished and primary relation of being to the "things," not because it disposes over an expressly appropriated transparency of Dasein, but on the ground of its not-going-into "the matters," because it is insensitive to all differences of level and genuineness. Publicness obscures everything and passes off what is thus covered as the known and accessible to everyone. The definition inverts the Enlightenment's honorific: publicness — the tribunal of open reason — is here the regime of groundless authority, whose peculiar power is negative (it is always right because it never engages the matters and so can never be refuted by them); its insensitivity to level and genuineness is not a failing of attention but its constitutive principle. The last sentence is § 7's concealment-doctrine socialized: the public covering presents itself as universal accessibility — disguise (Verstellung) in its collective form.

The seventh unit exposes the responsibility-mechanism. Das Man is everywhere present, yet so that it has always already stolen away wherever Dasein presses for decision. But because das Man pregives all judging and deciding, it takes responsibility away from the respective Dasein (nimmt... die Verantwortlichkeit ab). Das Man can, as it were, afford that "one" constantly appeals to it: it can most easily answer for everything, because no one is it who needs to stand for anything. Das Man always "was" it — and yet it can be said that "no one" was it. In Dasein's everydayness most things come about through that of which we must say: no one was it. The analysis of anonymous agency is exact enough for jurisprudence: the "one" is the universal defendant that cannot be arraigned — omnipresent in prescription, absent at the point of decision — and the everyday sentence "no one was it" (es war keiner) is elevated into the ontological signature of public action. Every later theory of structural irresponsibility (the bureaucratic "no one," collective action problems, Arendt's rule by Nobody) has this paragraph as ancestor.

The eighth unit names the exchange that secures the regime: das Man thus disburdens (entlastet) the respective Dasein in its everydayness. Not only that: with this disburdening of being it accommodates (kommt entgegen) Dasein, insofar as in Dasein lies the tendency to take things easily and make them easy; and because it constantly accommodates the respective Dasein with this disburdening of being, it retains and consolidates its stubborn dominion. The two verbs carry the doctrine — Entlastung and Entgegenkommen: the dictatorship is not imposed but purchased, meeting halfway a tendency of Dasein itself (the ease-seeking that § 68 will root in falling); domination by das Man is thus collusion, which is why no unmasking dissolves it — the disburdened party is a willing one.

The ninth unit strikes the coin: everyone is the other, and no one is himself. Das Man, with which the question of the who of everyday Dasein answers itself, is the nobody (das Niemand) to which all Dasein, in its being-among-one-another, has in each case already surrendered itself. Two sentences, the section's arch: the first states the exchange-structure of everyday identity (each defined through the others, none through himself), the second the answer to § 25's question in its starkest form — the who of everydayness is a nobody, and the surrender to it is always already accomplished, never an event one could have prevented.

The tenth unit converts the findings into a doctrine of everyday constancy — and blocks the moralizing reading. In the exhibited characters of being of everyday being-among-one-another — distantiality, averageness, leveling, publicness, disburdening of being, and accommodation — lies the nearest "constancy" (Ständigkeit) of Dasein: a constancy that concerns not the continual presence-at-hand of something but Dasein's mode of being as being-with. Being in these modes, the self of one's own Dasein and the self of the other have not yet found themselves — or have lost themselves: one is in the manner of non-self-constancy and inauthenticity (Unselbständigkeit und Uneigentlichkeit). This way to be signifies no diminution of Dasein's facticity, just as das Man, as the nobody, is no nothing; on the contrary, in this mode of being Dasein is an ens realissimum, if "reality" is understood as Dasein-like being. The unit answers § 25's demand (the constancy of the self needs existential interpretation) with a first, ironic installment: everydayness has its own constancy — the steadiness of the "one," identity outsourced to the public pattern — and § 64 will oppose to it the self-constancy of resoluteness. The double guard at the close is emphatic: inauthenticity is fully real, indeed the most real of the everyday (the scholastic superlative pointedly transferred), and das Man's being-nobody is not its being nothing — the moral and the nihilistic misreadings barred in one breath.

The eleventh unit fixes the phenomenon's peculiar mode of being. To be sure, das Man is as little present-at-hand as Dasein in general: the more openly it comports itself, the more ungraspable and hidden it is — but the less is it nothing. To unprejudiced ontic-ontological "seeing" it unveils itself as the "most real subject" of everydayness; and if it is not accessible like a present-at-hand stone, that decides nothing whatever about its mode of being. One may neither hastily decree that this Man is "really" nothing, nor cultivate the opinion that the phenomenon is ontologically interpreted when one "explains" it as the subsequently aggregated result of the co-presence of several subjects: rather, conversely, the working-out of the concepts of being must direct itself by these irrecusable phenomena. The methodological rule at the close is the section's deepest claim: ontology must be revised to fit das Man, not das Man explained away to fit ontology — the phenomena legislate to the categories (§ 7's priority of the Sachen, enforced against both eliminativism and social-aggregation theory).

The twelfth unit blocks the last classical shelter: nor is das Man anything like a "universal subject" hovering over the many. That conception can arise only if the being of the "subjects" is understood un-Dasein-like, as factually present-at-hand cases of an occurring genus — an approach that leaves ontologically only the possibility of understanding whatever is not a case in the sense of species and genus. Das Man is not the genus of the respective Dasein, nor can it be found as an abiding constitution in this being. That traditional logic too fails before these phenomena cannot surprise, once one considers that it has its foundation in an — moreover crude — ontology of the present-at-hand; hence it cannot be made fundamentally more supple by ever so many improvements and expansions: these "humanistically" oriented reforms of logic only increase the ontological confusion. The refused option is recognizably Hegelian-idealist (objective spirit as supra-individual subject) and its refutation is categorial: universal-over-cases is the genus/species logic of the vorhanden (§ 9), inapplicable where beings are not cases at all. The closing polemic — against the geisteswissenschaftlich reforms of logic (the Dilthey-school and value-philosophy's attempts to soften the categories for the human sciences) — repeats § 10's verdict: renovation upon the old foundation deepens the confusion it means to cure.

The thirteenth unit gives das Man its title and its history: das Man is an existential, and belongs as an original phenomenon to the positive constitution of Dasein. It has, in turn, various possibilities of its Dasein-like concretion: the penetration and explicitness of its dominion can change historically. The two sentences are the section's ontological verdict and its opening to history: das Man is neither corruption nor accident but constitutional (the "positive" is deliberate — a structure, not a fall from grace), and its rule is historically variable — an invitation the text does not take up, toward a history of publicness (how the dictatorship of the one differs in Athens, in Christendom, in the age of the newspaper) that §§ 74–77's historicity would license.

The fourteenth unit names the everyday self and describes the way back. The self of everyday Dasein is the Man-selbst — the they-self — which we distinguish from the authentic, that is, expressly seized self. As they-self, the respective Dasein is dispersed (zerstreut) into das Man and must first find itself. This dispersal characterizes the "subject" of that mode of being we know as concernful absorption in the nearest encountered world. If Dasein is familiar to itself as they-self, this means at once that das Man predelineates the nearest interpretation of the world and of being-in-the-world: das Man itself, for whose sake Dasein everyday is, articulates the reference-context of significance. Dasein's world frees encountered beings toward an involvement-totality familiar to das Man, and within the limits fixed with its averageness. Proximally, factical Dasein is in the averagely discovered with-world; proximally, it is not "I," in the sense of the own self, that "am," but the others, in the mode of das Man: from out of this and as this I am proximally "given" to myself. Proximally Dasein is das Man, and mostly it remains so. If Dasein discovers the world expressly and brings it near, if it discloses to itself its authentic being, then this discovering of "world" and disclosing of Dasein always comes to pass as a clearing-away of coverings and obscurings, as a breaking of the disguises with which Dasein bars itself against itself. The paragraph is the chapter's summit, and three theses must be lifted from it. The structural thesis: das Man occupies the Worumwillen — the anchor of significance (§ 18) is everyday held by the one, so the very intelligibility of my world is publicly pre-articulated; the dictatorship reaches into worldhood itself. The genetic thesis, in the most quoted sentence of the chapter: I am given to myself first from das Man and as das Man — the they-self is not a mask over a prior I but the first form of selfhood, from which any own self must be won. And the methodological thesis: authenticity is therefore reached only privatively, as the breaking of disguises — clearing-away, not construction — which fixes in advance the form of Division Two: anxiety, death, and conscience as the powers that break the public covering; and § 25's suspicion is retrospectively cashed: the loud "I" was the they-self's voice.
