The understood, held in fore-having and "fore-sightedly" targeted, becomes conceivable through the interpretation; the interpretation can draw the conceptuality belonging to the beings to be interpreted from these themselves, or force them into concepts that the beings, according to their mode of being, resist — however it may be, interpretation has in each case already decided, finally or with reservations, for a determinate conceptuality: it grounds in a fore-grasp (Vorgriff). The triad is minted here — Vorhabe, Vorsicht, Vorgriff: what one already has (the totality dwelt in), the angle from which one cuts, the concepts one brings — and the middle sentence quietly states the ethics of interpretation the section will make explicit: conceptuality drawn from the things themselves versus forced upon them; the destruction of § 6 (Greek concepts distorting Christian life; categories forced on Dasein) is exactly the diagnosis of violated fore-grasp.

The fifth unit applies it to philology's proudest claim. Interpretation of something as something is essentially founded through fore-having, fore-sight, and fore-grasp: interpretation is never a presuppositionless grasping of something pregiven. When the particular concretion of interpretation in the sense of exact text-exegesis likes to appeal to what "stands there" (was dasteht), then what proximally "stands there" is nothing other than the self-evident, undiscussed fore-opinion of the interpreter, which necessarily lies in every interpretive approach as that which is already "posited" with interpretation as such — pregiven in fore-having, fore-sight, fore-grasp. The sentence has become the charter-text of philosophical hermeneutics, and its edge should be kept sharp: the appeal to the bare text is not humility but concealed dogmatism — the "obvious meaning" is the interpreter's unexamined fore-structure enthroned as the given; rigor begins where the fore-structure is owned, not where it is denied.

The sixth unit poses the structural questions: how is the character of this "fore-" to be conceived? Is it done when one says, formally, "a priori"? Why does this structure belong to understanding, which was marked as a fundamental existential of Dasein? How does the "as"-structure belonging to the interpreted as such relate to it? The phenomenon is manifestly not to be dissolved "into pieces"; but does that exclude an original analytic? Are such phenomena to be accepted as "ultimates"? Then the question would still remain: why? Or do the fore-structure of understanding and the as-structure of interpretation show an existential-ontological connection with the phenomenon of projection — and does this point back into an original constitution of Dasein's being? The battery keeps § 28's rules in force (no dissolution, no lazy ultimates) and points the answer where the reader now expects it: fore- and as-structure as articulations of thrown projection — and, beyond, into the "original constitution" that temporality will name.

The seventh unit inserts the needed preliminary: before answering these questions — for which the equipment so far is far from sufficient — it must be investigated whether what is visible as fore-structure of understanding and as as-structure of interpretation does not itself present a unitary phenomenon, of which philosophical problematic makes abundant use, without the ontological explication matching the universality of the use. The unnamed universal is about to be named: Sinn — meaning — philosophy's most-used and least-examined coin.

The eighth unit defines meaning and expropriates it. In the projecting of understanding, beings are disclosed in their possibility; the possibility-character corresponds in each case to the mode of being of the understood beings. Innerworldly beings in general are projected upon world — upon a whole of significance in whose reference-relations concern, as being-in-the-world, has fastened itself in advance. When innerworldly beings are discovered with the being of Dasein — have come to understanding — we say: they have meaning (Sinn). But what is understood is, strictly, not the meaning but the beings, or being: meaning is that wherein the intelligibility of something holds itself. What is articulable in understanding disclosing we call meaning; the concept of meaning comprises the formal framework of what necessarily belongs to that which understanding interpretation articulates. Meaning is the fore-having-, fore-sight-, and fore-grasp-structured toward-which (Woraufhin) of the projection, from out of which something becomes intelligible as something. Insofar as understanding and interpretation constitute the existential constitution of the being of the Da, meaning must be conceived as the formal-existential framework of the disclosedness belonging to understanding: meaning is an existential of Dasein — not a property that adheres to beings, lies "behind" them, or floats somewhere as an "intermediate realm." Dasein only "has" meaning insofar as the disclosedness of being-in-the-world is "fillable" by the beings discoverable in it; hence only Dasein can be meaningful or meaningless — which says: its own being, and the beings disclosed with it, can be appropriated in understanding, or remain denied to non-understanding. The definition is the section's summit: meaning = the structured whither of projection, that from which anything is intelligible as what it is — and its polemical clause dispatches the era's three ontologies of meaning at once: not a property of things (naturalism), not behind them (metaphysical signification), not a floating third realm (Lotze's Geltung, Frege's and Husserl's ideal senses). Meaning is relocated into the disclosedness of the being that understands — an existential, not an entity of any realm.

The ninth unit accepts the hard consequence: holding fast this fundamentally ontological-existential interpretation of "meaning," all beings of non-Dasein-like mode of being must be conceived as unmeaning (unsinnig) — essentially bare of meaning altogether. "Unmeaning" here is no valuation but the expression of an ontological determination; and only the unmeaning can be counter-meaning (widersinnig): the present-at-hand, as encountered in Dasein, can, as it were, run against Dasein's being — for instance, breaking-in and destructive natural events. The stark corollary (nature is meaningless — not absurd but a-semantic, outside the dimension) is drawn without flinching, and the second clause converts it into an analysis of catastrophe: the flood is widersinnig, against-meaning — an assault registered as such only within a world of meaning it violates; absurdity is parasitic on significance.

The tenth unit turns the definition onto the book's own question: and when we ask about the meaning of being, the investigation does not become deep, nor does it brood on anything standing behind being; it asks about being itself, insofar as it stands into the intelligibility of Dasein. The meaning of being can never be set in opposition to beings, or to being as the supporting "ground" of beings — for "ground" becomes accessible only as meaning, even if this were itself the abyss (Abgrund) of meaninglessness. The paragraph deflates its own title-question with precision: "meaning of being" promises no hinter-world (§ 2's warning against the mython repeated at the level of Sinn) — it asks how being stands into intelligibility; and the last clause, with its play of Grund and Abgrund, is one of the book's forward-echoes: even should the ground prove an abyss, it could be met only within meaning — the sentence the later Heidegger will inhabit.

The eleventh unit lets the circle-objection assemble at full strength. Understanding, as the disclosedness of the Da, always concerns the whole of being-in-the-world; in every understanding of world, existence is co-understood, and conversely. All interpretation, further, moves in the characterized fore-structure: all interpretation that is to contribute understanding must already have understood what is to be interpreted. This fact has always been noticed, if only in the region of derivative modes of understanding and interpretation — in philological interpretation, which belongs within scientific cognition; and such cognition demands the rigor of grounding demonstration: scientific proof may not presuppose what it is its task to ground. But if interpretation must in each case already move in the understood and nourish itself from it, how is it to produce scientific results without moving in a circle — the more so as the presupposed understanding moves, moreover, in the common knowledge of man and world? Yet by the most elementary rules of logic the circle is circulus vitiosus; and so the business of historical interpretation remains a priori banished from the region of rigorous knowledge. So far as one does not remove this fact of the circle in understanding, historiography must resign itself to less rigorous possibilities of knowledge — allowed to compensate the lack somewhat through the "spiritual significance" of its "objects"; though it would be more ideal, in the historians' own opinion too, if the circle could be avoided and there were hope of one day creating a historiography as independent of the observer's standpoint as natural knowledge supposedly is. The objection is built to full contemporary height — the methodology-debate of the historical school, the envy of physics, the consolation-prize of "spiritual significance" — before the demolition; and the little word "supposedly" (vermeintlich) before the observer-independence of natural science plants the counter-charge in advance.

The twelfth unit delivers the doctrine of the circle. But to see a vitiosum in this circle, and to look about for ways to avoid it — even merely to "feel" it as an unavoidable imperfection — is to misunderstand understanding from the ground up. At issue is not assimilating understanding and interpretation to a determinate ideal of knowledge, which is itself only a variety of understanding that has strayed into the legitimate task of grasping the present-at-hand in its essential unintelligibility. The fulfillment of the basic conditions of possible interpretation lies rather in not misjudging it beforehand with respect to the essential conditions of its enactment: what is decisive is not to get out of the circle, but to come into it in the right way. This circle of understanding is not a ring in which any arbitrary kind of knowledge moves; it is the expression of the existential fore-structure of Dasein itself. The circle must not be degraded to a vitiosum, not even a tolerated one: in it hides a positive possibility of the most original knowing — a possibility genuinely seized only when interpretation has understood that its first, constant, and last task remains not to let fore-having, fore-sight, and fore-grasp be given to it by fancies and popular conceptions, but to secure the scientific theme in the working-out of these from the things themselves. Because understanding, in its existential sense, is Dasein's own potentiality-of-being, the ontological presuppositions of historical knowledge exceed in principle the idea of rigor of the most exact sciences: mathematics is not more rigorous than historiography, but only narrower with respect to the circuit of the existential foundations relevant to it. Every sentence of this celebrated paragraph carries a decision. The ideal of presuppositionless knowledge is itself unmasked as a founded variety of understanding (fitted to the essentially unintelligible present-at-hand — § 32's ninth unit paying off: exactness is calibrated to the meaningless); the imperative is re-directed from escape to right entry; the circle is identified with the fore-structure — Dasein's own being, not a defect of method; and the positive task is stated as a discipline: work out fore-having, fore-sight, fore-grasp from the things themselves against the drift of fancy and das Man's concepts — hermeneutic rigor as the perpetual audit of one's own presuppositions. The closing inversion (mathematics narrower, not stricter) re-scales the sciences by existential breadth: rigor is answerability to foundations, and historiography answers to more of Dasein than arithmetic does.

The closing unit banks the result and issues a final scruple: the "circle" in understanding belongs to the structure of meaning — a phenomenon rooted in the existential constitution of Dasein, in interpreting understanding. Beings for which, as being-in-the-world, their being is itself at issue have an ontological circle-structure. Yet, noting that "circle" belongs ontologically to a mode of being of presence-at-hand (subsistence), one must altogether avoid characterizing anything like Dasein ontologically by this phenomenon. The scruple is characteristic and instructive: having fought for the circle, Heidegger surrenders the word — "circle" is itself a figure of the present-at-hand (a closed subsisting line), and to keep it would smuggle the wrong ontology into the victory; the phenomenon stands, the geometry goes. The way is thereby clear for § 33's question: what becomes of interpretation when it flattens into the assertion — the derivative in which the tradition read the "as," the circle, and truth itself.

###### § 33. Assertion as a Derivative Mode of Interpretation

The opening unit places assertion in the derivation-order and refuses a definition. All interpretation grounds in understanding; what is articulated in interpretation as such, and predelineated in understanding in general as articulable, is meaning. Insofar as assertion (the "judgment") grounds in understanding and presents a derived form of the enactment of interpretation, it too "has" a meaning — but this meaning cannot be defined as what occurs "at" a judgment alongside the act of judging. The express analysis of assertion in the present context has a multiple purpose. The refused definition is Lotze's and the neo-Kantians': meaning as the ideal content attached to the psychic act — the two-component theory of judgment dismissed in a subordinate clause, since § 32 has already relocated Sinn into disclosedness.

The second unit gives the three purposes. First, assertion can demonstrate in what way the "as"-structure constitutive for understanding and interpretation is modifiable — understanding and interpretation thereby come into a still sharper light. Then, the analysis of assertion has a distinguished place within the fundamental-ontological problematic, because in the decisive beginnings of ancient ontology the logos functioned as the sole guiding thread for access to authentic beings and for the determination of their being. Finally, assertion counts from of old as the primary and authentic "place" of truth — a phenomenon so tightly coupled with the problem of being that the present investigation necessarily strikes upon the truth-problem in its further course, indeed already stands, though inexpressly, in its dimension; the analysis of assertion is to help prepare this problematic. The triple motivation is the book's architecture in cross-section: a structural yield (the as-structure's modifiability), a destructive yield (§ 6's logos-guided ancient ontology re-engaged), and a forward yield — § 44 announced: dethroning assertion as truth's place is the precondition for re-locating truth in disclosedness.

The third unit announces the procedure: three significations are assigned to the title "assertion," drawn from the phenomenon itself, connected among themselves, and delimiting in their unity the full structure of assertion. The method is § 7 B's again — one word, its senses ordered and unified from the phenomenon.

The fourth unit gives the first signification: assertion means primarily pointing-out (Aufzeigung). This holds fast the original sense of logos as apophansis: letting beings be seen from themselves. In the assertion "the hammer is too heavy," what is discovered for sight is no "meaning" but a being in the mode of its readiness-to-hand; even if the being is not in graspable and "visible" nearness, the pointing-out means the being itself — not a mere representation of it, neither a "merely represented" something nor a psychic state of the asserter, his representing of the being. The choice of example is polemical genius: the logician's specimen sentence is re-supplied with its workshop original — and the primary stratum of assertion is fixed as world-directed through and through: what the sentence exhibits is the too-heavy hammer, not a proposition, not an idea, not a mental act. Intentionality's realism, radicalized: § 7 B's apophansis governing the theory of judgment.

The fifth unit gives the second: assertion means predication — a "predicate" is "asserted" of a "subject," the latter determined by the former. What is asserted in this signification is not the predicate but "the hammer itself"; what does the asserting — the determining — lies in the "too heavy." What is asserted in the second sense, the determined as such, has undergone a contentual narrowing over against what is asserted in the first: every predication is what it is only as pointing-out. The second signification has its foundation in the first; the members of the predicative articulation — subject, predicate — grow within the pointing-out. Determining does not first discover; as a mode of pointing-out, it initially restricts the seeing precisely to what shows itself — the hammer — as such, in order, through the express restriction of the gaze, to make the manifest expressly manifest in its determinateness. Determining, faced with what is already manifest — the too-heavy hammer — first takes a step back; the "positing of the subject" dims the being down to "this hammer there," so that by the enactment of the un-dimming the manifest can be seen in its determinable determinateness. Subject-positing, predicate-positing, together with the com-positing, are through and through "apophantic" in the strict sense of the word. The micro-phenomenology of predication is among the book's finest technical passages: the subject-term is analyzed as a deliberate dimming (Abblendung) — a restriction of the gaze to the bare bearer — and the predicate as the staged un-dimming that lets the already-manifest reappear as determination. Predication thus adds no discovery; it re-organizes a prior manifestness — narrowing as its price, explicitness as its yield — and even the copulative synthesis is apophantic (a mode of letting-see), not a gluing of representations: § 7 B's reading of synthesis enforced inside grammar.

The sixth unit gives the third: assertion means communication (Mitteilung), speaking-forth. As such it has direct relation to assertion in the first and second significations: it is a letting-see-with (Mitsehenlassen) of what is pointed out in the manner of determining. This letting-see-with shares the being pointed out in its determinateness with the other; "shared" is the common seeing being toward what is pointed out — a being toward it that must be held fast as being-in-the-world, in that world, namely, from which the pointed-out is encountered. To assertion as communication so existentially understood belongs spokenness (Ausgesprochenheit): what is asserted, as communicated, can be "shared" by the others with the asserter without their having the pointed-out and determined being themselves in graspable and visible nearness. What is asserted can be "passed along" — the circuit of the seeing sharing-with-one-another widens. But at the same time, in the passing-along, the pointed-out can veil itself again — although even the knowledge and acquaintance growing in such hearsay still means the being itself and does not, say, "affirm" a circulated "valid meaning." Even hearsay is a being-in-the-world and a being toward what is heard. The analysis quietly contains the whole of § 35 in advance: communication as shared seeing-toward (not transport of contents — § 34 will say it), the widening circuit of the passed-along, and the re-veiling that widening brings — idle talk's mechanism, discovered inside assertion's own third moment. The closing barb keeps even degenerate speech world-directed: hearsay is about the being, not about a circulating validity — against the Geltungs-theory about to be arraigned.

The seventh unit conducts the arraignment. The theory of "judgment" today predominantly oriented to the phenomenon of "validity" (Geltung) is not to be discussed at length; it suffices to point to the multiple questionableness of this phenomenon, which since Lotze is readily passed off as an irreducible "primal phenomenon" — a role it owes only to its ontological unclarifiedness. The "problematic" that has settled around this word-idol (Wortgötze) is no less opaque. Validity means, first, the "form" of actuality accruing to the judgment-content insofar as it subsists unchangeably over against the changeable "psychic" judgment-process; given the state of the being-question characterized in the Introduction, it can hardly be expected that "validity" as "ideal being" is distinguished by particular ontological clarity. Validity means then, at once, the validity of the valid judgment-meaning of the "object" meant in it, and thus slides into the signification of "objective validity" and objectivity in general. And the meaning thus "valid" of beings — "timelessly" valid in itself — "is valid" then once more in the sense of holding for every rational judger: validity now means bindingness, "universal validity." If one further advocates a "critical" epistemology, according to which the subject does not "really" "get out" to the object, then validity as the object's validity — objectivity — is grounded on the valid subsistence of the true (!) meaning. The three significations set out — as the mode of being of the ideal, as objectivity, and as bindingness — are not only in themselves opaque; they constantly confuse themselves among one another. Methodical caution demands not choosing such iridescent concepts as the guiding thread of interpretation: we do not first restrict the concept of meaning to "judgment-content," but understand it as the characterized existential phenomenon in which the formal framework of what is disclosable in understanding and articulable in interpretation becomes visible. The demolition is the era's sacred cow slaughtered by disambiguation: Geltung — Lotze's legacy, backbone of the Windelband-Rickert school and of the young Husserl's anti-psychologism — is decomposed into three senses (ideal being, objectivity, bindingness) whose systematic conflation is exposed as the theory's engine: each sense borrows plausibility from the others, and the "word-idol" reigns by equivocation. The exclamation mark after "true" flags the theft: a validity-theory that grounds objectivity in the subsistence of true meaning has presupposed truth, the very thing at issue. § 7 B's derivation-method has become a weapon.

The eighth unit assembles the definition and verifies the fore-structure. Taking the three analyzed significations together in a unified view of the full phenomenon, the definition runs: assertion is a communicatively determining pointing-out (mitteilend bestimmende Aufzeigung). It remains to ask with what right assertion is grasped as a mode of interpretation at all: if it is such, the essential structures of interpretation must recur in it. The pointing-out of assertion is enacted on the ground of what is already disclosed in understanding or circumspectively discovered; assertion is no free-floating comportment that could of itself primarily disclose beings, but holds itself always already on the basis of being-in-the-world. What was shown earlier (§ 13) regarding knowing the world holds no less of assertion: it needs a fore-having of something disclosed in general, which it points out in the manner of determining. In the determining approach lies, further, an already directed taking-of-regard upon what is to be asserted: that with respect to which the pregiven being is targeted takes over, in the enactment of determining, the function of the determining element — assertion needs a fore-sight, in which the predicate to be lifted out and assigned is, as it were, loosened from its inexpress enclosedness in the being itself. To assertion as determining communication belong in each case a significative articulation of the pointed-out; it moves in a determinate conceptuality: the hammer is heavy, heaviness accrues to the hammer, the hammer has the property of heaviness. The fore-grasp always also lying in asserting remains mostly inconspicuous, because language in each case already harbors a developed conceptuality within it. Assertion has necessarily, like interpretation in general, its existential foundations in fore-having, fore-sight, and fore-grasp. The verification is exact and its last observation profound: the fore-grasp hides in the grammar — the three paraphrases (is heavy; accrues; has the property) are three ontologies smuggled by syntax, and language's sedimented conceptuality is why assertion seems presuppositionless: the Vorgriff has been institutionalized as idiom. § 32's fifth unit, applied to every sentence ever uttered.

The ninth unit poses the derivation-question through the logician's own examples. In what way, though, does assertion become a derivative mode of interpretation — what has been modified in it? The modification can be shown by holding to limit-cases of assertions that function in logic as normal cases and as examples of the "simplest" assertion-phenomena. What logic makes its theme with the categorical assertoric sentence — "the hammer is heavy" — it has, before all analysis, always already understood "logically": unexamined, the "meaning" of the sentence is already presupposed as: the hammer-thing has the property of heaviness. In concernful circumspection there are "at first" no such assertions; but circumspection has its specific ways of interpretation, which, with respect to the cited "theoretical judgment," may run: "the hammer is too heavy," or rather: "too heavy!", "the other hammer!" The original enactment of interpretation lies not in a theoretical assertoric sentence but in the circumspectively concernful laying-aside or exchanging of the unsuitable tool, "without wasting a word." From the absence of words one may not conclude the absence of interpretation. On the other hand, circumspectively spoken interpretation is not yet necessarily an assertion in the defined sense. Through which existential-ontological modifications does assertion arise from circumspective interpretation? The inversion of logic's self-understanding is complete: its "simplest normal case" is a limit-case — an achievement standing at the end of modifications — and the demonstration runs through the descending series of the workshop's own speech: sentence, exclamation, imperative, wordless exchange of tools. Interpretation bottoms out below language altogether (the silent laying-aside), so the equation of thought with proposition is refuted by the carpenter's hands.

The tenth unit exhibits the double switch. The being held in fore-having — the hammer, for instance — is at first ready-to-hand as equipment. If this being becomes the "object" of an assertion, then with the assertion-approach an overturn (Umschlag) in the fore-having is enacted in advance: the ready-to-hand with-which of having-to-do, of performance, becomes the "about-which" of the pointing-out assertion; the fore-sight aims at something present-at-hand in the ready-to-hand. Through this regard and for it, the ready-to-hand is veiled as ready-to-hand; within this discovering of presence-at-hand that covers up readiness-to-hand, the encountered present-at-hand is determined in its being-present-at-hand-thus-and-so. Only now does access open to anything like properties. The what, as which the assertion determines the present-at-hand, is drawn from the present-at-hand as such. The as-structure of interpretation has undergone a modification: the "as," in its function of appropriating the understood, no longer reaches out into an involvement-totality; it is cut off, as regards its possibilities of articulating reference-relations, from the significance that constitutes environmentality. The "as" is forced back into the uniform level of the merely present-at-hand; it sinks down to the structure of the determining letting-be-seen-only of the present-at-hand. This leveling (Nivellierung) of the original "as" of circumspective interpretation to the as of presence-at-hand-determination is the advantage (Vorzug) of assertion: only so does it gain the possibility of pure regarding demonstration. The paragraph is the section's engine-room. The Umschlag is doubly located: in the fore-having (Womit becomes Worüber — the handled becomes the topic) and in the as (hermeneutic reach into the totality cut, the "as" flattened to property-attribution) — § 16's breakdown-precipitation of presence-at-hand now shown producible at will by the assertion-stance itself. And the balance of the verdict must be kept: the leveling is called assertion's Vorzug — its distinction, its enabling advantage — for pure demonstration is real and precious (science lives on it); derivativeness, once more, is not disqualification but placement.

The eleventh unit fixes the terminology: so assertion cannot deny its ontological provenance from understanding interpretation. The original "as" of circumspectively understanding interpretation (hermēneia) we call the existential-hermeneutic "as," in distinction from the apophantic "as" of assertion. The two-as doctrine is the section's coinage and the whole hermeneutic tradition's inheritance: beneath every proposition's "S as P" operates the deeper "as" of dealings — and the Greek names assign the lineages: hermēneia beneath apophansis, § 7 C's hermeneutics beneath § 7 B's logos.

The twelfth unit refuses a clean dichotomy: between the interpretation still wholly enveloped in concernful understanding and the extreme counter-case of a theoretical assertion about the present-at-hand there are manifold intermediate stages — assertions about happenings in the environing world, depictions of the ready-to-hand, "situation-reports," the recording and fixing of a "state of affairs," the description of a circumstance, the narration of what has occurred. These "sentences" cannot be reduced to theoretical assertoric sentences without essential perversion of their meaning; they have, like these themselves, their "origin" in circumspective interpretation. The list is a standing rebuke to every two-level semantics: ordinary discourse — reports, descriptions, narratives — is not imperfect theory but a spectrum of intermediate as-structures with its own integrity; the reduction of all saying to the assertoric is named a perversion, and the philosophy of language is left a field (never worked out in the book) of graded modifications.

The thirteenth unit turns to history: with the progressing knowledge of the structure of the logos, it could not fail that this phenomenon of the apophantic "as" came into view in some shape; the way it was first seen is not accidental, and did not fail to affect the subsequent history of logic. The transition sets the destructive coda: how the "as" was first sighted — and mis-sighted — decided logic's fate.

The fourteenth unit reconstructs the Greek sighting. For philosophical consideration the logos is itself a being and, according to the orientation of ancient ontology, something present-at-hand: at first present-at-hand — findable like things — are the words and the word-sequence in which the logos speaks itself out. This first search for the structure of the logos thus present-at-hand finds a being-present-at-hand-together of several words. What founds the unity of this together? It lies — as Plato recognized — in this, that the logos is always logos tinos, of something: in view of the beings manifest in the logos, the words are composed into one word-whole. Aristotle saw more radically: every logos is synthesis and diairesis at once — not either the one (as "positive judgment") or the other (as "negative judgment"); every assertion, affirming or denying, true or false, is equiprimordially synthesis and diairesis: pointing-out is a taking-together and taking-apart. To be sure, Aristotle did not press the analytic question further to the problem: which phenomenon within the structure of the logos permits and demands characterizing every assertion as synthesis and diairesis? The reconstruction is a destruction in the strict § 6 sense: the first logic was an ontology of a present-at-hand word-thing (the logos itself vorhanden, its unity a puzzle about co-occurrent words) — the theory of judgment born as regional ontology of sentences; Plato's aboutness and Aristotle's synthesis-diairesis are honored as advances within the frame, and Aristotle's stopping-point is fixed exactly: he found the both-at-once but not its ground.

The fifteenth unit names what they were reaching for: what was to be phenomenally hit with the formal structures of "binding" and "separating" — more precisely, with their unity — is the phenomenon of the something as something. In accordance with this structure, something is understood with regard to something, in being taken together with it, in such a way that this understanding confrontation, interpreting and articulating, at once takes apart what has been taken together. If the phenomenon of the "as" remains covered — above all veiled in its existential origin from the hermeneutic "as" — then Aristotle's phenomenological approach to the analysis of the logos collapses into an external "theory of judgment," according to which judging is a binding or separating of representations and concepts. The § 21 principle (interpret the tendency, not the theses) here does constructive work: synthesis-diairesis was the as-structure seen through a glass darkly — taking-together that takes-apart is exactly how "something as something" articulates — and the counterfactual is the history of logic in one sentence: the "as" missed, Aristotle's phenomenology decays into the combination-theory of representations that § 7 B already arraigned.

The sixteenth unit follows the decay to its terminus: binding and separating can then be further formalized into a "relating"; logistically, the judgment is dissolved into a system of "coordinations" — it becomes the object of a "calculating," but not the theme of an ontological interpretation. The possibility and impossibility of the analytic understanding of synthesis and diairesis — of "relation" in the judgment in general — is closely knotted with the respective state of the fundamental ontological problematic. The trajectory (as → synthesis → relation → coordination-calculus) reaches, by name, the new logistics — Russell's and the emerging mathematical logic — and the verdict is placed with care: not false, but ontologically mute; calculability purchased at the price of the phenomenon, § 17's warning about "relation" and § 18's about function-concepts converging on formal logic itself. The closing sentence makes logic's depth a dependent variable of ontology's.

The seventeenth unit produces the strangest witness: the copula. How far the ontological problematic works into the interpretation of the logos, and conversely the concept of "judgment," by a remarkable counter-stroke, works back into the ontological problematic, is shown by the phenomenon of the copula. At this "bond" it comes to light that the synthesis-structure is at first posited as self-evident and has retained its authoritative interpretive function. But if the formal characters of "relation" and "binding" can contribute nothing phenomenally to the substantive structural analysis of the logos, then in the end the phenomenon meant by the title copula has nothing to do with bond and binding. The "is" and its interpretation — whether expressed in language or indicated in the verbal ending — moves, if assertion and understanding of being are existential possibilities of being of Dasein itself, into the problem-context of the existential analytic; the working-out of the question of being (cf. Part One, Division 3) will encounter this peculiar phenomenon of being within the logos again. The little word "is" — grammar's hinge — is liberated from the bond-theory in two moves: if relation explains nothing, the copula is not a coupling; and since asserting is an existentiell possibility of the being that understands being, the "is" in every sentence is a deposit of Seinsverständnis — the being-question hiding in syntax. The forward reference is poignant: the copula's ontology is remanded to the unwritten third division (GA 24 § 16 ff. executes the analysis the book only promises).

The closing unit draws the section's double balance: provisionally, the task was only to make clear, by demonstrating the derivativeness of assertion from interpretation and understanding, that the "logic" of the logos is rooted in the existential analytic of Dasein. The knowledge of the ontologically insufficient interpretation of the logos sharpens at the same time the insight into the non-originality of the methodical basis on which ancient ontology grew: the logos is experienced as something present-at-hand, interpreted as such, and likewise the beings it points out have the meaning of presence-at-hand — and this meaning of being remains itself indifferently unmarked against other possibilities of being, so that being in the sense of formal something-being fuses with it, without even a pure regional separation of the two being attainable. The final sentences close § 6's circle at its finest joint: the guiding thread of ancient ontology (the logos) was itself read through the ontology it produced (presence-at-hand) — instrument and product mutually confirming — with the last clause adding a subtle new charge: existential being, real presence, and the formal "something" were never even regionally sorted, an indistinction the analogia-problem (§ 20) inherited. Logic is thereby delivered to fundamental ontology, and the way is free for the phenomenon assertion presupposed all along: discourse.

###### § 34. Da-sein and Discourse. Language

The opening unit confesses a deliberate omission. The fundamental existentials constituting the being of the Da — the disclosedness of being-in-the-world — are disposedness and understanding; understanding harbors in itself the possibility of interpretation, the appropriation of the understood, and since disposedness is equiprimordial with understanding, it maintains itself in a certain understanding and admits likewise a certain interpretability. With assertion, an extreme derivative of interpretation was made visible; the clarification of its third signification, as communication (speaking-forth), led into the concept of saying and speaking, which had hitherto remained unattended — and deliberately so. That language only now becomes the theme is meant to indicate that this phenomenon has its roots in the existential constitution of Dasein's disclosedness: the existential-ontological foundation of language is discourse (Rede). Of this phenomenon constant use has already been made in the preceding interpretation of disposedness, understanding, interpretation, and assertion — but it was, as it were, withheld in the thematic analysis. The confession is architecture: language's late arrival is an argument — placed after everything it is usually taken to found, to display that it is founded; and the Rede/Sprache distinction is opened: discourse (the existential) beneath language (its worldly shape), the section's whole burden.

The second unit sets discourse in the constitution and states the founding order of meaning and word. Discourse is existentially equiprimordial with disposedness and understanding. Intelligibility is always already articulated, even before appropriating interpretation: discourse is the articulation of intelligibility — hence it already underlies interpretation and assertion. What is articulable in interpretation — more originally, then, already in discourse — we called meaning; what is structured in the discursive articulation as such we call the significance-whole (Bedeutungsganze), which can be dissolved into significations; significations, as the articulated of the articulable, are always meaningful (sinnhaft). If discourse — the articulation of the intelligibility of the Da — is an original existential of disclosedness, and disclosedness is primarily constituted by being-in-the-world, discourse too must essentially have a specifically worldly mode of being: the disposed intelligibility of being-in-the-world speaks itself out as discourse. The significance-whole of intelligibility comes to word: to significations, words accrue (den Bedeutungen wachsen Worte zu). But word-things are not fitted out with significations. The last two sentences are the section's most consequential and most quoted: the direction of accrual settles the philosophy of language in advance — meaning is not injected into sounds; words grow to an articulation already there — so every semantics that starts from the sign-vehicle plus conferred meaning (the tradition from the Cratylus to the theory of expression) has the genesis backwards. § 18's promissory note (significance founding significations founding language) is paid in full.

The third unit defines language and derives its vulnerability. The spokenness-forth of discourse is language (Sprache): this word-whole, in which discourse has an own "worldly" being, becomes thus findable, as an innerworldly being, like something ready-to-hand; language can be shattered into present-at-hand word-things. Discourse is existentially language because the being whose disclosedness it significantly articulates has the mode of being of thrown being-in-the-world, referred upon the "world." The definition is exact on both sides: language is discourse's worldly body (findable, usable, hence also dissectable into vocables — the linguist's corpus is discourse ontified), and the "because" is thrownness — a worldless spirit would need no tongue; language is the price and shape of a disclosedness that is thrown into a world. The word-thing into which language "can be shattered" names in advance the object of every science of language, and its derivative status.

The fourth unit posts the plan: as an existential constitution of Dasein's disclosedness, discourse is constitutive for its existence; to discoursing speech belong, as possibilities, hearing and keeping-silent — at these phenomena the constitutive function of discourse for the existentiality of existence first becomes fully clear. First, the structure of discourse as such. The inclusion of hearing and silence among discourse's own possibilities is already the doctrine: speech is not the whole of Rede — the section will end by finding discourse's depth precisely in its non-phonetic modes.

The fifth unit gives the structural inventory. Discoursing is the "significant" structuring of the intelligibility of being-in-the-world — to which being-with belongs, and which maintains itself in each case in a determinate way of concernful being-with-one-another. This is discursive as assenting and refusing, demanding, warning, as pronouncement, consultation, intercession, further as "making assertions" and as talking in the manner of "giving a speech." Discoursing is discourse about...; and the about-which of discourse does not necessarily — mostly not, in fact — have the character of the theme of a determining assertion: a command, too, is issued about something; the wish has its about-which; intercession does not lack its about-which. Discourse necessarily has this structural moment because it co-constitutes the disclosedness of being-in-the-world and is preformed in its own structure by this basic constitution of Dasein. What is talked about (das Beredete) in discourse is always "addressed" in a determinate regard and within certain limits; in every discourse lies a said-as-such (ein Geredetes), what is said as such in the respective wishing, asking, speaking-oneself-out about... — and in this said, discourse communicates itself. The inventory quietly accomplishes what analytic philosophy would later call the discovery of non-assertoric force: commands, wishes, warnings, intercessions all have their aboutness without being statements — the about-structure is wider than the propositional theme, because it descends from being-in-the-world, not from predication. § 33's demotion of assertion is thereby completed from below: the assertoric is one regional crystallization of a discursive field.

The sixth unit purges communication. The phenomenon of communication must be understood in an ontologically broad sense: asserting "communication" — notification, for example — is a special case of communication grasped existentially and in principle. In this, the articulation of understanding being-with-one-another constitutes itself: it accomplishes the "sharing" of co-disposedness and of the understanding of being-with. Communication is never anything like a transport of lived experiences — opinions and wishes, say — from the interior of one subject into the interior of another: co-Dasein is essentially already manifest in co-disposedness and co-understanding; being-with is in discourse "expressly" shared — that is, it already is, only unshared as not seized and appropriated. The transport-model — the conduit picture that still governs information-theory — is refused at the root: nothing crosses between interiors, because there are no interiors to cross between (§ 13's "always already outside," socialized); communication is the express appropriation of a sharedness that being-with already is. The formula "already, only unshared" is the section's finest: talk does not create community; it seizes one.

The seventh unit adds self-announcement — and locates poetry. All discourse about..., communicating in what it says, has at the same time the character of speaking-itself-out (Sichaussprechen): discoursing, Dasein speaks itself out — not because it is at first encapsulated as an "inside" against an outside, but because, as being-in-the-world, understanding, it already is "outside." What is spoken out is precisely the being-outside — the respective mode of disposedness (of mood), which was shown to concern the full disclosedness of being-in. The linguistic index of this attestation of disposed being-in lies in intonation, modulation, the tempo of discourse, "in the manner of speaking"; and the communication of the existential possibilities of disposedness — the disclosing of existence — can become the proper aim of "poetizing" discourse. Two discoveries share the paragraph. Expression is re-founded without an interior: what speech "expresses" is the being-outside itself — mood as world-disclosure sounding in tone, pace, cadence — so the prosodic dimension, mere ornament for logic, becomes ontologically load-bearing. And poetry receives its definition in a subordinate clause: discourse whose proper aim is the disclosure of existence through the communication of disposedness's possibilities — five lines that carry the whole later Heidegger on Dichtung.

The eighth unit assembles the moments and ranks them. Discourse is the significative structuring of the disposed intelligibility of being-in-the-world; its constitutive moments are: the about-which of discourse (what is talked about), the said as such, communication, and attestation (Bekundung). These are not properties that can be scraped up empirically from language, but existential characters, rooted in Dasein's constitution of being, which first make anything like language ontologically possible. In the factical linguistic shape of a determinate discourse, single moments can be lacking or remain unnoticed; that they often do not come to "verbal" expression is only the index of a determinate kind of discourse which, insofar as it is, must in each case be in the totality of these structures. The four-moment schema is the section's formal yield, and the modal claim is its force: the moments are transcendental for language (conditions of its possibility, not features found in it), and their occasional verbal absence indexes kinds of discourse — the schema classifies speech without being read off it.

The ninth unit measures the definitions of language against the schema: the attempts to grasp the "essence of language" have always taken their orientation from a single one of these moments, conceiving language along the guiding thread of the idea of "expression," of "symbolic form," of communication as "assertion," of the "making-known" of lived experiences, or of the "shaping" of life. Nothing would be gained for a fully sufficient definition of language by syncretistically shoving these various determination-pieces together: what remains decisive is to work out beforehand the ontological-existential whole of the structure of discourse on the ground of the analytic of Dasein. The catalogue names its era precisely — expression (the tradition), symbolic form (Cassirer), assertion (logic and the early Husserl), Kundgabe of experiences (Husserl's First Investigation), Gestaltung of life (Humboldt's descendants and Lebensphilosophie) — and the diagnosis applies § 34's own schema: each theory absolutizes one moment; and the § 11 anti-syncretism rule bars the eclectic repair. Only the prior whole — discourse as existential — orders the fragments.

The tenth unit derives hearing — and lets a friend's voice be heard. The connection of discourse with understanding and intelligibility becomes clear from an existential possibility belonging to discoursing itself: hearing. It is not by accident that we say, when we have not heard "rightly," that we have not "understood." Hearing is constitutive for discoursing; and as linguistic vocalization grounds in discourse, so acoustic perception grounds in hearing. Listening-to... is the existential being-open of Dasein, as being-with, for the other; hearing even constitutes the primary and authentic openness of Dasein for its ownmost potentiality-of-being — as hearing the voice of the friend whom every Dasein carries with it (bei sich trägt). Dasein hears because it understands; as understanding being-in-the-world with the others, it is "in thrall" (hörig) to co-Dasein and to itself, and in this thralldom belonging (zugehörig) to them. Hearing-one-another, in which being-with develops itself, has the possible ways of following and going-along, and the privative modes of not-hearing, resisting, defying, turning-away. The paragraph's structure repeats the section's master-pattern (vocal beneath existential: acoustics founded in hearing founded in understanding), and its center is the book's most enigmatic sentence — the friend's voice that every Dasein carries with it: unexplained, unrepeated, naming an openness to one's ownmost potentiality that comes through hearing another — a socialized precursor, perhaps, of the voice of conscience (§§ 54 ff.), and in any case the strongest word yet against the solipsist reading of authenticity. The etymological chord Hören–hörig–zugehörig (hearing, thralldom, belonging) binds obedience and belonging into hearing itself: acoustic community as the medium of existence.

The eleventh unit runs the derivation through hearkening. On the ground of this existentially primary ability-to-hear, something like hearkening (Horchen) is possible — itself phenomenally more original than what psychology "at first" determines as hearing: the sensing of tones and the perceiving of sounds. Hearkening too has the mode of being of understanding hearing: "at first" we never hear noises and sound-complexes, but the creaking wagon, the motorcycle; one hears the column on the march, the north wind, the knocking woodpecker, the crackling fire. The famous list needs no gloss beyond its own order: the heard world is a world of things and happenings, not of acoustic data — the auditory twin of § 32's refutation of the bare percept, delivered as a poem of everyday sounds.

The twelfth unit draws the anti-empiricist consequence: it requires a very artificial and complicated attitude in order to "hear" a "pure noise." That we at first hear motorcycles and wagons is the phenomenal testimony that Dasein, as being-in-the-world, in each case already dwells alongside the innerworldly ready-to-hand — and at first not at all alongside "sensations," whose swarm would first have to be formed to supply the springboard from which the subject leaps off finally to reach a "world." Dasein, as essentially understanding, is at first alongside the understood. The springboard-image ridicules the constructivist epistemology at its weakest joint: the sensation is not the given but the achieved (an artifact of a contrived attitude — § 32's Umstellung in the ear), and the supposed foundation of world-knowledge turns out to be a late abstraction from dwelling.

The thirteenth unit extends it to speech-perception: even in expressly hearing the discourse of the other, we at first understand what is said — more precisely, we are in advance already with the other alongside the beings the discourse is about. We do not, by contrast, at first hear the spoken-out of the vocalization: even where speaking is indistinct, or the language foreign, we at first hear unintelligible words, and not a manifold of tone-data. The refinement is decisive: even failure to understand is word-shaped — the foreign tongue gives unintelligible words, not acoustics — so the understanding-form goes deeper than comprehension itself; and the primary datum of conversation is named with precision: not the other's sounds, nor his meanings, but the being talked about, shared in advance.

The fourteenth unit places diction: in the "natural" hearing of the about-which of discourse we can at the same time hear the manner of its being-said, the "diction" — but this too only in a prior co-understanding of what is talked about; for only so is there the possibility of appraising the how of the being-said in its adequacy to the thematic about-which. Style is thereby made audible only through the matter: one hears how something is said by measuring it against what is being said — a small hermeneutics of tone with consequences for rhetoric and for the reading of philosophy itself.

The fifteenth unit adds the reply: likewise the counter-discourse, as answer, follows at first directly from understanding the about-which of the discourse, already "shared" in being-with. Dialogue is thus routed through the matter, not through the other's psyche: I answer from the shared about-which — conversation as joint being-toward the thing, the § 26 Sache-structure in miniature.

The sixteenth unit closes the hearing-analysis with its ground: only where the existential possibility of discoursing and hearing is given can anyone hearken; the one who "cannot hear" and "must feel" may perhaps, and precisely therefore, hearken very well. Merely-hearing-around is a privation of hearing understanding: discoursing and hearing ground in understanding — which arises neither through much talking nor through busy listening-around. Only one who already understands can listen. The proverb dismantled (the deaf who must feel — German idiom for the obstinate) and the closing epigram — nur wer schon versteht, kann zuhören — seal the founding order and prepare its dark twin in § 35: das Man's talk and listening as understanding's counterfeit.

The seventeenth unit gives silence its rank. The same existential foundation belongs to another essential possibility of discoursing: keeping-silent (Schweigen). One who is silent in talking-with-one-another can "give to understand" more authentically — that is, develop understanding — than the one who never runs out of words. Speaking much about something guarantees not in the least that understanding is thereby advanced; on the contrary, prolix talking-over covers up, and brings the understood into the semblance-clarity — that is, the unintelligibility — of triviality. But keeping-silent does not mean being mute: the mute has, conversely, the tendency to "speak"; a mute has not only not proven that he can be silent — he even lacks every possibility of proving it. And as little as the mute does one who by nature is accustomed to speak little show that he is silent and can be silent: one who never says anything is also unable, at the given moment, to be silent. Only in genuine discoursing is authentic silence possible: in order to be able to be silent, Dasein must have something to say — that is, must dispose over an authentic and rich disclosedness of itself. Then reticence (Verschwiegenheit) makes manifest, and strikes down "idle talk"; as a mode of discoursing, reticence articulates the intelligibility of Dasein so originally that from it stems the genuine ability-to-hear and the transparent being-with-one-another. The analysis is a small masterpiece of modal distinction: silence is not the absence of speech (the mute cannot be silent; the taciturn does not thereby keep silence) but a mode of discourse — an articulation performed by withholding, possible only for one who has something to say. The two future debts are visible: reticence as the discourse-mode of resoluteness (§ 60) and the silent call of conscience (§ 56) are both drawn on this account; and the closing clause — reticence strikes down Gerede — announces section B's antagonist by name.

The eighteenth unit re-derives the Greek definition of man and the program of a liberated grammar. Because discourse is constitutive for the being of the Da — for disposedness and understanding — while Dasein means being-in-the-world, Dasein as discursive being-in has already spoken itself out: Dasein has language. Is it an accident that the Greeks, whose everyday existing had displaced itself predominantly into talking-with-one-another, and who at the same time "had eyes" to see, determined the essence of man, in pre-philosophical as in philosophical interpretation, as zōon logon echon? The later interpretation of this definition as animal rationale, "rational living being," is not "false," but it covers up the phenomenal soil from which the definition was drawn: man shows himself as the being that talks — which means not that the possibility of vocal utterance is proper to him, but that this being is in the manner of discovering the world and Dasein itself. The Greeks have no word for language; they understood this phenomenon "at first" as discourse. But because for philosophical reflection the logos came into view predominantly as assertion, the working-out of the basic structures of the forms and constituents of discourse was carried out along the guiding thread of this logos: grammar sought its foundation in the "logic" of this logos, which however grounds in the ontology of the present-at-hand. The basic stock of "signification-categories" that passed over into subsequent linguistics, and is fundamentally authoritative still today, is oriented to discourse as assertion. Taking the phenomenon instead in the fundamental originality and breadth of an existential, there results the necessity of re-founding the science of language on ontologically more original foundations: the task of liberating grammar from logic requires beforehand a positive understanding of the a priori basic structure of discourse in general as an existential, and cannot be carried out after the fact through improvements and supplementations of the transmitted; with regard to it, one must ask after the basic forms of a possible significative structuring of everything intelligible — not only of innerworldly beings cognized in theoretical regard and expressed in sentences. The doctrine of signification (Bedeutungslehre) does not result of itself through the comprehensive comparing of as many and as remote languages as possible; nor does it suffice to take over, say, the philosophical horizon within which W. von Humboldt made language a problem: the doctrine of signification is rooted in the ontology of Dasein — its flourishing and perishing hang on the fate of that ontology. The folded-in note directs the reader, for the doctrine of signification, to Husserl's Logical Investigations (the First and the Fourth through Sixth) and to the more radical version of the problematic in Ideen I §§ 123 ff. — homage that dates and places the debt precisely: Husserl's pure grammar (the Fourth Investigation's a priori of signification-forms) is the nearest ancestor of the "liberation of grammar from logic," now to be re-rooted one level deeper. The paragraph re-runs § 10's deflation of animal rationale with its positive ground supplied — the definition sprang from a people who existed in conversation — and issues one of the book's great unredeemed programs: a grammar of everything intelligible (wishes, commands, moods, the unsaid), founded existentially, against the assertion-derived category-stock that still, as Heidegger correctly says of his own day and could of ours, governs linguistics.

The nineteenth unit asks the question no science of language asks: in the end, philosophical research must resolve for once to ask what mode of being belongs to language in general. Is it innerworldly ready-to-hand equipment, or has it Dasein's mode of being — or neither of the two? Of what kind is the being of language, that it can be "dead"? What does it mean ontologically that a language grows and decays? We possess a science of language, and the being of the beings it thematizes is obscure — even the horizon for the investigating question after it is veiled. Is it an accident that significations are at first and mostly "worldly," predelineated by the world's significance, indeed often predominantly "spatial" — or is this "fact" existentially-ontologically necessary, and why? Philosophical research will have to renounce "philosophy of language" in order to inquire after the "things themselves," and must bring itself into the position of a conceptually clarified problematic. The battery of questions is the section's testament: language's mode of being falls between the book's categories (tool? Dasein? neither?) — dead languages, growth and decay, the spatiality of significations (§ 23's Humboldt-material generalized) all resist the available ontology — and the renunciation demanded is precise: not less attention to language but the end of "Sprachphilosophie" as a regional annex, in favor of the question the later Heidegger will make his own: the being of language itself.

The closing unit states the section's modest office: the present interpretation of language was meant only to point out the ontological "place" of this phenomenon within Dasein's constitution of being, and above all to prepare the following analysis, which attempts to bring the everydayness of Dasein into view in an ontologically more original way, along the guiding thread of a fundamental mode of being of discourse in connection with other phenomena. With this, section A closes and its symmetry is armed: the constitution of the Da — disposedness, understanding, discourse — has been won precisely so that its everyday counterfeits — idle talk, curiosity, ambiguity — can be read as its modes; the fundamental mode of discourse announced for the sequel is Gerede, and the analysis of falling begins.

##### B. The Everyday Being of the Da and the Falling of Dasein

The preamble's first unit re-sets the frame. In going back to the existential structures of the disclosedness of being-in-the-world, the interpretation has in a certain way lost sight of Dasein's everydayness; the analysis must regain this thematically posited phenomenal horizon. The question now arises: what are the existential characters of the disclosedness of being-in-the-world, insofar as this, as everyday, maintains itself in the mode of being of das Man? Does das Man have a specific disposedness, a special understanding, discoursing, and interpreting? Answering becomes the more urgent when one recalls that Dasein proximally and mostly is absorbed in das Man and mastered by it: is not Dasein, as thrown being-in-the-world, thrown precisely at first into the publicness of das Man — and what does this publicness mean but the specific disclosedness of das Man? The closing identification is the section's warrant: § 27's publicness = a disclosedness — so the constitution of the Da just won (§§ 29–34) must have its everyday, public shape; and the word "thrown" links §§ 29 and 27 into one clamp: thrownness lands, first of all, in das Man.

The second unit states the method and the destination: if understanding must be conceived primarily as Dasein's potentiality-of-being, then from an analysis of the understanding and interpreting belonging to das Man it can be gathered which possibilities of its being Dasein as das Man has disclosed and appropriated to itself. These possibilities themselves will then reveal an essential tendency-of-being of everydayness, which finally, ontologically sufficiently explicated, must unveil an original mode of being of Dasein — such that from it the indicated phenomenon of thrownness can be exhibited in its existential concretion. The plan is a spiral in miniature: from public possibilities to a tendency (falling) to an original mode of being that concretizes thrownness — § 29's abstract Geworfenheit is to be cashed in the everyday.

The third unit issues the standing disclaimer: what is first required is to make visible the disclosedness of das Man — the everyday mode of being of discourse, sight, and interpretation — in determinate phenomena; and with regard to these the remark may not be superfluous that the interpretation has a purely ontological intent and is far removed from a moralizing critique of everyday Dasein and from "culture-philosophical" aspirations. The guard must be posted precisely because the coming pages read like satire: the analysis of Gerede, Neugier, Zweideutigkeit is structure, not sermon — and the barb at Kulturphilosophie (the era's Spenglerian decline-diagnostics) marks the difference: no epochal lament, but existentials.

###### § 35. Idle Talk

The opening unit founds the phenomenon in language's own being. The expression "Gerede" is not to be used here in a disparaging signification: terminologically it means a positive phenomenon that constitutes the mode of being of the understanding and interpreting of everyday Dasein. Discourse mostly speaks itself out and has always already spoken itself out: it is language. But in what is spoken out there lie, in each case already, understanding and interpretation: language, as spokenness, harbors in itself an interpretedness (Ausgelegtheit) of Dasein's understanding. This interpretedness is as little merely present-at-hand as language itself; its being is itself Dasein-like. To it Dasein is proximally, and within certain limits constantly, delivered over: it regulates and distributes the possibilities of average understanding and of the disposedness belonging to it. Spokenness preserves, in the whole of its articulated significance-connections, an understanding of the disclosed world and, equiprimordially, an understanding of the co-Dasein of others and of one's own being-in; the understanding thus already deposited in spokenness concerns both the discoveredness of beings attained and handed down in each case, and the current understanding of being, and the available possibilities and horizons for fresh interpretation and conceptual articulation. But beyond a mere pointer to the fact of this interpretedness of Dasein, the question must be asked after the existential mode of being of the spoken and self-speaking discourse: if it cannot be conceived as something present-at-hand, what is its being, and what does this say in principle about the everyday mode of being of Dasein? The paragraph is the ontology of tradition (§ 6) re-derived from § 34: because discourse must speak itself out, every language is a deposited interpretation of world, others, and self — die Ausgelegtheit — into which each Dasein is delivered; the vocabulary one inherits has already distributed what can be understood and even how one may be attuned. Idle talk will be this deposit's mode of being — which is why the term is declared positive before the description turns dark.

The second unit gives communication's tendency in three lines: self-expressing discourse is communication, whose tendency of being aims at bringing the hearer into participation in the disclosed being toward what the discourse is about. The compact restatement of § 34's sixth unit sets the standard from which the fall is about to be measured.

The third unit measures it. In accordance with the average intelligibility already lying in the language spoken in speaking-out, the communicated discourse can be widely understood without the hearer bringing himself into an originally understanding being toward the about-which of the discourse: one does not so much understand the beings talked about; one already listens only to the said-as-such (das Geredete als solches). This is understood; the about-which only approximately, superficially — one means the same, because one understands what is said in common in the same averageness. The mechanism is exact: language's average intelligibility (its blessing — § 34) permits uptake without appropriation; the said detaches from the matter, and consensus becomes agreement in averageness — "one means the same" precisely because no one has gone to the thing.

The fourth unit names the constitution of idle talk. Hearing and understanding have clamped themselves in advance onto the said-as-such; communication does not "share" the primary relation of being to the beings talked about — rather, being-with-one-another moves in talking-with-one-another and in attending to the said. What matters to it is that there be talking. Being-said, the dictum, the pronouncement now stand surety for the genuineness and matter-appropriateness of the discourse and its understanding. And because the discoursing has lost — or never gained — the primary relation of being to the beings talked about, it communicates itself not in the manner of an original appropriation of these beings but by way of passing-along and repeating (Weiter- und Nachreden): the said-as-such draws wider circles and takes on authoritative character. The thing is so, because one says so. In such repeating and passing-along — whereby the initial lack of groundedness escalates to complete groundlessness (Bodenlosigkeit) — idle talk constitutes itself. Nor does it remain restricted to vocal repetition: it spreads in what is written, as the "scribble" (das Geschreibe); repetition here feeds not so much on hearsay as on the skimmed (das Angelesene). The average understanding of the reader will never be able to decide what has been originally drawn and won and what repeated — more: average understanding will not even want such a distinction, will not need it, since it understands everything. The definition and the diagnosis are one: idle talk = discourse whose warranty has migrated from the matter to the dictum ("the thing is so because one says so" — authority by circulation, § 27's publicness given its linguistic engine). The extension to writing and skimming — Gerede become Geschreibe — indicts the print-public sphere by name; and the last sentence is the deepest cut: the leveling of the difference between the drawn-from-the-source and the repeated is not a failure average understanding suffers but a need it lacks — omniscience as the perfect form of not-understanding.

The fifth unit explains the success. The groundlessness of idle talk does not bar its entry into publicness; it favors it. Idle talk is the possibility of understanding everything without prior appropriation of the matter; it already protects against the danger of foundering in such appropriation. Idle talk, which anyone can pick up, not only releases from the task of genuine understanding: it develops an indifferent intelligibility to which nothing is closed any longer. The economics of § 27 recur precisely: disburdening (release from the task, insurance against failure) purchases dominion; and the closing formula — an intelligibility to which nothing is closed — is disclosure's counterfeit perfected: universal openness as total closure, the paradox the next unit makes doctrine.

The sixth unit converts disclosure into closure. Discourse, which belongs to Dasein's essential constitution of being and co-constitutes its disclosedness, has the possibility of becoming idle talk and, as such, of not so much holding being-in-the-world open in an articulated understanding as closing it off and covering up innerworldly beings. For this no intent to deceive is required: idle talk does not have the mode of being of consciously passing something off as something. The groundless being-said and being-passed-along suffices for the disclosing to invert into a closing-off — for what is said is at first always understood as "saying," that is, as uncovering: idle talk is thus, from the start, by its own omission of the return to the ground of what is talked about, a closing-off. The analysis dispenses with malice: no liar is needed — the truth-presumption of speech itself (the said taken as uncovering) plus mere circulation generates concealment; § 7 C's necessary covering (every proposition degenerates in transmission) here receives its everyday mechanism, and § 44's account of untruth its social base.

The seventh unit adds the retardation-effect: this closing-off is intensified anew in that idle talk — in which the understanding of what is talked about is supposedly attained — on the strength of this supposedness holds back every new questioning and all confrontation, suppresses them and retards them in a peculiar way. Idle talk is thus not only concealment but inhibition: the presumption of achieved understanding is the enemy of the question — § 1's forgottenness of the being-question, whose mechanics were historical there, here finds its everyday motor.

The eighth unit universalizes the condition and forecloses the exit. In Dasein this interpretedness of idle talk has in each case already established itself: much we come to know at first in this way, and not a little never gets beyond such average understanding. This everyday interpretedness, into which Dasein at first grows, it can never withdraw from: in it and out of it and against it all genuine understanding, interpreting, and communicating, all rediscovery and new appropriation, is accomplished. It is not the case that a Dasein, untouched and unseduced by this interpretedness, is ever set before the free land of a "world" in itself, merely to behold what it encounters. The dominion of public interpretedness has even already decided over the possibilities of being-attuned — over the basic way Dasein lets itself be concerned by the world: das Man predelineates disposedness; it determines what and how one "sees." The paragraph is the hermeneutic condition humaine: no zero-point outside the inherited interpretation — genuine understanding happens in, out of, and against it (the three prepositions are a whole methodology: even the destruction is a mode of this "against") — and the extension to mood completes the dominion: even attunement is publicly pre-tuned (§ 29's thirteenth unit on manufactured moods, now grounded). § 32's imperative — secure the fore-structure from the things against Einfälle und Volksbegriffe — receives here its adversary's portrait.

The ninth unit names the resulting mode of being: idle talk, closing off in the characterized way, is the mode of being of Dasein's uprooted understanding. Yet it does not occur as a present-at-hand condition in something present-at-hand: it is itself, existentially uprooted, in the manner of constant uprooting. Ontologically this means: Dasein maintaining itself in idle talk is, as being-in-the-world, cut off from the primary and originally genuine relations of being to the world, to co-Dasein, to being-in itself; it holds itself in a floating (Schwebe) and is in this way nevertheless always alongside the "world," with the others, toward itself. Only a being whose disclosedness is constituted by disposed-understanding discourse — which, in this ontological constitution, is its Da, is "in-the-world" — has the possibility of being of such uprooting, which so little constitutes a non-being of Dasein that it makes up rather its most everyday and most stubborn "reality." The double precision matters: the floating is still being-in-the-world (cut off from the primary relations yet always alongside — suspension, not absence), and the possibility of uprootedness is itself a distinction: only a disclosive being can float; stones cannot lose their ground. § 6's Bodenlosigkeit (there the erudite tradition's) is thus generalized: groundlessness is everydayness's most stubborn reality, not its rare disease.

The closing unit sounds the section's dark chord: in the self-evidence and self-assurance of the average interpretedness, however, it lies that under its protection the uncanniness (Unheimlichkeit) of the floating — in which Dasein can drift toward a growing groundlessness — remains hidden from the respective Dasein itself. The word Unheimlichkeit surfaces here for the first time in its weight-bearing use: the floating is uncanny, and the function of average interpretedness is precisely to hide this from the floater — the sentence on which § 40 will build (anxiety as the mood in which the hidden uncanniness breaks through the protection).

###### § 36. Curiosity

The opening unit recalls the apparatus: in the analysis of understanding and of the disclosedness of the Da in general, the lumen naturale was referred to, and the disclosedness of being-in was named the clearing of Dasein, in which alone anything like sight becomes possible; sight was conceived, with regard to understanding as the basic mode of all Dasein-like disclosing, in the sense of the genuine appropriation of the beings toward which Dasein can comport itself according to its essential possibilities of being. The recall fixes the standard: sight = appropriating disclosure — so that the coming phenomenon can be measured as its everyday counterfeit.

The second unit introduces the phenomenon and its Greek pedigree. The basic constitution of sight shows itself in a peculiar tendency-of-being of everydayness toward "seeing." We designate it with the term curiosity (Neugier), which is characteristically not restricted to seeing and expresses the tendency toward a peculiar perceiving letting-the-world-be-encountered. We interpret this phenomenon with a fundamental existential-ontological intent, not in the narrowed orientation to cognition — which already early, and in Greek philosophy not accidentally, is conceived from the "desire to see": the treatise that stands first in the collection of Aristotle's treatises on ontology begins with the sentence pantes anthrōpoi tou eidenai oregontai physei — in the being of man lies essentially the care of seeing (die Sorge des Sehens).
