But being toward the ownmost potentiality-of-being means ontologically: Dasein is, in its being, in each case already ahead of itself (sich vorweg). Dasein is always already "beyond itself" — not as a comportment toward other beings that it is not, but as being toward the potentiality-of-being that it itself is. This structure of the essential "it is at issue" we grasp as Dasein's being-ahead-of-itself. The derivation chains § 4's formula through § 31's projection to the first care-moment, and the crucial guard is set immediately: the "ahead" is not transcendence toward other things nor a planning futurism, but self-relation as possibility — Dasein outruns itself toward itself. Temporality's future is already legible under the phrase, unnamed.

The third unit adds the second moment and revisits worldhood. This structure concerns the whole of Dasein's constitution: being-ahead-of-itself does not mean an isolated tendency in a worldless "subject" but characterizes being-in-the-world — to which it belongs that, delivered over to itself, it is in each case already thrown into a world. Dasein's abandonment to itself shows itself originally and concretely in anxiety. Being-ahead-of-itself means, more fully grasped: ahead-of-itself-in-already-being-in-a-world. As soon as this essentially unitary structure is seen phenomenally, what was set forth earlier in the analysis of worldhood also clarifies itself: there it emerged that the reference-whole of significance, as which worldhood is constituted, is "fastened" in a for-the-sake-of-which. This interlocking of the reference-whole — the manifold relations of the in-order-to — with that which is at issue for Dasein signifies no welding-together of a present-at-hand "world" of objects with a subject: it is rather the phenomenal expression of the originally whole constitution of Dasein, whose totality is now explicitly lifted out as ahead-of-itself-in-already-being-in... Put otherwise: existing is always factical; existentiality is essentially determined by facticity. The paragraph performs the book's structural convergence: § 18's anchoring of significance in the Worumwillen was, it now appears, the care-structure seen from the side of world — the "fastening" neither weld nor synthesis but the expression of one whole being; and the formula grows its second member: the ahead is always already in — thrown projection (§ 31's yield) written into care's syntax.

The fourth unit adds the third: and again, Dasein's factical existing is not only in general and indifferently a thrown potentiality-for-being-in-the-world; it is always also already absorbed in the attended world. In this falling being-alongside..., the fleeing before uncanniness announces itself, expressly or not, understood or not — the uncanniness that mostly remains covered by latent anxiety, since the publicness of das Man suppresses all unfamiliarity. In ahead-of-itself-already-being-in-a-world there lies, essentially included, the falling being-alongside the attended innerworldly ready-to-hand. The third moment enters with its § 40 pedigree attached: Sein-bei is not neutral dwelling but flight-shaped absorption — falling as the everyday mode of the alongside — so care's third member carries the whole uncanniness-analysis within it.

The fifth unit states the definition. The formally existential totality of Dasein's ontological structural whole must therefore be grasped in the following structure: the being of Dasein means — ahead-of-itself-already-being-in-(the-world) as being-alongside (beings encountered within the world). This being fulfills the signification of the title care (Sorge), used purely ontologically-existentially; excluded from the signification remains every ontically intended tendency of being such as worry (Besorgnis) or carefreeness. The hyphenated monster — Sich-vorweg-schon-sein-in-(der-Welt-) als Sein-bei (innerweltlich begegnendem Seienden) — is the book's central formula, and its syntax is its doctrine: three moments in one breath, existentiality (ahead), facticity (already-in), falling (alongside), articulated but unsegmented. The exclusion-clause repeats § 12's guard at the summit: care is not worry — the ontic moods of burden and ease are both grounded in it (as § 12 promised), neither defines it.

The sixth unit re-derives the earlier terminology and blocks a reflexive misreading. Because being-in-the-world is essentially care, being-alongside the ready-to-hand could in the preceding analyses be grasped as concern, and being with the innerworldly encountered co-Dasein of others as solicitude: being-alongside... is concern because, as a way of being-in, it is determined by being-in's basic structure, care. Care characterizes not only existentiality, detached from facticity and falling; it embraces the unity of these determinations of being. Nor, therefore, does care mean primarily and exclusively an isolated comportment of the I toward itself: the expression "care of self" (Selbstsorge), on the analogy of concern and solicitude, would be a tautology. Care cannot mean a special comportment toward the self, because the self is ontologically already characterized by being-ahead-of-itself — in which determination the two other structural moments, already-being-in and being-alongside, are co-posited. The paragraph settles accounts backwards (Besorgen and Fürsorge were advances on care's account — § 12 and § 26 redeemed) and forwards: the tautology-argument quietly demarcates Sorge from every cura sui tradition (the Stoic-Christian care of the self, and Scheler's ordo amoris nearby) — self-care is redundant because care is the self's structure, not an attitude the self takes up.

The seventh unit handles inauthenticity's place in the definition. In being-ahead-of-itself as being toward the ownmost potentiality-of-being lies the existential-ontological condition of the possibility of being-free for authentic existentiell possibilities. The potentiality-of-being is that for the sake of which Dasein in each case is as it factically is; but since this being toward the potentiality-of-being is itself determined by freedom, Dasein can comport itself toward its possibilities also unwillingly — it can be inauthentic, and factically it is so proximally and mostly. The authentic for-the-sake-of-which remains unseized; the projection of one's own potentiality-of-being is left to the disposal of das Man. Thus in being-ahead-of-itself the "itself" means in each case the self in the sense of the they-self; even in inauthenticity Dasein remains essentially ahead-of-itself — just as Dasein's falling flight before itself still shows the constitution that this being is at issue for it. The unit forestalls the objection that care names only the authentic: the ahead persists in its own disowning — das Man occupies the Worumwillen (§ 27 recalled), yet the occupied position is still the position; even flight attests the at-issue (§ 40's method restated as ontology). Care is the invariant beneath both modes — exactly what § 39's third criterion demanded.

The eighth unit fixes care's apriority and dissolves the theory/practice frame. Care, as original structural totality, lies existentially-a priori "before" every factical "comportment" and "situation" of Dasein — that is, always already in them. The phenomenon therefore by no means expresses a priority of "practical" over theoretical comportment: the merely intuitive determining of something present-at-hand has the character of care no less than a "political action" or resting enjoyment. "Theory" and "practice" are possibilities of being of a being whose being must be determined as care. The guard is indispensable against the reception the tool-analysis invited: care is not praxis enthroned — contemplation, action, and idleness are equally its modes; the theory/practice distinction is regional within care, not care's definition. § 13's balance (knowing founded, not disparaged) is reaffirmed at the summit.

The ninth unit bars the conative derivation: hence the attempt also fails to trace the phenomenon of care, in its essentially untearable totality, back to special acts or drives such as willing and wishing or urge and propensity — or to construct it from them. The one-sentence unit posts § 39's anti-derivation rule at its station; the four candidates named will each be processed in turn.

The tenth unit states the founding order and the reservation about life. Willing and wishing are ontologically necessarily rooted in Dasein as care, and are not simply ontologically indifferent lived experiences occurring in a "stream" wholly indeterminate as to its sense of being. This holds no less of propensity and urge: they too, so far as they are purely exhibitable in Dasein at all, ground in care. This does not exclude that urge and propensity ontologically also constitute beings that merely "live": the basic ontological constitution of "living" is, however, a problem of its own, to be unrolled only by way of reductive privation from the ontology of Dasein. The double stroke repays notice: against the Erlebnisstrom (Husserl's and psychology's neutral flux — experiences are never ontologically indifferent, since they are care's), and the careful reservation of animal conativity — drives in mere life are conceded, but their ontology is again remanded to the privative method (§ 10, § 12's von Baer discussion): the same words, Drang and Hang, name founded modes in Dasein and something else in the merely living.

The eleventh unit calibrates the claim's scope: care is ontologically "earlier" than the named phenomena — which can of course always be adequately "described" within certain limits without the full ontological horizon becoming visible or even needing to be known. For the present fundamental-ontological investigation, which aspires neither to a thematically complete ontology of Dasein nor to a concrete anthropology, an indication of how these phenomena are existentially grounded in care must suffice. The concession is § 5's honesty repeated: regional psychology of will and wish keeps its descriptive rights; ontological priority does not annul ontic adequacy — and the analysis to come is expressly a sketch, not a doctrine of the passions.

The twelfth unit derives willing. The potentiality-of-being for the sake of which Dasein is has itself the mode of being of being-in-the-world; in it lies, therefore, ontologically the relation to innerworldly beings — care is always, even if only privatively, concern and solicitude. In willing, an understood being — one projected upon its possibility — is seized as something to be attended to, or to be brought into its being through solicitude; hence to every willing belongs a willed, which has already determined itself from a for-the-sake-of-which. For the ontological possibility of willing are constitutive: the antecedent disclosedness of the for-the-sake-of-which in general (being-ahead-of-itself), the disclosedness of something attendable (world as the wherein of already-being), and Dasein's understanding self-projection upon a potentiality-of-being toward a possibility of the "willed" being. In the phenomenon of willing the underlying totality of care shines through. The derivation is transcendental in exact form: three conditions of any act of will, each one of care's three moments — so the will, the tradition's candidate for the self's core (from Augustine through Kant to Schopenhauer's metaphysical inflation), is exhibited as a founded configuration of care; volition presupposes the whole it was supposed to explain.

The thirteenth unit describes the everyday will's world. Dasein's understanding self-projection, as factical, is in each case already alongside a discovered world; from it — and proximally according to the interpretedness of das Man — it takes its possibilities. This interpretation has in advance restricted the freely choosable possibilities to the circuit of the familiar, the attainable, the bearable, of what is fitting and proper. This leveling of Dasein's possibilities to the everyday proximally available accomplishes at the same time a dimming-down of the possible as such: average everydayness of concern becomes possibility-blind and tranquilizes itself with the merely "actual." This tranquilization does not exclude an extended busyness of concern but awakens it: willed then are not positive new possibilities, but the available is "tactically" altered in such a way that the semblance arises that something is happening. The paragraph is § 27 and § 38 replayed inside the theory of the will: das Man's four adjectives (familiar, attainable, bearable, proper) are the everyday will's whole option-space; possibility-blindness names the condition; and the closing sentence — tactical variation of the available producing the semblance of happening — is the Betrieb's mechanism given in one line: busy-ness as the counterfeit of the possible.

The fourteenth unit derives wishing. This tranquilized "willing" under the leadership of das Man does not mean an extinguishing of being toward the potentiality-of-being, but only a modification: being toward possibilities then shows itself mostly as mere wishing. In the wish, Dasein projects its being upon possibilities that not only remain unseized in concern but whose fulfillment is not even considered or expected; on the contrary, the predominance of being-ahead-of-itself in the mode of mere wishing brings with it a non-understanding of the factical possibilities. Being-in-the-world whose world is primarily projected as wish-world has lost itself, without a hold, to the available — in such a way, however, that the available, as the only ready-to-hand, in the light of the wished-for never suffices. Wishing is an existential modification of understanding self-projection which, fallen to thrownness, merely still hankers after (nachhängt) possibilities; such hankering closes off the possibilities — what is "there" in wishful hankering becomes the "actual world." Wishing presupposes care ontologically. The analysis is a phenomenology of daydream and disappointment in five sentences: the wish-world's double bind — lost to the available and never satisfied by it — derives romantic dissatisfaction from a modification of projection; and the pattern is now visible: each conative phenomenon is care with one moment hypertrophied and the others dimmed.

The fifteenth unit derives propensity. In hankering, already-being-alongside... has priority; being-ahead-of-itself-in-already-being is correspondingly modified. The falling hankering manifests Dasein's propensity (Hang) to be "lived" by the world in which it in each case is: propensity shows the character of being-out-for... (Aussein auf...). Being-ahead-of-itself has lost itself in a "merely-always-already-alongside..."; the "toward" of propensity is a letting-oneself-be-drawn by that after which the propensity hankers. When Dasein sinks, as it were, into a propensity, there is not merely still a propensity present-at-hand — the full structure of care is modified: grown blind, Dasein puts all possibilities in the service of the propensity. The formula "lived by the world" (from Dasein's own idiom — gelebt werden) fixes addiction's ontology: not a drive added to a self but care with its alongside-moment tyrannizing the whole — every possibility annexed as means; the moment-analysis proves its worth by rendering the difference between wish and craving as two distributions of the same structure.

The sixteenth unit derives urge and states the theorem. By contrast, the urge "to live" (Drang) is a "toward" that brings the impetus along from itself: it is "toward at any price." Urge seeks to crowd out (verdrängen) other possibilities; here too being-ahead-of-itself is inauthentic, even though the being-assailed by the urge comes from the urging itself. Urge can overrun the current disposedness and understanding — but Dasein is then not, and never, "mere urge" to which other comportments of mastering and steering are occasionally added: as a modification of full being-in-the-world it is always already care. The differential (propensity pulled by the world, urge pushing from itself; the one binding care, the other outrunning it) is fine-grained psychology in ontological notation — and the closing theorem is aimed at a whole metaphysics: Dasein is never "mere urge plus control," against every two-story picture of drives beneath and reason above (Schopenhauer, the drive-psychologies, the id avant la lettre): the urge is care's mode, not its basement.

The seventeenth unit closes the derivations with the pair's ineradicability and its consequence. In pure urge, care has not yet become free, though care first makes possible ontologically Dasein's being-pressed from itself; in propensity, by contrast, care is always already bound. Propensity and urge are possibilities rooted in Dasein's thrownness: the urge "to live" cannot be annihilated; the propensity to be "lived" by the world cannot be extirpated. But both — because, and only because, they ground ontologically in care — are ontically-existentielly modifiable by care as authentic. The paragraph balances tragedy and freedom in three clauses: the conative ground is ineradicable (thrownness's coin — no ascetic uprooting of urge, no cure of the world-pull), yet precisely their rootedness in care makes them modifiable by care in its authentic mode — the only doctrine of self-transformation the book allows: not eradication but the authentic modification of what one ineradicably is (§ 27's and § 38's modification-theorem now cashed for the passions).

The closing unit opens the abyss beneath the result. The expression "care" means an existential-ontological basic phenomenon that is nevertheless not simple in its structure. The ontologically elemental totality of the care-structure cannot be traced back to an ontic "primal element," as surely as being cannot be "explained" from beings; in the end it will show itself that the idea of being in general is just as little "simple" as the being of Dasein. The determination of care as ahead-of-itself — in-already-being-in... — as being-alongside... makes clear that this phenomenon too is in itself still structurally articulated. Is this not the phenomenal indication that the ontological question must be driven further, to the exhibition of a still more original phenomenon that ontologically bears the unity and totality of the structural manifold of care? Before the investigation pursues this question, there is need of a retrospective and sharpened appropriation of what has been interpreted so far, with a view to the fundamental-ontological question of the meaning of being in general. First, however, it must be shown that the ontologically "new" of this interpretation is ontically quite old: the explication of Dasein's being as care does not force this being under a contrived idea, but brings us existentially to concept what is ontically-existentielly already disclosed. The self-audit is the book's engine restarted at its own result: care is total but not simple — three members still articulate it — so the unity-question re-poses itself one level down; the "still more original phenomenon" is temporality, and this paragraph is Division Two's birth certificate. The aside on the idea of being (equally non-simple) quietly re-arms § 1's analogy-problem at the summit. And the last sentence hands the baton to § 42 with the § 39 promise: the new is old — the concept only lifts what Dasein always already told itself.

##### § 42. The Attestation of the Existential Interpretation of Dasein as Care from Dasein's Pre-ontological Self-Interpretation

The opening unit frankly measures the estrangement. In the preceding interpretations, which finally led to setting forth care as the being of Dasein, everything depended on winning the appropriate ontological foundations for the being that we ourselves in each case are and call "man"; for this, the analysis had from the outset to be twisted out of the direction of the transmitted, ontologically unclarified and fundamentally questionable approach pregiven by the traditional definition of man. Measured against that, the existential-ontological interpretation may seem strange (befremden) — especially when "care" is understood merely ontically as worry and grief. Therefore a pre-ontological testimony (Zeugnis) shall now be adduced, whose demonstrative force is, to be sure, "only historical." The concessive scare-quotes around "only historical" are the section's hinge: by the standards of proof the tradition acknowledges, a fable proves nothing; the next unit will re-found the standard.

The second unit does so. Consider, however: in this testimony Dasein speaks itself out about itself, "originally," undetermined by theoretical interpretations and without aiming at any; consider further that Dasein's being is characterized by historicity — which, to be sure, must first be demonstrated ontologically. If Dasein is "historical" in the ground of its being, then an assertion that comes out of its history and goes back into it, and that moreover lies before all science, acquires a special — though never purely ontological — weight: the understanding of being lying in Dasein itself speaks itself out pre-ontologically. The testimony adduced in what follows is to make clear that the existential interpretation is no invention, but as ontological "construction" has its ground, and with it its elementary predelineations. The argument is § 39's Bewährung-program given its epistemology: because Dasein is historical, its ancient self-utterances are data — not authorities but depositions of the pre-ontological understanding (§ 4's Faktum, now called to the stand); the fable's force is exactly that of § 32's fore-having made venerable. The double honesty is characteristic: historicity itself is an IOU (§§ 72 ff.), and the weight is never purely ontological — attestation corroborates, it does not demonstrate.

The third unit introduces the document, and the folded-in note gives its provenance: the following self-interpretation of Dasein as "care" is deposited in an old fable — upon which, the note records, the author came through Konrad Burdach's essay "Faust und die Sorge" (1923), which shows that Goethe took over the Cura-fable — transmitted as number 220 of the fables of Hyginus — from Herder and worked it into the second part of his Faust; the Latin text is cited after Bücheler, the translation after Burdach. The philological trail (Hyginus–Herder–Goethe–Burdach) is itself a small essay in historicity: the pre-ontological testimony reached Heidegger through the living tradition it attests — the fable working in Faust's Sorge-scene before it worked in fundamental ontology.

The fourth unit is the fable itself, given in Latin and in translation. As Care was crossing a river, she saw clayey soil; pondering, she took a piece and began to shape it. While she deliberates on what she has made, Jupiter approaches; Care asks him to give the shaped clay spirit, and he readily grants it. When she wished to bestow her own name on the figure, Jupiter forbade it, insisting his name be given; while Care and Jupiter disputed over the name, Earth (Tellus) arose and desired that her name be given, since she had offered it a piece of her body. The disputants took Saturn as judge, and Saturn gave this apparently just decision: "You, Jupiter, since you gave the spirit, shall receive the spirit at its death; you, Earth, since you gave the body, shall receive the body. But since Care first shaped this being, let Care possess it as long as it lives. And since there is dispute over the name, let it be called homo, since it is made from humus." The fable earns its place by its economy: creation, composition, possession, death, and name in twelve lines — a complete anthropology in narrative form, whose every clause the next units will read as pre-ontological doctrine.

The fifth unit performs the exegesis, and the attached note points to Herder's poem "Das Kind der Sorge." This pre-ontological testimony gains special significance in that it not only sees "care" in general as that to which human Dasein belongs "for its lifetime," but that this priority of care emerges in connection with the familiar conception of man as the composite of body (earth) and spirit. Cura prima finxit: this being has the "origin" of its being in care. Cura teneat, quamdiu vixerit: the being is not released from this origin but held fast, thoroughly ruled by it, as long as this being "is in the world" — "being-in-the-world" bears the ontological stamp of "care." The name (homo) this being receives not with regard to its being, but in relation to what it consists of (humus). And where the "original" being of this figure is to be seen — the decision rests with Saturn, "Time." The reading is a destruction performed on a fairy tale, and its findings are the book's architecture recognized in miniature: the dualist inventory (spirit to Jupiter, body to Earth) is conceded exactly the status § 10 allowed it — the composite view — while the fable itself subordinates it: what the components' donors receive at death is not what the being is while it lives; living being-in-the-world belongs to Care. Origin and possession (finxit, teneat) render care as both source and hold — § 41's a priori narrativized. The name-verdict (homo from humus) even encodes § 10's diagnosis: the tradition names man from his stuff, not his being. And the judge is Saturn — Time: the fable's own last word assigns the decision about man's original being to time, so that Sein und Zeit's title stands, pre-ontologically, at the end of a Roman fable.

The sixth unit mines the word's semantic history, and the note discloses the analytic's own genealogy. The signification-history of the ontic concept "cura" lets still further basic structures of Dasein shine through: Burdach calls attention to a double sense of the term, according to which it means not only "anxious effort" but also "carefulness," "devotion" (Hingabe) — so Seneca, in his last letter (ep. 124): among the four existing natures (tree, animal, man, God), the last two, alone endowed with reason, differ in that God is immortal, man mortal; in the one, God, his good is perfected by his nature — in the other, man, by care: unius bonum natura perficit, dei scilicet, alterius cura, hominis. The note adds that merimna was already a fixed term in the Stoa and recurs in the New Testament (Vulgate: sollicitudo) — and, decisively, that the direction of vision toward "care" followed in the present existential analytic grew upon the author in connection with attempts to interpret Augustinian — that is, Greek-Christian — anthropology with regard to the fundamental foundations reached in Aristotle's ontology. The Seneca-citation is chosen with a jeweler's eye: mortal man perfected by care, immortal God by nature — finitude and care paired against divine self-sufficiency, the fable's teneat quamdiu vixerit doctrinally confirmed. And the footnote is the section's quiet autobiography: the care-analytic descends from the early-1920s Augustine interpretations read against Aristotle — the book's deepest concept confessing its Greek-Christian provenance in small print.

The seventh unit reads the double sense structurally: the perfectio of man — becoming what he can be in his being-free for his ownmost possibilities (projection) — is an "accomplishment" of "care"; equiprimordially, care determines the basic manner of this being according to which it is delivered over to the attended world (thrownness). The "double sense" of cura means one basic constitution in its essentially twofold structure of thrown projection. The semantic split (anxious burden / devoted cultivation) is decoded as the care-structure itself: Hingabe is projection's face, ängstliche Bemühung thrownness's — the word's two moods are geworfener Entwurf heard ontically. Philology, once more, as fossilized phenomenology (§ 20's method vindicated on the book's own key term).

The eighth unit fixes the logical status of the move from cura to Sorge. The existential-ontological interpretation is not, over against the ontic exegesis, merely a theoretical-ontic generalization — which would say only: ontically, all of man's comportments are "care-laden" and guided by "devotion" to something. The "generalization" is a priori-ontological: it means not constantly occurring ontic properties, but an in-each-case already underlying constitution of being. This alone makes ontologically possible that this being can be ontically addressed as cura; the existential condition of the possibility of "life-care" and "devotion" must be conceived, in an original — ontological — sense, as care. The distinction is Husserl's formalization/generalization (§ 17's note) turned to a new use: the analytic does not induce "man is always worried" from cases — it names the constitution that makes worry and devotion possible ontically at all; the fable attests, it does not instantiate.

The ninth unit measures the breadth so won: the transcendental "universality" of the phenomenon of care and of all fundamental existentials has, on the other hand, that breadth by which the ground is pregiven on which every ontic-worldview interpretation of Dasein moves — whether it understands Dasein as "care-of-life" and distress, or in the contrary way. The claim quietly settles the pessimism/optimism quarrel by demotion: gloom-anthropologies and cheer-anthropologies alike move on care's ground — the existential is neutral soil, its ontic colorations equidistant derivatives (§ 12's "toil and gaiety both possible only because care" now formalized).

The tenth unit answers the emptiness-charge in two sentences: the "emptiness" and "universality" of the existential structures that ontically obtrude have their own ontological determinateness and fullness; the whole of Dasein's constitution is therefore, in its unity, not simple, but shows a structural articulation that comes to expression in the existential concept of care. The reply inverts the accusation: what looks empty from the ontic side is articulate from the ontological — care's three-membered formula is the fullness the abstraction-charge misses; § 41's closing (total but not simple) restated as defense.

The closing unit banks the attestation and turns the investigation. The ontological interpretation of Dasein has brought this being's pre-ontological self-interpretation as "care" to the existential concept of care. But the analytic of Dasein does not aim at an ontological groundwork of anthropology; it has a fundamental-ontological purpose, which — unspoken — determined the course of the considerations so far, the selection of phenomena, and the limits of the analysis's advance. Now, with a view to the guiding question of the meaning of being and its working-out, the investigation must expressly assure itself of what has been won; and this cannot be reached by an external summary of what was discussed — rather, what could only be roughly indicated at the beginning of the existential analytic must, with the help of what has been won, be sharpened toward a more penetrating understanding of the problem. The unit is the chapter's pivot: attestation complete, the anthropological reading barred one last time (§ 5's disclaimer at the harvest), and the remaining sections re-motivated — §§ 43 and 44 will not summarize but sharpen, turning care back onto the two concepts through which the tradition said being: reality and truth.

##### § 43. Dasein, Worldhood, and Reality

The opening unit re-grounds the whole enterprise in three sentences: the question of the meaning of being becomes possible at all only if something like an understanding of being is; to the mode of being of the being we call Dasein belongs understanding of being; the more appropriately and originally the explication of this being succeeds, the more surely will the further course of working out the fundamental-ontological problem reach its goal. The syllogism is the book's circle stated as a progress-report: the analytic's success is the being-question's capital — and the unit quietly re-poses § 2's structure (the inquirer's being as the first theme) at the harvest.

The second unit takes inventory of what disclosure has yielded. In pursuing the tasks of a preparatory existential analytic there grew the interpretation of understanding, meaning, and interpretation; the analysis of Dasein's disclosedness showed further that with it Dasein is equiprimordially unveiled — according to its basic constitution of being-in-the-world — with regard to world, being-in, and self. Moreover, in the factical disclosedness of world, innerworldly beings are co-discovered: this implies that the being of these beings is in a certain way always already understood, even if not appropriately conceived ontologically. The pre-ontological understanding of being does embrace all beings essentially disclosed in Dasein, but this understanding has not yet articulated itself according to the various modes of being. The last sentence names the deficit § 43 and § 44 address: the pre-ontological understanding is total but undifferentiated — being understood in the lump, its modes (readiness-to-hand, presence-at-hand, existence) unsorted; articulation is ontology's work.

The third unit explains why "reality" usurped the name of being. The interpretation of understanding showed at the same time that, according to the mode of being of falling, understanding has proximally and mostly displaced itself into the understanding of "world"; even where what is at issue is not merely ontic experience but ontological understanding, the interpretation of being at first takes its orientation from the being of innerworldly beings — the being of what is proximally ready-to-hand gets skipped over, and beings are first conceived as a present-at-hand thing-context (res). Being acquires the sense of reality; the basic determinateness of being becomes substantiality. Corresponding to this displacement of the understanding of being, even the ontological understanding of Dasein moves into the horizon of this concept of being: Dasein too is, like other beings, really present-at-hand. Thus being in general acquires the sense of reality; the concept of reality accordingly has a peculiar priority in the ontological problematic — a priority that obstructs the way to a genuine existential analytic of Dasein, indeed even the view of the being of what is proximally ready-to-hand innerworldly, and finally forces the problematic of being in general into a wrong direction: the remaining modes of being are determined negatively and privatively with regard to reality. The paragraph is the book's whole diagnosis in genetic form — § 38's falling supplying the motor for § 21's Descartes and § 25's substance-self: the displacement of understanding into the world (an existential movement) produces, at the level of ontology, the reign of res, realitas, substantia — with the final clause naming the cost precisely: every other way of being demoted to not-quite-real, life, mind, existence as privations of thing-actuality.

The fourth unit states the counter-program: hence not only the analytic of Dasein but the working-out of the question of the meaning of being in general must be twisted free of the one-sided orientation to being in the sense of reality; it must be demonstrated that reality is not only one mode of being among others, but stands ontologically in a determinate founding-context with Dasein, world, and readiness-to-hand — a demonstration requiring a fundamental discussion of the reality-problem, its conditions and limits. The two claims must be held together: reality is demoted (one mode among others) and situated (founded in the Dasein–world–tool nexus) — deposition plus genealogy, § 21's verdict now to be executed on the concept itself rather than on Descartes' version of it.

The fifth unit sorts the tangle and gives the section's map. Under the title "reality-problem" various questions mingle: (1) whether the beings supposedly "transcendent of consciousness" are at all; (2) whether this reality of the "external world" can be sufficiently proven; (3) how far these beings, if real, are knowable in their being-in-itself; (4) what the meaning of these beings — reality — signifies in general. The following discussion treats, with regard to the fundamental-ontological question, a threefold: a) reality as a problem of being and of the provability of the "external world"; b) reality as an ontological problem; c) reality and care. The four-question analysis is itself the first result: the "problem of the external world" is a confusion of an existence-question, a proof-question, a knowability-question, and a meaning-question — and the order of treatment will invert the tradition's: the meaning-question (4), which the schools took last or never, is the first in right.

###### a) Reality as a Problem of Being and of the Provability of the "External World"

The opening unit establishes the right order and what it presupposes. In the order of the enumerated questions, the ontological one — what reality signifies in general — is first. But so long as a pure ontological problematic and methodology were lacking, this question, if expressly posed at all, had to become entangled with the discussion of the "external-world problem"; for the analysis of reality is possible only on the ground of an appropriate access to the real. From of old, however, intuitive cognition counted as the mode of apprehending the real; this "is" as a comportment of the soul, of consciousness. Insofar as the character of the in-itself and of independence belongs to reality, the question of the meaning of reality couples itself with the question of the possible independence of the real "from consciousness," or of the possible transcendence of consciousness into the "sphere" of the real. The possibility of a sufficient ontological analysis of reality hangs on how far that from which independence is to obtain — that which is to be transcended — is itself clarified with regard to its being; only so does the mode of being of the transcending itself become ontologically graspable. And finally, the primary mode of access to the real must be secured, in the sense of deciding whether cognition can take over this function at all. The genealogy of the entanglement is precise: given intuition as the canonical access (§ 31's diagnosis) and intuition's residence in consciousness, "independence" had to mean independence-from-consciousness, and the meaning-question collapsed into the transcendence-question. The three prerequisites named — the being of the "subject," the being of transcending, the right of cognition to primacy — are exactly what the analytic has supplied.

The second unit certifies this: these investigations, lying in advance of any possible ontological question about reality, have been carried through in the foregoing existential analytic. According to it, cognition is a founded mode of access to the real; the real is essentially accessible only as innerworldly being; all access to such beings is ontologically founded in Dasein's basic constitution, being-in-the-world; and this has the more original constitution of care (ahead-of-itself — already-being-in-a-world — as being-alongside innerworldly beings). The unit is a receipt: §§ 13, 18, 41 itemized as the settled preconditions the epistemological tradition never possessed — the confrontation can now be conducted from secured ground.

The third unit dissolves the existence-question. The question whether a world is at all and whether its being can be proven is, as a question posed by Dasein as being-in-the-world — and who else should pose it? — without sense (ohne Sinn). Moreover it remains afflicted with an ambiguity: world as the wherein of being-in, and "world" as innerworldly beings (the whereat of concernful absorption), are thrown together, or not even first distinguished. But world is essentially disclosed with the being of Dasein; "world" is, with the disclosedness of world, in each case already discovered. To be sure, precisely innerworldly beings in the sense of the real, the merely present-at-hand, can still remain covered — but even the real is discoverable only on the ground of an already disclosed world, and only on this ground can the real still remain hidden. One poses the question of the "reality" of the "external world" without prior clarification of the world-phenomenon as such; factically the "external-world problem" constantly orients itself by innerworldly beings (things and objects), and so these discussions drift into an ontologically almost inextricable problematic. Every word is calibrated. "Without sense" is a technical verdict, not abuse: by § 32's definition, sense is the wherefrom of intelligibility — and the questioner, as being-in-the-world, is the disclosedness the question pretends to doubt; the parenthesis ("who else should pose it?") is the whole refutation in five words. The § 14 ambiguity (world/"world") is then shown to be the problem's fuel: about the world, doubt is senseless (disclosed with Dasein's being); about innerworldly things, concealment is possible but presupposes the disclosed world — so on neither reading does the classical question stand.

The fourth unit opens the Kant dossier. The entanglement of the questions — the confusion of what wants proving with what gets proved and with that by which the proof is conducted — shows itself in Kant's "Refutation of Idealism." Kant calls it "a scandal of philosophy and of universal human reason" that the compelling, skepticism-crushing proof for the "Dasein of things outside us" is still lacking; he himself presents such a proof, as grounding of the theorem: "the mere, but empirically determined, consciousness of my own Dasein proves the Dasein of objects in space outside me." The three-way confusion announced (goal, result, instrument of proof) is the analysis's grid; the choice of Kant is strategic — the strongest, most nearly ontological version of the proof, so that its failure convicts the genre.

The fifth unit fixes the terminology: it must first be expressly noted that Kant uses the term "Dasein" to designate the mode of being here called presence-at-hand; "consciousness of my Dasein" means for Kant: consciousness of my being-present-at-hand in Descartes' sense — the term covering both the presence-at-hand of consciousness and that of things. The philological note is a verdict in disguise: Kant's very vocabulary levels the modes of being (one word for the being of consciousness and of things), so the proof moves, before it begins, inside the ontology it should have questioned — and the book's own re-minting of "Dasein" is retroactively justified.

The sixth unit reconstructs the proof fairly. The proof for the "Dasein of things outside me" rests on this: that to the essence of time change and permanence belong equiprimordially. My being-present-at-hand — the presence-at-hand, given in inner sense, of a manifold of representations — is present-at-hand change; but temporal determinateness presupposes something permanently present-at-hand, which cannot be "in us," "because precisely my Dasein in time can be determined only through this permanent"; hence with the empirically posited present-at-hand change "in me" there is necessarily empirically co-posited something permanent present-at-hand "outside me" — the permanent as the condition of the possibility of the presence-at-hand of change "in me": the experience of the in-time-being of representations posits equiprimordially the changing "in me" and the permanent "outside me." The reconstruction preserves the proof's real elegance — a transcendental argument from time-determination, not an inference to causes — because the critique will need the proof at full strength: what fails must be the approach, not a repairable step.

The seventh unit locates the failure. The proof is indeed no causal inference and so not afflicted with its disadvantages; Kant gives, as it were, an "ontological proof" from the idea of a temporal being. At first it seems as though Kant had given up the Cartesian approach of an isolatedly findable subject — but that is semblance. That Kant demands a proof at all for the "Dasein of things outside me" already shows that he takes the footing of the problematic in the subject, with the "in me"; the proof itself is then carried through from the empirically given change "in me" — for only "in me" is the "time" that carries the proof experienced: time gives the ground for the demonstrative leap into the "outside me." Moreover Kant stresses that the problematic idealism which professes only our inability to prove an existence outside us by immediate experience is "reasonable and in accordance with a thorough philosophical manner of thought." The diagnosis is structural, not textual: the demand for proof is itself the Cartesian confession — whoever asks for a bridge has already posited the two banks; and the observation about time is the deep cut: the proof's engine (inner time) is located "in me," so the demonstration leaps from an interior it never questions. Kant's praise of problematic idealism as philosophically thorough seals the diagnosis from his own mouth.

The eighth unit measures what the proof would prove even if it worked. Even if the ontic priority of the isolated subject and of inner experience were given up, Descartes' position would still be retained ontologically. What Kant proves — granting the legitimacy of the proof and its basis — is the necessary co-presence-at-hand of changing and permanent beings; but this co-ordination of two present-at-hand things does not yet amount even to the co-presence-at-hand of subject and object. And even were that proven, the ontologically decisive thing would remain covered: the basic constitution of the "subject," of Dasein, as being-in-the-world. The co-presence-at-hand of the physical and the psychic is ontically and ontologically completely different from the phenomenon of being-in-the-world. The escalating concessions are the section's logical form: grant the proof — it yields two co-present things; grant their identification as subject and object — it yields a commercium of the present-at-hand (§ 28's refused "between"); at no stage does being-in-the-world even come into view. The proof cannot fail to miss what its categories cannot state.

The ninth unit exposes the presupposition and springs it. The difference and connection of the "in me" and "outside me" Kant presupposes — factically with right, but, in the sense of his proof-tendency, wrongly; likewise it is not demonstrated that what is established, along the guiding thread of time, about the co-presence-at-hand of the changing and the permanent also holds of the connection of the "in me" and "outside me." But if the whole of the difference and connection of "inside" and "outside," presupposed in the proof, were seen — if what is presupposed with this presupposition were ontologically conceived — then the possibility would collapse of holding the proof for the "Dasein of things outside me" to be still outstanding and necessary. The dilemma is exact: unexamined, the inside/outside distinction vitiates the proof (a gap between the temporal argument and the spatial conclusion); examined, it dissolves the demand for proof — for what the distinction rests on is being-in-the-world, in whose light nothing is "outstanding." The proof-problem cannot survive its own clarification.

The tenth unit re-names the scandal. The "scandal of philosophy" consists not in that this proof is still outstanding, but in that such proofs are expected and attempted again and again. Such expectations, intentions, and demands grow from an ontologically insufficient positing of that from which, independently and "outside," a "world" is to be proven as present-at-hand: not the proofs are insufficient, but the mode of being of the proving and proof-demanding being is under-determined. Hence the semblance can arise that with the demonstration of the necessary co-presence-at-hand of two present-at-hand things something has been proven — or is even provable — about Dasein as being-in-the-world. Rightly understood, Dasein resists (widersetzt sich) such proofs: for in its being it in each case already is what subsequent proofs hold it necessary to demonstrate to it. This is the section's most famous stroke — Kant's phrase turned around on its coiner: the scandal is the expectation, not the lack; philosophy's shame is that it keeps asking a being that is being-in-the-world to certify its world. The closing sentence gives the resistance its ground: demonstration comes too late, always — the theme of the next units.

The eleventh unit blocks the fideist exit, with Dilthey in the note. If one wished to conclude, from the impossibility of proofs for the presence-at-hand of things outside us, that this must therefore be "accepted merely on faith," the perversion of the problem would not be overcome: the pre-opinion would persist that at bottom, ideally, a proof ought to be possible. With the restriction to a "faith in the reality of the external world" the inappropriate approach is affirmed even when this faith is expressly given back its own "right": one fundamentally joins in the demand for a proof, though attempting to satisfy it by a way other than stringent demonstration. The folded-in note names the addressee: Dilthey's 1890 treatise on the origin of our belief in the reality of the external world and its right — and quotes Dilthey's own opening confession, that if there is to be universally valid truth for man, thinking must, by the method first indicated by Descartes, clear a path from the facts of consciousness to external actuality. The argument is a small classic of problem-criticism: faith is proof's understudy, not its overcoming — accepting "on belief" what "cannot be proven" ratifies the demand it waives; and Dilthey's quoted sentence convicts the era's most world-friendly philosopher of Cartesian method at the root — the path from consciousness outward, even when walked by Erlebnis rather than deduction.

The twelfth unit blocks the transcendental-presupposition exit: even if one wished to appeal to the claim that the subject must presuppose — and unconsciously always already does presuppose — that the "external world" is present-at-hand, the constructive positing of an isolated subject would still be in play; the phenomenon of being-in-the-world would be as little reached thereby as by the demonstration of a co-presence-at-hand of the physical and the psychic. With such presuppositions Dasein always comes "too late," for insofar as it enacts this presupposing as a being — and otherwise the presupposing is not possible — it is, as a being, in each case already in a world. "Earlier" than every Dasein-like presupposition and comportment is the "a priori" of the constitution of being in the mode of being of care. The refutation generalizes: even the subtlest repair (the world as necessary presupposition, tacitly always made) keeps the subject who presupposes — and presupposing is itself a comportment of a being already in the world; the act invoked to found the world presupposes it. The too-late theorem is care's apriority (§ 41) applied as a weapon.

The thirteenth unit gathers the whole family of attempts under one diagnosis: believing in the reality of the "external world," rightly or wrongly; proving this reality, sufficiently or insufficiently; presupposing it, expressly or not — all such attempts, not master of their own ground in full transparency, presuppose a proximally worldless subject, or one unsure of its world, which must at bottom first assure itself of a world. Being-in-a-world is thereby set, from the start, upon apprehending, supposing, being-certain, believing — a comportment that is itself always already a founded mode of being-in-the-world. The unit is the subsection's thesis-sentence: belief, proof, and presupposition differ only in etiquette; all three stage the world as something a worldless subject must acquire, and all three run on cognitive comportments that § 13 showed to be founded modes of the very being-in-the-world they would establish.

The fourteenth unit converts the problem into a symptom. The "reality-problem," in the sense of the question whether an external world is present-at-hand and provable, proves to be an impossible problem — not because its consequences lead to insoluble aporias, but because the very being that stands in this problem's theme, as it were, rejects (ablehnt) such a question-formulation. Not to be proven is that and how an "external world" is present-at-hand; to be exhibited is why Dasein, as being-in-the-world, has the tendency first to bury the "external world" "epistemologically" in nullity, in order then to prove it. The ground lies in Dasein's falling, and in the displacement, motivated therein, of the primary understanding of being onto being as presence-at-hand. If the question-formulation, in this ontological orientation, is "critical," it finds as the proximally and solely certain present-at-hand a mere "inside": after the shattering of the original phenomenon of being-in-the-world, the joining-together with a "world" is carried out on the basis of the remaining residue, the isolated subject. This is the subsection's deepest move: the task changes genre — from proving the world to explaining the proof-compulsion; and the explanation is § 38 doing epistemology: falling displaces the understanding of being onto Vorhandenheit; "critical" method then finds only the inner residue certain; the shattered phenomenon must be reassembled — burial first, resurrection by proof afterwards. Epistemology as the ritual of a self-inflicted loss.

The fifteenth unit refuses the eclectic settlement: the manifold attempted solutions of the "reality-problem," developed in the varieties of realism and idealism and their mediations, cannot be discussed at length here. As surely as a kernel of genuine questioning will be found in all of them, just so perverse would it be to want to win the tenable solution by casting up the balance of what is in each case correct: needed rather is the fundamental insight that the various epistemological directions go astray not so much as epistemological, but that, owing to the omission of the existential analytic of Dasein, they never even gain the ground for a phenomenally secured problematic — a ground also not to be won by subsequent phenomenological improvements of the concept of subject and consciousness, which do not guarantee that the inappropriate question-formulation does not persist. The § 11 anti-syncretism rule is enforced (no averaging of the standpoints), and the closing sentence carries a barb near home: even phenomenology's refined consciousness — the Husserlian repair of the subject — leaves the question-form intact; improvement of the subject-concept is not the destruction of the subject-approach.

The sixteenth unit fixes the relation to realism. With Dasein as being-in-the-world, innerworldly beings are in each case already disclosed. This existential-ontological assertion seems to accord with the thesis of realism, that the external world is really present-at-hand; insofar as it does not deny the presence-at-hand of innerworldly beings, it agrees in result — doxographically, as it were — with realism's thesis. But it differs in principle from every realism in this: realism holds the reality of the "world" to be in need of proof and also to be provable — both precisely negated in the existential assertion. What fully separates it from realism, however, is realism's ontological non-understanding: realism attempts to explain reality ontically, through real causal connections among the real. The three-step demarcation is exact bookkeeping: agreement in the ontic result (things are — no denial), disagreement on provability's need and possibility (both denied), and the decisive charge — explanation of being by beings, reality derived from causal traffic among the real: the ontological difference violated, which no shared "result" can offset.

The seventeenth unit grants idealism its strange priority. Over against realism, idealism — however opposed and untenable in result — has a fundamental priority, provided it does not misunderstand itself as "psychological" idealism. When idealism stresses that being and reality are only "in consciousness," there comes to expression the understanding that being cannot be explained through beings. But insofar as it remains unclarified what this understanding of being itself ontologically means, how it is possible, and that it belongs to Dasein's constitution of being, idealism builds the interpretation of reality into a void (ins Leere). That being is not explicable through beings, and that reality is possible only in the understanding of being, does not absolve from asking after the being of consciousness, of the res cogitans itself: in the consequence of the idealist thesis lies predelineated, as an unavoidable prior task, the ontological analysis of consciousness itself. Only because being is "in consciousness" — that is, understandable in Dasein — can Dasein also understand and bring to concept such characters of being as independence, the "in-itself," reality in general; only therefore are "independent" beings circumspectively accessible as innerworldly encountered. The verdict scandalized both parties and is precisely weighed: idealism's honor is the ontological difference dimly kept (being not a being, hence not explicable from beings — "in consciousness" as a garbled form of "in the understanding of being"); its bankruptcy is the unasked question of the being of the consciousness it invokes — the void into which it builds. And the closing derivation performs the transvaluation of § 39's thesis: independence and the in-itself are understood characters — intelligible only within the understanding of being — so idealism, corrected, grounds precisely the realism of everyday circumspection.

The eighteenth unit splits the word. If the title idealism means the understanding that being is never explicable through beings but is, for every being, always already the "transcendental," then in idealism lies the sole and right possibility of philosophical problematic — and then Aristotle was no less an idealist than Kant. If idealism means the tracing-back of all beings to a subject or consciousness distinguished only by remaining undetermined in their being, characterized at most negatively as "unthinglike," then this idealism is methodically no less naive than the crudest realism. The disambiguation is § 7 B's method turned on an -ism: "idealism" as the transcendentality of being (Aristotle and Kant in one lineage — the sentence that licenses reading the whole tradition as a single, stammering fundamental ontology) versus "idealism" as subject-reduction (naive exactly where realism is naive: an undetermined foundation). The book's own position is neither and the truth of both — which is why § 44 can refuse the realism/idealism alternative altogether.

The nineteenth unit dispatches the correlativist compromise: there remains the possibility of placing the reality-problematic before every "standpoint" orientation with the thesis: every subject is what it is only for an object, and conversely. But in this formal approach the members of the correlation, like the correlation itself, remain ontologically undetermined — while at bottom the whole of the correlation is necessarily thought as "somehow" being, hence with regard to a determinate idea of being. To be sure, if the existential-ontological ground is first secured through the exhibition of being-in-the-world, the named correlation can afterwards be recognized as a formalized, ontologically indifferent relation. The target is the era's most refined evasion (Rickert's and the phenomenologically inclined neo-Kantians' subject-object correlation, Husserl's noesis-noema nearby): correlativism postpones ontology and therefore smuggles it — the "somehow being" of the correlation is an unexamined idea of being; § 17's formalization-critique closes the trap: the correlation is the skeleton of being-in-the-world, harmless once the phenomenon is secured, vacuous as its substitute.

The closing unit of the subsection draws the conclusion — and the note settles with the ontological movement. The discussion of the unspoken presuppositions of the merely "epistemological" solution-attempts shows that the reality-problem must be taken back into the existential analytic of Dasein as an ontological problem. The appended note reckons with Nicolai Hartmann, who — following Scheler's lead — has grounded his ontologically oriented epistemology on the thesis of cognition as a "relation of being": both Scheler and Hartmann, for all the difference of their phenomenological starting points, fail to recognize that "ontology" in its traditional basic orientation fails before Dasein, and that precisely the "relation of being" enclosed in cognition compels its fundamental revision and not merely critical repair; the underestimation of the unspoken reach of an ontologically unclarified positing of the being-relation forces Hartmann into a "critical realism" at bottom wholly foreign to the level of the problematic he himself exposed. The note is the subsection's verdict applied to its nearest kin: the new ontological realists had the right instinct (cognition as Seinsverhältnis — § 13's own phrase) and the old ontology; revision, not repair — the § 43(a) result — separates fundamental ontology from the ontological renaissance it superficially resembles.

###### b) Reality as an Ontological Problem

The opening unit answers question four in the order of founding. If the title reality means the being of innerworldly present-at-hand beings (res) — and nothing else is understood by it — then for the analysis of this mode of being this signifies: innerworldly beings are ontologically conceivable only if the phenomenon of innerworldliness is clarified; innerworldliness grounds in the phenomenon of world, which in turn, as an essential structural moment of being-in-the-world, belongs to Dasein's basic constitution; and being-in-the-world is ontologically interlocked in the structural totality of Dasein's being, characterized as care. Therewith the foundations and horizons are marked out whose clarification alone makes possible the analysis of reality — and in this context the character of the in-itself, too, first becomes ontologically intelligible; from an orientation to this problem-context, the being of innerworldly beings was interpreted in the earlier analyses. The chain — res, innerworldliness, world, being-in-the-world, care — is the positive answer that subsection a) cleared space for: reality defined by its address in the founding-order; the meaning-question answered by locating the phenomenon's conditions, with the in-itself (§ 16's deposit) expressly included in the settlement.

The second unit honors and diagnoses Dilthey's resistance-analysis. Within certain limits, a phenomenological characterization of the reality of the real can indeed be given without the express existential-ontological basis: Dilthey attempted this in the treatise named above. The real is experienced in impulse and will; reality is resistance — more precisely, resistingness (Widerständigkeit). The analytic working-out of the resistance-phenomenon is the positive contribution of that treatise, and the best concrete confirmation of the idea of a "descriptive and analytic psychology." But the right effect of the analysis is held back by the epistemological reality-problematic: the "principle of phenomenality" does not let Dilthey come to an ontological interpretation of the being of consciousness. "The will and its inhibition arise within the same consciousness" — but the mode of being of this "arising," the sense of being of the "within," the being-relation of consciousness to the real itself: all this needs ontological determination. That it is missing lies finally in this, that Dilthey left "life" — behind which, to be sure, one cannot go back — standing in ontological indifference. But ontological interpretation of Dasein does not mean an ontic going-back to another being; and that Dilthey was refuted epistemologically cannot deter from making fruitful the positive element of his analyses, which precisely remained ununderstood in those refutations. The double gesture is § 10's Dilthey-treatment completed: the resistance-analysis is saluted as genuine phenomenology (and its psychology-program as sound), while the quoted sentence is dissected word by word — "arise," "within," consciousness's relation to the real: three ontological blanks in nine words. The famous concession (behind life one cannot go) is repeated with its rider: irreducibility is not clarification — and the closing defense of Dilthey against his refuters (Rickert's school) is a rare courtesy: they refuted what they had not understood.

The third unit brings the account to date with Scheler — the note recording, mid-proof, the just-published "Erkenntnis und Arbeit" (1926), with its fuller "voluntative theory of Dasein" and its appreciation and critique of Dilthey. Scheler has recently taken up Dilthey's reality-interpretation, advocating a "voluntative theory of Dasein" — Dasein understood here in the Kantian sense as presence-at-hand: the "being of objects is immediately given only in the relatedness of drive and will." Scheler not only stresses, like Dilthey, that reality is never primarily given in thinking and apprehending; he points out above all that cognition itself is not judging, and that knowing is a "relation of being." The unit registers the strongest contemporary form of the resistance-theory — will-relatedness as the primary givenness of the real, cognition demoted below judgment, knowledge as Seinsverhältnis — everything, in short, that sounds like the analytic itself; the demarcation must therefore cut fine, and the next unit cuts it.

The fourth unit performs the critique — the subsection's core argument. Of this theory too holds, in principle, what had to be said of the ontological indeterminacy of the foundations in Dilthey: the fundamental ontological analysis of "life" cannot be shoved in afterwards as a substructure — it bears and conditions the analysis of reality, the full explication of resistingness and its phenomenal presuppositions. Resistance is encountered in a not-coming-through, as hindrance of a willing-to-come-through; but with this, something is already disclosed upon which drive and will are out (aus sind). The ontic indeterminacy of this whereupon must not be overlooked ontologically, or grasped as a nothing. Being-out-for..., which strikes on resistance and alone can "strike," is itself already alongside an involvement-totality; the discoveredness of this totality, however, grounds in the disclosedness of the reference-whole of significance. Resistance-experience — the striving discovery of the resistant — is ontologically possible only on the ground of the disclosedness of world: resistingness characterizes the being of innerworldly beings. Resistance-experiences determine factically only the breadth and direction of the discovering of innerworldly encountered beings; their summation does not first initiate the disclosure of world but presupposes it. The "against" and "counter to" are, in their ontological possibility, borne by disclosed being-in-the-world. The argument is the § 30 fear-analysis and § 21 hardness-analysis fused and aimed at the strongest target: resistance is hindrance of a striving-through, striving is out-for a whither within an involvement-whole, the whole is discovered on disclosed significance — so the experience recruited to prove the world presupposes it twice over. The summation-clause kills the genetic version too: no accumulation of collisions builds a world; each collision is already worldly. Every counter is carried by the open.

The fifth unit completes the demotion and prices the theory. Nor is resistance experienced in a drive or will "arising" for itself: these prove to be modifications of care — only beings of this mode of being can strike upon the resistant as innerworldly. If, then, reality is determined by resistingness, a twofold must be noted: first, only one character of reality among others is thereby reached; second, for resistingness an already disclosed world is necessarily presupposed. Resistance characterizes the "external world" in the sense of innerworldly beings, never in the sense of the world; "consciousness of reality" is itself a way of being-in-the-world. To this existential basic phenomenon all "external-world problematics" necessarily comes back. The settlement invokes § 41's conative derivations at the decisive point (drive and will are care's modes, so the "voluntative theory" rests on the analytic it would replace), and the two-line audit fixes resistance's real yield — one character of the real, world-presupposing — with the § 14 disambiguation applied once more: resistance touches the "world" (things), never the world (the wherein). Realitätsbewußtsein itself is filed as a mode of being-in-the-world: the theory's master-term, domesticated.

The closing unit rewrites the cogito. Should the "cogito sum" serve as the point of departure of the existential analytic of Dasein, then it needs not only the inversion (Umkehrung) but a new ontological-phenomenal confirmation of its content. The first assertion is then: "sum" — and indeed in the sense: I-am-in-a-world. As such a being, "I am" in the possibility of being toward various comportments (cogitationes) as ways of being alongside innerworldly beings. Descartes, by contrast, says: cogitationes are present-at-hand; therein an ego is co-present as worldless res cogitans. The paragraph redeems § 6's promissory note (the destruction's second station executed in miniature): the sum first — read as being-in-a-world — with the cogitationes re-founded as modes of the alongside; against Descartes' order, where thinkings occur and a worldless thinking-thing is co-given inside them. The inversion-plus-refounding formula is exact: not merely sum before cogito (which Kierkegaard and others had said) but a new content for the sum — existence as being-in-the-world, whereby the cogito's entire inventory returns as care's comportments.

###### c) Reality and Care

The opening unit sorts the term's scope and demotes it. Reality, as an ontological title, refers to innerworldly beings. If it serves to designate this mode of being in general, then readiness-to-hand and presence-at-hand function as modes of reality; but if the word keeps its traditional signification, it means being in the sense of pure thing-presence-at-hand. Yet not every presence-at-hand is thing-presence-at-hand: the "nature" that "embraces" us is indeed an innerworldly being, but shows neither the mode of being of the ready-to-hand nor that of the present-at-hand in the manner of "natural thinghood." However this being of "nature" may be interpreted, all modes of being of innerworldly beings are ontologically founded in the worldhood of the world, and therewith in the phenomenon of being-in-the-world. From this springs the insight: reality has no priority within the modes of being of innerworldly beings, and this mode of being can characterize nothing like world and Dasein in an ontologically appropriate way. The unit executes § 43's fourth question in full: "reality," disambiguated (generic versus thing-actual), is stripped of both its pretensions — no priority among the innerworldly modes, no jurisdiction over world or Dasein — while the embracing nature of § 15's eleventh unit returns as a standing anomaly: a third innerworldly mode the tool/thing pair does not exhaust, left expressly open.

The second unit states the founding-thesis and immediately fences it: reality is, in the order of ontological founding-contexts and of possible categorial and existential demonstration, referred back to the phenomenon of care. That reality grounds ontologically in the being of Dasein cannot mean that the real could only be as what it is in itself if and as long as Dasein exists. The fence is erected before the thesis can be misread: dependence of reality on care is not dependence of the real on us — the idealist conclusion is barred in the same breath that concedes the idealist-sounding premise; the next unit will draw the distinction with the book's utmost care.

The third unit is the celebrated statement of that distinction. To be sure: only as long as Dasein is — that is, the ontic possibility of the understanding of being — "is there" being (»gibt es« Sein). If Dasein does not exist, then "independence" also "is" not, and the "in-itself" "is" not; such things are then neither understandable nor not understandable; then innerworldly beings, too, are neither discoverable nor can they lie in concealment; then it can be said neither that beings are nor that they are not. It can indeed now be said — as long as the understanding of being is, and therewith the understanding of presence-at-hand — that then beings will still continue to be. The paragraph must be read with the scare-quotes as load-bearing: being "is given" only while its understanding is — for "is," "independence," "in-itself," discovery and concealment, even the assertibility of "are" and "are not," are all items within disclosedness; with Dasein gone, not the things but the entire dimension of sense lapses, so that even the denial "then nothing would be" is barred (it too speaks from the understanding). And the final sentence performs its own doctrine: from within the now-existing understanding of presence-at-hand, we rightly say the beings will go on — realism's truth uttered from the only place it can be uttered. Being's dependence, beings' independence: the ontological difference as the resolution of the oldest quarrel.

The fourth unit converts the theorem into a prophylactic: this characterized dependence of being — not of beings — on the understanding of being, that is, the dependence of reality — not of the real — on care, secures the further analytic of Dasein against an uncritical interpretation of Dasein along the guiding thread of the idea of reality, an interpretation that nevertheless presses in again and again. Only the orientation to existentiality, positively interpreted ontologically, guarantees that in the factical course of the analysis of "consciousness" or "life" some sense of reality, however indifferent, is not after all laid at the ground. The formula-pair (Sein nicht Seiendes; Realität nicht Reales) is minted for permanent use, and its function named: a guard-rail for Division Two — since the pull toward reading Dasein as a real occurrence (the vorhanden idea's Rückstrahlung) is not an error once refuted but a standing gravitation, needing standing counter-orientation.

The closing unit re-states the human formula and knots the circle. That beings of Dasein's mode of being cannot be conceived from reality and substantiality, we expressed by the thesis: the substance of man is existence. But the interpretation of existentiality as care, and its demarcation against reality, do not mean the end of the existential analytic; they only let the problem-entanglements in the question of being and its possible modes, and of the meaning of such modifications, stand out more sharply: only if the understanding of being is, do beings as beings become accessible; only if beings are of Dasein's mode of being, is the understanding of being possible as a being. The § 25 thesis returns as settled coin, and the final chiasmus is the book's deepest circle stated as two conditionals locked into each other — being's accessibility conditioned on understanding, understanding's existence conditioned on a being that is — neither reducible to the other, the mutual implication that "Time and Being" would have had to unwind. On this knot the analysis turns to the phenomenon in which being and its accessibility were always jointly named: truth.

##### § 44. Dasein, Disclosedness, and Truth

The opening unit summons the tradition's own testimony for the pairing of being and truth. Philosophy has from of old put truth together with being. The first discovery of the being of beings by Parmenides "identifies" being with the perceiving understanding of being: to gar auto noein estin te kai einai. Aristotle, in his sketch of the discovery-history of the archai, stresses that the philosophers before him were, led by "the things themselves," compelled to question further: the matter itself made the way for them and forced them to seek; he marks the same fact with the words that Parmenides was compelled to follow what showed itself in itself, and elsewhere: compelled by the "truth" itself, they inquired. Aristotle designates this inquiring as philosophizing about the "truth," and as apophainesthai peri tēs alētheias — exhibiting letting-see with respect to and within the circuit of the "truth"; philosophy itself is determined as epistēmē tis tēs alētheias, science of the "truth" — and at the same time characterized as the science that considers beings as beings, that is, with regard to their being. The dossier is assembled with cunning: in Aristotle's own idiom, "truth" stands where we should expect "beings" or "being" — the compulsion exercised by the pragma, the phainomena, and the alētheia is one compulsion — so that the tradition's founding texts themselves use "truth" as a name for what shows itself. The equation to be explained is thus not a thesis of this book but a datum of the oldest philosophy.

The second unit sharpens the datum into a puzzle: what does "inquiring about the 'truth,'" science of the "truth," mean here? Is "truth" thereby made a theme in the sense of a theory of knowledge or of judgment? Manifestly not, for "truth" means the same as "matter" (Sache), "what-shows-itself." But what, then, does the expression "truth" mean, if it can be used terminologically as "beings" and as "being"? The puzzle is exact: on the traditional (propositional) concept, the Aristotelian usage is a category-mistake; either the founders were confused, or "truth" originally names something the judgment-theory cannot reach — the section will show the latter.

The third unit converts the puzzle into the fundamental-ontological question: if truth rightly stands in an original connection with being, then the truth-phenomenon moves into the circuit of the fundamental-ontological problematic. Must it not then be encountered already within the preparatory fundamental analysis, the analytic of Dasein? In what ontic-ontological connection does "truth" stand with Dasein and with its ontic determinateness, the understanding of being? Can the ground be exhibited from this, why being necessarily goes together with truth, and truth with being? The battery converts § 39's tenth unit into the section's program: the ancient companionship of on and alēthes is to be grounded, not merely registered — and grounded in Dasein, since only there do being and its unveiledness meet.

The fourth unit acknowledges the phenomenon's prior presence: these questions are not to be evaded.
