Because being does in fact "go together" with truth, the truth-phenomenon has already stood in the theme of the earlier analyses, though not expressly under this title; now, with a view to the sharpening of the being-problem, the truth-phenomenon is to be expressly delimited and the problems enclosed in it fixed. And in this, what was earlier laid apart is not to be merely summarized: the investigation takes a new approach (einen neuen Ansatz). The confession and the promise balance: disclosedness, discoveredness, the as-structure — the whole apparatus was truth-theory incognito; yet the section is no recapitulation but a fresh assault, from the tradition's side inward.

The fifth unit gives the map: the analysis departs from the traditional truth-concept and attempts to lay free its ontological foundations (a); from these foundations the original phenomenon of truth becomes visible, and from it the derivativeness of the traditional concept can be exhibited (b); the investigation makes plain that to the question of the "essence" of truth there necessarily belongs the question of truth's mode of being, and with it the clarification of the ontological sense of the phrase "there is truth" and of the kind of necessity with which "we must presuppose" that there "is" truth (c). The three-step (foundations, origin and derivation, mode of being and presupposition) repeats the § 43 pattern — and the scare-quoted "essence," "there is," and "must presuppose" flag in advance the three idols subsection c) will melt down.

###### a) The Traditional Truth-Concept and Its Ontological Foundations

The opening unit states the three theses: (1) the "place" of truth is the assertion (the judgment); (2) the essence of truth lies in the "agreement" (Übereinstimmung) of the judgment with its object; (3) Aristotle, the father of logic, both assigned truth to the judgment as its original place and set in motion the definition of truth as "agreement." The triad is the section's target drawn with care: two doctrinal theses plus one historical attribution — and the analysis will destroy the first two as derivative and the third as a misreading of the very texts it invokes.

The second unit disclaims a history: a history of the truth-concept, which could be presented only on the soil of a history of ontology, is not here intended; some characteristic pointers to familiar matters shall introduce the analytical discussions. The disclaimer is doctrine in passing — a history of "truth" would be a history of ontology, since (as the section proves) each epoch's truth-concept is its being-concept applied to the logos.

The third unit gives the lineage. Aristotle says: the "experiences" of the soul, the noēmata ("representations"), are likenings (homoiōmata) to the things. This assertion, by no means presented as an express essence-definition of truth, became one occasion for the development of the later formulation of truth's essence as adaequatio intellectus et rei. Thomas Aquinas — who refers for the definition to Avicenna, who in turn took it over from Isaac Israeli's tenth-century "Book of Definitions" — uses for adaequatio also the terms correspondentia and convenientia. The philology is a quiet demolition of thesis three: the canonical formula descends not from Aristotle's doctrine but from an occasional remark in De interpretatione, routed through Arabic-Jewish compilation into scholasticism — the "Aristotelian" correspondence-theory is a medieval artifact bearing his name.

The fourth unit convicts the moderns of the same inheritance. Nineteenth-century neo-Kantian epistemology often characterized this truth-definition as the expression of a methodically backward naive realism, incompatible with any question-formulation that has passed through Kant's "Copernican turn." But one overlooks — as Brentano already noted — that Kant too holds fast to this truth-concept, so firmly that he does not even bring it up for discussion: "the old and famous question with which one supposed one could drive the logicians into a corner... is this: what is truth? The nominal explanation of truth, that it is namely the agreement of cognition with its object, is here granted and presupposed..." The exposure is double-edged: the anti-realist school's own founder presupposes the "realist" definition — so the Copernican turn turned inside the adaequatio-frame, and the quarrel of realism and idealism (§ 43's result confirmed) was always internal to an unexamined concept.

The fifth unit lets Kant testify further: "if truth consists in the agreement of a cognition with its object, then this object must thereby be distinguished from others; for a cognition is false if it does not agree with the object to which it is related, even though it contains something that might well hold of other objects." And in the introduction to the transcendental dialectic: "truth or semblance are not in the object insofar as it is intuited, but in the judgment about it insofar as it is thought." The second citation quietly delivers thesis one from Kant's mouth (truth located in the judgment) — the two traditional theses thus documented as one continuous possession from the schools through the critique.

The sixth unit grants the formula its due and poses the real question: the characterization of truth as "agreement," adaequatio, homoiōsis, is very general and empty — yet it will have some right if it sustains itself unimpaired through the most varied interpretations of the cognition that bears this distinguishing predicate. We now ask after the foundations of this "relation": what is inexpressly co-posited in the relational whole adaequatio intellectus et rei? What ontological character has the co-posited itself? The move is the book's signature charity-plus-suspicion: the formula's persistence certifies a phenomenon (something sustains it); the inquiry goes beneath it, to what the relation silently posits — the § 19 method (interrogate the presupposed, not the thesis) applied to truth.

The seventh unit dismantles "agreement." What does the term mean at all? Agreement of something with something has the formal character of a relation of something to something; every agreement — hence also "truth" — is a relation, but not every relation is agreement: a sign points at the shown — a relation, but no agreement of sign and shown. Nor does every agreement mean the convenientia fixed in the truth-definition: the number 6 agrees with 16 minus 10 — the numbers agree, are equal with regard to the how-much. Equality is one way of agreement, and to it belongs structurally something like a "with-regard-to" (Hinblick auf). What is that with regard to which the terms related in the adaequatio agree? In clarifying the "truth-relation" the peculiarity of the relational members must be co-attended: with regard to what do intellectus and res agree? Do they, by their mode of being and essential content, yield anything at all with regard to which they could agree? If equality is impossible on account of their lacking homogeneity, are the two then perhaps similar? But cognition is supposed to "give" the matter as it is. The "agreement" has the relational character "so — as": in what way is this relation possible as a relation between intellectus and res? From these questions it becomes plain: for the clarification of the truth-structure it does not suffice simply to presuppose this relational whole; one must question back into the context of being that bears this whole as such. The analysis is § 17's relation-critique executed on the tradition's central formula: "agreement" without a stated respect is empty; with a respect, it demands commensurability — and mind and thing, categorially heterogeneous, offer none. The refutation is not that the formula is false but that, as it stands, it says nothing determinate: the relational whole floats, and the ground that carries it must be sought.

The eighth unit blocks the retreat into immanence and lets the content/act split assemble. Does this require unrolling the "epistemological" problematic of the subject-object relation, or can the analysis restrict itself to interpreting the "immanent consciousness of truth," remaining "within the sphere" of the subject? According to general opinion, cognition is true; cognition, however, is judging. In the judgment one must distinguish: the judging as real psychic process, and the judged as ideal content — of the latter it is said that it is "true," while the real psychic process is present-at-hand or not. The ideal judgment-content thus stands in the agreement-relation, which accordingly concerns a connection between ideal judgment-content and the real thing as that about which one judges. Is the agreeing, by its mode of being, real or ideal, or neither of the two? How is the relation between ideal being and real presence-at-hand to be grasped ontologically? It does subsist, after all — and in factical judgments it subsists not only between judgment-content and real object, but at the same time between ideal content and real enactment of judgment; and here manifestly still "more inwardly"? The reconstruction is Lotze's and the early Husserl's anti-psychologism at full strength — and the closing turn is the trap: the two-realm theory, built to save truth from psychic flux, generates a second, worse chasm inside the judging subject itself: between the ideal content and its own real enactment.

The ninth unit poses the forbidden question in three lines: or may the ontological sense of the relation between the real and the ideal (the methexis) not be asked about? The relation is supposed to subsist: what does subsistence (Bestand) mean ontologically? The Platonic word is placed with malice: the modern content/act theory has reinvented participation — and, like its ancestor, left it a name without an ontology.

The tenth unit indicts the impasse: what should bar the legitimacy of this question? Is it accidental that this problem has not budged from the spot for more than two millennia? Does the perversion of the question lie already in the approach — in the ontologically unclarified separation of the real and the ideal? The two-millennia clock (Plato's chōrismos to Lotze's Geltung as one unsolved problem) converts stagnation into diagnosis: an unmoving problem is a misposed one; § 1's suspicion about eternal questions applied.

The eleventh unit asks whether the separation itself survives — and gives psychologism its half-right: and with regard to the "actual" judging of the judged, is the separation of real enactment and ideal content justified at all? Is not the actuality of cognizing and judging broken apart into two ways of being and "layers" whose piecing-together never reaches the mode of being of cognition? Is psychologism not right to resist this separation — although it itself neither clarifies ontologically the mode of being of the thinking of the thought, nor even knows it as a problem? The balance is finely held: the refuted school (psychologism, § 34's standing foil) had the sound instinct — cognition is one being, not a composite of process and content — while lacking any ontology of that one being; both parties to the era's great quarrel thus fail at the same unasked question.

The twelfth unit redirects the whole inquiry to demonstration. In the question of the mode of being of the adaequatio, the recourse to the division of judgment-enactment and judgment-content does not advance the discussion; it only makes plain that the clarification of the mode of being of cognizing itself becomes unavoidable. The analysis necessary for this must try to bring into view, at the same time, the phenomenon of truth that characterizes cognition. When does truth become phenomenally express in cognizing itself? When cognizing demonstrates itself (sich ausweist) as true: self-demonstration secures its truth. In the phenomenal context of demonstration, therefore, the agreement-relation must become visible. The methodological turn is § 7 in action: instead of theorizing the relation, catch it in the act — verification is where truth shows itself; the analysis moves from the seminar to the case.

The thirteenth unit performs the celebrated demonstration. Suppose someone, with his back to the wall, makes the true assertion: "the picture on the wall hangs askew." The assertion demonstrates itself when the asserter, turning around, perceives the picture hanging askew on the wall. What is demonstrated in this demonstration — what is the sense of the confirmation (Bewährung) of the assertion? Is, say, an agreement of the "cognition" or the "cognized" with the thing on the wall ascertained? Yes and no, according as the expression "the cognized" is interpreted in a phenomenally appropriate way. To what is the asserter related when he judges without perceiving the picture, "merely representing" it? To "representations," perhaps? Certainly not, if representation means representing as psychic process; nor to representations in the sense of the represented, if this means an "image" of the real thing on the wall. Rather, the "merely representing" asserting is, by its ownmost sense, related to the real picture on the wall: this is meant, and nothing else. Every interpretation that here inserts something else, supposedly meant in the merely representing asserting, falsifies the phenomenal state of affairs about which the assertion is made. Asserting is a being toward the existing thing itself. And what is demonstrated by the perception? Nothing other than that it is the being itself that was meant in the assertion. What comes to confirmation is that the asserting being toward the asserted is a pointing-out of the being — that it discovers the being toward which it is: demonstrated is the being-discovering (Entdeckend-sein) of the assertion. In the enactment of demonstration, cognizing remains related solely to the being itself; at this itself, as it were, the confirmation plays itself out. The meant being itself shows itself so, as it in itself is — that is, that it in selfsameness is so, as which, as being, it is pointed out, discovered, in the assertion. Representations are not compared, neither among themselves nor in relation to the real thing; what stands for demonstration is not an agreement of cognizing and object, still less of the psychic and the physical — nor of "contents of consciousness" among themselves. What stands for demonstration is solely the being-discovered of the being itself — it, in the how of its discoveredness. This confirms itself in that the asserted — that is, the being itself — shows itself as the selfsame: confirmation means the being's showing-itself in selfsameness. Confirmation is accomplished on the ground of a self-showing of the being; it is possible only in that the asserting and self-confirming cognition is, by its ontological sense, a discovering being toward the real being itself. The folded-in note names the debt and the isolation: for the idea of demonstration as "identification," Husserl's Sixth Investigation, and on "evidence and truth" its §§ 36–39 — with the observation that the usual presentations of the phenomenological truth-theory stop at the critical Prolegomena and its link to Bolzano, leaving the positive interpretations, fundamentally different from Bolzano's theory, untouched; the only one outside phenomenological research to take those investigations up positively was Emil Lask, whose "Logic of Philosophy" (1911) is as strongly determined by the Sixth Investigation's account of sensuous and categorial intuition as his "Doctrine of Judgment" (1912) by the sections on evidence and truth. The analysis is the section's experimental heart, and every negation earns its place: no comparison of representations (the image-theory falsifies the aboutness — I mean the picture, not my picture of it), no psychic/physical adequation, no immanent coherence of contents — what verification exhibits is the thing showing itself as the same that the assertion uncovered it as. Truth caught in the act is identity of the self-showing, not correspondence of two relata; Husserl's Erfüllung and Identifizierung are hereby claimed, radicalized, and re-grounded — and the Lask-note is a small monument: the one logician who understood, dead at the front in 1915, honored as the exception that measures the reception's failure.

The fourteenth unit states the result. The assertion is true means: it discovers the being in itself (an ihm selbst); it asserts, it points out, it "lets be seen" (apophansis) the being in its discoveredness. Being-true (truth) of the assertion must be understood as being-discovering. Truth has, then, by no means the structure of an agreement between cognizing and object in the sense of a likening of one being (subject) to another (object). The definition lands with § 7 B and § 33 behind it: apophansis cashes as Entdecken — the assertion's truth is its uncovering accomplishment, an act-character, not a relation between entities; adequation is not corrected but out-flanked: the phenomenon verification shows never had two terms to adequate.

The closing unit of the subsection opens the descent: being-true as being-discovering is in its turn ontologically possible only on the ground of being-in-the-world; this phenomenon, in which we recognized a basic constitution of Dasein, is the foundation of the original phenomenon of truth — which is now to be pursued still more penetratingly. The ladder is set: assertion's truth (discovering) roots in the discoverer's constitution — subsection b) descends from the act to its ground.

###### b) The Original Phenomenon of Truth and the Derivativeness of the Traditional Truth-Concept

The opening unit answers the arbitrariness-charge with the oldest texts. Being-true means being-discovering — but is this not a highly arbitrary definition of truth? By such violent concept-determinations one may succeed in expunging the idea of agreement from the truth-concept; must this dubious gain not be paid for by thrusting the old "good" tradition into nullity? But the apparently arbitrary definition contains only the necessary interpretation of what the oldest tradition of ancient philosophy originally surmised and pre-phenomenologically also understood. The being-true of the logos as apophansis is the alētheuein in the manner of apophainesthai: to let beings be seen — taking them out of concealment — in their unconcealment (discoveredness). The alētheia that Aristotle, in the passages cited above, equates with pragma and phainomena means the "things themselves," what shows itself, beings in the how of their discoveredness. And is it accidental that in one of the fragments of Heraclitus — the oldest philosophical doctrines expressly treating the logos — the phenomenon of truth in the sense of discoveredness (unconcealment) shines through? To the logos, and to him who says and understands it, are opposed the uncomprehending; the logos is phrazōn hokōs echei — it says how beings comport themselves; to the uncomprehending, by contrast, what they do lanthanei, remains in concealment — epilanthanontai, they forget: it sinks back again for them into concealment. Thus to the logos belongs unconcealment, a-lētheia. The translation by the word "truth," and still more the theoretical concept-determinations of this expression, cover up the sense of what the Greeks, as pre-philosophical understanding, laid "self-evidently" at the ground of the terminological use of alētheia. The paragraph is the birthplace of the reading that would occupy Heidegger for four decades: alētheia as Un-verborgenheit — the alpha-privative heard, the word parsed as a deed of wresting-from-concealment — with Heraclitus's fragment as the exhibit: lanthanein and epilanthanesthai, concealment and the sinking-back of forgetting, standing in the text as the logos's own counter-terms. The charge of violence is thus reversed: the "arbitrary" definition is the tradition's own buried self-understanding; "truth" the covering translation.

The second unit posts the guard and the office: the adduction of such evidence must guard itself against unrestrained word-mysticism; nevertheless it is in the end the business of philosophy to preserve the force of the most elemental words in which Dasein speaks itself out, from being leveled by common understanding to unintelligibility — which functions in its turn as a source of pseudo-problems. The double sentence is the book's whole philosophy of language-history: against etymological conjuring and against the leveling that manufactures the very "problems" (agreement between what and what?) philosophy then labors over — § 1's trivialization-mechanism, with word-preservation as the counter-office.

The third unit banks the § 7 promissory note: what was earlier set forth about logos and alētheia in, as it were, dogmatic interpretation has now received its phenomenal demonstration. The proposed "definition" of truth is no shaking-off of the tradition but its original appropriation — and the more so if the demonstration succeeds that, and how, theory had to arrive at the idea of agreement on the ground of the original truth-phenomenon. The claim is the destruction-concept in one line (appropriation, not demolition), and the program-sentence is exacting: the derivation must show necessity — why the covering was no accident — which the later units deliver.

The fourth unit adds the source of the definition: the "definition" of truth as discoveredness and being-discovering is also no mere word-explanation; it grows from the analysis of those comportments of Dasein we are proximally accustomed to call "true." The provenance-claim matters: not lexicography but phenomenology of verification (subsection a's picture-case) — the definition earned at the phenomena, then found again in the old words.

The fifth unit takes the first step down: being-true as being-discovering is a way of being of Dasein. What makes this discovering itself possible must necessarily be called "true" in a still more original sense: the existential-ontological foundations of discovering itself first show the most original phenomenon of truth. The regress-rule is stated cleanly: whatever enables truth deserves the name more originally — the principle that will carry truth from assertion through discovering to disclosedness.

The sixth unit distinguishes the first pair: discovering is a way of being of being-in-the-world; circumspective concern, or concern that tarries and looks, discovers innerworldly beings — these become the discovered, "true" in a second sense. Primarily "true" — that is, discovering — is Dasein; truth in the second sense means not being-discovering (discovery) but being-discovered (discoveredness). The bookkeeping fixes the order the tradition inverted: the agent-sense first (Dasein discovers), the patient-sense derived (things stand discovered) — entdeckend before entdeckt.

The seventh unit reaches the ground. Through the earlier analysis of the worldhood of the world and of innerworldly beings it was shown: the discoveredness of innerworldly beings grounds in the disclosedness of the world; disclosedness, however, is the basic kind of Dasein according to which it is its Da. Disclosedness is constituted by disposedness, understanding, and discourse, and concerns equiprimordially the world, being-in, and the self. The structure of care — ahead-of-itself, already-being-in-a-world, as being-alongside innerworldly beings — harbors in itself the disclosedness of Dasein; with and through it is discoveredness — hence only with Dasein's disclosedness is the most original phenomenon of truth reached. What was earlier exhibited regarding the existential constitution of the Da, and regarding the everyday being of the Da, concerned nothing other than the most original phenomenon of truth. Insofar as Dasein essentially is its disclosedness — as disclosed, discloses and discovers — it is essentially "true": Dasein is "in the truth." This assertion has ontological sense: it does not mean that Dasein is ontically always, or even ever, introduced "into all truth," but that to its existential constitution belongs disclosedness of its ownmost being. The paragraph is the section's summit and the book's retrospective self-identification: Chapter Five was the truth-chapter all along — disclosedness is original truth, care harbors it, and "Dasein is in the truth" is a constitutional statement, expressly quarantined (against every gnostic or dogmatic reading) from possession of truths.

The eighth unit announces the fourfold explication: taking up what was won earlier, the full existential sense of the sentence "Dasein is in the truth" can be rendered through the following determinations. A colon-unit — but its function is architectural: the four points to come are Division One's four load-bearing results (disclosedness, thrownness, projection, falling) re-read as a doctrine of truth.

The first numbered unit: to Dasein's constitution of being belongs essentially disclosedness in general. It embraces the whole of the being-structure that became explicit through the phenomenon of care; to care belongs not only being-in-the-world but being alongside innerworldly beings. With the being of Dasein and its disclosedness, equiprimordially, is the discoveredness of innerworldly beings. The first determination sets the frame and its scope-clause matters: disclosedness reaches through care to the alongside — so the discoveredness of things is given with Dasein's being, not added by acts.

The second numbered unit: to Dasein's constitution of being — as a constituent of its disclosedness — belongs thrownness. In it is unveiled that Dasein in each case already is as mine and as this Dasein, in a determinate world and alongside a determinate circuit of determinate innerworldly beings. Disclosedness is essentially factical. Truth's first finitude: the open is always this opening — mine, here, among these things — disclosure indexed to a throw; no view from nowhere, because the Da is a where.

The third numbered unit: to Dasein's constitution of being belongs projection — the disclosing being toward its potentiality-of-being. Dasein can, as understanding, understand itself from the "world" and the others, or from its ownmost potentiality-of-being. The latter possibility means: Dasein discloses itself to itself in and as its ownmost potentiality-of-being. This authentic disclosedness shows the phenomenon of the most original truth in the mode of authenticity: the most original and authentic disclosedness in which Dasein can be as potentiality-of-being is the truth of existence — which receives its existential-ontological determinateness only in the context of an analysis of Dasein's authenticity. The third determination plants Division Two inside the truth-doctrine: die Wahrheit der Existenz — authenticity as truth's own superlative — the phrase on which §§ 54–60 (resoluteness as Dasein's original truth) will draw at sight.

The fourth numbered unit: to Dasein's constitution of being belongs falling. Proximally and mostly Dasein is lost to its "world"; understanding, as projection upon possibilities of being, has displaced itself thither. Absorption in das Man means the dominion of public interpretedness: the discovered and disclosed stands in the mode of disguisedness and closedness through idle talk, curiosity, and ambiguity. Being toward beings is not extinguished but uprooted; beings are not completely hidden but precisely discovered — and at the same time disguised: they show themselves, but in the mode of semblance. Likewise the previously discovered sinks back again into disguise and concealment. Dasein is, because essentially falling, by its constitution of being in "untruth." This title, like "falling," is used ontologically; every ontically negative "valuation" is to be kept far from its existential-analytic use. To Dasein's facticity belong closedness and coveredness. The full existential-ontological sense of the sentence "Dasein is in the truth" says equiprimordially: "Dasein is in untruth." But only insofar as Dasein is disclosed is it also closed; and only insofar as innerworldly beings are in each case already discovered with Dasein, are such beings, as possibly innerworldly encounterable, covered (hidden) or disguised. The fourth determination is the doctrine's scandal and its precision: untruth equiprimordial with truth — not error's occasional intrusion but a constitutional counter-movement, § 38's falling and § 7's semblance fused (things discovered and disguised, shown in the mode of seeming, the once-won sinking back) — with the founding-order keeping the balance: closure presupposes disclosure; only an open being can be shut.

The next unit draws the practical corollary: hence Dasein must essentially appropriate expressly, against semblance and disguise, what has also already been discovered, and must assure itself of discoveredness again and again. And a fortiori, all new discovery is accomplished not on the basis of complete concealment, but taking its departure from discoveredness in the mode of semblance: beings look like... — that is, they are in a certain way already discovered and yet still disguised. The corollary founds the labor-character of truth (§ 32's fore-structure discipline, § 26's getting-to-know: appropriation as standing task, never possession) and re-derives inquiry's own situation: research starts from the half-shown — § 7's "proximally and mostly" phenomenology, grounded.

The following unit gives the word its violence: truth (discoveredness) must always first be wrested (abgerungen) from beings; beings are torn from concealment. The respective factical discoveredness is, as it were, always a robbery (Raub). Is it accidental that the Greeks speak themselves out about the essence of truth in a privative expression (a-lētheia)? Does not an original understanding of its own being announce itself in such self-utterance of Dasein — the pre-ontological understanding that being-in-untruth constitutes an essential determination of being-in-the-world? The Raub-sentence is the section's most quoted, and it is argument, not rhetoric: because untruth is equiprimordial, every truth is a taking-from — and the alpha-privative is the pre-ontological deposit of exactly this: the Greek language filed truth under theft before Greek theory filed it under agreement.

The next unit reads Parmenides' goddess — with Reinhardt in the note. That the goddess of truth who leads Parmenides places him before the two ways, that of discovering and that of concealing, means nothing other than: Dasein is in each case already in truth and untruth. The way of discovering is won only in krinein logō — in the understanding distinguishing of the two and deciding for the one. The note credits Karl Reinhardt's "Parmenides and the History of Greek Philosophy" (1916) with having first conceived and solved the much-discussed problem of the connection of the two parts of the didactic poem, while not expressly exhibiting the ontological foundation of the connection of alētheia and doxa and its necessity. The exegesis closes the section's ring at its opening exhibit: the poem's structure — truth-part and opinion-part in one revelation — is the double constitution itself (in truth and untruth at once), and the goddess's demand for krisis makes discovering a decision: the existential reading supplies what Reinhardt's philology found but could not ground.

The next unit fixes the condition: the existential-ontological condition for being-in-the-world's being determined by "truth" and "untruth" lies in that constitution of Dasein's being which we marked as thrown projection — a constituent of the structure of care. The one-sentence unit is the fourfold's signature: geworfener Entwurf, § 31's formula, named as the root of the truth/untruth double — projection opening, thrownness and falling limiting and disguising.

The next unit tallies: the existential-ontological interpretation of the phenomenon of truth has yielded: (1) truth in the most original sense is the disclosedness of Dasein, to which belongs the discoveredness of innerworldly beings; (2) Dasein is equiprimordially in truth and untruth. The two theses are the subsection's yield in portable form — and the second is the one the tradition (and the later "Essence of Truth" essay's readers) would find hardest: untruth installed in the definition.

The next unit sets the remaining task: these sentences can become fully evident within the horizon of the traditional interpretation of the truth-phenomenon only if it can be shown: (1) that truth understood as agreement has its provenance from disclosedness, by way of a determinate modification; (2) that the mode of being of disclosedness itself leads to this — that proximally its derivative modification comes into view and guides the theoretical explication of the truth-structure. The double demand repeats the § 43(a) pattern: derive the derivative and explain the inversion — not only that adequation descends from disclosedness, but why disclosedness itself puts its offspring forward first.

The next unit gives the first derivation in outline: assertion and its structure, the apophantic as, are founded in interpretation and its structure, the hermeneutic as, and further in understanding, Dasein's disclosedness; truth, however, counts as a distinguishing determination of the assertion so derived — thus the roots of assertion-truth reach back into the disclosedness of understanding. But beyond this indication of the provenance of assertion-truth, the phenomenon of agreement must now be expressly exhibited in its derivativeness. The unit banks § 33's whole yield in two lines and names the residue: the derivation of the assertion is done; what remains is the derivation of the agreement-look — how uncovering came to look like correspondence.

The next unit begins that derivation at speech. Being alongside innerworldly beings — concern — is discovering; to Dasein's disclosedness, however, essentially belongs discourse. Dasein speaks itself out: itself — as discovering being toward beings — and, as such, about discovered beings, in the assertion. The assertion communicates beings in the how of their discoveredness; the Dasein that perceives the communication brings itself, in perceiving, into the discovering being toward the discussed beings. The spoken-out assertion contains, in its about-which, the discoveredness of beings: this discoveredness is preserved (verwahrt) in what is spoken out. The spoken-out becomes, as it were, an innerworldly ready-to-hand thing that can be taken up and spoken further; on the ground of the preservation of discoveredness, the ready-to-hand spoken-out has in itself a relation to the beings about which it is in each case an assertion. Discoveredness is in each case discoveredness of...; even in repeating, the repeating Dasein comes into a being toward the discussed beings themselves — but it is, and holds itself, exempted from an original re-enactment of the discovering. The paragraph sets the mechanism running: § 34's spokenness plus § 35's passing-along — discoveredness deposited in the sentence, the sentence a tool, the tool circulable — with the crucial conservation-law: the deposit keeps its of-relation (aboutness survives circulation), which is exactly what makes exempted repetition possible: one is toward the thing through the saying, without discovering.

The next unit follows the deposit into das Man and springs the transformation. Dasein need not bring itself before the beings themselves in "originary" experience, and yet remains in a being toward them; in large measure, discoveredness is appropriated not through one's own discovering but through hearsay of the said. Absorption in the said belongs to the mode of being of das Man. The spoken-out as such takes over the being toward the beings discovered in the assertion. But if these are to be expressly appropriated with regard to their discoveredness, this means: the assertion is to be demonstrated as discovering. The spoken-out assertion, however, is a ready-to-hand thing — such that, as preserving discoveredness, it has in itself a relation to the discovered beings. Demonstration of its being-discovering now means: demonstration of the relation of the discoveredness-preserving assertion to the beings. The assertion is a ready-to-hand thing; the beings to which it, as discovering, has a relation are innerworldly ready-to-hand or present-at-hand; the relation itself thus presents itself as present-at-hand. The relation, however, consists in this, that the discoveredness preserved in the assertion is in each case discoveredness of...: the judgment "contains something that holds of the objects" (Kant). The relation now itself acquires, through its switch-over (Umschaltung) into a relation between present-at-hand things, the character of presence-at-hand: discoveredness of... becomes the present-at-hand conformity (Gemäßheit) of one present-at-hand thing — the spoken-out assertion — to another present-at-hand thing — the discussed beings. And if the conformity is seen only still as a relation between present-at-hand things — that is, if the mode of being of the relational members is understood, without distinction, as merely present-at-hand — then the relation shows itself as present-at-hand agreement of two present-at-hand things. This is the promised derivation executed, and its logic deserves slow statement: the verification-demand arises inside hearsay (the exempted appropriation must sometimes be cashed — § 35's own economy generates the demand for Ausweisung); but what now stands for demonstration is the deposited sentence, a thing among things, related to things; the of-relation, read off two vorhanden relata, switches over into a vorhanden conformity — and adequation is born: correspondence as the ontology of quotation. Kant's own formula reappears at the exact joint where the theory crystallizes. The necessity claimed at the third unit is thereby delivered: given falling discourse and the leveling understanding of being, the original phenomenon had to show itself as agreement.

The next unit condenses it: the discoveredness of beings moves, with the spokenness of the assertion, into the mode of being of the innerworldly ready-to-hand; but insofar as, in it, as discoveredness of..., a relation to the present-at-hand sustains itself, discoveredness (truth) becomes for its part a present-at-hand relation between present-at-hand things (intellectus and res). The compression names the corpse in the formula: intellectus and res — subsection a's incommensurable relata — are the fossilized end-products of the switch-over; the adaequatio was never a theory of discovering but the ontology of the discovered-and-deposited.

The next unit gives the transformation its formula: the existential phenomenon of discoveredness, founded in Dasein's disclosedness, becomes a present-at-hand property that still harbors a relational character in itself — and, as such, is broken apart into a present-at-hand relation. Truth as disclosedness and as discovering being toward discovered beings has become truth as agreement between innerworldly present-at-hand things. Therewith the ontological derivativeness of the traditional truth-concept is exhibited. The task set at the beginning of b) is formally discharged — provenance (disclosedness), modification (deposit and switch-over), result (adequation) — the tradition not refuted but explained: its truth-concept is true of the truth-artifact.

The next unit explains the inversion of orders. Yet what is last in the order of existential-ontological founding-contexts counts ontically-factically as first and nearest — and this factum grounds, as to its necessity, in the mode of being of Dasein itself. In concernful absorption, Dasein understands itself from the innerworldly encountered; the discoveredness belonging to discovering is proximally found innerworldly, in the spoken-out. But not only truth is encountered as present-at-hand: the understanding of being in general understands all beings proximally as present-at-hand. The nearest ontological reflection on the "truth" that is proximally encountered ontically understands the logos (assertion) as logos tinos (assertion about..., discoveredness of...), but interprets the phenomenon, as something present-at-hand, with regard to its possible presence-at-hand. And because presence-at-hand is equated with the sense of being in general, the question whether this mode of being of truth, and its proximally encountered structure, are original or not, cannot become alive at all. The understanding of being of Dasein that proximally dominates, and even today is not fundamentally and expressly overcome, itself covers up the original phenomenon of truth. The paragraph answers the second demand (why the derivative leads): falling's Rückstrahlung — truth met first as a worldly deposit, ontologized with the only being-concept in circulation — and the closing sentence widens the indictment to the present tense: the covering is not a Greek episode but the standing regime, "even today."

The next unit balances the verdict — with the note pointing to Nicomachean Ethics Z and Metaphysics Θ 10: at the same time it must not be overlooked that among the Greeks, who first developed this nearest understanding of being scientifically and brought it to dominance, the original though pre-ontological understanding of truth was alive, and even asserted itself — at least in Aristotle — against the covering lodged in their ontology. The balance is § 6's double gesture at the finest grain: the same Aristotle who occasioned the adaequatio preserved, in the ethics' alētheuein-chapter and the metaphysics' treatise on the truth of the asyntheta, the deeper phenomenon — the tradition's founder as its best witness against it.

The next unit acquits him of thesis one: Aristotle never defended the thesis that the original "place" of truth is the judgment; he says rather that the logos is the way of being of Dasein that can be discovering or covering. This double possibility is the distinctive thing about the being-true of the logos: it is the comportment that can also cover. And because Aristotle never asserted that thesis, he also never came into the position of "extending" the truth-concept from the logos to pure noein: the "truth" of aisthēsis and of the seeing of the "ideas" is the original discovering — and only because noēsis primarily discovers can the logos too, as dianoein, have a discovering function. The acquittal is precise on both counts: Aristotle located in the logos not truth's home but its risk (the both-ways comportment — § 7 B's synthesis-ground of falsehood recalled), and the noein-passages the schools read as extending judgment-truth upward in fact record the original order: intuitive uncovering first, discursive uncovering founded. Thesis three of the subsection's opening triad falls with documents.

The next unit convicts the thesis on its content: the thesis that the genuine "place" of truth is the judgment not only appeals wrongly to Aristotle; by its content it is a misrecognition of the truth-structure. The assertion is not the primary "place" of truth but the reverse: the assertion, as a mode of appropriation of discoveredness and as a way of being-in-the-world, grounds in discovering — in Dasein's disclosedness. The most original "truth" is the "place" of the assertion, and the ontological condition of the possibility that assertions can be true or false (discovering or covering). The inversion is total and formulaic — truth is not in the judgment; the judgment is in truth — the topology of two millennia reversed: disclosedness as the region within which any sentence can succeed or fail.

The closing unit of the subsection banks and pivots: truth, understood in the most original sense, belongs to Dasein's basic constitution; the title means an existential. Therewith the answer is already predelineated to the question of truth's mode of being, and of the sense of the necessity of the presupposition that "there is truth." The pivot hands subsection c) its whole agenda in the settled register: truth an existential — so its "being" and its "must be presupposed" will have to be read from Dasein's being, against the eternal-truths idiom the next pages confront.

###### c) The Mode of Being of Truth and the Presupposition of Truth

The opening unit draws the consequence that scandalized the century. Dasein, as constituted by disclosedness, is essentially in the truth; disclosedness is an essential mode of being of Dasein. Truth "is given" (»gibt es«) only insofar and as long as Dasein is: beings are discovered, and disclosed, only when and only as long as Dasein is at all. Newton's laws, the principle of contradiction, every truth whatsoever, are true only as long as Dasein is; before there was any Dasein, and after there is no longer any Dasein, no truth was and none will be — for as disclosedness, discovery, and discoveredness, truth then cannot be. Before Newton's laws were discovered, they were not "true"; from this it does not follow that they were false, still less that they would become false if ontically no discoveredness were possible any longer. Just as little does this "restriction" involve a diminution of the being-true of "truths." The paragraph must be read with its own distinctions or it reads as madness: truth's being is disclosedness — an existential — so its "there is" is indexed to the being whose constitution it is; the temporal clauses quantify over truth, not over beings, and the bivalence-trap is refused in advance (pre-Newtonian nature was neither truly nor falsely lawful: the true/false alternative itself was not yet in being). The choice of examples is maximal provocation — mechanics and the principle of contradiction — precisely the "timeless" cases, so that the thesis cannot be mistaken for a remark about mutable opinion.

The second unit gives the saving clause its exact form. That Newton's laws were, before him, neither true nor false cannot mean that the beings which the laws discoveringly point out were not before; the laws became true through Newton — with them, beings became accessible in themselves for Dasein. And with the discoveredness of beings, these show themselves precisely as beings that already were before: so to discover is the mode of being of "truth." The paragraph is § 43(c)'s Sein/Seiendes distinction executed on truth: the real is untouched (the planets moved), truth happens (their motion's law entered unconcealment) — and the recoil-clause is the finest stroke: discovery's own content includes the antecedence of the discovered; that the beings already were is itself part of what becomes true. Retroactivity belongs to unconcealment's structure — the realism of the discovered secured inside the event-character of truth.

The third unit prices the eternal-truths idiom: that there "are eternal truths" will be sufficiently proven only when the demonstration succeeds that in all eternity Dasein was and will be; so long as this proof is outstanding, the sentence remains a fantastic assertion, which gains no legitimacy from being commonly "believed" by the philosophers. The demand is a precise modus tollens on the section's result: truths are as long as disclosedness is; eternal truths therefore require eternal Dasein — a theological premise smuggled as logic; and the closing barb (philosophers' common "belief") files aeternae veritates under das Man's dictums, § 35's authority-by-circulation inside philosophy itself.

The fourth unit meets the relativism-charge and inverts it. All truth is, according to its essential Dasein-like mode of being, relative to the being of Dasein. Does this relativity mean: all truth is "subjective"? If "subjective" is interpreted as "left to the subject's discretion," then certainly not: for discovering, by its ownmost sense, withdraws asserting from "subjective" discretion and brings discovering Dasein before the beings themselves. And only because "truth," as discovering, is a mode of being of Dasein, can it be withdrawn from Dasein's discretion. Even the "universal validity" of truth is rooted solely in this, that Dasein can discover and free beings in themselves: only so can these beings in themselves bind every possible assertion — every pointing-out of them. Is rightly understood truth in the least impaired by the fact that it is ontically possible only in the "subject," and stands and falls with the subject's being? The inversion is the subsection's philosophical center: objectivity is grounded in the "relativity," not threatened by it — because truth is Dasein's discovering being-toward, the discovered thing itself can bind all assertion; the binding force the tradition sought in a truth-realm beyond the subject is delivered by the structure of the "subject" rightly understood. Bindingness (§ 33's third sense of Geltung) is thus re-derived cleanly: things oblige speech only within uncovering.

The fifth unit turns to the presupposition and reverses its direction. From the existentially conceived mode of being of truth, the sense of the truth-presupposition also becomes intelligible. Why must we presuppose that there is truth? What does "presuppose" mean — what the "must" and the "we"? What does "there is truth" say? "We" presuppose truth because "we," being in the mode of being of Dasein, are "in the truth." We do not presuppose it as something "outside" and "above" us, toward which, alongside other "values," we also comport ourselves. Not we presuppose "truth"; rather truth is what makes it ontologically possible at all that we can be such that we "presuppose" anything: truth first makes possible anything like presupposition. The reversal is total and elegant: the transcendental argument's direction is flipped — presupposing is an accomplishment within disclosedness, so truth is not the greatest of our presuppositions but the enabling ground of presupposing as such; the "value" among values (Lotze's heaven again) is dissolved into the constitution of the presupposer.

The sixth unit analyzes the act and finds care beneath it. What does "presuppose" mean? To understand something as the ground of the being of another being; such understanding of beings in their contexts of being is possible only on the ground of disclosedness — of Dasein's being-discovering. Presupposing "truth" then means: understanding it as something for the sake of which Dasein is. But Dasein — this lies in its constitution of being as care — is in each case already ahead of itself: it is the being for which, in its being, its ownmost potentiality-of-being is at issue; to Dasein's being and potentiality-of-being as being-in-the-world belong essentially disclosedness and discovering. Dasein is concerned with its potentiality-for-being-in-the-world, and therein with circumspectively discovering concern for innerworldly beings. In Dasein's constitution of being as care, in being-ahead-of-itself, lies the most original "presupposing." Because this self-presupposing belongs to Dasein's being, "we" must presuppose also "ourselves," as determined by disclosedness. This "presupposing" lying in Dasein's being comports itself not toward non-Dasein-like beings that also are, besides, but solely toward Dasein itself. The presupposed truth — the "there is" by which its being is to be determined — has the mode of being, the sense of being, of Dasein itself. The truth-presupposition we must "make" because it is already "made" with the being of the "we." The derivation is care's crowning application: Sichvorwegsein as the primal presupposition — Dasein has always already "posited" itself ahead as the ground of its being-possible — so the epistemologist's "we must presuppose truth" is the ontological structure of the ahead, misread as an axiom-choice. The must is constitutional, the "making" always already made: § 43's too-late theorem, now on truth's side.

The seventh unit deepens the must into thrownness and takes the measure of the skeptic's refutation. We must presuppose truth; it must be, as the disclosedness of Dasein, just as Dasein itself must be, in each case as mine and as this. Has Dasein ever, as itself, freely decided — and will it ever be able to decide — whether it wants to come into "Dasein" or not? "In itself" it is not to be seen at all why beings should be discovered, why truth and Dasein must be. The customary refutation of skepticism — of the denial of the being or the knowability of "truth" — stops halfway: what it shows in formal argumentation is merely that when judgment is made, truth is presupposed. This is a pointer to the fact that "truth" belongs to assertion — that pointing-out is, by its sense, a discovering — while it remains unclarified why this must be so, wherein the ontological ground of this necessary connection of being between assertion and truth lies. Likewise the mode of being of truth, and the sense of the presupposing and of its ontological foundation in Dasein itself, remain wholly dark; moreover it is misjudged that even when nobody judges, truth is already presupposed insofar as Dasein is at all. The paragraph is the subsection's darkest and most honest: the must of truth is the must of thrownness — nobody chose disclosure, and no reason "in itself" underwrites it; hence the retorsion-argument against the skeptic (judging presupposes truth) is convicted not of invalidity but of shallowness — it registers a necessity it cannot ground, mistakes an existential structure for a logical one, and misses that the presupposition runs with Dasein's being, judgments or none.

The eighth unit finishes with the skeptic. A skeptic can no more be refuted than the being of truth can be "proven." The skeptic, if he factically is, in the manner of the negation of truth, also needs no refutation: insofar as he is, and has understood himself in this being, he has, in the despair of suicide, extinguished Dasein and therewith truth. Truth cannot be proven in its necessity because Dasein cannot, for itself, first be placed under proof. And as little as it is demonstrated that there "are eternal truths," just as little is it demonstrated that there ever "was" a "real" skeptic — which the refutations of skepticism, despite their undertaking, at bottom believe; perhaps more often than the harmlessness of the formal-dialectical attempts to overrun "skepticism" would like to have true. The passage is among the book's grimmest: refutation and proof both fail because both operate downstream of the fact they concern — Dasein's being cannot be established before Dasein; the only consistent skeptic is the suicide, who refutes nothing and extinguishes everything, negation carried out ontically because it cannot be carried out logically. And the double dagger at the close cuts both ways: the schools' "real skeptic" is as undemonstrated as their eternal truths — and perhaps, the last clause murmurs, more actual than their harmless dialectic dreams: despair is not a position in a debate.

The ninth unit turns to the ideal subject. So, in the question of the being of truth and the necessity of its presupposition, just as in the question of the essence of cognition, an "ideal subject" is posited. The express or inexpress motive for this lies in the justified — but ontologically still to be grounded — demand that philosophy has the "a priori" as its theme, and not "empirical facts" as such. But does the positing of an "ideal subject" satisfy this demand? Is it not a fantastically idealized subject? Does the concept of such a subject not precisely miss the a priori of the merely "factual" subject, of Dasein? Does it not belong to the a priori of the factical subject — to the facticity of Dasein — that it is equiprimordially in truth and untruth? The critique is aimed past the neo-Kantians at Husserl's door: the ideal subject is a fantastic idealization that forfeits precisely what it was built to secure — the a priori — because Dasein's a priori is factical (thrown, falling, in truth and untruth at once); apriority and facticity, the tradition's disjunction, are conjoined in the analytic's subject. § 23's transvaluation of the a priori and § 44(b)'s fourth determination meet here.

The tenth unit names the casualties: the ideas of a "pure I" and of a "consciousness in general" so little contain the a priori of "actual" subjectivity that they skip over, or do not see at all, the ontological characters of facticity and of the constitution of being of Dasein. Rejection of a "consciousness in general" does not mean the negation of the a priori, just as little as the positing of an idealized subject guarantees a materially grounded apriority of Dasein. The double negative is carefully balanced: no empiricist retreat (the a priori stands) and no idealist ascent (the pure I falls) — the third position, factical apriority, holds the line against both; Kant's Bewußtsein überhaupt and Husserl's reines Ich are filed together as the same skip.

The eleventh unit signs the genealogy: the assertion of "eternal truths," like the conflation of the phenomenally grounded "ideality" of Dasein with an idealized absolute subject, belongs to the residues of Christian theology within the philosophical problematic that have long since not yet been radically expelled. The sentence is § 6's destruction in a single stroke of the pen: aeternae veritates descend from the divine intellect, the absolute subject from the theology of spirit — secularized theologoumena passing as logic; the "not yet radically expelled" claims the exorcism as ongoing work, this subsection included. (That Heidegger, the theologians' student, writes the sentence gives it its edge: the residues are named by one who knows the house.)

The twelfth unit states the positive connection: the being of truth stands in original connection with Dasein; and only because Dasein is, as constituted by disclosedness — that is, by understanding — can anything like being be understood at all: understanding of being is possible. The unit knots truth back into the book's title-question: disclosedness is the possibility of Seinsverständnis — truth is the bridge from the analytic of Dasein to the meaning of being; § 4's Faktum receives its final grounding.

The thirteenth unit speaks the equiprimordiality and defers the deepest question. Being — not beings — "is given" only insofar as truth is; and truth is only insofar and as long as Dasein is. Being and truth "are" equiprimordially. What it means that being "is" — where being is after all to be distinguished from all beings — can be concretely asked only when the meaning of being and the reach of the understanding of being in general have been clarified; only then can it also be originally laid apart what belongs to the concept of a science of being as such, of its possibilities and variations; and in demarcating this research and its truth, research as discovery of beings, and its truth, will be ontologically determined. The paragraph pairs with § 43(c)'s "gibt es"-theorem to form the book's double axis — being dependent on understanding, being dependent on truth: one dependence, since disclosedness is both — and the deferred question (in what sense being "is," given the ontological difference) with the promised doctrine of ontological versus ontic truth is the exact agenda of the unwritten Division Three; GA 24's discussion of the »es gibt« and the later "Zeit und Sein" grow from this deferral.

The closing unit ends Division One with an audit and three questions. The answering of the question of the meaning of being still stands out. What has the fundamental analysis of Dasein carried through so far made ready for working out this question? Through laying free the phenomenon of care, the constitution of being of the being to whose being something like an understanding of being belongs was clarified; Dasein's being was therewith at once demarcated against the modes of being — readiness-to-hand, presence-at-hand, reality — that characterize non-Dasein-like beings. Understanding itself was elucidated, whereby at the same time the methodical transparency of the understanding-interpreting procedure of the interpretation of being is guaranteed. If with care the original constitution of Dasein's being has been won, then on this ground the understanding of being lying in care must also be brought to concept — the meaning of being delimited. But is with the phenomenon of care the most original existential-ontological constitution of Dasein disclosed? Does the structural manifoldness lying in the phenomenon of care give the most original totality of the being of factical Dasein? Has the investigation hitherto brought Dasein as a whole into view at all? The audit is exact — care won, the modes demarcated, the method made transparent to itself (the hermeneutic circle, § 32, now certified as the procedure's own self-knowledge) — and the three closing questions dismantle the achievement's finality in ascending order: originality, unity, and, last and decisive, wholeness. Dasein as a whole has not been in view — everydayness is Dasein between birth and death, never the whole — and this deficit is Division Two's opening wound: to have the whole of a being that is essentially ahead-of-itself would require having its end. With the question of the Ganzsein hanging, Division One closes: the preparatory analysis complete, its provisionality now itself demonstrated, and death standing unnamed in the last question.

### Division Two: Dasein and Temporality

##### § 45. The Result of the Preparatory Fundamental Analysis of Dasein and the Task of an Original Existential Interpretation of This Being

The opening unit draws the balance of Division One. What was won through the preparatory analysis of Dasein, and what is sought? Found was the basic constitution of the thematic being — being-in-the-world, whose essential structures center in disclosedness; the totality of this structural whole unveiled itself as care, in which the being of Dasein lies enclosed. The analysis of this being took as its guiding thread what was anticipatorily determined as the essence of Dasein: existence. The title says, in formal indication: Dasein is as understanding potentiality-of-being, for which, in its being, this being itself is at issue; the being that is in this manner am in each case I myself. The working-out of the phenomenon of care furnished insight into the concrete constitution of existence — into its equiprimordial connection with Dasein's facticity and falling. The audit is deliberately double-columned — found versus sought — and its terms are chosen with care: everything found (world, disclosedness, care) was found along the guiding thread of existence taken as formal indication; the entire first division thus stands or falls with the adequacy of that fore-sight, which this section will now audit.

The second unit re-states what is sought and the condition of finding it. Sought is the answer to the question of the meaning of being in general, and before that, the possibility of a radical working-out of this basic question of all ontology. But laying free the horizon in which something like being in general becomes intelligible amounts to clarifying the possibility of the understanding of being in general — which itself belongs to the constitution of the being we call Dasein. The understanding of being, however, can be radically clarified as an essential moment of Dasein's being only if the being to whose being it belongs is itself originally interpreted with regard to its being. The chain of conditions runs the Introduction's program backward to its pivot: horizon = possibility of Seinsverständnis = original interpretation of Dasein — so the question whether Division One was original is not scholastic bookkeeping but the being-question's own demand.

The third unit poses the audit-question with its criterion missing: may we claim the ontological characterization of Dasein qua care as an original interpretation of this being? By what standard is the existential analytic to be assessed as to its originality or non-originality? What, indeed, does originality of an ontological interpretation mean at all? The triple question is honest to the point of severity: the analytic has no external tribunal, so the criterion itself must first be derived — which the next units do, from the theory of interpretation the analytic itself produced.

The fourth unit derives it from § 32. Ontological investigation is a possible kind of interpretation, characterized as the working-out and appropriation of an understanding; every interpretation has its fore-having, fore-sight, and fore-grasp. If interpretation becomes the express task of a research, then the whole of these "presuppositions" — which we call the hermeneutical situation — needs prior clarification and securing from and in a fundamental experience of the "object" to be disclosed. Ontological interpretation, which is to lay beings free with regard to their own constitution of being, is bound to bring the thematic being into the fore-having through a first phenomenal characterization, to which all subsequent steps of the analysis measure themselves; these need at the same time guidance through the possible fore-sight upon the mode of being of the being in question; and fore-having and fore-sight then predelineate at once the conceptuality (fore-grasp) into which all structures of being are to be raised. The paragraph mints the term hermeneutische Situation — the fore-structure become methodological self-consciousness — and turns § 32's doctrine of the circle into a research-protocol: an interpretation is answerable for its situation, and "coming into the circle in the right way" now means: audit your fore-having, fore-sight, fore-grasp expressly. The book examines itself by its own theory of interpretation — reflexivity as rigor.

The fifth unit raises the bar for originality: an original ontological interpretation demands not only a hermeneutical situation secured in phenomenal appropriateness; it must expressly assure itself whether it has brought the whole of the thematic being into the fore-having. Likewise, a first predelineation of this being's being, though phenomenally grounded, does not suffice: the fore-sight upon being must reach it with regard to the unity of the belonging and possible structural moments. Only then can the question of the meaning of the unity of the being-totality of the whole being be posed and answered with phenomenal security. Originality is thus defined by two demands — the whole in the fore-having, the unity in the fore-sight — which map exactly onto § 44's closing questions; and their conjunction defines Division Two's program in advance: wholeness (death), unity (temporality).

The sixth unit asks the question of the division in two sentences: did the accomplished existential analysis of Dasein grow from such a hermeneutical situation that the originality demanded by fundamental ontology is guaranteed through it? Can one advance from the won result — the being of Dasein is care — to the question of the original unity of this structural whole? The interrogatives are rhetorical only in retrospect; here they open a genuine crisis of the enterprise, staged deliberately at its midpoint.

The seventh unit audits the fore-sight and finds it lacking. How does it stand with the fore-sight that has hitherto guided the ontological procedure? The idea of existence was determined as understanding potentiality-of-being for which its being itself is at issue; but as in each case mine, the potentiality-of-being is free for authenticity or inauthenticity or their modal indifference. The interpretation hitherto, beginning with average everydayness, restricted itself to the analysis of indifferent or inauthentic existing. To be sure, on this way too a concrete determination of the existentiality of existence could and had to be reached; nevertheless the ontological characterization of the existence-constitution remained afflicted with an essential lack: existence means potentiality-of-being — but also authentic potentiality-of-being. So long as the existential structure of authentic potentiality-of-being is not taken into the idea of existence, the fore-sight guiding the existential interpretation lacks originality. The verdict is exact and self-inflicted: § 9's methodical decision for everydayness, right as far as it went, left the fore-sight one-eyed — existence analyzed only in its indifferent and disowned modes — so the guiding concept itself is incomplete until authenticity is structurally included; Chapter Two's resoluteness is thereby demanded by the method, not by edification.

The eighth unit audits the fore-having and finds the deeper wound. And how does it stand with the fore-having of the hitherto hermeneutical situation? When and how did the existential analysis assure itself that, with the approach from everydayness, it forced the whole Dasein — this being from its "beginning" to its "end" — into the theme-giving phenomenological view? Care was indeed asserted to be the totality of the structural whole of Dasein's constitution; but does not the very approach of the interpretation already renounce the possibility of bringing Dasein as a whole into view? Everydayness is precisely the being "between" birth and death. And if existence determines Dasein's being, and its essence is co-constituted by potentiality-of-being, then Dasein, as long as it exists, being-able, must in each case not yet be something. A being whose essence is constituted by existence essentially resists its possible apprehension as a whole being. The hermeneutical situation has hitherto not only not assured itself of the "having" of the whole being; it becomes questionable whether this is attainable at all, and whether an original ontological interpretation of Dasein must not founder — on the mode of being of the thematic being itself. The paragraph converts § 44's third question into an antinomy: care's totality was structural (all the moments), never extensional (the whole span) — everydayness is the between, and the ahead-of-itself guarantees a standing not-yet — so wholeness seems barred by the very constitution the analysis discovered. The candor of the last clause should be felt: the enterprise contemplates its own necessary foundering; § 31's "genuine foundering" now names a live methodological possibility.

The ninth unit states the deficit as verdict: one thing has become unmistakable — the hitherto existential analysis of Dasein cannot raise the claim to originality; in the fore-having stood always only the inauthentic being of Dasein, and this as un-whole. If the interpretation of Dasein's being is to become original, as foundation of the working-out of the basic ontological question, then it must beforehand have brought Dasein's being to light existentially in its possible authenticity and wholeness. The sentence is Division One's epitaph written by its author: uneigentlich und unganz — the two privatives that name the entire remaining task; and the order of the "and" (authenticity and wholeness) will in fact be executed in reverse — wholeness first (death), authenticity second (conscience), their unity third (anticipatory resoluteness).

The tenth unit converts the wholeness-problem into the death-analysis and sketches the argument to come. Thus grows the task of placing Dasein as a whole into the fore-having — which means: first of all unrolling the question of this being's potentiality-of-being-whole. In Dasein, as long as it is, something in each case still stands out (steht aus) that it can be and will be; to this outstanding, however, belongs the "end" itself. The "end" of being-in-the-world is death. This end, belonging to the potentiality-of-being — that is, to existence — limits and determines the in-each-case possible wholeness of Dasein. But Dasein's being-at-an-end in death, and therewith this being's being-whole, can be drawn into the discussion of possible being-whole in a phenomenally appropriate way only if an ontologically sufficient — that is, existential — concept of death has been won. Dasein-like, however, death is only in an existentiell being toward death (Sein zum Tode); the existential structure of this being proves to be the ontological constitution of Dasein's potentiality-of-being-whole. The whole existing Dasein thus lets itself be brought into the existential fore-having. But can Dasein also exist authentically whole? How is the authenticity of existence to be determined at all, if not with regard to authentic existing — whence do we take the criterion? Manifestly Dasein itself must, in its being, pregive the possibility and manner of its authentic existence, if this can neither be forced upon it ontically nor invented ontologically. The attestation (Bezeugung) of an authentic potentiality-of-being is given by conscience (das Gewissen); like death, this Dasein-phenomenon demands a genuinely existential interpretation, which leads to the insight that an authentic potentiality-of-being of Dasein lies in wanting-to-have-a-conscience — an existentiell possibility that tends, by its sense of being, toward existentiell determination through being toward death. The paragraph is Division Two's argument compressed to one breath, and its two hinges deserve marking. First hinge: death enters the fore-having not as event but as being-toward — the whole becomes graspable because the end is a way to be, not an outstanding occurrence; the substitution of Sein zum Tode for Zu-Ende-sein is the chapter's whole discovery, stated in advance. Second hinge: the criterion-problem for authenticity is solved by attestation — no ontic imposition, no ontological invention, but Dasein's own testimony (conscience), § 29's methodological rule (let Dasein interpret itself; the analytic accompanies) elevated to the division's evidentiary principle.

The eleventh unit banks the projected result: with the exhibition of an authentic potentiality-of-being-whole, the existential analytic assures itself of the constitution of Dasein's original being — and the authentic potentiality-of-being-whole becomes visible at the same time as a mode of care. Therewith the phenomenally sufficient soil for an original interpretation of the meaning of Dasein's being is also secured. The guard-clause is essential: even the authentic whole remains a mode of care — no new faculty, no exit from the structure; § 27's and § 38's modification-theorem projected forward over the entire division.

The twelfth unit names the destination: the original ontological ground of Dasein's existentiality, however, is temporality (Zeitlichkeit). The articulated structural totality of Dasein's being as care first becomes existentially intelligible from it. But the interpretation of the meaning of Dasein's being cannot halt at this demonstration: the existential-temporal analysis of this being needs concrete confirmation — the previously won ontological structures of Dasein must be laid free, retrogressively, with regard to their temporal sense. Everydayness unveils itself as a mode of temporality; through this repetition (Wiederholung) of the preparatory fundamental analysis, the phenomenon of temporality itself becomes at the same time more transparent, and from it becomes intelligible why Dasein, in the ground of its being, is and can be historical, and, as historical, can develop historiography. The paragraph gives the division's second half its charter: temporality named as the sought unity (§ 41's "still more original phenomenon" identified at last), and the method for it named too — Wiederholung, the retrieving repetition: Division One to be re-read, structure by structure, for its temporal sense (Chapter Four), with historicity (Chapter Five) as the yield. The book's spiral architecture is here made explicit doctrine: progress as deepened return.

The thirteenth unit derives the everyday time-concept's place: if temporality constitutes the original sense of Dasein's being, and this being is concerned, in its being, with this being itself, then care must need "time" and hence reckon with "the time." Dasein's temporality develops "time-reckoning"; the "time" experienced in it is the nearest phenomenal aspect of temporality, out of which grows the everyday-vulgar understanding of time — and this unfolds into the traditional concept of time. The derivation-chain (temporality, reckoning, vulgar understanding, traditional concept) is Chapter Six in four links — and its logic repeats the book's constant pattern: the tradition's time-concept will be neither refuted nor adopted but derived, as the self-leveling of a more original phenomenon.

The fourteenth unit stakes the deepest claim: the illumination of the origin of the "time" "in which" innerworldly beings are encountered — time as within-time-ness (Innerzeitigkeit) — reveals an essential possibility of temporalizing (Zeitigung) of temporality; therewith the understanding prepares itself for a still more original temporalizing of temporality, in which grounds the understanding of being constitutive for Dasein's being. The projection of a meaning of being in general can accomplish itself in the horizon of time. The last sentence is the book's title cashed as a program-sentence: the horizon sought since § 1 is time — with the crucial word "can" (kann sich vollziehen) keeping the claim projective; the demonstration belonged to the never-published Division Three, and this paragraph is its most explicit advance notice within the text.

The closing unit gives the division's table — and, in the folded-in note, settles the debt to Kierkegaard. The investigation of this division runs through the following stages: Dasein's possible being-whole and being toward death (Chapter One); the Dasein-like attestation of an authentic potentiality-of-being, and resoluteness (Chapter Two); Dasein's authentic potentiality-of-being-whole, and temporality as the ontological sense of care (Chapter Three); temporality and everydayness (Chapter Four); temporality and historicity (Chapter Five); temporality and within-time-ness as the origin of the vulgar concept of time (Chapter Six). The note records that in the nineteenth century Kierkegaard expressly seized and penetratingly thought through the existence-problem as an existentiell one; but the existential problematic is so foreign to him that, in ontological regard, he stands wholly under the dominion of Hegel and of ancient philosophy as seen through Hegel — hence there is philosophically more to be learned from his "edifying" writings than from the theoretical ones, with the treatise on the concept of anxiety excepted. The table is the division's map; the note is its most consequential acknowledgment and demarcation in one: Kierkegaard honored as the discoverer of the existentiell (the very register §§ 46–60 will mine — death, anxiety, the moment, repetition all bear his fingerprints) and confined to it — existenziell, not existenzial; penetrating, not ontological; his conceptual apparatus Hegel's own. The preference for the edifying discourses over the pseudonymous works, with the Angst-book as sole exception, is a reader's judgment of great precision — and a quiet self-location: what Kierkegaard did for the existentiell, this division claims to do for its ontology.

#### Chapter One: The Possible Being-Whole of Dasein and Being toward Death
