##### § 46. The Apparent Impossibility of Ontologically Grasping and Determining Dasein-like Being-Whole

The opening unit sets the task and lets the obstacle speak: the insufficiency of the hermeneutical situation from which the foregoing analysis of Dasein sprang is to be overcome. With regard to the fore-having of the whole Dasein that must necessarily be won, it must be asked whether this being, as existing, can become accessible in its being-whole at all — for weighty grounds seem to speak for the impossibility of the demanded pre-giving, grounds lying in the constitution of being of Dasein itself. The section's title-word "apparent" (scheinbar) already tips the verdict, but the method is § 40's: the objection is to be built at full strength from the analytic's own results before it is dismantled.

The second unit builds it from care. To care, which forms the totality of the structural whole of Dasein, a possible being-whole of this being manifestly contradicts, by care's ontological sense. The primary moment of care, the ahead-of-itself, says: Dasein exists in each case for the sake of itself; "as long as it is," up to its end, it comports itself toward its potentiality-of-being. Even when, still existing, it has nothing more "before it" and has "closed its account," its being is still determined by the ahead-of-itself: hopelessness, for example, does not tear Dasein away from its possibilities but is only an own mode of being toward these possibilities; no less does the illusionless "being-prepared for everything" harbor the ahead-of-itself in itself. This structural moment of care says unambiguously that in Dasein something always still stands out which, as potentiality-of-being of itself, has not yet become "actual": in the essence of the basic constitution of Dasein lies, accordingly, a constant unclosedness (Unabgeschlossenheit). The un-wholeness means an outstanding (Ausstand) of potentiality-of-being. The argument's finest touches are the two counter-examples: despair and stoic readiness — the existentiell postures that seem to have finished with the future — are shown to be modes of the ahead, not its absence; even having-nothing-before-one is a way of being-before. The structural conclusion follows: as long as Dasein is, it is not yet — incompleteness constitutional, not accidental.

The third unit closes the pincer: but as soon as Dasein "exists" in such a way that in it absolutely nothing more stands out, it has therewith already become no-longer-being-there (Nicht-mehr-da-sein). The removal of the outstanding of being means the annihilation of its being. As long as Dasein is as a being, it has never attained its "wholeness"; but if it gains it, the gain becomes the loss of being-in-the-world as such — as a being it then never again becomes experienceable. The dilemma is now formally complete and elegant: wholeness never while being, being lost at wholeness — Dasein and its totality apparently never co-present; the epigram (gain as loss) has the exactness of a conservation law.

The fourth unit locates the impossibility rightly: the ground of the impossibility of experiencing Dasein ontically as a whole being, and hence of determining it ontologically in its being-whole, lies not in an imperfection of the cognitive faculty; the hindrance stands on the side of the being of this being. What cannot even be in the way an experience pretends to grasp Dasein withdraws in principle from experienceability. But does not the reading-off of the ontological totality of being from Dasein then remain a hopeless undertaking? The relocation matters methodologically: no better instrument would help — the limit is ontological, not epistemic — which is exactly why the resolution, when it comes, will consist in re-conceiving the "whole," not in sharpening the grasp.

The fifth unit turns on the argument itself. The ahead-of-itself, as an essential structural moment of care, cannot be struck out — but is what we concluded from it sound? Was the impossibility of grasping the whole Dasein not inferred in merely formal argumentation? Or was Dasein at bottom not inadvertently posited as something present-at-hand, ahead of which a not-yet-present-at-hand constantly shoves itself? Did the argumentation grasp the not-yet-being and the "ahead" in a genuine existential sense? Was there talk of "end" and "wholeness" in phenomenal appropriateness to Dasein? Did the expression "death" have a biological or an existential-ontological — indeed any sufficiently and securely delimited — signification? And have all possibilities of making Dasein accessible in its wholeness in fact been exhausted? The self-cross-examination is the section's pivot, and the second question is the diagnosis: the "weighty grounds" secretly read Dasein as a present-at-hand thing with an outstanding remainder — the not-yet as a missing piece, the end as a terminal slice — categories imported precisely where existentials were owed. The whole apparatus of §§ 48–49 (Ausstand versus not-yet, Verenden versus Sterben) is set by this battery of questions.

The closing unit converts perplexity into program: these questions demand answer before the problem of Dasein's wholeness can be set aside as null. The question of Dasein's wholeness — the existentiell question of a possible potentiality-of-being-whole as well as the existential question of the constitution of being of "end" and "wholeness" — harbors the task of a positive analysis of existence-phenomena hitherto deferred. In the center of these considerations stands the ontological characterization of Dasein-like being-at-an-end and the winning of an existential concept of death. The investigations divide as follows: the experienceability of the death of others and the possibility of grasping a whole Dasein (§ 47); outstanding, end, and wholeness (§ 48); the demarcation of the existential analysis of death against possible interpretations of the phenomenon (§ 49); the predelineation of the existential-ontological structure of death (§ 50); being toward death and the everydayness of Dasein (§ 51); everyday being toward death and the full existential concept of death (§ 52); existential projection of an authentic being toward death (§ 53). The table gives the chapter its rhythm — one detour (§ 47), two conceptual demarcations (§§ 48–49), structure (§ 50), everydayness (§§ 51–52), authentic projection (§ 53) — the § 28 pattern (constitution, everyday mode, authentic mode) applied to the darkest phenomenon.

##### § 47. The Experienceability of the Death of Others and the Possibility of Grasping a Whole Dasein

The opening unit states the impasse and the obvious way around it. The reaching of Dasein's wholeness in death is at the same time loss of the being of the Da: the transition to no-longer-Dasein lifts Dasein precisely out of the possibility of experiencing this transition and understanding it as experienced. Such may indeed remain denied to the respective Dasein with regard to itself — all the more penetrating, then, is the death of others: an ending of Dasein thus becomes "objectively" accessible. Dasein can, especially since it is essentially being-with with others, win an experience of death; this "objective" givenness of death must then also make possible an ontological delimitation of Dasein's wholeness. The proposal is drawn from the analytic's own resources (Mitsein supplies the data the first person cannot), which is what gives the coming refutation its weight: the detour fails not for lack of ingenuity but on the phenomenon.

The second unit poses the test-question in one sentence: does this obvious expedient — drawn from Dasein's mode of being as being-with-one-another — of choosing the Dasein of others that has come to its end as the substitute-theme (Ersatzthema) for the analysis of Dasein's wholeness, lead to the appointed goal? The word Ersatzthema is the section's scalpel: what is being tested is substitution itself.

The third unit describes the transition and coins its formula. The Dasein of others too, with its wholeness reached in death, is a no-longer-Dasein in the sense of no-longer-being-in-the-world. Does dying not mean going-out-of-the-world, losing being-in-the-world? The no-longer-being-in-the-world of the one who has died is nevertheless still — understood extremely — a being, in the sense of the mere-presence-at-hand of an encountered corporeal thing. In the dying of others that remarkable phenomenon of being can be experienced which lets itself be determined as the switch-over (Umschlag) of a being from the mode of being of Dasein (or of life) to no-longer-Dasein: the end of the being qua Dasein is the beginning of this being qua something present-at-hand. The Umschlag — § 33's word for the assertion's flattening of the tool — returns at mortality's threshold: death as the categorial switch in person; and the closing chiasmus (end qua Dasein, beginning qua Vorhandenes) states with terrible economy what the next units will complicate.

The fourth unit complicates it once: this interpretation of the switch-over from Dasein to mere-presence-at-hand misses the phenomenal stock insofar as the still-remaining being presents no pure corporeal thing. Even the present-at-hand corpse is, theoretically regarded, still a possible object of pathological anatomy, whose tendency of understanding remains oriented to the idea of life: the merely-present-at-hand is "more" than a lifeless material thing — with it is encountered an unliving something that has forfeited life. The correction is categorially exact: the corpse is a privative of life, not a specimen of matter — even anatomy reads it against the idea of life (§ 10's privative biology confirmed at the dissection table); the dead body is a mode of the once-living, not a thing among things.

The fifth unit is a single sentence raising the stakes: but even this characterization of the still-remaining does not exhaust the full Dasein-like phenomenal finding. The one-line unit is a hinge — from the corpse to the deceased.

The sixth unit finds the dead within solicitude. The "deceased" (der Verstorbene), who in distinction from the dead (dem Gestorbenen) has been torn from the "bereaved," is the object of "concern" in the manner of the funeral rite, the burial, the cult of graves — and this, again, because he is in his mode of being "still more" than a merely attendable, environmentally ready-to-hand item of equipment. In mournful-commemorative tarrying alongside him, the bereaved are with him, in a mode of honoring solicitude: the relation of being to the dead must therefore not be grasped as concernful being alongside something ready-to-hand. The terminological split (Verstorbener/Gestorbener — the deceased-for-us versus the one who died) carries the phenomenology: the funeral's object is neither corpse nor tool but a co-Dasein still met in Fürsorge — mourning as a mode of being-with; three sentences that found an entire phenomenology of grief and ritual, and quietly correct any reading of § 26 that would confine Mitsein to the living.

The seventh unit fixes the paradox of this being-with: in such being-with with the dead, the deceased himself is no longer factically "there" (da); but being-with always means being-with-one-another in the same world. The deceased has left our "world" and left it behind; from out of it those remaining can still be with him. The analysis is exquisite: the shared world survives the sharer — the bereaved are with the dead from the world he abandoned, a with-being sustained one-sidedly across the departure; Mitsein shown to be world-mediated so essentially that even the other's absence is met within it.

The eighth unit draws the negative conclusion. The more appropriately the no-longer-Dasein of the deceased is grasped phenomenally, the more clearly it shows itself that such being-with with the dead precisely does not experience the authentic having-come-to-an-end of the deceased. Death unveils itself indeed as loss — but more as the loss experienced by those remaining; in suffering the loss, the loss of being that the dying one "suffers" does not become accessible. We do not experience, in the genuine sense, the dying of others; we are at most always only "there alongside" (dabei). The verdict names the structural asymmetry with a mourner's precision: two losses, incommensurable — the survivors' loss of him, his loss of being — and only the first is given; Dabeisein, being-present-at, is the maximum: attendance, never access.

The ninth unit closes even the psychological loophole: and even if it were possible and feasible to clarify to oneself "psychologically" the dying of others in being-alongside, the way of being thereby meant — namely coming-to-an-end — would by no means be grasped. The question stands after the ontological sense of the dying of the dying one, as a possibility of being of his being — not after the way of the co-Dasein and still-Dasein of the departed with those left behind. The directive to take the death experienced in others as the theme for the analysis of Dasein's end and wholeness can give, neither ontically nor ontologically, what it supposed it could give. The distinction cuts the section's theme cleanly in two: the phenomenology of the deceased-with-the-bereaved (units six and seven — genuine, and hereby honored) is not the ontology of dying; the substitute-theme delivered a real phenomenon, only not the one sought.

The tenth unit digs to the presupposition: above all, the appeal to the dying of others as substitute-theme rests on a presupposition demonstrably a complete misjudgment of Dasein's mode of being — the opinion that Dasein can be arbitrarily replaced by another, so that what remains unexperienceable in one's own Dasein becomes accessible in the foreign one. But is this presupposition really so groundless? The question is posed with genuine openness — for the analytic itself (§ 26) established representability; the next unit grants it its full domain before the boundary is drawn.

The eleventh unit grants representability its realm. To the possibilities of being of being-with-one-another in the world belongs, incontestably, the representability (Vertretbarkeit) of one Dasein by another; in the everydayness of concern, manifold and constant use is made of it. Every going-to..., every fetching-of... is representable within the circuit of the nearest attended "environing world"; the wide manifold of representable ways of being-in-the-world extends not only to the worn-down modes of public being-with-one-another, but concerns equally the possibilities of concern restricted to determinate circles, cut to professions, estates, and ages. But such representation is, by its sense, always representation "in" and "alongside" something — in the concern for something; everyday Dasein, however, understands itself proximally and mostly from what it is accustomed to attend to: "one is" what one does. With regard to this being — the everyday absorption with one another in the attended "world" — representability is not only possible in general; it belongs even as a constitutive to being-with-one-another: here one Dasein can and even must, within certain limits, "be" the other. The paragraph is § 27's everydayness re-derived from the side of substitution: because everyday identity is occupation ("one is what one does"), and tasks are transferable, the everyday self is constitutionally deputizable — replaceability not a defect but a constituent of the public with-world; das Man's anonymity given its praxeological ground.

The twelfth unit draws the boundary. This possibility of representation, however, founders completely when it is a matter of representing the possibility of being that constitutes Dasein's coming-to-an-end and gives it, as such, its wholeness. No one can take the other's dying away from him (Keiner kann dem Anderen sein Sterben abnehmen). Someone can indeed "go into death for another" — but that always means: to sacrifice oneself for the other "in a determinate cause"; such dying-for... can never mean that the other's death is thereby in the least taken from him. Dying is what every Dasein must in each case take upon itself. Death is, insofar as it "is," essentially in each case mine; and indeed it means a peculiar possibility of being, in which the being of one's own Dasein is at issue absolutely. In dying it shows itself that death is ontologically constituted by mineness and existence. Dying is not an occurrence (Begebenheit) but a phenomenon to be understood existentially — and this in a distinctive sense still to be delimited more closely. The paragraph is among the book's most famous, and its logic must be kept as strict as its rhetoric is stark. The sacrifice-clause is not a concession weakening the thesis but its sharpest proof: even the substitute death — the maximum of dying-for — leaves the beneficiary's own dying untouched; what is transferred is an occasion, never the mortality. The verb abnehmen echoes § 27 with precision: das Man took Dasein's being from it — its choices, its responsibility — but here is the one thing structurally untakeable; death as the limit of the disburdening economy. And the conclusion re-founds § 9 at the extreme: Jemeinigkeit and existence, posited formally there, are constituted in death — the possibility in which mineness cannot be delegated is the possibility that individualizes.

The thirteenth unit generalizes to wholeness: but if "ending," as dying, constitutes Dasein's wholeness, then the being of the wholeness itself must be conceived as an existential phenomenon of the in-each-case own Dasein. In "ending" and in the being-whole of Dasein constituted through it, there is essentially no representation. The proposed way out misjudges this existential state of affairs when it puts forward the dying of others as substitute-theme for the analysis of wholeness. The inference transfers the non-transferability from death to totality: since the whole is whole only through the un-deputizable end, wholeness itself is in each case mine — no third-person totality exists to be observed.

The fourteenth unit banks the double yield: so the attempt to make Dasein's being-whole phenomenally accessible in an appropriate way has foundered anew. But the result of the considerations does not remain negative: they were carried out in an orientation to the phenomena, however rough. Death has been indicated as an existential phenomenon — which forces the investigation into a purely existential orientation to the in-each-case own Dasein. For the analysis of death as dying there remains only the possibility of bringing this phenomenon either to a purely existential concept, or else of renouncing its ontological understanding. The methodological fork is stated without softening: existential concept or silence — third-person routes exhausted, the phenomenon accessible only in the first-person structure of being-toward; the negative result thus positively narrows the field to what § 50 will occupy.

The closing unit adds the terminological harvest: further, in characterizing the transition from Dasein to no-longer-Dasein as no-longer-being-in-the-world, it showed itself that Dasein's going-out-of-the-world in the sense of dying must be distinguished from a going-out-of-the-world of the merely-living: the ending of a living thing we grasp terminologically as perishing (Verenden). The distinction can become visible only through a demarcation of Dasein-like ending against the end of a life; dying can, to be sure, also be conceived physiologically and biologically — but the medical concept of "exitus" does not coincide with that of perishing. The closing legislation opens the three-term register § 49 will complete (Verenden for the animal, exitus for medicine, Sterben for Dasein) — the privative method's last and gravest application: only a being that exists can die; what merely lives, perishes — and even the clinic's death-concept is flagged as sui generis, coinciding with neither.

##### § 48. Outstanding, End, and Wholeness

The opening unit (closing § 47's discussion and opening the new task) names the standing danger: from the discussion so far of the possibility of ontologically grasping death it becomes clear that substructions (Substruktionen) of beings of another mode of being — presence-at-hand or life — unnoticedly pressing forward, threaten to confuse the interpretation of the phenomenon, indeed already its first appropriate pre-giving. This can be countered only by seeking, for the further analysis, a sufficient ontological determinateness of the constitutive phenomena: end and wholeness. The word Substruktion names the enemy with precision — not false theses but smuggled foundations: thing-categories and life-categories laid under the phenomenon before analysis begins; § 46's self-diagnosis generalized into a rule of vigilance for the whole chapter.

The second unit measures the task against the book's own circle. The ontological characterization of end and wholeness can, within the frame of this investigation, be only provisional. Its sufficient accomplishment would require not only setting forth the formal structure of end in general and wholeness in general; it would need at the same time the unfolding of their possible regional — that is, de-formalized — structural variations, related to determinate "contentful" beings and determined from their being. This task presupposes in its turn a sufficiently unambiguous, positive interpretation of the modes of being that demand a regional division of the totality of beings; and the understanding of these ways of being demands a clarified idea of being in general. An appropriate accomplishment of the ontological analysis of end and wholeness founders not only on the breadth of the theme, but on the fundamental difficulty that mastering this task presupposes precisely what is sought in this investigation — the meaning of being in general — as already found and known. The confession is the hermeneutic circle at its most vertiginous: a complete doctrine of ends and wholes needs the regional ontologies, which need the meaning of being, which this analysis of the end is meant to help win — the book openly borrowing against its own unproven result; provisionality not as modesty but as structural necessity.

The third unit narrows to what is needed: the prevailing interest of the following considerations belongs to the "variations" of end and wholeness that, as ontological determinatenesses of Dasein, are to guide an original interpretation of this being. In constant regard to the already exhibited existential constitution of Dasein, we must try to decide how far the concepts of end and wholeness that at first press forward — however categorially indeterminate they remain — are ontologically inappropriate to Dasein; and the rejection of such concepts must be developed into a positive assignment to their specific region. Thereby the understanding of end and wholeness in their variation as existentials consolidates itself, which guarantees the possibility of an ontological interpretation of death. The method is § 48's whole procedure announced: rejection-plus-assignment — each inadequate concept not merely refused but escorted home to its proper region (sums to the ready-to-hand, completion to works, perishing to life) — the § 20 discipline of regional bookkeeping turned to the service of the existential concept.

The fourth unit blocks the deductive reading: if the analysis of Dasein's end and wholeness takes so wide-spanned an orientation, this nevertheless cannot mean that the existential concepts of end and wholeness are to be won by way of a deduction; conversely, the point is to take the existential sense of Dasein's coming-to-an-end from Dasein itself, and to show how such "ending" can constitute a being-whole of the being that exists. No taxonomy of ends will yield death as a special case; the direction runs from the phenomenon outward — § 7's maxim guarding the chapter's most tempting shortcut.

The fifth unit formalizes the state of the problem: what has been discussed so far about death can be formulated in three theses: (1) to Dasein, as long as it is, belongs a not-yet that it will be — the constant outstanding; (2) the coming-to-its-end of what in each case is not-yet-at-an-end (the removal, in the manner of being, of the outstanding) has the character of no-longer-Dasein; (3) coming-to-an-end encloses in itself a mode of being absolutely unrepresentable for the respective Dasein. The three theses are §§ 46–47 compressed for processing: the first two form the antinomy, the third the constraint on any solution — and the section's work is now the audit of thesis one's key word: may the not-yet be read as Ausstand?

The sixth unit performs the audit on the debt-example. In Dasein there is a constant "un-wholeness," which finds its end with death — this is uncrossable. But may the phenomenal fact that, to Dasein as long as it is, this not-yet "belongs," be interpreted as an outstanding? With regard to what kind of beings do we speak of outstanding? The expression means what indeed "belongs" to a being but is still missing: outstanding, as lacking, grounds in a belongingness. Outstanding is, for example, the remainder of a debt still to be received: what is outstanding is not yet available; the discharge of the "debt," as removal of the outstanding, means the "coming in" — the successive arrival of the remainder, whereby the not-yet is, as it were, filled up until the owed sum is "together." Outstanding therefore means: the not-yet-being-together of what belongs together. Ontologically this involves the unreadiness-to-hand of pieces still to be brought in, of the same mode of being as those already ready-to-hand — which for their part do not modify their mode of being through the remainder's arrival. The subsisting un-together is discharged by an accumulating piecing-together: beings in which something is still outstanding have the mode of being of the ready-to-hand. The together — and the un-together founded in it — we characterize as sum. The analysis is a small phenomenology of debt with each feature marked for the coming contrast: homogeneity of parts (installments like installments), indifference of the present to the missing, completion by external accrual — the sum as the ontological form of the outstanding; whatever the not-yet of Dasein is, the next unit shows it is not this.

The seventh unit applies the negative and refines the question. This un-together belonging to such a mode of the together — lacking as outstanding — can by no means determine ontologically the not-yet that belongs to Dasein as its possible death. This being does not have at all the mode of being of something ready-to-hand within the world. The together of the being that Dasein "in its course" is, until it has "completed its course," is not constituted by a "continuing" piecing-on of beings that, of themselves, are somehow and somewhere already ready-to-hand. Dasein is not first together when its not-yet has filled itself up — so little that precisely then it no longer is. Dasein always already exists in just such a way that its not-yet belongs to it. But are there not beings that are as they are, to which a not-yet can belong, without these beings having to have Dasein's mode of being? The refutation turns § 46's dilemma into the diagnosis's proof: on the sum-model, completion should perfect; for Dasein it annihilates — so the model was categorially wrong from the start. The closing question opens the comparative method: intermediate cases must be tested before the existential not-yet stands alone.

The eighth unit tests the moon. One can say, for example: the last quarter of the moon is still outstanding until it is full; the not-yet diminishes with the vanishing of the covering shadow — yet the moon is always already present-at-hand as a whole. Apart from the fact that even the full moon is never wholly graspable, the not-yet here by no means signifies a not-yet-being-together of the belonging parts, but concerns solely the perceiving apprehension. The not-yet belonging to Dasein, however, not only remains provisionally and at times inaccessible to one's own and others' experience — it "is" not yet "actual" at all. The problem concerns not the apprehension of the Dasein-like not-yet but its possible being or not-being: Dasein must, as itself, become — that is, be — what it is not yet. In order, therefore, to determine the Dasein-like being of the not-yet by comparison, we must take into consideration beings to whose mode of being becoming belongs. The lunar case eliminates the epistemic reading with elegance: the moon's not-yet is in the seeing, not in the moon — whereas Dasein's not-yet is ontological, a not-yet of being; hence the comparison must move from the orders of presence and perception to the order of becoming.

The ninth unit finds the ripening fruit. The unripe fruit, for example, goes toward its ripeness; in ripening, what it is not yet is by no means pieced on to it as a not-yet-present-at-hand. It itself brings itself to ripeness, and such self-bringing characterizes its being as fruit. Nothing conceivable that could be brought in would remove the fruit's unripeness, did this being not come of itself to ripeness. The not-yet of unripeness does not mean an other standing outside, which could be present-at-hand at and with the fruit, indifferent to it: it means the fruit itself, in its specific mode of being. The not-yet-complete sum is, as ready-to-hand, "indifferent" to the missing, unready-to-hand remainder — strictly taken, it can be neither un-indifferent nor indifferent to it. The ripening fruit, however, is not only not indifferent to unripeness as an other of itself: ripening, it is the unripeness. The not-yet is already drawn into its own being — and by no means as an arbitrary determination but as a constitutive. Correspondingly, Dasein too, as long as it is, in each case already is its not-yet. The folded-in note observes that the difference between whole and sum — holon and pan, totum and compositum — is familiar since Plato and Aristotle, though the systematics of the categorial variation enclosed in this division was not thereby recognized and raised to concept; for the beginning of an executing analysis of these structures it points to Husserl's Third Logical Investigation, on the doctrine of wholes and parts. The fruit-analysis is the section's positive gain and its precision is grammatical: the fruit is its unripeness (reifend ist sie die Unreife) — the not-yet as a way of being, not a missing piece; the copula does what no accrual could. The note's genealogy places the whole discussion inside a lineage (the ancient holon/pan distinction, Husserl's mereology) while claiming the step neither took: the categorial variation of "whole" by mode of being.

The tenth unit takes the yield and marks the residue: what constitutes the "un-wholeness" in Dasein — the constant ahead-of-itself — is neither an outstanding of a summative together, nor indeed a not-yet-having-become-accessible, but a not-yet that in each case a Dasein, as the being it is, has to be. Nevertheless the comparison with the fruit's unripeness shows, along with a certain agreement, essential differences; to heed them means to recognize the indeterminacy of the talk so far of end and ending. Two eliminations are banked (sum, apprehension) and the positive formula minted — the not-yet as zu-sein, to-be — but the analogy is immediately put on notice: agreement in the not-yet does not entail agreement in the end.

The eleventh unit breaks the analogy at the end. Even if ripening, the specific being of the fruit, as a mode of being of the not-yet (of unripeness), formally agrees with Dasein in that both, in a sense still to be delimited, in each case already are their not-yet, this cannot mean that ripeness as "end" and death as "end" coincide with regard to the ontological end-structure. With ripeness the fruit completes itself (vollendet sich). But is the death at which Dasein arrives a completion in this sense? Dasein has indeed with its death "completed its course" — but has it therewith necessarily exhausted its specific possibilities? Are these not rather precisely taken from it? Even "uncompleted" Dasein ends. On the other hand, Dasein so little needs first to come to ripeness with its death that it can already have passed beyond it before the end: for the most part it ends in incompletion, or else decayed and used up. The break is the section's darkest insight, delivered with terrible economy: death is not telos — no maturation-schema fits it, for it can fall before ripeness, after it, or upon the unripe indifferently; the Aristotelian teleology of living form, which the fruit-example seemed to invite, is refused exactly where it beckons. Death perfects nothing; it takes.

The twelfth unit is a two-line hinge: ending does not necessarily mean completing-itself; the question becomes more pressing in what sense death must be conceived as Dasein's ending. The negative widens: with completion gone, the whole lexicon of ending must be sorted.

The thirteenth unit sorts it. Ending means at first ceasing (Aufhören), and this again in ontologically different senses: the rain ceases — it is no longer present-at-hand; the road ceases — this ending does not make the road vanish, but the ceasing determines the road as this present-at-hand one. Ending as ceasing can accordingly mean: passing over into un-presence-at-hand, or precisely presence-at-hand first with the end. The latter ending can in turn either determine something unfinished present-at-hand — a road under construction breaks off — or constitute the "finishedness" of something present-at-hand — with the last brushstroke the painting is finished. The taxonomy is built with the workshop's own cases (rain, road, painting) and its axes are exact: vanishing versus bounding; breaking-off versus finishing — four modes of ceasing, all categorial, all awaiting the verdict.

The fourteenth unit ranks finishing and completing: but ending as becoming-finished does not include completion in itself; what wants to be completed must indeed reach its possible finishedness — completion is a founded mode of "finishedness," which is itself possible only as a determination of something present-at-hand or ready-to-hand. The micro-hierarchy (completion founded on finishedness, finishedness confined to things and works) quietly seals the eleventh unit's result from the other side: even the noblest ending in the thing-register cannot reach Dasein.

The fifteenth unit adds the consumption-modes: even ending in the sense of vanishing can still modify itself according to the beings' mode of being — the rain is at an end, that is, vanished; the bread is at an end, that is, used up, no longer available as ready-to-hand. The bread beside the rain completes the grid: vanishing itself splits by region (the present-at-hand ceases, the ready-to-hand is consumed) — a last demonstration that "end" varies with being.

The sixteenth unit passes the verdict: by none of these modes of ending can death be appropriately characterized as Dasein's end. If dying were understood as being-at-an-end in the sense of an ending of the kinds discussed, Dasein would thereby be posited as something present-at-hand or ready-to-hand. In death, Dasein is neither completed, nor simply vanished, nor become finished, nor wholly available as something ready-to-hand. The four negations tick off the grid case by case — no telos, no evaporation, no opus, no consumption — the entire categorial vocabulary of ending exhausted and dismissed; what remains must be existential.

The seventeenth unit states it — and lets a medieval voice say it first. Rather: just as Dasein constantly, as long as it is, already is its not-yet, so it also always already is its end. The ending meant with death signifies no being-at-an-end of Dasein, but a being toward the end (Sein zum Ende) of this being. Death is a way to be that Dasein takes over as soon as it is: "as soon as a human being comes to life, at once he is old enough to die" — the note giving the source: the Ackermann aus Böhmen, in Bernt and Burdach's edition. This is the chapter's central transformation accomplished: the end relocated from the terminus to the way — death not the last point of the line but a how of being the line at every point; Zu-Ende-sein replaced by Sein zum Ende, the genitive of arrival by the accusative of comportment. And the citation is a masterstroke of the § 42 method: the pre-ontological attestation again — a fifteenth-century plowman's lament (edited by the same Burdach who supplied the Cura-fable) uttering the existential concept five centuries early: old enough to die at birth, mortality as a qualification of the living, not a property of the dead.

The eighteenth unit assigns the consequences: ending as being toward the end demands its ontological clarification from Dasein's mode of being; and presumably only from the existential determination of ending will the possibility of an existing being of the not-yet that lies "before" the "end" become intelligible. The existential clarification of being toward the end also first gives the sufficient basis for delimiting the possible sense of talk of a wholeness of Dasein — if indeed this wholeness is to be constituted through death as "end." The order of explanation is reversed with the relocation: the not-yet is now to be understood from being-toward-the-end (not the end from the not-yet) — § 46's whole apparatus re-founded on the new concept; wholeness, if it comes, will be a wholeness of being-toward, not of completion.

The nineteenth unit audits the path: the attempt to reach an understanding of Dasein-like wholeness by starting from a clarification of the not-yet, via the characterization of ending, did not lead to the goal. It showed only negatively: the not-yet that Dasein in each case is resists interpretation as outstanding; the end toward which Dasein existingly is remains inappropriately determined by being-at-an-end. At the same time, the consideration should make plain that its course must be reversed: a positive characterization of the phenomena in question (not-yet-being, ending, wholeness) succeeds only in unambiguous orientation to Dasein's constitution of being — an unambiguousness secured negatively, against wrong ways, by insight into the regional belonging of the end- and wholeness-structures that run ontologically counter to Dasein. The self-audit is the § 7 method's honesty: the section's whole labor was clearing — sums, moons, fruits, rains, roads, paintings, bread, each assigned its region — and the positive account must now be built the other way round, from care downward.

The closing unit gives the directive: the positive existential-analytic interpretation of death and its end-character is to be carried through along the guiding thread of the basic constitution of Dasein won so far — the phenomenon of care. The one-sentence unit hands § 50 its method: death to be read off the care-structure, moment by moment — which is exactly what § 50 will do.

##### § 49. The Demarcation of the Existential Analysis of Death against Possible Other Interpretations of the Phenomenon

The opening unit states the section's office: the unambiguousness of the ontological interpretation of death shall first be consolidated by bringing expressly to consciousness what this interpretation does not ask about, and about what an information and directive from it would be expected in vain. A section of pure boundary-drawing — and the double formula (what it does not ask; what it cannot supply) marks both directions of possible confusion: imports into the analysis, exports demanded of it.

The second unit places death within life and Dasein above both. Death in the widest sense is a phenomenon of life; life must be understood as a mode of being to which a being-in-the-world belongs, and it can be ontologically fixed only in privative orientation to Dasein. Dasein too can be considered as pure life: for the biological-physiological question-formulation it then moves into the region of being we know as the animal and plant world. In this field, data and statistics on the life-span of plants, animals, and humans can be won by ontic ascertainment; connections between life-span, propagation, and growth can be recognized; the "kinds" of death, the causes, "arrangements," and ways of its occurrence can be investigated — the note pointing to Korschelt's comprehensive presentation of life-span, aging, and death, with its rich bibliography. The paragraph re-runs § 10's privative biology at the mortal boundary: life read down from Dasein, never Dasein up from life — while granting the life-sciences their entire field (the demography and thanatology of the day catalogued without irony); the demarcation is of foundations, not of facts.

The third unit orders the sciences and legislates the terms. This biological-ontic investigation of death is grounded in an ontological problematic: it remains to be asked how the essence of death determines itself from the ontological essence of life. In a certain way, the ontic investigation of death has always already decided about this: more or less clarified pre-concepts of life and death are operative in it, and these need a predelineation through the ontology of Dasein. Within the ontology of Dasein, which is superordinate to an ontology of life, the existential analysis of death is in its turn subordinate to a characterization of Dasein's basic constitution. The ending of the living we called perishing (Verenden). Insofar as Dasein also "has" its physiological, life-bound death — not, however, ontically isolated, but co-determined by its original mode of being — and insofar as Dasein can also end without authentically dying, while on the other hand, qua Dasein, it does not simply perish, we designate this intermediate phenomenon as demise (Ableben). Dying (Sterben), however, shall count as the title for the way of being in which Dasein is toward its death. Accordingly it must be said: Dasein never perishes; demise, however, Dasein can only so long as it dies. The medical-biological investigation of demise can win results that may become significant even ontologically, once the basic orientation for an existential interpretation of death is secured. Or must sickness and death in general — even medically — be conceived primarily as existential phenomena? The three-term legislation is the section's yield: Verenden (the animal's ending), Ableben (Dasein's physiological death — the "intermediate phenomenon," biologically describable yet co-determined by existence), Sterben (the being-toward). The two theorems that follow are strict consequences: Dasein never perishes (its ending is never merely organic), and can demise only while it dies — the clinical event is founded in the existential way of being, not conversely. The closing question — must medicine itself conceive sickness and death existentially? — throws a bridge far beyond the book (Zollikon is in it), left open as a question should be.

The fourth unit orders the human sciences likewise. The existential interpretation of death lies before all biology and ontology of life; but it also first founds all biographical-historical and ethnological-psychological investigation of death. A "typology" of "dying," as a characterization of the states and ways in which demise is "lived," already presupposes the concept of death; moreover, a psychology of "dying" gives information rather about the "living" of the "dying one" than about dying itself — which is only the reflection of the fact that Dasein does not first die, nor even authentically dies, in and with a lived experience of factical demise. Likewise the conceptions of death among primitives, their comportments toward death in magic and cult, illuminate primarily the understanding of Dasein, whose interpretation already needs an existential analytic and a corresponding concept of death. The paragraph's central aperçu deserves isolation: the psychology of the deathbed studies the dying one's life — for dying is not an experience among experiences but the being of the experiencer; the datum such psychology seeks (dying "from inside") does not exist as a datum. And the ethnological remark repeats § 11 at the grave: death-cults document Daseinsverständnis, and so presuppose the analytic they might seem to test.

The fifth unit draws the this-worldly boundary. The ontological analysis of being toward the end, on the other hand, anticipates no existentiell stance toward death. If death is determined as the "end" of Dasein — of being-in-the-world — no ontic decision thereby falls as to whether "after death" another, higher or lower being is possible, whether Dasein "lives on" or, "outlasting itself," is "immortal." About the "beyond" and its possibility as little is decided ontically as about the "this side" — as though norms and rules of comportment toward death were to be proposed for "edification." But the analysis of death remains purely "this-worldly" insofar as it interprets the phenomenon solely with regard to how, as a possibility of being of the respective Dasein, it stands into this Dasein. Meaningfully and rightfully, one can only then even ask with methodical security what is after death, when death is conceived in its full ontological essence; whether such a question represents a possible theoretical question at all remains here undecided. The this-worldly ontological interpretation of death lies before every ontic other-worldly speculation. The neutrality is § 38's theology-settlement applied to immortality — with the same juridical structure: no denial of the beyond (agnosticism, not atheism, and expressly no edification either), but priority — any meaningful survival-question presupposes the ontological concept of what would survive; and the further reservation (whether the question is theoretically possible at all) withholds even the promise that metaphysics can be resumed after the analysis.

The sixth unit excludes the metaphysics of death: finally, outside the district of an existential analysis of death stands what might be discussed under the title of a "metaphysics of death." The questions how and when death "came into the world," what "sense" it can and should have as evil and suffering in the totality of beings, presuppose necessarily an understanding not only of the being-character of death, but of the ontology of the totality of beings as a whole, and the ontological clarification of evil and negativity in general in particular. Theodicy is dismissed not as false but as premature twice over: it needs the concept of death (this analysis) and an ontology of the whole plus a doctrine of the negative (nowhere in sight) — the fall, the penalty of sin, cosmic evil all filed as questions whose presuppositions are unpaid.

The seventh unit ranks and warns. To the questions of a biology, psychology, theodicy, and theology of death, the existential analysis is methodically superordinate. Taken ontically, its results show the peculiar formality and emptiness of all ontological characterization; that, however, must not blind one to the rich and intricate structure of the phenomenon. If Dasein in general never becomes accessible as something present-at-hand, because being-possible belongs in its own way to its mode of being, even less may one expect simply to read off the ontological structure of death — if indeed death is a distinguished possibility of Dasein. The double caution balances the section: the analysis's yield will look empty beside the sciences' riches (§ 42's defense of formal fullness re-invoked), and the phenomenon will resist reading-off more than any — a possibility, and the distinguished one, is the least vorhanden of all "objects."

The eighth unit secures the phenomenal control and the existentiell abstinence. On the other hand, the analysis cannot hold itself to an idea of death contrived accidentally and at will; this arbitrariness is steered only by a prior ontological characterization of the mode of being in which the "end" stands into Dasein's average everydayness — for which the full presentification of the earlier exhibited structures of everydayness is needed. That in an existential analysis of death existentiell possibilities of being toward death also resonate lies in the essence of all ontological investigation; all the more expressly must existentiell non-bindingness (Unverbindlichkeit) go together with the existential concept-determination — and this especially with regard to death, in which Dasein's possibility-character lets itself be unveiled most sharply. The existential problematic aims solely at setting forth the ontological structure of Dasein's being toward the end. The methodological double-bind is stated with unusual candor: no analysis of death without existentiell resonance (the analyst too is mortal, and ontology draws on an existentiell source — § 63 will make this explicit), hence the express discipline of non-bindingness: structure, not exhortation — the guard posted precisely because the coming sections will read, to careless eyes, like a sermon.

The closing unit is the long note, and it is the chapter's intellectual map. Appended to the section's last sentence, it records: the anthropology worked out in Christian theology — from Paul to Calvin's meditatio futurae vitae — has always seen death together with the interpretation of "life." Dilthey, whose authentic philosophical tendencies aimed at an ontology of "life," could not mistake its connection with death: "and finally the relation that most deeply and universally determines the feeling of our Dasein — that of life to death; for the limitation of our existence by death is always decisive for our understanding and estimation of life." Recently Simmel too expressly drew the phenomenon of death into the determination of "life," though without clear separation of the biological-ontic and the ontological-existential problematics (Lebensanschauung, 1918). For the present investigation, Jaspers' Psychology of Worldviews is especially to be compared: Jaspers grasps death along the guiding thread of the phenomenon of the "limit-situation" (Grenzsituation) he set forth, whose fundamental significance lies above all typology of "attitudes" and "world-pictures." Dilthey's impulses were taken up by Rudolf Unger (Herder, Novalis und Kleist, 1922; and the lecture on literary history as problem-history), who sees clearly the significance of phenomenological research for a more radical founding of the "problems of life." The note is § 49's demarcations converted into a genealogy and an acknowledgment: the Pauline-Reformed tradition credited with never interpreting life without death (the meditatio futurae vitae as the ancestor of Sein zum Tode); Dilthey's sentence quoted as the thesis the chapter ontologizes (death's limitation decisive for the understanding of life); Simmel honored and corrected in one clause; and Jaspers' Grenzsituation — the nearest contemporary kin to the existential concept — saluted with the book's highest compliment, fundamentality above all typology. The whole lineage from which the death-analysis descends is thus filed in small print at its threshold — theology, Lebensphilosophie, existence-philosophy — each honored, each demarcated: they saw the phenomenon; the analytic claims its ontology.

##### § 50. The Predelineation of the Existential-Ontological Structure of Death

The opening unit sets the derivation from care. The considerations on outstanding, end, and wholeness yielded the necessity of interpreting the phenomenon of death as being toward the end from Dasein's basic constitution: only so can it become plain how far a being-whole constituted by being toward the end is possible in Dasein itself, in accordance with its structure of being. Care was made visible as Dasein's basic constitution; the ontological signification of the expression was expressed in the "definition": ahead-of-itself-already-being-in (the world) as being-alongside (innerworldly) encountered beings. Therewith the fundamental characters of Dasein's being are expressed: in the ahead-of-itself, existence; in the already-being-in..., facticity; in the being-alongside..., falling. If death belongs in a distinguished sense to Dasein's being, then it (or being toward the end) must let itself be determined from these characters. The procedure is announced with full formality: the care-formula's three members become the death-analysis's three axes — the section will read mortality off existence, facticity, and falling in turn, § 48's closing directive executed.

The second unit is the one-sentence program: it is first necessary to make plain, in a predelineating way, how Dasein's existence, facticity, and falling reveal themselves in the phenomenon of death. The word vorzeichnend keeps § 5's register: sketch first, full concept (§ 52) later.

The third unit converts the not-yet into imminence. The interpretation of the not-yet — and therewith also of the outermost not-yet, Dasein's end — in the sense of an outstanding was rejected as inappropriate, for it enclosed the ontological perversion of Dasein into something present-at-hand. Being-at-an-end means existentially: being toward the end. The outermost not-yet has the character of something toward which Dasein comports itself; the end stands before Dasein (steht bevor). Death is not something not yet present-at-hand, not the last outstanding reduced to a minimum, but rather an imminence (Bevorstand). The terminological pivot from Ausstand to Bevorstand is § 48's whole yield minted as one word-pair: not what is missing behind but what stands before — the not-yet relocated from the inventory to the facing.

The fourth unit sorts imminences of the worldly kind: but to Dasein as being-in-the-world much can be imminent; the character of imminence does not by itself distinguish death. On the contrary, this interpretation too could suggest that death must be understood in the sense of an imminent event encountered environmentally: imminent can be, for example, a thunderstorm, the remodeling of the house, the arrival of a friend — beings, accordingly, that are present-at-hand, ready-to-hand, or there-with. Imminent death does not have a being of this kind. The self-correction is immediate and necessary: Bevorstand alone would re-ontify death as an approaching occurrence (§ 30's fearsome!); the three examples span the three regions (nature, work, friend) so the exclusion is total.

The fifth unit sorts imminences of Dasein's own kind: but imminent to Dasein can also be, for example, a journey, a dispute with others, a renunciation of something that Dasein itself can be — own possibilities of being, grounded in being-with with others. Even the refined class (imminent possibilities of my being, not events) does not yet isolate death: journey, quarrel, renunciation are mine, but relational — grounded in Mitsein; the next unit's second predicate is thereby prepared.

The sixth unit delivers the triple determination. Death is a possibility of being that Dasein itself has in each case to take over; with death, Dasein stands before itself (steht sich... bevor) in its ownmost potentiality-of-being. In this possibility, Dasein's being-in-the-world is at issue absolutely: its death is the possibility of no-longer-being-able-to-be-there (Nicht-mehr-dasein-können). When Dasein stands before itself as this possibility of itself, it is completely referred to its ownmost potentiality-of-being; standing thus before itself, all relations to other Dasein are in it dissolved. This ownmost, non-relational possibility is at the same time the outermost: as potentiality-of-being, Dasein cannot outstrip (überholen) the possibility of death — death is the possibility of the absolute impossibility of Dasein (die Möglichkeit der schlechthinnigen Daseinsunmöglichkeit). Thus death unveils itself as the ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped possibility (die eigenste, unbezügliche, unüberholbare Möglichkeit). As such it is a distinguished imminence, whose existential possibility grounds in this, that Dasein is essentially disclosed to itself, in the manner of the ahead-of-itself: this structural moment of care has in being toward death its most original concretion. Being toward the end becomes phenomenally clearer as being toward the characterized distinguished possibility of Dasein. The paragraph is the structural heart of the chapter, and its grammar bears the doctrine. The reflexive turn — with death Dasein stands before itself — converts § 47's Jemeinigkeit into structure: the imminence is self-imminence; what impends is not an event but I myself as possible impossibility. The three predicates then fall in strict order from the care-analysis: ownmost (Jemeinigkeit at its maximum — the undelegable of § 47), non-relational (the dissolution of all Mitsein-relations in the standing-before — § 40's individuation stated from death's side), not-to-be-outstripped (no possibility lies beyond it for projection — the ahead's own limit). And the celebrated formula — possibility of the absolute impossibility — keeps death inside the modal register § 31 crowned: not the actuality that ends possibilities but the possibility of their impossibility, possible through and through; the whole of § 53 will live on this clause. The derivation-claim at the close (Sichvorweg's most original concretion) makes the first care-axis pay: existence reveals itself in death as being toward the ownmost possibility.

The seventh unit derives the second axis: thrownness into death, unveiled in anxiety. This ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped possibility Dasein does not procure for itself subsequently and occasionally in the course of its being: rather, if Dasein exists, it is also already thrown into this possibility. That it is delivered over to its death, and that death thus belongs to being-in-the-world, of this Dasein has proximally and mostly no express or even theoretical knowledge. Thrownness into death unveils itself to it more originally and penetratingly in the disposedness of anxiety: anxiety before death is anxiety "before" the ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped potentiality-of-being; the before-which of this anxiety is being-in-the-world itself; the about-which of this anxiety is Dasein's potentiality-of-being absolutely. Anxiety before death must not be thrown together with a fear of demise: it is no arbitrary and accidental "weak" mood of the individual, but, as a basic disposedness of Dasein, the disclosedness of the fact that Dasein exists as thrown being toward its end. Therewith the existential concept of dying clarifies itself as thrown being toward the ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped potentiality-of-being; and the demarcation gains sharpness against a pure vanishing, against a mere perishing, and finally against an "experiencing" of demise. The second axis pays in full: facticity reveals itself as thrownness into the possibility — mortality never adopted, always already delivered over — and § 40's anxiety receives its determinate object-structure at last: the indefinite threat of the earlier analysis was thrownness-toward-death all along, its before-which (world) and about-which (potentiality) now specified through the three predicates. The demarcation-clause closes § 49's register: dying, so defined, coincides with none of vanishing, perishing, or the lived deathbed.

The eighth unit derives the third axis and totals the structure. Being toward the end does not first arise through, and as, an occasionally emerging attitude; it belongs essentially to Dasein's thrownness, which unveils itself in disposedness (mood) in this way or that. The factical "knowing" or "not-knowing" prevailing in a Dasein about its ownmost being toward the end is only the expression of the existentiell possibility of holding oneself in this being in different ways. That factically many, proximally and mostly, know nothing of death may not be passed off as proof that being toward death does not belong "universally" to Dasein, but only as proof that Dasein, proximally and mostly, covers up its ownmost being toward death, in flight before it. Dasein dies factically as long as it exists, but proximally and mostly in the manner of falling: for factical existing is not only in general and indifferently a thrown potentiality-for-being-in-the-world, but is always also already absorbed in the attended "world" — and in this falling being-alongside, the flight out of uncanniness announces itself, which now means: flight before the ownmost being toward death. Existence, facticity, falling characterize being toward the end and are accordingly constitutive for the existential concept of death: dying grounds, with regard to its ontological possibility, in care. The third axis completes the triangle with the argument-form of § 40: everyday ignorance of death is not counter-evidence but the falling mode of being-toward it — one flees only what one is toward, so the covering attests the covered; the flight from uncanniness (§ 40's finding) receives its final address: what das Man's at-home shelters from is being-toward-death itself. And the closing theorem — dying grounds in care — discharges the section's title: the structure predelineated, all three care-moments verified at the phenomenon.

The closing unit sets the verification-task: but if being toward death belongs originally and essentially to Dasein's being, then it must — though proximally inauthentically — also be demonstrable in everydayness. And if being toward the end should even offer the existential possibility for an existentiell being-whole of Dasein, therein would lie the phenomenal confirmation for the thesis: care is the ontological title for the totality of Dasein's structural whole. For the full phenomenal justification of this proposition, however, a predelineation of the connection between being toward death and care does not suffice: it must above all become visible in Dasein's nearest concretion, its everydayness. The transition is the § 28 rhythm once more — structure won, everydayness owed — and the stakes are marked: the everyday demonstration will simultaneously verify care's totality-claim (§ 41) at its hardest case; §§ 51–52 take up exactly this.

##### § 51. Being toward Death and the Everydayness of Dasein

The opening unit sets the method from the everyday apparatus. The setting-forth of everyday average being toward death orients itself by the earlier won structures of everydayness. In being toward death, Dasein comports itself toward itself as a distinguished potentiality-of-being; but the self of everydayness is das Man, which constitutes itself in the public interpretedness that speaks itself out in idle talk. Idle talk must accordingly make manifest in what way everyday Dasein interprets to itself its being toward death; the foundation of interpretation is in each case an understanding that is always also disposed — attuned. So it must be asked: how has the disposed understanding lying in das Man's idle talk disclosed being toward death? How does das Man comport itself understandingly toward the ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped possibility of Dasein? Which disposedness discloses to das Man the deliverance over to death, and in what way? The protocol is exact: Chapter Five's machinery (das Man, Gerede, disposed understanding) is wheeled to the grave — and the three closing questions distribute the coming analysis along disclosedness's own axes: interpretation, understanding, mood.

The second unit records the public datum. The publicness of everyday being-with-one-another "knows" death as a constantly occurring happening (Begegnis), as a "case of death" (Todesfall): this or that neighbor or stranger "dies"; unknown persons "die" daily and hourly. "Death" is encountered as a familiar event occurring within the world, and as such it remains in the inconspicuousness characteristic of the everyday encountered. Das Man has also already secured an interpretation for this event; the spoken, or mostly reticent, "fleeting" talk about it means to say: one dies in the end also sometime, but proximally one remains oneself unaffected. The observation is phenomenally exquisite: death publicly present precisely as inconspicuous — filed with § 16's unobtrusive background, a standing item of the news — and the everyday sentence is transcribed whole ("man stirbt am Ende auch einmal, aber zunächst bleibt man selbst unbetroffen"), for the next unit will read it word by word: the section's entire evidence is one idiom of das Man.

The third unit performs the exegesis of "one dies." The analysis of the "man stirbt" unveils unambiguously the mode of being of everyday being toward death. In such talk, death is understood as an indeterminate something that must first arrive from somewhere or other, but that proximally is for oneself not yet present-at-hand and hence unthreatening. The "one dies" spreads the opinion that death, as it were, strikes das Man. The public interpretation of Dasein says "one dies" because therewith everyone else, and oneself, can talk oneself into it: in each case not precisely I — for this Man is the nobody. "Dying" is leveled down to an occurrence that indeed strikes Dasein but belongs to nobody in particular. If ambiguity ever belongs to idle talk, it does to this talk of death: dying, which is essentially and unrepresentably mine, is perverted into a publicly occurring event that das Man encounters. The characterized talk speaks of death as a constantly occurring "case"; it passes death off as always already "actual" and veils its possibility-character and, in one therewith, the belonging moments of non-relationality and not-to-be-outstrippedness. With such ambiguity Dasein puts itself in the position of losing itself in das Man with regard to a distinguished potentiality-of-being belonging to its ownmost self: das Man gives right and increases the temptation to cover over for oneself one's ownmost being toward death. The exegesis is the book's method at its most devastating: a three-word idiom decomposed into a complete ontology of evasion. The grammatical subject does the work — "one" dies, and the one is nobody, so the sentence performs the delegation it describes (each speaker exempted by the very form of the words); the tense does the rest — the possible passed off as a standing actuality (cases, statistics, the "real"), which is precisely the destruction of possibility: § 50's three predicates inverted one by one (mine → anyone's; non-relational → public; not-to-be-outstripped → an event among events). And the closing sentence files it all under § 38: temptation, das Man as accomplice of the flight.

The fourth unit follows the evasion to the deathbed — and lets Tolstoy testify in the note. The covering evasion before death dominates everydayness so stubbornly that, in being-with-one-another, the "neighbors" often still talk the "dying one" into the belief that he will escape death and soon return again to the tranquilized everydayness of his attended world. Such "solicitude" even means thereby to "console" him: it wants to bring him back into Dasein by helping him to veil completely his ownmost, non-relational possibility of being. Das Man in this way attends to a constant tranquilization about death — which holds, at bottom, not only for the "dying one" but just as much for the "consolers." And even in the case of demise, publicness is still not to be disturbed and disquieted in its attended carefreeness by the event: indeed, in the dying of others one not seldom sees a social inconvenience, if not downright tactlessness, from which publicness is to be protected. The folded-in note records that Tolstoy, in his story "The Death of Ivan Ilyich," has presented the phenomenon of the shattering and collapse of this "one dies." The paragraph is the sociology of the sickroom done as ontology: consolation unmasked as the community's self-defense — the comforting lie a Fürsorge that works for the comforters, tranquilization distributed on both sides of the bed; and the last observation (death as a breach of etiquette) anticipates by decades every analysis of the modern concealment of dying. The Tolstoy note is the § 42 procedure once more — the pre-ontological attestation, this time literary and contemporary: Ivan Ilyich's "Caius is mortal" syllogism, true of Caius and unbelievable of himself, is the "man stirbt" caught ontically in the act, and his agony its collapse.

The fifth unit uncovers the mood-regulation. But das Man at the same time puts itself in the right and in repute, with this tranquilization that pushes Dasein away from its death, through the tacit regulation of the way one is to comport oneself toward death at all. Already the "thinking of death" counts publicly as cowardly fear, insecurity of Dasein, and dark flight from the world: das Man does not let the courage for anxiety before death arise. The dominion of das Man's public interpretedness has also already decided about the disposedness from which the stance toward death is to determine itself. In anxiety before death, Dasein is brought before itself as delivered over to the not-to-be-outstripped possibility; das Man attends to converting this anxiety into fear before an oncoming event. The anxiety, made ambiguous as fear, is moreover passed off as a weakness that no self-assured Dasein may know. What "is proper" according to the silent decree of das Man is the indifferent calm regarding the "fact" that one dies; the cultivation of such a "superior" indifference alienates Dasein from its ownmost, non-relational potentiality-of-being. The paragraph is § 29's thirteenth unit (publicness makes its moods) executed at the extreme case, and its central coinage — der Mut zur Angst, the courage for anxiety — is among the book's finest: courage re-assigned from the suppression of the mood to its endurance, while the public ethics of composure (stoic calm, "superior" indifference) is unmasked as manufactured alienation. The mechanism is § 40's founding-order weaponized by das Man: anxiety deliberately re-cast as fear-of-an-event, because an event can be far off, improbable, someone else's — the ontological demotion performed as social discipline.

The sixth unit names the structure and springs the attestation. Temptation, tranquilization, and alienation, however, mark the mode of being of falling: everyday being toward death is, as falling, a constant flight before it. Being toward the end has the mode of an evasion before it — re-interpreting, inauthentically understanding, and veiling. That the in-each-case own Dasein factically always already dies — that is, is in a being toward its end — this factum it conceals from itself by re-minting death into the everyday occurring case of death among others, which at most assures us still more distinctly that "one oneself" indeed still "lives." But with the falling flight before death, the everydayness of Dasein attests (bezeugt) that das Man itself too is in each case already determined as being toward death, even when it does not expressly move in a "thinking about death": even in average everydayness, Dasein is constantly concerned with this ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped potentiality-of-being, if only in the mode of attending to an unmolested indifference toward the uttermost possibility of its existence. The unit's logic is the chapter's masterstroke, § 40's evasion-theorem brought home: flight is the proof — one can flee only before what one is; the everyday concealment of death is therefore the everyday's own testimony that being-toward-death belongs to Dasein universally. Even indifference is a mode of the being-toward (concern for untroubledness against the possibility — the gegen doing the work): das Man convicted of mortality by its very tranquility. The three falling-moments of § 38 (temptation, tranquilization, alienation) are found intact at the grave — falling's kinetics verified on the hardest case.

The closing unit converts the finding into method: the setting-forth of everyday being toward death gives at the same time the directive to attempt, through a more penetrating interpretation of falling being toward death as evasion before it, to secure the full existential concept of being toward the end. At the before-which of the flight, made phenomenally sufficiently visible, it must let itself be phenomenologically projected how the evading Dasein itself understands its death. The transition-sentence is the § 40 protocol cited by name (the note refers to the anxiety-analysis): read the fugitive's map — the evasion, fully described, will yield by reversal the full concept; § 52 executes exactly this.

##### § 52. Everyday Being toward the End and the Full Existential Concept of Death

The opening unit takes stock and reverses direction. Being toward the end was determined in existential predelineation as being toward the ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped potentiality-of-being; the existing being toward this possibility brings itself before the absolute impossibility of existence. Beyond this apparently empty characterization of being toward death, the concretion of this being unveiled itself in the mode of everydayness: in accordance with the falling-tendency essential to everydayness, being toward death proved to be a covering evasion before it. Whereas previously the investigation passed from the formal predelineation of the ontological structure of death to the concrete analysis of everyday being toward the end, now, in the reversed direction, the full existential concept of death is to be won through a supplementary interpretation of everyday being toward the end. The methodological chiasmus is announced cleanly: structure was read down into everydayness; everydayness will now be read back up into structure — the evasion itself mined for the predicates it evades.

The second unit isolates the residue in the idiom. The explication of everyday being toward death held to das Man's idle talk: one dies also sometime, but provisionally not yet. So far, only the "one dies" as such was interpreted. In the "also sometime, but provisionally not yet," everydayness concedes something like a certainty of death: nobody doubts that one dies. But this "not doubting" need not already harbor in itself the being-certain that corresponds to the way death — in the sense of the characterized distinguished possibility — stands into Dasein. Everydayness remains at this ambiguous conceding of the "certainty" of death — in order to weaken it, covering dying still more, and to lighten for itself the thrownness into death. The reading returns to the idiom for its unexploited clauses: the concession ("gewiß") and the deferral ("noch nicht") — two words, two predicates in hiding; and the diagnosis of the concession's function is exact: certainty admitted precisely as a technique of weakening — one grants "the fact" in order not to be certain.

The third unit poses the paradox in two lines: the covering evasion before death cannot, by its own sense, be authentically "certain" of death — and yet it is. How does it stand with the "certainty of death"? The formulation is deliberate: the evasion is certain of what it evades (§ 40's structure again) — and this double status demands the truth-analysis that follows.

The fourth unit grounds certainty in § 44. To be certain of a being means: to hold it for true as something true. But truth means discoveredness of beings, and all discoveredness grounds ontologically in the most original truth, the disclosedness of Dasein: Dasein, as disclosed-disclosing and discovering, is essentially "in the truth." Certainty, however, grounds in truth or belongs to it equiprimordially. The expression "certainty," like the term "truth," has a double signification: originally, truth means the same as disclosing-being — a comportment of Dasein; the derived signification means the discoveredness of beings. Correspondingly, certainty means originally being-certain (Gewißsein) as a mode of being of Dasein; in a derived signification, however, the being of which Dasein can be certain is also called a "certain" one. The paragraph transplants § 44's double register onto certainty with strict parallelism — Gewißsein as act-character first, the "certain" entity derived — so that the coming analysis can ask about a way of being rather than a property of propositions; death-certainty will be a mode of Dasein or nothing.

The fifth unit defines the honest mode: one mode of certainty is conviction (Überzeugung). In it, Dasein lets its understanding being toward the matter be determined solely by the testimony of the discovered (true) matter itself. Holding-for-true, as holding-oneself-in-the-truth, is adequate when it grounds in the discovered being itself and, as being toward the being so discovered, has become transparent to itself with regard to its appropriateness to it — something lacking in arbitrary invention or in the mere "view" about a being. Conviction is defined by its evidential discipline (the thing's own testimony, plus self-transparency about fit) — the standard against which the everyday "certainty" of death will be measured and found to be neither conviction nor doubt but a third thing: adequate-seeming inadequacy.

The sixth unit indexes adequacy to being: the adequacy of holding-for-true measures itself by the truth-claim to which it belongs; this claim receives its right from the mode of being of the being to be disclosed and the direction of the disclosing. With the diversity of beings, and according to the guiding tendency and reach of the disclosing, the kind of truth changes, and therewith the certainty. The present consideration remains restricted to an analysis of being-certain with regard to death, which in the end presents a distinguished certainty of Dasein. The principle is § 7's regionalism applied to evidence: no single scale of certainty across the modes of being — a doctrine whose payoff comes in § 53, where death-certainty will be exempted from the gradation of evidences altogether; the closing phrase (eine ausgezeichnete Daseinsgewißheit) posts the claim in advance.

The seventh unit classifies the everyday certainty. Everyday Dasein mostly covers over the ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped possibility of its being; this factical covering-tendency confirms the thesis: Dasein, as factical, is in "untruth." Accordingly, the certainty that belongs to such covering of being toward death must be an inappropriate holding-for-true — not, say, uncertainty in the sense of doubting. Inappropriate certainty holds that of which it is certain in coveredness: if "one" understands death as an event encountered environmentally, the certainty related to it does not reach being toward the end. The classification is fine-grained and crucial: the everyday stance is neither skepticism nor conviction but certified concealment — certainty with the wrong object (the event instead of the being-toward), the § 44(b) doctrine of equiprimordial untruth cashing itself at the deathbed: one can be quite sure, and precisely thereby covered.
