The eighth unit catches das Man in the act and names its evidence. One says: it is certain that "death" comes. One says it — and das Man overlooks that, in order to be able to be certain of death, in each case one's own Dasein must itself be certain of its ownmost, non-relational potentiality-of-being. One says death is certain, and thereby plants in Dasein the semblance that it is itself certain of its death. And where lies the ground of the everyday being-certain? Manifestly not in mere mutual persuasion — one experiences daily, after all, the "dying" of others: death is an undeniable "fact of experience." The double exposure works both ways: the impersonal subject smuggles the certainty past its rightful owner (the "one" is certain, so that no I need be), and yet the ground is not mere talk — the empirical basis is real, which sets up the next unit's "critical" refinement and its deeper failure.

The ninth unit lets everydayness be critical. The way everyday being toward death understands the certainty so grounded betrays itself when it attempts to "think" about death even critically-cautiously — that is, supposedly appropriately: all human beings, so far as one knows, "die"; death is for every human being in the highest degree probable, yet not "unconditionally" certain; strictly taken, "only" empirical certainty may be ascribed to death — it necessarily remains behind the highest certainty, the apodictic, which we reach in certain districts of theoretical cognition. The reconstruction is deadpan and deadly: the inductive-logic commonplace (all observed humans mortal; certainty merely empirical; apodicticity reserved for mathematics) is quoted as everydayness at its most reflective — the seminar-room version of the "noch nicht," Kant's Critique enlisted by das Man.

The tenth unit dismantles it. In this "critical" determination of the certainty of death and of its imminence there reveals itself, first of all, once again the misjudgment — characteristic of everydayness — of Dasein's mode of being and of the being toward death belonging to it. That demise, as an occurring event, is "only" empirically certain decides nothing about the certainty of death. Cases of death may be the factical occasion for Dasein's first becoming attentive to death at all; but remaining within the characterized empirical certainty, Dasein cannot become certain of death at all in the way it "is." And yet: although Dasein in das Man's publicness seemingly "talks" only of this "empirical" certainty of death, at bottom it does not hold itself exclusively and primarily to the occurring cases of death. Evading its death, everyday being toward the end is certain of death otherwise than it would itself like to admit in purely theoretical reflection. This "otherwise" everydayness mostly veils from itself; it does not dare to become transparent to itself in it. With the characterized everyday disposedness — the "anxiously" concerned, seemingly anxiety-free superiority over against the certain "fact" of death — everydayness concedes a "higher" than merely empirical certainty. One knows about the certain death and yet "is" not authentically certain of it. The falling everydayness of Dasein knows the certainty of death and evades the being-certain. But this evasion attests phenomenally, from that before which it evades, that death must be conceived as the ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped, certain possibility. The dismantling has two blades. Categorial: empirical certainty is calibrated to occurrences, and death is not one — the "criticism" is rigorous about the wrong object (demise), so its modesty is a category-mistake. Phenomenological: the theoretical downgrade is belied by the mood — the anxious concern beneath the composed "superiority" concedes a certainty higher than the induction admits; everydayness is surer than its epistemology. And the closing move mints the fourth predicate by the § 40 method: gewiß won from the evasion itself — what is fled must be certain, or the flight were needless.

The eleventh unit turns to the second clause of the idiom. One says: death comes certainly, but provisionally not yet. With this "but..." das Man denies death its certainty. The "provisionally not yet" is no merely negative assertion but a self-interpretation of das Man, with which it refers itself to what proximally still remains accessible and attendable for Dasein. Everydayness presses into the urgency of concern and divests itself of the fetters of a weary, "inactive thinking about death": death is deferred to a "later sometime," and this with appeal to the so-called "general estimate" (allgemeines Ermessen). Thus das Man covers over what is peculiar to death's certainty — that it is possible at every moment (daß er jeden Augenblick möglich ist). Together with the certainty of death goes the indeterminacy of its When. Everyday being toward death evades this indeterminacy by conferring determinateness upon it — which cannot mean calculating the When of the demise's arrival; before such determinateness Dasein rather flees. Everyday concern determines for itself the indeterminacy of certain death by pushing before it the surveyable urgencies and possibilities of the nearest workaday. The exegesis of the "aber" is the section's second harvest: the adversative clause as das Man's own act of certainty-denial — and its mechanism specified with care: not calculation of the date (which is also fled — actuarial precision would bring the threat near) but the interposition of the surveyable: the day's business as a screen erected before the every-moment. The italic clause — possible at every moment — is the fifth predicate's ground, won, once again, from what the evasion labors to hide.

The twelfth unit couples the two characters: the covering of the indeterminacy, however, strikes the certainty along with it. Thus the ownmost possibility-character of death veils itself: certain, and therewith indeterminate — that is, possible at every moment. The two-line unit welds the pair: certainty and indeterminacy are one character seen twice — the "when" indeterminate precisely because the possibility is certain now and now and now; covering either covers both.

The thirteenth unit assembles the full concept. The complete interpretation of das Man's everyday talk about death, and of the way death stands into Dasein, led to the characters of certainty and indeterminacy. The full existential-ontological concept of death now lets itself be delimited in the following determinations: death, as the end of Dasein, is the ownmost, non-relational, certain and as such indeterminate, not-to-be-outstripped possibility of Dasein (die eigenste, unbezügliche, gewisse und als solche unbestimmte, unüberholbare Möglichkeit des Daseins). Death is, as Dasein's end, in the being of this being toward its end. The five-predicate formula is the chapter's doctrinal summit, and its provenance is its proof: three predicates from the care-structure (§ 50), two from the everyday evasion (§ 52) — the full concept assembled half from constitution, half from flight, exactly as the reversed method promised; and the closing sentence re-states § 48's relocation in the completed vocabulary: death is in the being-toward — the end's mode of being is Dasein's comportment.

The fourteenth unit pays the concept back into the wholeness-problem. The delimitation of the existential structure of being toward the end serves the working-out of a mode of being of Dasein in which it can, as Dasein, be whole. That even everyday Dasein already is toward its end — that is, constantly settles with its death, though "fleetingly" — shows that this end, closing off and determining being-whole, is nothing at which Dasein only finally arrives in its demise. In Dasein, as being toward its death, its own uttermost not-yet, to which all others are pre-ordered, is always already included. Hence the formal inference from the not-yet of Dasein — interpreted, moreover, ontologically inappropriately as outstanding — to its un-wholeness does not stand. The phenomenon of the not-yet, taken from the ahead-of-itself, is so little an instance against a possible existent being-whole — as is the care-structure in general — that this ahead-of-itself first makes such being toward the end possible at all. The problem of the possible being-whole of the being that we in each case are rightly stands, if care, as Dasein's basic constitution, "hangs together" with death as the uttermost possibility of this being. The paragraph discharges § 46's antinomy formally: the argument from the ahead to impossible wholeness is reversed at its hinge — the ahead-of-itself, far from barring the whole, is what makes being-toward-the-end possible; the uttermost not-yet is included in existence, not appended after it. Wholeness re-defined: not completion but the inclusion of the end in the being-toward — care and death "hanging together" as the problem's positive form.

The fifteenth unit audits and finds the modal gap. It remains questionable, however, whether this problem has already been sufficiently worked out. Being toward death grounds in care; as thrown being-in-the-world, Dasein is in each case already delivered over to its death. Being toward its death, it dies factically — and indeed constantly, so long as it has not come to its demise. Dasein dies factically: this says at the same time that in its being toward death it has always already decided itself in this or that way. Everyday falling evasion before death is an inauthentic being toward death; but inauthenticity has possible authenticity as its ground. Inauthenticity marks a mode of being into which Dasein can displace itself, and mostly always has displaced itself, but into which it need not necessarily and constantly displace itself: because Dasein exists, it determines itself, as the being it is, in each case from a possibility that it itself is and understands. The audit's yield is the modification-theorem enforced at the extreme (§ 38's seventeenth unit recalled by the ground-clause: Uneigentlichkeit hat mögliche Eigentlichkeit zum Grunde): the everyday evasion, being a decided mode of being-toward, presupposes the undecided possibility of the authentic mode — the flight's very possibility is the warrant for asking after what is fled toward.

The sixteenth unit poses the question of the chapter's last section: can Dasein also authentically understand its ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped, certain and as such indeterminate possibility — that is, hold itself in an authentic being toward its end? So long as this authentic being toward death is not set forth and ontologically determined, an essential lack clings to the existential interpretation of being toward the end. The five predicates are recited into the question itself: authenticity would be their unweakened understanding — and the lack-clause repeats § 45's audit-logic at the local scale: the concept incomplete until its authentic mode is included.

The closing unit fixes the register: authentic being toward death signifies an existentiell possibility of Dasein; this ontic potentiality-of-being must for its part be ontologically possible. What are the existential conditions of this possibility? How is it itself to become accessible? The double question hands § 53 its office with the § 49 discipline intact: conditions of possibility, not exhortation — the existential structure of a possible existentiell stance, whose factical enactment the analysis neither supplies nor demands.

##### § 53. Existential Projection of an Authentic Being toward Death

The opening unit lets the objection speak first. Factically, Dasein holds itself proximally and mostly in an inauthentic being toward death. How is the ontological possibility of an authentic being toward death to be "objectively" characterized, if in the end Dasein never comports itself authentically toward its end, or if this authentic being must, by its own sense, remain hidden from the others? Is the projection of the existential possibility of so questionable an existentiell potentiality-of-being not a fantastic undertaking? What is needed for such a projection to get beyond a merely poetizing, arbitrary construction? Does Dasein itself give directives for this projection? Can grounds of its phenomenal legitimacy be taken from Dasein itself? Can the ontological task now posed let predelineations be given to it from the analysis of Dasein carried out so far, predelineations that force its project onto a secure course? The battery is the § 49 scruple radicalized: the object may be nowhere exhibitable (rare, or essentially hidden) — so the projection must show its papers; the demand for Anweisungen from Dasein itself repeats § 29's protocol at the point of greatest strain.

The second unit answers with the double predelineation: the existential concept of death has been fixed, and therewith that toward which an authentic being toward the end is to be able to comport itself; furthermore, inauthentic being toward death has been characterized, and therewith it is prohibitively predelineated how authentic being toward death cannot be. With these positive and prohibitive directives the existential construction (Bau) of an authentic being toward death must let itself be projected. The method is stated with architectural candor: the concept (five predicates) supplies the toward-which, the evasion the via negativa — authenticity to be constructed as the exact photographic negative of the flight, each covering reversed into an uncovering.

The third unit fixes the frame: Dasein is constituted by disclosedness — that is, by a disposed understanding. Authentic being toward death cannot evade the ownmost, non-relational possibility, nor cover it over in this flight, nor re-interpret it for the common sense of das Man. The existential projection of an authentic being toward death must therefore set forth the moments of such a being that constitute it as an understanding of death — in the sense of a being toward this possibility that neither flees it nor covers it over. The triple negation (no evasion, no covering, no re-interpretation) is § 51's portrait inverted clause by clause; and the frame-word is understanding — the analysis will run through Verstehen's own structure (being toward a possibility), which the next four units calibrate.

The fourth unit clears the first wrong mode: concern for realization. It is first necessary to characterize being toward death as a being toward a possibility — indeed toward a distinguished possibility of Dasein itself. Being toward a possibility — toward something possible — can mean: being out for something possible, as attending to its actualization. In the field of the ready-to-hand and present-at-hand such possibilities constantly encounter: the attainable, masterable, feasible, and the like. The concernful being-out-for something possible has the tendency to annihilate the possibility of the possible by making it available. The concernful actualization of equipment (as producing, readying, readjusting, and so on) is, to be sure, always only relative, insofar as even the actualized still — and precisely — has the being-character of involvement: though actualized, it remains, as actual, something possible for..., characterized by an in-order-to. The present analysis is meant merely to make plain how concernful being-out-for comports itself toward the possible: not in a thematic-theoretical contemplation of the possible as possible, still less with regard to its possibility as such, but in such a way that it circumspectly looks away from the possible to the for-what-possible. The analysis banks a precise phenomenology of practical possibility: concern consumes possibility (realization as its annihilation-by-availability), yet never wholly (the § 15 involution: even the finished work stays a possible-for) — and above all, concern constitutively looks past the possible to its issue; a mode of being-toward-possibility that can therefore never hold the possible as such.

The fifth unit applies the exclusion: the being toward death in question manifestly cannot have the character of the concernful being-out for its actualization. For one thing, death, as something possible, is no possible ready-to-hand or present-at-hand thing, but a possibility of being of Dasein. And then: attending to the actualization of this possible would have to mean a bringing-about of the demise — whereby Dasein would precisely withdraw from itself the ground for an existing being toward death. The second clause settles, in passing and with cold exactness, the question of suicide's place in the analysis: self-killing is not the authentic relation to death but its abolition — actualizing the possibility destroys the being-toward it, removes the very ground of the comportment; the realization-schema refuted by its own limiting case.

The sixth unit clears the second wrong mode: brooding. If, then, being toward death does not mean an "actualization" of it, neither can it mean: dwelling with the end in its possibility. Such comportment would lie in the "thinking about death": this thinking ponders the possibility — when and how it might perhaps actualize itself. This brooding over death does not, to be sure, take from it its possibility-character entirely — it is still brooded over as coming — but it weakens it through a calculating wanting-to-dispose over death: death is, as something possible, to show as little as possible of its possibility. In being toward death, by contrast — if it is to disclose, understandingly, the characterized possibility as such — the possibility must be understood unweakened as possibility, developed (ausgebildet) as possibility, and, in the comportment toward it, endured (ausgehalten) as possibility. The exclusion is delicately weighed: the memento mori tradition — meditation on the hour and manner — is not evasion's opposite but its subtle continuation: brooding calculates, and calculation is the will to dispose, which shrinks the possible toward the manageable; against it the triple imperative (understand, cultivate, endure the possibility as possibility) states the authentic relation formally before naming it.

The seventh unit clears the third and nearest mode: expecting. Toward something possible in its possibility Dasein comports itself, however, in expecting (Erwarten): for one tensed toward it, something possible can encounter unhindered and undiminished in its "whether, or not, or finally after all." But does the analysis, with the phenomenon of expecting, not strike upon the same mode of being toward the possible that was already characterized in the concernful being-out-for? All expecting understands and "has" its possible with regard to whether and when and how it will actually be present-at-hand. Expecting is not only occasionally a looking-away from the possible toward its possible actualization, but essentially a waiting for this. Even in expecting lies a leaping-off from the possible and a gaining-footing in the actual, for which the expected is expected: from the actual and toward it, the possible is drawn, expectation-wise, into the actual. The refutation of the best candidate is the section's finest dialectical moment: expectation seems to hold the possible open (the suspense of "ob oder ob nicht" — § 30's fear-structure), yet its grammar convicts it — one expects the actualization; the possible is had from the actual and for it, the leap-off (Abspringen) landing always on the far side. Being-toward-death cannot be awaiting one's death: the modal revolution requires a comportment with no foothold in the actual at all.

The eighth unit coins it. Being toward the possibility, as being toward death, is to comport itself toward death so that death reveals itself, in this being and for it, as possibility. Such being toward possibility we grasp terminologically as anticipation — running-ahead into the possibility (Vorlaufen in die Möglichkeit). But does this comportment not harbor an approach toward the possible, and does not, with the nearness of the possible, its actualization emerge? This nearing, however, does not tend toward a concernful making-available of something actual; rather, in the understanding coming-nearer, the possibility of the possible becomes only "greater." The nearest nearness of being toward death as possibility is as far as possible from anything actual. The more unveiledly this possibility is understood, the more purely does the understanding penetrate into the possibility as the possibility of the impossibility of existence in general. Death, as possibility, gives Dasein nothing "to be actualized" and nothing that it, as actual, could itself be: it is the possibility of the impossibility of every comportment toward..., of every existing. In anticipation into this possibility, it becomes "ever greater" — that is, it reveals itself as such a possibility as knows no measure at all, no more or less, but signifies the possibility of the measureless impossibility of existence. By its essence, this possibility offers no hold for being tensed toward something, for "picturing to oneself" the possible actual and thereby forgetting the possibility. Being toward death, as anticipation into the possibility, first makes this possibility possible and sets it free as such. The coinage-paragraph is the chapter's peak, and its paradoxes are all load-bearing. Vorlaufen — running-ahead — is a nearing whose approach intensifies possibility instead of consuming it (the inverse of § 23's de-severance, whose nearing makes available): the closest closeness to death is maximal distance from the actual, because what is neared has no actual face at all. The formula deepens § 50's: possibility of the impossibility of every comportment — death as the possible end of the possible itself, hence measureless (no more-or-less, since every measure belongs to the field it would close), hence proof against the imagination (nothing to picture — every deathbed image is already the flight into the actual). And the closing sentence gives anticipation its transcendental office: it does not confront a ready possibility but first frees it — Ermöglichung, the making-possible of the possible, § 31's crowned modality enacted as a comportment.

The ninth unit converts anticipation into self-understanding and sets the run-through. Being toward death is anticipation into a potentiality-of-being of that being whose mode of being is anticipation itself. In the anticipatory unveiling of this potentiality-of-being, Dasein discloses itself to itself with regard to its uttermost possibility. But to project oneself upon one's ownmost potentiality-of-being means: to be able to understand oneself in the being of the being so unveiled — to exist. Anticipation proves to be the possibility of understanding the ownmost, uttermost potentiality-of-being — that is, the possibility of authentic existence. Its ontological constitution must become visible with the setting-forth of the concrete structure of anticipation into death. How is the phenomenal delimitation of this structure to be accomplished? Manifestly by determining the characters of the anticipatory disclosing that must belong to it so that it can become the pure understanding of the ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped, certain and as such indeterminate possibility — where understanding means primarily not: gaping at a sense, but understanding oneself in the potentiality-of-being that unveils itself in the projection. The reflexive twist opens the paragraph: the runner's mode of being is the running — anticipation is not an act Dasein performs upon death but a way Dasein is itself; hence its yield is self-disclosure, and "authentic existence" enters the book by this door, defined (not exhorted): the ability to understand oneself from the uttermost possibility. The program then locks in: the five predicates become five demands on the disclosing — the remainder of the section runs death's full concept through anticipation, predicate by predicate — with § 31's anti-intellectualist gloss posted at the threshold (self-understanding in a Seinkönnen, not the beholding of a meaning).

The tenth unit runs the first predicate. Death is Dasein's ownmost possibility. Being toward it discloses to Dasein its ownmost potentiality-of-being, in which the being of Dasein is at issue absolutely. Therein it can become manifest to Dasein that, in the distinguished possibility of itself, it remains torn away from das Man — that is, anticipating, it can in each case already have torn itself away. But the understanding of this "can" first unveils the factical lostness in the everydayness of the Man-self. The eigenste pays as liberation: what § 47 established (the undelegable) becomes, anticipated, a wresting-free — the reflexive verb doing the work: not "is torn" but "can tear itself away" — and the fine last clause keeps the order honest: only from the possibility of ownedness does the lostness first show as lostness; das Man diagnosed retroactively from the exit.

The eleventh unit runs the second — and guards the social bond. The ownmost possibility is non-relational. Anticipation lets Dasein understand that it has to take over, solely from itself, the potentiality-of-being in which its ownmost being is at issue absolutely. Death does not "belong" indifferently only to one's own Dasein: it claims this Dasein as individual (als einzelnes). The non-relationality of death, understood in anticipation, individualizes Dasein onto itself. This individualization is a way of the disclosing of the "Da" for existence; it makes manifest that all being alongside the attended and every being-with with others fails (versagt) when one's ownmost potentiality-of-being is at issue. Dasein can authentically be itself only when it makes this possible for itself of its own accord. But the failing of concern and solicitude by no means signifies a severing (Abschnürung) of these modes of Dasein from authentic being-a-self: as essential structures of Dasein's constitution, they belong to the condition of the possibility of existence in general. Dasein is authentically itself only insofar as it projects itself, as concernful being-alongside and solicitous being-with, primarily upon its ownmost potentiality-of-being — not upon the possibility of the Man-self. Anticipation into the non-relational possibility forces the anticipating being into the possibility of taking over its ownmost being of its own accord, from itself. The paragraph carries the heaviest guard in the chapter, and the reception's oldest error dies here if read: individuation is not isolation — world and others fail as sources of the ownmost, not as structures of existence; the authentic self is the concernful, solicitous being-in-the-world projected from the ownmost instead of from das Man (§ 31's fork re-run at the extreme). Anticipation individualizes the who of Mitsein, never abolishes the Mitsein — § 26 intact at the graveside.

The twelfth unit runs the third — and turns freedom social. The ownmost, non-relational possibility is not to be outstripped. Being toward it lets Dasein understand that, as the uttermost possibility of existence, self-surrender (Selbstaufgabe) stands imminent for it. Anticipation, however, does not evade the not-to-be-outstrippedness, as inauthentic being toward death does, but frees itself for it. The anticipatory becoming-free for one's own death liberates from lostness in the possibilities that accidentally press forward — and this in such a way that it first lets the factical possibilities that lie before the not-to-be-outstripped one be authentically understood and chosen. Anticipation discloses to existence, as its uttermost possibility, self-surrender, and thus shatters every rigidification upon the existence in each case attained. Anticipating, Dasein guards itself against falling behind itself and the understood potentiality-of-being — against "becoming too old for its victories" (Nietzsche). Free for the ownmost possibilities, determined from the end — that is, understood as finite — Dasein banishes the danger of misjudging, from its finite understanding of existence, the existence-possibilities of the others that outreach it, or of misinterpreting them and forcing them back upon its own, and so divesting itself of its ownmost factical existence. As non-relational possibility, death individualizes only in order — as not-to-be-outstripped — to make Dasein, as being-with, understanding for the potentiality-of-being of the others. Because anticipation into the not-to-be-outstripped possibility discloses along with it all the possibilities lying before it, there lies in it the possibility of an existentiell anticipating (Vorwegnehmen) of the whole Dasein — that is, the possibility of existing as whole potentiality-of-being. The paragraph is the chapter's ethical center, delivered as pure structure. The unoutstrippable, anticipated, converts into finite freedom: possibilities understood as finite can for the first time be chosen (against the drift of the accidental) — mortality as the condition of resolve, not its defeat; the Zarathustra-phrase ("too old for its victories") seals the anti-rigidification clause — anticipation as the standing solvent of every achieved self. And the social turn completes the eleventh unit's guard with a positive theorem: my finitude, owned, frees the others into theirs — no measuring of their possibilities by mine, no annexation; death individualizes in order to make Dasein, as Mitsein, understanding for the others' Seinkönnen — the sentence that refutes, in advance and by itself, every solipsist reading of the chapter. The closing clause banks the chapter's quarry: since the last possibility, anticipated, discloses all before it, the whole is reachable — existierendes Ganzsein as anticipatory, § 46's antinomy dissolved in the running-ahead.

The thirteenth unit runs the fourth — and re-ranks the evidences. The ownmost, non-relational, and not-to-be-outstripped possibility is certain. The way of being certain of it determines itself from the truth (disclosedness) corresponding to it. But the certain possibility of death discloses Dasein as possibility only in such a way that, anticipating toward it, Dasein makes this possibility possible for itself as its ownmost potentiality-of-being: the disclosedness of the possibility grounds in the anticipatory making-possible. Holding-oneself in this truth — being-certain of what is disclosed — claims anticipation all the more. The certainty of death cannot be computed from ascertainments of encountered cases of death; it does not hold itself at all within the truth of the present-at-hand — which encounters most purely in its discoveredness for a merely onlooking letting-be-encountered of beings in themselves. Dasein must first have lost itself to states of affairs — which can be care's own task and possibility — in order to win the pure objectivity, that is, the indifference, of apodictic evidence. If being-certain with regard to death does not have this character, that does not mean it is of a lower grade than apodictic evidence, but: it does not belong at all within the gradation-order of evidences about the present-at-hand. The certainty-analysis of § 52 completes itself here in a re-ranking of the whole theory of evidence: death-certainty is enacted, not registered (grounded in the anticipatory Ermöglichung — one is certain of it only running-ahead), while apodicticity is unmasked as an achievement of self-loss — the "purity" of theoretical evidence purchased by indifference, itself a possible task of care (§ 13's founded knowing recalled at its proudest claim); the closing clause performs § 52's regionalism: not lower on the scale — off the scale.

The fourteenth unit presses the re-ranking to its scandal. The holding-for-true of death — death is in each case only one's own — shows another kind, and is more original, than any certainty regarding an innerworldly encountered being or the formal objects; for it is certain of being-in-the-world. As such, it claims not merely one determinate comportment of Dasein, but Dasein in the full authenticity of its existence. In anticipation, Dasein can first make itself certain of its ownmost being in its not-to-be-outstripped wholeness. Hence the evidence of the immediate givenness of lived experiences, of the I, and of consciousness must necessarily lag behind the certainty enclosed in anticipation — not because the corresponding mode of apprehension would not be rigorous, but because it in principle cannot hold for true (disclosed) what at bottom it wants to "have there" as true: the Dasein that I myself am and, as potentiality-of-being, can authentically be only anticipating. The paragraph dethrones the Cartesian-Husserlian court of last appeal by its own standard: the cogito's evidence, and the phenomenological self-givenness of Erlebnisse, want the I "there" — present, had — but the I is a Seinkönnen, had only in the running-ahead; immanent evidence thus structurally misses its own object, and the surest certainty of the tradition lags behind the mortal one. Death-certainty claims the whole existence because what it certifies is not a proposition but me, whole.

The fifteenth unit runs the fifth — and names the mood. The ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped, and certain possibility is indeterminate with regard to its certainty. How does anticipation disclose this character of the distinguished possibility? How does the anticipatory understanding project itself upon a certain potentiality-of-being that is constantly possible, in such a way that the When in which the absolute impossibility of existence becomes possible remains constantly indeterminate? In anticipating toward the indeterminately certain death, Dasein opens itself for a constant threat arising from its own Da itself. Being toward the end must hold itself in this threat, and can so little dim it down that it must rather cultivate (ausbilden) the indeterminacy of the certainty. How is the genuine disclosing of this constant threat existentially possible? All understanding is disposed; mood brings Dasein before the thrownness of its "that-it-is-there." But the disposedness that can hold open the constant and absolute threat of itself, arising from Dasein's ownmost individualized being, is anxiety. In it, Dasein finds itself before the nothing of the possible impossibility of its existence; anxiety is anxious about the potentiality-of-being of the being so determined, and thus discloses the uttermost possibility. Because anticipation individualizes Dasein absolutely and, in this individualization of itself, lets it become certain of the wholeness of its potentiality-of-being, to this self-understanding of Dasein from its ground belongs the basic disposedness of anxiety. Being toward death is essentially anxiety (Das Sein zum Tode ist wesenhaft Angst). The unmistakable, though "only" indirect, attestation of this is given by the characterized being toward death itself, when it perverts anxiety into cowardly fear and, with the overcoming of this fear, makes known its cowardice before anxiety. The fifth predicate completes the structure by demanding a mood — understanding alone cannot hold the every-moment open; only attunement sustains a standing threat — and § 40's anxiety receives its final determination: the nothing it disclosed is now named the possible impossibility of existence, its object-structure and death's coinciding. The italic theorem welds chapter to chapter: authentic being-toward-death is not accompanied by anxiety but is it, essentially — and the closing turn is the evasion-argument's last performance: das Man's proud conquest of the fear it manufactured attests, indirectly and unmistakably, the anxiety beneath: courage over fear as cowardice before anxiety, § 51's Mut zur Angst inverted into diagnosis.

The sixteenth unit gathers the whole into one sentence. The characterization of the existentially projected authentic being toward death lets itself be summarized thus: anticipation reveals to Dasein the lostness in the Man-self and brings it before the possibility — primarily unsupported by concernful solicitude — of being itself; itself, however, in the passionate freedom toward death (Freiheit zum Tode), released from the illusions of das Man, factical, certain of itself, and anxious. The summary-sentence is the book's most famous, and each of its five determinations is a section-result compressed: passionate (the possibility endured, not contemplated — the sixth unit's Aushalten), released from the illusions of das Man (the tenth unit's wresting), factical (thrown — no leap out of the situation), certain of itself (the thirteenth and fourteenth units' enacted certainty), anxious (the fifteenth's essential mood) — freedom toward death as their unity: not freedom from death nor for dying, but the freedom that the anticipated end first gives, finite freedom as the chapter's last word. The Fürsorge-clause repeats the eleventh unit's precision — primarily unsupported, not unaccompanied.

The seventeenth unit draws back to the exact status of the result. All the relations, belonging to being toward death, to the full content of the characterized uttermost possibility of Dasein gather themselves in this: to reveal, unfold, and hold fast the anticipation constituted by them as the making-possible of this possibility. The existentially projecting delimitation of anticipation has made visible the ontological possibility of an existentiell authentic being toward death. But therewith emerges the possibility of an authentic potentiality-of-being-whole of Dasein — yet only as an ontological possibility. The existential projection of anticipation did indeed hold to the Dasein-structures won earlier, and let Dasein itself, as it were, project itself upon this possibility, without holding up to it a "contentful" existence-ideal or forcing one upon it "from outside." And nevertheless this existentially "possible" being toward death remains, existentielly, a fantastic exaction (eine phantastische Zumutung). The ontological possibility of an authentic potentiality-of-being-whole of Dasein means nothing so long as the corresponding ontic potentiality-of-being has not been demonstrated from Dasein itself. Does Dasein ever factically throw itself into such a being toward death? Does it even demand, from the ground of its ownmost being, an authentic potentiality-of-being determined by anticipation? The self-limitation is as rigorous as the construction was bold: the projection kept § 49's discipline (no ideal imposed from outside — Dasein let project itself), and precisely therefore its yield is only ontological; existentielly the whole edifice remains an exaction, fantastic, until Dasein's own testimony is produced. The two closing questions demand not examples but a structural witness: an attestation from the ground of Dasein's being.

The eighteenth unit names the required evidence: before answering these questions, it must be investigated to what extent at all, and in what way, Dasein gives testimony (Zeugnis), from its ownmost potentiality-of-being, of a possible authenticity of its existence — in such a way that it not only makes this known as existentielly possible, but demands it of itself. The demand is calibrated beyond mere possibility: the testimony must show authenticity demanded, not just available — the criterion that conscience, with its call and its "guilty!," will be shown to satisfy.

The closing unit sets the hinge to Chapter Two: the hovering question of an authentic being-whole of Dasein and of its existential constitution will be brought onto load-bearing phenomenal soil only when it can hold itself to a possible authenticity of Dasein's being attested by Dasein itself. If it succeeds in phenomenologically uncovering such an attestation and what is attested in it, then the problem arises anew: whether the anticipation of death, hitherto projected only in its ontological possibility, stands in an essential connection with the attested authentic potentiality-of-being. The chapter closes with its own incompleteness made into the next chapter's program — the § 45 architecture executing itself: death has given the whole (ontologically); conscience must give the witness (ontically-existentielly); and § 62 is silently reserved for their identity — whether Vorlaufen and the attested Seinkönnen are one. With this double question hanging, Chapter One ends: the existential concept of death complete, the freedom toward death projected, and the analysis, by its own strictest standards, still owing its proof.

#### Chapter Two: The Dasein-like Attestation of an Authentic Potentiality-of-Being, and Resoluteness

##### § 54. The Problem of the Attestation of an Authentic Existentiell Possibility

The opening unit states the evidentiary requirement. Sought is an authentic potentiality-of-being of Dasein that is attested by Dasein itself in its existentiell possibility. Beforehand, this attestation must itself let itself be found: if it is to "give Dasein to understand" itself in its possible authentic existence, it will have its root in Dasein's being — the phenomenological exhibition of such an attestation therefore includes in itself the demonstration of its origin from Dasein's constitution of being. The requirement is double, and both halves matter: the witness must exist (be findable as a phenomenon) and must be homegrown (rooted in the constitution, not imported) — § 53's closing demand converted into a two-part burden of proof that §§ 55–57 (origin) and §§ 58–60 (content) will discharge.

The second unit recalls the self and poses the modification-question. The attestation is to give an authentic potentiality-of-being-a-self to understand. With the expression "self" we answered the question of Dasein's who; Dasein's selfhood was determined formally as a way of existing — not as a present-at-hand being. The who of Dasein is mostly not I myself but the they-self; authentic being-a-self determines itself as an existentiell modification of das Man, which is to be delimited existentially. What lies in this modification, and what are the ontological conditions of its possibility? The unit re-opens § 27's deposit at its exact wording (authenticity as existentiell modification of das Man) and converts the formula into the chapter's question: the modification must now be given its structure and its conditions — the deferred check finally presented for payment.

The third unit derives the choice of the choice. With lostness in das Man, the nearest factical potentiality-of-being of Dasein — the tasks, rules, standards, the urgency and reach of concernful-solicitous being-in-the-world — is in each case already decided. Das Man has always already taken the seizing of these possibilities of being away from Dasein; it even conceals the silently accomplished disburdening from the express choice of these possibilities. It remains indeterminate who "authentically" chooses. This choiceless being-carried-along by nobody, whereby Dasein entangles itself in inauthenticity, can be reversed only in such a way that Dasein expressly fetches itself back to itself from the lostness in das Man. But this fetching-back must have that mode of being through whose omission Dasein lost itself into inauthenticity: the self-retrieval from das Man — the existentiell modification of the they-self into authentic being-a-self — must accomplish itself as the making-up of a choice (Nachholen einer Wahl). Making up the choice, however, means choosing this choice (Wählen dieser Wahl) — deciding for a potentiality-of-being from one's own self. In choosing the choice, Dasein first makes possible for itself its authentic potentiality-of-being. The derivation is a small masterpiece of structural symmetry: what was omitted (the choice — § 27's disburdening concealed even its own operation, so that no one ever chose the not-choosing) can be reversed only in its own currency; hence the doubled genitive — not choosing this or that, but choosing choice itself, retrieving the very dimension das Man confiscated. Kierkegaard's either/or (choosing oneself) is audibly near, re-cast as structure: the modification's form is the recovered choice.

The fourth unit adds the prior condition: but because Dasein is lost in das Man, it must first find itself. In order to find itself at all, it must be "shown" to itself in its possible authenticity: Dasein needs the attestation of a potentiality-of-being-a-self that, according to possibility, it in each case already is. The three-step (lost, hence to be found, hence needing to be shown) grounds the whole chapter's necessity: the choice cannot be made blind — the chooser must first be exhibited to himself — and the closing clause keeps the ontology straight: what is attested is no new acquisition but what Dasein possibly already is; the witness reveals, it does not confer.

The fifth unit names the witness — and the note dates the analysis. What is claimed in the following interpretation as such an attestation is familiar to Dasein's everyday self-interpretation as the voice of conscience (Stimme des Gewissens). That the "fact" of conscience is disputed, its function as a court of appeal for Dasein's existence variously assessed, and "what it says" manifoldly interpreted, could mislead one into abandoning the phenomenon only if this "dubiousness" of the factum, or of its interpretation, did not precisely prove that an original phenomenon of Dasein lies here. The following analysis places conscience into the thematic fore-having of a purely existential investigation with fundamental-ontological intent. The folded-in note records that these considerations, preceding and following, were communicated in thesis-form on the occasion of a public Marburg lecture on the concept of time (July 1924). The nomination follows § 42's logic once more: an everyday self-interpretation (the "voice") taken as pre-ontological testimony — and the inversion of the skeptical inference is characteristic: the endless quarrel over conscience (theological, psychological, moral) is read as the signature of an original phenomenon, contested precisely because it lies deep; disputedness as credential. The note quietly dates the conscience-death-time complex to the 1924 lecture "Der Begriff der Zeit" — the book's germ-cell acknowledged in small print.

The sixth unit draws the demarcations: first, conscience shall be traced back to its existential foundations and structures and made visible as a phenomenon of Dasein, holding fast to the constitution of being of this being won so far. The ontological analysis of conscience so begun lies before any psychological description and classification of conscience-experiences, just as it stands outside any biological "explanation" — that is, dissolution — of the phenomenon; but no smaller is its distance from a theological exegesis of conscience, or any employment of this phenomenon for proofs of God or for an "immediate" God-consciousness. The § 49 pattern repeats exactly: psychology (Erlebnis-classification), biology (explanation as dissolution — the word Auflösung recalling § 28's ban), and theology (including the era's Gottesbeweis-aus-dem-Gewissen and Schleiermacherian immediacy) each dismissed to its region; the existential analysis claims the ground floor beneath all three.

The seventh unit fixes the phenomenon's peculiar factuality. Nevertheless, even with this restricted investigation, its yield may be neither exaggerated nor placed under perverse claims and diminished. Conscience, as a phenomenon of Dasein, is no occurring and occasionally present-at-hand fact: it "is" only in Dasein's mode of being, and makes itself known as factum in each case only with and in factical existence. The demand for an "inductive empirical proof" of the "factuality" of conscience and of the legitimacy of its "voice" rests on an ontological perversion of the phenomenon — a perversion shared, however, by every superior critique of conscience as a merely occasionally occurring, not "universally ascertained and ascertainable fact." Under such proofs and counter-proofs the factum of conscience cannot be placed at all: that is no lack, but only the mark of its ontological difference from the environmentally present-at-hand. The paragraph applies § 43(c)'s guard-rail to conscience: believer and debunker convicted of the same category-mistake — both submit an existential to the evidential regime of things; the empirical prover and the "superior" critic (the psychologistic unmaskers of conscience) refuted in one clause, and the phenomenon's resistance to their tribunal booked as its ontological signature.

The eighth unit gives the formal thread and the theses. Conscience gives "something" to understand: it discloses. From this formal characteristic springs the directive to take the phenomenon back into Dasein's disclosedness — the basic constitution constituted by disposedness, understanding, falling, and discourse. The more penetrating analysis of conscience unveils it as call (Ruf); calling is a mode of discourse. The call of conscience has the character of the appeal (Anruf) to Dasein toward its ownmost potentiality-of-being-a-self, and this in the manner of the summons (Aufruf) to its ownmost being-guilty. The unit is the chapter in miniature: disclosure locates the phenomenon (Chapter Five's apparatus once more), discourse specifies it (call as Rede — § 34's non-vocal doctrine about to pay its greatest dividend), and the double formula — Anruf to the self, Aufruf to guilt — pre-announces §§ 56 and 58 respectively.

The closing unit maps the chapter: this existential interpretation lies necessarily far from everyday ontic common sense, though it sets forth the ontological foundations of what the vulgar interpretation of conscience has, within certain limits, always understood and brought to concept as a "theory" of conscience — hence the existential interpretation needs confirmation through a critique of the vulgar interpretation (§ 59). From the exhibited phenomenon it can be gathered how far it attests an authentic potentiality-of-being of Dasein. To the call of conscience corresponds a possible hearing; the understanding of the appeal unveils itself as wanting-to-have-a-conscience (Gewissenhabenwollen). In this phenomenon lies the sought existentiell choosing of the choice of a being-a-self, which, according to its existential structure, we call resoluteness (Entschlossenheit). The articulation is thereby pregiven: the existential-ontological foundations of conscience (§ 55); the call-character of conscience (§ 56); conscience as the call of care (§ 57); understanding of the appeal, and guilt (§ 58); the existential interpretation of conscience and the vulgar interpretation (§ 59); the existential structure of the authentic potentiality-of-being attested in conscience (§ 60). The map's chain of coinages — hearing, wanting-to-have-a-conscience, resoluteness — names the chapter's terminus in advance: Entschlossenheit as the structural form of the chosen choice; and the § 44 pattern governs the architecture again: construction first, derivation-cum-critique of the vulgar concept after (§ 59 as the truth-section's twin).

##### § 55. The Existential-Ontological Foundations of Conscience

The opening unit places the phenomenon and raises the stakes. The analysis of conscience departs from an indifferent finding: that it in some way gives someone something to understand. Conscience discloses, and belongs therefore in the circuit of the existential phenomena that constitute the being of the Da as disclosedness. The most general structures of disposedness, understanding, discourse, and falling have been laid apart; bringing conscience into this phenomenal context is not a schematic application of those structures to a special "case" of Dasein's disclosure — rather, the interpretation of conscience will not only carry the earlier analysis of the Da's disclosedness further, but grasp it more originally with regard to Dasein's authentic being. The methodological claim is worth pausing on: conscience is not an example filed under Chapter Five but that chapter's radicalization — disclosedness itself re-read from the side of authenticity; the analytic's spiral (§ 45's Wiederholung) enacted locally.

The second unit derives the necessity of the call. Through disclosedness, the being we call Dasein is in the possibility of being its Da; with its world it is there for itself — proximally and mostly in such a way that it has disclosed its potentiality-of-being to itself from the attended "world." The potentiality-of-being as which Dasein exists has in each case already abandoned itself to determinate possibilities — because it is a thrown being, whose thrownness is disclosed, more or less clearly and penetratingly, through being-attuned. To disposedness (mood) belongs equiprimordially understanding; thereby Dasein "knows" what it is at with itself, insofar as it has projected itself upon possibilities of itself or let these be pregiven to it, absorbed in das Man, through its public interpretedness. This pre-giving, however, is existentially made possible by the fact that Dasein, as understanding being-with, can hear on others (auf Andere hören). Losing itself into the publicness of das Man and its idle talk, it fails to hear (überhört) its own self in listening to the they-self. If Dasein is to be able to be fetched back from this lostness of failing-to-hear itself — and indeed by itself — then it must first be able to find itself: itself, which has failed to hear itself and fails to hear in listening-away to das Man. This listening-away must be broken — that is, the possibility of a hearing that interrupts it must be given to Dasein by Dasein itself. The possibility of such a breach lies in being appealed to without mediation. The call breaks the self-overhearing listening-away of Dasein to das Man if it, in accordance with its call-character, awakens a hearing that is in everything contrarily characterized in relation to the lost hearing: if the lost hearing is captivated by the "noise" of the manifold ambiguity of everyday "new" idle talk, the call must call noiselessly, unambiguously, without foothold for curiosity. That which, calling in this manner, gives to understand is conscience. The paragraph is the section's engine, and it runs entirely on § 34's acoustics. The everyday self is constituted by hearing (hörig to das Man — § 34's thralldom), so its lostness is an Überhören, a failing-to-hear-oneself in the listening-to-them; the remedy must therefore be auditory too — a counter-hearing awakened by a call — and the call's three negative marks are deduced, not described: noiseless (against Gerede's Lärm), unambiguous (against Zweideutigkeit), offering curiosity no foothold (against Neugier). Conscience is thus derived before it is named: whatever breaks the public audition must have exactly this form — the deduction of the voice from the structure of everyday deafness.

The third unit legitimates the call-language and gives its phenomenal marks. We grasp calling as a mode of discourse; discourse articulates intelligibility. Characterizing conscience as call is by no means only an "image," like, say, the Kantian representation of conscience as a court of justice. One must only not overlook that for discourse — and so for the call too — vocal utterance is not essential: every pronouncing and "calling out" already presupposes discourse. If the everyday interpretation knows a "voice" of conscience, what is thought is not so much an utterance — which is factically never findable — but "voice" is grasped as the giving-to-understand. In the call's disclosing tendency lies the moment of the jolt (Stoß), of the abrupt shaking-up (Aufrütteln). Called is from afar into afar (aus der Ferne in die Ferne). Reached by the call is the one who wants to be fetched back. The paragraph cashes § 34's deepest doctrine (Rede without Verlautbarung — silence and hearing as discourse's own modes) at the precise point where it is needed: the "voice" that never sounds is not a metaphor gone soft but discourse in its non-phonetic essence; Kant's tribunal is demoted to imagery while the call stands as structure. The two closing sentences are the section's poetry and its rigor at once: the distance-formula (from the far of uncanniness into the far of lostness, past all the near of the attended world) and the condition on reception — the call reaches the one who wants to be fetched back — which plants § 58's Gewissenhabenwollen and quietly concedes that the call can be refused.

The closing unit clears the faculty-psychology. With this characterization of conscience, only the phenomenal horizon for the analysis of its existential structure is outlined: the phenomenon is not compared with a call but understood, as discourse, from the disclosedness constitutive for Dasein. The consideration avoids from the outset the way that first offers itself for an interpretation of conscience: one traces conscience back to one of the soul's faculties — understanding, will, or feeling — or explains it as a mixed product of these. Facing a phenomenon like conscience, the ontological-anthropological insufficiency of a free-floating framework of classified soul-faculties or personal acts leaps to the eye. The appended note surveys the literature: besides the conscience-interpretations of Kant, Hegel, Schopenhauer, and Nietzsche, are to be noted Kähler's historical study and encyclopedia article, Ritschl's essay, and finally the just-published monograph of H. G. Stoker (1925, in Scheler's series) — a broadly conceived investigation that brings a rich manifold of conscience-phenomena to light, critically characterizes the possible ways of treating the phenomenon, and registers further literature (incomplete regarding the history of the concept). Stoker's monograph differs from the above existential interpretation already in its approach, and therewith in its results, notwithstanding many agreements: Stoker underestimates from the outset the hermeneutical conditions for a "description" of the "objectively actually subsisting conscience"; with this goes the blurring of the boundaries between phenomenology and theology — to the damage of both. Regarding the anthropological foundation of the investigation, which takes over Scheler's personalism, compare § 10 above. Stoker's monograph nevertheless signifies a noteworthy advance over the previous interpretation of conscience — but more through the comprehensive treatment of the conscience-phenomena and their ramifications than through the exhibition of the phenomenon's ontological roots. The closing polemic re-runs § 29's dossier-method (the tripartite psychology named as the standing evasion — conscience parceled to intellect, will, or feeling, or mixed from them), and the long Stoker-note is a model of the book's scholarly conscience: a rival treated at length, credited precisely (richness, critique, bibliography, advance), and faulted precisely — hermeneutical naivety (the "objectively subsisting conscience" as if description had no fore-structure: § 32 and § 45 applied as review-criteria), theology and phenomenology blurred to mutual damage, Scheler's personalism inherited with its § 10 liabilities.

##### § 56. The Call-Character of Conscience

The opening unit lays out discourse's grid: to discourse belongs the about-which that is talked over; discourse gives information about something, in a determinate regard; from the so-talked-over it draws what it, as this discourse, says — the said as such; in discourse as communication this becomes accessible to the co-Dasein of others, mostly by way of vocal utterance in language. The § 34 inventory (Worüber, Geredetes, Mitteilung, and — implicitly — Bekundung) is wheeled into position: the call, being discourse, must answer to each moment; the section proceeds through them as through a form.

The second unit fills the first slot. What is talked over — that is, appealed to (angerufen) — in the call of conscience? Manifestly Dasein itself. This answer is as incontestable as it is indeterminate: had the call so vague a target, it would remain at most an occasion for Dasein to attend to itself. But to Dasein belongs essentially that, with the disclosedness of its world, it is disclosed to itself, so that it always already understands itself. The call reaches Dasein in this everyday-average concernful always-already-understanding-itself; the they-self of concernful being-with with others is reached by the call. The refinement matters: the call's addressee is specified not abstractly (Dasein) but concretely in its everyday constitution — the Man-selbst is what picks up; the call must reach Dasein where it factically lives, in the midst of its public self-understanding, or reach nothing.

The third unit fills the whither — and stages the collapse of das Man. And to what is it appealed? To one's own self. Not to what Dasein counts for, can do, or attends to in the public with-one-another, nor to what it has seized upon, committed itself to, let itself be carried along by. The Dasein that it is, worldly understood, for others and for itself, is passed over (übergangen) in this appeal; the call to the self takes not the least notice of it. Because only the self of the they-self is appealed to and brought to hear, das Man collapses in itself (sinkt in sich zusammen). That the call passes over das Man and the public interpretedness by no means signifies that it does not also strike it: precisely in the passing-over, it thrusts the Man, avid for public regard, into insignificance. The self, however, robbed by the appeal of this lodging and hiding-place, is brought to itself by the call. The paragraph's central device is the Übergehen: the call defeats das Man not by argument but by disregard — passed over, the public self loses the only currency it has (regard), and collapses exactly as the world's involvements collapsed in anxiety (§ 40's sinkt in sich zusammen deliberately repeated: the call is anxiety's acoustic twin). The closing image — the they-self as Unterkunft und Versteck, lodging and hideout, of the self — compresses § 38's whole flight-analysis into two nouns.

The fourth unit guards the self so summoned: the they-self is appealed to toward the self — though not the self that can become an "object" of appraisal, not the self of the excited-curious and unrestrained dissection of its "inner life," not the self of an "analytic" gaping at psychic states and their backgrounds. The appeal to the self in the they-self does not force it upon itself into an inside, so that it should close itself off from the "external world": the call leaps over all that and disperses it, in order to appeal solely to the self — which is nevertheless not otherwise than in the manner of being-in-the-world. The triple negation is aimed with § 38's thirteenth unit behind it: introspective self-dissection was falling's refined form, so the call cannot be summoning to it — no inward turn, no psychic spelunking, no analytic Begaffung (the era's psychoanalysis within range of the word); the self called for is being-in-the-world, § 31's transparency rather than any interior — worldliness preserved at the very moment of individuation.

The fifth unit fills the said-slot with the section's scandal. But how are we to determine what is spoken in this discourse — what does conscience call to the one appealed? Strictly taken: nothing. The call asserts nothing, gives no information about world-events, has nothing to tell; least of all does it strive to open a "soliloquy" in the self appealed to. To the appealed self "nothing" is called to (zu-gerufen); rather, it is called forth (aufgerufen) to itself — to its ownmost potentiality-of-being. In accordance with its call-tendency, the call does not put the appealed self up for a "negotiation" (Verhandlung); rather, as summons to the ownmost potentiality-of-being-a-self, it is a calling-forth — a calling-forward (Vor-(nach-»vorne«-)Rufen) — of Dasein into its ownmost possibilities. The nothing is doctrine, not deflation: the call's content-lessness follows from § 34 (assertion is one derivative mode of discourse; the call is another, non-assertoric — a summons, not a report) and from § 31 (the possible, thematically stated, is destroyed as possible — so a call to possibility must state nothing). The bracketed etymology — the Vor-rufen glossed as calling toward the front, forward — quietly aligns conscience's direction with death's: the call calls forth as anticipation runs ahead; the two comportments already converging toward § 62.

The sixth unit gives silence its office. The call lacks any vocal utterance; it does not even first bring itself to words — and remains nevertheless nothing less than dark and indeterminate. Conscience speaks solely and constantly in the mode of keeping-silent (im Modus des Schweigens). Thus it not only loses nothing of perceptibility, but forces the Dasein appealed to and summoned into the reticence (Verschwiegenheit) of itself. The lack of a verbal formulation of what is called does not shove the phenomenon into the indeterminacy of a mysterious voice, but only indicates that the understanding of the "called" may not cling to the expectation of a communication. The paragraph redeems § 34's seventeenth unit at full value: silence as a positive mode of discourse, and here the mode — conscience the standing case of the reticent saying that gives most to understand; and the effect matches the medium: the silent call silences, forcing the hearer into Verschwiegenheit (resoluteness's discourse-mode, § 60, already sounding). The last clause disciplines the phenomenology: no secret message awaited — whoever listens for words has already re-routed the call into das Man's register.

The seventh unit secures the call's aim against its apparent vagueness. What the call discloses is nevertheless unambiguous, even though it may receive varying interpretation in the individual Dasein according to its possibilities of understanding. Over against the apparent indeterminacy of the call's content, the sure direction of its impact (Einschlagsrichtung) cannot be overlooked. The call needs no groping search for the one to be appealed, no distinguishing mark of whether he is the one meant or not. The "deceptions" in conscience arise not through a mis-calling (Sichver-rufen) of the call, but only from the way the call is heard — from the fact that, instead of being authentically understood, it is drawn by the they-self into a negotiating soliloquy and perverted in its disclosing tendency. The unit distributes error with juridical care: the call is infallible in address (the artillery-word Einschlagsrichtung: it lands on its man, unmistakably), fallible only in reception — all conscience's notorious "deceptions" relocated from the caller to the hearing, from the phenomenon to das Man's re-processing of it; the doctrine that keeps the attestation trustworthy while explaining its everyday distortions.

The eighth unit fixes the formula: it is to be held fast — the call, as which we characterize conscience, is the appeal to the they-self in its self; as this appeal, the summons of the self to its potentiality-of-being-a-self, and therewith a calling-forth of Dasein to its possibilities. The three-clause formula (Anruf an, Aufruf zu, Vorrufen auf) banks the section: whom (the they-self in its self), whereto (its own potentiality), in what direction (forward, into possibilities).

The closing unit poses the harder question: an ontologically sufficient interpretation of conscience is won only when it can be clarified not only who is called by the call, but who itself calls; how the one appealed stands to the caller; how this "relation" must be grasped ontologically as a connection of being. The pivot to § 57 is set with the quotation-marks doing the work: the caller-question, which every theology and psychology of conscience answered first (God, society, the super-ego avant la lettre), is here reached last and flagged as an ontological relation — the "Verhältnis" to be read as Seinszusammenhang, not as traffic between two entities.

##### § 57. Conscience as the Call of Care

The opening unit assembles the double indeterminacy. Conscience calls the self of Dasein forth from the lostness in das Man. The self appealed to remains indeterminate and empty in its what: what Dasein, proximally and mostly, understands itself as — in the interpretation from what it attends to — is passed over by the call; and yet the self is unambiguously and unmistakably reached. Not only is the one appealed meant by the call "without regard to person"; the caller too holds itself in a striking indeterminacy. To the questions after name, station, origin, and repute, it not only refuses answer but — though it in no way disguises itself in the call — gives not the least possibility of making it familiar for a "worldly" oriented understanding of Dasein. The caller of the call — this belongs to its phenomenal character — keeps every becoming-acquainted absolutely away from itself; it goes against the manner of its being to let itself be drawn into a considering and discussing. The peculiar indeterminacy and indeterminability of the caller is not nothing, but a positive distinction: it makes known that the caller is absorbed solely in the calling-forth to..., that it wants to be heard only as such and not further talked about. But is it then not appropriate to the phenomenon if the question who the caller is remains unasked? For the existentiell hearing of the factical call of conscience — yes; not, however, for the existential analysis of the facticity of the calling and the existentiality of the hearing. The paragraph's method is the § 40 conversion again: the caller's anonymity — the datum every interpretation rushes past — is held fast as a positive phenomenal character (no name, station, origin, repute: the four coordinates of das Man's world refused), and the closing distinction licenses the analysis without violating the phenomenon: existentielly the question falls silent before the call; existentially it must be posed.

The second unit refuses the easy identity: is there any necessity to pose the who-question expressly at all — does it not answer itself for Dasein as unambiguously as the question of the one appealed? Dasein calls, in conscience, itself. This understanding of the caller may be more or less awake in the factical hearing; ontologically, however, the answer that Dasein is caller and appealed at once is by no means sufficient. Is Dasein as appealed not "there" otherwise than as calling? Does perhaps the ownmost potentiality-of-being-a-self function as caller? The self-identity — the enlightened commonplace ("conscience is just yourself") — is granted ontically and refused as ontology in one breath: the sameness conceals a difference of mode ("da" otherwise as calling than as called) that is exactly what wants explaining; the vulgar answer stops where the problem begins.

The third unit fixes the phenomenal finding in three strokes. The call is precisely not and never planned by us ourselves, nor prepared, nor voluntarily accomplished: "it" calls (»es« ruft), against expectation and even against will. On the other hand, the call doubtless does not come from an other who is with me in the world. The call comes from me and yet over me (aus mir und doch über mich). The three sentences are the section's evidence-base, and the formula that closes them is the whole problem in seven words: involuntariness (no act of mine), immanence (no other's voice), transcendence-in-immanence (from me, yet over me) — the datum that every theory must save and that most theories, the next unit shows, destroy.

The fourth unit arraigns the two standard theories. This phenomenal finding is not to be interpreted away. It has indeed been taken as the point of departure for interpreting the voice as an alien power projecting into Dasein; proceeding in this direction of interpretation, one supplies the so-fixed power with a possessor, or takes the power itself as a person making itself known (God). Conversely, one attempts to reject this interpretation of the caller as expression of an alien power, and therewith to explain conscience away "biologically" altogether. Both interpretations spring too hastily over the phenomenal finding; the procedure is eased by the unspoken, guiding, ontologically dogmatic thesis: what is — that is, anything as factual as the call — must be present-at-hand; what does not let itself be objectively demonstrated as present-at-hand, is not at all. Theology and naturalism are convicted as the same mistake twice: both read the "over me" through the vorhanden-axiom — the theist reifying the transcendence into a person behind the voice, the biologist, unable to find the thing, explaining the voice away; supply a possessor or deny the phenomenon, one dogma with two signs. § 43's guard-rail (the uncritical idea of reality pressing in "again and again") catches its predicted quarry.

The fifth unit states the counter-method: over against this methodical over-hastiness, it is necessary not only to hold fast the phenomenal finding in general — that the call, coming from me and over me, reaches me — but also the ontological predelineation lying therein of the phenomenon as one of Dasein: the existential constitution of this being can offer the sole guiding thread for the interpretation of the mode of being of the "it" that calls. The rule is § 55's rooting-requirement enforced: the caller must be sought within Dasein's constitution — but, after the second unit, not in Dasein taken as flat self-identity: somewhere in the constitution there must be a "from me yet over me."

The sixth unit finds the place: thrownness. Does the analysis so far show a way to make the caller's mode of being ontologically intelligible? That the call is not expressly accomplished by me, that rather "it" calls, does not yet justify seeking the caller in a non-Dasein-like being. Dasein exists in each case factically; it is no free-floating self-projecting, but, determined by thrownness as factum of the being that it is, it was in each case already, and remains constantly, delivered over to existence. Dasein's facticity, however, differs essentially from the factuality of something present-at-hand: existing Dasein does not encounter itself as an innerworldly present-at-hand thing. Nor does thrownness cling to Dasein as an inaccessible character irrelevant to its existence: as thrown, it is thrown into existence; it exists as a being that, as it is and can be, has to be. The paragraph opens the answer by re-deepening § 29's Geworfenheit: the "es" of "es ruft" is to be housed in the throw — the dimension of Dasein that is mine without being my doing; delivered-over-ness as the structural original of "from me yet over me."

The seventh unit brings the throw to its mood. That it factically is may be hidden with regard to the why; the "that" itself, however, is disclosed to Dasein. The thrownness of this being belongs to the disclosedness of the Da and unveils itself constantly in the current disposedness. This brings Dasein, more or less expressly and authentically, before its "that it is and, as the being that it is, has to be, able-to-be." Mostly, however, the mood closes off the thrownness: Dasein flees before it into the relief of the supposed freedom of the they-self. This flight was characterized as flight before the uncanniness that at bottom determines individualized being-in-the-world. Uncanniness unveils itself authentically in the basic disposedness of anxiety and, as the most elemental disclosedness of thrown Dasein, places its being-in-the-world before the nothing of the world, before which it is anxious in anxiety about its ownmost potentiality-of-being. What if this Dasein, finding itself in the ground of its uncanniness, were the caller of the call of conscience? The paragraph gathers §§ 29, 38, and 40 into a single approach-run — the naked Daß, the flight, the Unheimlichkeit, anxiety's structure — and then poses the identification as a question, held in the subjunctive: the caller as Dasein in the ground of its uncanniness; the hypothesis earned, not asserted.

The eighth unit is the two-line verdict: nothing speaks against it — but for it, all the phenomena hitherto set forth in characterizing the caller and its calling. The brevity is confidence: the proof follows point by point.

The ninth unit runs the identification through the marks. The caller is in its who determinable by nothing "worldly": it is Dasein in its uncanniness, the original thrown being-in-the-world as not-at-home, the naked "that" in the nothing of the world. The caller is unfamiliar to the everyday they-self — something like an alien voice. What could be more alien to das Man, lost in the attended, manifold "world," than the self individualized upon itself in uncanniness, thrown into the nothing? "It" calls, and yet gives the concernfully curious ear nothing to hear that might be passed along and publicly talked over. But what should Dasein even report from the uncanniness of its thrown being? What else remains to it than its own potentiality-of-being, unveiled in anxiety? How else should it call than as summons to this potentiality-of-being, which alone is at issue for it? The verification is total and elegant: every "strange" feature of the call now falls out as necessity — the anonymity (the uncanny self has no worldly coordinates), the alienness (nothing is stranger to das Man than the individualized self: the "alien power" theory explained as das Man's accurate report of its own estrangement), the silence and contentlessness (the uncanny self has no events to report; its only "matter" is the Seinkönnen anxiety unveils), the summons-form (what else could it call to?). The theological datum — the voice as alien — is thus saved and relocated: alien indeed, but the alien is myself at bottom.

The tenth unit re-derives the call's mode and its cold accuracy: the call reports no occurrences; it calls even without any utterance. The call speaks in the uncanny mode of silence — and only because the call does not call the one appealed into the public idle talk of das Man, but calls him back out of it into the reticence of the existent potentiality-of-being. And whereupon rests the uncanny, by no means self-evident cold assurance with which the caller strikes the one appealed, if not on this: that Dasein, individualized upon itself in its uncanniness, is for itself absolutely unmistakable? What so radically deprives Dasein of the possibility of misunderstanding itself from elsewhere and mistaking itself, if not the forsakenness (Verlassenheit) in the deliverance to itself? The unit answers § 56's seventh (the sure Einschlagsrichtung) with its ground: the call cannot miss because, in uncanniness, there is nothing else left to hit — individuation strips every alias; the marksman's certainty is the forsakenness itself. The silence, likewise, is functional: a call out of the public cannot use the public's medium.

The eleventh unit crowns the identification. Uncanniness is the — though everyday covered — basic kind of being-in-the-world. Dasein itself calls, as conscience, from the ground of this being.
