The "it calls me" is a distinguished discourse of Dasein. The call, attuned by anxiety, first makes possible for Dasein the projection of itself upon its ownmost potentiality-of-being. The call of conscience, existentially understood, first makes known what was earlier merely asserted: uncanniness pursues Dasein and threatens its self-forgotten lostness. The paragraph settles the "es ruft" without dissolving it: the impersonal pronoun is kept — a distinguished discourse of Dasein, spoken not by the ego but from the ground — and § 40's IOU (the claim that uncanniness pursues Dasein, there "merely asserted") is formally redeemed: conscience is the pursuit, uncanniness's standing voice in everydayness.

The twelfth unit gives the section its title-formula. The sentence "Dasein is caller and appealed at once" has now lost its formal emptiness and self-evidence. Conscience reveals itself as the call of care: the caller is Dasein, in thrownness (already-being-in...) anxious about its potentiality-of-being; the one appealed is this same Dasein, called forth to its ownmost potentiality-of-being (ahead-of-itself...); and Dasein is called forth, by the appeal, out of the falling into das Man (already-being-alongside the attended world). The call of conscience — that is, this itself — has its ontological possibility in the fact that Dasein, in the ground of its being, is care. The mapping is exact and completes the § 50 pattern's twin: as death was run through care's three moments, so conscience — caller from facticity, call toward existence, calling-out-of falling — one structure, three offices; the identity-with-difference of the second unit resolved (caller and called the same being in different moments of its care), and the "from me yet over me" grounded: the throw is mine and over me. Care calls.

The thirteenth unit dismisses the alien powers and locates the theories' root. So there is no need of refuge in non-Dasein-like powers — especially as recourse to them so little clarifies the uncanniness of the call that it rather annihilates it. Does the ground of the devious "explanations" of conscience not lie, in the end, in this: that one has taken the gaze too short already for fixing the phenomenal finding of the call, and silently presupposed Dasein in an accidental ontological determinateness or indeterminateness? Why seek information from alien powers before making sure that, in the approach of the analysis, Dasein's being has not been assessed too low — that is, posited as a harmless, somehow occurring subject equipped with personal consciousness? The critique reaches its economical depth: God is invoked over conscience because the self was undersold — a harmless subject cannot contain the "over me," so transcendence must be outsourced; raise the ontology of the self (thrown, uncanny, care) and the phenomenon houses itself. The theological reading annihilates the very uncanniness it means to honor, domesticating the alien into a familiar Person.

The fourteenth unit exposes the "objectivity" of the power-thesis as flight: and yet, in interpreting the caller — who, worldly seen, is "nobody" — as a power, there seems to lie the unprejudiced acknowledgment of something "objectively findable." But rightly seen, this interpretation is only a flight before conscience — an escape-route of Dasein, along which it steals away from the thin wall that, as it were, separates das Man from the uncanniness of its being. The named interpretation gives itself out as acknowledgment of the call in the sense of a "universally" binding voice that speaks "not merely subjectively"; more: this "universal" conscience is heightened to a "world-conscience," which, by its phenomenal character, is an "it" and "nobody" — hence, after all, that which speaks there in the individual "subject" as this indeterminate. The image of the thin wall (die dünne Wand) is among the book's finest: das Man dwells one partition from its own uncanniness, and the pious "objectification" of conscience is the sound of someone tiptoeing away from it. The Weltgewissen (the era's idealist upgrade — a universal moral voice) is caught in self-contradiction: advertised as more-than-subjective, it is phenomenally an "it" and "nobody" — the anonymity smuggled back at the top.

The fifteenth unit turns the knife: but this "public conscience" — what is it other than the voice of das Man? Dasein can arrive at the dubious invention of a "world-conscience" only because conscience, in ground and essence, is in each case mine — and this not only in the sense that in each case the ownmost potentiality-of-being is appealed to, but because the call comes from the being that I in each case myself am. The exposure is complete: the universal conscience unmasked as das Man's own voice given metaphysical rank — publicness canonized — and the double mineness (mine as addressee, mine as source) is fixed as the phenomenon's essence, which every "world-conscience" precisely deletes.

The sixteenth unit settles subjectivity and objectivity. With the foregoing interpretation of the caller — which purely follows the phenomenal character of the calling — the "power" of conscience is not diminished and made "merely subjective." On the contrary: only so do the inexorability and unambiguousness of the call become free. The "objectivity" of the appeal first receives its right through the interpretation's leaving it its "subjectivity" — which, to be sure, denies the they-self its dominion. The chiasmus is § 44(c)'s truth-argument replayed for conscience: objectivity through rightly-understood subjectivity — the call binding because mine (the thrown self cannot be haggled with), not despite it; and the parenthesis prices the doctrine: the "subjectivity" that grounds the call's authority is precisely not the they-self's — mineness against publicness, not privacy against validity.

The seventeenth unit lets the natural experience object. Nevertheless, against the accomplished interpretation of conscience as call of care, the counter-question will be posed: can an exegesis of conscience hold water that removes itself so far from "natural experience"? How is conscience to function as summoner to the ownmost potentiality-of-being, when proximally and mostly it only reproves and warns? Does conscience speak so indeterminately-emptily about an ownmost potentiality-of-being — and not rather determinately and concretely, with reference to failures and omissions that have occurred or are intended? Does the asserted appealing stem from the "bad" conscience or the "good"? Does conscience give anything positive at all — does it not function rather only critically? The objection is assembled from the phenomenon's entire everyday inventory — reproof, warning, the determinate misdeed, the good/bad polarity, the essentially critical office — and given its full voice: the existential call, contentless and forward-directed, seems to fit nothing anyone has ever "heard."

The eighteenth unit grants the right and stays the verdict. The right of such reservations is not to be contested. From an interpretation of conscience it can be demanded that "one" recognize in it the phenomenon in question as it is everyday experienced. But satisfying this demand does not mean, in turn, acknowledging the vulgar ontic understanding of conscience as the first court of appeal for an ontological interpretation. On the other hand, the reservations adduced are premature so long as the analysis they concern has not been brought to its goal: hitherto it was only attempted to lead conscience back, as a phenomenon of Dasein, to the ontological constitution of this being — as preparation for the task of making conscience intelligible as an attestation, lying in Dasein itself, of its ownmost potentiality-of-being. The double ruling is § 59 in advance: recognition owed, jurisdiction denied — the everyday experience a datum the interpretation must save, never the tribunal before which it stands; and the analysis's own incompleteness is entered on the record: the guilt-content (§ 58) and the vulgar critique (§ 59) are still outstanding, so the objection has fired early.

The nineteenth unit derives the necessity of the hearing-analysis. What conscience attests comes to full determinateness only when it is sufficiently clearly delimited what character the hearing genuinely corresponding to the calling must have. The authentic understanding "following" the call is not an addendum merely attaching itself to the conscience-phenomenon, an occurrence that may set in or fail to appear: only from the understanding of the appeal, and in one with it, does the full conscience-experience let itself be grasped. If caller and appealed are in each case one's own Dasein itself at once, then in every failing-to-hear the call, in every mis-hearing of oneself, lies a determinate mode of being of Dasein. A free-floating call, upon which "nothing follows," is, existentially seen, an impossible fiction; "that nothing follows" means, Dasein-like, something positive. The paragraph completes the phenomenon's structure from § 34's side: to discourse belongs hearing — the call is whole only with its reception — and the identity of caller and called yields the sharp corollary: since I am both ends, even deafness is a deed; the ignored conscience is not a call that failed but a mode of my being (the Überhören of § 55 now weighted as positive comportment). No verdict "in absentia" is possible where the absent one is the court.

The closing unit hands the analysis its next word: so only the analysis of the understanding of the appeal can lead to the explicit discussion of what the call gives to understand. But only with the preceding general ontological characterization of conscience is the possibility given of conceiving existentially the "guilty!" called in conscience: all experiences and exegeses of conscience agree that the "voice" of conscience somehow speaks of "guilt" (Schuld). The transition names the one point where every party to the conscience-quarrel — theological, Kantian, psychological, vulgar — concurs: the voice speaks of guilt; and precisely this unanimous datum, the "schuldig!", is what § 58 must now win back from its moral and juridical encrustations into an existential concept. With the guilt-question posed, the call's formal analysis is complete: caller identified (care from uncanniness), addressee (the they-self in its self), content (nothing — a summons forward), mode (silence), and now the one word the silence says.

##### § 58. Understanding of the Appeal, and Guilt

The opening unit fixes the level of the analysis. To grasp phenomenally what is heard in understanding the appeal, one must return anew to the appeal. Appealing to the they-self means calling the ownmost self forth to its potentiality-of-being — and indeed as Dasein, that is, as concernful being-in-the-world and being-with with others. The existential interpretation of that to which the call calls forth cannot, if it rightly understands its methodical possibilities and tasks, want to delimit any concrete single possibility of existence: what can and will be fixed is not what is in each case called existentielly into the respective Dasein, but what belongs to the existential condition of the possibility of the in-each-case factical-existentiell potentiality-of-being. The register-guard is posted first: the analysis names no vocation — conscience's concrete counsel is each Dasein's own affair; ontology delimits the condition, never the content. And the parenthetical reminder (the Seinkönnen called to is worldly and with-others) extends § 53's eleventh unit into the conscience-chapter: the summons is to no worldless self.

The second unit gives the criterion of authentic hearing: the existentiell-hearing understanding of the call is the more authentic, the more non-relationally Dasein hears and understands its being-appealed, the less what one says, what is fitting and accepted, perverts the call's sense. And what lies essentially in the authenticity of understanding the appeal — what is in each case essentially given to understand in the call, even if not always factically understood? The comparative grammar (um so eigentlicher, je...) makes authenticity of hearing a matter of degree along one axis: insulation from das Man's acoustic interference — the death-predicate unbezüglich transferred to reception.

The third unit adds the whence and completes the call's form. We have already assigned the answer with the thesis: the call "says" nothing that could be talked over; it gives no knowledge of occurrences. The call points Dasein forward to its potentiality-of-being, and this as call out of uncanniness. The caller is indeterminate — but the whence from which it calls does not remain indifferent to the calling: this whence — the uncanniness of thrown individuation — is called along in the calling, that is, co-disclosed. The whence of the calling, in the calling-forth to..., is the whither of the calling-back. The call gives no ideal, universal potentiality-of-being to understand; it discloses it as the in-each-case individualized potentiality of the respective Dasein. The call's disclosure-character is fully determined only when we understand it as the calling-back that calls forth (vorrufender Rückruf). The paragraph completes the call's vector-geometry: the origin is part of the message (uncanniness co-disclosed — the caller's address sounds in the call), and the two directions close into one figure — whence = whither, the call-forward is a call-back — the formula vorrufender Rückruf minted here and cashed at the section's center as the temporal double-structure of care itself. The anti-idealist clause guards it: no universal Seinkönnen, only the individualized one — conscience never speaks in maxims.

The fourth unit turns to the unanimous datum and disciplines its use. Is not the question of what the call says answered more easily and surely by the "simple" reference to what is heard, or failed to be heard, throughout all conscience-experiences: that the call addresses Dasein as "guilty," or, as warning conscience, refers to a possible "guilty," or, as "good" conscience, confirms a "conscious of no guilt"? If only this "unanimously" experienced "guilty" were not so utterly variously determined in the conscience-experiences and interpretations! And even if the sense of this "guilty" could be grasped unanimously, the existential concept of this being-guilty lies in the dark. Yet if Dasein addresses itself as "guilty," whence should the idea of guilt be drawn if not from the interpretation of Dasein's being? But the question rises anew: who says how we are guilty and what guilt means? The idea of guilt cannot be arbitrarily thought up and forced upon Dasein. If an understanding of the essence of guilt is possible at all, this possibility must be predelineated in Dasein. How are we to find the trace that can lead to the unveiling of the phenomenon? All ontological investigations of phenomena like guilt, conscience, death must begin with what the everyday interpretation of Dasein "says" about them. In Dasein's falling mode of being lies at once that its interpretation is mostly inauthentically "oriented" and does not reach the "essence," because the originally appropriate ontological question-formulation remains foreign to it. But in every mis-seeing there is co-revealed a directive toward the original "idea" of the phenomenon. Whence, however, do we take the criterion for the original existential sense of the "guilty"? From this: that this "guilty" turns up as predicate of the "I am." Does what is understood in inauthentic interpretation as "guilt" perhaps lie in the being of Dasein as such — in such a way that, insofar as it in each case factically exists, it is also guilty? The paragraph is the section's methodological charter, and its two rules deserve isolation. First, the hermeneutics of the vulgar: begin with what everydayness says (there is no other entry), expect distortion (falling guarantees it), and read the mis-seeing itself as a pointer — § 44(b)'s semblance-doctrine turned into a research instrument. Second, the criterion: the "guilty" appears as a predicate of the I am — grammar again as fossil ontology: whatever guilt is, it is said of being, not of deeds; the section's destination (guilt as a determination of Dasein's being as such) extracted from the copula of the everyday confession.

The fifth unit is the two-sentence discipline: appeal to the unanimously heard "guilty" is therefore not yet the answer to the question of the existential sense of what is called in the call; this must first come to its concept, in order to make intelligible what the called "guilty" means, and why and how it is perverted in its signification by the everyday interpretation. The consensus is data, not doctrine — the concept owed, and the distortion to be explained, not merely corrected.

The sixth unit opens the semantic ledger: debts. Everyday common sense takes "being-guilty" proximally in the sense of "owing," "having something on the slate with someone": one is to give back to the other something on which he has a claim. This "being-guilty" as "having debts" is a way of being-with with others in the field of concern — as procuring, supplying; modes of such concern are also withdrawing, borrowing, withholding, taking, robbing — failing in some way to satisfy the possessory claim of others. Being-guilty of this kind is related to the attendable. The German Schuld does double duty (debt/guilt), and the analysis exploits the accident philosophically: the first stratum of the word is pure Besorgen — obligation as traffic in the ready-to-hand, breach as failed procurement — guilt's everyday home the ledger.

The seventh unit adds the second sense: being-guilty then has the further signification of "being guilty of" — being cause, author of something, or "being occasion" for something. In the sense of this "having guilt" for something, one can "be guilty" without owing anything to another or becoming "indebted"; conversely, one can owe another something without being oneself to blame for it — another can "incur debts" with others "for me." The second stratum is causality — authorship — and the two senses are shown logically independent by the two counterexamples: blameless debt, debtless blame; the vulgar concept already a compound.

The eighth unit compounds them and distills the formal concept. These vulgar significations of being-guilty as "having debts with..." and "having guilt for..." can go together and determine a comportment we call "making oneself guilty" — that is, by having guilt for a having-debts, to violate a right and make oneself punishable. But the demand one fails to satisfy need not be related to possession; it can regulate public being-with-one-another in general. The "making oneself guilty" so determined, as violation of right, can at the same time have the character of a "becoming guilty toward others" (Schuldigwerden an Anderen): this happens not through the violation of right as such, but through my having guilt for the other's being endangered in his existence, misled, or even broken. This becoming-guilty toward others is possible without violation of "public" law. The formal concept of being-guilty in the sense of having-become-guilty toward another can thus be determined: being-ground for a lack in the Dasein of an other, in such a way that this being-ground itself determines itself as "lacking" from its for-which. This lackingness is the failure to satisfy a demand that addresses the existing being-with with others. The paragraph climbs the ladder to its top ontic rung: from debt through liability to the deepest everyday sense — becoming guilty toward another's existence (endangered, misled, broken: three verbs that carry a whole ethics of Mitsein), expressly severed from legality; and from it the formal skeleton is read off: Grundsein für einen Mangel — being-the-ground-of-a-lack — the two components (ground; not) that the existential concept will keep while discarding the lack.

The ninth unit brackets the demand-question and dismisses the quality-answer. Let it remain open how such demands arise and how, on the basis of this origin, their demand- and law-character must be conceived. In any case, being-guilty in the last-named sense, as violation of a "moral demand," is a mode of being of Dasein — as are being-guilty as making oneself punishable, having debts, and every "having guilt for": these too are comportments of Dasein. If one takes "laden with moral guilt" as a "quality" of Dasein, little is said thereby; on the contrary, it only becomes manifest that this characterization does not suffice to demarcate ontologically this kind of "determinateness of being" from the previous comportments. The concept of moral guilt is, indeed, so little clarified ontologically that interpretations of the phenomenon could become and remain dominant which include in its concept the idea of deserving punishment, indeed even of having-debts, or determine it from these ideas — whereby the "guilty" is again thrust off into the district of concern, of the balancing settlement of claims. The bracket (whence moral demands — the entire question of the origin of normativity deferred, a deferral GA 24 and the later work never fully close) is honest bookkeeping; the polemic that follows names the standing corruption: moral guilt theorized through punishability and debt — Nietzsche's Genealogy (Schuld from Schulden) hovering unnamed — which re-books existence into the ledger.

The tenth unit states the required inversion in one sentence: the clarification of the guilt-phenomenon — which is not necessarily related to having-debts and violation of right — can succeed only if beforehand the being-guilty of Dasein is asked after in principle: the idea of "guilty" conceived from Dasein's mode of being. The direction of derivation reversed: not Dasein's guilt from the ledger's, but the ledger's from Dasein's.

The eleventh unit performs the formalization. To this end the idea of "guilty" must be formalized so far that the vulgar guilt-phenomena related to concernful being-with fall away. The idea of guilt must not only be lifted beyond the district of calculating concern, but detached from the relation to an ought and a law against which, failing, someone loads guilt upon himself; for here too guilt is necessarily still determined as lack — the missing of something that ought to be and can be. Missing, however, means not-being-present-at-hand: lack, as the not-presence-at-hand of an obligated, is a determination of being of the present-at-hand. In this sense, nothing can essentially be lacking in existence — not because it would be perfect, but because its character of being remains distinct from all presence-at-hand. The double detachment is radical: not only debt but the ought itself is stripped away — because "ought" still measures by lack, and lack is a thing-category (the missing piece, § 48's Ausstand in moral dress); the closing sentence has the book's signature severity: existence cannot lack anything, not from perfection but from category — a being of possibility has no missing pieces.

The twelfth unit distills the existential concept. Nevertheless, in the idea of "guilty" lies the character of the not (Nicht). If the "guilty" is to be able to determine existence, the ontological problem arises of clarifying existentially the not-character of this not. Further, to the idea of "guilty" belongs what expresses itself indifferently in the concept of guilt as "having guilt for": being-ground for... The formal existential idea of the "guilty" we therefore determine thus: being-ground for a being determined by a not — that is, being-ground of a nullity (Grundsein einer Nichtigkeit). If the idea of the not lying in the existentially understood concept of guilt excludes relation to a possible or demanded present-at-hand — if Dasein is not to be measured at all against anything present-at-hand or valid that it is not itself, or that is not in its way (does not exist) — then the possibility falls away of reckoning what is thus ground, with regard to its being-ground for a lack, as itself "lacking." From a Dasein-like "caused" lack — the non-fulfillment of a demand — one cannot simply reckon back to the lackingness of the "cause": the being-ground for... need not have the same not-character as the privativum grounding in it and springing from it; the ground need not first receive its nullity back from what it grounds. But therein lies: being-guilty does not first result from an indebtedness (Verschuldung); rather, the latter first becomes possible "on the ground" of an original being-guilty. Can such a thing be exhibited in Dasein's being, and how is it existentially possible at all? The formalization keeps exactly the two moments the eighth unit isolated — the ground and the not — and discards the lack: Grundsein einer Nichtigkeit, with the not now a constitutional character, not a deficit. The logical lemma that follows (ground and grounded may differ in their not-character; the ground need not import its nullity from its effects) is what licenses the great inversion of the closing sentence: guilt before guilts — indebtedness founded on being-guilty, the moral order's ontological precedence reversed; and the question that ends the unit hands the derivation its task.

The thirteenth unit begins the derivation: the throw. The being of Dasein is care; it comprises in itself facticity (thrownness), existence (projection), and falling. Being, Dasein is thrown — not brought into its Da by itself; being, it is determined as potentiality-of-being that belongs to itself and yet has not given itself to itself as itself. Existing, it never gets back behind its thrownness, so as ever expressly to release this "that it is and has to be" from its own being-a-self and lead it into the Da. Thrownness, however, does not lie behind it as an event that factually befell and fell away again — something that happened to it; rather Dasein is constantly, as long as it is, as care, its "that." As this being, delivered over to which it can exist solely as the being that it is, it is, existing, the ground of its potentiality-of-being. Though it has not itself laid the ground, it rests in its weight, which mood makes manifest to it as burden. The paragraph is § 29's thrownness thought to its aporia: the ground is mine (I am it, existing) and not mine (never laid by me, never retrievable — the nie zurück behind the throw); the throw not a past event but a standing tense of care; and § 29's Last returns with its ontological receipt — the burden mood discloses is the weight of an unfounded ground.

The fourteenth unit states the bind in three lines: and how is it this thrown ground? Solely by projecting itself upon possibilities into which it is thrown. The self, which as such has to lay the ground of itself, can never become master of it — and yet, existing, has to take over being-the-ground. To be its own thrown ground is the potentiality-of-being at issue for care. The tightest formulation in the book of finite existence: obligated to what cannot be mastered — the ground to be laid that was never mine to lay, taken over in the only currency available: projection upon thrown possibilities.

The fifteenth unit derives the first not. Being-ground — that is, existing as thrown — Dasein constantly lags behind its possibilities: it is never existent before its ground, but in each case only from it and as it. Being-ground accordingly means: never to be master of one's ownmost being from the ground up. This not belongs to the existential sense of thrownness: being-ground, it is itself a nullity of itself. Nullity by no means signifies not-being-present-at-hand, not-subsisting, but means a not that constitutes this being of Dasein — its thrownness. The not-character of this not determines itself existentially: being a self, Dasein is the thrown being as self — released from the ground not through itself but to itself, in order to be as this ground. Dasein is not itself the ground of its being, insofar as the ground first springs from its own projection; but as being-a-self it is the being of the ground (das Sein des Grundes). The ground is always only ground of a being whose being has to take over being-the-ground. The first nullity is minted with maximal care: never before one's ground, never master of it from the bottom — existence structurally in arrears to itself; and the guard is doubled (nullity is not non-subsistence; the self is released to itself, not by itself) so that the formula can stand: Dasein is not the ground of its being but the being of the ground — the finest chiasmus in the book, existence as the having-to-be of an unowned origin.

The sixteenth unit derives the second not. Dasein is its ground existing — that is, in such a way that it understands itself from possibilities and, so understanding itself, is the thrown being. But therein lies: being-able-to-be, it stands in each case in one or another possibility; constantly it is not another, and has waived it in the existentiell projection. Projection is not only, as in each case thrown, determined by the nullity of being-ground; as projection it is itself essentially null (nichtig). This determination again by no means signifies the ontic property "unsuccessful" or "worthless," but an existential constitutive of the being-structure of projecting. The nullity meant belongs to Dasein's being-free for its existentiell possibilities: freedom, however, is only in the choice of the one — that is, in bearing the not-having-chosen and not-also-being-able-to-choose the others. The second nullity is choice's shadow: every projection is a waiving — to be one possibility is constantly not to be the others — and the exclusions are constitutive, not regrettable (the guard against "unsuccessful, worthless" keeps the register ontological). The closing definition of freedom is among the book's greatest sentences: freedom is only in choosing the one, that is, in bearing not having chosen and not being able also to choose the others — finite freedom as the carried weight of the foregone; Kierkegaard's either/or given its ontology.

The seventeenth unit totals the structure. In the structure of thrownness as in that of projection lies essentially a nullity; and it is the ground for the possibility of the nullity of inauthentic Dasein in falling, as which it in each case already factically is. Care itself is in its essence thoroughly permeated by nullity. Care — the being of Dasein — accordingly means, as thrown projection: the (null) being-ground of a nullity (das (nichtige) Grund-sein einer Nichtigkeit). And that means: Dasein is as such guilty — if indeed the formal existential determination of guilt as being-ground of a nullity rightly stands. The summation runs the not through all three care-moments (thrownness null, projection null, falling's nullity grounded in both) and closes the circuit with the twelfth unit's formula: care = null ground of a nullity = the formal concept of guilt — therefore Dasein is guilty as such, by constitution; the ontological Schuldigsein demonstrated, before and beneath every deed.

The eighteenth unit fences the result: existential nullity by no means has the character of a privation, of a lack over against a posted ideal not attained in Dasein; rather, the being of this being is, before everything it can project and mostly attains, as projecting, already null. The nullity therefore also does not turn up occasionally at Dasein, to cling to it as a dark quality that it, far enough advanced, could remove. The double guard bars the two waiting misreadings: no ideal-shortfall (nullity precedes every standard — the perfectionist reading dead) and no removable stain (no progress retires it — the therapeutic and the Pelagian readings dead together); § 38's fourth-unit pattern (no fall from purity) repeated for guilt.

The nineteenth unit confesses the open depth. Nevertheless, the ontological sense of the notness of this existential nullity remains obscure — but this holds of the ontological essence of the not in general. Ontology and logic have, to be sure, exacted much of the not, and thereby made its possibilities visible stretch by stretch, without unveiling it itself ontologically: ontology found the not before it and made use of it. But is it so self-evident that every not signifies a negativum in the sense of a lack? Is its positivity exhausted in constituting the "transition"? Why does all dialectic take refuge in negation, without grounding such a thing dialectically itself — without even being able to fix it as a problem? Has the ontological origin of notness ever been made a problem at all — or, before that, even the conditions sought on whose ground the problem of the not, its notness, and their possibility can be posed? And where should these be found, if not in the thematic clarification of the meaning of being in general? The paragraph is one of the book's great open doors: the not itself unthought — logic a user, not an unveiler, of negation; Hegel's dialectic arraigned in one clause (negation employed everywhere, grounded nowhere, not even fixed as a problem); the transition-function (the Hegelian Übergang) refused as the not's whole positivity — and the trail pointed, as always, to the meaning of being. "Was ist Metaphysik?" (1929), with its nothing older than negation, grows straight from this unit.

The twentieth unit draws the consequence against the good. Already for the ontological interpretation of the guilt-phenomenon, the moreover scarcely transparent concepts of privation and lack do not suffice — though, grasped formally enough, they admit of far-reaching employment. Least of all can the existential phenomenon of guilt be approached through orientation to the idea of evil, the malum as privatio boni: for the bonum and the privatio have the same ontological provenance from the ontology of the present-at-hand — which also accrues to the idea of "value" "drawn off" from it. The demolition is aimed at the entire Augustinian-scholastic axiology and its modern heirs in one clause: good, privation, and value — the whole apparatus by which the tradition thought evil — descend from thing-ontology; guilt cannot be reached through malum because malum was never existentially conceived. § 21's value-critique completes itself at ethics' foundation.

The twenty-first unit orders morality and guilt. A being whose being is care can not only load itself with factical guilt, but is guilty in the ground of its being — which being-guilty first gives the ontological condition for Dasein's being able, factically existing, to become guilty. This essential being-guilty is equiprimordially the existential condition of the possibility of the "morally" good and evil — that is, for morality in general and its factically possible formations. Original being-guilty cannot be determined by morality, because morality already presupposes it for itself. The founding-order is stated with its full scandal: ontological guilt beneath moral good and evil alike — the condition of morality, hence undeterminable by it; not an indictment (the guilt is not a wrong) but a ground: only a being in arrears to itself can owe anything.

The twenty-second unit answers the evidence-question by inversion: but what experience speaks for this original being-guilty of Dasein? One should not forget the counter-question: "is" guilt only "there" when a consciousness of guilt awakens — or does precisely the original being-guilty make itself known in the fact that guilt "sleeps"? That it proximally and mostly remains undisclosed, held closed by Dasein's falling being, only unveils the said nullity: being-guilty is more original than any knowledge of it. And only because Dasein is guilty in the ground of its being, and, as thrown falling, closes itself off from itself, is conscience possible — if indeed the call gives this being-guilty at bottom to understand. The evidential inversion is § 51's argument-form at the deepest layer: the sleep of guilt is its testimony (concealment as the falling mode of what is concealed), and the whole existence of conscience is re-derived from it — the call possible only because there is something structurally covered to call about; conscience as the voice of the sleeping guilt.

The twenty-third unit unites call and content. The call is call of care. Being-guilty constitutes the being we call care. In uncanniness Dasein stands originally together with itself; uncanniness brings this being before its undisguised nullity, which belongs to the possibility of its ownmost potentiality-of-being. Insofar as, for Dasein as care, its being is at issue, it calls itself, from uncanniness, as the factically falling they-self, forth to its potentiality-of-being. The appeal is the calling-back that calls forth: forward — into the possibility of taking over, existing, the thrown being that it is; back — into the thrownness, in order to understand it as the null ground that it has to take up into existence. This calling-back-calling-forth of conscience gives Dasein to understand that it — null ground of its null projection, standing in the possibility of its being — is to fetch itself back to itself out of the lostness in das Man: that is, that it is guilty. The paragraph is the chapter's keystone: §§ 56–57's formal call and § 58's guilt-content welded — the vor-rufender Rückruf now with its cargo: forward into the taking-over, back into the throw understood as null ground; and the closing equation performs a small grammatical miracle: "that it is guilty" and "that it is to fetch itself back" made one clause — the indicative of guilt and the summons of conscience the same understanding. The temporal skeleton is barely concealed: forward and back at once — anticipation and retrieval — temporality's ecstases sounding through the call's two directions.

The twenty-fourth unit lets the perverse objection form: what Dasein thus gives itself to understand would then be a piece of knowledge about itself, and the hearing corresponding to such a call a taking-cognizance of the factum "guilty." But if the call is to have the character of a summons, does this interpretation not lead to a complete perversion of the conscience-function? Summons to being-guilty — does that not mean summons to wickedness? The objection is built at full absurdity (conscience as recruiter for evil) so that its dissolution can fix the concept's register once and for all.

The twenty-fifth unit is the two-line hinge: this call-sense not even the most violent interpretation will want to lay upon conscience. But what then is "summons to being-guilty" still to mean? The concession sharpens the demand: the formula must be readable without the perversion.

The twenty-sixth unit reads it. The call-sense becomes clear when understanding, instead of laying under it the derived concept of guilt — the indebtedness "arisen" through a deed or omission — holds to the existential sense of being-guilty. To demand this is no arbitrariness, if the call of conscience, coming from Dasein itself, directs itself solely at this being. Then the summons to being-guilty means a calling-forth to the potentiality-of-being that I in each case already am as Dasein. This being does not first need to load a "guilt" upon itself through failures or omissions; it is only to be authentically the "guilty" that it is (es soll nur das »schuldig« — als welches es ist — eigentlich sein). The resolution is the modification-theorem's most compressed statement: the summons is not to acquire guilt but to be it authentically — the existential imperative always of the form: be what you are, owned; Pindar's "become what you are" (§ 31) heard now in conscience's silence, with guilt as its matter.

The twenty-seventh unit defines right hearing as self-choice. Right hearing of the appeal then amounts to a self-understanding in one's ownmost potentiality-of-being — to projecting oneself upon the ownmost authentic ability-to-become-guilty. Understandingly letting oneself be called forth to this possibility includes in itself Dasein's becoming free for the call: the readiness for the ability-to-be-appealed. Understanding the call, Dasein is in thrall (hörig) to its ownmost possibility of existence. It has chosen itself. The paragraph converts audition into election: hearing rightly = projecting on the ability-to-become-guilty (not on innocence — the direction that matters) = readiness for the call = self-choice; and § 34's Hörigkeit is redeemed at its depth — the thralldom that constituted everyday listening to das Man now re-bound to the ownmost possibility: obedience relocated, not abolished. The two-word closing sentence — Es hat sich selbst gewählt — discharges § 54's Wählen der Wahl: the chosen choice found.

The twenty-eighth unit names the choice's yield and coins the term. With this choice Dasein makes possible for itself its ownmost being-guilty, which remains closed to the they-self. Das Man's common sense knows only satisfying and failing the handy rule and public norm; it reckons up infractions and seeks settlements; from the ownmost being-guilty it has stolen away, in order to talk the more loudly about mistakes. But in the appeal, the they-self is appealed to toward the ownmost being-guilty of the self. Understanding the call is choosing — not of conscience, which as such cannot be chosen; chosen is having-a-conscience, as being-free for the ownmost being-guilty. Understanding the appeal means: wanting-to-have-a-conscience (Gewissen-haben-wollen). The paragraph draws the class-portrait of das Man's ethics in three strokes (rule-satisfaction, infraction-accounting, loud fault-talk as flight from the quiet guilt) and then makes the decisive scholastic distinction: conscience is not chosen (it calls unbidden — the throw again); chosen is having it — the readiness; whence the coinage that names the attested phenomenon the whole chapter sought.

The twenty-ninth unit fences the coinage: this does not mean wanting to have a "good conscience," just as little a voluntary cultivation of the call, but solely readiness for being-appealed. Wanting-to-have-a-conscience is as far from seeking out factical indebtednesses as from the tendency to a liberation from guilt in the sense of the essential "guilty." The double fence excludes the pharisee (the good conscience wanted) and the scrupulant (guilt-hunting), and — subtler — the redeemer-fantasy: no liberation from the essential guilt is sought, for none is possible; readiness, not remission.

The thirtieth unit pays the concept into action — and mints the section's darkest gold. Wanting-to-have-a-conscience is rather the most original existentiell presupposition for the possibility of factical becoming-guilty: understanding the call, Dasein lets its ownmost self act in itself out of its chosen potentiality-of-being. Only so can it be answerable (verantwortlich). But all action is factically necessarily "conscienceless" — not only because it does not avoid factical moral indebtedness, but because, on the null ground of its null projecting, it has, in being-with with others, in each case already become guilty toward them. Thus wanting-to-have-a-conscience becomes the taking-over of the essential consciencelessness, within which alone the existentiell possibility subsists of being "good." The paragraph is the book's ethics in four sentences, and each is a blade. Responsibility grounded (answerability possible only from the chosen self acting in one — Verantwortung from Antwort, answering the call); the tragic theorem — all action necessarily "conscienceless": finite, null-grounded agency always already guilty toward others in the Mitsein, before and beneath every code; and the resolution that refuses consolation: goodness possible only inside the owned consciencelessness — no clean hands, only hands that have taken over their unclean-ness. Weber's ethics of responsibility, and every later "dirty hands" debate, stand in this unit's shadow.

The thirty-first unit banks the attestation: though the call gives nothing to cognizance, it is not only critical but positive: it discloses Dasein's most original potentiality-of-being as being-guilty. Conscience thereby reveals itself as an attestation belonging to Dasein's being, in which it calls Dasein itself before its ownmost potentiality-of-being. Can the potentiality so attested be determined existentially more concretely? The verdict answers § 57's seventeenth-unit objection at its center (only critical?) with the section's whole yield: the call's positivity is the disclosure of the ownmost Seinkönnen as guilty — the required attestation (§ 54) formally delivered; and the question that closes opens § 60's office.

The closing unit poses the credibility-question and assigns § 59: antecedently, the question arises whether the accomplished exhibition of a potentiality-of-being attested in Dasein itself can claim sufficient evidence, so long as the strangeness has not vanished — that here conscience was one-sidedly interpreted back into Dasein's constitution, with hasty passing-over of all the findings familiar to the vulgar interpretation. Can the conscience-phenomenon, as it "actually" is, be recognized at all in the foregoing interpretation? Has not an idea of conscience been deduced, with all-too-confident candor, from Dasein's constitution of being? To secure access, even for the vulgar understanding, to the last step of the conscience-interpretation — the existential delimitation of the authentic potentiality attested in conscience — the connection of the ontological analysis's results with the everyday conscience-experiences must be expressly demonstrated. The self-accusation is voiced in the reader's words (deduction! one-sidedness!) and converted into the next section's task: § 59 as the owed audit — the § 44(b) pattern (construction, then derivation of the vulgar concept) applied to conscience.

##### § 59. The Existential Interpretation of Conscience and the Vulgar Interpretation of Conscience

The opening unit defines the parties. Conscience is the call of care from the uncanniness of being-in-the-world, which summons Dasein to its ownmost ability-to-be-guilty; the corresponding understanding of the appeal proved to be wanting-to-have-a-conscience. The two determinations cannot without further ado be brought into accord with the vulgar interpretation — they seem even to contradict it directly. We call the interpretation vulgar because, in characterizing the phenomenon and marking its "function," it holds to what one knows as conscience — how one follows it or fails to follow it. The term is defined without contempt: "vulgar" names the interpretation indexed to das Man's knowing — what "one" knows of conscience — a technical register, the phenomenon in its public self-showing.

The second unit files the prior suspicion: but must the ontological interpretation agree with the vulgar exegesis at all? Does the latter not fall under a fundamental ontological suspicion? If Dasein understands itself proximally and mostly from what it attends to, and interprets all its comportments as concern, will it not interpret — falling and covering — precisely that mode of its being which, as call, wants to fetch it back from lostness in the concerns of das Man? Everydayness takes Dasein as a ready-to-hand thing that is attended to — that is, administered and reckoned; "life" is a "business," whether or not it covers its costs. The suspicion is structural, not ad hominem: the call is anti-concern by office, so concern's self-interpretation must distort it — the witness for the prosecution is the defendant; and the closing epigram (life as a business, solvent or not) is the vulgar ontology in nine words, the household-Dasein that the section's last units will meet again.

The third unit draws the double consequence. So, with regard to the vulgar mode of being of Dasein itself, there is no guarantee that the interpretation of conscience springing from it, and the conscience-theories oriented to it, have won the appropriate ontological horizon. Nevertheless, even the vulgar experience must somehow — pre-ontologically — reach the phenomenon. From this follows a twofold: the everyday interpretation cannot count as the last criterion for the "objectivity" of an ontological analysis; and the latter, on the other hand, has no right to set itself over the everyday understanding of conscience and to pass over the anthropological, psychological, and theological conscience-theories grounded on it. If the existential analysis has laid the phenomenon free in its ontological rooting, precisely from it must the vulgar interpretations become intelligible — not least in that wherein they miss the phenomenon and why they cover it. Since, however, the conscience-analysis stands, in the problem-context of this treatise, only in the service of the fundamental ontological question, the characterization of the connection between the existential interpretation and the vulgar exegesis must content itself with an indication of the essential problems. The paragraph fixes the audit's constitution: neither party is sovereign — the vulgar not the criterion, the ontological not exempt from explaining it — and the burden is stated in the book's signature form: the analysis must derive the distortions (wherein and why the vulgar misses), § 44(b)'s Umschlag-obligation transferred to conscience.

The fourth unit tables the objections: what the vulgar interpretation would object against the presented interpretation of conscience as summons of care to being-guilty is a fourfold: (1) conscience has an essentially critical function; (2) conscience speaks in each case relative to a determinate performed or willed deed; (3) the "voice" is, according to experience, never so radically related to Dasein's being; (4) the interpretation takes no account of the basic forms of the phenomenon — the "evil" and "good," the "reproving" and "warning" conscience. The four counts (§ 57's seventeenth unit formalized) set the section's docket; they will be heard in reverse order.

The fifth unit opens the fourth count with the bad conscience. Let the discussion begin with the last-named reservation. In all interpretations of conscience the "evil," "bad" conscience has priority: conscience is primarily "bad." Therein is made known that all conscience-experience first experiences something like a "guilty." But how, in the idea of the bad conscience, is the making-known of being-evil understood? The "conscience-experience" turns up after the performed deed or omission; the voice follows upon the transgression and points back to the occurred event through which Dasein has loaded itself with guilt. If conscience makes known a "being-guilty," this cannot happen as summons to..., but as remembering reference back to incurred guilt. The reconstruction concedes the datum (bad conscience's priority — itself evidence that conscience speaks guilt) and states the rival reading at full strength: the voice as after-voice, retrospective, indicting the deed — the temporal order (act, then voice, then reference back) doing all the theoretical work.

The sixth unit dismantles the after-voice. But does the "fact" of the voice's coming-after exclude that the call is at bottom nevertheless a calling-forth? That the voice is taken as a stirring of conscience that follows after does not yet prove an original understanding of the phenomenon. What if the factical indebtedness were only the occasion for the factical calling of conscience? What if the described interpretation of the "bad" conscience stopped halfway? That it does so becomes clear from the ontological fore-having into which the phenomenon is brought by that interpretation: the voice is something that turns up, has its place in the sequence of present-at-hand lived experiences, and follows upon the experience of the deed. But neither the call, nor the deed that has happened, nor the guilt taken on, are occurrences with the character of the present-at-hand that runs its course. The call has the mode of being of care: in it Dasein "is" ahead of itself, in such a way that it at the same time directs itself back upon its thrownness. Only the proximal positing of Dasein as a sequence-context of successive lived experiences makes it possible to take the voice as something coming after, later, and therefore necessarily referring back. The voice does call back, but back over the deed that has happened, into the thrown being-guilty, which is "earlier" than every indebtedness; and the call-back calls at the same time forth to being-guilty, as something to be seized in one's own existence — so that authentic existentiell being-guilty precisely "follows after" the call, not conversely. The bad conscience is at bottom so little only reproving-and-pointing-back that it rather calls back, pointing forward, into thrownness. The sequence-order of elapsing experiences does not give the phenomenal structure of existing. The refutation is the chapter's methodological jewel: the after-voice reading convicted not of misdescription but of Erlebnis-ontology — the fore-having (Dasein as experience-sequence) generating the temporal order it then finds; against it, the call's own time is exhibited — back over the deed, into the guilt older than deeds; forward to the guilt still to be seized — so that the true sequence inverts: the existentiell guilt follows the call. Care's double direction (ahead, back upon the throw) shows through the argument as its skeleton; § 65's ecstatic temporality is being demonstrated here on a moral phenomenon, one chapter early.

The seventh unit turns to the good conscience and hands it to the pharisee. If already the characterization of the "bad" conscience does not reach the original phenomenon, this holds still more of the "good" — whether one takes it as an independent form of conscience or as one essentially founded in the "bad." The "good" conscience would have to make known, as the "bad" a "being-evil," the "being-good" of Dasein. One sees easily that thereby conscience — formerly the "outflow of the divine power" — now becomes the servant of pharisaism: it is to let a man say of himself "I am good"; who can say that, and who would less want to confirm it of himself than precisely the good man? From this impossible consequence of the idea of the good conscience only this comes to light: that conscience calls a being-guilty. The reductio is classical in form and Lutheran in flavor: the good conscience, taken seriously, issues the one certificate the good cannot accept — self-attested righteousness — so the concept collapses into pharisaism (the divine voice demoted to its flatterer), and its impossibility testifies backward: the call's one word is guilty.

The eighth unit dispatches the privation-repair — with Scheler in the note. To escape the named consequence, one has interpreted the "good" conscience as privation of the "bad," determining it as "experienced lack of the bad conscience" — the note citing Scheler's Formalismus. It would then be an experiencing of the non-emergence of the call — of the fact that I have nothing to reproach myself with. But how is this "lack" "experienced"? The supposed experience is no experiencing of a call at all, but a making-oneself-certain that a deed imputed to Dasein was not committed by it and that it is therefore innocent. Becoming certain of not-having-done has in no way the character of a conscience-phenomenon; on the contrary, it can rather signify a forgetting of conscience — a stepping-out of the possibility of being able to be appealed. The named "certainty" harbors in itself the tranquilizing suppression of wanting-to-have-a-conscience — that is, of understanding the ownmost, constant being-guilty. The "good" conscience is neither an independent nor a founded form of conscience — it is no conscience-phenomenon at all. The refutation runs on § 29's mood-logic (a lack is not experienced as a call's absence; what is actually present is a self-certification) and ends in excommunication: the good conscience expelled from the phenomenon's genus entirely — not conscience at rest but conscience forgotten, the readiness (§ 58's Gewissen-haben-wollen) tranquilized; Scheler's repair honored with exact citation and refused at the root.

The ninth unit generalizes the diagnosis: insofar as talk of a "good" conscience springs from the conscience-experience of everyday Dasein, the latter only betrays thereby that even when it speaks of the "bad" conscience it at bottom does not reach the phenomenon — for factically the idea of the "bad" orients itself by that of the "good." The everyday interpretation holds itself in the dimension of the concernful reckoning and balancing of "guilt" and "innocence"; within this horizon the voice of conscience is then "experienced." The turn is elegant: the good conscience, just expelled, is shown to have been secretly governing the bad one too — both poles of the vulgar pair calibrated to the ledger (guilt/innocence as debit/credit), § 58's sixth unit returning as the horizon of the whole vulgar experience.

The tenth unit settles the reproving/warning pair. With the characterization of the originality of the ideas of a "bad" and "good" conscience, the distinction of a forward-pointing-warning and a backward-pointing-reproving conscience is also already decided. The idea of the warning conscience seems, to be sure, to come nearest the phenomenon of the summons to...: it shares with it the character of pointing-forward. But this accord is only semblance. The experience of a warning conscience sees the voice again only oriented to the willed deed from which it wants to preserve; the warning, as suppression of the willed, is possible only because the "warning" call aims at Dasein's potentiality-of-being — at its self-understanding in being-guilty, on which the "willed" first shatters. The warning conscience has the function of the moment-wise regulation of a remaining-free from indebtednesses; the experience of a "warning" conscience sees the call-tendency again only so far as it remains accessible to das Man's common sense. The nearest counterfeit gets the most careful treatment: the warning voice shares the forward direction and misses the target — still deed-indexed, a moment-wise deed-brake, whereas the true call aims at the Seinkönnen against which the willed deed shatters; the shared vector shown to be borrowed — warning possible only because the deeper summons operates beneath it.

The eleventh unit hears the third count: it appeals to the fact that everyday conscience-experience knows nothing like a being-summoned to being-guilty. This must be conceded. But does everyday experience thereby already guarantee that in it the full possible call-content of the voice is heard? Does it follow that the conscience-theories grounded on vulgar experience have made sure of the appropriate ontological horizon for the analysis of the phenomenon? Does not rather an essential mode of being of Dasein — falling — show that this being understands itself proximally and mostly ontically from the horizon of concern, but ontologically determines being in the sense of presence-at-hand? From this, however, grows a twofold covering of the phenomenon: the theory sees a sequence of experiences or "psychic processes" — a sequence mostly wholly indeterminate in its mode of being; the experience encounters conscience as judge and admonisher, with whom Dasein negotiates by reckoning (rechnend verhandelt). The concession is full (everydayness hears no such summons — granted) and the rebuttal jurisdictional: the ear is not the measure of the call; falling explains the deficit and predicts the two coverings — theoretical (the Erlebnis-sequence, § 59's sixth unit generalized) and practical (the judge one bargains with — § 56's Verhandlung returning as the vulgar relation to conscience: litigation instead of hearing).

The twelfth unit places Kant and the value-ethics. That Kant lays the "representation of the court of justice" at the basis of his interpretation of conscience is not accidental, but suggested by the idea of the moral law — though his concept of morality remains far removed from utility-morals and eudaimonism. Value-theory too, whether formally or materially conceived, has a "metaphysics of morals" — that is, an ontology of Dasein and existence — as its unspoken ontological presupposition: Dasein counts as a being to be attended to, which attending has the sense of "realizing values" or fulfilling norms. The historical placement is double-edged and exactly weighed: Kant honored (no eudaimonist) and diagnosed (the tribunal follows from the law-idea — the juridical frame not chosen but inherited); and the whole axiological succession, formal and material alike (Kant to Scheler in one sentence), convicted of an unexamined ontology in which existence is a concern-object and the good a production-target: Wertverwirklichung as the vulgar ontology's ethical dialect.

The thirteenth unit closes the third count: the appeal to the circuit of what everyday conscience-experience knows, as the sole court for the interpretation of conscience, can set itself in the right only if it has first considered whether in that experience conscience can become authentically accessible at all. The count is dismissed on standing: the tribunal's competence was the question, and it cannot certify itself.

The fourteenth unit takes the second count. Therewith the further objection also loses its force — that the existential interpretation overlooks that the call of conscience in each case relates itself to a determinate "actualized" or willed deed. That the call is frequently experienced in such a call-tendency cannot, again, be denied; the question remains only whether this call-experience lets the call fully "call itself out" (sich ausrufen). The common-sense exegesis may suppose it holds to the "facts," and has in the end, precisely through its common sense, already restricted the call's disclosive reach. As little as the "good" conscience lets itself be placed in the service of a "pharisaism," so little may the function of the "bad" be pressed down to an indicating of present-at-hand or a thrusting-away of possible indebtednesses — as though Dasein were a "household" (Haushalt) whose debts need only be properly balanced, so that the self can stand "beside" these experience-sequences as an uninvolved spectator. The count falls to the same jurisdictional ruling (frequency of the deed-indexed experience conceded; its completeness as hearing denied — the call not allowed to call itself out), and the closing image gathers the section's whole polemic: Dasein as household — debts squared, self a spectator at its own books — the vulgar ontology of conscience drawn in one caricature and dismissed.

The fifteenth unit reaches the first count and turns it. If for the call the relatedness to factically "present" guilt or factically willed guilty deed is not primary, and hence the "reproving" and "warning" conscience express no original call-functions, then the ground is also withdrawn from the first-named reservation — that the existential interpretation misjudges the "essentially" critical accomplishment of conscience. This reservation too springs from a sight of the phenomenon genuine within certain limits: in fact, nothing can be exhibited in the call-content that the voice "positively" recommends and commands. But how is this missed positivity of the conscience-accomplishment understood — does the "negative" character of conscience follow from it? The count is granted its datum (no positive commandments in the call — true) and the inference challenged: what concept of positivity is doing the accusing?

The sixteenth unit answers with the section's finest distinction. A "positive" content in what is called is missed out of the expectation of a currently usable indication of available, calculable, secure possibilities of "action." This expectation grounds in the interpretive horizon of common-sense concern, which forces Dasein's existing under the idea of a regulable course of business. Such expectations — which in part also underlie, unspoken, the demand for a material value-ethics as against a "merely" formal one — are, to be sure, disappointed by conscience. Such "practical" directives the call does not give, solely because it summons Dasein to existence, to its ownmost potentiality-of-being-a-self. With the expected, unambiguously reckonable maxims, conscience would deny to existence nothing less than — the possibility of acting. Because conscience manifestly cannot be "positive" in this way, neither does it function in the same way "only negatively": the call discloses nothing that could be positive or negative as something attendable, because it means an ontologically wholly other being — existence. In the existential sense, by contrast, the rightly understood call gives the "most positive" — that is, the ownmost possibility that Dasein can give itself, as calling-back that calls forth into the in-each-case factical potentiality-of-being-a-self. To hear the call authentically means: to bring oneself into factical action. But the fully sufficient interpretation of what is called in the call is won only by setting forth the existential structure that lies in the authentically hearing understanding of the appeal as such. The paragraph is the book's answer to every demand for an ethics, delivered as a category-analysis: the "positivity" missed is recipe-positivity — usable, calculable maxims — and the devastating counter-theorem holds the center: maxims would deny existence the possibility of acting, for action is the projection of the self upon its situation, and a supplied answer pre-empts precisely that (the deepest ground of the book's refusal to legislate: not reticence but the ontology of action). The call is beyond the positive/negative of the attendable because its referent is existence; existentially it gives the most positive — the ownmost possibility. Hearing = bringing oneself into factical action: conscience's yield is not a content but the agent.

The seventeenth unit states the section's double result: it was first to be shown how the phenomena solely familiar to the vulgar interpretation, understood ontologically appropriately, point back to the original sense of the call; then, that the vulgar exegesis springs from the limitedness of Dasein's falling self-interpretation and — because falling belongs to care itself — is, for all its self-evidence, by no means accidental. The audit closes on both books: the vulgar data saved (each pointing back, rightly read, to the call of care) and the vulgar distortion derived (necessary, not accidental — falling's own child); § 44(b)'s standard met for conscience.

The closing unit guards against the moralizing of the critique. The ontological critique of the vulgar interpretation could fall under the misunderstanding that, with the demonstration of the existential non-originality of everyday conscience-experience, something is to be judged about the existentiell "moral quality" of the Dasein that holds itself in it. As little as existence is necessarily and directly impaired by an ontologically insufficient understanding of conscience, so little is the existentiell understanding of the call guaranteed by an existentially appropriate interpretation: seriousness (der Ernst) is not less possible in the vulgar experience than unseriousness in a more original understanding. Nevertheless, the existentially more original interpretation also discloses possibilities of more original existentiell understanding — so long as ontological conceiving does not let itself be cut off from ontic experience. The closing distinction is the book's ethics of its own readership: ontology confers no existentiell rank — the plain believer in his vulgar conscience may be serious where the reader of this analysis is frivolous — and yet the interpretation is not idle: deeper concepts open deeper possibilities, provided concept and experience stay joined. With this double humility posted, the way is free for § 60: the existential structure of what the authentic hearing itself is — resoluteness.

##### § 60. The Existential Structure of the Authentic Potentiality-of-Being Attested in Conscience

The opening unit gathers the chapter for its last step. The existential interpretation of conscience is to set forth an attestation, being in Dasein itself, of its ownmost potentiality-of-being. The way conscience attests is no indifferent making-known, but the summons, calling forth, to being-guilty; what is so attested is "grasped" in the hearing that understands the call undisguised, in the sense intended by the call itself. The understanding of the appeal, as a mode of being of Dasein, first gives the phenomenal stock of what is attested in the call. Authentic understanding of the call we characterized as wanting-to-have-a-conscience: this letting the ownmost self act in itself, from itself, in its being-guilty, represents phenomenally the authentic potentiality-of-being attested in Dasein itself. Its existential structure must now be laid free: only so do we penetrate to the basic constitution, disclosed in Dasein itself, of the authenticity of its existence. The recapitulation fixes the section's exact object: not the call (§§ 56–57) nor its content (§ 58) but the hearing itself as a mode of being — the attested phenomenon is the response, and its structure is what "authenticity" will henceforth mean structurally.

The second unit sets the analytic frame: wanting-to-have-a-conscience is, as self-understanding in the ownmost potentiality-of-being, a way of Dasein's disclosedness; besides understanding, disclosedness is constituted by disposedness and discourse. Existentiell understanding means: projecting oneself upon the in-each-case ownmost factical possibility of the potentiality-of-being-in-the-world — and the potentiality is understood only in existing in this possibility. The frame is Chapter Five's triad once more (the third run: constitution, everydayness, now authenticity) — and the closing sentence bars the spectator-reading in advance: this understanding is had only in the existing, never in contemplation of it.

The third unit fills the mood-slot and the discourse-slot. Which mood corresponds to such understanding? Understanding the call discloses one's own Dasein in the uncanniness of its individuation; the uncanniness co-revealed in understanding is genuinely disclosed by the disposedness of anxiety belonging to it. The factum of conscience-anxiety (Gewissensangst) is a phenomenal confirmation that Dasein, in understanding the call, is brought before the uncanniness of itself: wanting-to-have-a-conscience becomes readiness for anxiety (Bereitschaft zur Angst). The third essential moment of disclosedness is discourse. To the call, as original discourse of Dasein, there corresponds no counter-discourse — say, in the sense of a negotiating talking-over of what conscience says. The understanding hearing of the call denies itself the counter-discourse not because overpowered by a "dark force" that crushes it, but because it appropriates the call-content un-covered. The call places before the constant being-guilty and thus fetches the self back from the loud idle talk of das Man's common sense. Accordingly, the mode of articulating discourse belonging to wanting-to-have-a-conscience is reticence (Verschwiegenheit). Keeping-silent was characterized as an essential possibility of discourse: whoever wants to give to understand in silence must "have something to say." Dasein gives itself, in the appeal, its ownmost potentiality-of-being to understand; hence this calling is a keeping-silent. The discourse of conscience never comes to utterance. Conscience calls only silently — that is, the call comes from the soundlessness of uncanniness and calls the summoned Dasein, as one that is to become still, back into the stillness of itself. Wanting-to-have-a-conscience therefore understands this silent discourse appropriately only in reticence: it withdraws the word from the common-sense idle talk of das Man. The paragraph fills two of the three slots with matched precision. The mood: conscience-anxiety — § 53's essential anxiety re-found on the conscience-side, and the fine coinage Bereitschaft zur Angst as authenticity's affective form: not courage over the mood but readiness for it (§ 51's Mut zur Angst institutionalized). The discourse: reticence, with the guard that matters — no counter-speech, not from being overpowered (the dark-force theory dismissed once more) but from appropriation: answering back is already das Man's litigation (§ 56's Verhandlung); the silent call is heard silently, stillness answering soundlessness, and das Man is defeated by the withdrawal of the word.

The fourth unit turns das Man's positivism inside out: the silent speaking of conscience gives the common-sense interpretation — which holds itself "strictly to facts" — occasion to pass conscience off as not ascertainable and not present-at-hand at all. That one, hearing and understanding only loud idle talk, can "register" no call, is shifted onto conscience with the excuse that it is "dumb" and manifestly not there. With this interpretation das Man only covers over its own failing-to-hear the call and the shortened reach of its "hearing." The diagnosis is § 34's founding-order applied forensically: the ear calibrated to noise certifies the silence as nothing — the deafness projected onto the phenomenon as its muteness; empiricism about conscience unmasked as an audiogram of das Man.

The fifth unit assembles the definition: the disclosedness of Dasein lying in wanting-to-have-a-conscience is accordingly constituted by the disposedness of anxiety, by understanding as self-projection upon the ownmost being-guilty, and by discourse as reticence. This distinguished, authentic disclosedness, attested in Dasein itself by its conscience — the reticent, anxiety-ready self-projection upon the ownmost being-guilty — we call resoluteness (Entschlossenheit). The coinage is the chapter's summit, and its construction is its doctrine: the three disclosedness-moments each in its authentic mode (anxiety, guilt-projection, reticence) welded into one formula — das verschwiegene, angstbereite Sichentwerfen auf das eigenste Schuldigsein. The word itself works: Ent-schlossenheit as un-closedness — resoluteness heard as disclosedness's own superlative (the German ties Entschluß to Erschließen), not as a clenched will; the next unit makes the etymology official.

The sixth unit ranks it in the truth-doctrine: resoluteness is a distinguished mode of Dasein's disclosedness. But disclosedness was earlier interpreted existentially as the original truth — primarily no quality of "judgment" nor of any particular comportment, but an essential constitutive of being-in-the-world as such: truth as fundamental existential. The ontological clarification of the sentence "Dasein is in the truth" pointed to the original disclosedness of this being as truth of existence, and referred, for its delimitation, to the analysis of Dasein's authenticity. The unit cashes § 44's promissory note by name: the "truth of existence" there deferred to the authenticity-analysis is about to be paid — resoluteness as its face.

The seventh unit pays it, and runs the modification through world and others. Now, with resoluteness, the most original — because authentic — truth of Dasein has been won. The disclosedness of the Da discloses equiprimordially the in-each-case whole being-in-the-world: world, being-in, and the self that, as "I am," this being is. With the disclosedness of world, innerworldly beings are in each case already discovered; the discoveredness of the ready-to-hand and present-at-hand grounds in the disclosedness of world, for the freeing of the current involvement-totality demands a pre-understanding of significance. Understanding significance, concernful Dasein circumspectly refers itself to the encountered ready-to-hand. The understanding of significance, as disclosedness of the current world, grounds in turn in the understanding of the for-the-sake-of-which, to which all discovering of the involvement-totality goes back. The for-the-sake of shelter, of sustenance, of advancement are nearest and constant possibilities of Dasein, upon which this being — for which its being is at issue — has always already projected itself. Thrown into its "Da," Dasein is factically in each case referred to a determinate — its — "world." In one therewith, the nearest factical projections are led by the concernful lostness in das Man; this lostness can be appealed to by one's own Dasein, and the appeal can be understood in the manner of resoluteness. This authentic disclosedness then modifies, equiprimordially, the discoveredness of the "world" founded in it and the disclosedness of the co-Dasein of others. The ready-to-hand "world" does not become "contentually" another; the circle of the others is not exchanged; and yet the understanding, concernful being toward the ready-to-hand, and the solicitous being-with with the others, are now determined from their ownmost potentiality-of-being-a-self. The paragraph is the modification-theorem's most explicit statement, and its double negative is the doctrine: same world, same others — nothing exchanged, nothing added — but the whole determined otherwise, from the ownmost Seinkönnen instead of from das Man. § 18's founding-chain (things from significance from the Worumwillen) is re-run to show exactly where the modification enters: at the for-the-sake-of, the chain's anchor, so that one changed anchoring re-tunes everything hung from it. Authenticity as re-anchoring, not relocation.

The eighth unit bars the isolation-reading once more: resoluteness, as authentic being-a-self, does not detach Dasein from its world, does not isolate it upon a free-floating I. How should it — when, as authentic disclosedness, it is nothing other than being-in-the-world, authentically? Resoluteness brings the self precisely into the current concernful being alongside the ready-to-hand and thrusts it into the solicitous being-with with the others. The three-sentence guard repeats § 53's eleventh unit at the chapter's peak, with the rhetorical question doing the ontological work: resoluteness is disclosedness, disclosedness is being-in-the-world — the isolation-reading is grammatically impossible; and the verb stößt (thrusts) gives the doctrine its force: authenticity propels into the with-world, it does not excuse from it.

The ninth unit derives authentic community. From the for-the-sake-of-which of the self-chosen potentiality-of-being, resolute Dasein frees itself for its world. The resoluteness toward itself first brings Dasein into the possibility of letting the others who are with it "be" in their ownmost potentiality-of-being, and of co-disclosing this in the solicitude that leaps ahead and liberates. Resolute Dasein can become the "conscience" of the others. From the authentic being-a-self of resoluteness first springs authentic being-with-one-another — not from the ambiguous and jealous stipulations and the talkative fraternizations in das Man and what one wants to undertake.
