The world is, as it were, already "further outside" than any object can ever be. The "transcendence-problem" cannot be brought to the question: how does a subject get out to an object? — where the totality of objects is identified with the idea of world. To be asked is: what makes it ontologically possible that beings can encounter innerworldly and, as encountering, be objectified? The regress to the ecstatically-horizonally founded transcendence of the world gives the answer. The paragraph settles a century's epistemology in four sentences: the Kantian form-imposition (categories over sense-stuff — the Netzwerk von Formen) refused with its worldless subject; the bridge-problem (§ 43's scandal) dissolved by the geometry — the world outside all objects because it is the horizon from which they meet; transcendence relocated from a feat of the subject to the constitution of the Da. "Vom Wesen des Grundes" is this unit expanded to an essay.

The eighth unit coins the paradox: if the "subject" is conceived ontologically as existing Dasein, whose being grounds in temporality, then it must be said: world is "subjective." But this "subjective" world, as temporally-transcendent, is then "more objective" than any possible "object." The two-sentence unit is the book's most quotable dialectical stroke: subjectivity radicalized until it out-objects objectivity — the world mine (Dasein's) and precisely therefore prior to and firmer than every object; idealism and realism each given their word and both overtaken.

The closing unit certifies and defers: through the leading-back of being-in-the-world to the ecstatic-horizonal unity of temporality, the existential-ontological possibility of this basic constitution of Dasein is made intelligible. At the same time it becomes plain that the concrete working-out of the world-structure in general, and of its possible variations, can be taken in hand only when the ontology of possible innerworldly beings is oriented, sufficiently securely, to a clarified idea of being in general; the possible interpretation of this idea demands, beforehand, the setting-forth of Dasein's temporality, which the present characterization of being-in-the-world serves. The section closes on the book's constant figure: the achievement banked (In-der-Welt-sein grounded), the completion deferred to the idea of being — the world-variations (other cultures' worlds, the work-world, nature's world) expressly awaiting the horizon Division Three was to supply.

##### § 70. The Temporality of Dasein-like Spatiality

The opening unit poses the apparent limit. Although the expression "temporality" does not mean what the talk of "space and time" understands by time, spatiality too seems to constitute a corresponding basic determinateness of Dasein, as temporality does: the existential-temporal analysis therefore seems to come, with Dasein's spatiality, to a limit, so that this being would have to be addressed, in co-ordination, as "temporal" "and also" as spatial. Has the analysis been halted by the phenomenon we came to know as Dasein-like spatiality, belonging to being-in-the-world? The objection is staged fairly: the und auch — the coordinating "and also" of the tradition's space-and-time — as the analytic's possible boundary-stone.

The second unit rules out the coordination and marks the distance from Kant. That, in the course of the existential interpretation, talk of Dasein's "spatio-temporal" determinateness cannot mean this being is present-at-hand "in space and also in time," needs no further discussion. Temporality is the sense of the being of care: Dasein's constitution and its ways to be are ontologically possible only on the ground of temporality, regardless of whether this being occurs "in time" or not. But then Dasein's specific spatiality too must ground in temporality. On the other hand, the demonstration that this spatiality is existentially possible only through temporality cannot aim at deducing space from time, or dissolving it into pure time. If Dasein's spatiality is "embraced" by temporality in the sense of existential founding, then this connection is also different from the priority of time over space in Kant's sense: that the empirical representations of what is present-at-hand "in space" run their course, as psychic occurrences, "in time," so that the "physical" also occurs mediately "in time," is no existential-ontological interpretation of space as a form of intuition, but the ontic ascertainment of the running-off of the psychically present-at-hand "in time." The paragraph sets the claim's exact strength: founding, not deduction (space not dissolved into time — the anti-reduction axiom again) and not Kant's priority either, which is convicted of running through the psychic detour: inner sense's mediation an ontic thoroughfare, not an ontological ground.

The third unit recalls how Dasein is spatial. We are to ask, existential-analytically, after the temporal conditions of the possibility of Dasein-like spatiality, which in its turn founds the discovery of innerworldly space. First we must recall in what way Dasein is spatial: Dasein can be spatial only as care, in the sense of factically falling existing. Negatively this means: Dasein is never — not even proximally — present-at-hand in space; it does not fill out a piece of space as a real thing or tool does, so that its boundary against the surrounding space would itself only be a spatial determination of space. Dasein takes space in — in the literal sense (nimmt Raum ein): it is by no means merely present-at-hand in the piece of space that the body (Leibkörper) fills. Existing, it has in each case already made room for itself a leeway (Spielraum); it determines its own location in each case in such a way that it comes back, from the room made, upon the "place" it occupies. To be able to say that Dasein is present-at-hand at a position in space, we must beforehand grasp this being in an ontologically inappropriate way. Nor does the difference between the "spatiality" of an extended thing and that of Dasein lie in Dasein's knowing about space; for taking-space-in is so little identical with a "representing" of the spatial that the latter presupposes the former. Nor may Dasein's spatiality be interpreted as an imperfection that clings to existence on the ground of the fatal "linkage of the spirit with a body": Dasein can rather, because it is "spiritual," and only therefore, be spatial in a way that remains essentially impossible for an extended corporeal thing. The paragraph re-banks §§ 22–24 with three new sharpenings: the literalized einräumen (Dasein spatial as room-making, returning from its opened leeway upon its place — inhabitation before location); the anti-intellectualist order (representing space presupposes taking it in); and the paragraph's famous scandal, aimed at the whole Platonic-Christian tradition of the soul's imprisonment: spirit is not in space despite itself — only because Dasein is "spiritual" can it be spatial as no body can; embodiment's dignity derived from existence, the "fatal linkage" dissolved. (The Leib/Körper distinction flickers here in one compound word, the phenomenology of the lived body deferred — as Heidegger later admitted — almost entirely.)

The fourth unit derives making-room from temporality. Dasein's making-room-for-itself is constituted by directionality and de-severance; how is such a thing existentially possible on the ground of temporality? The founding function of temporality shall be indicated briefly, only so far as necessary for the later discussion of the ontological sense of the "coupling" of space and time. To Dasein's making-room belongs the self-directing discovery of something like a region (Gegend): with this expression we mean first the whither of the possible belonging-somewhere of environmentally ready-to-hand, placeable equipment. In all finding, handling, moving and clearing-away of equipment, region is already discovered. Concernful being-in-the-world is directed — directing itself. Belonging-somewhere has an essential relation to involvement; it determines itself factically always from the involvement-context of the attended equipment. The involvement-relations are intelligible only in the horizon of a disclosed world; their horizon-character first makes possible the specific horizon of the whither of regional belonging. The self-directing discovery of region grounds in an ecstatically retaining awaiting of the possible thither and hither. Making-room is, as directed awaiting of region, equiprimordially a nearing (de-severing) of the ready-to-hand and present-at-hand: out of the pre-discovered region, concern comes back, de-severing, upon the nearest. Nearing, and likewise the estimating and measuring of distances within the de-severed innerworldly present-at-hand, ground in a making-present belonging to the unity of temporality, in which directionality too becomes possible. The derivation runs § 22's pair through the schemata: region as the spatial whither, discovered in a retaining awaiting of thither-and-hither; nearing as the presenting's return from the pre-opened region upon the closest — space's two existentials re-founded as temporalizations; the "coupling" of space and time (the tradition's und) re-assigned to a founding order and deferred (§ 80's world-time will collect).

The fifth unit banks the portable space: because Dasein, as temporality, is ecstatic-horizonal in its being, it can factically and constantly take along a made-room space (einen eingeräumten Raum mitnehmen). With regard to this ecstatically taken-in space, the Here of the current factical position or situation never means a space-position, but the leeway — opened in directionality and de-severance — of the circuit of the nearest-attended equipment-whole. The unit answers § 23's puzzle (the here that travels) with its ground: the portable leeway carried because the ecstases carry their horizons; the Hier indexed to the situation, never to co-ordinates.

The sixth unit explains the illusion of the mere thing in space: in the nearing that makes possible the handling and being-busy "absorbed in the matter," the essential structure of care — falling — announces itself. Its existential-temporal constitution is distinguished by this: that in it, and thus also in the "presently" founded nearing, the awaiting forgetting leaps after the making-present. In the nearing making-present of something from its thence, the making-present loses itself in itself, forgetting the thither. Hence it comes that, when "contemplation" of innerworldly beings begins in such a making-present, the semblance arises that "proximally" only a thing is present-at-hand — here, indeed, but indeterminately, in a space in general. The paragraph derives the starting-point of every empiricism as an artifact: the "mere thing here in space" is the residue left when the presenting, falling, forgets the region it neared from — the Dorther dropped, the leeway effaced; the epistemologist's primitive datum unmasked as the fallen present's amnesia.

The closing unit totals the section — and explains language's spatial cast. Only on the ground of ecstatic-horizonal temporality is the irruption (Einbruch) of Dasein into space possible. The world is not present-at-hand in space; yet space lets itself be discovered only within a world. The ecstatic temporality of Dasein-like spatiality makes intelligible precisely the independence of space from time — but conversely also Dasein's "dependence" on space, which reveals itself in the familiar phenomenon that Dasein's self-interpretation, and the stock of significations of language in general, are pervasively ruled by "spatial representations." This priority of the spatial in the articulation of significations and concepts has its ground not in a specific power of space, but in Dasein's mode of being: essentially falling, temporality loses itself in making-present and understands itself not only circumspectly from the attended ready-to-hand, but takes from that which the making-present constantly meets at it as present — from the spatial relations — the guiding threads for articulating what is understood and interpretable in understanding at all. The section ends on a double stroke: the Einbruch-sentence (Dasein's irruption into space grounded in the ecstases — with the world/space order fixed: space discoverable only within a world, never the converse), and the answer to a puzzle the book itself instantiates — why all language, its own included, speaks in spatial figures (horizon, ground, in, before...): not space's power but falling's — the presenting, lost among the present, borrows its articulation-threads from what presence shows, spatial relations first; metaphor's spatial gravity derived from the fallen present. The confession is quietly reflexive: the analytic's own vocabulary stands under the diagnosis it delivers.

##### § 71. The Temporal Sense of Dasein's Everydayness

The opening unit takes the chapter's stock: the analysis of concern's temporality showed that the essential structures of Dasein's constitution — interpreted, before the setting-forth of temporality, with the intent of leading toward it — must themselves be taken back existentially into temporality. In its first approach the analytic chose as theme not a distinguished possibility of existence, but oriented itself by the inconspicuous, average way of existing: the mode of being in which Dasein proximally and mostly holds itself we called everydayness. The retrospect closes the loop the chapter opened: the repetition performed (§§ 68–70), the starting-horizon itself now due for audit — the word that carried the whole preparatory analytic called to account.

The second unit confesses the darkness: what this expression at bottom, ontologically delimited, means remained dark; at the investigation's beginning there was no way even to make the existential-ontological sense of everydayness a problem. Now the sense of Dasein's being is illuminated as temporality: can a doubt still prevail regarding the existential-temporal signification of the title "everydayness"? And yet we are far from an ontological concept of this phenomenon — it remains even questionable whether the explication of temporality carried through so far suffices to delimit the existential sense of everydayness. The double movement is the book's honesty at its most exposed: the illumination granted (everydayness obviously temporal now) and the concept withheld — the section will be a problem-exhibition, not a solution.

The third unit reads the word. Everydayness manifestly means the manner of existing in which Dasein holds itself "every day" (alle Tage). And yet the "every day" does not mean the sum of the "days" allotted to Dasein in its "lifetime"; though it is not to be understood calendrically, such a time-determinateness still resonates in the signification of "everyday." Primarily, however, the expression means a determinate how of existence that rules through Dasein "for life" (zeitlebens). In the foregoing analyses we often used the expressions "proximally and mostly": "proximally" means the way in which Dasein is "manifest" in the with-one-another of publicness, even if "at bottom" it has existentielly "overcome" everydayness precisely; "mostly" means the way in which Dasein shows itself for everyman — not always, but "as a rule." The exegesis performs the book's method on its own most-used adverbs: alle Tage read past the calendar to the how (the daily as a manner, not a tally), and the standing formula zunächst und zumeist finally defined — the first indexing publicness's face (which even the authentic wear outwardly), the second the statistical rule; the analytic's ground-terms shown to be temporal through and through.

The fourth unit paints the how. Everydayness means the how in accordance with which Dasein "lives into the day" (in den Tag hineinlebt), whether in all its comportments or only in certain ones predelineated by being-with-one-another. To this how belongs further the comfort of habituation (das Behagen in der Gewohnheit), even if habit forces upon one the burdensome and "repugnant." The tomorrow that everyday concern remains awaiting is the "eternal yesterday" (das »ewig Gestrige«). The monotony of everydayness takes as variety whatever the day happens to bring. Everydayness determines Dasein even when it has not chosen das Man for its "hero." The paragraph is the book's small masterpiece of existential portraiture, each phrase a temporal finding: living into the day (the future shortened to the day's rim), comfort-in-habit even when habit chafes (the retention that has renounced retrieval), the awaited morrow as the eternal yesterday (Gewärtigen collapsed into repetition-without-Wiederholung — the future a replay of the been), monotony consuming novelty as its own diet (§ 68c's manufactured new). And the closing sentence bars the loophole with a phrase that quietly answers Nietzsche and Carlyle at once: everydayness reigns also over those who have not chosen das Man as their hero — heroic self-election does not exempt; even the exception keeps the everyday.

The fifth unit gives everydayness its mood and its mastery-clause. These manifold characters by no means mark everydayness as a mere "aspect" that Dasein offers when "one" "looks at" the doings of men: everydayness is a way to be, to which public manifestness indeed belongs. But as a way of its own existing, everydayness is also more or less familiar to the respective "individual" Dasein — through the disposedness of pallid untunedness. Dasein can "suffer" dully from everydayness, sink into its dullness, evade it in such a way that it seeks new distraction for its dispersal into business. But existence can also master the everyday in the moment of vision — and often, to be sure, only "for the moment" — though it can never extinguish it. The paragraph does three things with strict economy: bars the sociological reading (everydayness no spectator-aspect but each one's own way to be), gives it its disclosure (the fahle Ungestimmtheit of § 68b — the gray known from inside, in dull suffering, sinking, or the flight into fresh distraction), and legislates the limit that governs the whole book's ethics: the everyday can be mastered augenblicklich, never extinguished — authenticity as recurrent seizure, not permanent estate; "oft auch nur für den Augenblick" the most honest clause in the division.

The sixth unit converts familiarity into enigma: what is ontically so familiar in Dasein's factical interpretedness that we do not even heed it, harbors, existential-ontologically, riddle upon riddle. The "natural" horizon for the first approach of the existential analytic is only seemingly self-evident. The two-line unit is § 1's opening move re-executed on the analytic's own ground: the trivial as the deepest covering — the book's starting-point itself de-trivialized.

The seventh unit turns the audit on the explication itself. But do we find ourselves, after the interpretation of temporality carried through so far, in a more promising position for the existential delimitation of everydayness? Or does precisely this confusing phenomenon make manifest the insufficiency of the foregoing explication of temporality? Have we not hitherto constantly immobilized (stillgelegt) Dasein in certain positions and situations, and "consistently" disregarded that it, living into its days, stretches itself "temporally" along in the sequence of its days? The monotony, the habit, the "as yesterday, so today and tomorrow," the "mostly" — these cannot be grasped without going back to the "temporal" stretching-along of Dasein. The self-accusation is exact and epoch-making: the analysis has worked in stills — resolute moments, situations, seizures — while everydayness is duration: the day-after-day, graspable only from the Erstreckung; the confession that commissions § 72's connectedness-of-life problem and, with it, the whole historicity-chapter.

The closing unit adds the reckoning and defers the concept. And does there not belong to existing Dasein also the factum that, spending its time, it daily takes account of "time" and regulates the "account" astronomically and calendrically? Only when the everyday "happening" of Dasein, and the reckoning with "time" attended to in this happening, are drawn into the interpretation of Dasein's temporality does the orientation become comprehensive enough to make the ontological sense of everydayness as such a problem. But because with the title everydayness at bottom nothing other is meant than temporality, while temporality makes possible Dasein's being, the sufficient conceptual delimitation of everydayness can succeed only in the frame of the fundamental discussion of the sense of being in general. The chapter thus closes on a double handover: the stretching (Chapter Five) and the reckoning (Chapter Six) named as the two owed analyses — everydayness the seam where they meet — and the final deferral is total: everydayness at bottom is temporality, so its concept waits upon the meaning of being itself; the humblest word in the book assigned to the missing division.

#### Chapter Five: Temporality and Historicity

##### § 72. The Existential-Ontological Exposition of the Problem of History

The opening unit re-fixes the one goal: all efforts of the existential analytic serve the one aim of finding a possibility of answering the question of the sense of being in general. The working-out of this question demands a delimitation of the phenomenon in which anything like being becomes accessible — the understanding of being; this belongs to Dasein's constitution. Only when this being is first interpreted sufficiently originally can the understanding of being enclosed in its constitution itself be conceived, and on this ground the question be posed of the being understood in it and of the "presuppositions" of this understanding. The chapter opens, as § 45 did, from the fundamental-ontological summit — every analysis, historicity's included, indexed to the being-question; the reader is not to mistake what follows for philosophy of history.

The second unit lets the achievement pose as completion: though in detail many structures still lie in the dark, it seems that with the illumination of temporality as the original condition of the possibility of care, the demanded original interpretation of Dasein has been reached. Temporality was set forth with regard to Dasein's authentic potentiality-of-being-whole; the temporal interpretation of care confirmed itself through the demonstration of the temporality of concernful being-in-the-world. The analysis of the authentic potentiality-of-being-whole unveiled the equiprimordial connection, rooted in care, of death, guilt, and conscience. Can Dasein be understood still more originally than in the projection of its authentic existence? The rhetorical close invites complacency in order to break it: the question sounds unanswerable — and the next unit answers it.

The third unit springs the wound: birth. Though we see no possibility of a more radical approach, a heavy scruple awakens precisely with regard to the foregoing discussion of everydayness: has the whole of Dasein, with regard to its authentic being-whole, in fact been brought into the fore-having of the existential analysis? The question-formulation related to Dasein's wholeness may possess genuine ontological unambiguousness; the question itself may even have found its answer with regard to being toward the end. But death is only the "end" of Dasein — formally taken, only the one end that encloses the Dasein-whole; the other "end," however, is the "beginning," "birth." Only the being "between" birth and death presents the sought whole. Accordingly, the hitherto orientation of the analytic remained, for all its tendency toward existing being-whole and despite the genuine explication of authentic and inauthentic being toward death, "one-sided": Dasein stood in the theme only as it exists, as it were, "forward" and leaves everything been "behind it." Not only did being toward the beginning remain unheeded, but above all the stretching-along of Dasein between birth and death; precisely the "connectedness of life" (Zusammenhang des Lebens), in which Dasein constantly somehow holds itself, was overlooked in the analysis of being-whole. The paragraph is the division's second great self-correction (after § 45's): the death-analysis convicted of one-sidedness by its own standard — one end secured, the other (birth) never thematized, and with it the between, the stretch, Dilthey's Lebenszusammenhang named as the overlooked phenomenon; the analytic caught existing only forward.

The fourth unit refuses the retreat: must we then — though what is addressed as "connectedness" between birth and death is ontologically wholly dark — take back the approach of temporality as the sense of the being of the Dasein-whole? Or does the exhibited temporality rather first give the ground for bringing the existential-ontological question of that "connectedness" into an unambiguous direction? Perhaps it is already a gain, in the field of these investigations, that we learn not to take the problems too lightly. The alternative is posed and the tone set: no retraction — the scruple to be converted into the deeper confirmation; and the closing sentence is the book's pedagogy in one line.

The fifth unit reconstructs the vulgar answer. What seems "simpler" than characterizing the "connectedness of life" between birth and death? It consists of a succession of experiences "in time." If one pursues this characterization, and above all its ontological pre-opinion, more penetratingly, something remarkable results: in this succession, "authentically" only the experience present-at-hand "in the current now" is "actual"; the past and the just-arriving experiences, by contrast, are no longer or not yet "actual." Dasein traverses the time-span allotted to it between the two boundaries in such a way that, "actual" only in the now, it hops, as it were, through the now-sequence of its "time" (die Jetztfolge seiner »Zeit« gleichsam durchhüpft). Hence one says Dasein is "temporal." In this constant change of experiences the self maintains itself in a certain selfsameness; opinions diverge in determining this persistent element and its possible relation to the change of experiences. The being of this persisting-changing connectedness of experiences remains undetermined — but at bottom, whether one wishes to admit it or not, something present-at-hand "in time," though of course "unthinglike," has been posited in this characterization of the life-connectedness. The reconstruction is devastating in its fairness: the Erlebnis-theory (Dilthey's school and every empirical psychology) rendered at full strength — and its picture caught in one unforgettable verb: existence hopping across the nows, actual only at the point of contact; while the divergent "opinions" about the persisting self (substrate, act-unity, Gestalt) are all convicted of the same unexamined positing: an untinglike thing in time.

The sixth unit passes the verdict: with regard to what was worked out as the sense of the being of care under the title temporality, it shows itself that, along the guiding thread of the vulgar interpretation of Dasein — justified and sufficient within its limits — a genuine ontological analysis of the stretching-along between birth and death not only cannot be carried through: it cannot even be fixed as a problem. The verdict's precision matters: the vulgar view keeps its ontic rights (within limits); ontologically it cannot even pose the question — the problem itself is invisible from inside the now-hopping picture.

The seventh unit demolishes the frame-picture: Dasein does not exist as the sum of momentary actualities of experiences that arrive one after another and vanish; nor does this succession gradually fill up a frame. For how should the frame be present-at-hand, when in each case only the "actual" experience is "actual," and the frame's boundaries — birth and death — as past and only arriving, lack actuality? At bottom, even the vulgar conception of the "life-connectedness" does not think of a frame spanned "outside" Dasein and embracing it, but rightly seeks it in Dasein itself. But the tacit ontological positing of this being as something present-at-hand "in time" makes every attempt at an ontological characterization of the being "between" birth and death founder. The demolition proceeds by the theory's own arithmetic: a frame whose ends lack actuality cannot be filled — the picture collapses under its actuality-criterion; and the vulgar view's sound instinct (the connectedness sought in Dasein, not outside) is saved from its categorial ruin.

The eighth unit speaks the positive doctrine. Dasein does not first fill up, through the phases of its momentary actualities, a somehow present-at-hand track and stretch "of life": it stretches itself along (erstreckt sich selbst) in such a way that in advance its own being is constituted as stretching-along (Erstreckung). In Dasein's being already lies the "between" with relation to birth and death. By no means, conversely, "is" Dasein actual in a time-point and, in addition, "surrounded" by the non-actual of its birth and death. Existentially understood, birth is not, and never is, something past in the sense of the no-longer-present-at-hand, just as little as death has the mode of being of the not-yet-present-at-hand, arriving outstanding. Factical Dasein exists natively (existiert gebürtig), and natively it also already dies, in the sense of being toward death. Both "ends" and their "between" are, as long as Dasein factically exists, and they are in the sole way possible on the ground of Dasein's being as care: in the unity of thrownness and fleeing or anticipating being toward death, birth and death "hang together" in the Dasein-like manner. As care, Dasein is the "between" (Als Sorge ist das Dasein das »Zwischen«). The paragraph is the chapter's foundation-stone, and every clause bears weight. The self-stretching (no track filled; the being is the stretching — Erstreckung as an existential, not a measure); birth de-pastified exactly as death was de-futurized (§ 48's operation now performed on the other end: born-ness a way I am, not an event behind me — gebürtig existieren, the beautiful coinage); dying already in being born (the Ackermann's sentence structurally redeemed); and the closing identification that dissolves the between-problem: Dasein does not occupy the between — it is it; care itself the span. The connectedness of life is not to be assembled from moments because existence never was punctual.

The ninth unit names the new phenomenon: happening. The constitutional totality of care, however, has the possible ground of its unity in temporality; the ontological clarification of the "life-connectedness" — of Dasein's specific stretching-along, movedness, and persistence — must accordingly be approached in the horizon of this being's temporal constitution. The movedness (Bewegtheit) of existence is not the motion of something present-at-hand; it determines itself from the stretching-along of Dasein. The specific movedness of the stretched self-stretching we call the happening (Geschehen) of Dasein. The question of Dasein's "connectedness" is the ontological problem of its happening; laying free the happening-structure and its existential-temporal conditions of possibility means winning an ontological understanding of historicity. The unit mints the chapter's central term with its whole pedigree attached: Geschehen — the movedness proper to a self-stretching being (no local motion, no process) — and the equation is drawn in two steps: connectedness-question = happening-problem; happening-structure = historicity. Geschichte to be read from Geschehen: history from the way existence happens.

The tenth unit reconnects to the self: with the analysis of the specific movedness and persistence proper to Dasein's happening, the investigation comes back to the problem touched immediately before the laying-free of temporality: the question of the constancy of the self, which we determined as the who of Dasein. Self-constancy is a way of being of Dasein and grounds therefore in a specific temporalizing of temporality; the analysis of happening leads before the problems of a thematic investigation of temporalizing as such. The retrieval is exact: § 64's Selbst-ständigkeit — the stand won — now revealed as the historicity-question in nuce: how a self persists is how it stretches and happens; and the closing clause promises the deepest stratum: Zeitigung itself as theme.

The eleventh unit fixes the problem's place against the theory of science. If the question of historicity leads back into these "origins," then the place of the problem of history is thereby already decided: it may not be sought in historiography (Historie) as the science of history. Even when the science-theoretical treatment of the "history"-problem aims not only at the "epistemological" clarification of historical apprehension (Simmel) or the logic of concept-formation of historical presentation (Rickert), but orients itself also toward the "object-side," history is, in this question-formulation, in principle accessible always only as the object of a science. The basic phenomenon of history — which lies before and underlies a possible thematization by historiography — is therewith irretrievably set aside. How history can become a possible object for historiography can be gathered only from the mode of being of the historical, from historicity and its rootedness in temporality. The demarcation names the era's two reigning programs (Simmel's epistemology of historical knowing, Rickert's logic of concept-formation — the Baden school's whole industry) and convicts both, even in their "objective" turn, of the same displacement: history pre-cast as science's object, the phenomenon lost before the analysis begins; the order re-fixed: historicity first, Historie derived — § 10's rule (the sciences from the mode of being, never conversely) at its most consequential application.

The twelfth unit declares the method: if historicity is to be illuminated from temporality, and originally from authentic temporality, then it lies in the essence of this task that it can be carried through only by way of a phenomenological construction; the existential-ontological constitution of historicity must be conquered against the covering vulgar interpretation of Dasein's history. The existential construction has its determinate holds in the vulgar understanding of Dasein and its guidance through the hitherto won existential structures. The method-clause invokes § 63 by citation: construction — the owned, violent projection — with its two securities named (the vulgar understanding as foothold, the won existentials as guide); historicity to be wrested, like everything before it, im Gegenzug.

The thirteenth unit gives the entry-plan: the investigation first procures, through a characterization of the vulgar concepts of history, an orientation over the moments commonly held essential to history; therein it must become plain what is originally addressed as historical — and therewith the point of insertion for the exposition of the ontological problem of historicity is marked. The plan is § 58's protocol (begin with what everydayness says; read the mis-seeing as pointer) — § 73 commissioned.

The fourteenth unit states the derivation-rule and files everydayness: the guiding thread for the existential construction of historicity is offered by the accomplished interpretation of the authentic potentiality-of-being-whole and the analysis of care as temporality grown from it. The existential projection of Dasein's historicity only brings to unveiling what already lies enveloped in the temporalizing of temporality. Corresponding to the rootedness of historicity in care, Dasein exists in each case as authentically or inauthentically historical; what stood in view, under the title everydayness, as the nearest horizon of the existential analytic, clarifies itself as Dasein's inauthentic historicity. The paragraph carries two theses of the first rank in three sentences: the unveiling-clause (historicity no new stratum — the temporalizing itself, unwrapped: nothing added to § 65, everything unfolded from it), and the identification that answers § 71's riddle at a stroke: everydayness is inauthentic historicity — the day-after-day the fallen mode of the stretch; the two chapters welded.

The fifteenth unit orders historiography's genealogy: to Dasein's happening belong essentially disclosure and interpretation; from this mode of being of the historically existing being grows the existentiell possibility of an express disclosing and grasping of history. Thematization — the historiographical disclosure of history — is the presupposition for the possible "construction of the historical world in the human sciences." The existential interpretation of historiography as science aims solely at the demonstration of its ontological provenance from Dasein's historicity; only from here are the boundaries to be staked out within which a theory of science oriented to the factical research-operation may expose itself to the contingencies of its question-formulations. The unit sets § 76's program with Dilthey's late title quoted verbatim (the Aufbau der geschichtlichen Welt claimed as founded, not refuted) and puts the science-theorists on notice: their empirical orientation licensed only inside ontologically staked bounds.

The sixteenth unit states the chapter's thesis in one antithesis: the analysis of Dasein's historicity attempts to show that this being is not "temporal" because it "stands in history," but that, conversely, it exists and can exist historically only because it is temporal in the ground of its being. The inversion is the chapter's whole argument compressed: history does not temporalize Dasein; temporality historizes it — the common picture (in history, therefore in time) reversed at the root.

The seventeenth unit grants within-time-ness its due and fixes the order of exposition. Nevertheless, Dasein must also be called "temporal" in the sense of being "in time": factical Dasein, even without developed historiography, needs and uses calendar and clock; what happens "with it" it experiences as happening "in time," and in the same way the processes of lifeless and living nature encounter "in time" — they are within-time. Hence it would be tempting to place before the discussion of the connection between historicity and temporality the analysis — deferred to the next chapter — of the origin of the "time" of within-time-ness from temporality. But in order to take from the vulgar characterization of the historical, by means of the time of within-time-ness, its seeming self-evidence and exclusiveness, historicity shall first — as the "substantive" connection also demands — be purely "deduced" from Dasein's original temporality. Insofar, however, as the time of within-time-ness also "stems" from Dasein's temporality, historicity and within-time-ness prove equiprimordial: the vulgar interpretation of the temporal character of history therefore keeps, within its limits, its right. The paragraph settles the chapter-order with strategic candor (historicity before clock-time, lest dates seem history's essence) and files the equiprimordiality-theorem: both descend from temporality, so the datable side of history is genuine — the vulgar view once more preserved in its limits at the very moment of its demotion.

The eighteenth unit takes the measure of the task — and names Dilthey. Does it still need, after this first characterization, the express assurance that the following investigation does not believe it can solve the problem of history by a coup de main? The poverty of the available "categorial" means and the insecurity of the primary ontological horizons become the more obtrusive, the more the problem of history is brought to its original rootedness. The following consideration contents itself with indicating the ontological place of the problem of historicity. At bottom, the following analysis is solely concerned to further, in its own part and in a way-preparing manner, the appropriation of Dilthey's researches — an appropriation that still stands before the present generation. The confession-paragraph is the chapter's signature of intellectual honesty: no Handstreich, categories admitted poor, horizons insecure — and then the dedication, unique in the book: the whole chapter placed in Dilthey's service, its office the preparation of an appropriation the generation still owes; the § 77 homage announced, fundamental ontology presenting itself as Dilthey's executor.

The closing unit tables the chapter: the exposition of the existential problem of historicity — necessarily limited, moreover, by the fundamental-ontological aim — has the following articulation: the vulgar understanding of history and Dasein's happening (§ 73); the basic constitution of historicity (§ 74); Dasein's historicity and world-history (§ 75); the existential origin of historiography from Dasein's historicity (§ 76); the connection of the foregoing exposition with the researches of Dilthey and the ideas of Count Yorck (§ 77). The table sets the five stations — vulgar concept, constitution, world-history, science, and the closing conversation with Dilthey and Yorck — the last a chapter-ending unlike any other in the book: a correspondence given the final word.

##### § 73. The Vulgar Understanding of History, and Dasein's Happening

The opening unit fixes the entry: the next aim is to find the point of insertion for the original question of the essence of history — for the existential construction of historicity; this point is marked by what is originally historical. The consideration therefore begins with a characterization of what is meant, in the vulgar interpretation of Dasein, by the expressions "history" and "historical" — which are ambiguous. The protocol is § 44(a)'s and § 58's once more: the everyday word as the phenomenon's first deposit, its ambiguities the trail.

The second unit clears the first ambiguity: the nearest-lying, often noted, but by no means "approximate" ambiguity of the term "history" announces itself in that it means both the "historical actuality" and the possible science of it; the signification of "history" in the sense of historical science (Historie) we provisionally exclude. The exclusion enforces § 72's place-decision terminologically: Geschichte versus Historie — the happening versus its science — the German's luck (two words where English has one) made to carry the whole founding-order.

The third unit takes the first and dominant sense: the past. Among the significations that mean the being itself — not necessarily objectified — that one claims privileged use in which this being is understood as past (das Vergangene): the sense announced in the phrase "this and that already belongs to history." "Past" here means: no longer present-at-hand, or else still present-at-hand but without "effect" on the "present." But the historical as the past also has the opposite signification, when we say: one cannot evade history — here history means the past that nevertheless still works after (das Vergangene, aber gleichwohl noch Nachwirkende). However taken, the historical as past is understood in a positive or privative effect-relation to the "present" in the sense of what is actual "now" and "today." "Pastness" has thereby yet a remarkable double sense: the past belongs irretrievably to the earlier time, belonged to the events of that time — and can nevertheless still be present-at-hand "now": for example, the remains of a Greek temple; a "piece of the past" is still "present" with it. The analysis catalogues the first sense's internal strains with a collector's care: past as inert versus past as still-working (the two idioms — "belongs to history" and "no escaping history" — contradicting each other from within the same word), and both indexed to the now; the temple-fragment planted as the exhibit the museum-analysis will interrogate.

The fourth unit takes the second sense: provenance. History then means not so much the "past" as the derivation (Herkunft) from it: what "has a history" stands in the connectedness of a becoming, wherein the "development" is now rise, now decline; what "has a history" in this way can at the same time "make" history — "epoch-making," it determines "presently" a "future." History here means an event- and "effect-connectedness" drawing itself through "past," "present," and "future"; the past has here no special priority. The second sense corrects the first's tense-bias: history as the through-running nexus (having and making history — the idiom-pair again doing the work), with all three dimensions engaged.

The fifth unit takes the third: the region. History means further the whole of beings that changes "in time" — and indeed, in distinction from nature, which likewise moves "in time," the transformations and destinies of men, human associations, and their "culture." History here means not so much the mode of being, the happening, as the region of beings that one distinguishes from nature with regard to the essential determination of man's existence by "spirit" and "culture" — although nature too, in a certain way, belongs to history so understood. The third sense is the Geisteswissenschaften's charter-concept (spirit's realm against nature's) — registered with its instability noted in the concessive clause: nature keeps leaking back in (landscape, climate, soil — § 75's geschichtlicher Boden waiting).

The sixth unit takes the fourth in one sentence: and finally, the "handed-down" as such counts as historical — whether historiographically known, or taken over as self-evident and concealed in its provenance. The fourth sense is tradition (das Überlieferte) — with the decisive rider that will carry §§ 74–76: the handing-down works also, and mostly, incognito.

The seventh unit gathers them: taking the four significations together, we get — history is the specific happening of existing Dasein occurring in time, in such a way that the happening that is "past" in being-with-one-another and at the same time "handed down" and still working counts as history in the emphatic sense. The synthesis is deliberately provisional (the vulgar concept's own sum, not yet the existential one): happening, in time, with-others, past-yet-transmitted-yet-working — four moments awaiting their ground.

The eighth unit finds the common root and poses the question-battery. The four significations hang together in that they relate to man as the "subject" of events. How is the happening-character of these to be determined? Is the happening a succession of processes, a changing emergence and vanishing of occurrences? In what way does this happening of history belong to Dasein? Is Dasein first factically "present-at-hand," to get then occasionally "into a history"? Does Dasein first become historical through an interweaving with circumstances and occurrences? Or is the being of Dasein first constituted through the happening, so that only because Dasein is historical in its being are such things as circumstances, occurrences, and destinies ontologically possible? And why, in the "temporal" characterization of Dasein happening "in time," has precisely the past the emphasized function? The battery is the section's engine: the common root (man as history's "subject") granted and immediately radicalized — the alternative posed in the book's constant form (does Dasein fall into history, or does historicity first make circumstance and destiny possible?), with the past's strange priority flagged as the riddle the museum-piece will crack.

The ninth unit sets the method from the riddle: if history belongs to Dasein's being, and this being grounds in temporality, then it is natural to begin the existential analysis of historicity with those characters of the historical that manifestly have a temporal sense: the sharper characterization of the remarkable priority of the "past" in the concept of history shall prepare the exposition of historicity's basic constitution. The transition licenses the coming case-study: interrogate the vulgar concept at its temporal center — the Vergangenheits-primacy — and let its incoherence yield the phenomenon.

The tenth unit interrogates the museum-piece — the section's celebrated analysis. "Antiquities" preserved in the museum — household gear, for example — belong to a "past time" and are nevertheless still present-at-hand in the "present." How far is this equipment historical, when it is not yet past? Only, say, because it became an object of historical interest, of curatorship and regional lore? But such equipment can be a historiographical object only because it is in itself somehow historical. The question repeats: with what right do we call this being historical, when it is not past? Or do these "things," though still present-at-hand today, have "something past" "about them"? Are they, the present-at-hand, then still what they were? Manifestly the "things" have changed; the gear has become, "in the course of time," brittle and worm-eaten. But the specific past-character that makes it something historical does not lie in this transience, which continues also during its presence-at-hand in the museum. What, then, is past about the equipment? What were the "things" that they today no longer are? They are still the determinate use-gear — but out of use. However, supposing they stood, like many heirlooms in the household, still in use today: would they then not yet be historical? Whether in use or out of use, they are nevertheless no longer what they were. What is "past"? Nothing other than the world within which they, belonging to an equipment-context, encountered as ready-to-hand and were used by a concernful Dasein being-in-the-world. The world is no longer. But what was formerly innerworldly in that world is still present-at-hand. As world-belonging equipment, what is now still present-at-hand can nevertheless belong to the "past." What, however, does the no-longer-being of world mean? World is only in the manner of existing Dasein, which is factical as being-in-the-world. The analysis is among the book's most perfect: every naive answer eliminated in sequence — not curatorial interest (which presupposes the historicity it would confer), not decay (worms work in the museum too — transience is not pastness), not disuse (the heirloom in service is historical still) — until the remainder stands alone: what is past is the world; the jug outlives the household, the temple its Greece — the thing present, its world gone. Secondary historicity discovered by subtraction, and the world-concept (§ 18, § 69c) cashed at the vitrine: world is only as existing Dasein's, so a world can cease while its furniture persists.

The eleventh unit draws the ontological consequence — da-gewesen. The historical character of the still-preserved antiquities grounds, then, in the "past" of the Dasein to whose world they belonged. According to this, only "past" Dasein would be historical, not "present" Dasein. But can Dasein be past at all, if we determine "past" as "now no longer present-at-hand or ready-to-hand"? Manifestly Dasein can never be past — not because it is imperishable, but because it can essentially never be present-at-hand: rather, if it is, it exists. Dasein that no longer exists, however, is, in the ontologically strict sense, not past but having-been-there (da-gewesen). The still-present antiquities have a "past"- and history-character on the ground of their equipmental belonging to, and provenance from, a been world of a Dasein that has-been-there; this Dasein is the primarily historical. But does Dasein first become historical by no longer being there? Or is it not precisely historical as factically existing? Is Dasein only been in the sense of the having-been-there — or is it been as making-present-futural, that is, in the temporalizing of its temporality? The paragraph completes § 65's lexical legislation at history's door: vergangen barred from Dasein by category (never vorhanden, hence never past) — the dead are da-gewesen, having-been-there: existence's perfect, not presence's lapse; and the closing question-pair springs the section's trap: if the departed are the primarily historical, history would be an affair of the dead — the next unit's assertion will reverse it.

The twelfth unit summarizes the preliminary yield: from this analysis of the still-present and yet somehow "past" equipment it becomes plain that such beings are historical only on the ground of their world-belonging; the world, however, has the mode of being of the historical because it constitutes an ontological determinateness of Dasein. Further it shows itself: the time-determination "pastness" lacks unambiguous sense and manifestly distinguishes itself from beenness, which we came to know as a constitutive of the ecstatic unity of Dasein's temporality. But therewith the riddle finally only sharpens: why is it precisely "pastness" — or, more appropriately spoken, beenness — that predominantly determines the historical, when beenness temporalizes itself equiprimordially with present and future? The audit banks two results (world-belonging as secondary historicity's ground; Vergangenheit ≠ Gewesenheit) and re-poses the eighth unit's riddle at the deeper level, now in the corrected vocabulary — the question § 74 will answer through the Erbe and Wiederholung.

The thirteenth unit legislates the order: primarily historical — we assert — is Dasein; secondarily historical, however, is the innerworldly encountered — not only ready-to-hand equipment in the widest sense, but also environing nature as "historical ground" (geschichtlicher Boden). We call the non-Dasein-like beings that are historical on the ground of their world-belonging the world-historical (das Weltgeschichtliche). It can be shown that the vulgar concept of "world-history" springs precisely from the orientation to this secondarily historical; the world-historical is not first historical on the ground of a historiographical objectification, but as the being that it, innerworldly encountering, in itself is. The unit mints the chapter's second great term: das Weltgeschichtliche — things, works, institutions, and even the land itself (the geschichtlicher Boden: soil, river, coast as history's ground) historical in themselves through world-belonging, before and without any historian; the vulgar "world-history" diagnosed as this secondary stratum mistaken for the primary.

The fourteenth unit draws the anti-chronological consequence: the analysis led not only back to Dasein as the primarily historical, but made doubtful whether the temporal characterization of the historical may be oriented primarily to the being-in-time of something present-at-hand at all. Beings do not become "more historical" with their moving-off into an ever more distant past, so that the oldest would be the most authentically historical; and the "temporal" distance from the now and today has, again, no primarily constitutive significance for the historicity of authentically historical beings — not because they are not "in time" and are timeless, but because they exist so originally temporally as something present-at-hand "in time," passing or arriving, by its ontological essence never can be. The paragraph kills antiquarianism's axiom in one clause (age is not historicity — the oldest not the most historical) and grounds the kill correctly: not timelessness (no Platonic exit) but a more original temporality than any date can register; distance-from-now a parameter of the secondary stratum only.

The closing unit meets the shrug. Circumstantial reflections, one will say — that human Dasein is at bottom the primary "subject" of history no one denies, and the cited vulgar concept says it plainly enough. But the thesis "Dasein is historical" means not only the ontic factum that man presents a more or less important "atom" in the machinery of world-history and remains the plaything of circumstances and events; it poses the problem: how far, and on the ground of what ontological conditions, does historicity belong, as essential constitution, to the subjectivity of the "historical" subject? The section closes by converting the concession into the task: everyone grants man history's subject — the thesis asks what a subject must be, in its being, to be capable of history at all; the atom-and-plaything picture (historicism's man, Weltgetriebe's pawn) set aside for § 74's answer: the being whose happening is resolute self-transmission.

##### § 74. The Basic Constitution of Historicity

The opening unit states the thesis and the reduction: Dasein has factically in each case its "history," and can have such, because the being of this being is constituted by historicity. This thesis is to be justified with the intent of exposing the ontological problem of history as an existential one. Dasein's being was delimited as care; care grounds in temporality; within its circuit we must accordingly seek out a happening that determines existence as historical. Thus the interpretation of Dasein's historicity proves at bottom only a more concrete working-out of temporality — which we unveiled first with regard to authentic existing, characterized as anticipatory resoluteness. How far does an authentic happening of Dasein lie herein? The frame is set with the unveiling-clause of § 72 enforced: historicity as temporality worked out, nothing more — and the site fixed once more at the authentic summit: the happening to be read off vorlaufende Entschlossenheit.

The second unit finds the gap in resoluteness. Resoluteness was determined as the reticent, anxiety-ready self-projection upon one's own being-guilty; it gains its authenticity as anticipatory resoluteness, in which Dasein understands itself with regard to its potentiality-of-being in such a way that it goes under the eyes of death (dem Tod unter die Augen geht), so as to take over wholly, in its thrownness, the being that it itself is. The resolute taking-over of one's own factical "Da" means at the same time the resolution into the situation. What Dasein in each case factically resolves upon, the existential analysis on principle cannot discuss; but the present investigation excludes even the existential projection of factical possibilities of existence. Nevertheless it must be asked whence, in general, the possibilities can be drawn upon which Dasein factically projects itself. The anticipatory self-projection upon the unoutstrippable possibility of existence — death — vouches only for the wholeness and authenticity of resoluteness; the factically disclosed possibilities of existence are not to be taken from death. And this the less, as anticipation into the possibility means no speculation about it, but precisely a coming-back upon the factical Da. Should, then, the taking-over of the self's thrownness into its world disclose a horizon from which existence wrests its factical possibilities? Was it not moreover said that Dasein never gets back behind its thrownness? Before deciding overhastily whether Dasein draws its authentic possibilities from thrownness or not, we must assure ourselves of the full concept of this basic determinateness of care. The paragraph opens the section's real question with exemplary honesty: the whole apparatus of Division Two certifies the form of authentic existence (whole, owned) and supplies no content — death gives no programs (the anticipation returns to the Da empty-handed of directives); so whence the possibilities? The suspicion falls on thrownness — guarded at once by the nie zurück of § 58 — and the demand is for thrownness's full concept: the throw about to show itself as inheritance.

The third unit fills the concept: the throw is worldly and shared. Thrown, Dasein is indeed delivered over to itself and its potentiality-of-being — but as being-in-the-world: thrown, it is dependent upon a "world" and exists factically with others. Proximally and mostly the self is lost in das Man; it understands itself from the possibilities of existence that "circulate" in the current "average" public interpretedness of Dasein — mostly made unrecognizable by ambiguity, yet still familiar. Authentic existentiell understanding so little withdraws from the traditional interpretedness that it in each case seizes the chosen possibility in the resolution from it, and against it, and yet again for it (aus ihr und gegen sie und doch wieder für sie). The paragraph is the section's hinge and one of the book's most compressed formulas: the possibilities circulate — thrownness is always thrownness into a stocked, interpreted with-world — and the authentic relation to that stock is the triple preposition: from it (no other source), against it (wrested from ambiguity), for it (returned, renewed). Authenticity as critical inheritance: no creation ex nihilo, no submission — the whole doctrine of tradition in nine words.

The fourth unit mints heritage and fate. Resoluteness, in which Dasein comes back upon itself, discloses the current factical possibilities of authentic existing from the heritage (Erbe) that it, as thrown, takes over. The resolute coming-back upon thrownness harbors in itself a self-transmitting (Sichüberliefern) of traditional possibilities — though not necessarily as traditional. If everything "good" is heirloom (Erbschaft), and the character of "goodness" lies in the making-possible of authentic existence, then in resoluteness there constitutes itself, in each case, the handing-down of a heritage. The more authentically Dasein resolves itself — that is, understands itself unambiguously from its ownmost, distinguished possibility in anticipating death — the more unambiguous and unaccidental is the choosing finding of the possibility of its existence. Only anticipation into death drives out every accidental and "provisional" possibility; only being-free for death gives Dasein its goal absolutely (das Ziel schlechthin) and thrusts existence into its finitude. The seized finitude of existence tears one back out of the endless manifold of the nearest offering possibilities — of comfort, taking-lightly, shirking — and brings Dasein into the simplicity of its fate (Schicksal). With this we designate the original happening of Dasein, lying in authentic resoluteness, in which it hands itself down to itself, free for death, in a possibility that it has inherited and yet chosen (in einer ererbten, aber gleichwohl gewählten Möglichkeit). The paragraph is the chapter's doctrinal center, and its terms must be weighed singly. Erbe: the possibilities' source named — the throw as legacy, answered to the second unit's question; the incognito-clause (not necessarily known as inherited) keeping the phenomenon wider than antiquarian consciousness. The goodness-sentence, the book's nearest approach to an axiology: the good is what enables authentic existence, and all of it is inherited. The finitude-mechanism: death as selector — the running-ahead burning off the accidental, the finite freedom concentrating the dispersed manifold into simplicity. And the definition itself: Schicksal — not what befalls (the next unit severs that) but the happening of resolute self-transmission, its formula the hendiadys that carries everything: inherited and yet chosen — thrownness and projection, the two nullities of § 58, fused in one possibility; fate as owned inheritance. Amor fati re-thought without amor's resignation: the chosen throw.

The fifth unit severs fate from fortune: Dasein can be struck by blows of fate only because, in the ground of its being, it is fate in the characterized sense. Existing fatefully in self-transmitting resoluteness, Dasein is, as being-in-the-world, disclosed for the "coming-toward" of "fortunate" circumstances and the cruelty of accidents. Fate does not first arise through the collision of circumstances and occurrences: even the irresolute one is driven about by them — more than the one who has chosen — and can nevertheless "have" no fate. The severance is exact and paradoxical in the right way: Schicksalsschläge presuppose Schicksal — only the fated can be struck (the resolute alone has the openness in which fortune and cruelty register as such); while the irresolute, most buffeted, has no fate at all: mere weather, no destiny. Fate an achievement of resoluteness, not a quantum of happenings.

The sixth unit deepens the power-structure and widens to destiny. When Dasein, anticipating, lets death become powerful in itself, it understands itself, free for death, in the own super-power (Übermacht) of its finite freedom — which "is" only in the having-chosen of the choice — so as to take over, in this freedom, the powerlessness (Ohnmacht) of abandonment to itself and to become clear-sighted for the accidents of the disclosed situation. But if fateful Dasein, as being-in-the-world, exists essentially in being-with with others, its happening is a co-happening (Mitgeschehen) and determined as destiny (Geschick): with this we designate the happening of the community, of the people (das Geschehen der Gemeinschaft, des Volkes). Destiny does not compose itself out of individual fates, any more than being-with-one-another can be conceived as a coming-together of several subjects; in being-with-one-another in the same world, and in resoluteness for determinate possibilities, the fates are already guided in advance. In communication and in struggle (In der Mitteilung und im Kampf) the power of destiny first becomes free. The fateful destiny of Dasein in and with its "generation" constitutes the full, authentic happening of Dasein — the note referring, for the concept of "generation," to Dilthey's 1875 treatise on the study of the history of the sciences of man, society, and state. The paragraph carries the chapter's heaviest freight. The power-dialectic first: finite freedom as Übermacht that consists in taking over Ohnmacht — the super-power of the powerless, might won by owning the might-less throw; the deepest formula of finite agency in the book. Then the extension that the century would read in its own darkening light: fate shared is Geschick — the happening of the community, of the Volk — with the anti-summative guard immediately posted (destiny no aggregate of fates, on § 26's authority: Mitsein no plurality of subjects) and the media of its liberation named: communication and struggle, Mitteilung und Kampf. The commentary must be double here. Structurally, the step is rigorous: if the throw is shared (the third unit's circulating possibilities), the resolute retrieval is co-retrieval — a generation's destiny the with-world's fate; and Dilthey's sober concept of the generation is the note's anchor. Historically, the sentence would be conscripted: within seven years its author would lend Geschick, Volk, and Kampf to a movement that read them as license — and while the text's own guards (destiny grounded in individual resoluteness; no collective subject; the community's possibilities inherited-and-chosen, not decreed) forbid the totalitarian reading, the vocabulary's availability for it belongs to the sentence's history. The commentary registers both: the analysis stands; the danger was real, and was realized by the author himself.

The seventh unit totals the conditions: fate — as the powerless super-power, readying itself for adversities, of the reticent, anxiety-ready self-projection upon one's own being-guilty — demands as the ontological condition of its possibility the constitution of being of care, that is, temporality. Only when death, guilt, conscience, freedom, and finitude dwell together equiprimordially in the being of a being, as in care, can it exist in the mode of fate — that is, be historical in the ground of its existence. The summation gives fate its complete formula (ohnmächtige, den Widrigkeiten sich bereitstellende Übermacht — the powerless super-power making itself ready for adversity) and its condition-list: the five co-dwellers (death, guilt, conscience, freedom, finitude) whose one house is care — historicity possible only for the being so built.

The eighth unit gives the temporal derivation in a single sentence-cascade: only a being that is essentially futural in its being, so that, free for its death and shattering against it (an ihm zerschellend), it can let itself be thrown back upon its factical Da — that is, only a being that, as futural, is equiprimordially having-been — can, handing down to itself the inherited possibility, take over its own thrownness and be in the moment of vision for "its time" (augenblicklich sein für »seine Zeit«). Only authentic temporality, which is at the same time finite, makes possible something like fate — that is, authentic historicity. The cascade is § 65 recited as historicity's deduction: future (free for death), the shattering rebound (zerschellend — anticipation's recoil off the impossible possibility, the book's most violent verb for the gentlest structure: the future's finitude as the springboard back), beenness (the inherited possibility), the moment (for "its time" — the Augenblick historicized: contemporaneity as achievement). Fate = finite temporality enacted; the italic theorem closing the derivation.

The ninth unit mints repetition — and the choice of the hero. That resoluteness expressly knows the provenance of the possibilities upon which it projects itself is not necessary. But in Dasein's temporality, and only in it, lies the possibility of fetching the existentiell potentiality-of-being expressly from the traditional understanding of Dasein: the resoluteness that comes back upon itself and hands itself down then becomes the repetition (Wiederholung) of a traditional possibility of existence. Repetition is express handing-down — the going-back into possibilities of the Dasein that has-been-there. The authentic repetition of a been possibility of existence — that Dasein choose its hero (daß das Dasein sich seinen Helden wählt) — grounds existentially in anticipatory resoluteness; for in it the choice is first chosen that frees for the contending succession and fidelity to the repeatable (die kämpfende Nachfolge und Treue zum Wiederholbaren). But the repeating self-transmission of a been possibility does not disclose the Dasein that has-been-there in order to actualize it once again: the repetition of the possible is neither a bringing-back of the "past" nor a binding-back of the "present" to the "outmoded." Springing from a resolute self-projection, repetition does not let itself be talked over by the "past" into merely letting it return as the formerly actual. Repetition rather rejoins — replies to (erwidert) — the possibility of the existence that has-been-there. But the rejoinder to the possibility in the resolution is at the same time, as momentary (augenblickliche), the revocation (Widerruf) of that which, in the today, is working itself out as "past." Repetition neither abandons itself to the past nor aims at a progress: both are indifferent to authentic existence in the moment of vision. The paragraph is the chapter's finest, and its concept the book's answer to historicism entire. Wiederholung defined: express retrieval — the incognito inheritance (fourth unit) raised to knowing appropriation; possible only where the choice is chosen (§ 54's formula returning at full depth). The hero-clause — sich seinen Helden wählt — the book's single concession to exemplarity: authentic tradition as elective succession, kämpfende Nachfolge, contending discipleship (fidelity that fights its model, not copies it). Then the triple guard that severs repetition from every restoration: not re-actualization (the possible retrieved as possible, § 31's modality preserved in transmission), hence Erwiderung — the rejoinder: repetition answers the been possibility, converses with it — and Widerruf: the same act revokes the pseudo-past working in the today (the dead tradition disempowered by the living retrieval). And the closing indifference — neither passéism nor progress — places authentic historicity outside the nineteenth century's whole alternative: the moment neither conserves nor advances; it retrieves. Kierkegaard's Gjentagelse honored and out-built; Nietzsche's second Untimely Meditation (§ 76 will cite it) already answered.

The tenth unit re-weights history onto the future. Repetition we characterize as the mode of self-transmitting resoluteness by which Dasein exists expressly as fate. But if fate constitutes Dasein's original historicity, then history has its essential weight neither in the past nor in the today and its "connectedness" with the past, but in the authentic happening of existence, which springs from Dasein's future. History, as a way of being of Dasein, has its root so essentially in the future that death, as the characterized possibility, throws anticipating existence back upon its factical thrownness and thus first lends beenness its peculiar priority in the historical. Authentic being toward death — that is, the finitude of temporality — is the hidden ground of Dasein's historicity (der verborgene Grund der Geschichtlichkeit des Daseins). Dasein does not first become historical in repetition; rather, because it is historical as temporal, it can take itself over repeatingly in its history. For this, no historiography is yet needed. The paragraph answers § 73's riddle at last and inverts the obvious: the past's priority in history is lent by the future — the rebound off death (the eighth unit's zerschellend) is what charges the been with weight; the italic sentence enthroning finitude as historicity's hidden ground is the chapter's deepest theorem — mortality, not memory, makes us historical; and the closing pair of clauses fixes both orders: repetition presupposes historicity (no bootstrap), historiography presupposes both (no scholar needed for a people to have a past).

The eleventh unit consolidates the lexicon: the anticipatory self-transmission, lying in resoluteness, to the Da of the moment of vision we call fate; in it is co-grounded destiny, by which we understand the happening of Dasein in being-with with others. Fateful destiny can be expressly disclosed in repetition with regard to its attachment to the traditional heritage; repetition first makes manifest to Dasein its own history. The happening itself, and the disclosedness belonging to it — or the appropriation of this — grounds existentially in this: that Dasein, as temporal, is ecstatically open. The consolidation stacks the four coinages in their founding order (fate, destiny, repetition, and the disclosure repetition brings) and roots the whole in the one structure: ecstatic openness — history happenable and knowable because existence stands out.

The twelfth unit names the result and re-opens the wound. What we have hitherto characterized as historicity, in conformity with the happening lying in anticipatory resoluteness, we call Dasein's authentic historicity. From the phenomena of handing-down and repetition, rooted in the future, it became plain why the happening of authentic history has its weight in beenness. But it remains all the more enigmatic in what way this happening, as fate, is to constitute the whole "connectedness" of Dasein from birth to death. What can the recourse to resoluteness bring by way of clarification? Is a resolution not, after all, in each case again only a single "experience" in the succession of the whole experience-connectedness? Is the "connectedness" of authentic happening to consist, say, of a gapless sequence of resolutions? Whereby is it that the question of the constitution of the "life-connectedness" finds no sufficiently satisfying answer? Whether the investigation, in the end, in its haste, hangs too much on the answer, without first having tested the question for its legitimacy? Nothing has become so plain from the analytic's course as the factum that the ontology of Dasein falls again and again prey to the temptations of the vulgar understanding of being. This is to be met methodically only by pursuing the origin of the so very "self-evident" question of the constitution of the Dasein-connectedness, and determining in what ontological horizon it moves. The self-objection is staged at full strength (resolutions as beads on the Erlebnis-string again — the fifth unit of § 72 threatening to reabsorb the whole doctrine) and the reply redirected at the question itself: the standing rule of the book (audit the question before serving the answer) invoked with the confession that the vulgar understanding's gravity never ceases — the temptation clause the analytic's permanent weather-report.

The closing unit commissions § 75: if historicity belongs to Dasein's being, then inauthentic existing too must be historical. What if Dasein's inauthentic historicity determined the direction of the question after a "connectedness of life" and blocked (verlegte) the access to authentic historicity and its peculiar "connectedness"? However that may stand: if the exposition of the ontological problem of history is to be sufficiently complete, we cannot in any case dispense with the consideration of Dasein's inauthentic historicity. The handover carries its hypothesis openly: the life-connectedness question itself may be a product of fallen historicity — the questioner's horizon the obstacle; § 75 to test exactly this.

##### § 75. Dasein's Historicity and World-History

The opening unit re-derives the everyday self-reckoning. Proximally and mostly Dasein understands itself from the environmentally encountering and circumspectly attended. This understanding is no mere taking-cognizance of itself that merely accompanies all Dasein's comportments: understanding means self-projection upon the current possibility of being-in-the-world — that is, existing as this possibility; thus understanding, as common sense, constitutes also das Man's inauthentic existence. What encounters everyday concern in the public with-one-another are not only equipment and work, but at the same time what "goes on" with these: the "businesses," undertakings, incidents, accidents. The "world" is at once ground and stage, and as such belongs to the everyday traffic and dealings. In the public with-one-another the others encounter in that bustle in which "one" oneself "swims along"; one knows it, discusses it, furthers it, combats it, retains and forgets it, always in the primary regard to what is thereby driven forward and what "jumps out" (herausspringt). We reckon the progress, standstill, adjustment, and "balance" of the individual Dasein at first from the course, standing, change, and availability of the attended. However trivial this reference to the everyday understanding of Dasein may be, ontologically it is by no means transparent. But why, then, should Dasein's "connectedness" not be determined from the attended and "experienced"? Do not equipment and work, and everything Dasein dwells alongside, belong with it to "history"? Is the happening of history only the isolated running-off of "experience-streams" in the individual subjects?
