The paragraph reinstates the ledger-self of § 59 as the historical self: the day's businesses as one's biography — Fortgang, Stillstand, Fazit computed from the attended — and then, characteristically, gives the everyday view its genuine question: things do belong to history (the reproach against subject-historicism is sound); the isolated experience-stream is indeed too little.

The second unit answers with the world's historicity. In fact history is neither the motion-connectedness of alterations of objects nor the free-floating experience-sequence of "subjects." Does the happening of history then concern the "linkage" of subject and object? If one assigns the happening to the subject-object relation, one must also ask after the mode of being of the linkage as such, if it is this that at bottom "happens." The thesis of Dasein's historicity says not that the worldless subject is historical, but the being that exists as being-in-the-world: the happening of history is the happening of being-in-the-world; Dasein's historicity is essentially the historicity of world, which, on the ground of ecstatic-horizonal temporality, belongs to its temporalizing. Insofar as Dasein factically exists, innerworldly discovered beings also already encounter: with the existence of historical being-in-the-world, the ready-to-hand and present-at-hand are in each case already drawn into the history of the world. Equipment and works — books, for example — have their "fates"; buildings and institutions have their history. But nature too is historical — precisely not, indeed, insofar as we speak of "natural history," but rather as landscape, as region of settlement and exploitation, as battlefield and cult-site. These innerworldly beings are as such historical, and their history does not mean something "external" that merely accompanies the "inner" history of the "soul." We call these beings the world-historical — the note commending, on the question of the ontological demarcation of "natural happening" against the movedness of history, Gottl's long-undervalued Die Grenzen der Geschichte (1904). The paragraph pays § 73's coinage in full: both reductions refused (object-alterations, subject-streams) and the middle theory (linkage) impaled on its own unasked question; then the positive doctrine — history happens as being-in-the-world, so world itself temporalizes historically — cashed in the book's warmest concreta: books with fates, buildings with histories, and nature historical as landscape, settlement, battlefield, and shrine (the geschichtlicher Boden of § 73 unfolded into four words that hold a whole cultural geography); the inner/outer picture of history (soul's history accompanied by external scenery) dismissed in a clause.

The third unit fixes the double sense and the ring's enigma. Note the double signification of the chosen, here ontologically understood expression "world-history": it means, first, the happening of world in its essential, existent unity with Dasein; at the same time, insofar as innerworldly beings are in each case discovered with the factically existent world, it means the innerworldly "happening" of the ready-to-hand and present-at-hand. Historical world is factically only as world of innerworldly beings. What "happens" with equipment and work as such has an own character of movedness, which so far lies wholly in the dark. A ring, for example, that is "presented" and "worn" does not simply suffer changes of place in this being: the movedness of the happening in which something "happens with it" cannot be grasped at all from motion as change of place. This holds of all world-historical "processes" and events, and in a certain way also of "natural catastrophes." We can here pursue the problem of the ontological structure of world-historical happening the less — apart from the necessary overstepping of the theme's limits — as it is precisely the intent of this exposition to lead before the ontological enigma of the movedness of happening in general. The paragraph legislates the term's two registers (world's happening; the happening within it) and then, in the ring, gives the book one of its most quietly radical examples: the wedding-band given and worn — its "happening" (betrothal, fidelity, widowhood) invisible to kinematics; the movedness of meaning irreducible to locomotion, and expressly left as enigma: the ontology of the event confessed missing (the later Ereignis-thinking germinates in this ring).

The fourth unit derives the vulgar view's necessity in three "becauses": it is only necessary to delimit the circuit of phenomena ontologically co-meant in talk of Dasein's historicity. On the ground of the temporally founded transcendence of the world, world-historical things are, in the happening of existing being-in-the-world, in each case already "objectively" there — without being historiographically grasped. And because factical Dasein, falling, is absorbed in the attended, it understands its history at first world-historically. And because, further, the vulgar understanding of being understands "being" indifferently as presence-at-hand, the being of the world-historical is experienced and interpreted in the sense of something present-at-hand that arrives, is present, and vanishes. And because, finally, the sense of being in general counts as the self-evident absolutely, the question of the mode of being of the world-historical and of the movedness of happening in general is "after all really" only the unfruitful circumstantiality of verbal sophistry. The triple weil is a genealogy in miniature: world-historical objectivity prior to all historians (transcendence's gift); the fallen self reading its history off its businesses; the vorhanden-ontology flattening the happening into arrival-presence-vanishing; and the terminus — the shrug: the question itself dismissed as Wortklügelei, word-quibbling; the section's own reception predicted inside its argument.

The fifth unit springs the origin of the connectedness-question. Everyday Dasein is dispersed into the manifold of what daily "passes" (passiert). The opportunities and circumstances that concern, "tactically" awaiting, keeps in view in advance, yield "fate" [in the vulgar sense]; from the attended, inauthentically existing Dasein first computes its history. And because, driven about by its "businesses," it must first gather itself together (sich... zusammenholen) out of the dispersion and the disconnectedness of what has just "passed," if it wants to come to itself, there first arises, from the horizon of understanding of inauthentic historicity, the question of a "connectedness" of Dasein to be instituted — in the sense of the experiences of the subject that are "also" present-at-hand. The possibility of this question-horizon's dominion grounds in irresoluteness, which constitutes the essence of the self's non-constancy (Un-ständigkeit). The paragraph executes § 74's closing hypothesis: the life-connectedness question unmasked as a symptom — asked by the dispersed self that must retro-assemble itself from the day's debris; the demand for a unity to be instituted arising exactly where lived unity is missing. The question's origin its refutation: Dilthey's problem diagnosed rather than solved.

The sixth unit formalizes the exposure: therewith the origin of the question of a "connectedness" of Dasein — in the sense of the unity of the linkage of experiences between birth and death — is exhibited; and the provenance of the question betrays at the same time its inappropriateness with regard to an original existential interpretation of the wholeness of Dasein's happening. Given the predominance of this "natural" question-horizon, it becomes explicable, on the other hand, why precisely Dasein's authentic historicity — fate and repetition — looks as though it could least of all supply the phenomenal ground for bringing what the question of the "connectedness of life" at bottom intends into the shape of an ontologically grounded problem. The double result is exact: the question's pedigree convicts it (a fallen self's demand cannot legislate for the whole phenomenon), and the appearance is explained away: fate and repetition look useless for the connectedness-problem only from inside the horizon that generated the pseudo-problem.

The seventh unit reverses the question and answers it. The question cannot run: whereby does Dasein win the unity of connectedness for a subsequent linking of the arrived and arriving succession of "experiences" — but: in which mode of being of itself does it lose itself in such a way that it must, as it were, only subsequently gather itself together out of dispersion, and think up for itself an embracing unity for the together? Lostness in das Man and in the world-historical was earlier unveiled as flight before death; this flight before... makes manifest being toward death as a basic determinateness of care. Anticipatory resoluteness brings this being toward death into authentic existence. But the happening of this resoluteness — the anticipating self-transmitting repetition of the heritage of possibilities — we interpreted as authentic historicity. Does there lie in it, perhaps, the original, unlost stretchedness of the whole existence, needing no connectedness? The self's resoluteness against the non-constancy of dispersion is in itself the stretched steadiness (die erstreckte Stätigkeit) in which Dasein, as fate, holds birth and death and their "between" "included" in its existence — in such a way that, in such constancy, it is in the moment of vision for what is world-historical in its current situation. In the fateful repetition of been possibilities, Dasein brings itself back "immediately" — that is, temporally-ecstatically — to what has already been before it; but with this self-transmission of the heritage, the "birth" is, in the coming-back out of the unoutstrippable possibility of death, caught up (eingeholt) into existence — so that existence may, to be sure, only accept the thrownness of its own Da more free of illusion. The paragraph is the chapter's resolution, and its logic completes the book's deepest figure. The question inverted (§ 63's method): not how the pieces join, but how the self shattered — dispersion the derivative, needing explanation, not unity. Then the positive: resolute existence is the stretched steadiness — erstreckte Stätigkeit, the § 72 Erstreckung now in its authentic mode — which needs no connectedness because it never fell apart: birth and death held included in the fate that lives them; and the closing clause performs what § 72 demanded: birth caught up (eingeholt — the twin of § 68's Wiederholung) into existence from the rebound off death — natality retrieved through mortality, the other end reached at last, and reached soberly: the caught-up birth yields no myth of origin, only the throw accepted illusionsfreier. The connectedness-problem does not get solved; it gets dissolved — the authentic whole was never in pieces.

The eighth unit gives constancy its ethics: fidelity and reverence. Resoluteness constitutes the fidelity (Treue) of existence to its own self. As anxiety-ready resoluteness, fidelity is at the same time possible reverence (Ehrfurcht) before the sole authority that a free existing can have: before the repeatable possibilities of existence. Resoluteness would be ontologically misunderstood if one supposed it actual as "experience" only as long as the "act" of resolving "lasts": in resoluteness lies the existentiell constancy that, by its essence, has already anticipated every possible moment of vision springing from it. Resoluteness as fate is the freedom for the possibly situation-required giving-up of a determinate resolution; thereby the steadiness of existence is not interrupted but precisely confirmed in the moment. Steadiness does not first form itself through and from the adjoining of "moments"; rather these spring from the already stretched temporality of the futurally-beening repetition. The paragraph is the book's ethics of constancy complete in five sentences: Treue — the self's fidelity to itself as resoluteness's very form (§ 64's Selbst-ständigkeit given its moral name); Ehrfurcht — reverence, the one authority a free existence acknowledges: the repeatable possibilities (not persons, not laws, not values — the heritage as the free one's only sovereign: authority and freedom reconciled in the Erbe); the duration-fallacy barred (resolve no episode — its constancy has pre-anticipated its moments); and § 62's retraction-clause re-derived as fate's freedom: the revoked resolution confirms steadiness rather than breaking it, because the moments spring from the stretch, not the stretch from the moments — the final inversion of the Erlebnis-arithmetic.

The ninth unit draws the counter-portrait — inauthentic historicity. In inauthentic historicity, by contrast, the original stretchedness of fate is concealed. Non-constant as the they-self, Dasein makes present its "today"; awaiting the next new thing, it has also already forgotten the old. Das Man evades choice; blind for possibilities, it cannot repeat what has been — it only retains, and receives, the left-over "actual" of the world-historical that has been, the remnants (Überbleibsel) and the present-at-hand information about them. Lost in the making-present of the today, it understands the "past" from the "present." The temporality of authentic historicity, by contrast, is, as anticipating-repeating moment of vision, a de-presenting (Entgegenwärtigung) of the today and a weaning (Entwöhnung) from the usages of das Man. Inauthentically historical existence, however, seeks the modern, laden with the legacy of a "past" that has become unrecognizable to it. Authentic historicity understands history as the "return" of the possible, and knows that the possibility returns only when existence is open for it, fateful-momentarily, in resolute repetition. The counter-portrait completes the chapter's diptych, each stroke matched: the today presented, the old forgotten (§ 68's signature at the scale of epochs); choice evaded, hence repetition impossible — only Überbleibsel retained: relics and reports, the antiquarian's whole estate; the past read from the present (historicism's method as fallenness's optics). Against it, the two great coinages of the authentic present: Entgegenwärtigung — the de-presenting of the today, the moment as counter-thrust to the present's tyranny — and Entwöhnung, the weaning from das Man's customs: authenticity as withdrawal-cure from the current. And the closing sentence, the chapter's epigram: history as the return of the possible — Wiederkehr des Möglichen, eternal recurrence transposed from actuality into possibility — returning only to the open; the possible knocks once more only where resolute repetition has left the door unbarred. The seeker of the modern, dragging an unrecognized inheritance, is the century's portrait in one clause.

The closing unit confesses the shadow and hands over: the existential interpretation of Dasein's historicity constantly falls, unawares, into the shadow; the obscurities are the less to be stripped off as even the possible dimensions of appropriate questioning are not disentangled, and in all of them the enigma of being — and, as has now become plain, of motion — carries on its essence (sein Wesen treibt). Nevertheless, a projection of the ontological genesis of historiography as science from Dasein's historicity may be ventured; it serves as preparation for the clarification, to be accomplished in what follows, of the task of a historiographical destruction of the history of philosophy. The chapter's penultimate word is its most candid: the double enigma — being and movement (the ring's unresolved Bewegtheit now ranked with being itself: kinēsis, Aristotle's abyss, named as the analysis's standing shadow) — confessed as undispelled; and the handover names § 76's stake precisely: the science of history to be derived so that § 6's destruction of the tradition — the book's own historiographical deed — may finally understand itself.

##### § 76. The Existential Origin of Historiography from Dasein's Historicity

The opening unit sets the question above sociology: that historiography, like every science, is, as a mode of being of Dasein, factically and in each case "dependent" on the "ruling worldview," needs no discussion; beyond this factum, however, the ontological possibility of the origin of the sciences from Dasein's constitution of being must be asked after. This origin is still little transparent; in the present context the analysis is to make the existential origin of historiography recognizable in outline only so far as thereby Dasein's historicity, and its rootedness in temporality, come still more clearly to light. The frame concedes the sociology-of-knowledge platitude in a subordinate clause and passes it: dependence on the age is ontic weather; the question is what a being must be for sciences to spring from it at all — with the office-clause honest: historiography analyzed here for historicity's sake, not its own.

The second unit distinguishes the double presupposition: if Dasein's being is fundamentally historical, then manifestly every factical science remains bound to this happening; but historiography has Dasein's historicity as its presupposition in yet an own and distinctive way. The distinction is the section's hinge: all sciences happen historically (they are done by historical beings); historiography alone has the historical as its theme — bound twice.

The third unit deepens the presupposition and refuses the abstraction-method. One might at first clarify this by the reference that historiography, as science of Dasein's history, must "presuppose" the originally historical being as its possible "object." But not only must history be, so that a historiographical object becomes accessible; and not only is historical cognition, as a happening comportment of Dasein, historical: the historiographical disclosure of history is in itself — whether factically accomplished or not — by its ontological structure rooted in Dasein's historicity. This connection is what the talk of the existential origin of historiography from Dasein's historicity means; to illuminate it means, methodically: to project ontologically the idea of historiography from Dasein's historicity. Conversely, it is not a matter of "abstracting" the concept of historiography from a factical scientific operation of today, or of assimilating it to this. For what guarantees, seen fundamentally, that this factical procedure in fact represents historiography in its original and authentic possibilities? And even if that holds — over which we withhold every decision — the concept could be "discovered" at the factum only along the guiding thread of the already understood idea. But conversely, the existential idea of historiography is not placed in a higher right by the historian's confirming the agreement of his factical comportment with it; nor does it become "false" by his contesting such agreement. The paragraph fixes the method's independence in both directions: the idea projected from historicity, not distilled from the guild's practice (whose representativeness no one can certify); and the working historian neither its licensor nor its refuter — the same status § 62 gave the existential projection of authenticity: neither provable nor damageable by the ontic vote.

The fourth unit applies thematization and finds the condition: in the idea of historiography as science lies that it has seized the disclosure of historical beings as its own task. Every science constitutes itself primarily through thematization: what is pre-scientifically familiar in Dasein, as disclosed being-in-the-world, is projected upon its specific being; with this projection the region of beings is bounded, the accesses to it receive their methodical "direction," the structure of the interpretive conceptuality gains its predelineation. If we — postponing the question of the possibility of a "history of the present" — assign historiography the disclosure of the "past" as its task, then the historiographical thematization of history is possible only if, in general, "past" is in each case already disclosed. Quite apart from whether sufficient sources for a historical envisaging of the past are available, the way to it must in general be open for the historiographical return into it; that such a thing holds, and how it becomes possible, by no means lies in the open. The unit runs § 69b's machinery (thematization: projection, region, direction, conceptuality) on the historical field and isolates the wonder positivism never sees: before all source-criticism, the sheer openness of the way back — that a past is accessible at all — stands as the unexplained condition.

The fifth unit supplies it: insofar as Dasein's being is historical — that is, on the ground of ecstatic-horizonal temporality, open in its beenness — the thematization of the "past," accomplishable in existence, has in general free passage. And because Dasein, and only it, is originally historical, what historiographical thematization pregives as possible object of research must have the mode of being of Dasein that has-been-there. With factical Dasein as being-in-the-world there is in each case also world-history: if Dasein is no longer there, then the world too is having-been-there (dagewesen). This does not conflict with the fact that the formerly innerworldly ready-to-hand nevertheless does not yet pass away, and becomes, as the unpassed (Unvergangenes) of the been world, "historiographically" findable for a present. The answer is § 65's Gewesenheit cashed as historiography's transcendental condition: the way back is open because the historian is his been — ecstatic openness as the archive before all archives; and § 73's museum-result is re-stated in the strict lexicon: worlds da-gewesen, their furniture unvergangen — the relic defined as the unpassed of the passed world.

The sixth unit orders material and understanding: still-present remains, monuments, reports are possible "material" for the concrete disclosure of the Dasein that has-been-there. Such things can become historiographical material only because, by their own mode of being, they have world-historical character; and they become material only through being understood in advance with regard to their innerworldliness. The already projected world determines itself by way of the interpretation of the world-historically "preserved" material. The procuring, sifting, and securing of material does not first set the return to the "past" in motion, but presupposes the historical being toward the Dasein that has-been-there — that is, the historicity of the historian's existence. This founds historiography as science existentially, down to its most inconspicuous, "handicraft" arrangements — the note referring, for the constitution of historical understanding, to Spranger's essay in the Volkelt-Festschrift. The paragraph settles the order the source-positivists invert: no heap of documents starts history's return — the historian's own historicity is the engine, working already in the card-catalogue and the collation (the handwerkliche clause the exact twin of § 69b's microscope-preparations); and the double condition on material (world-historical in itself; understood in advance as innerworldly) locks § 73 and § 32 together: no datum without fore-having, at the archive as at the workshop.

The seventh unit fixes the authentic theme — and lets the scandal speak. If historiography thus roots in historicity, then from here it must also be determinable what is "authentically" the object of historiography. The delimitation of the original theme will have to be accomplished in conformity with authentic historicity and its disclosure of the having-been-there — repetition: this understands the Dasein that has-been-there in its been authentic possibility. The "birth" of historiography from authentic historicity then means: the primary thematization of the historiographical object projects the Dasein that has-been-there upon its ownmost possibility of existence. Is historiography then to have the possible for its theme? Does not its whole "sense" aim solely at the "facts" — at how it actually was? The unit derives the thesis that overturns the discipline's self-image — history's object the possible, not the actual — and gives the outraged Ranke-formula (wie es eigentlich gewesen, audible in the paraphrase) its full voice for the next unit's reply.

The eighth unit answers with the still power of the possible. But what does it mean: Dasein is "factual"? If Dasein is "authentically" actual only in existence, then its "factuality" constitutes itself precisely in resolute self-projection upon a chosen potentiality-of-being. What "factually" authentically has-been-there is then the existentiell possibility in which fate, destiny, and world-history factically determined themselves. Because existence in each case is only as factically thrown, historiography will disclose the still power of the possible (die stille Kraft des Möglichen) the more penetratingly, the more simply and concretely it understands the having-been-in-the-world from its possibility, and "only" presents it. The reply dissolves the fact-cult in its own term: the factual of an existing being is its enacted possibility — facticity constituted in resolute projection, so the truest fact about the dead is what they chose to be able to be; and the closing phrase is among the book's most beautiful mintings: die stille Kraft des Möglichen — the possible's quiet power, disclosed best by the simplest presentation; the historian's art defined as making the been possibility strike home, wie es möglich gewesen against wie es eigentlich gewesen.

The ninth unit dissolves the law/individuality quarrel: when historiography, itself growing from authentic historicity, unveils, repeating, the Dasein that has-been-there in its possibility, it has also already made manifest the "universal" in the unique (im Einmaligen das »Allgemeine«). The question whether historiography has for object only the sequence of unique, "individual" events, or "also laws," is missed at the root: its theme is neither the only-once-happened nor a universal hovering above it, but the factically existent been possibility. This possibility is not repeated as such — that is, authentically historiographically understood — if it is perverted into the pallor of a supratemporal model (in die Blässe eines überzeitlichen Musters). Only factical authentic historicity, as resolute fate, can disclose the been history in such a way that in repetition the "power" of the possible strikes into (hereinschlägt) factical existence — that is, comes toward it in its futurity. Historiography therefore — as little as the historicity of unhistoriographical Dasein — by no means takes its departure in the "present" and from what is "actual" only today, in order to grope its way back from there to a past: even historiographical disclosure temporalizes itself from the future. The "selection" of what is to become possible object for historiography is already made in the factical, existentiell choice of Dasein's historicity — in which historiography first arises, and uniquely is. The paragraph is the section's densest yield: the Windelband–Rickert alternative (nomothetic law versus idiographic uniqueness — the era's methodological civil war) dismissed at the root, both parties sharing the wrong ontology (actuality, once or always); the theme a third thing, the been possibility — which also bars the exemplar-reading: retrieval that fades the possibility into a timeless pattern (die Blässe of the classicist's "eternal Greece") is its second death. And the temporal thesis completes § 74's inversion at the writing-desk: even the historian's disclosure comes from the future — the archive's "selection-problem" (Rickert's Wertbeziehung) solved existentially: chosen already, in the choosing of one's historicity.

The tenth unit turns the objectivity-tables: the historiographical disclosure of the "past" grounded in fateful repetition is so little "subjective" that it alone guarantees the "objectivity" of historiography. For the objectivity of a science regulates itself primarily by whether it can bring the thematic beings belonging to it, in the originality of their being, undisguised to the understanding, against it. In no science are the "universal validity" of standards, and the claims to "universality" that das Man and its common sense demand, less possible criteria of "truth" than in authentic historiography. The inversion repeats § 44(c)'s and § 69c's figure at the historian's bench: objectivity = fidelity to the object's own mode of being — and since the object is been existence, only the fateful reader reaches it; Allgemeingültigkeit unmasked once more as das Man's epistemology, at its weakest exactly where it shouts loudest (the "scientific history" of the seminar).

The eleventh unit grounds the fact-orientation and the tradition-detour: only because the central theme of historiography is in each case the possibility of the existence that has-been-there, and this always exists factically world-historically, can historiography demand of itself the inexorable orientation to the "facts." Hence factical research ramifies manifoldly, making equipment-, work-, culture-, spirit-, and idea-history its object. History is at the same time, in itself, as self-transmitting, in each case in an interpretedness belonging to it, which itself has its own history — so that historiography mostly penetrates to the having-been-there itself only through the history of the transmission (Überlieferungsgeschichte). Therein lies why concrete historical research can hold itself in varying nearness to its authentic theme: the historian who from the outset "throws" himself upon the "worldview" of an age has thereby not yet proven that he understands his object authentically historically and not merely "aesthetically"; and on the other hand, the existence of a historian who "only" edits sources can be determined by an authentic historicity. The paragraph is generosity and rigor in balance: the fact-rigor derived, not disdained (the possible exists world-historically, so its retrieval passes inexorably through things and documents); the doubled historicity of tradition (the sources' own history of interpretation as the standing detour — § 6's insight institutionalized); and the closing pair of portraits, the book's kindest sentence about scholarship: the Geistesgeschichte-virtuoso possibly a mere aesthete, the silent editor of sources possibly the authentic one — the hierarchy of genres revoked in favor of the hierarchy of existences.

The twelfth unit reads historicism as symptom: so too the dominion of a differentiated historical interest, extending to the most distant and primitive cultures, is in itself no proof of the authentic historicity of a "time." In the end, the emergence of a problem of "historicism" is the clearest sign that historiography strives to alienate Dasein from its authentic historicity — which does not necessarily need historiography: unhistoriographical ages are not as such also unhistorical. The diagnosis inverts the age's self-congratulation (universal historical curiosity as culture's crown): omnivorous Historie can be flight — and the very existence of the historicism-crisis (Troeltsch's problem, the relativist vertigo) is read as pathology's symptom: a science estranging its bearers from what it treats. The closing distinction (unhistorisch ≠ ungeschichtlich) frees the archaic ages: peoples without archives, historical in the fullest sense.

The thirteenth unit meets Nietzsche. The possibility that historiography in general can be either of "advantage" or "disadvantage" "for life" grounds in this: that life is historical in the root of its being, and hence, as factically existing, has in each case already decided itself for authentic or inauthentic historicity. Nietzsche recognized what is essential about the "use and disadvantage of historiography for life" in his second Untimely Meditation (1874) and said it unambiguously and penetratingly. He distinguishes three kinds of historiography — the monumental, the antiquarian, and the critical — without expressly exhibiting the necessity of this triad and the ground of its unity. The threefoldness of historiography is predelineated in Dasein's historicity; this at the same time lets us understand how far authentic historiography must be the factically concrete unity of these three possibilities. Nietzsche's division is not accidental; the beginning of his "Meditation" allows the surmise that he understood more than he made known (daß er mehr verstand, als er kundgab). The homage is exactly weighed, in the book's highest style of acknowledgment: the title-question itself grounded (use-for-life possible only because life is historical and has always already decided how), the triad saluted as essential and convicted of groundlessness — necessity and unity unshown — with the analytic offering itself as the missing deduction; and the closing compliment, reserved in the whole book for Nietzsche alone in this form: he understood more than he communicated — the meditation's opening (the beast's unhistorical bliss, the horizon-doctrine) read as cryptic possession of the existential ground.

The fourteenth unit performs the deduction. As historical, Dasein is possible only on the ground of temporality, which temporalizes itself in the ecstatic-horizonal unity of its raptures. Dasein exists authentically as futural in the resolute disclosure of a chosen possibility; resolutely coming back upon itself, it is, repeating, open for the "monumental" possibilities of human existence — the historiography springing from such historicity is "monumental." As beening, Dasein is delivered over to its thrownness; in the repeating appropriation of the possible there lies at the same time predelineated the possibility of the reverent preservation (verehrende Bewahrung) of the existence that has-been-there, at which the seized possibility became manifest — as monumental, authentic historiography is therefore "antiquarian." Dasein temporalizes itself, in the unity of future and beenness, as present; the present discloses, as moment of vision, the today authentically. But insofar as the today is interpreted from the futurally-repeating understanding of a seized possibility of existence, authentic historiography becomes the de-presenting of the today (Entgegenwärtigung des Heute) — the suffering release (das leidende Sichlösen) from the falling publicness of the today: monumental-antiquarian historiography is, as authentic, necessarily critique of the "present." Authentic historicity is the foundation of the possible unity of the three modes; the ground of the foundation of authentic historiography, however, is temporality as the existential sense of being of care. The deduction is a small masterpiece of architectonic: Nietzsche's three kinds mapped one-to-one onto the ecstases — monumental from the future (the repeatable greatness as coming possibility), antiquarian from beenness (reverence, § 75's Ehrfurcht, preserving the site where the possibility shone), critical from the moment (the Entgegenwärtigung of § 75 — critique as the present's de-presenting, and leidend: a suffering release, detachment that costs) — with the unity-theorem Nietzsche owed supplied: authentic historiography is all three at once because temporality is its ecstases at once; the triad's necessity is time's own.

The closing unit hands over to Dilthey and Yorck: the concrete presentation of the existential-historical origin of historiography accomplishes itself in the analysis of the thematization constituting this science. Historiographical thematization has its chief piece in the development of the hermeneutical situation which, with the resolution of historically existing Dasein to the repeating disclosure of the having-been-there, opens itself. From the authentic disclosedness ("truth") of historical existence, the possibility and structure of historiographical truth are to be exposed. But because the basic concepts of the historical sciences — whether they concern their objects or their manner of treatment — are existence-concepts, the theory of the human sciences presupposes a thematically existential interpretation of Dasein's historicity. This is the constant goal that Dilthey's research-work seeks to bring nearer, and which is illuminated more penetratingly by the ideas of Count Yorck von Wartenburg. The handover compresses the undone program (historiographical truth from existential truth; the hermeneutical situation as the historian's chief instrument — § 45's concept given to the discipline) and states the thesis that licenses § 77: the Geisteswissenschaften's basic concepts are Existenzbegriffe — Dilthey's lifelong goal named as this book's own, with Yorck as its sharper seer.

##### § 77. The Connection of the Foregoing Exposition of the Problem of Historicity with the Researches of W. Dilthey and the Ideas of Count Yorck

The opening unit declares the debt: the accomplished laying-apart of the problem of history has grown from the appropriation of Dilthey's work; it was confirmed, and at the same time consolidated, by the theses of Count Yorck, found scattered in his letters to Dilthey — the note citing the Briefwechsel of 1877–1897, published 1923. The declaration is unique in the book — a whole chapter's provenance confessed in one sentence — and the section's peculiar form follows from it: not a critique but a reading, the analytic stepping back to let its ancestors speak.

The second unit shatters the received portrait: the picture of Dilthey still widely current today is this — the "sensitive" interpreter of the history of spirit, especially of literature, who "also" strives for a demarcation of the natural and human sciences, assigning a distinguished role to the history of these sciences and likewise to "psychology," and letting the whole blur into a relativistic "philosophy of life." For superficial observation this sketch is "correct"; but it misses the "substance" — it covers more than it unveils. The demolition of the feuilleton-Dilthey (the fine-fingered essayist dissolving into relativism) is conducted with the book's own category: richtig but covering — correctness as the mask of the essential, § 44's semblance-doctrine applied to a reputation.

The third unit gives the true portrait. Schematically, Dilthey's research-work divides into three districts: studies on the theory of the human sciences and their demarcation from the natural sciences; researches on the history of the sciences of man, society, and the state; efforts toward a psychology in which the "whole fact of man" is to be brought to presentation. Science-theoretical, science-historical, and hermeneutic-psychological investigations constantly interpenetrate and cross; where one direction of view predominates, the others are already motive and means. What looks like dividedness and insecure, accidental "trying-out" is the elementary unrest toward the one goal: to bring "life" to philosophical understanding, and to secure for this understanding a hermeneutical foundation from "life itself." Everything centers in the "psychology" that is to understand "life" in its historical development- and effect-context, as the way in which man is, as possible object of the human sciences, and as the root of these sciences at once. Hermeneutics is the self-clarification of this understanding, and only in derived form a methodology of historiography. The portrait re-founds Dilthey-interpretation for a century: the scattered oeuvre read as one elementare Unruhe — the elemental unrest toward life's self-understanding out of life itself (the hermeneutics of facticity's own ancestral formula); and the last sentence performs the decisive re-ranking: hermeneutics as understanding's self-illumination first, method of the humanities only derivatively — Dilthey rescued from his methodologist admirers with his own deepest tendency.

The fourth unit excuses the surface: Dilthey did, in consideration of contemporary discussions that one-sidedly forced his foundational researches into the field of science-theory, often orient his publications in this direction; but the "logic of the human sciences" is as little central for him as his "psychology" is striven for "only" as an improvement of the positive science of the psychic. The excuse is philologically shrewd: the epistemological Dilthey a concession to the neo-Kantian weather — the man's publications skewed by his critics' agenda; the center elsewhere.

The fifth unit names the shared interest: Dilthey's ownmost philosophical tendency, in the communication with his friend Count Yorck, is once brought unambiguously to expression when Yorck points to "our common interest in understanding historicity" (the author's emphasis; Briefwechsel p. 185). The appropriation of Dilthey's researches, only now becoming accessible in full compass, needs the steadiness and concretion of fundamental confrontation; this is not the place for a detailed discussion of the problems that moved him, and of how they moved him. The formula is lifted from the correspondence like a relic — Geschichtlichkeit zu verstehen, the two friends' watchword adopted as the chapter's own title-concept — with the ongoing edition (the Gesammelte Schriften then appearing) noted as the appropriation's future field.

The sixth unit turns to Yorck on psychology — the first quotation-block. The tendency of Yorck, alive in communication with Dilthey's question and work, shows itself precisely in his stance toward the tasks of the founding discipline, analytic psychology. He writes on Dilthey's academy-treatise "Ideas concerning a Descriptive and Analytic Psychology" (1894): self-reflection as primary means of knowledge, analysis as primary procedure, are firmly set up, and propositions formulated that one's own finding verifies — but there is no advance to a critical dissolution, an explanation and thereby inner refutation, of constructive psychology and its assumptions; this abstention hangs together, Yorck judges, with the concept and position Dilthey assigns to epistemology: only an epistemology gives the explanation of the inapplicability [of natural-scientific method] — it has to give account of the adequacy of scientific methods and to ground the doctrine of method, instead of methods being taken, as now, from the individual fields "at haphazard." The block (with the folded note renouncing fuller Dilthey-exposition since Misch's great introduction is available) lets Yorck state the demand the analytic itself obeys: description is not enough — the friend's descriptive psychology must become critical dissolution of constructivism, and method must be grounded, not borrowed auf gut Glück; the Junker correcting the professor toward radicality.

The seventh unit reads the demand and states the friends' difference. In this demand of Yorck's — it is at bottom that of a logic striding ahead of the sciences and leading them, as the Platonic and Aristotelian was — lies enclosed the task of working out, positively and radically, the different categorial structure of the beings that are nature and the beings that are history (Dasein). Yorck finds that Dilthey's investigations "too little stress the generic difference between the ontic and the historical" (the author's emphasis). "In particular, the procedure of comparison is claimed as method of the human sciences. Here I part from you... Comparison is always aesthetic, always adheres to the shape (Gestalt). Windelband assigns shapes to history. Your concept of the type is a wholly inner one. Here it is a matter of characters, not of shapes. For him history is a series of images, of individual shapes, an aesthetic demand; for the natural scientist there remains, beside science, only aesthetic enjoyment as a kind of human tranquilizer. Your concept of history is nevertheless that of a nexus of forces, of unities of force, to which the category 'shape' should be applicable only in a transferred sense." The paragraph mints the chapter's watchword from Yorck's letter — the generic difference of the ontic and the historical — and glosses the demanded discipline as pre-cursive logic in the ancient style (Plato's and Aristotle's, which led the sciences instead of trailing them: § 3's crisis-doctrine in Yorck's voice); while the quoted polemic against comparison and Gestalt cuts deeper than its target: Windelband's picture-gallery history (and every morphology of cultures — Spengler within range) convicted of ocular aesthetics, with Dilthey half-implicated and half-defended (his types inner, his history a force-nexus).

The eighth unit is a bridging sentence: from the sure instinct for the "difference of the ontic and the historical," Yorck recognizes how strongly traditional historical research still holds itself in "purely ocular determinations" that aim at the corporeal and shape-like. The link-unit isolates Yorck's diagnostic category — Okularität, the eye-bound — the tradition's history as portraiture; the term the next quotations will wield.

The ninth unit lets Yorck strike Ranke and the historical school. "Ranke is a great ocular, for whom what has vanished cannot become actualities... From Ranke's whole manner is also to be explained the restriction of historical material to the political: only this is the dramatic." And: the modifications the course of time has brought appear to Yorck inessential — "the so-called historical school I hold to be a mere side-current within the same river-bed, representing only one member of an old, continuing opposition. The name has something deceptive: that school was no historical school at all [author's emphasis] but an antiquarian one, construing aesthetically, while the great dominating movement was that of mechanical construction; hence what it added methodically to the method of rationality was mere general feeling." The double execution is delivered in Yorck's own aristocratic prose and glossed by placement alone: Ranke — the guild's saint of wie es eigentlich gewesen — a great eyeglass to whom the vanished never becomes actual (the dead as spectacle, hence the political-dramatic diet); and the Historische Schule itself, historicism's mother, un-historical: antiquarian aesthetics in the same river-bed as mechanism — the nineteenth century's two giants, empathic history and causal construction, exposed as one ocular family; § 76's Nietzsche-triad audible beneath (antiquarian without monumental or critical).

The tenth unit assembles Yorck's positive credo from the letters. "The genuine philologist conceives historiography as a cabinet of antiquities: where nothing is palpable — whither only living psychic transposition leads — these gentlemen do not come; at heart they are natural scientists, and become skeptics the more because the experiment is lacking. From all such rubbish — how often, say, Plato was in Magna Graecia or Syracuse — one must keep quite clear: no livingness hangs on it. This external manner, which I have now critically reviewed, comes at last to a great question-mark and is put to shame by the great realities: Homer, Plato, the New Testament. Everything actually real becomes a phantom when it is considered as a 'thing in itself,' when it is not lived." The "scientists" stand over against the powers of the time like the refined French society of the revolutionary era: formalism, cult of form; determinations-of-relation the last word of wisdom. Such a direction of thought has, Yorck means, its own — as he holds, not yet written — history: "the groundlessness of thinking and of the belief in such thinking — regarded epistemologically, a metaphysical comportment — is a historical product." "The wave-oscillations called forth by the eccentric principle that more than four hundred years ago brought up a new age seem to me to have become extremely broad and flat; cognition has advanced to the point of annulling itself, man so far removed from himself that he no longer catches sight of himself. The 'modern man' — that is, the man since the Renaissance — is ready to be buried." And against all this: "All truly living historiography, and not merely one reflecting life's shimmer, is critique." "But knowledge of history is for the best part knowledge of the hidden sources." "With history it is so, that what makes a spectacle and is striking to the eye is not the main thing; the nerves are invisible, as the essential in general is invisible. As it is said: 'if you were still, you would be strong,' so too the variant is true: if you are still, you will perceive — that is, understand." "And then I enjoy the still soliloquy and the intercourse with the spirit of history — who did not appear to Faust in his cell, nor to Master Goethe either. They would not have shrunk back in terror from him, however earnest and gripping the apparition may be: for it is brotherly, kin to us in another, deeper sense than the dwellers of bush and field. The effort resembles Jacob's wrestling — a sure gain for the wrestler himself; and that is what matters first of all." The assembled credo is the correspondence's heart, and the commentary need only mark its convergences: the philologist's Antiquitätenkasten and the Syracuse-rubbish (positivism's facts as the unlived — Yorck's erlebt anticipating the analytic's existenziell); the Renaissance-verdict, four centuries of the eccentric principle flattening into self-annulling cognition — modern man ready for burial (a destruction of the modern age in one letter, more violent than § 6's); the counter-canon: living history as critique (§ 76's third mode in Yorck's words), the hidden sources against the spectacle, the invisible nerves — and the stillness-doctrine, quoting Isaiah's "in quietness shall be your strength" into hermeneutics: stillness as the condition of perceiving, § 60's reticence given its scriptural ancestor. The Faust-passage at the close — the spirit of history brotherly, the wrestling Jacob's — is the century's most intimate image of historical understanding: gain for the wrestler, whatever the angel yields.

The eleventh unit reaches Yorck's deepest stratum: virtuality and the historicity of philosophy itself. Yorck gains the clear insight into the basic character of history as "virtuality" from the knowledge of the being-character of human Dasein itself — thus precisely not science-theoretically from the object of historical observation: "That the whole psycho-physical datum is not [being = being-present-at-hand of nature, the author notes] but lives, is the germ-point of historicity. And a self-reflection directed not at an abstract I but at the fullness of my self will find me historically determined, as physics knows me as cosmically determined. Just as I am nature, so I am history..." And Yorck, who saw through all inauthentic "determinations of relation" and "groundless" relativisms, does not hesitate to draw the last consequence: "But then, given the inner historicity of self-consciousness, a systematics separated from historiography is methodologically inadequate. As physiology cannot abstract from physics, so philosophy — precisely if it is critical — cannot abstract from historicity... Self-comportment and historicity are like breathing and air-pressure, and — however paradoxical it may sound — the non-historicizing of philosophizing appears to me, in methodical regard, a metaphysical residue." "Because philosophizing is living, there is — do not be alarmed — in my opinion a philosophy of history: who could write it! Certainly not as it has hitherto been conceived and attempted, against which you have declared yourself irrefutably: the hitherto question-formulation was simply false, indeed impossible — but it is not the only one. Hence there is further no actual philosophizing that would not be historical; the separation between systematic philosophy and historical presentation is essentially incorrect." "The ability to become practical is, to be sure, the real ground of right of all science; but mathematical praxis is not the only one. The practical aim of our standpoint is the pedagogical, in the widest and deepest sense of the word: it is the soul of all true philosophy, and the truth of Plato and Aristotle." "You know what I hold of the possibility of an ethics as science. Nevertheless it can always be done a bit better. For whom, actually, are such books? Registries upon registries! The only noteworthy thing, the drive to come from physics to ethics." "If one conceives philosophy as manifestation of life, not as the expectoration of a groundless thinking — groundless-seeming because the gaze is turned away from the ground of consciousness — then the task is as sparse in result as it is intricate and toilsome in the winning; freedom from prejudice is the presupposition, and already this is hard to win." The unit gathers Yorck's testament: the sentence the book most needed — that the psycho-physical is not but lives, the Keimpunkt of historicity ("is" glossed by the author, in his one intervention, as Vorhandensein: Yorck's instinct given the analytic's term); the symmetry-formula gerade so wie Natur bin ich Geschichte; and the consequences that read like the book's own program written twenty years early: philosophy's non-historicizing a metaphysical residue (§ 6's destruction demanded from the other side), the systematic/historical divide essentially false, breathing-and-air-pressure as the figure for self-comportment and historicity. The pedagogical passage and the ethics-registries jab complete the man — Plato's truth as education, moral treatises as filing-cabinets — and the last quotation grounds it all in the humblest demand: presuppositionlessness itself hard-won, philosophy as Lebensmanifestation.

The twelfth unit records Yorck's own struggle with expression: that Yorck himself set out to bring the historical (as against the ontic, the ocular) categorially into grip, and to raise "life" into the appropriate scientific understanding, becomes plain from his indication of the kind of difficulty of such investigations: the aesthetic-mechanistic manner of thought "finds verbal expression more easily — explicable from the broad provenance of words out of ocularity — than an analysis that goes back behind intuition... What, by contrast, penetrates into the ground of livingness withdraws from exoteric presentation; hence all its terminology is not commonly intelligible, but symbolic and unavoidable. From the particular kind of philosophical thinking follows the particularity of its linguistic expression." And: "you know my predilection for paradox, which I justify by this — that paradoxicality is a mark of truth, that the communis opinio is certainly nowhere in the truth, being the elementary precipitate of a generalizing half-understanding, related to truth as the sulfur-vapor the lightning leaves behind. Truth is never element. It would be a state-pedagogical task to decompose elementary public opinion and, so far as possible, to make possible, formatively, individuality of seeing and looking. Then, instead of a so-called public conscience — this radical externalization — individual consciences, that is, conscience, would again become powerful." The block is the book's own apologia found ready-made: § 70's diagnosis (language's ocular provenance) in Yorck's words, with the consequence the analytic lives daily — the terminology of livingness necessarily symbolic, uncommon, unavoidable; § 63's violence and § 65's word-torsions pre-justified by the Count. And the paradox-passage joins § 57 across the decades: communis opinio as lightning's sulfur-trail, truth never element — with the closing political theology of conscience (public conscience as radical externalization; the state's true pedagogy the re-empowering of the singular Gewissen) reading like § 54–60 in aristocratic shorthand.

The thirteenth unit radicalizes the friends' watchword. The interest in understanding historicity brings itself before the task of working out the "generic difference between the ontic and the historical"; therewith the fundamental goal of the "philosophy of life" is fixed. Nevertheless the question-formulation needs a fundamental radicalization: how else is historicity, in its difference from the ontic, to be philosophically grasped and "categorially" conceived, than by bringing "the ontic" as well as "the historical" into a more original unity of possible comparison and distinguishability? That, however, is possible only if the insight grows: (1) the question of historicity is an ontological question after the constitution of being of historical beings; (2) the question of the ontic is the ontological question after the constitution of being of non-Dasein-like beings, of the present-at-hand in the widest sense; (3) the ontic is only one district of beings. The idea of being embraces "the ontic" and "the historical"; it is this idea that must let itself be "generically differentiated." The paragraph is the chapter's — and in a sense the book's — argument in three numbered steps: Yorck's difference honored and shown to demand what Yorck lacked: a common ground of comparison, which can only be the idea of being itself — the friends' Lebensphilosophie driven to fundamental ontology as its own truth; the generic difference possible only within the generically differentiable Seinsidee.

The closing unit explains the terminology's confession and speaks the dedication. It is not accidental that Yorck calls the non-historical beings the ontic simply: that is only the reflection (Widerschein) of the unbroken dominion of traditional ontology, which, deriving from the ancient question after being, holds the ontological problematic in a fundamental narrowing. The problem of the difference between the ontic and the historical can be worked out as a research-problem only if it has beforehand assured itself of the guiding thread through the fundamental-ontological clarification of the question of the sense of being in general. Thus it becomes plain in what sense the preparatory existential-temporal analytic of Dasein is resolved to cultivate the spirit of Count Yorck in order to serve the work of Dilthey (den Geist des Grafen Yorck zu pflegen, um dem Werke Diltheys zu dienen). The closing diagnosis is delicate: even Yorck's word "ontic" (for nature alone) betrays the old ontology's reach — being still tacitly equated with presence, so that the historical must stand outside "the ontic" instead of within a wider being; the narrowing only fundamental ontology can undo. And then the sentence with which the chapter ends — among the most gracious in philosophical literature: the analytic resolved (entschlossen — the term of art, deliberately) to cultivate Yorck's spirit in the service of Dilthey's work: the seer honored through the laborer, insight through the oeuvre; Chapter Five signing itself as an act of the very repetition it taught — the retrieval of a been possibility, the friends' interest taken over, inherited and yet chosen.

#### Chapter Six: Temporality and Within-Time-ness as the Origin of the Vulgar Concept of Time

##### § 78. The Incompleteness of the Foregoing Temporal Analysis of Dasein

The opening unit restores the everyday's confiscated word. To demonstrate that and how temporality constitutes Dasein's being, it was shown: historicity, as constitution of being of existence, is "at bottom" temporality. The interpretation of history's temporal character was accomplished without regard to the "fact" that all happening runs off "in time"; to the everyday understanding of Dasein, which factically knows all history only as "within-time" happening, the word remained withdrawn in the course of the existential-temporal analysis of historicity. But if the existential analytic is to make Dasein ontologically transparent precisely in its facticity, then the factical "ontic-temporal" interpretation of history must also expressly be given back its right. The time "in which" beings encounter deserves fundamental analysis the more necessarily, as, besides history, natural processes too are determined "by time." More elementary, however, than the circumstance that the "time-factor" occurs in the sciences of history and nature is the factum that Dasein, before all thematic research, "reckons with time" and directs itself according to it. And here, again, Dasein's "reckoning" "with its time" remains decisive — the reckoning that precedes all use of measuring-equipment cut to time-determination: that reckoning goes before this use and first makes anything like the use of clocks possible. The chapter opens with a debt-payment announced (§ 72's suspended right restored: the everyday's in-der-Zeit was silenced for method's sake, now to be honored by derivation) and the order of analysis fixed at the deepest layer: beneath the sciences' time-factor, beneath the instruments, the pre-instrumental reckoning-with-time — Dasein counting on its time before any counting of it; the clock's condition, not its product.

The second unit poses the everyday questions: factically existing, the respective Dasein "has time" or "has none"; it "takes time for itself" or "can allow itself no time." Why does Dasein take "time," and why can it "lose" it? Whence does it take time? How does this time relate to Dasein's temporality? The four questions are lifted straight from the idiom-hoard (Zeit haben, sich Zeit nehmen, Zeit verlieren) — the vernacular of time-economy set as the section's data, exactly as "man stirbt" and "schuldig" were before.

The third unit states the gap in the analysis so far: factical Dasein takes account of time without understanding temporality existentially; the elementary comportment of reckoning with time needs clarification before the question what it means that beings are "in time." All comportment of Dasein is to be interpreted from its being — from temporality; it must be shown how Dasein, as temporality, temporalizes a comportment that relates to time by taking account of it. The foregoing characterization of temporality is therefore not only incomplete in general, in that not all dimensions of the phenomenon were heeded — it is fundamentally defective (grundsätzlich lückenhaft), because to temporality itself there belongs something like world-time, in the strict sense of the existential-temporal concept of world. How that is possible, and why it is necessary, shall be brought to understanding; thereby the vulgarly familiar "time" "in which" beings occur, and in one therewith the within-time-ness of these beings, gain illumination. The self-audit is severe and precise: not a missing chapter but a structural gap — Weltzeit belongs to temporality itself (as world belonged to the ecstatic horizon, § 69c), so the account of time without its worldly self-publication is defective at the root; the chapter's task the closing of this gap.

The fourth unit gives the derivation-program: everyday Dasein, taking time for itself, finds time proximally at the innerworldly encountering ready-to-hand and present-at-hand; the time so "experienced" it understands in the horizon of the nearest understanding of being — that is, itself as something somehow present-at-hand. How and why the vulgar concept of time comes to formation demands clarification from the temporally founded constitution of being of time-concerned Dasein. The vulgar concept of time owes its provenance to a leveling (Nivellierung) of original time; the demonstration of this origin becomes the justification of the earlier interpretation of temporality as original time. The program repeats the book's constant genetic figure at its last station: time met among things, hence read as a thing — and the Nivellierung-thesis stated with its methodological payoff: derive the level from the original and the original's title is thereby proven (§ 65's a potiori claim to be cashed).

The fifth unit stations Hegel. In the formation of the vulgar concept of time a remarkable wavering shows itself, whether time is to be ascribed a "subjective" or "objective" character: where it is taken as being in itself, it is nevertheless assigned pre-eminently to the "soul"; and where it has "consciousness-like" character, it nevertheless functions "objectively." In Hegel's interpretation of time both possibilities are brought to a certain sublation: Hegel attempts to determine the connection between "time" and "spirit," in order to make intelligible from it why spirit, as history, "falls into time." In its result, the foregoing interpretation of Dasein's temporality and of world-time's belonging to it seems to agree with Hegel; but because the present analysis of time distinguishes itself fundamentally from Hegel already in its approach, and is oriented, in its goal — the fundamental-ontological intent — precisely contrarily to him, a brief presentation of the Hegelian conception may serve to clarify indirectly, and provisionally to conclude, the existential-ontological interpretation. The station-paragraph explains the strange guest of § 82: Hegel admitted because the resemblance is dangerous (spirit falling into time sounds like thrown temporality) — the confrontation to establish that the agreement is of results only, approach and aim contrary; the book securing its flank against its greatest neighbor.

The closing unit defers the being of time and tables the chapter: the question whether and how a "being" pertains to time, why and in what sense we call it "being," can be answered only when it is shown how far temporality itself, in the whole of its temporalizing, makes possible anything like understanding of being and addressing of beings. The chapter's articulation: Dasein's temporality and the concern for time (§ 79); the attended time and within-time-ness (§ 80); within-time-ness and the genesis of the vulgar concept of time (§ 81); the contrast of the existential-ontological connection of temporality, Dasein, and world-time with Hegel's conception of the relation between time and spirit (§ 82); the existential-temporal analytic of Dasein and the fundamental-ontological question of the sense of being in general (§ 83). The deferral is the deepest in the book — whether time "is" waits upon the enabling of Seinsverständnis by temporality's whole temporalizing, i.e., upon Division Three — and the table names the five last stations of the published torso.

##### § 79. Dasein's Temporality and the Concern for Time

The opening unit finds time already spoken in the workshop. Dasein exists as a being for which, in its being, this being itself is at issue; essentially ahead of itself, it has projected itself, before all mere and subsequent observation of itself, upon its potentiality-of-being; in the projection it is revealed as thrown; thrownly abandoned to the "world," it falls, attending, upon it. As care — existing in the unity of the falling thrown projection — this being is disclosed as Da. Being-with with others, it holds itself in an average interpretedness, articulated in discourse and spoken out in language; being-in-the-world has always already spoken itself out, and as being alongside innerworldly encountering beings it constantly speaks itself out in addressing and discussing the attended itself. Circumspectly understanding concern grounds in temporality, in the mode of the awaiting-retaining making-present; as attending reckoning, planning, providing, and preventing, it always already says — audibly or not: "then" shall that happen, "beforehand" that other find its settlement, "now" that be made up which "at that time" miscarried and escaped. The paragraph opens the derivation at its true source — not the astronomer but the shop: care's whole formula recited, § 34's spokenness invoked, and then the discovery: the workshop already speaks time — dann, zuvor, jetzt, damals embedded in every planning sentence, sounded or silent; time's first words are concern's own adverbs.

The second unit assigns the adverbs to the ecstases: in the "then" concern speaks itself out awaitingly; retaining, in the "at-that-time" (damals); making-present, in the "now." In the "then" lies, mostly unexpressed, the "now not yet" — that is, it is spoken in the awaiting-retaining, or awaiting-forgetting, making-present; the "at-that-time" harbors in itself the "now no longer" — with it, retaining speaks itself out as awaiting making-present. "Then" and "at-that-time" are understood together with regard to a "now": the making-present has a peculiar weight. It always temporalizes itself, indeed, in unity with awaiting and retaining, even where these are modified to unawaiting forgetting — in which mode temporality entangles itself in the present, which, making-present, says pre-eminently "now-now." What concern awaits as nearest is addressed in the "right away" (sogleich); what has just been made available or lost, in the "just now" (soeben). The horizon of the retaining that speaks itself out in the "at-that-time" is the "earlier"; that of the "then," the "later-on" ("in future"); that of the "now," the "today." The mapping is complete lexicography of the ecstases in the vernacular: then/awaiting, at-that-time/retaining, now/presenting — each with its implicit counter-clause (not yet, no longer) and its horizon-word (later, earlier, today) — with the present's peculiar weight registered and the falling signature identified inside grammar: the now-now of the entangled present, § 68c's leaping run into speech.

The third unit discovers datability. But every "then" is, as such, a "then, when..."; every "at-that-time" an "at-that-time, as..."; every "now" a "now, that..." (jetzt, da...). This apparently self-evident relational structure of the "now," "at-that-time," and "then" we call datability (Datierbarkeit). It must here still be wholly disregarded whether the dating is factically accomplished with regard to a calendrical "date": even without such "dates," the "now," "then," and "at-that-time" are more or less determinately dated; if the determinateness of the dating stays away, this does not mean the structure of datability is lacking or accidental. The coinage names the section's central find: the time-words are constitutionally relational — every now a now-that (the door slams), every then a then-when — datedness before all calendars, the structure surviving even indeterminate filling; the everyday sentence carrying an ontological joint no theory had seen.

The fourth unit interrogates the self-evident: what is that to which such datability essentially belongs, and wherein does it ground? Can a more superfluous question be posed? With the "now, that..." we mean, "as everyone knows," a "time-point"; the "now" is time. Incontestably we understand the "now-that," "then-when," "at-that-time-as" in a certain way as hanging together with "time" — but that such things mean "time" itself, how that is possible, and what "time" means, is not already conceived with the "natural" understanding of the "now." Is it, then, even self-evident that we "understand without further ado" and "naturally" utter something like "now," "then," and "at-that-time"? Whence do we take these "now, that..."? Have we found such things among innerworldly beings, the present-at-hand? Manifestly not. Were they then found at all? Have we ever set out to seek and ascertain them? "At any time" we dispose over them, without ever having expressly taken them over, and constantly we make use of them, though not always in an utterance: the most trivial, everyday spoken discourse — for example, "it is cold" — co-means a "now, that..." Why does Dasein, in addressing the attended, co-utter — though mostly without vocalization — a "now, that," "then, when," "at-that-time, as"? Because the interpreting addressing of... speaks itself out along with it — that is, the circumspectly understanding being alongside the ready-to-hand, which lets this encounter discoveringly; and because this self-co-interpreting addressing and discussing grounds in a making-present and is possible only as this. The paragraph performs the book's oldest maneuver on its last phenomenon: the trivial word arraigned (§ 1's forgotten question in miniature — whence the now?), the empiricist source eliminated (never found among things, never sought, always already possessed), and the answer given from § 34: every address of beings co-addresses the addresser's presenting — "it is cold" says the sayer's now because saying is a temporalizing that speaks itself along.

The fifth unit names the interpreted presenting "time": the awaiting-retaining making-present interprets itself; and this in turn is possible only because it — in itself ecstatically open — is for itself in each case already disclosed, and articulable in the understanding-discoursing interpretation. Because temporality constitutes the clearedness of the Da ecstatically-horizonally, it is originally always already interpretable in the Da, and therewith familiar. The self-interpreting making-present — that is, the interpreted, addressed in the "now" — we call "time." Therein is merely made known that temporality, recognizable as ecstatically open, is proximally and mostly familiar only in this concernful interpretedness; the "immediate" intelligibility and familiarity of time does not exclude, however, that both original temporality as such, and the origin, temporalizing itself in it, of the uttered time, remain unknown and unconceived. The definition-paragraph is the chapter's keystone: "time," the everyday word, defined as temporality's self-interpretation — the ecstases speaking themselves in the now/then/at-that-time; the § 69 Gelichtetheit supplying the possibility (the open interprets itself); and the double familiarity-clause holding the paradox: time perfectly familiar, its origin perfectly hidden — the phenomenology of § 1's "self-evident concept" completed.

The sixth unit converts datability into proof: that the structure of datability belongs essentially to what is interpreted with the "now," "then," and "at-that-time" becomes the most elementary proof of the provenance of the interpreted from self-interpreting temporality. Saying "now," we always already co-understand, without co-saying it, a "— that this and that..." Why? Because the "now" interprets a making-present of beings: in the "now, that..." lies the ecstatic character of the present. The datability of the "now," "then," and "at-that-time" is the reflection (Widerschein) of temporality's ecstatic constitution, and therefore essential to the uttered time itself: the structure of datability is the evidence that these — sprung from the stem of temporality — are themselves time. The interpreting utterance of the "now," "then," and "at-that-time" is the most original giving-of-time (Zeitangabe). And because in the ecstatic unity of temporality — which is understood, unthematically and unrecognizably as such, with datability — Dasein is in each case already disclosed to itself as being-in-the-world, and innerworldly beings are discovered in one therewith, the interpreted time in each case also already has a dating from the beings encountering in the Da's disclosedness: now, that — the door slams; now, that — the book is missing to me, and the like. The proof-paragraph delivers the chapter's central inference with its own image: datability as the Widerschein — the reflection — of ecstasy: the now points beyond itself to an event because the present is a rapture toward beings; the relational grammar of the time-words is temporality's fingerprint on language. And the two homely datings (the slamming door, the missing book) place the whole doctrine in a study at evening.

The seventh unit extends it to the horizons: on the ground of the same origin from ecstatic temporality, the horizons belonging to the "now," "then," and "at-that-time" also have the character of datability — as "today, when...," "later-on, when...," and "earlier, when..." The one-sentence unit completes the system: even the frame-words (today, later, earlier) are dated — the horizon-terms of the second unit drawn into the proof.

The eighth unit unfolds spannedness. If awaiting, understanding itself in the "then," interprets itself, and thereby, as making-present, understands what it awaits from out of its "now," then in the "giving" of the "then" there already lies the "and now not yet": the making-present awaiting understands the "until-then" (bis dahin). Interpretation articulates this "until-then" — namely that it "has its time" — as the meanwhile (das Inzwischen), which likewise has the datability-relation, coming to expression in the "during which..." (während dessen). Concern can articulate the "during" itself again, awaitingly, through further "then"-specifications: the "until-then" is divided by a number of "from-then-till-thens," which, however, are "embraced" in advance in the awaiting projection of the primary "then." With the awaiting-presenting understanding of the "during," the "lasting" (das Währen) is articulated: this duration is, again, the time manifest in temporality's self-interpretation — the time understood, unthematically, as "span" (Spanne) in concern. The awaiting-retaining making-present "interprets" a spanned "during" only because it is thereby disclosed to itself as the ecstatic stretchedness of historical temporality, even if unrecognized as such. And here a further peculiarity of the "given" time shows itself: not only the "during" is spanned, but every "now," "then," and "at-that-time" has, with the datability-structure, in each case a spannedness of varying span-width: "now" — in the recess, at the meal, in the evening, in summer; "then" — at breakfast, on the climb, and the like. The paragraph adds the second structural moment — Gespanntheit — with its derivation from § 72: duration interpretable only by a being that is its stretch (the between of birth and death reflected in every "meanwhile"); and the closing series (now in the pause, at supper, in summer — then at breakfast, on the ascent) settles an old dispute in passing: the lived now is never a point — the instant of the theorists an artifact, the everyday now as wide as its dating.

The ninth unit reads the everyday's leaky time: the awaiting-retaining-presenting concern "allows itself" time thus or thus, and gives it to itself concernfully, even without any and before all specifically reckoning time-determination. Time here dates itself, in the current mode of the concernful allowing-oneself-time, from what is currently attended environmentally and disclosed in disposed understanding — from what one does "the day through." The more Dasein, awaiting, is absorbed in the attended and, unawaiting of itself, forgets itself, the more its time too — the time it "allows" itself — remains covered by this way of "allowing": in the everyday concernful "living-along," Dasein never understands itself as running along a continuously lasting sequence of pure "nows." The time Dasein allows itself has, on the ground of this covering, as it were holes (Löcher): often we can no longer bring a "day" together, when we come back upon the "used" time. But this un-together of the holed time is no fragmentation, but a mode of the temporality in each case already disclosed, ecstatically stretched.
