The way the "allowed" time "runs its course," and the manner in which concern more or less expressly gives it to itself, can be phenomenally appropriately explicated only if, on the one hand, the theoretical "representation" of a continuous now-flow is kept far off, and, on the other, it is conceived that the possible ways in which Dasein gives and allows itself time are to be determined primarily from how it, corresponding to its current existence, "has" its time. The paragraph is a phenomenological gem hiding in the derivation: the day that will not add up — gelöcherte Zeit, time with holes, the evening's failed audit of the hours — read rightly: not fragmentation of a stream (there is no stream) but the self-forgetting mode of the one stretched temporality; the continuous now-flow expelled as theory's fiction even for describing everydayness, and the economics of time indexed, finally, to existence: how one has time follows from how one is.

The tenth unit contrasts the two time-economies. Earlier, authentic and inauthentic existing were characterized with regard to the modes of the temporalizing of temporality founding them: according to that, the irresoluteness of inauthentic existence temporalizes itself in the mode of an unawaiting-forgetting making-present — the irresolute one understands himself from the nearest events and accidents, encountering in such making-present and pressing in changingly; busily losing himself at the attended, he loses at it his time — whence the talk characteristic of him: "I have no time." Just as the inauthentically existing one constantly loses time and never "has" any, so it remains the distinction of the temporality of authentic existence that in resoluteness it never loses time and "always has time." For the temporality of resoluteness has, with regard to its present, the character of the moment of vision; the moment's authentic making-present of the situation does not itself have the lead, but is held in the beening future. Momentary existence temporalizes itself as fatefully whole stretchedness in the sense of the authentic, historical constancy of the self; the temporal existence of this kind has "constantly" its time for what the situation demands of it. But resoluteness discloses the Da only as situation: hence the disclosed can never encounter the resolute one in such a way that he could irresolutely lose his time at it. The paragraph is the book's ethics of time complete, hung on two idioms: "ich habe keine Zeit" diagnosed — the busiest as the poorest, time lost at the attended because the self is lost there — against the resolute one's constant having: never losing time not by better scheduling but by the Augenblick's constitution: whatever meets him meets him in the situation, where nothing solicits dispersal. Wealth in time as a mode of selfhood: § 75's erstreckte Stätigkeit cashed as the quiet superabundance of the resolved.

The eleventh unit gives both their ground in one sentence: factically thrown Dasein can "take" time for itself and lose it only because to it, as ecstatically stretched temporality, with the disclosedness of the Da grounded in this temporality, a "time" is allotted (beschieden). The one-line unit banks the pair: taking and losing alike presuppose the allotment — time first given with the Da; economy possible only for the endowed.

The closing unit derives publicness and hands over: as disclosed, Dasein exists factically in the manner of being-with with others; it holds itself in a public, average intelligibility. The "now, that..." and "then, when..." interpreted and uttered in everyday being-with-one-another are understood fundamentally, even though they are unambiguously dated only within certain limits: in the "nearest" being-with-one-another, several can say "now" "together," each dating the said now differently — now, that this or that occurs. The uttered "now" is said by each in the publicness of being-with-one-another-in-the-world; the interpreted, uttered time of the respective Dasein is therefore, as such, on the ground of its ecstatic being-in-the-world, in each case already published (veröffentlicht). Insofar, now, as everyday concern understands itself from the attended "world," it knows the "time" it takes not as its own; attending, it uses up the time that "is given" (»es gibt«), with which one reckons. The publicness of "time" is the more penetrating, the more expressly factical Dasein attends to time by expressly taking account of it. The closing derivation adds the third structural moment: the now public constitutionally — sayable together, differently dated, understood by all (the common now no metaphysical mystery but Mitsein's own utterance) — and the expropriation named that § 80 will unfold: the everyday knows its time not as its own; one spends the time "es gibt," the anonymous stock one reckons with — das Man's genitive over the hours.

##### § 80. The Attended Time and Within-Time-ness

The opening unit poses the being-question of public time: provisionally it was only to be understood how Dasein, grounding in temporality, existing attends to time, and how time publishes itself for being-in-the-world in the interpreting concern; thereby it remained wholly undetermined in what sense the uttered public time "is" — whether it can be addressed as being at all. Before every decision whether public time is "after all only subjective," or "objectively actual," or neither of the two, its phenomenal character must first be more sharply determined. The section opens on § 78's wavering (subjective/objective) with the standing rule: phenomenal determination before ontological verdict.

The second unit fixes the publication's necessity: the publication of time does not happen subsequently and occasionally; rather, because Dasein, as ecstatic-temporal, is in each case already disclosed, and understanding interpretation belongs to existence, time has also already published itself in concern. One directs oneself according to it, so that it must somehow be findable for everyman. The two-sentence unit bars the convention-theory: public time no social afterthought — published with disclosedness itself; everyman's time as old as the Da.

The third unit grounds time-reckoning in thrownness. Although the concern for time can accomplish itself in the characterized manner of dating from environmental events, this happens at bottom always already in the horizon of a concern for time that we know as astronomical and calendrical time-reckoning. This does not occur accidentally, but has its existential-ontological necessity in Dasein's basic constitution as care. Because Dasein essentially exists as thrown, falling, it interprets its time, attending, in the manner of a time-reckoning; in this the "authentic" publication of time temporalizes itself, so that it must be said: Dasein's thrownness is the ground for there "being" time publicly (daß es öffentlich Zeit »gibt«). To secure intelligibility for the demonstration of public time's origin from factical temporality, the time interpreted in concern's temporality had first to be characterized in general — if only to make plain that the essence of the concern for time does not lie in the application of numerical determinations in dating: the existential-ontologically decisive element of time-reckoning is therefore not to be seen in the quantification of time, but must be conceived more originally from the temporality of the Dasein that reckons with time. The paragraph delivers the chapter's boldest founding-sentence — thrownness the ground of public time — the calendar's necessity derived from abandonment (the thrown one must read its time off the world it is delivered to); and the anti-quantitative rule posted: number is not the essence of reckoning — the count comes late, the accounting early.

The fourth unit defines the theme: "public time" proves to be the time "in which" innerworldly ready-to-hand and present-at-hand beings encounter — which demands calling these non-Dasein-like beings within-time (innerzeitig). The interpretation of within-time-ness procures a more original insight into the essence of "public time" and at the same time makes possible the delimitation of its "being." The definition-unit converts § 66's advance-coinage into the section's official theme: Innerzeitigkeit as the time-determinateness of things — the "in" of "in time" now the exact object.

The fifth unit derives the need for daylight. Dasein's being is care; this being exists as thrown, falling. Abandoned to the "world" discovered with its factical Da, and attending, referred to it, Dasein is awaiting of its potentiality-for-being-in-the-world in such a way that it "reckons" with and upon that with which, for the sake of this potentiality, it has in the end a distinguished involvement. Everyday circumspect being-in-the-world needs the possibility of sight — that is, brightness (Helle) — to be able to deal, attending, with the ready-to-hand within the present-at-hand. With the factical disclosedness of its world, nature is discovered for Dasein; in its thrownness it is delivered over to the change of day and night: day, with its brightness, gives the possible sight; night takes it. The derivation begins at the body's oldest fact, rigorously placed: circumspection is sight, sight needs light, light is allotted and withdrawn by the sky — the thrown worker delivered to the alternation; nature entering the time-analysis not as object but as the condition of the workshop's eyes.

The sixth unit derives the day. Circumspectly attending, awaiting the possibility of sight, Dasein — understanding itself from its day's work — gives itself its time with the "then, when it dawns." The attended "then" is dated from what stands, in the nearest environmental involvement-context, with the coming-light: the sunrise. Then, when it rises, it is time for... Dasein thus dates the time it must take from what encounters, within the horizon of the abandonment to the world, as something with which it has a distinguished involvement for its circumspect potentiality-for-being-in-the-world: concern makes use of the "readiness-to-hand" of the sun, which bestows light and warmth. The sun dates the time interpreted in concern; from this dating grows the "most natural" time-measure — the day. And because the temporality of the Dasein that must take its time is finite, its days are also already counted (sind seine Tage auch schon gezählt). The "while it is day" gives the attending awaiting the possibility of determining providently the "thens" of what is to be attended — of dividing the day; and the division is accomplished, again, with regard to what dates time: the wandering sun. Sunset and midday, like sunrise, are distinguished "places" this heavenly body occupies; its regularly recurring passage Dasein, thrown into the world, temporalizingly giving itself time, takes into account. Dasein's happening is, on the ground of the dating time-interpretation predelineated from thrownness into the Da, a day-by-day one (tagtäglich). The paragraph is the derivation's most beautiful stretch: the sun as the first tool of time — dated from because light-giving involvement, its stations (rising, noon, setting) the first "places" of the then; the day derived, and with it, in one scriptural clause, the count: because temporality is finite, the days are numbered — Psalm 90 folded into the deduction; and everydayness itself (§ 71's riddle) given its cosmological etymology: das tagtägliche Geschehen, existence day-by-day because thrown under the sun.

The seventh unit derives the clock. This dating, accomplished from the light-and-warmth-bestowing heavenly body and its distinguished "places" in the sky, is a giving-of-time performable in being-with-one-another "under the same sky," for "everyman" at any time and in the same way, within certain limits at first unanimously. What dates is environmentally available and yet not restricted to the currently attended equipment-world: in the latter, rather, environing nature and the public environment are always already co-discovered. On this public dating, in which each gives himself his time, everyman can at once also "count": it uses a publicly available measure. This dating reckons with time in the sense of a time-measurement, which accordingly needs a time-measurer — a clock. Therein lies: with the temporality of the thrown Dasein, abandoned to the "world," giving itself time, something like a "clock" is also already discovered — that is, a ready-to-hand thing that, in its regular recurrence, has become accessible in the awaiting making-present. The thrown being alongside the ready-to-hand grounds in temporality: temporality is the ground of the clock (Sie ist der Grund der Uhr). As the condition of the possibility of the clock's factical necessity, temporality at the same time conditions its discoverability; for only the awaiting-retaining making-present of the sun's course, encountering with the discoveredness of innerworldly beings, makes possible — and at the same time demands, as self-interpreting — the dating from the publicly, environmentally ready-to-hand. The paragraph reaches the chapter's most quoted theorem — die Zeitlichkeit ist der Grund der Uhr — with its full derivation attached: the sky as the first public instrument (same heaven, everyman, unanimous within limits — § 79's publicness given its dome), the clock defined ontologically (any regular recurrence accessible to awaiting presenting), and its double conditioning: temporality necessitates the clock and makes it findable — the horologe's metaphysics complete before a wheel is cut.

The eighth unit orders natural and artificial: the "natural" clock, always already discovered with the factical thrownness of Dasein grounding in temporality, first motivates and at the same time makes possible the production and use of handier clocks — in such a way that these "artificial" ones must be "set" to the "natural," if they are, for their part, to make accessible the time primarily discovered in the natural clock. The one-sentence unit fixes the founding order every chronometer obeys: the works regulated to the sky — Greenwich the sun's clerk; artifice as the natural clock's deputy, never its replacement.

The ninth unit sets the further course: before characterizing the main traits of the development of time-reckoning and clock-use in their existential-ontological sense, the time attended in time-measurement is first to be characterized more completely. If time-measurement first "authentically" publishes the attended time, then in pursuing how the dated shows itself in such "reckoning" dating, the public time must become phenomenally unveiled and accessible. The transition-unit orders the analysis: the measured time's structure first, the measuring's history-in-essence after.

The tenth unit discovers appropriateness and mints world-time. The dating of the "then" interpreting itself in concernful awaiting includes: then, when it dawns, it is time for the day's work. The time interpreted in concern is always already understood as time for... (Zeit zu ...); the respective "now, that this and that" is, as such, in each case suited or unsuited. The "now" — and every mode of interpreted time — is not only a "now, that...," but, as this essentially datable, is at the same time essentially determined by the structure of suitedness or unsuitedness: interpreted time has from the house out the character of "time for..." or "untime for..." (Unzeit für ...). The awaiting-retaining making-present of concern understands time in a relation to a for-which, which in its turn is finally fastened in a for-the-sake-of-which of Dasein's potentiality-of-being. The published time reveals, with this in-order-to relation, the structure we earlier came to know as significance: it constitutes the worldhood of the world. The published time, as time-for..., has essentially world-character; hence we call the time publishing itself in the temporalizing of temporality world-time (die Weltzeit) — and this not because it is present-at-hand as an innerworldly being, which it can never be, but because it belongs to the world in the existential-ontologically interpreted sense. How the essential relations of the world-structure — the "in-order-to," for example — hang together, on the ground of the ecstatic-horizonal constitution of temporality, with public time — the "then, when," for example — must show itself in what follows. Now at any rate the attended time can be structurally completely characterized: it is datable, spanned, public, and, as so structured, belongs to the world itself; every naturally-everyday uttered "now," for example, has this structure and is understood as such — though unthematically and pre-conceptually — in the concernful allowing-itself-time of Dasein. The paragraph completes the structure with its fourth and deepest moment: appropriateness — time constitutionally the time-for and the untime-for (kairos naturalized into the workday: right time and wrong time as original as the now); the chain run home to the Worumwillen (time's fitness anchored, like every in-order-to, in existence's for-the-sake-of); and the coinage delivered with its exact warrant: Weltzeit — time belonging to the world as significance belongs to it, worldly without being innerworldly (the guard against reification posted in the same breath); the four-fold structure (datable, spanned, public, worldly) the section's tabled yield.

The eleventh unit sets the developmental question: in the disclosedness of the natural clock, belonging to Dasein existing thrown-falling, lies at the same time a distinguished publication of attended time, in each case already accomplished by factical Dasein — which heightens and consolidates itself in the perfection of time-reckoning and the refinement of clock-use. The historical development of time-reckoning and clock-use is not to be presented here historiographically in its possible variations; rather it is to be asked existential-ontologically: which mode of the temporalizing of Dasein's temporality becomes manifest in the direction of development of time-reckoning and clock-use? With the answering of this question there must grow a more original understanding of this: that time-measurement — that is, at the same time, the express publication of attended time — grounds in Dasein's temporality, and indeed in a wholly determinate temporalizing of it. The question-unit converts horology's history into ontology's index: not the museum of clocks but the temporalizing their refinement betrays — the direction of development as symptom.

The twelfth unit compares "primitive" and "advanced": if we compare the "primitive" Dasein, which we laid at the basis of the analysis of "natural" time-reckoning, with the "advanced," it shows itself that for the latter the day and the presence of sunlight no longer possess a pre-eminent function, because this Dasein has the "advantage" of being able to make even the night into day. Likewise, for ascertaining the time, an express, immediate look at the sun and its position is no longer needed: the manufacture and use of proper measuring-equipment permits reading the time directly off the clock produced expressly for this. The what-o'clock (Wieviel-Uhr) is the "how-much-time." Though it may remain covered to the respective time-reading, even the use of clock-equipment grounds — because the clock, in the sense of making possible a public time-reckoning, must be regulated to the "natural" clock — in the temporality of Dasein, which, with the disclosedness of the Da, first makes possible a dating of the attended time at all. The understanding of the natural clock, developing with the advancing discovery of nature, gives the directive for new possibilities of time-measurement, relatively independent of the day and of any express observation of the sky. The comparison carries the modern condition in one clause — the Dasein that makes night into day (electric light's ontology: emancipation from the sun's allotment as the "advance") — with the founding kept intact beneath the emancipation: even the wristwatch, blind to the sky, is the sky's tenant through its regulation; independence relative, never absolute.

The thirteenth unit reads the peasant-clock. In a certain way, however, even "primitive" Dasein makes itself independent of a direct reading of time off the sky, insofar as it does not ascertain the sun's position in the heavens but measures the shadow cast by a being available at any time. This can happen first in the simplest form of the ancient "peasant-clock": in the shadow that constantly accompanies everyman, the sun encounters with regard to its changing presence at different places. The shadow-lengths, varying through the day, can be paced off "at any time"; even if the body- and foot-lengths of individuals differ, the ratio of the two remains constant within certain limits of exactness. The public time-determination of a concernful appointment then takes the form: "when the shadow is so many feet long, we will meet there" — the equality of the latitude of the "place" being unexpressly presupposed in the being-with-one-another within the narrower bounds of a nearest environment. This clock Dasein does not even need first to carry with it: in a certain way, it is this clock itself (es ist sie in gewisser Weise selbst). The vignette is the section's most delightful and most profound: the Bauernuhr — one's own shadow paced by one's own feet, the ratio self-correcting (tall man, long shadow, long feet), the appointment made in shadow-lengths — and the closing sentence that no philosophy of instruments has surpassed: Dasein is its own first clock; the body under the sun the original chronometer, measurement's zero-point the measurer himself.

The fourteenth unit poses the sundial's riddle: the public sundial, on which a shadow-line moves, counter to the sun's course, along a numbered track, needs no further description. But why do we find, at the place the shadow occupies on the dial, something like time? Neither the shadow nor the divided track is time itself, nor their spatial relation to each other. Where, then, is the time we thus read directly off the "sundial," and off every pocket-watch? The riddle is posed with maximal simplicity — the instrument dismantled into shadow, track, relation, none of them time — the reading's object missing from its apparatus; the everyday act of glancing at the watch turned inside out into the chapter's central mystery.

The fifteenth unit answers it: what does time-reading mean? "Looking at the clock" cannot mean only: observing the ready-to-hand equipment in its change and following the hand's positions. Ascertaining, in the clock's use, the what-o'clock, we say — expressly or not: now it is so-and-so much; now it is time for...; there is still time... namely now, until... The looking-at-the-clock grounds in, and is guided by, a taking-time-for-oneself. What already showed itself in the most elementary time-reckoning becomes plainer here: the self-directing according to time that looks at the clock is essentially a now-saying (Jetzt-sagen). This is so "self-evident" that we do not heed it at all, and know still less expressly that here the now is in each case already understood and interpreted in its full structural stock of datability, spannedness, publicness, and worldhood. The answer relocates time from the dial to the reader: the glance is a saying — every consultation an implicit "now it is... time to..." — the instrument mute without the now-saying it serves; and the four-fold structure certified present, entire and unnoticed, in the most banal act of the modern day.

The sixteenth unit derives measurement's present and its yield. Now-saying, however, is the discoursing articulation of a making-present that temporalizes itself in unity with a retaining awaiting. The dating accomplished in clock-use proves to be a distinguished making-present of something present-at-hand: the dating does not simply refer to a present-at-hand thing — the referring itself has the character of measuring. The measure-number can, to be sure, be read off immediately; but therein lies: it is understood that the standard is contained in a stretch to be measured — that is, the how-often of its presence in it is determined. Measuring constitutes itself temporally in the making-present of the present standard in the present stretch. The unchangingness lying in the idea of the standard means that it must be present-at-hand, in its constancy, for everyman at any time. Measuring dating interprets the attended time in a making-present regard to the present-at-hand, which becomes accessible, as standard and as measured, only in a distinguished making-present. Because in measuring dating the making-present of the present has a special priority, the measuring time-reading on the clock also speaks itself out, in an emphasized sense, with the now: in time-measurement, therefore, a publication of time is accomplished according to which time encounters, in each case and at any time, for everyman, as "now and now and now." This time, "universally" accessible on the clocks, is found, as it were, like a present-at-hand now-manifold — without the time-measurement being thematically directed at time as such. The paragraph is the genetic engine of the whole vulgar concept, isolated at the dial: measurement is presenting doubled (standard present in the stretch present — the how-often of an Anwesenheit), so the clock's time speaks in the emphatic now; and the yield is named in the run of three — "jetzt und jetzt und jetzt" — the now-manifold lying on the dials like a thing, minted by the measuring present without anyone ever having looked at time itself. § 81's Jetztfolge is born here, at the watch-glass.

The seventeenth unit settles time and place — the relativity note attached. Because the temporality of factical being-in-the-world originally makes possible the disclosure of space, and spatial Dasein has in each case assigned itself a Dasein-like here from a discovered there, the time attended in Dasein's temporality is, with regard to its datability, in each case bound to a place of Dasein. Not time is knotted to a place; rather temporality is the condition of the possibility that the dating can bind itself to the spatially-local, and in such a way that this binds as measure for everyman. Time is not first coupled with space; rather the "space" supposedly to be coupled encounters only on the ground of the time-attending temporality. In conformity with the founding of clock and time-reckoning in Dasein's temporality — which constitutes this being as historical — it can be shown how far clock-use is itself ontologically historical, and every clock as such "has a history." The folded-in note declines to enter the relativity-theoretical problem of time-measurement: the clarification of the ontological foundations of this measurement already presupposes the clarification of world-time and within-time-ness from Dasein's temporality, as well as the illumination of the existential-temporal constitution of nature-discovery and of the temporal sense of measurement in general; an axiomatics of physical measurement-technique rests on these investigations, and can for its part never unroll the time-problem as such. The paragraph settles § 70's deferred "coupling" (space-time bound only through temporality — the sundial's latitude, the meridian's authority, grounded existentially, and the clock itself historical: every timepiece with its history, from the gnomon to the escapement); and the note is the book's one sentence to Einstein, exactly weighed: no evasion but a founding-order — relativity's measurement presupposes what fundamental ontology investigates; physics' axiomatics can refine the metric and never touch the time-problem — the same ruling § 3 gave every regional crisis.

The eighteenth unit blocks the spatialization-thesis: the time published in time-measurement by no means becomes space through the dating from spatial measure-relations; nor is the existential-ontologically essential element of time-measurement to be sought in the fact that dated "time" is numerically determined from spatial stretches and the change of place of a spatial thing. The ontologically decisive lies rather in the specific making-present that makes measurement possible. The dating from the "spatially" present-at-hand is so far from being a spatialization of time that this supposed spatialization means nothing other than the making-present of the being that is present-at-hand for everyone in every now, in its presence. In the time-measurement that essentially-necessarily says now, the measured as such is, over the winning of the measure, as it were forgotten — so that beyond stretch and number nothing is to be found. The paragraph is the answer to Bergson thirty years early promised and here delivered: no Verräumlichung occurs — what the clock does to time is not spatialization but presentification: the presenting of the omnipresent present-at-hand; and the closing clause diagnoses the loss with precision: measurement forgets its measured over the measure — the operation succeeds and its object vanishes, leaving track and number: positivism's time as measurement's amnesia.

The nineteenth unit reads the watch's economics: the less time the time-attending Dasein has to lose, the more "precious" time becomes, and the handier must the clock be; not only shall the time be specifiable "more exactly," but the time-determining itself shall claim as little time as possible, and yet at the same time agree with the time-specifications of the others. The two-line unit is a sociology of the wristwatch in ontological grammar: scarcity, precision, speed, synchrony — the modern chronometric regime derived from time-poverty; § 79's "ich habe keine Zeit" wearing its instrument.

The twentieth unit banks and defers — with the habilitation note. Provisionally it was only necessary to show in general the "connection" of clock-use with the time-taking temporality: just as the concrete analysis of developed astronomical time-reckoning belongs to the existential-ontological interpretation of nature-discovery, so the foundation of calendrical-historiographical "chronology" can be laid free only within the task-circle of the existential analysis of historical cognition. The folded-in note refers, as a first attempt at the interpretation of chronological time and the "historical number" (Geschichtszahl), to the author's Freiburg habilitation-lecture of 1915, "The Concept of Time in the Science of History" (published 1916); the connections between historical number, astronomically computed world-time, and the temporality and historicity of Dasein need further investigation — with references besides to Simmel's "Problem of Historical Time" and, as the two foundational works on the formation of historical chronology, Scaliger's De emendatione temporum (1583) and Petavius's Opus de doctrina temporum (1627), with Bilfinger, Diels on the ancient clock, and Rühl on medieval and modern chronology. The deferral assigns the two calendars their homes (astronomy's to nature-discovery, the historian's to § 76's circle), and the note is quietly autobiographical: the 1915 lecture — the young Privatdozent's first published thoughts on time, on the date as the historian's number — cited as this chapter's own ancestor: the book's problem twelve years old, the erudition (Scaliger to Diels) attesting that the derivation of the calendar was won from the calendar's own history.

The twenty-first unit gathers world-time's transcendence: time-measurement accomplishes a pronounced publication of time, so that on this way there first becomes familiar what we commonly call "the time." In concern, to every thing "its time" is ascribed; it "has" it, and can — like every innerworldly being — only "have" it, because it is at all "in time." The time "wherein" innerworldly beings encounter we know as world-time: on the ground of the ecstatic-horizonal constitution of the temporality to which it belongs, it has the same transcendence as the world. With the disclosedness of world, world-time is published, so that every temporally attending being alongside innerworldly beings understands these circumspectly as encountering "in time." The gathering-unit fixes the "in" at last: things have their time as they have their place — through world-belonging; Weltzeit transcendent as world is (§ 69c's geometry extended): the wherein of encounter, prior to every encountered.

The twenty-second unit dismantles the objective and its Kantian detour: the time "in which" the present-at-hand moves and rests is not "objective," if by that the being-present-at-hand-in-itself of innerworldly encountering beings is meant; but just as little is it "subjective," if we understand by that being-present-at-hand and occurring in a "subject." World-time is "more objective" than every possible object, because, as the condition of the possibility of innerworldly beings, it is always already "objected" ecstatically-horizonally with the disclosedness of world. Hence — against Kant's opinion — world-time is found just as immediately at the physical as at the psychic, and not at the physical only by the detour over the psychic: "the time" shows itself proximally precisely at the sky — there where, in the natural directing-oneself according to it, one finds it — so that "time" is even identified with the sky. The paragraph replays § 69c's dialectic on time itself — more objective than any object, as its condition — and lands its Kant-correction with the oldest evidence: time first at the heavens, not in inner sense (the first Critique's detour through the psyche refuted by every shepherd who reads the hour off the sky); Anaximander's and the common tongue's identification of time with heaven called as witness.

The twenty-third unit completes the chiasmus and draws the strict lexicon: but world-time is also "more subjective" than every possible subject, because — in the well-understood sense of care as the being of the factically existing self — it first co-makes this being possible. "Time" is present-at-hand neither in the "subject" nor in the "object," neither "inside" nor "outside," and "is" "earlier" than every subjectivity and objectivity, because it presents the condition of the possibility even for this "earlier." Has it then any "being" at all? And if not, is it then a phantom — or "more in being" (seiender) than every possible being? The investigation proceeding in the direction of such questions will strike against the same "limit" that already erected itself for the provisional discussion of the connection of truth and being. However these questions may be answered in what follows — or first originally posed — it is proximally to be understood that temporality, as ecstatic-horizonal, temporalizes something like world-time, which constitutes a within-time-ness of the ready-to-hand and present-at-hand: these beings can then, in the strict sense, never be called "temporal"; they are, like every non-Dasein-like being, untemporal (unzeitlich), whether they really occur, arise, and pass away, or "ideally" subsist. The paragraph completes the § 69c chiasmus (more subjective than any subject: care's own enabling) and then reaches the book's outermost edge in three questions: time earlier than the earlier itself — its "being" undecidable at the very Grenze where § 44 stalled (the same limit for truth's being and time's: both "given" with Dasein, both outrunning the meaning of "is") — the Third Division's door once more, marked and shut. And the strict lexicon closes the terminological system begun in § 65: things, even eternal ones, are unzeitlich — within time and untemporal — temporality reserved for the being that is its time; the triple register (zeitlich/innerzeitig/unzeitlich, with the ideal's outside-time included in the untemporal) complete.

The closing unit sets § 81's course: if world-time thus belongs to the temporalizing of temporality, it can be neither "subjectivistically" volatilized nor "reified" in a bad "objectification"; both are avoided from clear insight — and not merely from an insecure wavering between the two possibilities — only if it can be understood how everyday Dasein, from its nearest understanding of time, conceives "the time" theoretically, and how far this concept of time, and its dominion, block for Dasein the possibility of understanding what is meant in it from original time — that is, as temporality. Everyday time-giving concern finds "the time" at the innerworldly beings that encounter "in time": hence the illumination of the genesis of the vulgar concept of time must take its departure from within-time-ness. The handover restates § 78's wavering as the thing to be dissolved (not adjudicated) by genesis: the vulgar concept to be derived from Innerzeitigkeit — the leveled read from the deposit, § 81's exact commission.

##### § 81. Within-Time-ness and the Genesis of the Vulgar Concept of Time

The opening unit finds time at the pointer. How does something like "time" first show itself for everyday, circumspect concern? In which concernful, equipment-using dealings does it become expressly accessible? If, with the disclosedness of world, time is published, and is always already attended along with the discoveredness of innerworldly beings belonging to world's disclosedness — insofar as Dasein, reckoning with itself, calculates time — then the comportment in which "one" expressly directs oneself according to time lies in clock-use. Its existential-temporal sense proves to be a making-present of the wandering pointer: the presenting following of the pointer-positions counts. This making-present temporalizes itself in the ecstatic unity of an awaiting retaining: to retain, making-present, the "at-that-time" means — saying now, to be open for the horizon of the earlier, the now-no-longer; to await, making-present, the "then" means — saying now, to be open for the horizon of the later, the now-not-yet. What shows itself in such making-present is time. The paragraph fixes the phenomenal site of the vulgar concept with the book's characteristic concreteness: the eye on the dial — following, counting, now-saying — the whole ecstatic apparatus operative but bent through the present: earlier and later already reformulated as no-longer-now and not-yet-now; the leveling caught at its workbench.

The second unit reads Aristotle's definition as its own confirmation. What, accordingly, is the definition of the time manifest in the horizon of circumspect, time-taking, concernful clock-use? It is the counted that shows itself in the presenting, counting following of the wandering pointer — in such a way that the presenting temporalizes itself in ecstatic unity with the retaining and awaiting horizonally open toward the earlier and later. But this is nothing other than the existential-ontological exegesis of Aristotle's definition of time: touto gar estin ho chronos, arithmos kinēseōs kata to proteron kai hysteron — "for this is time: the counted at the motion encountering in the horizon of the earlier and later." However strange this definition may seem at first glance, it is "self-evident" and genuinely drawn, once the existential-ontological horizon from which Aristotle took it is delimited. The origin of the time thus manifest does not become a problem for Aristotle; his interpretation of time moves rather in the direction of the "natural" understanding of being. But because this itself, and the being understood in it, is made fundamentally into a problem by the present investigation, the Aristotelian analysis of time can be thematically interpreted only after the solution of the question of being — in such a way that it then gains fundamental significance for the positive appropriation of the critically limited question-formulation of ancient ontology in general. The paragraph is one of the book's great acts of philology-as-philosophy: the Physics definition — number of motion with respect to before and after, the West's founding time-formula — translated word for word into the just-derived structure (the counted = the now-said; the motion = the wandering pointer; the proteron kai hysteron = the ecstatic horizons of retaining and awaiting), so that twenty-three centuries of time-theory stand certified as the correct phenomenology of the clock; Aristotle honored as genuine (echt geschöpft) and located: the origin unasked, the natural understanding of being his unexamined element. And the deferral is once more Division Two of Part One's unwritten neighbor: the thematic Aristotle-interpretation scheduled after the Seinsfrage's solution — GA 24's brilliant Physics-chapter would pay the first installment on this note.

The third unit fixes the tradition and mints Jetzt-Zeit: all subsequent discussion of the concept of time holds itself fundamentally to the Aristotelian definition — that is, it makes time its theme as it shows itself in circumspect concern. Time is the "counted" — that which is uttered and (though unthematically) meant in the making-present of the wandering pointer (or shadow); in the presenting of the moved in its motion one says: "now here, now here, and so forth." The counted are the nows; and these show themselves "in every now" as "right-away-no-longer" and "just-now-not-yet." The world-time thus "sighted" in clock-use we call the now-time (die Jetzt-Zeit). The unit legislates the history (from Aristotle through every subsequent theory, one unbroken thematization of clock-sighted time) and names the product: Jetzt-Zeit — world-time as it looks when only the counted now is retained; the term under which the remainder of the section will conduct the audit.

The fourth unit derives the flow-picture: the more "naturally" time-giving concern reckons with time, the less it tarries at the uttered time as such — it is lost to the attended equipment, which in each case has its time. The more "naturally" — that is, the less thematically directed at time as such — concern determines and specifies time, the more the presenting-falling being alongside the attended says, without ceremony, with or without vocalization: now, then, at-that-time. And so, for the vulgar understanding, time shows itself as a sequence of constantly "present-at-hand" nows, at once passing and arriving: time is understood as a succession, as the "flow" of nows, as the "course of time." What lies in this interpretation of the attended world-time? The derivation catches the picture at its birth: absorption breeds the bare now (the less one looks at time, the purer the "now" one says), and the said nows, regarded, line up into the river — the Fluß der Zeit as sedimented inattention; the question posed for the audit.

The fifth unit conducts the audit: we receive the answer by going back to the full essential structure of world-time and comparing with it what the vulgar understanding knows. As the first essential moment of attended time, datability was exhibited — grounding in the ecstatic constitution of temporality: the "now" is essentially a now-that...; the datable now understood in concern, though not grasped as such, is in each case a suited or unsuited one — significance belongs to the now-structure, whence we called the attended time world-time. In the vulgar interpretation of time as now-sequence, both datability and significance are lacking: the characterization of time as pure succession does not let these two structures "come to appearance" — the vulgar interpretation covers them. The ecstatic-horizonal constitution of temporality, in which the now's datability and significance ground, is leveled by this covering: the nows are, as it were, shorn (beschnitten) of these relations and, as so shorn, merely range themselves one after another to make up the succession. The audit is exact double-entry: two structural moments (the relational and the practical — now-that and time-for) missing from the vulgar ledger; and the leveling given its image: the pruned nows — each cut back to a stump of itself, then strung; the sequence not a finding but the residue of an amputation.

The sixth unit derives the covering's necessity: this leveling covering of world-time, which the vulgar understanding accomplishes, is not accidental. Precisely because the everyday interpretation of time holds itself solely in the sight-direction of concernful common sense and understands only what "shows itself" in its horizon, these structures must escape it. The counted in concernful time-measurement — the now — is co-understood in the attending to the ready-to-hand and present-at-hand; insofar as this time-concern comes back to the co-understood time itself and "regards" it, it sees the nows — which are indeed also somehow "there" — in the horizon of that understanding of being by which this concern itself is constantly guided. The nows are therefore, in a certain way, co-present-at-hand: that is, beings encounter, and also the now. Although it is not expressly said that the nows are present-at-hand like things, they are ontologically "seen" in the horizon of the idea of presence-at-hand. The nows pass away, and the passed ones make up the past; the nows arrive, and the arriving ones bound the "future." The vulgar interpretation of world-time as now-time does not dispose at all over the horizon in which such things as world, significance, datability could be made accessible: these structures remain necessarily covered — the more so, as the vulgar interpretation consolidates the covering through the manner in which it conceptually develops its characterization of time. The paragraph runs § 44(b)'s machinery one last time: the covering necessary, not culpable — common sense sees what its horizon shows; the nows, regarded at all, regarded as quasi-things (co-vorhanden, seen under presence's idea without anyone asserting it) — the ontological contraband smuggled in the mere act of looking; and past and future degraded in one stroke to the passed and pending stock of nows.

The seventh unit finds Plato at the picture's source: the now-sequence is apprehended as something somehow present-at-hand, for it itself moves "into time." We say: in every now, the now is; in every now it also already vanishes. In every now the now is now — hence constantly present as the same, even if in every now another may, arriving, vanish. As this changing thing it nevertheless shows at the same time the constant presence of itself — whence already Plato, with this direction of view upon time as the arising-passing now-sequence, had to call time the image of eternity: "he bethought himself to make a moving image of eternity, and, in ordering the heaven, makes of the eternity abiding in the One an eternal image proceeding according to number — that which we have named time" (Timaeus 37d). The paragraph is a small destruction executed with complete respect: the now's double face (always another, always the same "now") read as the constant presence the tradition demanded — and Plato's definition derived as forced (nennen mußte): once time is the now-sequence, its strange self-same flux can only be understood as eternity's moving copy; the Timaeus formula the picture's oldest and noblest monument.

The eighth unit dissolves the continuity-aporia: the now-sequence is uninterrupted and gapless; however "far" we advance in "dividing" the now, it is always still now. One sees time's steadiness in the horizon of an indissoluble present-at-hand; in the ontological orientation to a constantly present-at-hand thing one seeks the problem of time's continuity — or leaves the aporia standing. Thereby the specific structure of world-time must remain covered: that it is spanned, in one with the ecstatically founded datability. The spannedness of time is not understood from the horizonal stretchedness of the ecstatic unity of temporality, which has published itself in time-concern. That in every now, however momentary, there is in each case already now, must be conceived from what is still "earlier," from which every now stems: from the ecstatic stretchedness of temporality, which is foreign to every continuity of a present-at-hand thing, but for its part presents the condition of the possibility of access to a continuous present-at-hand. The paragraph settles the oldest paradox in the philosophy of time (Aristotle's aporia, Zeno's shadow, the mathematical continuum's philosophical career) by exhibiting its frame: continuity sought among things must either be constructed or abandoned; but the now's inexhaustibility — always still now, under every division — is the Widerschein of the stretch: each now inherits its width from the ecstatic Erstrecktheit it levels; the continuum a pensioner of temporality.

The ninth unit confronts the infinity-thesis — the section's center. Most penetratingly, the main thesis of the vulgar interpretation — that time is "infinite" — reveals the leveling and covering of world-time, and thereby of temporality in general, lying in such interpretation. Time gives itself proximally as uninterrupted sequence of nows; every now is also already a just-now or a right-away. If the characterization of time holds primarily and exclusively to this sequence, then in it as such no beginning and no end can in principle be found: every last now is, as now, in each case already a right-away-no-longer — hence time in the sense of the no-longer-now, the past; every first now is in each case a just-now-not-yet — hence time in the sense of the not-yet-now, the "future." Time is therefore "endless on both sides." This time-thesis becomes possible only on the ground of the orientation to a free-floating in-itself of a present-at-hand now-course — in which the full now-phenomenon, with regard to datability, worldhood, spannedness, and Dasein-like locality, is covered and sunk down to an unrecognizable fragment. If "one thinks" the now-sequence "to the end," in the direction of presence-at-hand and non-presence-at-hand, an end can never be found; from the fact that this thinking-to-the-end of time must in each case always still think time, one concludes: time is infinite. The analysis is the book's finale-argument in nuce: infinity derived, not discovered — a valid inference inside the leveled picture (no first or last now findable in a sequence whose every member is transitional), and the picture itself convicted: the premise a freischwebendes An-sich, the now shrunk to an unrecognizable fragment of itself; endlessness the exact geometry of the fragment. What the tradition took for time's majesty is the shadow cast by an amputation.

The tenth unit names the ground: das Man never dies. But whereon grounds this leveling of world-time and covering of temporality? In the being of Dasein itself, which we preparatorily interpreted as care. Thrown-falling, Dasein is proximally and mostly lost to the attended; in this lostness, however, announces itself the covering flight of Dasein before its authentic existence, characterized as anticipatory resoluteness. In the concernful flight lies the flight before death — a looking-away from the end of being-in-the-world; this looking-away from... is in itself a mode of the ecstatically futural being toward the end. The inauthentic temporality of falling-everyday Dasein must, as such looking-away from finitude, misrecognize authentic futurity and therewith temporality in general. And if, indeed, the vulgar understanding of Dasein is guided by das Man, then the self-forgotten "representation" of the "infinity" of public time can first consolidate itself. Das Man never dies, because it cannot die — insofar as death is in each case mine, and is authentically understood, existentielly, only in anticipatory resoluteness. Das Man, which never dies and misunderstands being toward the end, nevertheless gives the flight before death a characteristic interpretation: until the end "it always still has time." Here a having-time announces itself in the sense of being-able-to-lose it: "now first this, then that, and only that still, and then..." Here the finitude of time is not, say, understood — on the contrary: concern is out to snatch (erraffen) as much as possible from the time that still comes and "goes on." Time is, publicly, something that everyone takes and can take: the leveled now-sequence remains wholly unrecognizable, with regard to its provenance from the temporality of the individual Dasein, in the everyday with-one-another. How, indeed, should "time" be touched in the least in its course, if a man present-at-hand "in time" no longer exists? Time goes on — as indeed it already "was" when a man "entered into life." One knows only the public time, which, leveled, belongs to everyman — and that means to no one (jedermann und das heißt niemandem gehört). The paragraph is the section's deepest and darkest stroke, and its argument runs the derivation of infinity home to death. Time's endlessness is the fugitive's cosmology: the looking-away from the end, itself a mode of being toward the end, projects a time without ends; and das Man — the dying-less public of § 51 — supplies the subject this time needs: the one who always still has time, whose having is a being-able-to-lose, whose economy is the snatching (erraffen — greed's verb) of the oncoming hours. The two closing sentences are among the book's bitterest and most perfect: the observation no one disputes — time flows on over every death, flowed before every birth — unmasked as the phenomenology of the leveled view itself (of course the ownerless sequence outlasts its "contents"); and public time's title finally read out: everyman's, therefore no one's — the genitive of das Man, § 27's Niemand, stamped on the hours.

The eleventh unit catches everydayness knowing more than it admits. But just as, even in evasion before death, death follows the fleeing one, and he must see it precisely in turning away from it — so too the merely running-off, harmless, infinite sequence of nows lays itself, in a remarkable enigmaticness, "over" Dasein. Why do we say: time passes (vergeht) — and not, with equal emphasis: it arises? With regard to the pure now-sequence, both may be said with equal right. In the talk of time's passing, Dasein finally understands more of time than it would like to admit (mehr von der Zeit, als es wahrhaben möchte): the temporality in which world-time temporalizes itself is, for all covering, not completely closed off. The talk of time's passing gives expression to the "experience" that time does not let itself be halted; this "experience" is in turn possible only on the ground of a wanting-to-halt time. Herein lies an inauthentic awaiting of the "moments," which already forgets the gliding-away ones; the presenting-forgetting awaiting of inauthentic existence is the condition of the possibility of the vulgar experience of time's passing. Because Dasein is futural in the ahead-of-itself, it must, awaiting, understand the now-sequence as gliding-away, passing: Dasein knows the fleeting time from the "fleeting" knowledge of its death. In the emphatic talk of time's passing lies the public reflection (Widerschein) of the finite futurity of Dasein's temporality; and because death can remain covered even in the talk of time's passing, time shows itself as a passing "in itself." The paragraph is the section's finest turn: the asymmetry-argument — vergehen, never entstehen, though the bare sequence licenses both equally — as everydayness's involuntary confession: the direction of lament betrays the finitude the picture denies; time flees for one who wanted to hold it, and one wants to hold it who fleetingly knows he ends. The Widerschein-figure of § 79 returns at the deepest level: even in the fugitive's proverb, finite temporality shows through — and, death staying covered, the passing is booked to time "itself": the last displacement, mortality laundered into cosmology.

The twelfth unit derives irreversibility: but even at this in-itself passing, pure now-sequence, original time reveals itself through all leveling and covering. The vulgar interpretation determines the time-flow as an irreversible succession. Why can time not be reversed? In itself — and precisely in the exclusive look at the now-flow — it is not to be seen why the sequence of nows should not once re-establish itself in the reversed direction. The impossibility of reversal has its ground in the provenance of public time from temporality, whose temporalizing — primarily futural — "goes" ecstatically to its end, in such a way that it already "is" to the end. The last audit-item is the strongest: irreversibility — the one feature the leveled picture cannot fund (a bare sequence runs as legibly backward) — funded only by the origin: time cannot turn because temporalizing is a going-to-the-end that already is its end; the arrow of time, physics' standing embarrassment, grounded in mortality.

The thirteenth unit renders the verdict with both hands. The vulgar characterization of time as an endless, passing, irreversible now-sequence springs from the temporality of falling Dasein; the vulgar representation of time has its natural right. It belongs to Dasein's everyday mode of being and to the proximally ruling understanding of being; hence proximally and mostly even history is publicly understood as within-time happening. This time-interpretation loses its exclusive and pre-eminent right only if it claims to convey the "true" concept of time and to be able to predelineate the sole possible horizon of time-interpretation. Rather it has resulted: why and how world-time belongs to temporality becomes intelligible only from Dasein's temporality and its temporalizing. The interpretation of world-time's full structure, drawn from temporality, first gives the guiding thread for "seeing" at all the covering lying in the vulgar concept and for estimating the leveling of the ecstatic-horizonal constitution of temporality. The orientation to Dasein's temporality makes it possible at the same time to demonstrate the provenance and the factical necessity of this leveling covering, and to test the vulgar theses about time for their ground of right. The verdict repeats the book's constant jurisprudence at its final defendant: the three predicates (endless, passing, irreversible) all genuine — natural right confirmed, everydayness's title deed honored — and all derivative; only the exclusivity-claim struck down; and the methodological asymmetry stated once more: from the origin the level is visible and derivable, never conversely.

The fourteenth unit secures the title "original": conversely, temporality remains inaccessible in the horizon of the vulgar understanding of time. But because now-time not only must be oriented primarily to temporality in the order of possible interpretation, but also temporalizes itself only in the inauthentic temporality of Dasein, the addressing of temporality as original time justifies itself with regard to the derivation (Abkunft) of now-time from it. The two-sentence unit closes § 78's promised proof: the a potiori title earned twice over — interpretative order (the level readable only from the origin) and ontological genesis (now-time temporalized in inauthentic temporalizing); ursprüngliche Zeit no honorific but a derivation-certificate.

The closing unit draws the last severances — with the four notes folded in. Ecstatic-horizonal temporality temporalizes itself primarily from the future; the vulgar understanding, by contrast, sees the basic phenomenon of time in the now — the pure now, shorn of its full structure, which one calls the "present." From this it can be gathered that it must remain in principle hopeless to clarify from this now, or even derive from it, the ecstatic-horizonal phenomenon of the moment of vision belonging to authentic temporality. Correspondingly, the ecstatically understood future — the datable, significant "then" — does not coincide with the vulgar concept of "future" as the pure nows not yet arrived and only arriving; just as little do the ecstatic beenness — the datable, significant "at-that-time" — and the concept of the past as the passed pure nows fall together. The now is not pregnant with the not-yet-now; rather the present springs from the future, in the original ecstatic unity of the temporalizing of temporality (Das Jetzt geht nicht schwanger mit dem Noch-nicht-jetzt, sondern die Gegenwart entspringt der Zukunft). Although the vulgar experience of time proximally and mostly knows only "world-time," it nevertheless always also gives it a distinguished relation to "soul" and "spirit" — and this even where an express and primary orientation of philosophical questioning to the "subject" still lies far off. Two characteristic attestations may suffice: Aristotle says, "but if nothing other than soul, and in soul the nous, were of a nature to count, time would be impossible, soul not being..." (Physics D 14, 223a25); and Augustine writes: "hence it appeared to me that time is nothing other than a distention; but of what thing, I know not — and it were a marvel if not of the mind itself" (Confessions XI.26). Thus even the interpretation of Dasein as temporality does not, in principle, lie outside the horizon of the vulgar concept of time. And Hegel has already made the express attempt to set forth the connection of vulgarly understood time with spirit — whereas in Kant, time is indeed "subjective," but stands unconnected "beside" the "I think." Hegel's express grounding of the connection between time and spirit is suited to clarify indirectly the foregoing interpretation of Dasein as temporality and the demonstration of world-time's origin from it. The folded notes carry four last charges. First, the eternity-note: that the traditional concept of eternity, in the signification of the "standing now" (nunc stans), is drawn from the vulgar understanding of time and delimited in orientation to the idea of "constant" presence-at-hand needs no lengthy discussion; if God's eternity could be philosophically "constructed," it might be understood only as a more original and "infinite" temporality — whether the via negationis et eminentiae could offer a possible way hereto is left open. Second and third, the source-citations for soul-time: Aristotle's no-soul-no-time and Augustine's distentio animi — the two ancient testimonies that time, even vulgarly sighted, points to the "soul." Fourth, the Kant-note: how far, in Kant, a more radical understanding of time nevertheless breaks through than in Hegel, is shown by the first section of the second part of this treatise. The closing unit thus performs the section's whole yield as lexical law — Augenblick never from the now, Zukunft never the pending nows, Gewesenheit never the spent ones — crowned by the finale-sentence that reverses the tradition's obstetrics: the now does not go pregnant with the not-yet (Aristotle's and Hegel's generative present refused by name in advance); the present springs from the future. The soul-testimonies are placed with exquisite fairness: Aristotle's counting soul and Augustine's distended mind prove the vulgar horizon itself gestures toward the "subject" — hence the analytic's own thesis (Dasein as temporality) does not exit that horizon by fiat but must earn its difference; Hegel admitted as the tradition's most express connector of time and spirit, Kant noted as leaving time unjoined beside the I think. And the fourth note is the torso's most poignant self-citation: the promised proof of Kant's deeper radicality assigned to "the first section of the second part of this treatise" — the Kant-destruction of the never-published continuation; the book here cites, as though extant, the part it would never receive, and the Kantbuch of 1929 would be its executor.

##### § 82. The Contrast of the Existential-Ontological Connection of Temporality, Dasein, and World-Time with Hegel's Conception of the Relation between Time and Spirit

The first preamble-unit poses Hegel's problem: history, which is essentially history of spirit, runs its course "in time" — thus "the development of history falls into time." But Hegel does not content himself with setting down the within-time-ness of spirit as a factum; he seeks to understand the possibility of spirit's falling into time — into time, which is "the unsensuous sensuous." Time must, as it were, be able to receive spirit; and spirit in turn must be akin to time and its essence. Hence a double point is to be discussed: (1) how does Hegel delimit the essence of time? (2) what belongs to the essence of spirit, that makes it possible for it "to fall into time"? The answering of both questions serves solely a contrasting clarification (abhebende Verdeutlichung) of the foregoing interpretation of Dasein as temporality; it makes no claim to even a relatively complete treatment of the problems necessarily co-resonating in Hegel — the less so, as it does not occur to it to "criticize" Hegel. The contrast of the exposed idea of temporality against Hegel's concept of time suggests itself above all because Hegel's concept presents the most radical and too-little-heeded conceptual elaboration of the vulgar understanding of time. The preamble fixes the confrontation's terms with unusual courtesy: not critique but Abhebung — setting-off, the profile won by contrast — and the compliment that licenses the whole section: Hegel the vulgar concept's radicalste Ausformung, the leveled now thought through to the end; to measure oneself against the completion, not the average.

The second preamble-unit states Hegel's own kinship-requirement: das unsinnliche Sinnliche — Lasson's Hegel quoted — time the sensuous that is not sensed; the fall demands receivability on time's side and kinship on spirit's; the double question the section's two subsections.

###### a) Hegel's Concept of Time

The opening unit reads the system's map: the "systematic place" at which a philosophical interpretation of time is carried through can count as criterion for the guiding basic conception of time. The first transmitted, thematically detailed exegesis of the vulgar understanding of time is found in Aristotle's Physics — that is, in the context of an ontology of nature: "time" stands together with "place" and "motion." Hegel's analysis of time, faithful to the tradition, has its place in the second part of his Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences, titled Philosophy of Nature; its first division treats Mechanics, whose first section is devoted to the discussion of "space and time" — they are the "abstract outside-one-another." The criterion-argument is the section's method in one move: where a philosophy files time is what it thinks time is — Aristotle filed it in physics, Hegel, twenty-two centuries later, in the same drawer (nature, mechanics, beside space); the systematic place as confession.

The second unit follows the dialectical transition: although Hegel puts space and time together, this does not happen merely in an external stringing — space "and also time": "this 'also' philosophy combats." The transition from space to time does not mean the adjoining of the paragraphs treating them; rather "space itself goes over." Space "is" time — that is, time is the "truth" of space: if space is thought dialectically in what it is, this being of space unveils itself, according to Hegel, as time. How must space be thought? The unit registers Hegel's genuine superiority over the mere "and": the und auch fought, the transition earned — space itself passing over; the question posed as Hegel poses it.

The third unit thinks Hegel's space: space is "the unmediated indifference of nature's being-outside-itself" — the abstract multiplicity of the points distinguishable in it. Space is not interrupted by these; nor does it arise from them, least of all by way of assembly. Space, distinguished by the distinguishable points, which are themselves space, remains for its part without distinction: the distinctions are themselves of the character of what they distinguish. But the point, insofar as it distinguishes anything at all in space, is the negation of space — yet in such a way that, as this negation (the point is, after all, space), it itself remains in space; the point does not lift itself out of space as something other than space. Space is the distinction-less outside-one-another of the point-manifold; but space is not, say, point — it is, as Hegel says, "punctuality" (Punktualität). The reconstruction is scrupulous: Hegel's space rendered in Hegel's grammar (the point as self-remaining negation, the whole as Punktualität) — the material for the coming derivation laid out without caricature.

The fourth unit quotes the derivation-sentence: "But negativity, which relates itself as point to space and develops in it its determinations as line and surface, is, in the sphere of being-outside-itself, just as much for itself, and its determinations therein — yet, as positing in the sphere of being-outside-itself, appearing at the same time indifferent toward the quiet side-by-side. Negativity, thus posited for itself, is time" (Encyclopedia § 257). The quotation-block sets the section's exhibit: Hegel's own sentence in which space's negativity, posited für sich, is time — the text the next unit must make speak.

The fifth unit makes it speak: if space is represented — that is, immediately intuited in the indifferent subsistence of its distinctions — the negations are, as it were, simply given; but this representing does not yet grasp space in its being. That is possible only in thinking, as the synthesis that has passed through thesis and antithesis and sublates them: space is thought, and thus grasped in its being, only when the negations do not simply remain subsisting in their indifference but are sublated — themselves negated. In the negation of the negation (that is, of punctuality) the point posits itself for itself and thereby steps out of the indifference of subsisting; as posited for itself, it distinguishes itself from this one and that one: it is no longer this and not yet that. With the self-positing for itself, it posits the succession in which it stands — the sphere of being-outside-itself, which is henceforth the sphere of the negated negation. The sublation of punctuality as indifference means a no-longer-lying-still in the "paralyzed rest" of space: the point "spreads itself up" (spreizt sich auf) over against all other points. This negation of the negation as punctuality is, according to Hegel, time. If this discussion has any demonstrable sense at all, it can mean nothing other than: the self-positing-for-itself of every point is a now-here, now-here, and so forth — every point "is," posited for itself, a now-point. "In time the point thus has actuality." That through which the point can in each case posit itself for itself, as this one here, is in each case a now: the condition of the possibility of the point's self-positing is the now. This possibility-condition makes up the point's being, and being is at the same time thought-ness; hence, because the pure thinking of punctuality — of space — in each case "thinks" the now and the being-outside-itself of the nows, space "is" time. How is time itself determined? The paragraph performs the section's central act of translation: the dialectical machinery (negation of negation, für-sich-setzen, the point's revolt against paralyzed rest) rendered until its cash-value appears — the point's self-positing is a now-saying, the now the condition of the point's actuality — Hegel's deduction of time from space exposed as running, at every joint, on the now; and the author's careful conditional (if the discussion has demonstrable sense at all) marks the method: charity as instrument, the maximal sense sought and found to be Jetzt.

The sixth unit quotes the definition: "Time, as the negative unity of being-outside-itself, is likewise something simply abstract, ideal. — It is the being that, in that it is, is not, and in that it is not, is: intuited becoming; that is, the distinctions — which are, to be sure, simply momentary, immediately self-sublating — are determined as external, yet external to themselves" (Encyclopedia § 258). Time unveils itself, for this exegesis, as "intuited becoming" — which means, according to Hegel, transition from being to nothing or from nothing to being: becoming is arising as much as passing; being "goes over," or non-being. What does this say with regard to time? The being of time is the now; but insofar as every now "now" also already is-no-longer, or in each case now is previously not-yet, it can also be apprehended as non-being. Time is "intuited" becoming — that is, the transition that is not thought, but simply offers itself in the now-sequence. If the essence of time is determined as "intuited becoming," then it becomes manifest: time is primarily understood from the now — and indeed as it is findable for pure intuition. The unit reads the famous § 258 formula (the being that, being, is not — the most dialectical sentence ever written about time) down to its operational base: the paradox funded entirely by the now's double face (seventh unit of § 81), and the participle angeschaut convicting the concept: the transition not thought but looked at — time read off the intuitable now; Hegel's time an ocular time, in Yorck's term.

The seventh unit renders the verdict in two sentences: it needs no circumstantial discussion to make plain that Hegel, with his interpretation of time, moves wholly in the direction of the vulgar understanding of time. Hegel's characterization of time from the now presupposes that the now remains covered and leveled in its full structure, so that it can be intuited as an — albeit "ideal" — present-at-hand. The verdict applies § 81's audit to the summit: the shorn now (no datability, no significance, no span, no place) the very unit of Hegel's construction; "ideal" presence still presence.

The closing unit of a) documents and totals — with the great Aristotle–Hegel–Bergson note folded in. That Hegel accomplishes the interpretation of time from the primary orientation to the leveled now is attested by these sentences: "The now has a monstrous right — it 'is' nothing but the single now; but this exclusive thing, in its spreading-up, is dissolved, flowed apart, dispersed to dust as I utter it" (§ 258, Zusatz); "for the rest, in nature, where time is now, there is no 'subsisting' distinction of those dimensions" — past and future (§ 259); "in the positive sense of time one can therefore say: only the present is; the before and after is not; but the concrete present is the result of the past, and it is pregnant with the future. The true present is thus eternity" (§ 259, Zusatz). If Hegel calls time "intuited becoming," neither arising nor passing has a priority in it; nevertheless he occasionally characterizes time as the "abstraction of consuming" (Abstraktion des Verzehrens) — and so brings the vulgar experience and interpretation of time to the most radical formula. On the other hand, Hegel is consistent enough not to concede, in the authentic definition of time, any priority to consuming and passing — such as is rightly held fast in everyday time-experience; for Hegel could ground this priority dialectically as little as the "circumstance," introduced by him as self-evident, that the now emerges precisely with the point's self-positing-for-itself. And so, even in characterizing time as becoming, Hegel understands this in an "abstract" sense, which lies still beyond the representation of the "flow" of time: the most adequate expression of the Hegelian conception of time therefore lies in the determination of time as negation of the negation (of punctuality). Here the now-sequence is formalized in the extremest sense and unsurpassably leveled (unüberbietbar nivelliert). Only from this formal-dialectical concept of time can Hegel establish a connection between time and spirit. The folded note carries the section's scholarship and its widest claim. From the priority of the leveled now it becomes plain that Hegel's conceptual determination of time follows the train of the vulgar understanding — and that means at once the traditional concept: it can be shown that Hegel's concept of time is drawn directly from Aristotle's Physics. In the Jena Logic, drafted at the time of Hegel's habilitation, the Encyclopedia's time-analysis is already developed in all essential pieces; the section on time reveals itself to the roughest examination as a paraphrase of the Aristotelian treatise on time. Already in the Jena Logic Hegel develops his conception of time within the frame of the philosophy of nature, whose first part bears the title "System of the Sun"; the analysis of space is there still subordinate. Though the dialectic already breaks through, it does not yet have the later rigid, schematic form, but still permits a loosened understanding of the phenomena. On the way from Kant to Hegel's developed system, a decisive irruption (Einbruch) of Aristotelian ontology and logic takes place once more: as a factum this has long been known — but way, manner, and limits of the influence remain to this day obscure; a concrete comparative philosophical interpretation of Hegel's Jena Logic and Aristotle's Physics and Metaphysics will bring new light. For the above consideration some rough indications may suffice: Aristotle sees the essence of time in the nyn, Hegel in the now; Aristotle apprehends the nyn as horos (limit), Hegel takes the now as "boundary"; Aristotle understands the nyn as stigmē (point), Hegel interprets the now as point; Aristotle characterizes the nyn as tode ti, Hegel calls the now the "absolute this"; Aristotle, following the tradition, brings chronos into connection with the sphaira, Hegel stresses the "circular course" of time. To Hegel escapes, to be sure, the central tendency of the Aristotelian time-analysis: to uncover a founding-connection (akolouthein) between the nyn, horos, stigmē, and tode ti. With Hegel's thesis that space "is" time, Bergson's conception — for all difference of grounding — agrees in the result: Bergson says only, conversely, time (temps) is space. Bergson's conception of time too has manifestly grown from an interpretation of the Aristotelian treatise on time: it is not merely an external literary connection that, simultaneously with Bergson's Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience, where the problem of temps and durée is exposed, a treatise of his appeared under the title Quid Aristoteles de loco senserit. With regard to the Aristotelian determination of time as arithmos kinēseōs, Bergson prefixes to the analysis of time one of number: time as space (Essai p. 69) is quantitative succession; duration is described, from the counter-orientation to this concept of time, as qualitative succession. For a critical confrontation with Bergson's concept of time and the other contemporary conceptions, this is not the place; so far as anything essential beyond Aristotle and Kant is won at all in today's analyses of time, it concerns rather the apprehension of time and "time-consciousness." The indication of the direct connection between Hegel's concept of time and the Aristotelian analysis is not meant to reckon up a "dependence" against Hegel, but to draw attention to the fundamental ontological bearing of this filiation for the Hegelian Logic.
