(On "Aristotle and Hegel" compare Nicolai Hartmann's essay of that title, 1923.) The closing unit's own dialectic deserves the last word of the subsection: Hegel's documented sayings — the now's monstrous right dissolved in the utterance; nature knowing no subsisting past and future; only the present is, and the true present eternity — assemble the complete vulgar theology of the now (the Timaeus's conclusion re-derived, the concrete present "pregnant with the future" the exact obstetrics § 81's finale-sentence refused); the Verzehren-formula saluted as the vulgar experience's radicalest expression — time the consumer, Kronos devouring — and Hegel's consistency in withholding this priority from the definition proper turned into the diagnosis: what everyday experience rightly holds (passing's priority), the dialectic cannot fund, any more than it can fund the now's emergence at the point's self-positing; the un-groundable imported as self-evident. And the note is the book's deepest single piece of destruction-philology: the Jena paraphrase exposed (Hegel's time Aristotle's, via the System of the Sun), the five-term parallel table (nyn/Jetzt, horos/Grenze, stigmē/Punkt, tode ti/absolutes Dieses, sphaira/Kreislauf) — with the one Aristotelian excellence Hegel missed: the akolouthein, the founding-order among the terms; Bergson annexed to the same filiation from the other side (his durée the mere counter-image of the Aristotelian-quantitative time, his Latin thesis the paper-trail), so that the nineteenth century's two extremities — absolute idealism and vitalism — stand revealed as two readings of Physics Delta; and contemporary phenomenology itself (Husserl unnamed in "Zeitbewußtsein") credited only with progress in the apprehension of time, not in time's being. The generosity-clause seals the method: no Abhängigkeit reckoned — filiation exhibited for its ontological bearing; the destruction, as § 6 promised, a positive appropriation.

###### b) Hegel's Interpretation of the Connection between Time and Spirit

The opening unit asks after spirit's essence: how is spirit itself understood, that it can be said to be in accordance with it to fall, with its actualization, into time determined as negation of the negation? The essence of spirit is the concept (der Begriff) — by which Hegel understands not the intuited universal of a genus, as the form of something thought, but the form of the self-thinking thinking itself: the conceiving of itself — as the grasping of the not-I. Insofar as the grasping of the not-I presents a distinguishing, there lies in the pure concept, as the grasping of this distinguishing, a distinguishing of the distinction. Hence Hegel can determine the essence of spirit formally-apophantically as negation of the negation: this "absolute negativity" gives the logically formalized interpretation of Descartes' cogito me cogitare rem, wherein he sees the essence of conscientia. The unit reconstructs the second term of the kinship with the same scruple as the first: spirit's essence not genus but self-thinking's form — the distinguishing of the distinction — and the genealogy drawn in one clause: Hegel's absolute negativity as the logical formalization of the Cartesian cogito me cogitare; German idealism's spirit the algebra of Descartes' consciousness.

The second unit assembles Hegel's I: the concept is accordingly the self-conceiving conceivedness of the self, as which the self authentically is what it can be — free. "I is the pure concept itself, which as concept has come to existence (Dasein)." "But I is this first pure self-relating unity — and this not immediately, but in that it abstracts from all determinateness and content and goes back into the freedom of limitless equality with itself." Thus the I is "universality," but just as immediately "singularity." The quotation-work fixes spirit's formula in Hegel's own words (the I as existent concept; freedom as the abstractive return into limitless self-equality; universality and singularity in one) — the material against which the fall must be measured.

The third unit gives spirit's restlessness: this negating of the negation is at once the "absolutely restless" (das absolut Unruhige) of spirit and its self-revelation, which belongs to its essence. The "progression" of the spirit actualizing itself in history carries "a principle of exclusion" in itself; this exclusion, however, does not become a detachment from the excluded, but its overcoming. The self-freeing that overcomes and at the same time endures characterizes the freedom of spirit: "progress" therefore never means a merely quantitative more, but is essentially qualitative — of the quality of spirit; the "progressing" is known, and knows itself in its goal. In every step of its "progress" spirit has to overcome "itself" as the truly hostile obstacle (das wahrhaft feindselige Hindernis) of its own aim; the goal of spirit's development is "to reach its own concept," and the development itself is "a hard, endless struggle against itself." The paragraph lets Hegel's philosophy of history speak at full stature — the restless negativity, exclusion-without-detachment, qualitative progress, spirit its own enemy, the endless self-war — the passages the closing units must both honor and place; the resonance with the analytic's own vocabulary (struggle, self-overcoming, the self as its own obstacle) deliberately audible: § 74's Kampf finding its idealist ancestor.

The fourth unit derives the fall: because the restlessness of the development of the spirit bringing itself to its concept is the negation of the negation, it remains in accordance with spirit, actualizing itself, to fall "into time" as the immediate negation of the negation. For "time is the concept itself that is there (der da ist), and presents itself to consciousness as empty intuition; hence spirit appears necessarily in time, and it appears in time so long as it does not grasp its pure concept — that is, does not annul (tilgt) time. Time is the outer, intuited pure self not grasped by the self, the merely intuited concept" (Phenomenology of Spirit, closing chapter). Thus spirit appears, necessarily by its essence, in time. "World-history is therefore, in general, the exegesis of spirit in time, as the idea in space exegetes itself as nature." The "excluding" belonging to the movement of development harbors in itself a relation to non-being: that is time, understood from the self-spreading now. The unit reaches the kinship-theorem: spirit falls into time because both are negation of negation — time the immediate, spirit the mediated form of the same structure; time "the concept itself that is there," the daseiende Begriff, spirit's alienated portrait as empty intuition — annulled (getilgt) when the concept grasps itself; and the Phenomenology's world-history formula (spirit's exegesis in time as nature is the idea's in space) quoted as the doctrine's monument.

The fifth unit fixes time's powerlessness: time is the "abstract" negativity; as "intuited becoming" it is the immediately findable, distinguished self-distinguishing — the "existing" (daseiende), that is, present-at-hand concept. As something present-at-hand, and thus external to spirit, time has no power over the concept; rather, the concept "is the power of time" (Encyclopedia § 258). The two-sentence unit completes Hegel's account with its decisive asymmetry: time vorhanden, external, powerless — the concept time's master; the fall a condescension, the annulment its telos.

The sixth unit renders the structural verdict: Hegel shows the possibility of the historical actualization of spirit "in time" by going back to the selfsameness of the formal structure of spirit and time as negation of the negation. The emptiest formal-ontological and formal-apophantic abstraction, into which spirit and time are externalized, makes possible the establishing of a kinship of the two. But because time is at the same time conceived in the sense of the utterly leveled world-time, and its provenance thus remains completely covered, it simply stands over against spirit as something present-at-hand — whence spirit must first of all fall "into time." What, indeed, this "falling" and the "actualization" of the spirit that is master of time and authentically "is" outside it mean ontologically remains dark. As little as Hegel illuminates the origin of the leveled time, so completely does he leave unexamined the question whether the essential constitution of spirit, as the negating of the negation, is at all possible otherwise than on the ground of original temporality. The verdict is the section's yield in three strokes: the kinship purchased at the price of double emptying (both terms formalized to the same algebraic husk — negation of negation the emptiest common denominator); the fall unintelligible on Hegel's own books (time a thing outside spirit, the "into" and the "actualization" ontologically dark); and the counter-question that turns the tables — whether negation-of-negation itself, spirit's very essence, is thinkable except on the ground of original temporality: Hegel's structure as a formalized shadow of the ecstases.

The seventh unit honors the drive — the closing Phenomenology quotation. Whether Hegel's interpretation of time and spirit and their connection stands rightfully, and rests at all on ontologically original foundations, cannot yet be discussed; but that the formal-dialectical "construction" of the connection of spirit and time can be ventured at all reveals an original kinship of the two. Hegel's "construction" has its impetus from the effort and struggle for a conceiving of the "concretion" of spirit — as this sentence from the closing chapter of his Phenomenology of Spirit attests: "Time appears therefore as the fate and the necessity of the spirit that is not complete within itself — the necessity to enrich the share that self-consciousness has in consciousness, to set in motion the immediacy of the in-itself (the form in which substance is in consciousness), or, conversely — the in-itself taken as the inward — to realize and reveal what is at first inward: that is, to vindicate it to the certainty of itself." The unit is the confrontation's most gracious moment: the adjudication deferred (whether Hegel's foundations are original — a question for the missing horizon), the venture itself read as evidence — that the construction could be dared at all betrays a real kinship of time and spirit; and Hegel's deepest sentence on time (time as the fate and necessity of incomplete spirit) quoted at length, its pathos honored: the effort toward the Konkretion acknowledged as genuine — Hegel reaching, with formal-dialectical means, for what the analytic reaches for with existential ones.

The closing unit speaks the counter-thesis — the confrontation's last word. The foregoing existential analytic of Dasein, by contrast, sets in with the "concretion" of factically thrown existence itself, in order to unveil temporality as what originally makes it possible. "Spirit" does not first fall into time, but exists as the original temporalizing of temporality (existiert als ursprüngliche Zeitigung der Zeitlichkeit); this temporalizes world-time, in whose horizon "history" can "appear" as within-time happening. "Spirit" does not fall into time; rather: factical existence "falls," as falling, out of original, authentic temporality (fällt als verfallende aus der ursprünglichen, eigentlichen Zeitlichkeit). This "falling," however, itself has its existential possibility in a mode of the temporalizing belonging to temporality. The final antithesis is built as a perfect chiasmus, and it closes the section, the chapter, and the book's whole confrontation with the tradition in four sentences: where Hegel begins in the formal and struggles toward concretion, the analytic begins in the concretion (the thrown factical existence) and unveils its enabling; the fall re-assigned — not spirit into time, but existence, falling, out of authentic temporality: verfallen replacing fallen, the direction reversed (not from eternity down into the nows, but from original time down into the leveled nows) — and even this fall kept inside time's own household: falling itself a mode of temporalizing, § 68c's theorem (the origin of lostness is authentic temporality itself) standing as the last word against every two-world picture. Hegel's problem — how spirit and time belong together — is answered by dissolution: they were never two; "spirit" is temporality's own temporalizing, and what Hegel called the fall into time is inauthentic temporality's descent from itself.

##### § 83. The Existential-Temporal Analytic of Dasein and the Fundamental-Ontological Question of the Sense of Being in General

The opening unit takes the book's final inventory. The task of the foregoing considerations was to interpret the original whole of factical Dasein — with regard to the possibilities of authentic and inauthentic existing — existential-ontologically from its ground: as this ground, and thus as the sense of being of care, temporality revealed itself. What the preparatory existential analytic of Dasein made ready before the laying-free of temporality has now been taken back into temporality, the original structure of Dasein's totality of being; from the analyzed possibilities of temporalizing of original time, the structures earlier only "exhibited" have received their "grounding." But the setting-forth of Dasein's constitution of being remains, for all that, only a way: the goal is the working-out of the question of being in general. The thematic analytic of existence needs, for its part, first the light from the previously clarified idea of being in general. This holds above all if the sentence expressed in the Introduction is held fast as the measure of every philosophical investigation: philosophy is universal phenomenological ontology, taking its departure from the hermeneutics of Dasein, which, as analytic of existence, has fastened the end of the guiding thread of all philosophical questioning at the point from which it springs and to which it strikes back. Of course this thesis too may not count as dogma, but as the formulation of the still "enveloped" fundamental problem: can ontology be grounded ontologically, or does it need even for this an ontic foundation — and which being must take over the function of founding? The paragraph is the torso's honest self-assessment: the two divisions' whole achievement stated (the exhibited structures grounded in temporalizing) and immediately relativized — nur ein Weg, only a way; the analytic itself confessedly awaiting light from the idea of being it was to prepare — the hermeneutic circle of the whole book named at book's end; § 7's definition of philosophy recited as measure and instantly de-dogmatized into the deepest question the book possesses: whether ontology can ground itself, or must borrow its ground from a being — fundamental ontology's own foundation posed as problem in the final section.

The second unit dissolves the last complacency — the reification-question. What appears as evident as the distinction between the being of existing Dasein and the being of non-Dasein-like beings (reality, for example) is nevertheless only the point of departure of the ontological problematic, but nothing at which philosophy can set its mind at rest. That ancient ontology works with "thing-concepts," and that the danger exists of "reifying consciousness," one has long known. But what does reification mean? Whence does it spring? Why is being "conceived" precisely "proximally" from the present-at-hand — and not from the ready-to-hand, which lies still nearer? Why does this reification come again and again to dominion? How is the being of "consciousness" positively structured, so that reification remains inappropriate to it? Does the "distinction" between "consciousness" and "thing" suffice at all for an original unrolling of the ontological problematic? Do the answers to these questions lie along the way? And can the answer even be sought, so long as the question of the sense of being in general remains unposed and unclarified? The paragraph fires the book's last question-battery at its own nearest allies: the era's whole critical consciousness (the warnings against reification — Lukács's word two years old, phenomenology's and Lebensphilosophie's common coin) convicted of resting in the slogan: everyone knows the danger, no one asks what reification is, whence it springs, why presence wins over the nearer readiness, why it always returns, what consciousness positively is that reification wrongs it — and whether consciousness-versus-thing is even the right first distinction; and the terminal question folds them all back into the one the book began with: none answerable while the Seinsfrage sleeps.

The third unit refuses abstraction and confesses the way: the origin and possibility of the "idea" of being in general can never be investigated with the means of formal-logical "abstraction" — that is, without a secure horizon of question and answer. It is necessary to seek a way to the illumination of the fundamental ontological question, and to go it; whether it is the sole way, or the right one at all, can be decided only after the going (kann erst nach dem Gang entschieden werden). The strife regarding the interpretation of being cannot be settled, because it has not yet even been kindled (noch nicht einmal entfacht); and in the end it does not let itself be "picked from the fence" — the kindling of the strife already needs an equipping (Zurüstung). Toward this alone is the present investigation under way. Where does it stand? The paragraph is the book's methodological last testament: the idea of being no abstractum (genus-logic barred at the door one final time, § 1's ruling upheld); the way confessedly ventured — its rightness decidable only in the going, the hermeneutic wager stated without security; and the gigantomachia of the opening page revisited with the bitterest honesty: the battle over being not merely unsettled but unlit — the whole book a Zurüstung, an arming for a strife still to be kindled; the investigation unterwegs, and asking, in its own last interrogative before the final one: where does it stand?

The closing unit ends the book in questions. Something like "being" is disclosed in the understanding of being that belongs, as understanding, to existing Dasein; the antecedent, though unconceptual, disclosedness of being makes it possible for Dasein, as existing being-in-the-world, to comport itself toward beings — toward the innerworldly encountering as well as toward itself as existing. How is disclosive understanding of being, in the manner of Dasein, possible at all? Can the question gain its answer by going back to the original constitution of being of the Dasein that understands being? The existential-ontological constitution of Dasein's totality grounds in temporality; accordingly, an original mode of temporalizing of ecstatic temporality itself must make possible the ecstatic projection of being in general. How is this mode of temporalizing of temporality to be interpreted? Does a way lead from original time to the sense of being? Does time itself reveal itself as the horizon of being? (Führt ein Weg von der ursprünglichen Zeit zum Sinn des Seins? Offenbart sich die Zeit selbst als Horizont des Seins?) The final unit compresses the whole book into a single ascending chain and then — instead of a conclusion — opens: the understanding of being (the book's first phenomenon) restated as the last problem; the answer's direction fixed (a temporalizing-mode of temporality must enable the projection of being — the doctrine Division Three was to deliver as the Temporalität of being itself, the horizonal schemata of § 69c raised to being's own horizon) — and then the two questions with which Sein und Zeit ends, its title dissolved into its interrogatives: whether a way leads from original time to the sense of being; whether time itself reveals itself as being's horizon. The commentary's last word can only mark what the ending is: not a peroration but a threshold — the book breaks off, by design and then by fate, on the questions it was written to make askable; the projected Third Division ("Time and Being") and the whole Second Part (the destruction of Kant, Descartes, and Aristotle) remained unwritten, and the path went on otherwise — the 1930 turn, the Beiträge, the 1962 lecture that took the missing division's title. But the questions stand as posed: the strife equipped, the way opened, the going — as the book's own last sentence-form insists — still to be decided by the going.
